🧟‍♂️🏚 Resident Evil HD Remaster Review 🏚🧟‍♂️

🕹 Length: 10–15 hours (per playthrough) | 20+ hours replaying both characters
💰 Price vs. Content: Excellent — multiple campaigns and high replayability
⚙ Optimization: Excellent; runs flawlessly on modern systems
🎮 Difficulty: Moderate to hard; classic survival horror design

🎮 Gameplay

Resident Evil HD Remaster is the modern version of the original Resident Evil, and it remains one of the most important and influential survival horror games ever made. Set in the iconic Spencer Mansion, the game builds tension through limited resources, clever puzzles, and a constant feeling of vulnerability.

You can play as Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield, each offering a slightly different experience. Jill has more inventory space and a more accessible playthrough, while Chris offers a tougher challenge with fewer resources. This dual-character system adds replayability and variety.

The gameplay sticks to the classic formula: fixed camera angles, tank controls, backtracking, and inventory management. For players new to this style, it can feel slow and even frustrating at first — but once it clicks, the tension and pacing are incredibly rewarding.

Compared to Resident Evil 0, this game feels more refined and better balanced, especially thanks to the return of the item box system, which makes inventory management far less tedious.

✅ The Good:
✔ One of the most important survival horror games ever made
✔ Incredible atmosphere and level design (the mansion is iconic)
✔ Two playable characters with different experiences
✔ Much better pacing and balance than Resident Evil 0
✔ Excellent HD remaster visuals

❌ The Bad:
✖ Tank controls and fixed cameras may feel outdated
✖ Backtracking is frequent
✖ Can be tough for newcomers to the genre

💻 Technical Aspects

🎨 Graphics: Beautiful remastered environments with detailed pre-rendered backgrounds
🎶 Sound: Outstanding atmosphere with subtle, tense audio design
🐞 Bugs: Very stable; no major issues

⭐ Final Verdict

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a true classic that still holds up thanks to its masterful atmosphere, level design, and survival mechanics. It improves on the ideas seen in Resident Evil 0 and delivers a more polished and memorable experience.

Even today, it stands as one of the best examples of classic survival horror — though like RE0, it would be incredible to see it get a full modern remake in the style of newer entries.

👉 Rating: 9/10 🧟‍♂️

Resident Evil is an incredible, highly replayable, memorable, tense, and beautiful game. And it's really unfortunate that this remaster is kinda... bad. The gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds of the 2002 GameCube original have been completely destroyed with over-sharpened, blotchy, poorly rendered upscales. There's also an intense contrast filter slapped on top of it that leads to extreme cases of crushed blacks and loss of visual detail. The music plays too fast and is higher pitched than it should be. The mouse cursor doesn't go away. The resolution caps at 1080p and the framerate caps at 60. I also find it crazy that after numerous re-releases, the remake, and the remake's various ports and releases, you're STILL not able to skip the door animations. It's safe to say this remaster is pretty rough.

So, why do I recommend it then? Two things, really. First, the game itself is still amazing, and everyone should play it. Second, there's mods that fix literally every issue I just listed.

The first mod is the most important one, and that is ThirteenAG's Resident Evil Fusion Fix. This mod fixes the resolution and framerate cap, lets you turn off the contrast filter, lets you skip door animations, hides the mouse cursor, and more.

The second mod is RESCALE. This is the current best backgrounds replacement mod the community has to offer, and it works wonders to this game's visuals. The shoddy 2015 upscales done by Capcom are completely overhauled with, albeit somewhat flawed, modern AI upscaling technology, greatly improving visual clarity and detail. This one is a must-have, but it does come with a fairly hefty download.

The last mod is the Normalized Music Mod. This fixes the strangely quiet and sped-up music tracks the game has out of the box.

All these mods are very easy to install, being just simple drag-and-drop replacements of game files, so please, play this game and install these mods, and enter the survival horror.

If you enjoy slow-paced, methodical gameplay and classic survival horror design, Resident Evil is absolutely worth your time.

There are a couple of downsides. The camera system can be frustrating at times—angles sometimes change right when you need them to stay still, especially during tense moments. Also, recovery items feel a bit too generous; green herbs, sprays, and other healing items are quite abundant, which slightly reduces the survival pressure.

That said, once everything clicks, the experience becomes very satisfying and immersive.

A solid remake that respects the original and still holds up today.

Recommended.
8.5/10 is the sweet spot—it feels honest, not inflated, and builds trust.

[h2] A legendary classic that deserves respect, but doesn’t hold up well for first-time players in modern gaming [/h2]


I went into Resident Evil HD completely fresh, having never played a single game in the series before. I wanted to start from the very beginning to understand its roots.

I played for 10.5 hours as Jill on Easy difficulty (which is insane in hindsight) and eventually stopped midway after reaching the catacombs. After losing 40 minutes of progress to a one-shot death from a hunter, I realised I just wasn’t enjoying myself anymore.

I started the first couple of hours blind but quickly got completely lost and had to restart using a guide just to figure out what I was supposed to be doing.

[h3]The Good[/h3]

The atmosphere is genuinely fantastic. Every room has its own tension, and the use of music (especially in the safe rooms) creates these moments of relief that feel incredibly rewarding after struggling through the mansion or any other area that you are in.

Visually, the remaster is seriously impressive. Compared to the original 1996 version, the upgrade is massive. The lighting, character detail, and environments all look great even by today’s standards. For a game that’s over 20 years old, it holds up extremely well graphically.

The fixed camera angles, while frustrating, do add to the tension. You never quite know what’s around the corner, and that uncertainty definitely enhances the horror element.

There are also some memorable and unexpected moments, like the residence area with the giant plant and the completely random shark tank section, which helped break up the mansion gameplay.

[h3]The Bad[/h3]

Unfortunately, this game was more of a negative experience for me than a positive one.

Firstly, the saving system completely ruined the experience for me.

Limited saves using ink ribbons might have worked back in the day, but in 2026 it just feels outdated and unnecessarily punishing. I don’t always have hours to commit to gaming, and this system actively punishes shorter play sessions. Sometimes life gets in the way of gaming and I need to turn off the PC, but I can’t save unless I back track or keep pushing on until I find another save area. Also, having a limited number of ribbons In the game? I was not a fan. Losing 40 minutes of progress because you didn’t save at the “right” time isn’t tension, it’s just frustrating.

The lack of direction is another major issue. I understand that exploration is part of survival horror, but the game gives you almost no guidance at all. Without a guide, I genuinely think this game would take 4–5x longer, purely from trial and error.

Backtracking is excessive and often tedious. You’re constantly going back and forth managing inventory, grabbing items, and trying to figure out where to go next, only to sometimes realise you’ve come to an area too early and can’t progress anyway.

The camera system, while adding tension, is more annoying than immersive by modern standards. 
Combined with clunky controls, it makes already difficult encounters even more frustrating.

Combat and resource management never felt satisfying, just stressful. You’re constantly under-equipped, never sure what’s coming next, and often punished for not bringing the “right” items into an area you had no way of predicting.

Story-wise, a lot of things feel poorly explained. Enemies like hunters just appear with no context, and major characters like Lisa are barely introduced unless you’re using external guides, granted I am sure that it’s explained a lot more at the end, but without the guide I would have had no idea what that chewing gum looking monstrosity was that I bumped into in the cabin

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

I can fully respect what this game did for the survival horror genre and understand why it’s so highly regarded. But as someone playing it for the first time in 2026, I just didn’t enjoy the experience.

In 2026, I would still suggest this game to hardcore fans of the series or players who appreciate retro design, but not for newcomers used to modern quality-of-life features.

I might come back and finish it one day, but right now, it’s more frustrating than fun.

Starting an iconic franchise so late into the game is somewhat daunting, I’d heard it all about fixed camera angles, tank controls  and the difficult puzzles and inventory restrictions. Living up to such a reputation was to be a big task and somehow it did and surpassed them.

Taking place in a mansion after S.T.A.R.S. is investigating disappearances in the area we get to choose between two characters, Jill who comes with more inventory, a lockpick for easier access to some doors and less health, or Chris who comes with less inventory a lighter (which will be discussed later) and more health. To start I pick Jill. I’ll start by saying this is an absolutely gorgeous game, looking around the mansion you can easily see the detail of the textures that still look impressive even today this immediately creates an unforgettable atmosphere of something dark and terrible.

My first foray into the mansion is rough, the controls feel uncomfortable and I’m not sure how anything works, to save you have to use a resource, an ink ribbon, I do so right when I get one. Another aspect to get used to is the fixed camera angles, these are strange and often at odds with where the character is going. One thing the camera angles does allow is showing off the beautiful graphics and artstyle, some of the shots are beautiful and convey great emotion and atmosphere for the moments of the game. My first encounter with a zombie doesn’t go well, shooting is a bit odd and combined with the movement it doesn’t go well. I explored a few more rooms but it’s not going well. About an hour in I’ve gotten more familiar with things and am much more in control, I decide to restart. Restarting is a great idea as it allows me to breathe easier and optimize my limited saves and ammo. 

Exploring the mansion is engaging and tense, never knowing what is going to be around any corner maintains a level of uncertainty throughout the game. After a while I have become very competent with the fighting and enjoy them. Throughout the mansion are many odd puzzles similar to point-and-click adventure games or escape room puzzles, I excel at these. Each puzzle is creative and well thought out with a solution that is able to be figured out, I never get stuck really. Like all great games near the end I play more and more, when I complete Jill’s story I immediately jump into Chris’s, which goes significantly smoother than Jill’s and faster. Being armed with the knowledge of what to do for most of the game helps immensely. All of this is coupled with stellar music, from the darker ambiences that play throughout the mansion to the coziness and safety of the safe room music it evokes exactly the mood it needs to. It also knows when to hold back on the music and just let the sounds play, footsteps or distinct sounds of the different enemies to both inform and frighten you. Tense moments often play out devoid of music which is a great decision.  

Some aspects remain a bit of a downer, managing the inventory can be quite annoying as you run back from the universal storage item box to wherever you need to go, more of a nuisance than anything but not terrible. Controls are alright once you get used to them but still feel somewhat unnatural and for certain enemies (DOGS!!!) can be quite a pain. While the story is engaging enough and voice acted quite well it’s a bit standard and is more about background details and notes rather than a big main story, the notes are interesting and where the story excels.

There are few games that manage to evoke such a strong sense of atmosphere while having the gameplay be the most engaging part. I'll be thinking about this one for a long time, a fantastic start to the series.

Ive played though most of the RE games of the TPS era (RE 4-6, both revelations) and the mere thought of playing a game with tank controls sounded ridiculous and just straight up not fun, like i remember literally rolling my eyes at " boomers" who wanted tank controls to come back, like what the hell man, stop suggesting that, tank controls is dead for a reason, i thought

Well with the hype of RE Requiem i wanted to see where it all began and decided to take the plunge and play the first REmake, just for" testing the waters", " ill drop it inmediately if the controls are awful"  are some of the things i said

well, 30h later and after beating the game 2 times with both characters this are my impressions
its a masterpiece, like legitimately
lets start with the graphics, like from the moment i had control of jill i was like, wth, if you told me this was a AA game released this year by a mid sized team id totally believe it, it looks AMAZING, second the movement and gamefeel, this may be the most important part of the review

the Tank controls will be probably unlike anything youve played before and they will take some getting used to, you HAVE to get into the mindset that this is not a TPS like RE 4-6 or the REmakes, that youre not supposed to see the whole screen and you are supposed to have blind spots, thankfully the controls are responsive and controlling jill or chriss feels really good

on that note theres 2 options for tank controls, the " Alternative" and the " Original" , if youre on the fence you can try the Alternative first, that makes the controls somewhat easier, but after getting used to the tank controls and camera id strongly advise switching to the Original, after all that was the way its meant to be played, because if you start with original controls it may be too much at once and you may get overwhelmed, at least i think i wouldve

and on topic, unless you are used games like this and somewhat know what youre doing i also strongly recommend playing with Jill first, as chris is basically the "hard" mode

another " tip" this is a game that gets significantly easier the more knowledge you have on where the items, enemy are, so if you reach a  point where youre outta bullets dont be afraid to load up an earlier save or hell restart the game, if it took yuou say 5 hours to get to a point, if you restart  you can do it in easily half and with much more items

but this game truly made me a believer that Tank control games can be not only good, but excellent, and im at most  mechanically average, like i took like almost double of the usual time to beat this game but i enjoyed basically every second

[b] Positives [/b]
Nice graphics that still hold up today. I love the character designs and the mansion was a really nice area to explore!
The fixed cam did a good job at scaring me. I’ve had more jumpscares in this game than any other! Really helps set the scary atmosphere.

[b] Gameplay and Items [/b]
Fixed cam + tank controls is the worst combination on earth. I am semi-used to tank controls as I have played such games before, but fixed cam is just not me. During my 15 hour playthrough, I never got used to it and it continued to bother me through all of it. I don’t understand why there has to be five camera angles of the same hallway, all from different directions.
The fixed cam disoriented me, leaving me to spend half of my game on the map. Every time I had sat through yet another door animation, I had to pull up my map to see where to go. The constant different camera angles prevented me from learning the layout of the mansion.
The door animations ruined every bit of immersion. I spent more time on door animations than actual gameplay. I don’t mind backtracking in games, and I like large areas like the mansion. But when I found out I had missed an item or my inventory was full when I found a new one, realizing I had to backtrack to an item box, I contemplated on just quitting. I don’t mind a bit of inventory management, but knowing how long it would take me to backtrack just made me dislike it.
As I said, the mansion was nice to explore, but when I was on hour 12 of backtracking, I just wanted to get out of there.
Speaking of the map, it lacked a lot of detail. A lot of my time was spent trying to unlock doors, checking rooms for items, since I didn’t know what was where due to lack of information on the map.
The one-way doors are unnecessary and annoying.

[b] Combat and Weapons [/b]
The combat was okay. My biggest “issue” is the fact that you can’t move while aiming. The shotgun is really satisfying to shoot, and I enjoyed killing the enemies. The boss fights were not fun, as I felt really vulnerable because I couldn’t move while aiming, and the bosses felt quite fast compared to the fact that I had to stand still to shoot.

[b] Enemies [/b]
The enemies were okay, not really memorable. The crimson heads and hunters did a good job at scaring the heck out of me! Some of the bosses like Yawn and Black Tiger confused me and seemed out of place. But I don’t have an issue with this game’s enemies.

[b] Puzzles [/b]
The worst puzzles in any game I’ve ever played. Super, super, super vague and confusing, I wondered how anyone figured them out back in 2002. I had to google [u]every single puzzle[/u], and just when I thought I had figured out something on my own, I was so far from the correct solution. Every time I searched it up and saw the solution, my only thought was always [i]I would never in my life have figured that out.[/i] Same goes for things you had to do to progress. I always go in blind on my first playthroughs, but for this game I eventually just pulled up a guide and followed it. Every time I reached the next step, I thought [i]I would never have known I had to do this.[/i]

[b] Ending (Spoilers) [/b]
The ending was cute, and the final boss fight was fun and scary. I saved both Barry and Chris, so the ending where all three escape was a nice way to end my long playthrough. Not much to say, good ending.

[b] Conclusion [/b]
I had high expectations for this game as it’s regarded as a masterpiece and fan favorite. But I just didn’t get the hype. I wouldn’t recommend this game to someone unless they’re used to older games. I’d love to see this game as a modern remake.
If I play this game again, it will probably be to try out Chris and farm achievements.

I do not believe in the idea of »definitive versions«. But if there were to be one, it would probably be this.

I like to play original titles and consider updated re-releases and remakes largely to be their own thing. Games have a bad habit of just adding stuff on top, with little thought to how it meshes with the existing experience and direction. This is often exasperated by the tendency of great games getting the remake treatment. It's the classics, not the misses that get a second chance.

But while Resident Evil 1 is definitely a classic, it almost has the spirit of a miss to me. Not that it's tedious or hard to play in a modern sense. On the contrary, my biggest surprise getting to know these games are how smooth they are to play — despite a few bumps here and there. And the PS1-era sensibility of the visual and design language of the classic Resident Evil games are such a large part of their charm. If you had asked me previously whether they needed a remake for the GameCube, I would probably have scoffed at the idea. The modern remakes of 2 and 3 I get, since those seem like complete overhauls. But this? The exact same game, but with a new coat of paint? It seems unnecessary.

It isn't though. in 1996 ,Resident Evil 1 had not yet quite hit the tone and vibe that 2 and 3 would nail down. Playing it — even for the first time with no knowledge of the series — it kinda felt like there was an underlying vision that had not been realized. The remake taps into that feeling and makes the core vibe of the game snap into sharp focus. The Spencer Mansion stands here — in all its wicked pomp and pageantry — and has never been more inviting as a playspace.

Even as a definitive version — the perfect entry point — there are clever wrinkles and remixes of the original's framework that keep things spicy for players returning to the mansion. The most noteworthy here is honestly how seamlessly it all blends into the existing game. Additions like this would normally be the type of thing I would balk at, but here it is (mostly) for the better of the overall balance of the game.

Despite my praise, I think I still somehow prefer the original. While I often found it tedious and annoying in the moment, the brisk pace and dramatic curve was so masterfully done. And were I to have a main gripe with the remake, it would be that it still ends up feeling a bit bloated. Despite the thoughtfulness of the additions, there are just one too many detours and distractions to make the remake able to keep up the pace.
It’s a remake that cuts nothing and only adds more.

Resident Evil HD Remaster has many of the same strengths and weaknesses as Resident Evil 0, but I ended up liking it less overall due to a few specific design decisions that made the experience more frustrating than engaging.

Visuals & Presentation:
Like Resident Evil 0, the game holds up well visually for its age. The pre-rendered backgrounds are detailed and atmospheric, and the cinematic camera angles do a good job of creating tension and mood. That said, the frequent camera shifts make navigation more difficult than it needs to be, often working against the player rather than enhancing the experience.

Characters & Narrative:
This was one of the bigger disappointments for me. Playing as Chris, I felt like there was very little story or character engagement compared to Resident Evil 0. Without a partner, the experience feels much more isolated, and the lack of interaction makes it harder to stay invested. I understand that Jill’s campaign introduces more interaction through an additional character, but based on my experience, the game leans far more heavily into gameplay systems than narrative or character development.

Gameplay:
The core gameplay is very similar to Resident Evil 0, but the issues feel more pronounced here. The camera system is more disruptive due to how often it changes perspective, which makes movement and combat feel less consistent. Combined with clunky aiming, this creates frequent moments where I felt like I was fighting the controls more than the enemies.

Inventory & Design Friction:
The inventory system is where the game really started to break down for me. Having only six inventory slots without a partner makes management significantly more difficult than in Resident Evil 0. On top of that, the game leans more heavily into puzzle-solving, which requires holding onto multiple items and figuring out the correct combinations at the right time.

This led to constant backtracking:
- Running to item boxes to store and retrieve items  
- Trying to remember where certain doors or puzzles were  
- Rechecking areas repeatedly due to uncertainty  

The map design makes this worse. With so many locked doors and unclear progression paths, I found myself revisiting the same areas over and over again, often without clear direction. It felt less like exploration and more like trial-and-error navigation.

Overall Experience:
I found the game more frustrating than enjoyable for large portions of my playthrough. While it has strong atmosphere and a solid foundation, the heavy emphasis on puzzles, limited inventory, and constant backtracking made it feel like a chore at times.

It’s clear the game is more focused on gameplay systems than story or characters, and if you enjoy puzzle-heavy design with a lot of backtracking and uncertainty, there’s something here to appreciate. For me, though, that design focus made it much harder to stay engaged.

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil HD Remaster is an important entry in the series with strong atmosphere and classic survival horror design, but the restrictive inventory, heavy puzzle focus, and constant backtracking made it a less enjoyable experience than Resident Evil 0.

Worth playing for completion or historical context, but not something I found particularly compelling on its own. If your goal is to experience the full series from beginning to end, like I aim to do, I would recommend waiting a few years to see if they release a remake, as I feel that is inevitable, and will likely be much more enjoyable compared to this entry as it currently is presented.

In response to all the negative reviews calling this game outdated and archaic: I hate to say this, because it sounds like gatekeeping, and that is not my intention here. However, I don't think this game was necessarily made for modern audiences. I'm not saying it can't appeal to younger demographics, but given that it sticks so close to the original PS1 game in playstyle, graphics, and overall feel, I believe it was made for the people who played it back in the day and want a modern way to play the game they love with better visuals and a slightly updated control scheme. Otherwise, as far as I can discern from the opening section, it's the same game as it ever was, and unless that is an experience you are already familiar with, then it most likely is not going to be something you have the patience for.

All that said, as someone who was a teenager when the PS1 game came out, and loved it, this game is awesome. A fitting love note to the original with just the right touch of modernism to alleviate the worst of the frustration with the controls (while leaving the option to switch between them at any time), but not trying reinvent the wheel.  A nice PS2'esque update to the graphics, and better voice acting, which can be seen as a good or bad thing depending on your POV. It all just feels right.

I would love to see a complete remake in the vein of RE2 and 3, but this version seems to me to be the definitive way to play Resident Evil now. If you loved it back in the 90's you'll love it now, and if it's new to you, I'd say it's well worth going back to see where it all began.

This game was a lot cooler than I ended up anticipating. I love when games are unique to themselves and show why, especially retroactively since I am a very new fan of the series, why they are so popular to begin with or why they blew up. Resident Evil 1 remake is certainly one of the best games I have played, and is certainly the best horror game in that margin. What will stand out first to many playing this game are fixed camera angles and limited saves, both uniquely add to the environment by A. creating tense moments when you know something is in the room with you but you can’t see it because of the camera angle, forcing you to wait or possibly charge in and get grabbed by something, a uniquely intense situation that you will find yourself in over and over. But also B. limited saves make you think really hard about the decisions you make throughout the game as you dont know when the next time you will get ink ribbons to do so, or if a major fight or encounter is gonna come soon after that you would have rather have saved some ribbons for adding to the intensity overall. The story/setting of this game is really cool from the starting cutscene all the way to the end I felt the vibe that this game was going for from the get-go. Exploring this desolate mansion with limited ammo, communication and general unknowingness gave you dread, but you also felt confident enough to press on as the game gives you JUST enough defense tools to make you feel somewhat protected. In combination with the actual writing of the game which I enjoyed, the gameplay, and the decision making make Resident Evil remake stand out as an extremely unique experience and a great entrypoint to the series. The combat in this game is actually pretty satisfying and unique, especially the controls. Original tank controls are not my favourite but I did not mind them entirely, I would use them if I had to but I chose to only do it the one time. Guns feel great especially the better ones, your starter pistol feels bad and I think that is actually a good thing, you are unequipped early to fight the evil in this place, but later you get your hands on some pretty heavy stuff that can feel great if you get a headshot. The characters, music at times especially in safe rooms to give you a moment to breathe, and underlying storytelling throughout the game really make you feel like you’re trying to solve SOMETHING but mostly you are just trying to survive. If you couldn’t tell, dread is probably the best way I could describe this game but in the best meaning of that word possible. I highly recommend checking this game out if you are interested in the series.

By slowly unwrapping a single mansion, you become intimately familiar with every room and camera angle.  Your traversal becomes second nature, which has its own satisfaction to it.  Bosses are straightforward and exciting.  Puzzles can be obtuse but on repeat playthroughs the logic holds.

The story is also very satisfying.  Simple and sometimes silly in presentation, there is some genuine characterization from the entire cast.  I adored every line of dialogue and cutscene I got to watch.  The game is oozing personality and style.  There are just enough cutscenes to keep me invested, but not so many that it detracts from the core experience - the gameplay.

I sincerely hope Capcom returns to this format in the future.

**Resident Evil (Remake) – Steam Review**

**Playtime:** ~9.5 hours
**Played as:** Jill Valentine
**Difficulty:** Normal
**Recommendation:** 👍 *Yes (once)*

---

I went into this with pretty limited experience in the series. I’ve only played *Resident Evil 4* and *Resident Evil 7: Biohazard*, and I’m now playing everything in canonical order after beating *Resident Evil 0*.

That said, I’ve got history with this game—I grew up watching my mom play the original on PS1 when I was a kid. Coming back to it almost 30 years later and actually playing it myself was a weirdly nostalgic experience. I even caught myself remembering certain moments before they happened.

---

### 👍 **What I Liked**

* **Atmosphere & visuals** – The remake still looks great. Lighting, reflections, and the mansion itself carry the experience.
* **Story (especially hidden lore)** – Reading notes and piecing things together was genuinely enjoyable.
* **Lisa Trevor storyline** – Easily the standout part of the game. No spoilers, but it hits hard.
* **Puzzle design** – The game is loaded with puzzles. Some are simple, others require actually reading notes and paying attention. A couple even have randomized elements, which makes blindly following a guide less reliable and adds some freshness.
* **Boss variety** – Mechanically simple, but still cool to experience. Fighting the various "BOW" creatures was pretty cool even if the fights boil down to “shoot, kite, repeat,” the variety keeps it interesting.

---

### 👎 **What I Didn’t Like**

* **Inventory system is awful**
  You can’t drop items. You can’t swap items. You’re constantly backtracking to item boxes.
  If you’re a completionist, this becomes miserable.

* **Fixed camera angles**
  Movement changes with camera cuts. Feels clunky and outdated.

* **Door animations everywhere**
  Every room transition = slow cutscene.
  When you get lost (which you will), it turns into a door simulator.

* **No direction at all**
  No quest log, no markers. If your navigation isn’t solid, expect a lot of wandering.

* **Combat is stiff**
  Auto-aim + limited control. It works, but it doesn’t feel good.

* **Cheesy dialogue**
  Even in the remake, the voice acting is rough. Kinda charming, but still rough.

---

### ⚠️ **Tips**

* Play as **Jill**, not Chris (inventory is more forgiving)
* Stick to **Easy/Normal** unless you enjoy suffering
* Use a guide if you don’t want to waste time backtracking

---

### 🧠 **Final Thoughts**

This game is **dated**, no question. Even as a remake, a lot of its systems feel archaic and frustrating.

But… I’m still glad I played it.

Between the atmosphere, the puzzle-solving, and the variety of encounters, there’s still something here that holds up. It’s not always fun moment-to-moment, but it’s definitely **worth experiencing at least once**, especially if you care about the series.

---

**Score:** 6.5 / 10

[h1] A Beautifully Aged Horror Title [/h1] 


I'm still impressed how much depth this game holds even 30 years after it's initial release. It stands on it's own legs pretty well and doesn't try to sell itself to the player too hard like some titles try to. Here, the player has to slowly churn through. It's a game that can't really be rushed. More of a slow burner. 

This may be a turn off for some people, but if you have patience and you're a fan of classic horror games, this one's for you. 

[h3] Pros [/h3] 

[list] 
[*] IMO, the atmosphere of this game is unmatched compared to the other resident evil games. The colours, lighting, camera angles, and music all fit together nicely to create an experience that instills dread to the player. This game would've scared the ♥♥♥♥ out of me if i was eight. 

[*] Sparse resources and limited safe areas create an interesting challenge where the player must be mindful with what resource to use and when. Conservation is rewarded with having extra items at your disposal which can be fun, especially if you're playing on higher difficulties. 

[*] This game is packed with puzzles. If you're someone who likes to pay attention to detail and solve problems, you'll like some of the levels. 
[/list]


[h3] Cons [/h3] 

[list] 
[*]The game, even as a HD remaster, still shows signs of age. One prominent sign is the use of fixed camera angles. Understandably, this approach to rendering the game would've made sense due to hardware limitations back in the late 90's, but in the height of 2015, it doesn't. Navagating the map can sometimes be a little annoying as you'll constantly be needing to adjust the controls of your character as you move around. It also makes it difficult to see objects in the game because the camera simply doesn't cover it. 

Arguably, you get used to it after a while. It certainly brings a unique feel to the game. 

[*] Another feature that can make this game really tiresome is, of course, the door loading screens. 

Again, would've made sense due to old hardware, but come on. Making me wait five seconds every time I want to enter another room? In the mid 2010's? 

Like the camera angles, it definatly brings a unique 'feel' to the game. But after a while, it REALLY makes the game drag on when you have [spoiler] 116 [/spoiler] ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rooms to clear out. This is especially true when you need to manage space and back-track to other rooms in order to progress in the game. Generally, just moving around in this game is a pain in the ass. It's not for people with ill patience. 
[/list]

[h1]The Residents Were in Fact Evil[/h1]

After putting in almost 19 hours on my first run through this game as Jill, I have finally beaten Resident Evil 1. Thus far I have played RE 2, 4, 7, 8 and Requiem and am happy to now add 1 to the list. This is not an easy game. 

The puzzles were genuinely challenging at times and there were multiple points in this game I had to backtrack and do a process of elimination to figure out what to do next. I highly recommend/suggest playing this game without a guide, even if it is frustrating at times. The satisfaction from solving where to go next and some of the more intricate puzzles are immensely satisfying once you figure it out. The combat is very tense and makes you feel on edge whenever you're turning a corner and going through long hallways. The music is also fantastic in this game. Every time I found a new safe room, hearing that music as a moment of peace from all the chaos was always so eerily satisfying, like a breath of fresh air.

My biggest gripe with this game is the fixed camera angles can really do you dirty, especially when you're fighting bossess as the camera will constantly shift while youre moving around certain rooms. It is escpecially frustrating when you are holding a direction that you want to move in and the game remembers the last direction you are going which can cause you to constantly switching back and forth between directions you dont want to go. The tank controls I got used to pretty quickly though there were definitley times where the aiming was very finicky. Also ♥♥♥♥ the [spoiler]dogs, absolute bane of my existence in this game lmao.[/spoiler]

Those were really my only gripes with this game though, and overall I would highly recommend anyone looking to get into resident evil to play through this game. I give RE 1 a solid 8/10. On to Resident Evil 3 Nemesis...

There isn't much to say about this game that hasn't already been said. It's a one of the earliest survival horror games that made the genre mainstream. The remake is almost a different game in terms of visual presentation. For anyone who was put off by the 3D polygonal characters and simple pre-rendered backgrounds of the original game, you will find that this remake and remastered version, it is practically completely overhauled with new puzzles and areas. If you're a veteran of original or someone who is looking to get into the series for the first time, you can't go wrong starting here.

Graphics and art design is second to none. The pre-rendered backgrounds are beautifully rendered. Zombies look creepy and the creature designs in the game are memorable. It has antialiasing, filters, and HD graphical enhancements. Trust me, the pictures don't do it justice! The lighting, environment, visual effects and attention to detail is absolutely fantastic, even in today's standards. It's a timeless visual masterpiece.

Sound is exceptional. The music and sound effects are chilling. The voice acting isn't the best, but it doesn't take away from the overall feel of the game. Zombies drag their feet, make creepy sounds and some of the more dangerous creatures can scare the crap out of you by just their sound alone,

Gameplay is fun, yet challenging. There are many quality of life enhancements the game adds over the original. Defense items are a great feature, along with the addition of the 180 degree turn and enemy lock on mechanic. It may not have the modern controls of a third person shooter, but if you give it some time and trust the process, you'll find that the controls work pretty well with the fixed camera angles.

Story is fantastic. It's the start of the virus outbreak everyone has heard about. There are notes left behind in the game you read to fill in the back story and cut scenes you watch playout to move the story along. The games level design, puzzles and characters are memorable that set the mood and tone right from the start. With multiple ends for each character and varies set pieces depending on who you play as, there is plenty of world building to discover.

Atmosphere and mood of the game is a masterpiece. The design of the mansion, courtyard, caverns and underground lab are perfectly depicted. Just about every area in the game and gameplay moments you have will have a lasting appeal. From the background details, character models and creature design, you'll be hooked from start to finish.

Difficulty is fair. There is a Very Easy, Easy, Normal and Hard difficulty, along with additional game modes that challenge the player even further. Extra game modes such as Real Survivor  (which is played in hard difficulty and unconnected item boxes) and the Invisible Enemy (which as name suggests, all enemies are invisible). There is one other additional feature that the game throws at you upon beating the game with both characters, but I wont spoil that for you.

Replay Value consist of the two game modes I mentioned above, along with a Widescreen or Original Display, Digital Instructions Manuel which is really neat and quite comprehensive I might add. There is a Global and Friends leaderboard you can view. A Video Gallery of the games various endings you can achieve and unlockable infinite weapons you can use by beating the game in under specific time limits. There are multiple character outfits you can unlock along with two characters you can play through the game as (Jill or Chris). There are also steam trading cards, profile backgrounds, and achievements.

I don't know what else to say, it's a brilliant game from top to bottom. if you can get used to the controls and fixed camera angles, you probably won't find a better classic zombie survival horror game out there. It's a perfect blend of survival, item management, puzzle solving, dark, moody atmospheric and beautiful, yet haunting experience. It's personally one of my favorite games of all time and I believe anyone who enjoys this type of genre should play it once in their lifetime.

Having little experience between the original and this HD remaster, I was honestly really impressed with how much this got right having gone back to look at the original for cross comparing while also letting this stand on its' own two feet.

Ignoring the obvious massive graphical improvements, there's a lot of additional quality of life that makes the game more enjoyable without undercutting the original's design - like how there's not too much changed from a combat perspective, outside of now having a proper quick turn to get out of bad situations more reliably. 
The story is entertaining as a campy B-movie zombie horror experience in every way you can likely think of, the dialogues vary between serious when necessary, cheesy for proper comedic relief, and it doesn't hold your hand to spoonfeed you the entire story through obvious "OH MY GOD" statements but still has them for aforementioned relief.
OST is OK, I lean more towards praising it than hating it though I think the default volume mixing leaves a lot to be desired - especially during the first few minutes where it drones the same eerie tune to hurry you into the next story event.
Gameplay its' self is great, balancing between managing your resources and picking your fights carefully - as early you start with very little, and later on it will punish you directly for [spoiler]fighting too many zombies, and not burning the corpses with another resource that needs managing, by making them come back as Crimsons; a very fast very rapid attacking and much tankier zombie.[/spoiler]

The puzzles aren't that difficult compared to some of the other games, as much as they are a challenge of inventory management and patience to backtrack or using a guide/memory on a second+ runthrough to bring the right key items to the right rooms.

Playing this as someone that never played a resident evil game and started from the first one is difficult. I’m sure at the time it was truly a masterpiece and for those that played it back then it will be a very nice nostalgia trip. But it sure does not feel that way playing it today.

Unfortunately, the age of this game shows. Not in the graphics, those are actually quite good, but in the design philosophy. The controls and the predetermined camera positions are particularly where the age shows. Controlling your movement, especially when the camera switches positions as you move, is a constant exercise in frustration.

It is downright annoying to have the character move controls switch up based on camera angle and to do so inconsistently also. Sometimes you can hold the controls you had before the camera switched and the character won’t change direction and sometimes It will and you have to adapt your directions to the new camera angle. 

On top of that you have the extremely slow aiming where the button that’s supposed to make it fast, which should adjust aim to nearby enemies, does not work more than half the time. 
The camera angles also are downright confusing at times. They make it unclear which direction to go through. “Hiding” pathways purely because the angle is not the best. Making items hard to get in the range necessary to pick them up or use them. It’s a mess in that regard.

This means that in time sensitive situations like time puzzles, particularly intense fights or situations when you need to run, it all becomes a frustrating mess trying to wrestle the controls to get them to do what you need. 

Outside of that the age also shows through:

- Unnecessary time padding elements. One particular example is when a door becomes unusable after repeated use to force you to go through a corridor where a bunch of new enemies show up. However, after you get rid of those enemies, the door is still unusable and the path just becomes elongated unnecessarily.
- Then you have the door “loading screens” that at the time probably made perfect sense because of hardware limitations and needing a ton of separate loading for areas. However, in this case where you know your hardware could handle loading the entire mansion probably, it’s just veryyyy slow. Slow to go through the map and slow to manage your inventory (as you have to make multiple runs to item boxes to manage the very limited inventory space)


So if you never played the series and want to start with this one bear in mind there will be some pain involved. And I don’t think you can get the story through the cutscenes available online alone. Since the cutscenes are actually not that good from a writing/story point of view. They often make little sense in what the characters are doing and how they react. Most of the good story comes from the environment, the items, the texts via books/journals. That’s what truly sets the basis for the story and the world. And that, you can only get by playing the game and struggling through the controls. 

If you have played it however, I'm sure you'll have a great time, since you're most likely used to the controls.

Ironically, I played every other main series entry in this franchise before I played RE1. My experience with the franchise is built on over-the-shoulder cameras, heavy action, and much more modern gameplay systems. And yet, despite that, RE1 might just be the best in the franchise. At the very least, it is the best representation of true survival horror that this series has to offer. The pacing, level design, enemy encounters, inventory management, split-protagonist narrative, it all works to perfection. Despite its age, this remake still looks very good and plays very smooth on modern hardware.

Other titles in this series, especially ever since they started remaking some of the other games like RE2 and 4, are better with their storytelling and acting, and the gameplay is a lot more fast-paced and exciting. If you're more of an action game fan, RE1's devotion to pure survival horror will not appeal to you. However, even saying that, this game is the purest representation of the series' core, and I would recommend that any fan of the series give it a try if they haven't played it before.

This was a disorienting experience at first. The controls were not intuitive and as a result I died frequently and could not move in the way I wanted to. I felt discouraged, but I pushed through. And I’m glad I did, because this is a great game. 

The tank controls add a necessary friction that results in a tense but rewarding experience. Combat is difficult, and your choices must be deliberate, including properly allocating your resources. Exploration is a careful venture when you do not know what dangers are lurking behind the fixed angles. These same fixed-camera angles also display beautiful, pre-rendered backgrounds. So many shots and sight lines inside the mansion are richly dark, baroque, and intriguing. The art is so memorable. It felt like I was traversing rooms and hallways that had been lived in and intentionally designed. I also loved the soundtrack – how can I not mention the safe room theme? An immediate wave of relief would wash over me any time I entered a room and heard that song play.

There’s so many positive things to say about this game. Which is why I was so surprised at how poorly Jill was written. It’s not entirely apparent at first, but over the course of the game, you realize Jill is an empty shell. We know nothing about her past. She has nothing to say and no real inner world. We are told, at least, that she is a skilled professional, capable of overcoming difficult obstacles, yet the writing forces her to be saved time and time again.

[h3]Jill’s Awful Characterization[/h3]

I was reading about the game when I found a review that considered the "Narrative Impact and Character Interactions." Here is what the GLS Team, as recently as March 4, 2025, had to say about Jill:

[quote=GLS Team]Jill’s interactions with Barry Burton are particularly noteworthy. Their dynamic provides a sense of camaraderie and dependence, influencing the player’s perception of the unfolding events […] These […] character interactions add depth to the narrative and provide additional insight into the personalities of the S.T.A.R.S. members. [1] [/quote]

This, to me, cannot be further away from the truth. Jill is written incompetently. It is hard to care about her beyond a superficial concern for her safety. Jill has virtually nothing to say about the bizarre events she’s experiencing, even when she knows information that could serve as a basis for her to say anything. She barely communicates at all with her team. Notably, we also know nothing from her past. [2] 

One example of this poor writing is the brief exchange Barry and Jill have after he rescues her from Plant 42.

[quote=Jill and Barry]Jill: “I thought I was finished.”
Barry: “Yeah.”
Jill: “That was close. Thanks again.”
Barry: “Don’t mention it. But what was that. What the hell is going on in this place?”[/quote]

Then, the scene ends while Jill just stares blankly into the distance. This is when I first noticed how awful her characterization is. Not only is this the third time she’s had to be saved by Barry, but she has no insight to provide. Nothing to report. There's no depth to be found. Which is outrageous, considering that immediately before this cutscene, for example, Jill read Dr. Sarton’s report on Plant 42 [3] and concocted the V-Jolt to significantly weaken this monstrosity. Surely that’s enough of a basis of knowledge for her to say something, rather than nothing, even if that something is just informing Barry about her findings.

Jill also never confronts Barry about the secret conversation she overhears before the fight with Plant 42. The same secret conversation where Barry mentions a “deal,” the “destr[uction] of S.T.A.R.S,” or his concern for his family's safety? And to go even further, I cannot believe that the writers so blatantly gaslight Jill. That was devastating. Jill barely gets to ask a single question before Barry easily convinces her that he was simply talking to himself. He makes her doubt her recollection - what she just experienced moments ago was not real. No follow-up. Not even an inner reflection from Jill to the player. 

Another egregious example is Barry’s traitorous reveal. Jill reaches Wesker at the laboratory, and Barry aims his revolver at her, and Jill’s only response is: “Well, whaddaya know.” Jill, [b]you knew![/b] This is somehow worse than Leon’s camp. This is not the first time Barry has aimed his gun directly at Jill's face. He tried to kill her during the last encounter with Lisa Trevor – something which, again, she never brings up again. We also know Jill overheard Barry’s secret conversation and, as one other person put it, "[failed to] even tell Barry there’s a traitor among the [S.T.A.R.S.] members? That’s crucial information!” [5] 

Jill is there to investigate. This is made clear to us multiple times throughout our time with her. Investigate, find an exit, and survive. Yet, she has no theories of her own. No conclusions. No report on her findings. What are her thoughts on all that she's learned? Who knows, who cares. The little that we do know about her interior, for example, that she forgives Barry for his betrayal to the S.T.A.R.S., is similarly unexamined. Barry aided and abetted Wesker’s murder of Enrico. He tried to kill her (twice!). He betrayed the team. Surely there’s a conversation to be had.

I didn’t enjoy Resident Evil 0, but I still had some hope going into Resident Evil. After all, this is the game that defined the series. And to be fair… it is slightly better. But only slightly.

The most noticeable improvement is the item box system. Unlike Resident Evil 0, where inventory management felt like a constant punishment, here it actually works. It doesn’t remove the limitations, but it makes them tolerable. You still have to plan ahead, but at least the game respects your time a bit more.

Another positive is the level design. The mansion is genuinely well-crafted. It feels interconnected, and there’s a sense of progression as you unlock shortcuts and revisit areas. Compared to the more fragmented feeling of Resident Evil 0, this is a clear step up.

But beyond that, many of the same issues remain.

The controls are still extremely stiff. Movement feels outdated and unnecessarily restrictive. Instead of adding tension, it often just leads to frustration. Fighting enemies or even navigating tight spaces becomes more about wrestling with the controls than actually playing the game.

The pacing also suffers from old design choices. Door opening animations return, and while they might have been used to build tension back in the day, now they just slow everything down. After a while, they stop being atmospheric and start feeling like interruptions.

Combat isn’t particularly satisfying either. It lacks responsiveness, and encounters often feel clunky rather than intense. The game wants to create fear, but most of the time it just creates annoyance.

I can understand why this game was important. It clearly laid the foundation for the survival horror genre, and longtime fans probably see it very differently. But playing it today, especially as a newcomer, it’s hard to ignore how outdated it feels.

There are glimpses of what made it special—the mansion design, the atmosphere, the sense of isolation—but they’re buried under mechanics that didn’t age well.

In the end, Resident Evil is a step up from Resident Evil 0, but not by much. It’s more structured, slightly less frustrating, and occasionally engaging. Still, for a modern player, it’s difficult to recommend beyond curiosity.

Resident Evil (2002 Remake) – A Masterclass in Atmosphere and Survival Horror

The 2002 remake of Resident Evil is not merely a graphical update of a PlayStation classic—it is a meticulous reimagining that elevates nearly every aspect of the original game into something timeless. Developed by Capcom for the Nintendo GameCube (and later remastered for modern platforms), this version stands as one of the finest examples of how to revisit and refine a beloved title without compromising its identity.

Atmosphere: The Mansion as a Living Nightmare

From the moment you step into the Spencer Mansion, the remake establishes an oppressive, almost suffocating atmosphere. Every corridor, every creaking door, and every flicker of candlelight feels deliberate. The game trades the slightly campy tone of the original for a more grounded and sinister aesthetic. Pre-rendered backgrounds are rendered with astonishing detail, blending realism with gothic horror in a way that still holds up decades later.

Lighting plays a crucial role. Shadows obscure threats, forcing the player to move cautiously, never quite certain what lies ahead. The mansion itself feels like a character—ancient, hostile, and filled with secrets that seem to resist discovery.

Gameplay: Tension Through Limitation

At its core, Resident Evil Remake is about restraint. Inventory space is limited, ammunition is scarce, and saving your game requires consumable ink ribbons (unless playing on easier modes in later versions). These mechanics are not inconveniences—they are the foundation of the experience.

Combat is intentionally stiff, with tank controls that demand commitment to movement. While this may feel archaic to newcomers, it reinforces vulnerability. Every encounter becomes a calculated risk: do you spend precious bullets, or attempt to dodge and conserve resources?

The remake introduces a significant new mechanic: Crimson Heads. Zombies that are not properly disposed of can return as faster, more aggressive enemies. This transforms what was once a solved problem into a persistent threat, forcing players to think long-term. Do you burn the corpse now, using limited fuel, or risk facing a deadlier version later?

Exploration and Puzzle Design

Exploration is methodical and rewarding. The mansion unfolds gradually, revealing new areas as players acquire keys, solve puzzles, and piece together its dark history. The design is intricate but logical, encouraging careful observation and memory.

Puzzles strike a satisfying balance between challenge and clarity. They rarely feel arbitrary; instead, they are integrated into the environment and narrative. Solving them provides a genuine sense of progression, reinforcing the feeling that you are unraveling a mystery rather than simply advancing through levels.

Narrative: Subtlety Over Spectacle

The story remains largely faithful to the original: members of the S.T.A.R.S. team investigate a series of grisly murders and uncover a conspiracy involving the Umbrella Corporation. However, the remake refines the delivery. Dialogue is more natural, voice acting is improved, and environmental storytelling is significantly enhanced.

Files scattered throughout the mansion provide chilling insights into the experiments that took place there. Rather than relying on exposition, the game allows players to piece together the narrative themselves. This approach deepens immersion and adds to the sense of dread.

Audio Design: Silence as a Weapon

Sound design is one of the remake’s greatest strengths. Music is used sparingly, often giving way to ambient noise—footsteps echoing on wooden floors, distant thunder, or the faint groan of something unseen.

When music does appear, it heightens tension rather than overpowering it. The result is a soundscape that keeps players on edge, making even quiet moments feel dangerous.

Visuals: Timeless Craftsmanship

Even by modern standards, the remake’s visuals are striking. The use of pre-rendered backgrounds allows for a level of detail that was far ahead of its time. Character models, especially in later HD remasters, blend seamlessly with these environments.

Camera angles are fixed, but they are carefully chosen to enhance tension and composition. Each shot feels intentional, often obscuring threats or emphasizing isolation. This cinematic approach contributes significantly to the game’s identity.

Replayability and Dual Protagonists

Players can choose between Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield, each offering a slightly different experience. Jill has more inventory space and access to lockpicking, making her campaign more accessible. Chris, on the other hand, is more challenging, with fewer resources but greater combat resilience.

These differences encourage multiple playthroughs, as do branching choices, hidden items, and alternate endings.

Legacy and Impact

Resident Evil Remake is often cited as one of the greatest remakes ever created—and for good reason. It demonstrates that a remake can do more than update graphics; it can reinterpret and refine a game’s core ideas while preserving what made it special.

It also serves as a benchmark for survival horror. Many modern games attempt to replicate its tension and atmosphere, but few achieve the same balance of fear, strategy, and immersion.

Final Verdict

Resident Evil (2002 Remake) is a near-perfect example of survival horror design. It respects its source material while enhancing it in meaningful ways, resulting in an experience that feels both classic and timeless.

For fans of horror, it is essential. For newcomers, it may require patience—but those willing to embrace its deliberate pacing and mechanics will find a deeply rewarding and unforgettable journey into one of gaming’s most iconic nightmares.

I don't have anything new to say about this game that haven't been said by many reviewers and game critics before, so I'll stick to my experience.

I first played RE1 in the PSX in 1996 with my brother and my neighbor. I was six at the time, my brother nine and my neighbor 11. They held the controller, I watched from the sidelines. We never made it too far into the game - we played at night, and I clearly remember the first zombie scene, trying to flee the mansion, and the corridor with dogs. I think we dropped the game shortly after because I can't remember anything else from that time, and I was absolutely terrified of it. That was the beginning of the end for me when it came to horror games, I just felt I couldn't handle them.

Fast forward some 25 or almost 30 years later, and I'm playing games again, now as an adult. Recently tackled some scarier games like FEAR, SIGNALIS (abandoned, couldn't handle it), Hellblade (does that count?), Little Nightmares, and some unsettling but lighter games such as Daniel Mullin's The Hex and Pony Island, Fatum Betula, Limbo, System Shock 2, The Last of Us, etc. Then I finally felt ready to return to this game. Got this remake and booted it up, hoping for the best.

The experience I had was incredible. The game looks really, really good. Textures, models, pre-rendered backgrounds, the lightning, the sounds of footsteps, the growls, moans, and screams, it's a whole vibe. For the first two-thirds of the game, while I was still getting me bearings around the mansion and unsure of what was to come or where or when, I felt EXTREME pressure. It was unrelenting. And I feel that's what makes the first Resident Evil so special, to the point it coded and established the survival horror genre. You're never sure if now is the right time to save, because you might run out of ink ribbons when you need them the most. You're never sure if this is the zombie it's worth burning or even shooting, because you don't know if you'll be returning to that room or not, or where's the next ammo cache or fuel canister. Also, can you spare the inventory for that green herb? A first, blind playthrough of RE is marvelous in that sense, you're always on the edge and always second-guessing your decisions at every turn. I had some cheap deaths throughout my play, but luckily never really ran out of resources (showing I was over-conservative with them)

Voice acting and cutscenes are a bit cheesy, soapy and melodramatic, but I feel that's what they were going for and it lands. I think I would prefer a more serious style, it would blend better with the atmosphere, but what's on display there is not too bad.

And there you have it - my take on this great game, and the perfect way to cultivate a new Resident Evil fan, and someone who might one day pick SIGNALIS again and this time not suck entirely hahaha

I do not think this game is awful. If Steam had a middle review rating, I would give it that. But I've got a lot of problems. I've just completed Chris's campaign, have not touched Jill's.

-Difficulty:
     I selected the wrong difficulty because the game basically lies to you. Before you clear the game for the first time, you only have Very Easy, Easy, and Normal. But the game phrases it in a way that strongly implies that they are Easy, Normal, and Hard. So I picked what I thought was Normal. By the time I realized it, I was a few hours in and couldn't be bothered to start again.

-Camera:
     The camera is a total disaster. I've heard people say that the fixed angles help the atmosphere and horror. In my opinion, they take away from both. To me, having less agency in this way makes the horror/scares feel cheap and obvious, whereas scares that are my fault are much scarier. As for the atmosphere, I find the camera angles and switches extremely distracting. For example, there are several narrow, non-branching halls where the camera changes drastically 4-5 times in the hallway for genuinely no reason. This bothers me immensely. Often, after going through a door, the first angle is a close up of Chris's goofy face (or Jill's I guess but I did not play her mode yet), and then it changes as soon as I move a millimeter.

-Horror:
     I did not find the game to be scary at all. Not because I'm some tough guy or something. I vacated my bowels in RE7 or example. I just think there is very little that is spooky in this one. This may in part be because of my high expectations for horror in the game due to so many people complaining that RE4 "moved away from horror."

-Cutscenes:
     The cutscenes are quite not good. The acting is interesting and they all only last like 25 seconds with dumb dialogue. It is funny though.

-Controls:
     The game offers both the Classic (tank) controls and Modern (normal?) controls. I tried both. The Modern controls kinda fight you with the camera angles, but I still prefer them over the awkwardly slow spinning of the Classic. Overall pretty clunky.

-Combat:
     Nothing interesting about the combat. It auto aims, and you're just fighting the awkward camera and sluggish movement. I know that combat isn't the main thing in the game, but it still comes up quite frequently, so it's definitely an important factor. Can't remember any entertaining bosses either.

-Puzzles:
     I do gotta be upfront here: I played the first half of the game 10 months ago, and the second half in the last few days. So I just straight up don't remember most of the early puzzles. But the ones I can remember and those from the second half are largely unimpressive. Frankly, I haven't been very impressed by most puzzles in the RE games I do actually like (such as RE2 remake and RE7), but it seems to be a bigger focus here.

-Conclusion:
     The game is fine. If you're interested in more Resident Evil and there's a nice sale on this one, pick it up. But I do not care much for the game.

Resident Evil (2002) is one of the best remakes ever made, and honestly, I think it is better than the original in almost every way that matters.

And I say that as someone who really loves the original. This is not one of those remakes that throws away the soul of the game and replaces it with modern shiny nonsense. This is a real remake. A proper one. It keeps the story, keeps the identity, keeps the structure, keeps the feeling. It is basically a 1:1 remake in spirit, and that is exactly why it works.

What I love the most is that they did not "reimagine" Resident Evil 1 into something unrecognizable. They respected it. The mansion, the characters, the pacing, the exploration, the weird charm, all of it is still here. You can feel that the people making this actually understood why the original mattered.

At the same time, the best thing about this remake is not what it changed, but what it added.

The Trevor family story is one of the best additions in any RE game. George Trevor and his family bring a much darker, sadder, more haunted tone to the mansion. It makes the place feel less like just a video game map and more like an actual cursed place with history buried inside it. That extra layer of tragedy fits Resident Evil so well. It made the mansion feel more alive, and somehow more dead at the same time.

And that goes for the whole game really. The mansion in this remake has life. The original had many rooms that felt almost empty or just there to connect one area to another. Here, the mansion feels dense. More detailed. More believable. Every room has purpose, or at least atmosphere. It feels like a real place that slowly reveals itself to you. On a first playthrough, the mansion is so huge and so cleverly designed that you honestly can't even piece it together in your head yet. You are lost, then less lost, then lost again. And that is part of what makes it so good.

The fixed camera is another reason this game is a masterpiece. I know a lot of people now are too used to over-the-shoulder third person camera because of the later remakes, but the fixed camera here is not some outdated limitation. It is art. It is design. It is deliberate. The angles are chosen so carefully. Some shots are low and strange, like the game is watching you from under the furniture. Some angles are there to disorient you on purpose. Some are there to hide things. Some are there to show you danger in the mirror before you see it directly. Some close-up shots make the lighting hit the character's face in a way that makes the scene feel almost painted. It creates tension without trying too hard. It turns every hallway into a threat. And honestly, I still think this game has the best atmosphere in the entire series.

The cinematic cutscenes were clearly held back. They look like they were pulled almost directly from the original game, and for a remake that improved so much else, they look weirdly old. I really hate that part. You go from this beautiful, oppressive mansion atmosphere into cutscenes that look so dated it kind of hits you in the face. It is not enough to ruin the game, obviously, but it does stand out, and not in a good way.

Same thing with the pre-rendered backgrounds. Let me be clear: artistically, they are amazing. The atmosphere they create is unmatched. But technically? Yeah, the resolution is low. Very low. You can tell these backgrounds came from older material and were upscaled with whatever magic or crime against pixels they had back then. Most of the time it still works because the art direction is so strong, but there were definitely moments where I looked at the floor or a table and thought, what am I even looking at here? Still, even with that flaw, the backgrounds and camera angles together create something special that modern games almost never do.

Voice acting is way better than the original too. The original RE1 voice acting is legendary, yes, but let's be honest, it is legendary because it is hilariously bad. Here, the lines are still awkward sometimes, because Resident Evil will always have a little of that weird DNA in it, but the delivery is much better. Much more believable. Much less cringe-inducing. It keeps some charm without sounding like everybody recorded their lines half asleep in a garage.

Music is also very strong. Not my favorite soundtrack in the series, but still really good. The remake does a great job reinterpreting the original music instead of just copying it mindlessly. It knows when to be quiet, when to be eerie, and when to let the room itself do the talking.

This game also understands something that a lot of horror games forgot: horror is not just monsters jumping at you. Horror is place, silence, uncertainty, angle, sound, delay, and not knowing what is in the next room. Resident Evil Remake gets that. That is why it still works. That is why it still feels superior to so many horror games that came after it.

For me, this is not just one of the best Resident Evil games. It is one of the best remakes ever made, period.

It respects the original.
It adds meaningful new material.
It improves the acting.
It deepens the atmosphere.
It makes the mansion unforgettable.

And yes, I really do think it is better than the original.

If the original Resident Evil was the blueprint, this is the perfected nightmare.
