I am a big fan of this franchise, and I have played most of its entries. However, I've never played the originals of 2 and 3, nor had I played Resident Evil 0 and 1 before. Unfortunately I must encourage anyone who doesn't have nostalgia for this game to skip it. This is actually a 2015 Remaster of a 2002 Remake of Resident Evil. From what I've seen, the differences are minimal, barely enough to call it a remake in the first place. In fact, a lot of puzzles in the Remake seem longer than in the original forcing you to do more tedious backtracking.

Every door, elevator, ladder and any other room transition plays a long, unskippable transitioning cutscene. I'm sure these were necessary back when the game came out. I cannot imagine these being necessary in 2002 and definitely not in 2015. Besides this massive annoyance, the game seems entirely based around causing as much friction and tedium between it and the player as possible. The handgun, a usually reliable first option in Resident Evil games is practically useless in Resident Evil 1. At the point in the game where I have stopped (and I'm unsure if I'll continue) I have 118 handgun rounds in my item box and 14 in the gun's chamber, because there are literally no use cases for it anymore.

The game has the same save system that a lot of other Resident Evil games would use, most recently Resident Evil Requiem. You have typewriters and in order to save at a typewriter, you need an ink ribbon. This would be fine, if it wasn't for the fact that things that would take five minutes in any other Resident Evil game take half an hour in Resident Evil 1, due to unskippable cutscenes, zombie and zombie dog grab animations that feel like they go on for years, a map layout that is purposefully designed for you to have to backtrack as much as humanly possible and ludicrously limited, non-upgradeable inventory space. The inventory managment system itself is also painfully slow and tedious. For every horribly dubbed, skippable cutscene in this game there are a 100 more unskippable cutscenes of riveting things like turning a crank and turning an item incrementally five times to properly assemble it into the necessary sequence (each time having to confirm, sometimes even twice, that you indeed want to turn it further).

So many sections where I lost half an hour, 45 minutes or even over an hour to the game suddenly throwing some absolute BS at me. A horrendously obtuse timed puzzle, a sudden boss encounter for which the game did not prepare me in the slightest (in fact, the first half of the game teaches you to run away from anything resembling a boss, only for the second half to force you to fight them, without clear delineation), a sudden horde of enemies bursting through the windows and stun locking me till next Sunday. There are moments where you can see, clear as day, that the only intention of the designers was to prolong the game time. If this was remade today, in the style of the three modern RE Remakes and nothing was changed, no new content was added, the puzzles were simply made less tedious and obtuse, with less unnecessary backtracking and more sensible design and controls, less overly long, unskippable animations and animation locks (especially in combat or while picking up items) and gunplay that didn't absolutely suck, you'd be looking at a four hour first time playthrough at the absolute most. Instead all of the difficulty comes from awful camera angles, that help enemies attack you from the border of the screen, inconsistent weapon damage, random 1-hit kill attacks (with no counter ofc) and other miscellaneous BS concerning the environment, enemies or puzzles. There are also plenty of block pushing puzzles with, ofc, the slowest pushing I might’ve ever come across in a video game before.

The game never actually makes you genuinely scared in a fair way past the introductory hour or so. You're less scared of the zombies and more scared of having to fight them with the godawful controls and of potentially having to endure the same tedium you went through for half of your game session again.

[h3]Side Tangent Rant[/h3]
This game is lauded as something truly one of a kind and profound, but in 2026, the only thing that is profound about it, is how it can be used as the poster child for an issue that has persisted in gaming since its humble beginnings: busywork, padding, fake playtime inflation, an utter disrespect and waste of the player’s time. This doesn’t happen in any other medium, quite like it does in video games. Imagine if you bought a book and the book was 500 pages long, but 400 of those pages were just the author smashing their face on their keyboard to create absolute gibberish. Intermittently you’d randomly find pages that were part of the other 100 of something actually coherent and maybe even worth reading: the reading public would be in an uproar, the books would be mass refunded and returned and the author would never get to publish anything under their real name again. Unfortunately this sort of design is not only accepted in video games, it is respected, beloved and fervently lauded. And it’s even worse in gaming than in my fictional book example. In a book you can skip pages, in gaming you cannot skip anything that the developer doesn’t allow you to. The only way tedium such as this is skipped in the gaming landscape, is the mental skipping that occurs only through older player’s nostalgia, when they recount how supposedly amazing games of yore were compared to today.

If you do decide to play this regardless: there are three difficulty modes to choose from, Normal, Easy and Super Easy (though the game instead gives you a vague question about how hard you like your games). Don't choose Normal, choose "Easy" or even "Very Easy" for your first playthrough. Normal is not fun, unless you already know the entire game like the back of your hand. And trust me... I know, because I played on Normal. Also, change from "Alternate" controls to original (or use d-pad), trust me!

[h3]Update after finishing the game + full story summary[/h3]
I finished the game and stand by what I said. This game isn't even all that important. All you have to know is: [spoiler]A rich megalomaniac Ozwell E. Spencer (whose mansion is full of contrived puzzles) built a massive lab complex under his mansion where he experimented on people with a virus he had 20 years prior to create the "T-Virus" (that turns folks into zombies) and develop the first "Tyrant" (a massive, humanoid Bio-Organic Weapon with superhuman strength and athleticism). A special police unit, S.T.A.R.S. arrive from the police department of the local Racoon City to investigate, but are betrayed by one of their police officers, Albert Wesker. Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, Barry Burton and Rebecca Chambers barely escape the self-destructing lab, blow up the Tyrant with a rocket launcher and are rescued by their last remaining comrade, Brad, in a helicopter.[/spoiler] 

You can learn 99% of this through cutscenes, notes and a million other references in the later Resident Evil games, which feature much more robust narratives, with much better acting, cutscenes and gameplay. Just do yourself the favor and skip 0, Code Veronica and 1 for now and start with the remakes of Resident Evil 2 and 3, unless you're super hellbent on trying these games yourself for whatever reason, but then you probably wouldn't be reading this review, certainly not this far in. For these remaining games, you may look up story summaries online or wait for them to be remade. It seems Capcom is retconning a whole bunch of their lore and earlier games (through new remakes) anyway, so it might even be a better idea to just wait for all of the new versions. According to credible leaks remakes for Resident Evil 0, Code Veronica and 5 are in the works. If 0 is being remade then a modernization of this archaic piece of software will likely also follow soon enough.

A blast from the past, it was really interesting to see where the series started, getting to explore the mansion, the setup for future games, & the first impressions of some long lasting characters in the series, mainly being Chris, Jill, & Wesker. It really was an experience you’d have to try yourself.

I found that I adapted pretty quickly to the tank controls, which I saw as a novelty tied to this game with its history in gaming & all. Even though it was clunky at times, the majority of puzzles were easy enough to figure out, with only 1 or 2 stumping me for a while.

The bonus modes, Real Survival & Invisible Enemies, were a nice touch which provided a decent challenge, both also taking away your ability to lock onto enemies, forcing you to utilise more of the tank controls.

Now for my biggest gripe with it… I know the original was released in 1996 while this remake was 2014/2015, but one thing that bugged me was the “multiple” endings. While the process of getting the different endings was intriguing, the payoff wasn’t worth it. A lot of the endings were just reused cutscenes, not really acknowledging the “choices” you could make through your actions/inaction, which I just found disappointing.

I also wish I knew about the “door skip” mod before playing, as all the door animations you go through seriously add up to a few hours after a while.

Nevertheless, this is a faithful remaster of the original & a must-try for any Resident Evil fan or anybody interested in gaming history.

After having just completed the game for the first time, here are my thoughts.

This is my first actual Resident Evil game. While I've tried demos in the past and watched videos, this is the first RE game that I have played fully myself, and I loved it. I can see why Resident Evil/Biohazard got so popular to the point of having roughly twelve main entry games, plus spin-offs. But I will say, many things I love about this game, I also hate, (It's very 50/50) such as the camera angles, the saving system, and the lack of guidance. Let me begin with the camera angles. I love fixed camera angles and I think it's unique. However, it also causes some issues with the movement and having creatures off screen. There were many times where I would pass a corner where a zombie resides and I would successfully pass, but due to the camera angle changing and my movement getting confused, I'd walk straight into the zombie, thus taking damage anyways. Then there's the save system. I love the idea that your saves are tied to in-game items, making you really have to think about spacing out your saves. This also contributes to the "resource management" thing the Resident Evil series is kind of known for. But this only becomes an issue with player ignorance as I used many ribbons in the beginning, not thinking about long term, so that's more of my own fault than the game. Lastly, there's the lack of guidance. I like that this game barely gives you any notice of what to do. The majority of objectives in this game crumble down to "figure it out" and I honestly really like that. You, the player, have to figure out the puzzles through context clues, reading notes, and really using your brain. But, because of this, you can find yourself stuck throughout many moments in the game due to not having any idea of what to do. Sure, it's great that the game tests your own intelligence, but it does NOT feel great to be going room to room again trying to understand what you're missing. Props to everyone who played this back in the day without guides.

So, overall, I absolutely love this game. Even with the aspects of the game that I have problems with, they have their upsides and make the game more worth playing. I highly recommend for anyone trying to get into survival horror, or even just fans of the newer games as this game is kind of history when it comes to not just Resident Evil, but the horror genre as a whole.

The strict item management forces you into true survival mode, the limited saves make every decision feel weighty, and the fixed camera angles heighten the tension, especially within the mansion’s eerie atmosphere.
That said, I still recommend this game. It’s a unique experience. However, tbh I don’t see myself replaying it :P

First off the graphics are simply incredible. This is easily one of the best looking games I've seen, the character models aged gracefully, the backgrounds are top notch, the lighting is so tasteful. The fixed camera not only adds to the gameplay and visual storytelling, but provides movie-esque cinematography. Jill Is GORGEOUS 

A great example of this, in the mansion, you often run past hallways with glass windows, the camera holds an uncomfortable angle that puts the windows as the focus while you run by, suddenly, out of no where, a horde of zombies breaks through the glass during a run though the mansion, now the next time the camera is set to the same angle, you are struck with a high degree of tension, not knowing if another window breaking event is coming. 

This is why its important to preserve the original camera systems of these games. Whether it be the OG resident evil angles, or the stiff locked camera of RE4, these games lose a ton of tension with an over the shoulder camera, or in the case of RE4 remake, a free aim movement option with a free camera. 

It goes beyond the gameplay. The camera often makes use of classic horror film cinematography to great effect. Dutch angles make you feel unsteady and tense, low angles  cut off your sight and force you to be brave, uncomfortable close ups of Chris or jill, both of you staring right into each other as the ambience kicks in. Its very intentional and its honeslty incredible how a game can blend this level of cinematography while being very fun and playable. I often found myself just sitting there appreciating these moments as if I was taking in a really good film. Very good artistic choices 

And the lighting... this game was way ahead of its time in terms of style and fidelity. It looks far better than the ue5 asset slop we get these days. You can tell a carefully picked art team spent countless hours on so many details. Bravo.

The sound design is fantastic. Incredible music that relies more on ambience and texture over typical arrangements. The sound of enemy steps are so perfectly clear, you can paint a picture of the room the second you walk into it, its the evolution of the monster sound design found in  DOOM. Don't get me started on the foot steps, they are so perfectly recorded for each surface. Occasionally the music cuts and you are met with silence, birds making noise, wind, and of course foot steps. Oh and the shotgun headshot? Perfection. Top tier audio design

The gameplay is fantastic... mostly.  The game starts off as a perfect survival horror game in my view; inventory management is crucial as you occasionally have to carry kerosene and a lighter around, for you see, you simply can't just hoard ammo and kill every zombie you see, if you don't burn the corpse with kerosene, hit them with a flame grenade, or land a critical shotgun headshot, the zombies will come back as ultra aggressive crimson heads, which basically sprint at you, and have much tighter dodge windows. 

The Mansion is... its perfection. Somehow very Cozy and lived in, yet so scary and enigmatic. The visual storytelling is so strong in this game, you can paint a head canon of the day to day in the Spencer Mansion as you read all the files and flavor text. The rooms and hall ways are so familiar, by the end of the game I felt like I myself grew up in that mansion. The way the floors and rooms connect, its obvious this game was a huge inspiration for the interconnected design of DARK SOULS. 

The start of the game with the ink ribbons and kerosene management is fantastic. You're constantly weighing your inventory versus the route you want to take, and it leads to some incredible tension. Zombies will even roam at times, which is a counter to strict route memorization. Pretty good puzzles, nothing on the level of something like SIgnalis or Silent Hill 2 however...

The game has tight responsive controls and incredible feedback on weapons. Its the opposite of SILENT HILL 2, that game intentionally controls clunky to add to the the haze like dreamy feel of it, whereas RE1 has very tight and controlled gameplay, which plays into its speed run ranking system. Until the advent of the RE engine, resident evil has always been a gold standard in control and responsiveness.

The new movement system is broken basically, if you practice a bit you can really dodge just about anything, and there is no hard mode to start off, which leads me to the first flaw in the game; its too easy to snowball and ruin the second half of this game. You get so good at dodging, you start accumulating a dozen or so defense items, herbs, ammo, you start using the shotgun to pop heads on some routes, and suddenly, you're unstoppable. The bosses are no challenge basically, Capcom has always struggled with boss fights out side of DMC and Monster Hunter. 

Second, as with many Japanese game developers, the latter parts of the game aren't as good in my opinion. The lab feels way too quick and sudden, and basically provides 0 challenge and exploration. You are so overpowered by then that the game loses all of its tension

A smaller nitpick, can these guys chill out with the puzzle density at around the 60 percent mark? Jeezas, it was getting tedious! 

Having hard at the start would greatly benefit this game. Its necessary for og gamer UNCS such as myself.

The story, well you would think its pretty bad, its engaging enough, but nothing beyond a dumb horror summer zombie flick, right? Youre wrong 

The story itself is serviceable, but the visual storytelling, let's just say the Japanese, from film, to anime and in video games excel at visual story telling. The way the rooms are either tidy or scattered, the way books are open, lab equipment thrown about, a messy rug here, a book open on a desk facing out into the forest, there's a story that isnt written here, but told through the mansion, and its one youll have to see for yourself. In this regard, this game is fantastic. Visual storytelling, a lost art in modern media...

This game is at its best when you are wandering through a hall way, with minimal ammo, trying to figure out what to do, when suddenly, as a bolt of lightning hits, a bunch of zombies break through the windows. In a sheer panic you decide to sprint to an adjacent hallway, just to be greeted by a crimson head, because of course you aren't carrying a lighter around, so you end up sprinting into a random room in sheer panic

This game as its worst when you hit that point where your inventory management skills, and dodge skills result in you walking around with an entire arsenal. 

Overall, this game is mandatory for any fans of survival horror period. It doesn't hit the puzzles and writing, or the incredible ambience of SILENT HILL 2, nor does it hit the highs of a game like Signalis, but there is something about this game that just draws you in. Arguably the best game Capcom has made along side DMC 3 and RE4

This is how you do a remake, you bring in the minds behind original artistic / gameplay direction, and allow them to fully break past the limitations of the previous generation. You don't hire a random team to taint the direction of the source.

The (remake) of the first Resident Evil ever. Many say that this game is the definitive survival horror experience and it's not hard to see why that is. 

The atmosphere, sound design and music are unreal. It gives off such an eerie feel to the game that fits the whole vibe of the game. It is extremely good, arguably the best atmosphere in any horror games though the Silent Hill games may just be slightly better in this department. 

Also, this game is scary. Enemies can suddenly ambush you from nowhere, you have to manage your limited inventory well, you have very limited ammo especially in the first half of the game and you only have limited saves so the fear of having to restart a large portion is very intense. The fixed camera angle also helps add to the horror as you never know if there's going to be an enemy when you go into a new room or when you turn a corner. 

Gameplay wise, it's really solid. Of course not everyone's gonna love tank controls and fixed camera angles. I personally don't mind it. Playing DMC and the old Silent Hill games have gotten me relatively experienced. There are also a variety of options when it comes to your weapons so it's fun to mix and match in different types of situations. Though this game is quite hard, especially for newcomers. I struggled a lot during the first 30%-ish of the game. It definitely takes some getting used to but once you do it's smooth onwards. 

As for the story, it's quite simple though that's not a bad thing. I've only played Jill's but I will definitely come around to play Chris' eventually. The characters and dialogue definitely do a lot of the heavy lifting. This game has the old style of survival horror voice acting. It's cheesy, kinda bad (but in a good way). 

I believe this is an excellent Resident Evil game. It's not my favourite as I do prefer the gameplay of some of the newer ones but I 100% understand the universal praise for this game from the RE community.

I am writing this review after completing the Resident Evil 2 and 3 remakes, which I got as part of the March sale for very cheap. I was interested in playing Requiem, but wanted to dive into the franchise from the beginning first. I was very impressed with RE1. The tank controls and camera angles were definitely something to get used to, but only for the first hour or so of gameplay was it jarring. You will end up backtracking through areas a lot on a blind first playthrough to solve puzzles and return for items you couldn't get before, so you end up getting a feel for when and where the camera changes inside each room. It really is not bad, and this game is so good that I think it would be a shame to give up on experiencing it solely because of the control scheme. It really is not as clunky as it seems after just spending some time with it.


My playthrough was as Chris and at the hardest difficulty. Playtime was split between my PC and my Steam Deck, probably a 20/80 split. The game is challenging, the puzzles felt rewarding to solve, and the resource management/survival horror aspects were well executed. I was continuously impressed with the design of Spencer Mansion, visually and gameplay-wise, and how well the game fills you with a sense of dread. Every corner becomes a risk, and every encounter with enemies is a puzzle of its own in a way, since you have to manage your resources and make decisions about how to deal with enemies. Some, like hunters or crimson heads, leave you little choice but to fight. Sometimes, you may be able to just run past enemies and into the next doorway. You have to choose how you will deal with every enemy, and the answer changes depending on what defensive items you have, or how much shotgun ammo you have, or other things like that. 

Overall I think the game holds up really well, and it made me excited to play the newer games. I think this has been the scariest of the RE games I have played so far, despite it being older, just because of the constant uneasiness and the overall sense of dread you can feel playing the game.

Still, that's one thing RE0 has over this on PC; RE0 looks amazing right out of the box, while RE1 needs a bit of work. The alternate control scheme works well, so you don't have to suffer through the tank controls if you don't want to. Overall, this is one for the ages, and even though it plays differently than the recent games in the series, it still comes highly recommended.

From the start, I was hooked with the introduction of the main characters first playing as Jill Valentine then Chris Redfield on later playthroughs with the game's fixed camera angles adding to the unforeseen terror awaiting at every corner and tight gameplay that makes every encounter dangerous. The inventory system was a fun gameplay mechanic in how to best proceed forward with certain items unsure of what you might need and properly organizing yourself to meet the challenge in the next room. While I didn't play the game using the "tank" controls, I found the alternate controls to be suitable with enough adjustment with the refined movement feeling fluid enough where I was able to dodge almost every zombie in the game. The guns feel satisfying to use as while ammo is abundant the consequence of Crimson Heads add a layer of unease to how you approach every enemy unsure of whether or not fight or flight is best given the scenario. The game is hauntingly beautiful with the camera angles fixed to where you're able to appreciate each and every room to where the game still holds up graphically to this day with how each character is silhouetted within the environment. The story while not the most complex was satisfactory for the first entry in the series to introducing players to the characters and world where future titles will build upon it. My favorite aspect of the game would be the puzzles as each one became satisfying to solve with no singular one being annoying to the point of frustration as every element is blended together well. The layout of the mansion is perfect imitating a metroidvania in appearance as every single element of where to go in each area is crafted to flow into each other well to where you're able to route out perfectly where to go based on where you are. Through this, repeat playthroughs were a joy to play as knowledge of the layout and puzzles leads you to blaze through the game unlike your first playthrough which is such a gratifying feeling.

My only true complaint of the game would be the controls aren't the most responsive at times due to the camera angles. With adjustment I am able to properly handle them, but I can definitely name a couple sections where I was stuck within a camera interval as momentum stays between sections and I am unsure of how to proceed given the switch or not. Another minor gripe is the controls for aiming as with the alternate controls the directions are fixed to up, line of sight, or beneath you and at times I want to aim between these intervals which wasn't possible without using up some ammo for adjustment. I was able to adjust to it, but a slightly better aiming system would've definitely enhanced the gun-play.

For achievements, the game is pretty comprehensive in what you must accomplish to 100% it with multiple playthroughs as both Chris & Jill on multiple difficulties. Some were simple and fun like the knife-only & Invisible Enemy modes as on lower difficulties they aren't too much trouble and are pretty fun in execution due to the shift in gameplay. The hardest achievement would have to be Real Survivor as item boxes aren't linked and your auto-aim is turned off, although these conditions are in place I didn't find the game too much harder as knowledge of multiple playthroughs still helped to streamline the experience simply the hardest task I did. The speedrun achievements were fun to try and optimize my runs with my time getting lower and lower with my fastest time being 1:52 and using the bonus weapons were a fun reward for playing well.

Overall, I had a fantastic time playing through the first Resident Evil game. This has set the bar pretty high for the series and with so many titles ahead of me I can't wait to see what the rest have in store. I believe this game is timeless and a must play if you are curious at all at what the true essence of survival-horror entails and just an enjoyable game in general.

The music is relatively memorable, and it sounds instinctive enough to know which areas you’re in. Whether it be the save or the rewards room, it kept you calm throughout the storm of this zombie apocalypse. The game gives some replay value where you can play as Chris or Jill, and they have their advantages and disadvantages. Jill has more inventory space, but has smaller health. While most of it is relatively the same, the cutscenes are completely different, which was interesting. There are some dated aspects, like the voice acting and dialogue, that weren’t the best, which felt more like a product of its time. A nearly unique Resident Evil experience in this day and age. Along with RE0, this is the last holdout of pre-rendered fixed camera Resident Evil games on Steam and it provides a completely different, but completely worthwhile, experience compared to the more modern over the shoulder or first person entries.

I got into the series with the aforementioned modern titles so it was quite challenging to play a fixed camera game at first and I had quite a few false starts before it finally clicked. I'd recommend starting on the easiest difficulty as this game is quite challenging - doubly so if you're not used to the camera perspective - and using the modern analogue controls instead of the tank controls. After a few rooms I think you'll find the gameplay feels much more natural. Just bear in mind that the easiest difficulty trivialises the ink ribbon and ammo conservation vs lighter fluid mechanics as you always have more than enough ammo to kill everything, and way more ink ribbons than you need - so if you want these mechanics to play more of a part be sure to select a harder difficulty. I'd play as Jill first as the extra item slots vs Chris will help avoid backtracking to item boxes for your first playthrough.

The visual style of this game is really striking and everything just looks incredibly cool. There's a super charming 2000s aesthetic to the environments but since the backgrounds are pre-rendered they are far more detailed than anything else at the time and look fantastic. I'd recommend the RESHADE mod (takes 2 min to install) as this release is now over 10 years old and it definitely feels it - some of the upscales Capcom did at the time do not do the original artwork justice and some environmental text and images are hard to read: this is completely fixed by RESHADE. The atmosphere is excellent with creepy sound design, really engaging music (and often none at all), enemy ambushes that are perfectly timed to catch you out etc. It's not a scary game at all but it's got a great atmosphere. The story unfolds naturally and some of the voice acting/CGI is a little goofy by today's standards but overall holds up well. There are a number of choices in the story and it plays out a little differently each time if you make different choices, including between the two playable characters.

The combat is tricky but this is because a lot of the time you are expected to avoid enemies instead of engaging them. There's a good variety of weapons that feel great. Puzzles are spread out throughout the game and there's loads to sink your teeth into. None are particularly hard but they're not trivial either and add a lot of enjoyment to unpicking the mansion and beyond. The mansion unfolds gradually and is easily top 3 RE puzzle-box locations: up there with RE2 RPD and RE9 care centre. The only slightly frustrating thing is there can be a lot of backtracking to item boxes to get an item you need to solve a puzzle, or to put a gun away to make room for puzzle items. This, coupled with the mandatory 8 second animation whenever you go through a door can be a little frustrating but I'd still say its worth playing with the door animations on for the first playthrough for the deliberate, slow paced, gameplay they encourage, and the tension they build when you don't know what's on the other side. They can be modded out later if you hate them.

My first playthrough took about 10 hours but its designed to be incredibly replayable and most people could probably get at least 2-4 playthroughs out of it (the subsequent ones getting faster) without getting bored. There's lots of achievements and rewards to go for if that helps keep you engaged.

I look forward to the over-the-shoulder RE1 remake that's coming out in the future but it'll by no means replace this game because of the gorgeous graphics, great atmosphere, and unique gameplay. It's a shame we never got to see RE2 or RE3 in this style and they're now consigned to the outdated PS1 versions forever.

[h1] GEM OF A GAME [/h1]

I've played every mainline Resident Evil game, including 0, and finally built up the courage to get past the tank controls once again. This game is a masterpiece—the DEFINITIVE RESIDENT EVIL EXPERIENCE. Anyone interested in playing the Resident Evil franchise HAS to finish this one.

If you're a newcomer to the Resident Evil series and have played the remakes alongside 7, 8, and 9, expect a bit of a learning curve when getting into this game. Especially dealing with Tank-controls

At first, it'll feel god awful. You'll get frustrated, wish they'd just release a modern remake, and maybe even start to wonder if it would be easier to watch a let's play instead. DON'T. This game is a gem in its own right, and once you push past that initial barrier, everything begins to click. After some time getting lost in the mansion and fumbling through the controls, you start to find your footing—and that’s when the game really opens up. What once felt clunky begins to feel intentional, and you start appreciating the experience for all its quirks.

[b] GRAPHICS: 10/10 [/b]

The graphics in this game give it an incredible amount of charm. The best way I can describe the atmosphere is that it feels like an "I-SPY" book brought to life—creepy, detailed, and strangely captivating. Every screen feels handcrafted, with an attention to detail that pulls you in and keeps you searching every corner. It’s a style that truly stands out, and honestly, it deserves to be studied. No other Resident Evil—aside from RE 0—really captures this same feeling.

[b] MAP DESIGN: 9/10 [/b]

The map design here represents the peak of Resident Evil—arguably even more so than the RPD. The developers nailed the balance between openness and structure, creating an environment where progression feels natural once you understand the game’s logic. Every puzzle, corridor, and accessible door ties into a larger system that rewards observation and intuition.

That said, the beginning can feel overwhelming. With so many doors accessible early on, it's easy to lose track of what you should be doing next (something I definitely experienced). But this confusion is part of the design. As you explore and experiment, patterns start to emerge. I'd say that after the dog whistle segment, the game begins to reveal its structure more clearly. From that point on, navigation becomes far more manageable, and even satisfying.

[b] GAMPLAY AND COMBAT 7/10 [/b]

The tank controls play a huge role in shaping the gameplay. While they may feel stiff at first, they ultimately enhance the tension and horror. Movement becomes deliberate, and every encounter carries weight because of it.

Combat itself isn't meant to be the highlight—and that’s by design. The original Resident Evil titles—1, 2, 3, REmake, and RE 0—prioritize puzzles and survival over action. Here, combat is a resource management tool, not an opportunity to go all John Wick on some weathered-ass fleshy creatures. Ammo is scarce, and every shot matters.

Each weapon has a purpose: grenade launchers and magnums are best saved for stronger enemies, shotguns are useful for permanent kills, and handguns are often used to create space or, with the right approach, finish enemies efficiently. Misusing your resources can quickly put you in a bad position, so careful planning is essential. In that sense, the combat perfectly complements the survival horror experience.

[b] PUZZLES 9/10 [/b]

At a glance, many of the game's puzzles seem simple—often boiling down to "find this item and bring it here." However, what makes them engaging is the layered design behind them. The items you need are often locked behind additional puzzles, requiring exploration and backtracking to obtain or use (like the stone and metal emblem).

Yes, this can feel repetitive at times—especially if you missed something earlier and need to retrace your steps—but it rarely feels pointless. The game is carefully designed to loop you back through areas in a way that reinforces familiarity rather than frustration.

Once you get over the initial learning curve, most puzzles become intuitive, and solving them starts to feel genuinely satisfying.

[b] STORY (SPOILERS) [/b]

The story may come across as campy to some, but that’s part of its 90s charm—and it works. To fully appreciate it, you NEED to read the files scattered throughout the game. They add depth, provide progression hints, and flesh out the world in ways cutscenes alone simply can't.

Through these files, you gain a better understanding of Spencer's Mansion, Umbrella, and the origins of the virus-infected creatures roaming the halls. Especially for newcomers, this added context is essential to fully grasp the scope of the narrative.

If there’s one criticism, it’s that the ending feels a bit rushed. Not in terms of gameplay—exploring Spencer’s labs is still engaging—but in how quickly major story beats unfold. Wesker’s betrayal and the introduction of the Tyrant happen in rapid succession, all within a matter of minutes. The final boss fight itself is also surprisingly brief, often lasting less than a minute.

Still, despite that, the overall experience remains unforgettable. [b] 9/10 [/b]

TL;DR: There's a great game here, but it really does hinge on personal preference. But I do recommend you play through once, if not just for seeing where things all started. The updated controls make it a lot easier to digest the relatively obtuse puzzles and item gathering. 

Up till today, I've complete multiple Resident Evil games in my life, some of which include:
-Resident Evil 2 and 3 Remakes
-Resident Evil 4 Wii Edition
-Resident Evil 5
-Resident Evil 7

But for the longest time, I've tried playing Resident Evil 1. Tried first on PS1 (on PS3) and had a hard time adjusting to the controls. It was also difficult to know where to go and when. Then I finally tried RE1 HD after hearing it "fixed" the controls. Boy, the alternate control scheme went a long way for me.

While I had my gripes with the very foundation of this game's playstyle, I can't really hold that against the game as an objective fault. I used a guide all the way through, didn't read everything properly and had to backtrack several times. I truly admire how unique the inventory management makes this game and how the statistics at the very end encourage you to put all the pieces in the right order to beat it as fast as possible. 

If this is your first Resident Evil experience, that's actually great from a narrative standpoint. But it will take some time to adjust to inventory management and truly learning the value of item boxes. You will learn to take what you really need and nothing else. Engaging in combat with every single zombie you meet is ill-advised for multiple reasons. Leaving corpses unburned/with their heads on is also ill-advised for multiple reasons. Many bad habits will eventually catch up with you the further you play.

Combat itself is rigid and stiff by design. Aiming has its own wind-up and requires you to keep the appropriate distance needed for the enemy at hand. This can be hard to manage in the many, MANY tight corridors. But you soon learn how to lead zombies along into favorable positions to either kill or avoid. 

Presentation-wise, this game still looks pretty good! The colors, atmosphere, lighting are all great. Be aware that the game utilizes FMVs that were unfortunately not upscaled, re-rendered, etc. to look better at higher resolutions. That said, the game itself was not fussy playing on my 3440x1440 ultrawide, though this made FMVs look noticeably worse. The models themselves hold up well too, with some of the derpy eye movements adding to the charm.

Audio design is also good, even chilling at times when you enter a hallway and hear a zombie grumbling or Crimson Head awakening. There's not much in the way of conventional music, as RE instead opts for ambient tracks with low, brooding bass and tame, haunting strings. It ramps up for action scenes when needed as well. The voice acting pulls back a bit from the PS1 original's campiness, but still retains enough of it as to not ruin the B-movie aura of the narrative. 

Resident Evil is a good time. I don't see myself ever going back to it, I don't feel a need to improve or optimize how I played. I get the idea of the game and acknowledge what it wants from the player, but I'm not interested in that kind of deep dive. However, if a game of juggling inventory management, careful exploration and playing through a cheesy horror movie sounds like fun to you... Go for it!

[h1] A Survival Horror Experience You Can’t Forget [/h1]

I’ve never been a fan of the franchise. I’ve always been scared of horror games, mainly because of experiences on the PS1 when I was 5-6 years old. Now, as an adult and with all the hype around RE Requiem, I decided to give the genre a third chance and start with Resident Evil 1.

For a classic game, even in its HD Remastered version, I was genuinely surprised by how smooth the controls feel. I didn’t need any major mods, just a simple graphics mod easily found on Nexus Mod.

So far, I’ve completed only one run as Jill, and the game is gripping in every sense : from the story to the lore, the environments, and the enemies. It’s not scary in the strict sense, but it constantly keeps you on edge every door you open or corner you turn could spell danger, often deadly.

[h3] Positive Points : [/h3]
[list]
[*][b] Incredible atmosphere :[/b] The mansion isn’t just a maze map, it feels like a living character, integral to the story.
[*][b] Satisfying puzzles :[/b] Well-designed and rewarding to solve.
[*][b] Constant tension :[/b] Limited resources and ammo force you to play strategically, often avoiding unnecessary fights.
[*][b] Sense of progression :[/b] Every action matters, making the experience consistently rewarding.
[/list]

[h3] Negative Points : [/h3]
[list]
[*][b] Ink ribbon save system :[/b] A clever design choice in line with the survival horror spirit, but it can be frustrating in practice. You often have to redo sections you’ve already completed, and ribbons are limited. A great idea on paper, less convenient in real gameplay.
[/list]

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

This isn’t a game for everyone, but if you embrace its slow pace and constant tension, RE1 delivers an experience that modern games often forget. Personally, I loved it after playing several RE titles, the original remains unbeatable for me.

Resident Evil HD is one of those games that reminds you why survival horror became such an iconic genre in the first place. Even though it’s a remaster of a much older title, the atmosphere still feels incredibly strong. The Spencer Mansion is tense, mysterious, and sometimes downright unsettling. Every corridor, every door you slowly open, carries that quiet sense that something is waiting for you.
At first, the classic “tank controls” might feel a bit unusual, especially if you’re used to more modern games. But after a little time, you start to appreciate how much they contribute to the tension and the pacing. Movement feels deliberate, resources are limited, and every decision matters. Do you spend that ammo now, or save it for something worse around the corner?
That said, I wouldn’t say the game is particularly difficult. What it really asks from the player is patience and a bit of precaution. If you take your time, manage your resources wisely, and pay attention to your surroundings, the game becomes much more manageable and enjoyable.
The visual upgrade is also impressive. The environments look beautiful while still preserving the original atmosphere. Combined with the sound design and music, the game constantly keeps you on edge.
What I really enjoy about this game is how it respects its roots. It doesn’t try to modernize everything or turn itself into something it’s not. Instead, it preserves that classic survival horror feeling where exploration, puzzles, and careful planning are just as important as combat.
If you enjoy survival horror or want to experience one of the foundations of the genre, this game is absolutely worth playing. It’s a classic for a reason. 8/10

Resident Evil is a franchise I've been a big fan of since the second half of my college years, but the reasons why I couldn't easily get into this monumentally important entry at first are the same reasons I'd probably have trouble recommending it to most of my friends I know. It can feel antagonistic and obtuse, in both controls and design. 

Its design is very intentional though. It's that intent that helps drive you forward to complete this game. It's not impossible, but it's made to certainly look and feel like it is at first. The journey that starts with you shakily raising a pistol towards a walking cadaver, muttering curses under your breath with every missed or wasted shot, or every extra bullet you couldn't take with you, ends with you eager to shove the end of a magnum revolver you've been saving for a special occasion towards the jowls of something soon to be dead a second time, as you gnarl through gnashed teeth, "open wide and say AHHH".

It's those same reasons that make me love this game, and a good chunk of this franchise, and a greater chunk of the survival horror genre, which Resident Evil originally coined the name for waaaaaay back in '96. The 2002 remake is, to put it as bluntly as I can, intentional. All the stiff controls and frustrating inventory not only add to the game's effective dread, but to your own sense of triumph when you finally overcome all the game's challenges.


...This game will most likely inevitably get remade, again. I don't think many of us have the power to stop it from happening. As much as I understand many will champion either a third-person or first-person perspective as a means of making many aspects of this game accessible for a modern audience, I would like to say that it's the limitations of this original title that make it what it is. It's those limitations that this 2002 remake celebrates, indulges in, and absolutely relishes. The fixed cameras might limit your perspective, but your imagination? Your fears? Those are running wild. 

For what drives dread and discomfort more than to not be able to understand something? To not be able to see around a corner up ahead? To have the last thing you see of something only be its sharp teeth? To only hear that something as it approaches you. You can't see it yet, but you can hear it, can't you? It's getting closer, and you can tell, as its chains are rattling, and it's moaning loudly. It's cold. Restless. Hungry.

For Classic RE Fans Only (Updated 2026-03-16 | 8:41 PM Central Time)

30 years ago, I played the original Resident Evil on the Sony PlayStation: the one that came in its monolithic rectangle box with a crazed-looking semi-realistic Chris on the cover. It was an amazing game for me at the time and something that would influence my tenets of gameplay and game design. I never bothered to check out the GameCube remake, upon which this port is based (some may appropriately call this a remaster of said remake, but for clarity, I use "port"). I thought it looked pretty, but I had also already played through three Resident Evil games at that point, and I didn't think a return to the Spencer Mansion was necessary. By the time RE4 was released three years later, I was pleased enough with how the future was looking for Resident Evil, and passed on this until just recently finishing Resident Evil Requiem.

[+] GRAPHICS | The graphics in this game still look great. I played with HD+ resolution with fullscreen mode for no letterbox cropping (they had to crop it to get widescreen). This makes it so there is no scrolling, and no part of the gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds are cut off. The chiaroscuro lighting is something you can't achieve so easily with modern perspective-based rendering, so this is very nice looking, like staring into an oil painting.

[+] ENEMIES | Great variety of enemies including zombies, crimson heads, dogs, birds, giant spiders, Chimeras, and my favorite, the Hunters~ ❤️

[+?] MOVEMENT | New control method replaces tank controls with directional control based on the POV of the current camera. Easier for general movement, but still tricky in cases when the camera does a 180. If you don't keep holding the same direction, you can get confused and end up moving in circles.

[-] PROGRESSION | Backtracking really sucks in this game. There is way too much of it. You have to guess what you might need need, and if you're wrong, you have to run all the way back to the item room and get the proper item. I would say about half of this game is running back to the item room to grab something, and that's already playing as Jill (8 slots versus Chris's 6). I feel like it would have been better if key items didn't take up inventory slots on normal/easy difficulties. Too much of this game's design feels like it's based on replaying the game on harder difficulties where you already have knowledge of what you need where (which is great for replay value, but the first time experience should be the top priority). Seven years ago, I finished RE2 Remake on Hardcore, so I know how this stuff works.

[-] COMBAT (CAMERA) | Attacking enemies outside of the view of the camera is annoying. Yes, it is challenging and can feel rewarding when you get it right. I appreciate the mirrors and reflections added in some rooms to let you see the enemies and add tension. But it's just a really jank mechanic that makes combat far too situational. And sometimes enemies can be just around the corner with no audiovisual cues to help you out.

[-] COMBAT (AIMING) | Attacking in general is annoying. I remember in the original, I could aim up slightly with my gun and get close enough to zombies to get headshots. I can't seem to pull that off in this game. Furthermore, aiming goes back to tank controls, even when you're using new controls. They give you a lock on button, thankfully, but it is bound to the same shoulder side as aiming, so I have to two finger it with LT(L2) and LB(L1) just to properly target an enemy before shooting. Instead of letting you map keys directly, they have a crusty old selection of 5 different button layouts which doesn't just have a simple swap of specific buttons.

[-] UI | Lots of UI jank carried over from the original RE. Including having to nuzzle the bounds of the room and mash the action button to pick up items that are invisible or nearly so.

Does this remake need a remake? No. RE Requiem is the best remake currently available (I don't mean "remake" literally, but I do mean that in the sense of how RE9 combines many elements from the series). Rhodes Hill Care Center > Spencer Mansion. Now, rumor has it that a new RE1 remake is already in the works. If this is true, I'll play it, and I'm sure I'll love it, but they're gonna have to do some big changes to keep things fresh.

FINAL VERDICT: To give credit where credit is due, I will say this game is good! It improves upon the 1996 original with new features and modernizes some elements as would appropriate for its GameCube release circa 2002 (with some PC improvements and QOL for this port). But now that it's 2026, I can't really recommend this to anyone. It's so old that some younger gamers don't even understand that this was a remake and not a remaster (pedantically: this game is a port/remaster of a remake). Overall, it remains one of the strongest examples of classic survival horror design.

Crash on Launch Fix (Windows 11 / Some GPUs)

As of 12/03/2026, the game may crash immediately when opening on Windows 11 for some players.

What fixed it for me (NVIDIA GPU):
Disable G-SYNC.

Steps:

Open NVIDIA Control Panel

Go to Display → Set up G-SYNC

Uncheck “Enable G-SYNC / G-SYNC Compatible”

If you use multiple monitors, disable G-SYNC for each monitor

Click Apply and launch the game again

After turning G-SYNC off, the game launched normally for me.

I can only confirm this fix for NVIDIA GPUs, but if you're having the same crash-on-launch issue, it’s worth trying. Hopefully this helps someone.

I think it’s unfair that Capcom is still selling the game in this state. I understand this is an older title, but that shouldn’t matter when the game does not launch at all on some GPUs.

Until this problem is fixed, or a reliable workaround is confirmed for everyone, buyers should be aware that the game may crash on startup and be completely unplayable on certain systems.


There are also other issues. For example, the game does not allow you to select higher resolutions in the in-game settings. To change the resolution, you need to manually find the “Config.ini” file and edit the resolution values there.

Until these issues are properly fixed, buyers should be aware that the game may be unstable or require manual fixes just to run properly.

Short review: Genre defining classic and must play.

LONG review: Resident Evil 1 (2002) is a game that I find myself replaying multiple times a year in a variety of formats, because I truly can not think of a single area it doesn't succeed in. For a game that only came out SIX years after the original, it's got truly breathtaking visuals that still hold up to this day, the pre-rendered backgrounds are truly gorgeous, and the overall art direction of the game especially keeps it stunning. Each area features truly gorgeous lighting and use of shadows and color that give the game a truly cinematic feel that never gets old. 
On the gameplay front, this is tense survival horror at it's finest. The remake takes everything about Resident Evil 1 and cranks it up to flow even better than imagined. For people who find tank controls in old school horror games too hard (Which I'd argue is just a matter of a learning curve, everyone is capable of it!) this version supports analogue controls with snappier, instant movement (Although this can trivialize the game in some aspects). When playing in the original, intended experience however, the game flows beautifully. The tank controls and Fixed Camera angles add a beautiful cinematic feel to the game, every enemy encounter remains tense and full of interesting decision making. The addition of Crimson Heads in the remake is another fantastic change that mixes the formula up on a fantastic level. The already tense resource management of the original takes on an entirely new lens the second the player's made aware of this new threat. Every zombie having the potential to come back in a more menacing and deadly way means that even already 'cleared out' areas are now tense to track back through. Burning bodies and the location of the closest kerosene are things that constantly need to be thought about in the back of your mind, adding even more to the amount of resources you need to struggle. Resident Evil is a game that expects you to plan out your next steps methodically, execute them well, and reap the rewards. The remake also does several other things to keep the enemies snappy as well, variety is better and the expanded areas keep things fresh variety wise. Yawn in particular is a much more interesting boss than in the original. On top of that, even once you've finished all the official content, community mods such as randomizers can add thousands of hours of potential fun, keeping the game playable for longer than you could dream.
 
Plot wise, this game aims for a much different tone than the original, which was the perfect move in my opinion. Compared to the 2002 remake, the original 1996 Resident Evil sets itself apart through it's much brighter color pallete and extremely campy tone. The original re1 is clearly not taking itself seriously, and is a love letter to campy b horror movies, full of corny jokes and crazy voice deliveries. While these are extremely beloved by fans (For good reason, few lines are as timeless as Jill Sandwich) the remake opts to set itself apart through taking the story more seriously. The tone here shifts to more of a gothic horror setting, the colorful mansion of the original is reimagined as a spooky haunted house, with dark lighting and shadows illuminating every corner, and the plot shifts around to accommodate, with the campy delivery of the original replaced with more serious muted dialogue.  The silly jokes of the original are toned much further down here, as the characters react more appropriately to the nightmare in which they find themselves. The loss of the cast's fellow teammates is mourned, the character's visibly struggle with the nightmare they find themselves in. While both versions are beloved for a reason, the remake's a much more atmospheric ride than a fun comedic romp like the original. The only area I'd argue it falls flat in is it's portrayal of Rebecca Chambers. Shinji Mikami has gone on record to voice his distaste for her character several times, and unfortunately some aspects of that shine through here. This remake was developed alongside Resident Evil 0 (My personal favorite game in the series!) which shows the nightmare Rebecca endured and how she survived the 24 hours before alpha team arrived at the mansion. To keep things brief, Rebecca grows tremendously over the course of 0 and her character arc in it, but several scenes in Re1 still portray her as overwhelmed and vulnerable, in a way that feels like it's robbing her of a lot of her agency. This isn't to say all the content does her a disservice, a few scenes in which she mourns the teammates she's lost and shows the stress of the situation wearing her down do a lot to make her feel more rounded and human, but I'd still argue that they could have done much more to better represent the character she's become. 

Resident Evil is a beloved classic for a reason, the game is a genre defining classic and the remake in particular is considered one of the best in video game history. Many modern players find themselves too afraid of tank controls to engage with it, but I promise if you do you'll find a treat unlike any other, the game is simply timeless in a way few are, it's tense, scary, and comforting, in a way very few horror experiences tend to nail the blend of. It's a game I've played dozens of times on dozens of platforms, and I promise, you will never, ever go wrong by giving it a shot.

Resident Evil (2002) is honestly one of the best remakes ever made and easily my favorite entry in the entire Resident Evil series. What Capcom accomplished here is incredible. They managed to take the original Resident Evil and modernize it while still respecting everything that made the game special in the first place.

The atmosphere in this game is absolutely unmatched. The Spencer Mansion feels darker, creepier, and far more oppressive than it ever did in the original version. Everything from the lighting to the sound design helps create this constant sense of unease while you're exploring the mansion.

The gameplay loop and pacing are also incredibly tight. Moving through the mansion, slowly unlocking new areas, managing resources, and solving puzzles never stops being satisfying. It captures the exact formula of the original game but polishes it to near perfection.

Visually, the game is still stunning even more than two decades later. The pre rendered backgrounds are incredibly detailed, and the character models blend into those environments far better than they did in the original release. It is honestly kind of crazy how good the game still looks 24 years later.

One of the most impressive things about the remake is how faithful it is to the original. Rather than cutting content, the developers actually expanded on it. New areas, enemies, and story elements were added without taking anything away from the original experience. The tone is also much creepier and more serious this time around, which fits the setting perfectly.

I also liked some of the little connections and callbacks to later games like RE2 and Code Veronica, which help the game feel more connected to the overall Resident Evil storyline.

The only thing that really bothered me was one specific moment involving Rebecca Chambers. There is a scene where she is basically portrayed as a damsel in distress, which feels strange considering she literally just survived the events of Resident Evil Zero. After everything she went through there, seeing her cowering in a corner here feels a little out of character.

Aside from that one moment though, Resident Evil Remake is an incredible game. The atmosphere, pacing, and presentation all come together to create what is probably the definitive version of the original Resident Evil and one of the strongest survival horror experiences ever made.

Chris having a lighter for a special item is ok, but you really only use the lighter 3 times, while the lockpick for Jill is used with around 5-6 doors in the game. Well, I did it. I beat RE1 and have officially completed the entire mainline Resident Evil series (not the originals, just the remakes—sorry). I gotta say, I wish I had played this sooner. I always turned a blind eye to this game because of the tank controls, fixed camera angles, and limited saves. I was a Resident Evil noob. But after playing 7 and 8 and really enjoying them, then the 2, 3, and 4 remakes, and finally playing 5 and 6 with my buddy, I was hooked on the series. With Requiem coming out, I decided I HAD to play the OG and get the mainline series under my belt.

All this to say, this game is awesome. It’s the epitome of that classic Resident Evil feel that sparked the genre and the series. I have a newfound appreciation for this game and the series as a whole. The atmosphere was thick, and surprisingly, the fixed camera angles grew on me. They actually added tension when I could hear scary sounds but couldn’t see the threat until I got closer or until the monster rushed me. This gave me a whole new sense of panic and tension. Plus, the camera angles made it feel cinematic in a way.

The puzzles felt a lot more involved than in the other games, too. Some were a little vague, but I enjoyed how many required exploring the entire mansion and courtyard for key items, switches, and solutions.

My biggest complaint was the six-slot inventory, which forced me to backtrack to item boxes way more than necessary because you can’t drop or discard anything. It made it hard to carry weapons, ammo, health items, key items, and puzzle pieces all at once. But that’s a small grievance, and I actually got over it pretty quickly.

All in all, this was a fantastic game and a super interesting look into the classic game that birthed a legendary franchise. It’s crazy that this remake came out only six years after the original and how good it looks and feels comparatively. I highly recommend this game

[b]Resident Evil – Gameplay & Mechanics Review[/b]

[i]Classic survival horror distilled into tense exploration and resource-limited combat.[/i]

[b]Core Loop & Survival Tension[/b]  
What defines this game is its survival-first design. You’re constantly balancing scarce resources — ammo, health items, and inventory space — against exploration goals. Every decision matters: do you take that extra herb now or save it for later? This isn’t a run-and-gun experience, it’s meticulous risk management. 

[b]Exploration & Puzzle Integration[/b]  
Fixed camera angles and pre-rendered environments create an unsettling sense of space. Progression often hinges on finding keys and solving environment puzzles, not just fighting enemies. Backtracking is baked into design, turning familiar areas into threats you’ve previously bypassed.

[b]Combat & Resource Scarcity[/b]  
Combat isn’t about high-octane shooting — it’s a deliberate, rhythm-based affair. Weapon feel is weighty and deliberate, and ammo is precious, which means each encounter is a choice rather than a chore. The iconic inventory puzzle is a mechanical pillar of the experience. Limited slots force prioritisation of healing items versus combat tools. Managing space becomes as strategic as the fights themselves — and supplies you hoard early can dictate how comfortably you survive later zones.

My first experience with Resident Evil and Resident Evil 0 was honestly pretty rough. Coming from the more modern titles in the series, the difference was huge. The fixed camera angles were the most frustrating part at first 
they can hide enemies, make movement feel clunky, and force you to carefully plan every step. Because of that, I initially gave up and started the series with Resident Evil 2, then continued with the newer entries.

After finishing the modern games, I decided to go back to the roots of the franchise and properly complete the classics. It turned out to be a serious challenge. These older titles don’t hold your hand. They don’t constantly guide you or clearly tell you what to do next. You have to explore carefully, read files, remember locations, and pay close attention to details. Resource management is crucial  it’s easy to waste bullets, and every encounter can cost you valuable health.

The Ink Ribbon save system adds another layer of tension. The fact that you can’t save whenever you want forces you to play more carefully and think twice about every decision. Even while using a guide at certain points, I still got lost or stuck on some puzzles. These are not games that “spoon-feed” the player, and that can be frustrating if you're used to modern design standards.

That being said, those very elements are what create their unique atmosphere and identity. The puzzles, the backtracking, the constant feeling of vulnerability, and the limited resources all contribute to a tense and authentic survival horror experience. Every bit of progress feels earned, not given.

There were definitely moments where the games seriously annoyed me, but at the same time, I had fun and grew to appreciate their design. They truly test your patience and attention to detail. They’re not for everyone, especially if you prefer fast-paced, more accessible experiences.

Honestly, I don’t think I’d replay them anytime soon because of the difficulty and slower pace. Still, I’m glad I finished them. They have a unique charm and offer a real sense of accomplishment once you see them through to the end.

My final score for the classic titles: 8/10.

I will begin by saying that my first Resident Evil game was Resident Evil 7, followed by Resident Evil Village. I only recently played Resident Evil HD Remaster, and I intend to play every title from 1 to 9 (the remakes, where available) and achieve 100% completion in all of them.

I want to make it clear that I genuinely love this series and am truly excited to experience every installment to its fullest. Any complaints or criticisms I may have should not diminish anyone else’s enjoyment. Even if I find myself appreciating one entry slightly less than another, my admiration for the series as a whole remains unwavering. Otherwise, I would not even attempt to complete each game in its entirety.

It is wonderful to return to Resident Evil, and this version does an admirable job of delivering a visual update while warmly welcoming both veteran players and newcomers alike. With its graphical and audio enhancements, along with modernized and more fluid controls, this edition gives newer players the opportunity to experience one of the defining pillars of the survival-horror genre. Offered at an accessible price, Resident Evil HD Remaster is highly recommended for longtime fans who have followed the series since its earliest days and wish to relive the nostalgia of replaying one of the greatest games of all time.

Although certain environmental imperfections may slightly hinder the experience, the gameplay remains deeply engaging, sustained by its tense atmosphere. The series has always been built upon mood, scarcity of ammunition and resources, and the ever-present danger lurking behind every door. This remaster faithfully preserves the essence of the original classic.

[spoiler]Beyond its gameplay and atmosphere, however, what truly stayed with me was how deeply emotional the experience became. I love how this game made me reflect, not only about the story, but about life itself. It taught me quiet, meaningful lessons, the kind that linger long after the screen fades to black. Lessons I now carry with me into every game I play.

Just as Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil Village did, this entry reminded me that beneath all the horror, there is something profoundly human beating at the center of it all. Ethan’s story, especially, touched my heart in a way I did not expect. His love for his family, his unwavering determination to protect them, no matter the cost, felt so pure, so painfully beautiful.

By the end of his journey in Village, I found myself deeply moved. It wasn’t just the conclusion of a character’s arc; it felt like the closing of something sacred. His sacrifice, his devotion, his quiet strength… it all spoke to the idea that the true meaning of life is found in the people we love and the bonds we choose to protect. That love, selfless, steadfast, enduring, is what gives everything else meaning.

It was one of the most beautiful experiences I have had in gaming. Truly. It touched me in a place I didn’t even know needed to be touched. And even now, I still carry Ethan’s story with me. In many ways, it was the end of his journey in Resident Evil Village that solidified my love for this franchise.

[b]In this installment, while zombies may appear to be the primary threat, the true antagonist is the Umbrella Corporation, and the betrayal of Albert Wesker, a fellow human and teammate who sacrifices loyalty for profit and power. The most dangerous threats are often not the obvious monsters before us, but rather the selfishness, greed, and corruption of those in positions of authority.[/b]

The entire tragedy unfolds from the Umbrella Corporation’s relentless pursuit of biological weapons for financial gain, coupled with Wesker’s personal ambition for evolution and dominance. Unchecked ambition, and the willingness to treat humanity as expendable in the name of personal advancement, inevitably leads to destruction. And, if we reflect honestly, we have witnessed more than enough examples of that in our own lives, have we not?[/spoiler][hr][/hr]The remarkable visual and sound effects make the player feel truly immersed in the narrow corridors, opening ominous doors and venturing into suspicious places. Playing at night, alone in the living room or bedroom, is an experience reserved for the bravest. And woe to those who believe themselves immune to the shivers that begin at the base of the spine and freeze the very soul: they will be the first to lose their composure within the opening hours of the game.

The fear factor, already intense in the original version, has only increased with the new visual and audio effects implemented for the PC release. The entire sinister atmosphere has gained additional detail, and the realism is such that you will shudder simply at the sight of a zombie dragging itself toward you, no exaggeration.

Compared to the original version, Resident Evil HD Remaster features new rooms and areas to explore, new enemies, and additional animations. The original puzzles have been preserved, and several more complex ones have been added in the newly introduced areas.

Players may move freely throughout the mansion, without a strictly defined route. However, it is crucial to follow the “correct” path, as ammunition is scarce, the rule is conservation, and inventory space is limited. If you fill every slot in your inventory, you will be unable to collect any additional items. There is no option to discard unwanted equipment. Storage chests are scattered throughout the game, and only in these chests may you deposit unused items and equipment. The contents of one chest are shared among all others; that is, if you deposit an item in a chest on the third floor, it will be available in every other chest in the mansion.

Combine items such as ammunition clips with weapons, herbs that restore health, Ink Ribbons, and other useful objects. When playing as Chris, you will gather a set of disposable keys, each used to open a single door. In short, strategic thinking and careful item management are essential, as is knowing the right moment to run.[hr][/hr]For newcomers and interested players, the following points should be noted:

[list][*]No cutting-edge graphics; no support for VR headsets or related devices;
[*]Large mansion and secret laboratory: many rooms must be revisited; no linear “corridor” levels;
[*]No autosave: saving requires Ink Ribbons at typewriters;
[*]No auto-healing;
[*]Limited ammunition: reckless shooting is not rewarded;
[*]Limited inventory space: the female protagonist manages her bag better than her male counterpart;
[*]No directional indicators if you lose your way;
[*]Defeated enemies are not necessarily gone for good;
[*]The objective is survival, not eliminating every enemy (see limited ammunition);
[*]No DLCs and no monthly subscription (sorry, I simply could not resist).[/list][hr][/hr]A timely recommendation for fully enjoying the game: use high-volume stereo sound and play in dim lighting, but only if you have the courage.

[b]Words can hardly convey the emotions, describe the environments, or capture the terror the game evokes. The only way to experience it all is to gather your courage… and play.[/b]

I would recommend Resident Evil HD Remaster — but mainly for Resident Evil fans rather than as a first entry into the series.

The game keeps the fixed camera angles and classic tank-style movement. This can make navigation feel clunky at times, especially compared to modern entries like the Resident Evil 2, 3 and 4 Remakes.

However, this is very much a legacy Resident Evil mechanic. It preserves the original survival horror feel and brings a strong sense of nostalgia for players familiar with the early games.

The downside is that it doesn’t align with the modernised direction of later remakes. Compared to the fluid controls and over-the-shoulder perspective of titles like RE2 Remake, this can feel dated.

It’s hard to say whether I’d universally recommend it — not because it’s a bad game (it isn’t), but because its design choices may alienate those now accustomed to modern Resident Evil, as well as newcomers used to the more recent style.

That said, Capcom likely kept this structure intentionally to preserve the original experience. For long-time fans, this works.

The Spencer Mansion remains a highlight. While it isn’t near as atmospheric as the RPD Police Station in Resident Evil 2 Remake, the evolving enemy threats help maintain tension. Zombies can later develop into faster and more dangerous forms, alongside other quicker enemies, which keeps the player engaged.

It’s also worth noting that enemies in these earlier titles feel less intelligent compared to those in the modern Resident Evil games. In a way, it’s interesting to see how far the series has evolved since then.

The Lisa Trevor shack, the Residence section, and some of the later laboratory areas were less enjoyable for me compared to the main mansion exploration. One minor annoyance however, was the amount of backtracking between the West and East Wings. It’s not a major issue, but it can become slightly repetitive.

Playing as Jill and Chris was a positive. It’s interesting to see how both characters evolve across the series — Jill from RE1 to RE3, and Chris from RE1 through to later entries like RE5 and RE8.

Overall, Resident Evil HD Remaster is best viewed as a preserved classic rather than a modern remake.

For fans of the series, it’s worth experiencing despite its dated mechanics. For newcomers, it may feel like a step back.

Resident Evil is an incredible, highly replayable, memorable, tense, and beautiful game. And it's really unfortunate that this remaster is kinda... bad. The gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds of the 2002 GameCube original have been completely destroyed with over-sharpened, blotchy, poorly rendered upscales. There's also an intense contrast filter slapped on top of it that leads to extreme cases of crushed blacks and loss of visual detail. The music plays too fast and is higher pitched than it should be. The mouse cursor doesn't go away. The resolution caps at 1080p and the framerate caps at 60. I also find it crazy that after numerous re-releases, the remake, and the remake's various ports and releases, you're STILL not able to skip the door animations. It's safe to say this remaster is pretty rough.

So, why do I recommend it then? Two things, really. First, the game itself is still amazing, and everyone should play it. Second, there's mods that fix literally every issue I just listed.

The first mod is the most important one, and that is ThirteenAG's Resident Evil Fusion Fix. This mod fixes the resolution and framerate cap, lets you turn off the contrast filter, lets you skip door animations, hides the mouse cursor, and more.

The second mod is RESCALE. This is the current best backgrounds replacement mod the community has to offer, and it works wonders to this game's visuals. The shoddy 2015 upscales done by Capcom are completely overhauled with, albeit somewhat flawed, modern AI upscaling technology, greatly improving visual clarity and detail. This one is a must-have, but it does come with a fairly hefty download.

The last mod is the Normalized Music Mod. This fixes the strangely quiet and sped-up music tracks the game has out of the box.

All these mods are very easy to install, being just simple drag-and-drop replacements of game files, so please, play this game and install these mods, and enter the survival horror.
