There’s a reason Resident Evil is synonymous with survival horror. It literally popularized the term. While it wasn’t the first horror game ever made (it was inspired in part by the limitations of Sweet Home), this is the game that set the template: limited ammo, scarce resources, creepy environments, and constant tension.

When the original dropped in 1996, I rented it from Blockbuster… and returned it the next day. I was way too young, couldn’t handle the tank controls, and the Cerberus crashing through the window absolutely wrecked me as a kid. I’ve genuinely wondered if younger-me could’ve emotionally survived finishing it.

Ironically, I didn’t actually beat the game until years later with the HD Remaster. I’m pretty sure I finished RE4, 5, and 6 before I ever completed this one. And technically? I still haven’t beaten the original PS1 version—just the remake. But this remake holds up surprisingly well for being over 20 years old. The pre-rendered environments are beautifully creepy. Even without zombies, I wouldn’t want to spend a single second inside the Spencer Mansion.

Yes, the fixed camera can still be frustrating. There’s one puzzle involving moving walls and a statue where I felt like I was fighting six different camera angles more than the puzzle itself. But after replaying RE0, this honestly felt smooth by comparison.

You choose between Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine, and the differences matter. Chris has more health and starts with a lighter. Jill has extra inventory slots and a lockpick that saves you from hunting down keys. Both start with just a knife and a Beretta M92FS, and ammo is scarce—because this game basically wrote the rulebook on making every bullet count.

Each character also has a partner—Rebecca Chambers for Chris and Barry Burton for Jill. Depending on your actions, they can live or die, which affects the ending. It adds replay value and reinforces that classic survival horror tension.

Crimson Heads are the real game-changer here. If you don’t burn zombies after killing them, they come back faster and deadlier. I already try to avoid killing enemies to conserve ammo, so this mechanic adds a whole new layer of strategy. On one hand, I love what they bring to the game. On the other? Fighting a Crimson Head absolutely sucks.

The boss fights felt easier this time around—maybe I just had better luck avoiding poison—but the atmosphere and tension still carry the experience. The story is silly, sure, but that’s part of the charm. And honestly? It’s way more coherent than RE0’s.

Also worth noting: it ran flawlessly on Steam Deck, which made this marathon replay a lot easier.

Item boxes returning after RE0 was a blessing. I never thought I’d be so happy to see one. Backtracking is part of the design, but at least here it feels intentional—not like an excuse to remove a core mechanic.

As someone who has played Resident Evil all my life, any game from this IP has a soft spot for me. I never played the original, and was only interested when I got my hands on an original copy of the PS1 version. I fell in love immediately, finishing that game and instantly buying the HD remake. This game is such a gem and despite me being a huge horror buff, this game did scare me at times.

It does horror in such a great way, from the fixed camera hiding some enemies until you run into them, to the quality of life changes from the original such as better controls and auto aim. This game is one of the BEST remakes of any game ever. To think that this came out on the game cube back in the day is absolute insanity. It holds up to this day both graphically, and gameplay wise. This is what Resident Evil is known for, and I don't think anyone can dispute that.

The story is great, it captivated me, and created a sense of urgency during the certain timed parts. I preferred Chris' playthrough, with the added difficulty, and how Chris reacts to things. Jill's playthrough is still amazing, just not my favorite. I do think that Jill's playthrough feels more fleshed out and as close to "canon" as possible. You get constant scenes with Barry, and it feels like they are both exploring the mansion, giving that great sense of immersion. 

Now, I do think the 100% grind is a little much in certain ways. So, you have to do a minimum of around 4 playthroughs, which is A LOT. Even if you know the answers to all the puzzles, it really can become a grind. I think for the average person, who comes and goes to other games, it would be fine. But once I set my mind to something, I cannot stop until it's done. So having to play multiple playthroughs over and over really bored me. With the door transitions too, it really just was horrible. Another thing that irked me is the only way to get the infinite rocket launcher and handgun is to beat the game in under 3 hours on NORMAL or above. I think if the achievement was made to be that way as well, as opposed to just under 3 hours in general. It would've saved me a playthrough, It was a real bummer when I finished the game in under 3 hours on easy, see the achievement pop, just to not get the weapons sucked.

Overall, I think this game is a joy and for the average gamer, will be a 10/10. For me, the grind to 100% was rough enough to really dock it a little for me, so 8/10. I think this is a game anyone who likes horror should play, because this IS THE BLUEPRINT. Also the game goes on sale a lot, so there's that.

To have the grand-daddy of all survival-horror available to us on Steam is something we really shouldn't take for granted. I guess you can't say Resident Evil's 2002 remake is precisely perfect, but it's damn near close. It's an extremely well-refined and iconic game, taking what was good about the original 1996 game and trimming off the fat. The remake adds lots of new stuff as well, and that includes redoing the voice lines - thank GOD for that. if you know, you know.

For this remake to have originally come out on the GameCube only six years after the original launched and to look THIS good is honestly baffling. This remastered port helps makes things look even better, running at a gorgeous 60 F.P.S. The game's unique design with its cinematic camera angles make it feel like you're playing one big cutscene, and the way the characters move is inexplicably very satisfying to me for some reason. The environments in and around the sinister Spencer Mansion are nothing short of iconic - this right here is a game that's got it all: a spooky mansion, disgusting flesh-eating ghouls, hideous mutant monsters, booby-traps, and a classic horror-driven story that goes the sci-fi route toward the end. I mean, you fight gigantic tarantulas, sharks and snakes in this game, how is that not badass? The gloomy rooms you explore occasionally light up with a crash of thunder and lightning, which sets the tone of this gruesome adventure wonderfully. It is a bit stupid that the lightning all but vanishes as soon as you step outside, but whatever. 

I see a rather embarrassing number of negative reviews that criticise the camera angles and the tank controls, and this makes me want to hack up some phlegm and spit on my screen. If you can't appreciate the classic style (that helped define an entire GENRE) then maybe you should stick to your kiddie-games. I hate to gatekeep, but really, tank controls are a significantly excellent control scheme once you master them, and the cinematic camera angles help make this one of the most intense, uncomfortable, and yes, scary games I've played. I really don't care if the franchise moved on from the fixed angles; these days Resident Evil is once again a mainstream series topping charts everywhere, so this attracts a lot of new fans. I hate to break it to you, but don't call yourself a real fan of RE if you aren't able to even spend the time learning to appreciate the style of this kind of gameplay. Need I remind you that Silent Hill, Dino Crisis and Haunting Ground are games that are well-regarded, and their most popular titles all had 3-D controls. 

This remake can be a hard game to learn to love (getting killed by that first zombie is almost guaranteed and will surely leave a bad taste in your mouth) but stick with it. This game sadly came about just as the series began to depart from its horror roots and this reflected poorly on its sales, despite it being an undisputed masterpiece. The different outfits and weapons to unlock add some replayability, even though I feel like the game is almost too huge to make want to keep redoing it. Invisible Enemy mode and Real Survival mode are must-plays for any veterans of the series or for fans who are keen to try to the game in a different way. There's a ton of alternative cutscenes to see and a combination of multiple ways to end the game as well, but that's really just a bonus for the completionists who like seeing everything. The game sadly can't be 100%'d apparently, as the Gallery menu seems to be glitched and won't actually allow you to 'unlock' certain endings even when you already got them. Two of Jill's endings aren't on my menu, and after some research on the internet, I know I'm not the only one with this problem.  

The decision of being able to play as either Chris or Jill is a pretty neat feature, and really feels like kind of a unique thing in a game that probably would have been fine with a traditional sole protagonist. Playing as both characters is great - I don't believe either of the two are better than each other as they both have their own pros and cons.

As I already said, we're truly blessed to actually have a computer port of this game - there's very few games on Steam I can compare this to. So hop aboard that chopper with the rest of Alpha Team, go deep into the Arklay mountains and witness the true and terrifying beginning of this predominant game franchise.

[h1]Resident Evil | Old But Gold[/h1]

TL;DR - It's less of a survival horror and more of a puzzle game. It's not scary, except for when you realize you forgot to save your last 30 minutes, but it is a great challenge and entirely unforgiving. The setting is also refreshing from all the old forests and broken down space stations. Voice acting is infamously bad, but in a charming way. But be warned: THIS GAME REQUIRES YOU TO THINK.    

[h2]Game Overview[/h2]
[i] Resident Evil [/i] is marketed as a survival horror with puzzle elements, but it's definitely more of a puzzle game with survival horror elements. There was never a time I found it scary, but that's largely in part to the game be old. If you're someone who wants to get into the RE series, I'd recommend playing the RE2 Remake first. You don't need to play this one to understand that game, and it's genuinely great.

Now, that's not to say that RE1 is bad. Far from it. But, it's a bit slow and unapologetic. The mansion setting is intriguing and fresh, but it's also hell to navigate. There were so many times where I had to check the map just to see if I was still heading the right way; that's doubled by the fact that a door-opening cutscene plays every single time you open a door. It's unskippable, and thought it takes 2 seconds, it feels like 3 minutes. 

Speaking of the map, it doesn't show you items you've left behind. Meaning if you fill up your non-upgradeable EIGHT items spots you'll have to leave that key item behind, as all items are held in the same zip lock bag. So, you better have a good memory or write down where that item was cuz it's gonna be a long walk back to the storage box. 

[h2]Game Mechanics[/h2]
The storage mechanic in this game is both my biggest grievance and my highest praise. You get eight item slots, for ALL of your things. This means one will for your handgun, one for your handgun ammo, one for any healing item, one for your knife, one for that key you just picked up, one for the shotgun, one for shotgun ammo, maybe another healing item, and now you're full. Like I said, it can be hella annoying, but this mechanic also encourages the player to actually think.

Now, you need to actually plan out what you're gonna bring with you. Do you REALLY need that knife? You're pretty sure the zombies are all dead in that area, so do you REALLY need 2 healing items? Should I REALLY be using shotgun ammo on basic zombies? So on and so forth. There's a definite learning curve with it, but it actually makes the game feel 10x more rewarding if you bring the right gear.

One thing the Resident Evil franchise is known for is resource management. This game is the KING of that. Unlike future games, there's no ammo crafting, so you can't go around shooting out every zombie you see. You'll have to pick-and-choose your battles, while making sure to save enough ammo for boss fights. That goes double for healing items, there's no passive healing, so you have to extra conservative on those.

The final thing you need to conserve are Ink Ribbons, AKA the item that lets you SAVE THE GAME. That's right, in this game you need an item to save. Run out? Then you better get real good real soon, cause that last save is all you got. There's no autosave and no checkpoints. If you die to ANYTHING you'll be set back to your last save, even bosses. No starting outside their door on death. This also means that ALL your progress will be gone. I personally lost 20 minutes worth of exploration to getting stun-locked by a super zombie (will get to that). Luckily, the game will provide you with more every time you find a new save spot, as well as sprinkle some around the map, but they need to be used wisely. Because once they're gone, they're gone. 

[h2]Enemies[/h2]
The zombies in this game are very different from your Left 4 Dead 2 zombies. A single headshot won't kill them (unless your lucky enough to get a critical), and killing one zombie can have you go from 50 bullets to 15. And dead is a very loose term. As the zombies can also, y'know, get back up. You can 'kill' a zombie and have them be dead for the remainder of the time your in the room, but every time you leave there's a chance they'll just get back up. 

There's only 3 ways to truly kill a zombie. One, get lucky and blow its head off with a critical. Two, burn the corpse with kerosene. Or three, kill it enough times that it dies for real. Each of these has its own problems. One is unreliable as it's just pure luck, kerosene takes up an item slot and is ALSO something you can run out of, and three will just eat up your ammo. So, it's best to just leave them on the ground, right? Well...

If you don't dispatch of the zombie using either the first or second methods, it will turn into a stronger variant. It moves faster, hits harder, and can literally chain hit you to death if you're unlucky. The trigger for this is time, ranging from either 5 minutes to 1 hour depending on difficulty. Meaning every time you walk into a room there's a chance you'll get a super zombie. 

There are other monsters you'll encounter, but I'll let those be a surprise.

[h2]Story[/h2]
The story of this game is written in the same vain as Dark Souls. Not in content, but in execution. 90% of this games story is pieced together from collectibles you can find around the mansion; everything from what happened to this place, to a mini side story. However, the main story that gets told through the cutscenes & dialogue is...fine?

Well, there's technically two separate stories you can play. Chris Redfield's and Jill Valentine's. While you CAN play them both in either order, I'd recommend starting with Chris's first. It has a better flow to the pacing, whereas Jill's story was written in way that expected the player to already know everything.

Moving onto the voice acting, it's bad. Like, famously bad, but in a charming way. Here's a quick ranking of the main cast:
#1: Wesker - Although this is mainly cause he has very few lines, but each one still delivered well.
#2: Barry (Jill Run Only Character) - Same with Wesker, he doesn't have many lines, but the delivery and tone was consistent with the scene.
#3: Chris - His tone is stiff, and most of the time his delivery is that out of a 2000's video game commercial, but he at least as SOME energy.
#4: Rebecca (Chris Run Only Character) - Honestly, I'd have her tied with Chris. But, sometimes her tone is pretty inconsistent with what's happening. 
#5: Jill - It feels like she's reading straight off the script. Anyone whose done her run will tell you about the notorious 'sandwich' line; it felt like her energy was being drained as she read those lines. And I loved it.

[h2]Conclusion: 8/10[/h2]
This game isn't for everyone, especially those of the survival horror genre. It's clunky, has a poorly paced story, and an annoying door cutscene. (I've seen the 'Door Opening Simulator' review at least 7 times). But, if you're willing to brave through it, you'll find an extremely rewarding and charming game.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is not only one of the best remakes ever made, it’s a masterclass in survival horror that still puts many modern games to shame.

What makes this remake so special is how faithful it is to the original vision, while massively improving everything that mattered. The pre-rendered backgrounds were completely redone in HD and they still look incredible to this day. The atmosphere is unmatched: the Spencer Mansion feels oppressive, mysterious, and dangerous at every corner. This game simply does not age.

The fixed camera angles, often criticized by newcomers, are actually one of its greatest strengths. They enhance tension, limit information, and turn simple hallways into sources of genuine fear. Every door you open feels risky because you never fully know what’s waiting for you. Modern over-the-shoulder cameras just don’t create this level of suspense.

Limited saves with ink ribbons are another brilliant design choice. They force you to plan, manage resources, and think twice before taking risks. Every decision matters, and every mistake can be costly. This is survival horror in its purest form — not an action game pretending to be scary.

The gameplay is slow, methodical, and tense. Enemy placement, sound design, and pacing are near perfect. Even veterans will respect how punishing and fair the game can be. Add to that multiple characters, alternate paths, puzzles, and unlockables, and you have a game with huge replay value.

Resident Evil HD Remaster proves that great game design is timeless. It respects its roots, understands what made the original iconic, and refines it without watering it down. If you want to experience true survival horror — not just nostalgia, but quality — this is an absolute must-play.

Resident Evil shot into the zeitgeist back in ‘96 (good year) by collecting and mutating the great spooky works before it. Horror: now accessible to the gaming masses — addictive exploration, tense combat, and undeniable charm all bundled, stamped and shipped. The foundations were immediately strong, even if a few aspects were found wanting. 

The 2002 release is, for most people, the definitive way to experience RE1. Whether you like remakes or not, it’s hard to argue that they didn’t do a great job here. This is an elevation of the core essence into a more polished exterior, but still different enough that you can (and should!) play both. 

Spencer Mansion is as creepy as ever: dust of past tragedies is displaced as you clunk your way through a plethora of interesting, vividly detailed rooms, each one an adventure in itself. Delve deeper and deeper into whatever layer of hell suits you. Uncover ethical nightmares, solve dynamic puzzles, inhale herbs like your life depends on it (spoiler: it does). 
Strange sounds precede your vision; fixed cameras control the flow for unsuspecting players. Doors are more dangerous than ever — the game plays with your expectations of separate cells, thereby almost justifying how tedious the frequent loading screens really are. Almost.

I’m not sure I like the item limitations here. Inventory management has always been a staple of Resident Evil, and Chris having less slots in the original was because he was a different difficulty for the player. Here, we have different characters as well as difficulty options — management as a result feels more annoying than it needs to be, especially when you’re not optimising a route on your 10th no-saves/no-deaths/no-grass-touched speedrun. 

There is a secret sauce here that undeniably captures people’s attention. It’s a slicker, smoother experience — one that’s aged very well against the ‘96 version. Against the more drastic remakes of 2 - 4 (and whatever else they have planned), I’m not sure it justifies its existence enough, but it sure as hell is appreciated. 
Anyone who is trying to dip their toes into the series should start here. You may not finish it — you’ll probably snag against the tank controls, the loading screens, the backtracking — but you’ll understand the heart of the series, and appreciate any modern take on its sensibilities so much more. In that regard: this remake is truly a success.

After finishing Studio System: Guardian Angel, I was left craving more similar survival horror experiences, so I asked around and, among others, Resident Evil 1 (and the saga itself for that matter) was the one I chose to satisfy my hunger of all things creepy.

I had never played a fixed camera game before stusys, but from the first one or two hours, I was already sold on the idea. The fact that RE1 Remake kept that, instead of making it into an over-the-shoulder 3rd person game like its other remakes, is something I greatly appreciate. Clunky and annoying as it can sometimes be, the personality and atmosphere it brings to the game makes it so worth it. It is not without flaws, though, and some angles felt unnecessarily annoying or awkward, but not either of those enough to really become a serious issue. Most of the times the angles added to what a certain scene was trying to tell.

I absolutely LOVED every bit of the mansion. Exploring it and feeling trapped in a giant maze that is both trying to kill you but expecting you to open up its secrets felt very unique. From the ways you solve the puzzles to the interactions with the objects themselves, like having to inspect or rotate them to find a key, open them up, etc... It just oozes charisma and uniqueness in a way that also immerses you greatly. You don't just press a button to make a text pop up saying whether there was an item inside or not. Instead, you have to actually rotate the item in your inventory and press the button once the lock is "in front" of you. Imho, such interactions makes the player feel like they are actually doing something in the game rather than just playing it, if that makes sense. It's like pressing a button and automatically doing a cool ass combo, as opposed to actually having to press a set of buttons, all doing rather simple actions, that, in the end, amount to a cool ass combo.

The atmosphere is GREAT. Even if some things can feel a bit predictable, I never felt safe outside of a save room, or until I killed every zombie and burnt their bodies. This was a lesson that a friendly crimson head in a random hallway taught me well. Thanks and ♥♥♥♥ you. Scariest enemy in the whole game.
Regardless, both music and ambience keeps you on your toes at all times. If you aren't tense, you'll at least have an uneasiness chasing you constantly. And well, I guess that's part of the point.

I think the story was good. Progression was nice, and I really enjoyed how it gets weirder and weirder until it climaxes at the labs. All the little notes and books depicting what was going on really added to the depressing and eerie vibe of the mansion, especially those scientists who had to off themselves or lost someone close to them. Aside from that, the story itself does feel veeery short, and I wish some characters, like Barry, had a bit more screen time or development (although I liked him overall). Same goes for Wesker, but I think all gets expanded upon in future games, but I felt it was noteworthy.

Now... this game is not free of sins, and the inventory system is a bit ass. Limited slots are fine, great even. I love having to plan ahead. But not being able to replace items you find on the ground with the ones you are already carrying just feels too clunky. Also, and I may be wrong about this as I don't remember this well, but I have the memory of being annoyed at the inventory system when I had my pockets full and couldn't pick up ammunition for my depleted gun. Stuff like that just feels awkward and annoying for no real valid reason.

Running back and forth between puzzles wasn't something I was too fond of either, especially when key items for a puzzle would show up way before the puzzle itself, in a rather unrelated room at the opposite wing of the mansion. Just feels a tad bit too unstructured, and while it adds to the feeling of being trapped in a maze, sometimes it becomes tedious.

Lastly, one of the things I actually liked because I thought was silly, was some of the very over-the-top things you can find in the mansion. Like, I'm sure nothing weird would go on in the mansion that has FOUR DEATH MASKS scattered around. Or the signpost with 4 directions pointing to THE VALLEY OF DESTRUCTION or THE PATH OF REVENGE surely means normal activities are being carried out in it! The owner must be a well-adjusted person for sure! It was funny to ease some of the tensions by being reminded I'm literally walking through the domains of a twirly mustache supervillain, plotting and scheming EVIL things in his VERY EDGY Mansion of Total World Domination or something. It's kinda charming and a good contrast to the actual horrors the scientists took part in.
Also, the notes where the scientists or workers turn into zombies going like "mm itchy, yummy. Still itches, food good" are just hilarious.

Overall, despite its age clearly showing both in visuals and gameplay, it is just a gem of a game that I would recommend to anyone trying to get into survival horrors, even if they'll have to endure through tank controls and fixed camera. That's just a rite of passage.

This forces players to think before acting, creating tension that modern horror games often struggle to replicate. Enemy placement and sound design work together to keep players constantly on edge, even during moments of silence.

While newcomers may find the controls and slower pace challenging, Biohazard HD REMASTER never compromises its vision. It understands exactly what it is and executes it flawlessly.

The Birthplace of Survival Horror - A Review of Resident Evil

Overall Rating: 9.75/10

Resident Evil stands as one of the most important survival horror games ever created, and its modern release preserves everything that made it legendary while subtly refining the experience. Set within the infamous Spencer Mansion, the game is a masterclass in tension, atmosphere, and deliberate pacing. Rather than relying on constant action, it builds fear through confinement, uncertainty, and the ever-present threat of the unknown. This is survival horror in its purest, most disciplined form.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 9.5/10
The mansion remains one of gaming’s most iconic locations. Pre-rendered backgrounds are richly detailed, filled with shadowy hallways, decaying rooms, and unsettling stillness. Every environment feels carefully composed, using fixed camera angles to frame danger just outside the player’s view. Lighting and environmental detail elevate the setting into something oppressive yet elegant, making exploration both mesmerizing and nerve-wracking. The mansion itself feels hostile, as if every corridor and room is actively working against your survival.

Story and Narrative: 9/10
Resident Evil tells its story with restraint and confidence, allowing the player to uncover its secrets through exploration rather than direct explanation. Journal entries, environmental details, and subtle story beats piece together a slow, unsettling descent into biological horror. The tragedy of the mansion’s past reveals itself gradually, while the larger Umbrella conspiracy looms in the background with pulpy, genre-defining flair. The narrative works hand in hand with the gameplay, reinforcing tension and discovery while naturally supporting the game’s deliberate survival-focused design.

Gameplay and Survival Mechanics: 9.5/10
This is where Resident Evil defines the genre. Limited resources, deliberate movement, and careful inventory management create constant tension. The presence of item boxes provides strategic relief, turning backtracking into a thoughtful risk-versus-reward system rather than pure frustration. Combat is intentionally stiff, reinforcing vulnerability and making every encounter a decision rather than a reflex. Exploration, puzzle-solving, and survival are perfectly intertwined.

Sound Design and Music: 10/10
The soundscape is nothing short of iconic. Ambient silence is frequently more terrifying than any musical cue, broken only by distant footsteps, creaking floors, or the sudden moan of the undead. When music does surface, it’s deliberate and unforgettable—haunting melodies that heighten tension without overwhelming it. The soundtrack understands restraint, using music as punctuation rather than constant accompaniment.

Immersion and Replayability: 10/10
Resident Evil rewards multiple playthroughs through alternate characters, routes, and item placements. Familiarity never dulls the experience; instead, it deepens appreciation for its design. Speed runs, challenge modes, and mastery of the mansion layout keep the game engaging long after the first completion.

Conclusion: 9.75/10
Resident Evil is a benchmark for survival horror, proving that fear doesn’t come from excess—but from control. Its careful balance of atmosphere, mechanics, and sound design creates a slow-burning tension few games have ever matched. Every door opened feels earned, every bullet spent feels costly, and every moment inside the mansion feels dangerous.

Final Verdict:
A masterclass in survival horror design, Resident Evil remains as effective today as it was at release. Its deliberate pacing, oppressive atmosphere, and interconnected systems work in harmony to create an experience where tension is constant and every decision matters. Few games understand fear through limitation as completely—or as confidently—as this one.

Great remake of a great game. Yeah sure if you put it up against modern RE games it's relatively "clunky" and "annoying" but that just adds to the tension. The limitations make the game scarier, not worse. You never know what you need to carry or how much ammo you should use or when you should save. This game induces dread not through scares but mostly through resource management, which is exactly what a survival horror game should do.

Unfortunately, that's a double-edged sword. Once you've finished the game, the second playthrough (which I do recommend doing) is not nearly as scary. You know exactly what you need to do, what you need to carry, and when you need to carry it. But that's when you get to the second layer of fun that is perfecting your run and getting a better score. Hell, the game encourages you to shave your time down to less than 3 hours if you're a completionist. 

In terms of story and characters, I think that it's a "side-grade" from the original. Yeah sure the lines aren't as overtly dumb anymore but the characters all still feel... off. Like these aren't how normal humans act and it doesn't help that they aren't allowed to talk or interact outside of cutscenes. Maybe that'll be distracting, maybe that'll add to the atmosphere for you. 

This is a great starting point for the series IF you are patient and willing to engage with it. Please give it a shot and don't be afraid to turn down the difficulty on your first playthrough if you're really having trouble. Because you can always kick it up a notch on the second go-round once you're feeling more confident.

what is a problem, i feel, is that the gameplay systems don't seem to be balanced or designed to accommodate the above constraints. on the hardest difficulty, zombies take 10+ handgun shots to kill, none of which stun the zombie (bizarre?). ammo is extremely scarce anyway, and on full health you die in just two bites. oftentimes making a turn that leads to a camera angle switch will reveal a conveniently-positioned enemy ready to take a bite, and the frustrating RNG minigame of trying to dodge a zombie attack isn't fun in the slightest, especially in tight corridors and hallways. 

if the game featured more traditional third-person "top-down" controls (where pulling a stick in a certain direction leads to your character IMMEDIATELY turning and moving in that direction, relative to the camera), this would all be a lot more bearable, but probably still feel "off" as the zombies' attacks just feel clunky and inconsistent in general.

balance is hard, especially in shooters, but here the difficulty feels very artificial, and a product of its time.

i'll be waiting for the inevitable remake.

As someone who has played this game since its original release on the Gamecube two decades ago, I've always considered this the absolute best Resident Evil game ever made.
Not only does it truly embody the core formula of survival horror and puzzles, but its graphics are still excellent at conveying the desired atmosphere to this day. If not to one's liking, there's always shaders and texture mods to improve what is already an excellent experience.

The acting and writing have been greatly improved from the original on the PS1, as have the mechanics and environment. Sure, there still are nowhere near enough bathrooms in the Spencer Mansion grounds, and the mansion layout is bonkers, but the changes made are an undeniable, objective improvement over the original, particularly the "Aqua Ring" section. Those who somehow prefer the oldschool dialogue lines, cheesier than a Parmigiano Reggiano vault in Italy, can always just mod the goofy old voices back in, there's ways to cater to such inferior taste. Free country.

The controls in this PC port allow for a new control scheme that deviates from the tank controls of old, for those of us who aren't interested in participating in that traditional, perhaps antiquated and claustrophobic style that in my opinion conveys much of the tension through player disempowerment. You're not an action hero, you're a lonesome little person with no pockets and outgunned from the start.
Still, I thoroughly insist you play with a controller. Mouse and Keyboard controls are just... unbecoming of this. Games like SIGNALIS and HOLSTIN are much better examples of a well-done keyboard + mouse control scheme in this type of game.

All in all, a truly excellent example of where the genre started, where it should return to on occasion, and otherwise every element of a classic.

Man, I remember as a kid when I first played Resident Evil, seeing that first zombie, ingrained in my memory!

Fast forward, 20+ years later, here we are, decided to play through the whole franchise from start! And how does this one hold up? I'm going to be honest, when I first started to play this one, I hated it! In fact, I loathed it, it was horrible! Tank controls, camera angles, the horrible door loading, not knowing what the f*** to do and where to go... Yeah, I rage quit some time after, but something inside of me was calling me back to it... I had that itch, to give it another chance. I did in the end, and boy did I made the right call.

The good:

- I never cared for the RE lore that much, but this game made me dug deeper, and it surprised me how good  it actually is.
- The mansion. It's just amazing, huge puzzle area. 
- That zombie introduction is iconic!
- Art style, some of the back drops and camera angles are so creepy and perfect looking.
- For the most part, game is not scary, however I had 2-3 amazing and super scary moments, which I loved.
- I love the fact that there is barely any music, mind the very few exceptions.
- Once you get used to controls, it's great fun. Give it a chance newcomers.
- This might sound weird, but I just love that are not that many enemies in the game, when you consider it. Sometimes, less is more. For example, common video game logic is usually you start the game pretty easy and over time, they throw you more and more enemies until the end. However, in the last part of this game, you'll have few enemies at most. 
- Multiple different endings and modes to complete the game. 
- Story spoilers [spoiler] Lisa Trevor and her family's story is so depressing, tragic and sad... perfectly fits with the tone of the game, I love it. Everytime I replayed this game, I would read their diaries and symphatize with their tragedy. [/spoiler]

That's pretty much it, now for the bad stuff:

- Doors loading. Let me explain: When you enter any area or room, you will see doors opening animation and you walking through them. This usually last for 7-8 seconds. So what's the issue? You will back track. A LOT. You will run through areas so fast, that sometimes you will only see those God forsaken doors. I hated this with a passion, UNTIL I found a mod that removes that stupid animation! It cuts the load time from 7-8 seconds to 2 seconds. You barely notice it now and it's such a relief.
- Back tracking. In a sense that most of the time you will be running through corridors and nothing will happen. It gets boring sometimes really fast.
- Underground cave area (3/4 of the game) is the worst part. It's such a slog and borefest.
- Most of the bosses are ass. Barely a challenge. 
- Some of the puzzles are baffling and make zero sense. I had to look for guides for a decent chunk of a game. 
- There are some places where you can soft lock yourself, so beware.
- Voice acting is horrible sometimes.

That's pretty much it, maybe some minor nitpicks here and there. In the end, I ended up loving this game. For the newcomers, give it a chance. It will be rough at first, but it's soooo worth it.

Overall, Resident Evil still holds up extremely well if you can either put up with the old school game design or use a guide to help you along. At first I didnt really care for this game. Zombies are hard to kill, the controls take a while to become accustomed to, saves are limited, there's a decent amount of backtracking, and the quick camera switching is disorienting. Eventually I got frustrated with the game and gave it another try with the difficulty bumped down a bit. And after having played through it on easy mode, I can say I really enjoyed this game. Once I got the hang of it, I ended up replaying it with Chris and Jill again a few times on the regular difficulty.

This game requires you to think and manage your inventory. Not only do you need to figure out which items you need for a puzzle but you also need to choose what weapons to bring, if you want to be able to save along the way, if you want to be able to permanently kill zombies or just get them out of the way temporarily, and if you should bring extra heals. Navigating and combat requires strategy, but if you're skilled enough you can conserve items and ammo by dodging zombies.

The story was solid but the most interesting thing is the dialogue. The dialogue is definitely a sign of the times with how goofy the lines and acting are. It feels like a parody of old horror movies and I'm glad they kept that style in this remake.

Overall a great game with great replayability

[h1][b]Resident Evil 1 (HD Remaster)[/b][/h1]
[b]Genre:[/b] Survival Horror
[b]Perspective:[/b] 3rd Person (Fixed Camera-Angles)
[b]My Rating:[/b] ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[i]The iconic first main-entry of the Resident Evil series. You play either as Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield, both members of S.T.A.R.S - a group of elite law enforcement officers from the Racoon City Police Station. There have been mysterious murder-cases all over Racoon City where victims were appearantly partially eaten. Losing contact to the STARS Alpha-Team, the Bravo-Team decides to go investigate and eventually Jill and Chris find themselves in the iconic Mansion within the Racoon City forest, fighting for their survival, trying to save their comrades/friends.[/i]

[h3][b]The Positives[/b][/h3]
[list][*]Resident Evil 1 still has the beautifully pre-rendered backgrounds and fixed camera-angles complimented by gloomy lighting! Sound effects like the thunder outside and various others along with nice musical tunes here and there create a wonderfully creepy atmosphere! In many shots there is also almost just dreadful silence, the only sound you hear your footsteps. It truly makes you feel alone within that huge mansion even though you do get to meet your comrades occasionally. ...speaking of music, the tune when you are in the water-ring-area... so creepy and nice!
[*]We do have pewpews but you're supposed to use them when needed and not just shoot everything on sight as ammo is limited. Many times the smart choice is to avoid the zombies rather than to brawl with them. The game gives you plenty of ways for this as zombies can't attack you when they're on stairs (they only puke) and they are very slow so you can bait them into grabbing at you and then running past. Or just slowly lead your new rotten friend around furniture :')
[*]I love the story, many notes and extra treats to find for more lore and it has very tragic parts (Lisa for example). There are multiple endings and playing as Jill or Chris really compliments each other as you find out even more details!
[*]There are quite a few puzzles but the way the game puts them in, they aren't out of place or feel to just be there to have something to do- they are a part of the mansion. If you play through the game for the first time you might not feel like it but the game is actually quite linear as well. Once you figure it all out, there is a clear straight line of events and puzzles you can take, it's a lot of fun figuring it out.
[*]The game added modern controls if you struggle with tank controls. But let me tell you: This game feels and plays a lot better with the original intended tank controls given the fixed camera-angles. And they aren't clunky, they are quite smooth! :)
[*]I love how Jill and Chris both have their pros and cons with certain goodies the other doesn't have - it slightly changes the gameflow. And we need to talk about how great they both are written (imo). Jill isn't an onedimensional bossbabe that has no emotions, she is vulnerable but fights through and is both caring but also knows when she has to be tough. Chris isn't an alphamale that runs around huffing, he is also caring and vulnerable at times but still strong and determined. Ya know, like actual humans. You don't see that so often nowadays anymore...  
[/list]
[h3][b]The “Not So Goods”[/b][/h3]
[list][*]You wanna know what's bad? That I can't ever experience this game for the first time ever again. I generally love it all around.
[/list]

A fantastic remake of the original 1996 Resident Evil, launching exclusively on Nintendo GameCube in 2002 (Japan: March 22, NA: April 30), timed perfectly as a GameCube system-seller from Capcom legend Shinji Mikami. 

I remember the graphics were absolutely state-of-the-art for the era: real-time lighting and shadows (a GC first), hyper-detailed 3D character models with facial animations that aged like fine wine, upgraded pre-rendered backgrounds, and creepy effects like dripping blood, earning it a near-perfect 96 Metacritic score and "Game of the Year" everywhere. 

They even refined the tank controls over the PS1 original, adding quick 180-degree spins, smarter auto-aim, and smoother responsiveness while keeping that classic fixed-camera tension. Like RE2 (2019), RE3 (2020), and RE4 (2023) remakes, it overhauled RE1 with fresh content: Crimson Head zombies that resurrect fiercer, expanded puzzles/areas, the tragic Lisa Trevor subplot, new enemies, and story tweaks for deeper horror, making the Spencer Mansion feel alive (and terrifying) all over again.

Having only seen stuff from the 4th installment onward being very much action-focused with the only thing I knew about this game was the always ridiculed voice acting I thought I had to just endure the slog that was going to be the first one to get into the series.

But instead, [b]Resident Evil[/b] (1996) had become one of the most positively engrossing experiences I had with a game in quite some time.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You run around a mansion and areas surrounding it scavenging for items, some of them used to survive the undead that stalk the hallways, some to treat yourself, and others to solve puzzles and progress through the game.

The game has “tank conrolls” meaning that the up and down arrows/stick moves the character forwards and backwards relative to it’s orientation not yours, while left and right steer the character orientation.
This while stiff means that the frequent change of camera angles won’t affect your character movement in the slightest

[h1]Story[/h1]
A small police task force is sent to investigate the murder of people and sightings of strange creatures in a forested mountainous area, here a mansion lies at the center of this mystery as what remains of the team investigates the strange place.

The story unraveling the mystery naturally comes about as you discover notes, diaries, and more evidence while also running into your team again providing some more info as you find ways to get ever deeper into the mansion.

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
I was actually surprised about how well these dreaded “tank controls” worked along the fixed camera angle and less action-centric nature of this game to create a mare cinematic experience adding to the suspense of the game, with a complete lack of UI emphasizing this even more.

I don’t know if it’s nostalgia blinding me, but I felt that this was a mystery-horror with focus on mystery rather than horror, making the feel of the game eerie but on the serene side, reorganizing your inventory in a save room, moving through empty hallways while a light breeze blows outside and no enemies in sight is strangely soothing.

The control system also works because defeating enemies isn’t a twitch action reflex challenge but more of a calculated question of how many times you’ll need to go through a certain place vs how many bullets you are willing to use to clear a room as ENEMIES DO NOT respawn. 

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
One would say the voice acting, but it’s honestly charming in a cheesy and campy way, and the most AMERICAN voice acting possible, probably not to please westerners but Japanese players who wanted that American movie experience in videogame format back then.

The fixed camera angles while cool have the bad side-effect of “binding” you to a lot of stuff, if a baddie is right in front of your face you won’t see it unless you get an angle that lets you see it (however often you can hear their steps which improves the experience considerably).

The doors are infamous for how long they take to open and close but aren’t actually that bad, having the game restart on you because you took a bite too many or trudging all around the mansion because you forgot an item however is what slightly lessens the game’s enjoyment for me.

The prototypical survival horror game with HD graphics and updated controls.

I wasn't interested in playing the Resident Evil series when it came out on PlayStation decades ago because I was never a fan of that console's graphics and tank controls. But when the HD remakes started coming out over the last decade, I decided to give them a try. I'm not a fan of the survival horror genre because I never want to get stuck mid-game where I can't progress, but the graphics, controls, and internet guides (to help prevent you from having to restart) made it worth playing again.

I played through this game several years ago and figured I would never 100% the achievements because of how many times you'd have to play it (and my first run through was well over 10 hours). But, after the remakes of 2, 3, and 4 came out (with 3R's brevity inspiring me to run through it for 100% achievements only to go back to 2R and buy 4R to 100% those), I went back to 0, 100%ed that, and then felt the urge to finish the 5-part OG completionist by reinstalling this game. It's a lot of fun, though the achievements are nerve-racking.


The Positives
-With much better graphics and controls than the PlayStation but the same great survival horror and fun unlocks as the original, I enjoyed this game. The pickups are much more accurate than 0, and the original story and diverse bosses are interesting.

-Capcom really mastered the "feels impossible, but then you memorize the game and you can speedrun it and beat enemies that used to kill you in seconds" game structure. I still can't believe I play its games over like 15 hours the first playthrough and then hit 2h15m by the end.

-The story is fun. They do a great job of combining FMV, in-game cutscenes, and document pickups to build the world you're in. The intrigue it builds while it unfolds is suspenseful, and you always like learning the next piece of lore about the world.

-I appreciate the quality-of-life features they added like auto-aim and the linked item boxes. They added a mode that eliminated those, but all that does is add to the time-consuming, annoying aspects of the game and so they made the right decision to include those by default.


The Negatives
-You have to beat the game quite a few times to get all of the achievements. Not an issue with the game at all; just something to keep in mind if you are a completionist that you'll have to play it like 5-6 times (twice as Jill and twice as Chris for the costumes, a no-save run, a knife-only run, and real survivor and invisible enemy modes—you can combine some runs, but not many).

-Some actions are still clunky. Item pickup was much easier than 0, and I only have 1-2 issues. Same with the camera angle changes, which occasionally have you running back the way you came by accident. I was amazed at how well I could eventually dodge enemies, but there are some positioned where dodging them by running right past is near-impossible and, with the knife-only run, you're getting bitten a bunch of times with the few enemies you actually have to defeat (it's amazing how the basic zombie is one of the most dangerous enemies in the game because of how much it can take out of your health if your zig-zag dodge misses).

-Difficulty varies greatly. Some enemies are easy, others are hard, some are easy or hard based on luck. On the knife-only run, your toughest enemies will be the dog with the collar, the crimson head boss, and Plant 42. Strangely, the Tyrant was the easiest enemy I fought in the Very Easy knife-only run. However, on the invisible enemy mode, the Tyrant killed me twice because I couldn't see it (though I was only using the grenade launcher because I didn't have the magnum). Hunters and Lisa Trevor can insta-kill you, so you have to be very careful on those parts of the no-save run. Do the bad ending for challenge modes to save yourself a boss (trying to hit an invisible second Tyrant with a rocket launcher is insane). And the sharks and little snakes can hit you 0-2 times when you run past, causing damage and poison, respectively based on luck.


I can't believe how much graphics and controls can help me like a game more. I was never a fan of the PS1 era (I liked 8-bit, 16-bit, and 64-bit games better), but with the enhancements of these remakes, I really enjoy(ed) the series. I still don't like the survival horror genre in general, and I have to play these games on weekends when I have time and get nervous about mistakes, ammo, dying, and saving when playing...but when I memorize the route and do it well, it feels very rewarding.

If you like the genre, this is one of the games that defined it. If you like the series, you'll like this one, which started it all. The only things you might not like are the controls and camera angles, the low inventory, ammo, and saving, and maybe how its difficulty is inverted (hard at first and gets easier at the end). But it's a classic, so I recommend trying it. I hear people want to see an RE2/3/4-like modernization of the OG, but I don't see why. This version is just fine—and I say that having liked the modernized 2/3/4 versions more than their PS1 originals. It would be interesting, but it's not necessary. This classic is great—just feel free to start on a low difficulty if the inventory/ammo/health/save limitations will cause you too much anxiety. Learn the game and then you can play it on higher difficulties later when you know what you need to do so you won't run out of anything mid-game.

[h1] Look How They Used to Look and Tell Me This Isn’t Better [/h1]

Back in 2002 my Dreamcast was already buried, and twelve‑year‑old me was drowning in Resident Evil fever after Code Veronica—so desperate I was emailing some Spanish walkthrough site just to kill the Tyrant on that damn plane.

That’s when Chris Redfield became my guy—not Leon with his shampoo‑model hair and smug quips, but the action hero who bleeds, stumbles, and still gets it done. The one you [b] trust [/b]. 

All while watching Jill’s origin story after playing her as some kind of Sarah Connor in RE3.

No GameCube for me, just Club Nintendo magazines dangling this mythical RE1 remake while classmates cried about how “unfair” it was. Fast‑forward to 2025, nostalgia pile‑drives me back into the Spencer Mansion with RE0 bundled in, reminding me why I once made clay monsters and embarrassing fanfics—and shockingly, it still slaps, even if the difficulty curve feels like a flatline.

Play one old‑school Resident Evil and you’ve basically got the survival‑horror Bible: zombies soak up bullets like they’re on payroll, so you dodge, live in the map, and backtrack like a lunatic. My way of making it fun? Start on easy, learn the dance, then crank it up for unlockables and speed‑run glory. I went in sweating, thinking this would be the hardest RE1 ever, and five minutes later I’m calm as a monk—tank controls, fixed cameras, eerie hum—it’s horror yoga with teeth even when you crank it up to hard mode.

The mansion’s emptier than I remember, but Crimson Heads are evil genius: burn them, plan routes, play chess instead of wasting ammo. The remaster? Gorgeous, definitive. And the nostalgia payoff—unlocking Chris’ Code Veronica outfit—wasn’t fan service, it was my full‑circle victory lap, controller in the air, personal trophy earned.

All base character models? Peak design on the S.T.A.R.S. team. Barry, Jill, Rebecca—perfection.

I liked that they even included some RE5 skins from the start! But one gripe for the future: stop turning Chris into a square‑jawed trauma billboard. He’s supposed to be grounded grit with big‑bro energy (think Bruce Willis in The Last Boy Scout), not a walking testosterone factory with night terrors. Somehow the rookie cop handled his trauma better. Explain that one.

This game is relaxing, rewarding, and aged like forbidden wine in a dusty cellar. Still worth every second. But beware—the real final boss lives in the forums. That’s where you survive the horror of bad grammar and the actual monsters: gatekeepers who chant “tank controls” like a curse and flatten newcomers for sport. Avoid them like a lit Crimson Head. Old or new, Resident Evil 1 is eternal. 

And until it’s remade [b]again[/b] with mounted camera, this is still the ultimate mansion crawl.

So why should i play them again with different guns, if i needed to push myself through the tedium of finishing them in the first place. 

That's what makes RE1 so special. Here, this progression past the first run doesn't only make sense. It excels in pushing you to go in again and again. Guns with unlimited ammo make inventory management quicker, zombies loaded with grenades force you to think on your toes, each new modifier you unlock serves to heighten the speed of playthroughs. The challenges the game poses to unlock the objectively best equipment, like the unlimited rocket launcher, seem manic while you are stuck on your first playthrough. Finish a run in under 3 hours. Only use your knife. Never save. And at the very end play with invisible enemies? How do you even manage to do that? I'm shocked there isn't an achievement for finishing the entire game with your eyes closed, or playing it with a steering wheel. 

But after closing the book on a hard run in under 5 hours, I SEE THE LIGHT. Suddenly, the survival horror turned into a feverish arcade about highscores and playtimes. The addiction speaks for itself, when a whole third of players who finished the game on both the A and B sides completed ALL of the further challenges.

Having never played the original Resident Evil, this HD remaster was my first true encounter with the game that started it all and it didn’t disappoint. Even without the nostalgia factor, it manages to deliver a tense, atmospheric experience that gives a clear sense of how revolutionary the original must have been.

This remaster is visually appealing, maintaining the eerie mood and claustrophobic tension of the mansion while improving lighting, textures, and animations. As with most Resident Evil games, the puzzles are tricky sometimes even frustrating but that’s part of the charm and sense of accomplishment when you finally figure them out.

The map design is brilliant, constantly evolving as you unlock new areas and shortcuts through exploration. This creates a satisfying loop of progress and discovery, though it also introduces new enemies to keep you on edge. The boss fights are challenging and well-balanced, demanding both resource management and quick reflexes. However, I have to admit that two particular enemies really tested my patience the Hunters and the Crimson Head zombies (especially when I forgot to burn a corpse and it came back stronger).

The limited inventory space and restricted save system add a layer of tension that’s both thrilling and occasionally frustrating. There were moments when I found myself debating whether to carry a healing item or a crucial key, knowing I might not have enough space or enough ink ribbons to save.

This was my first experience with the classic survival-horror formula, as my introduction to the franchise was Resident Evil 4 on the PS2. While Resident Evil 1 HD feels slower and more methodical, it offers a different kind of satisfaction one built on atmosphere, fear, and smart resource management rather than pure action.

Overall, Resident Evil 1 HD is a strong remaster that respects its roots while remaining accessible to newcomers. It may feel dated in some mechanics, but its design, tension, and atmosphere hold up remarkably well. It’s not a perfect game, but it’s an unforgettable one a true survival-horror experience that every fan of the genre should play at least once.

[h2] Classic Resident Evil horror. [/h2]
The story of the original from 1996 got overhauled and expanded. No other title in the series has this much atmosphere.

Getting into the game might take some time since it doesn't hold your hand like modern games. There's a lot of trial and error if you don't pay close attention. 
Inventory management is key since you can't drop or replace items unless you use an item box. Until you find your first save room with one, you'll have to carefully decide which items to pick up and which to leave for later. 
Saving regularly is also important: there are [b][u] NO checkpoints [/u][/b] and [b][u] NO autosaves [/u][/b]. This means if you haven't saved in a while, all progress since your last save will be lost. 
However, this makes progress feel all the more rewarding.

There’s a good variety of enemies, with the well-known zombie having received a nice twist that keeps it scary even later in the game. 
The difficulty curve introduced by new enemy types is pretty gradual.

Controls can be challenging, as the game was originally made in 2002 with tank controls and fixed camera angles in mind. It's best played with a controller using the D-pad for movement. 
Other control schemes work, but the character may change direction when switching between camera angles.
Using weapons - especially the knife - requires some good positioning, since attacking is fairly slow in this game.

The story is quite cheesy, which gives the game a unique charm. While there are some plot holes, they'll only become apparent after finishing the game a few times.

[b] Personally, it's one of my favorites in the Resident Evil series. [/b]

The fixed camera, saving mechanic, and inventory management can all be somewhat annoying if you're not used to it but it's all worth it for the nostalgia of a game like this. Don't be afraid to look at a guide online since some of the puzzles aren't the most intuitive. Playing as Jill first and then as Chris was great advice before upping the difficulty (essentially the same main story but small differences). I'll probably come back to this game many more times in the future.

I'll start this off with saying no I don't hate this game in a way most negative reviews may lead off with.  I've played or at least tried out every Resident Evil game on steam.  Resident Evil one was one of my final projects to hop into and tackle.  Going in I was already aware it would NOT be played like the remakes or even RE4 2005.  To an extent, I actually enjoy the old mechanics of this game.  However, I feel it's incredibly punishing going in with a blind perspective other than knowing it'll be an older game.  You'll constantly get blamed for this in a RE1 community who praise this game top to bottom, for even mentioning this.  An issue me and most likely many others faced early into the game is not having a storage box within the first save room.  After grabbing an ink ribbon [Even returning the plate on the fireplace back to it's original spot for space.]  It is all TOO easy to accidentally soft lock yourself without any way to properly dispose of these items.  You're offered a statue on the top floor which hands you a blue diamond, now with ammo, a gun, knife, ink ribbon, the diamond, a herb, etc.  You accidentally soft lock yourself within the first 20 minutes of the game rendering your first or second run useless needing to start over if you weren't aware of it.

I can agree, this doesn't make this game UNPLAYABLE for that reason but it certainly isn't a very kind introduction for someone trying to feel good about this game.  As for other issues people leave negative for this game I didn't have any issues with.  Examples being: Limited saves, Standing in place whilst aiming [Same in RE5], and combat in general after some practice.  However, the camera angles are probably one of the most irritating experiences and you feel punished just trying to see the game to the end.  Yes I've heard it all with "That's how it makes it scary!  It's the horror experience!"  I feel even without the crappy camera angles you'd feel tension with just how limited resources can be and really changes our perspective of how alone you truly are in this game which I enjoyed.

I linger on the camera angles because it feels as if you're tormented constantly.  You get into chase scenes with a giant rock and you try to turn the corner consider yourself dead because you just walked right back into the rock by mistake.  [I didn't actually die to this in particular but I can already picture many did if they didn't try their damned hardest to work with the angles ahead of time.]  Enemies are often out of frame and you need to prepare yourself down a hallway ahead of time to even accurately or properly get a shot in the dark.  

Some enemies are placed in such a way where if you first walk into a new room they're behind a wall your camera angle doesn't even reveal to you and then once again you find yourself walking right into it and wasting supplies due to a mechanic out of your control.  Does it make it impossible and am I to quit because of this obstacle? No, but again anyone who is trying to play for the story of the game would probably be put off by this.  My only other actual complaint on this game is the overly tedious backtracking that somehow is the worst I've seen in all RE games.

I understand the whole concept of Resident Evil from day one is the puzzle backtracking which can be tedious at times but nothing to drive you insane.  Resident Evil one however turns the dial up on this in a way that mostly just has to do with both the camera angles and the map itself of the mansion tormenting you as a slap in the face.  I never usually use maps once but in this game I 100% had to because of how confusing it was with fixed angles making doors sometimes hardly visible you might miss it.  Therefore this leads you on a journey constantly realizing you missed things or the common "That's a door and not just a wall?"  

That being the least of my issue, the real thing that made it so tedious was how the mansion will often times purposely block off working doors so they're an only one way exit.  If I wanted to put something in storage after coming back from the courtyard, I can enter through the door next to the Spencer Crest door but afterward I cannot re-enter that door.  It purposely makes me have to run all the way back around for absolutely no reason other than being irritating.  I can't logically think of how that would make "The game scarier or make you think on your resources" kind of mentality.

All of these small 2 issues really made this game end up feeling like more of a chore rather than an experience that should've been a fun challenge to crack.  I've played Resident Evil 0 before re-tackling one again for the third time.  Somehow even Resident Evil 0 with the same time of mechanics made it more enjoyable just on the fact that you can drop items and return to them with proper planning.  Call this funny, but I didn't quite like but didn't hate Resident Evil 1.  

I feel people who have valid reactions to the issues I listed here are often swept under the rug by people who praise this game for everything it stands for or just the fact "It's a classic how dare you."  I'll say for those kinds of people, I agree in a way.  It's indeed a great remaster to it's original.  I think the graphics and art style are amazing and overall if not for those issues I listed I would've probably liked playing this game more.  In a way I felt proud after being able to finally progress and get passed everything that stopped me before from playing it.

However, not everyone is like me. If someone with 0 prior Resident Evil knowledge were to pick this up because they wanted to play it in order, they'd probably have a bad introduction to the series which is a shame.  I'll admit it was an interesting experience to work with the odd game play but honestly I wouldn't find this to be something I'd rave to recommend anyone anytime soon.  If I had to give an ACTUAL rating rather than just "Recommended or Negative."  I'd give this game a 8/10.  This is a game definitely for fans of the franchise as a whole, but not for newer players to the games.  If you're new to Resident Evil, I suggest you do what I did and tackle this one later if you feel up for it.  Even play RE0 first, somehow that feels a little more tolerable.  I respect anyone who does love this title, but honestly it wasn't my favorite out of the series and that's fine I got the game done and this is just my honest review after giving it a proper run.

I wanna preface this review with 2 things that need to be addressed.

1. I understand why this game is seen as good or even great by many players over the years. It originated one of the most successful gaming IPs of all time, and its atmosphere is undeniably great.

2. This is not a 33 minute review despite the caption. I played several hours during an internet outage, and that time didn't get recorded.

Now the actual review. While, as I already said, I understand the positive reactions to this game, I'm gonna offer a point of view of a person that has no pre-existing relationship with Resident Evil before playing it and no nostalgic feelings for old school jank mechanics from 90s gaming, so I don't have any rose tinted glasses to make my experience better with this game. As a player that tried out this game in 2025, I didn't have fun in it at all, because it is simply not up to the standards set out by hundreds of better games that released after it. I'm sure it was great in the PS1 era, but it isn't now.

When you take the nostalgia filter away, it is basically a game about finding objects in different shapes and then finding a hole that has the same shape as the object you found, while managing a very limited inventory that doesn't let you hold a lot of shapes at once. So, for example, if you have a square key and a diamond emblem, but to progress you need a triangle key and a heart emblem, there is a big chance you're gonna have to run several laps around the mansion just to swap the 2 items from your inventory that you have to the 2 items that you need. It's not hard to find them. If you have an ok memory or a piece of paper, it's not even a bit difficult. And this is basically the whole puzzle and thinking part of this game.

Now everything else. While doing these laps around the mansion to find shapes and shape-shaped holes, you're gonna be controlling an elite S.T.A.R.S. member, which is the in-universe equivalent to a spec ops operator. The best the military can offer, designated only for the most dangerous missions. So obviously your character has physical, survival, and marksmanship skills of a half-baked potato. They will refuse to aim at the head of a barely moving enemy and their first experience with using a knife was apparently 3 minutes before they got dropped into the mansion full of undead.

Your enemies on the other hand will be zombies that are sometimes killable, sometimes not, sometimes on a specific route never changing it, and sometimes just appearing out of nowhere in a previously empty room. Which one is which? Nobody knows. And the game will not tell you how any of its mechanics work, so have fun using your very limited save attempts to figure it out over several hours, go watch a guide and spoil everything for yourself, or just endlessly avoid the same enemies in the same spots, looping them around furniture while you look for shape no. 34 that you need to insert into hole no. 23.

Overall, the game has a lot of arcade practices that found their way into the early PC and console gaming era, before they were phased out as they were meant to waste time and get more coins out of players. Like not telling the player about the rules and mechanics to encourage trial and error gameplay with a lot of time repeating the same things before you can get back to the spot you were in, or changing the established rules mid playthrough without warning to catch the player off guard and send them to a previous save spot that might be very far away. Even the beloved backtracking around the whole mansion and limited inventory are just artificial ways to milk playtime.

At this point it is obvious that I did not enjoy this game, but I wanna point out one more thing. I did not complain about anything that is related to the technological limitations of 1996 when the OG released. The camera angles to save memory, the jank aiming system or anything controls related. I understand that it's an old game and it has its limitations. However, the things I listed here were bad even in 1996. Players just didn't know better back then and today they get nostalgic over something that in a new game would be called out immediately.

So to end this review, if you're starting your journey with Resident Evil in 2025, then just google this game's entire 3 paragraphs of story and move on to the actual remakes that are way better.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 452:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆☆☆☆☆ (4/10)

Hmm. I can easily see how groundbreaking [i] Resident Evil[/i] was when it first released. But to me, a modern gamer, it doesn't quite hold up, especially with Capcom releasing incredible RE remakes and new games so recently. The atmosphere is still incredible, the setting beautiful, the tight resource management—it’s all very old-school horror. But that’s also the issue: it’s too old-school.

🔑[b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Classic survival horror atmosphere. It's honestly amusing how this game unnerved me, even when there's no jump scares, and the zombies are slow af. The pacing is slow, which works well. You're not given any answers as you're forced to move from one room to another. Hallways are narrow and claustrophobic; lighting is moody.

[*] Atmospheric sound design. Eerie silence, echoing footsteps pattering on carpet, and zombie moans build real dread. Honestly, it was actually sort of relaxing, running around in the beginning safe zone.

[*] Beautiful setting. The Spencer Mansion is practically a character itself: grand, ornate, decaying, and filled with unsettling secrets behind every door.

[*]Replay value. There's different playable characters (Jill and Chris), unlockable modes, and speedrun potential.
[/list]

🪬 [b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Absolute mind-numbing door opening loading screens. I would have preferred a black screen instead, honestly.

[*] Voice acting and dialogue are dated. I mean, it's not bad, per se, but it kinda has that “B-movie camp” energy (aka "Jill sandwich).

[*] “Oldschool” puzzles are unfortunately just very tedious and sometimes borderline impossible key hunts. I found it difficult to see what was interactable and what was part of the setting. 🤷‍♀️

[*] Limited saves. Saving is tied to an ink ribbon that you come across in the mansion. Since bag space is extremely limited, it's enormously cumbersome that your ability to save the game takes up a spot, along with juggling a ton of random crap in your inventory. I don't usually mind it, but I found it frustrating to have to redo sections because I couldn't go back to the typewriter after having to backtrack BECAUSE I couldn't pick up a key item I needed because of that.

[*] Fixed cameras. Oh boy. Yeah, it's a deliberate design choice. Sure, it adds tension and surprise. Is a zombie literally just around the corner or not? But many times, I found myself accidentally turning the wrong direction back and forth. Having this issue when attempting to run for my life was super annoying.

[*] Combat. I found myself fighting the aiming system. The fact that you can't move while aiming alone feels totally wrong to me. Once your gun is up, you can "aim" at enemies that may be moving around you or even off-screen. There's very little in the way of feedback as to if your shots are even hitting the target sometimes. 
[/list]

If you asked me to define "survival horror" as pure as I could, I would say Resident Evil 1 "Remastered". This game gets basically everything right for survival horror, it is almost perfect, however, the Resident Evil franchise after re1 embedded a lot more action into their games. And in my opinion, it is way more fun when you have the perfect mix/balance of survival horror and action, giving you that huge satisfaction of game progression with a slightly better gun or simply just ammo for a more powerful gun. However, that doesn't take away from this game at all, it is, in my opinion, a perfect survival horror game, even if its not my favourite RE game, or the one I enjoy the most. 

spoilers beyond:

You may notice I put "remastered" in quotations - thats because this game is not a remaster, even if it says it is. Yes, they improved the graphics (pre-rendered backgrounds), character models, voice acting, etc just like a remaster does. However, they added stuff that wasn't in the original. There are more rooms than in the original games, there's literally a whole new enemy type in this game that forces you to make so many extra decisions, and also a new boss fight. The new enemy type is the crimson head, making you decide which enemies you should kill, leave or burn. Also these enemies are terrifying when you see it running towards you. Genius. The new boss of course is Lisa Trevor, which is such an iconic enemy in the RE series now, and has some dark lore behind her. She is also absolutely terrifying and packs one hell of a punch.

I do also want to mention the endings. There is no canon ending. Either Jill is locked up all game or Chris is locked up all game, and it cant be either. Chris has to meet rebecca, but Jill has to be there for Barry, as both of these characters show up at least once either in another canon game or movie. Although this review is about RE1, I would like to share a theory that RE2 Remake also has no canon "scenario order", due to the scenarios being a bit weird (Mr X dying in one, but still showing in the other or stuff done from the other character not seen in the current scenario and more). The original RE2 executed scenarios perfectly, which I wish they did in the remake, but anyways, I like to believe that maybe RE2 doesn't really have a canon scenario order, just like how RE1 doesn't.
Quickly I would like to maybe "criticise" that they don't have door skips in this version (2015 HD version). Just a tad annoying, and I got a bit tired of it towards the end of my 100% journey. It would've been possible here, and I nearly downloaded a mod for it. That's all. 

One thing I forgot to add is I really love the opening scene with Jill watching Joseph get mauled apart by dogs. The way she stands there frozen, repeatedly pulling the trigger although the gun is empty is genius. I think it really highlights the start of her trauma/PTSD that we get a look at in RE3.

I don't feel I have much else to say about this game, it is the first Resident Evil in its best form, and to be honest, this game is not for everyone. Some people are looking for more action, a modern control format and a classic first person or over-the-shoulder view, which is completely fine, although I'd urge everyone to at least give this game a chance. A remake of this game, I am actually more than open to. Will they mess it up and try to appeal to modern audiences? maybe. But seeing the mansion with a modern graphics overhall, exploring the tight narrow hallways in an over-the-shoulder or potentially first person view (if optional) and a modern control scheme would be absolutely awesome. They are probably bound to mix in some more action if they remade this, due to money, but I can cope with that as long as its not RE6. 

Also, I would love to see more of Barry in future games (I know he's in rev2) and more of Rebecca. Can't believe Barry was one of the first to see the T-Virus, the start of bio-weapons and RE, and we only see him once more, in a revelations game. Although to be fair, he was awesome in that game.
