I'd played the original PS1 entries before, and I've beaten RE4 (the original) and RE5. But I never actually beat those PS1 originals.
Then I got this game on a bundle pack along with most of the others a while back, and figured it was as good of an excuse as any to actually give the first entry a proper shot.
...And then I ended up 100%ing it over 8 playthroughs.

It was just THAT good.


Okay so, context for those not in the loop. Original RE1, PS1 game, 1996. The start of survival horror, with the bad dialogue, ugly visuals and clunky controls and inventory management we all know and love.
Then in 2002, once the Gamecube's already come around, they release this game for that, as a full remake of that original game.

But it's not a remake in the same way as, say, the current RE2-4 remakes are. This one is as faithful as faithful can be in terms of gameplay and structure, keeping the same fixed camera perspective gameplay and the same inventory management, while upgrading basically EVERYTHING.

The level design, the mansion, is "the same", nothing's really missing, but it's also got a TON of new additions on top. New routes, new shortcuts, a couple new little areas and things to do to expand on the original even more and make navigation and backtracking more comfortable with the added routes and options.


And honestly?
Going fixed camera is probably one of the best choices they could've made here.
This game is [b]GORGEOUS[/b]. Like [i]"how the hell was this running on Gamecube"[/i] gorgeous. This looks like a PS3 game, especially with the unlocked resolution and widescreen that this PC port added on top.

You know how they did that?
All the backgrounds are still 2D. Prerendered. Sorta like what they did back on PS1. Meaning they could focus on putting absolutely all of the heavy work and detail into the really detailed character models which there's only a couple of on screen at any given time.
And then you combine that with this RIDICULOUSLY smartly put together lighting system, that dynamically casts shadows to and from the character models, that somehow also PERFECTLY LAYER OVER THE PRERENDERED BACKGROUNDS.
Like you'll have moonlight coming in through a window, have your character walk past it, and see their shadow perfectly cast onto the wall behind them along the way. It's [i]insanely[/i] well made, and I can't even begin to imagine the amount of meticulous work that must've gone into putting it together this way, especially back in 2002.



Anyway, gushing about the visuals aside, lemme talk about the actual [b]gameplay[/b] real quick.
This version gives you two options for control schemes: [i]"classic"[/i] and [i]"modern"[/i].

Classic leaves everything as-is, from the PS1 original; tank controls, up goes forward, left and right slowly turn you like a tank, down walks backwards. You can play that way if you want!

But Modern really gives you the best of both worlds here. The left stick just lets you freely move around, which is extremely quick, responsive and snappy, and makes it a lot more feasible to maneuver around monsters and even juke them out if you're good enough.
And you'd think [i]"oh well, clearly that's going to break when the fixed camera cuts to a different angle"[/i]. And you'd be right, kind of!
But that's why you still have the d-pad on hand. Because Modern mode [i]keeps the tank controls on the d-pad[/i].
Essentially, this means you can switch back and forth pretty much instantly, without going into any menus! Just lift your fat thumb off the left stick and move it over to the dpad and voila, you can now run forward uninterrupted without worrying about any of the camera angles. It's [i]great[/i].
You even get a quick 180 turn move bound to flicking the right stick, which is perfect since you have no camera control so it wouldn't get any use outside of that.

But yeah, it's a survival horror game. THE survival horror game, just updated to feel less dated. You run along the mansion, collecting items, solving puzzles, and managing your limited resources and inventory to try and make sure you don't run out of ammunition or tools to ensure your survival. To make sure you don't make things harder for yourself later on.
It's super fun! The level design's great, and although the very beginning can be a bit rough if you're not used to the genre, it really picks up from basically the moment you get the first key and start finding more weapons and items to help you.


The story's decent too! It's not like, Shakespearean or whatever, but it's a gigantic improvement from the infamous PS1 cutscenes. It's still got just the right amount of cheese, just with competent voice acting and writing that doesn't make you want to tear your ears off.


Anyway, in terms of content, your first playthrough will probably run you somewhere in the ballpark of 8-10 hours, depending on how much you know what you're doing. And after that you can unlock a bunch of costumes and (if you beat the speedrun times) even special weapons for NG+.
There's also extra difficulties and challenge modes that unlock after your first clear, and there's a TON of achievements to give you more stuff to do.
That's where my playtime comes from; again, I 100%ed the game over 8 playthroughs. And by the end of it I had it down to a science and could beat the game in one sitting in under 3 hours without really trying. There's a moment where it just "clicks" and you effortlessly start going through the game without breaking a sweat, completing the various challenges they offer.

Admittedly [spoiler]Invisible Enemy[/spoiler] mode is kind of a complete dickmove, and [spoiler]Real Survival[/spoiler] mode can be very annoying to inventory manage given the rules it runs off of, but honestly once you're used to the game it kind of becomes a FUN sort of dickishness. It's an extra challenge on top of a really really solid base, and it works alright if you're trying to get more out of the game.
IDK if I'd prefer every game has this many ballbusting sidemodes, I'd rather they condense it into less playthroughs, but it was still fun overall!


[b]Anyway yeah, I really, REALLY recommend this game. It's absolutely GREAT.[/b]

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a masterclass in survival horror, taking one of the most iconic games in gaming history and polishing it to near perfection. From the first step into the eerie Spencer Mansion, the tension is palpable. Every creaking floorboard, flickering light, and distant moan creates an atmosphere of dread that keeps you on edge throughout the game.

The remaster shines in both visuals and gameplay. The updated HD graphics bring the mansion to life, enhancing the atmosphere without losing the charm of the original design. Character models are sharper, environments are more detailed, and lighting effects heighten the suspense. At the same time, the controls and camera have been modernized to feel smoother and more responsive, making exploration and combat more intuitive without compromising the classic feel.

What truly sets this version apart is how it balances nostalgia with quality-of-life improvements. Inventory management, aiming, and puzzles have been refined while keeping the challenge and tension intact. The audio is outstanding, with haunting sound design and chilling music that makes every corner of the mansion feel alive—and dangerous.

The story, full of intrigue and horror, remains as compelling as ever. Encountering the terrifyingly relentless enemies, discovering hidden secrets, and piecing together the events of the mansion makes for a deeply satisfying experience. Resident Evil HD Remaster isn’t just a faithful recreation—it’s an elevated experience that honors the original while making it accessible and thrilling for modern audiences.

For fans of survival horror, or anyone curious about the roots of the genre, this remaster is a must-play. It’s tense, terrifying, and endlessly rewarding—proof that classic horror never goes out of style.

Resident Evil 1 Remake — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… the *Spencer Mansion*. Where it all began.

The 2002 remake of *Resident Evil* is not merely a recreation—it is a resurrection. A refined specimen born from the flawed DNA of its 1996 predecessor. A second chance at perfection… though, as always, humanity falls just short.

From the first moment one steps into that grand, decaying hall, the atmosphere is palpable. Every flicker of candlelight, every echoing footstep… the mansion itself *breathes.* It is not just a setting—it is a living organism, consuming those foolish enough to enter. A perfect testing ground for Umbrella’s research.

Graphically, the remake is exquisite. The lighting and texture work conjure a realism that borders on oppressive. You can almost smell the mildew, the rot… the fear. Even I Albert Wesker must commend such attention to detail—it’s the kind of precision I admire in both science and slaughter.

The gameplay retains its deliberate pace—some call it “tank-like.” I call it discipline. Every encounter demands foresight, every bullet carries consequence. It teaches players restraint, a lesson most of humanity refuses to learn.

And then there are the *Crimson Heads*. An elegant evolution. The dead returning with newfound aggression—a reminder that adaptation always favors the ruthless. Beautiful creatures, really.

Of course, my role within this narrative remains… understated. The calm within the chaos. The architect watching his experiment unfold. It’s almost touching, watching the S.T.A.R.S. members stumble about in the dark, unaware that their commander is already ten steps ahead.

The remake’s sound design, too, is superb. The groan of distant doors, the whisper of rain against the windows, the heartbeat beneath the silence—it all conspires to keep the player uneasy. Fear, after all, is the most reliable motivator.

In the end, this remake transcends nostalgia. It is rebirth through refinement—a mirror of evolution itself. Not perfect… but close.

My verdict:
A masterful reconstruction of terror.

There is some level of replay-value with the fact you can play as two different characters with loosely different events that unfold for each other's story despite both stories taking place in the exact same area.

Some puzzles are somewhat confusing and it is not always clear what you may need to do next, that is where exploration comes into play, though some of it feels like padding. You explore a mansion mainly and a view other smaller areas though there is a lot of backtracking through the entire game which makes the game-time feel inflated by "loading screens" and constant moving back and fourth between places you've already been.

This game requires some level of patience in both just navigating the areas and figuring out the puzzles. The enemy variety is fine; zombies, zombies that come back to life, frog-like mutants, zombie dogs, evil sentient plant, sharks, spiders, snakes, and insects. Most function exactly the same though outside of their speed and attack range though it's mostly just don't get near them and you're fine.

I had more fun on subsequent runs rather than my first which was somewhat frustrating and confusing. But once you understand the layout of the world it is fun to run through and can be somewhat of a challenge. The achievements are fine, but most of them are just "clear game with X criteria met", which makes it less of a fun challenge and more of a cycle of doing the same thing just slightly differently. If these criteria were more distinct beyond "help X character", or "leave X character", and actually affected the way the rest of the game plays out in a somewhat major way, it could be significantly more fun to "grind" the achievements.

You do unlock new things when you finish your first two playthroughs of the game those things being costumes, game modifiers, two new difficulties, sometimes weapons. You do not unlock all of these at once though, which is completely fine and allows for more content to be seen periodically. 

However, the same issue with the achievements applies to the general unlocked content too, there isn't enough distinctive features within these unlocks and mostly provide cosmetic changes. You won't be gawking at the amount of content there is left after the first playthrough, but will instead be saying "oh nice".

As someone who loves to get the most out of their games, replay-value is an important feature to me, though I also understand that is not the intention of this game's existence and respect that.

Overall 7/10. Recommended if you enjoy puzzle and exploration mixed with loose sci-fi and horror elements, but if you are looking for a high octane, high suspense, and a high fear factor experience; then this is not going to suffice that craving. 

Definitely not a game for everyone, but I would still recommend you give it a shot if you just enjoy puzzle, exploration, or horror.

[h1]The Spencer Mansion: Where It All Began[/h1]

[i]The game that defined the survival-horror genre is back! Check out the remastered HD version of Resident Evil.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Set in July 1998, the game follows the S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team—Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield—as they investigate a series of bizarre murders in the outskirts of Raccoon City. Their investigation leads them to the eerie Spencer Mansion, where they encounter terrifying creatures and uncover the sinister Umbrella Corporation's experiments.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil HD Remaster is a high-definition re-release of the 2002 GameCube remake of the original 1996 Resident Evil. Resident Evil is a survival horror game. The character is controlled from a third-person perspective using fixed camera angles and tank controls.

To progress, you explore a mansion and its surroundings, avoiding, outsmarting, or defeating monsters. You can open doors, push objects, climb obstacles, and collect items, which are stored in a limited inventory and can be used, examined, or combined to solve puzzles and access new areas.

While firearms are available, Resident Evil emphasizes evasion due to limited ammo. Health decreases when attacked, but can be restored with herbs, which can also be combined for stronger effects. Some monsters can poison you, gradually draining health until cured with serum or special herbs.

You can play as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, each with strengths and weaknesses: Chris deals and takes more damage, while Jill can carry more items and use a lock pick. Both can equip defensive weapons—like a dagger, taser (Jill), or stun grenade (Chris)—usable only when grabbed by a monster.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
Resident Evil features a variety of enemies, from classic zombies to terrifying mutated creatures. Zombies are slow but deadly in groups, and those not beheaded or burned can revive as faster, stronger Crimson Heads. Zombie dogs are fast and agile, often attacking in packs, while Hunters are lethal, reptilian humanoids capable of long leaps and heavy damage. Spiders can ambush you by crawling on walls and ceilings. These are just a few examples of all the threats. The game also includes several bosses, which I won’t spoil.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
Most of the game takes place in the Spencer Mansion, a sprawling Gothic estate filled with hidden passages, locked doors, secret rooms, grand halls, and ornate chambers—many of which require solving intricate puzzles. Narrow hallways create tension during zombie encounters. Underground labs expand the environment, adding layers of exploration and danger. Some areas outside the mansion, such as courtyards or gardens, provide brief reprieves from the claustrophobic interiors but often hide enemies and traps. Enemies are strategically placed to create suspense, ambushes, and memorable scares.

The game features an automap to help you navigate the different areas of the game. Additionally, you can find and pick up maps of certain sections to reveal unexplored areas.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
Enjoy remastered textures and improved lighting that bring the haunting mansion to life. Witness smoother character movements and more detailed environments. Switch between the original 4:3 and a new 16:9 widescreen mode to suit your preference. Each room has a distinct look, often themed (libraries, laboratories, dining halls) with intricate details that make the mansion feel lived-in yet sinister. Dim lighting, flickering lights, and shadows create suspense, making the environment feel alive and threatening.

Immerse yourself in the atmospheric audio with 5.1 surround sound support. Environmental sounds—creaking floors, distant growls from monsters, and dripping water—create tension and make the mansion feel alive and haunting. Spiders' presence within a room can be known to you if you listen out for their low-bass thumping noise as they scurry around. Crimson Heads announce themselves with fast footsteps and screeches as they sprint to attack.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
The fixed camera angles and tank controls feel awkward at first and take some time to get used to.

The voice acting is not the best.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil was groundbreaking for its time back in 1996. It’s credited for defining the survival horror genre and returning zombies to popular culture. I was born in 1993, and remember the first time I saw this game. It was when I was maybe six-eight years old, and I watched my big sister play this game. She completely freaked out, and so did I. I thought it was very scary.

What I like the most about this game is its haunting and eerie atmosphere and the ambient sound design and music. You never feel safe, and the game is good at scaring you and effectively induce panic with sudden enemy occurrences like zombies and dogs. The awkward controls can be frustrating at first, but they also heighten the panic and horror of tense situations. Once you get a hang of it, it’s very satisfying to pull off headshots with the shotgun on zombies. The puzzles are also well-made and fun.

Overall, if you can look past getting used to the movement and controls, I strongly recommend you play this fantastic remaster of one of the most defining games in the history of survival horror, and the start of this fantastic franchise.

[h2]Rating: 8/10[/h2]

[h1]Passing of the Torch[/h1]

Even though Resident Evil REmake isn't a bad game, I wouldn't recommend it anymore. The indie scene has taken the torch from the father of survival horror and is doing a splendid job. Games like Crow Country, Tormented Souls, Signalis, and many more make the REmake feel almost redundant in today's gaming landscape.

The biggest issue is the amount of filler. It is painfully obvious how little confidence the developers had in the puzzles, so they stretched them as much as they could. It might have been a good idea 23 years ago, but it doesn't work anymore.

Meaningless backtracking and an abundance of materials (even on normal mode, which is the hardest you can go on the first playthrough) make the experience lacking in terms of the survival horror feel.

With all that said, it is still an OK-ish game when taken on its own merits. It's just nowhere near the standard it used to be held to. It was once the best there was, but it is time to pass the torch on.

[h1]A NOTE BEFORE BUYING[/h1]

Resident Evil 1, despite being a remake, has a game design that is a little dated and presents itself as a backtracking nightmare for someone who has a bad memory, coupled with the door loading screen every time the player enters a different room and the locked camera.

I get it if someone born from the 90's finds some enjoyment from these limitations. I for one consider myself a hardcore player that does not prefer playing games on easy difficulties the first time, but even I reached the point of frustration that I'm questioning my own intelligence. [b][i]This game is cleverly designed to F*CK WITH YOU [/i][/b] and make things that may seem obvious not obvious at all.

But despite the frustrations, I still managed to push through, finish the game and  find some satisfaction completing it even if I had to look up guides for specific moments at random times. The game also offers multiple replayability by reacting to your actions and having it affect the ending, so rest assured I will be playing it again and pretend like I'm smart enough to know that [spoiler] you have to use the square crank two times just to enter the lab behind the waterfall [/spoiler]

[h1]PRO TIP IF YOU DO DECIDE TO PLAY THIS GAME:[/h1]
1. Press interact with every thing on the wall even those that are beyond what the camera can see 
2. Examine each object you find that isn't ammo or healing items
3. Check every corner you can find in a room even if there are enemies guarding blocking that corner 
4. Manage your inventory (segregate healing, ammo and keys/puzzle objects), 
5. Don't keep reloading a save to try and save your healing items or you will end up forgetting where you are therefore getting you lost. [i]In a nutshell: Don't be a f*cking p*ssy[/i] 

Ignore these and you'll be spending most of your time searching for guides and getting yourself accidentally spoiled by a Gemini.

Goodluck!

For all intents and purposes, this REmake should not be held in such high esteem on the surface. REmake was done less than 10 years since the original Resident Evil came out, and if we were to talk with it by today's standards, too soon for one. It was locked to the GameCube for years because of an exclusive deal that saw its sales numbers be lower because of its exclusivity (directly leading to the much bemoaned existence of Resident Evil 4, 5 and 6 for some people, pushing things to action to sell better, because of this decision to lock it to just that console). But even after all of Capcom's further REmakes of their classic Resident Evil games, this is one is still by far their best one that they have done. But why is that?

REmake does something the others really kind of don't, or aren't, by any nature: it is quite possibly, the definitive version of the game it is remaking. Living in a world rife with remakes, this probably seems preposterous, since many elect to modernize the control schemes or change things for the sake of it, or due to the (mostly) new developers' intentions with the games. Not this one though, this game basically plays like a better version of the original, with some slight additions like the quick turn being added in, and subweapons, to not get damaged by monsters if grabbed from the front, on the control side. It also barely cuts anything from the original, instead adding on to it, very much so for its story (such as dealing with the Trevors), likewise with the gameplay of being in the mansion, and beyond it. A lot of things have been expanded upon, and even people who have played the original will get a new experience too. Some zombies can never truly die, adding to the tense decision making of using ammo to shoot zombies at the risk of them coming back stronger than ever, if not done in by a lucky headshot, or by burning its cadaver. You can even aim downwards with the unlockable rockets, meaning dogs are no longer the bane of your existence if just using that weapon. Character-wise, it is also very true to the original. While the lines they say are different, they still really feel like the characters we were introduced to in 1996, something that most remakes, and even Capcom's own future REmakes, often fail to capture. 

Yeah, the mansion is a hell of a lot darker and moodier than its original counterpart, but this darker ambience serves a purpose, unlike swears being injected into every 5th sentence a REmake 2 and up character might say for the sake of appearing "serious". The overtly serious tone REmakes 2 and above do clash with the older, campier tone that I favour more, here it is a bit more serious too, but not overtly so. Barry still alludes to the Jill Sandwich line, and Chris, while not saying it in such a hammy way, does get to the root of the problem in one part of the game. It honors and respects the original while adding layers on to it. The Lisa Trevor storyline still works very well, in spite of all of this. It helps that Shinji Mikami came back to direct this, so it makes sense the reverence for the source material is here, and felt a lot more than other remakes of this calibre.

It's not perfect as a complete replacement though. As said earlier, the mansion is a lot darker and menacing than it used to be, changing the ambience and mood drastically. There is more of a predetermined order of using the keys and accessing doors, allowing less freedom on subsequent runs to do things differently(still better than the randomised items that 3 did). Some scenes that were optional in the original are done by default in this version. An Easter Egg you can find that references later characters directly contradicts some story elements found in the later games. Zombies can resurrect and be a stronger version of themselves, leading to the tried and true "shotgun to the head" method to not even be as effective sometimes. The walking with the fuel section sucks, even if it's short (Mostly because that's where a no save run went awry for me from getting grabbed from a Crimson Head).

These are very small issues when compared to the myriad of benefits and changes that adds to the game, leading to the often said statement that this is the best remake, and REmake, of all time. I am inclined to agree with both of those statements. Even if it is not my favourite Resident Evil, it is still a damn good game you owe to yourself to play for not only its historical value, but for its significance on survival horror as a whole, especially now that it isn't locked to just the damn GameCube.

TL;DR: Not for everyone, but essential if you value nostalgia, atmosphere, Resident Evil games and the roots of survival horror.

It is not a game that will appeal to everyone. It is a product of its time, even in its remade form, and it shows it. The fixed camera angles, tank-style controls, and deliberate pacing can feel slow or even clunky compared to modern standards. If you’re expecting fast action, quick reloads, and constant set-pieces like in the newer games, you’ll probably walk away frustrated(like me, as it was my first RE game, and when I tried it for the first time i was lost a walked away frustrated).

One the other hand - that’s exactly what makes this game special. The remake stays faithful to the spirit of the original survival horror formula: limited resources, slow exploration, and a constant sense of dread where every bullet and every herb matters. The mansion itself feels like a character — claustrophobic, mysterious, and packed with atmosphere.

This game rewards patience. It wants you to slow down, pay attention, and let the tension build naturally. If you grew up with the original PlayStation release or you’re curious about the roots of the franchise, it’s an incredible nostalgic trip that still delivers a unique experience.

If you don’t have the patience for older design philosophies, stick to the newer Resident Evil games. But if you want to experience the franchise’s origins in the best possible form, this remake is a must-play.

The good:
-Great spooky atmosphere and environments. Even when in areas I knew were safe, I was always at least a little on edge.
-Good puzzles. None of the puzzles were that complicated or difficult, but they were enough to be fun to solve.
-Resource management. Mainly with ammo, I was constantly on the edge of running out and had to prioritise clearing rooms vs just dodging. Playing on normal. In my opinion it was balanced quite well to keep me in this state, though by the end game I had ammo to spare.
-Exploration/game flow. Thanks to the previously mentioned great atmosphere, exploring was always good. The way you have to backtrack over past areas as you get items that enable you to access previously locked rooms in those past areas is interesting. The game stops you from being complacent when going back to these past areas by surprises.
-Story/characters/world: It feels like a cheesy horror movie. The characters are goofy/fun. The story and world were engaging enough. Though, possibly because I played quite slowly, the balance between gameplay and story leaned towards gameplay. 

The mixed:
-The fixed camera angles: Sometimes they can really add to the atmosphere and create a fell like you're playing a horror movie. Other times, they can just be really annoying...
-The limited saves: They play into the resource management gameplay, but can be inconvenient. I had to unlearn some saving habits to avoid using up ink too much.

The bad:
-The movement controls. I played with the alternative control scheme with a keyboard/mouse, because that is what I started with and I never bothered to change it. Especially in rooms with varied camera angles this could get awkward/annoying to control sometimes. While I had mostly adapted by the end of the game, there were still places where it was annoying. It didn't detract from the game too much, it was just sometimes annoying.

Overall: recommend if you like spooky games with puzzle elements. (don't recommend if you have arachnophobia)

I've had an odd experience with resident evil as a franchise. So my experience before this is revelations 2, the first 2 movies, a demo for revelations 1 on 3ds before I actually played the port of the first game on ds and played umbrella corps. I tried out the multiplayer games after I got every re game in a bundle.

So I decided to play 0 first, that was a mistake, it's bad.
Now I've played through this which is much better.
Having deadly silence as context makes this game somewhat surreal. I know this game, but so much is changed and added upon they might as well be 2 different games. It feels like I played a prototype of this game on the ds which is good for this game, but I also feel that what the game does expand on here isn't really necessary.
Honestly a lot of what I enjoyed here felt worse from being dragged out. Sure there's more content, but the crimson heads don't do anything other than discourage the player from killing the base zombies and slowly waiting for an angle to run past them, it makes the pistol then useless since you're never going to be using it for any other threat. I felt the hunters for being as big a deal as they were, were much worse off being relegated to around 2 encounters in the same spot which just makes them forgettable here compared to how ds just didn't have anywhere else to put them. I felt the chimeras were a cool enemy, and I really like the vent crawling section for the M.O. disc, but they're so easy to deal with at that point from how much ammo you've likely been saving that it makes it a breeze. 

So while this game is prettier, and has substantially more. I really feel this version ends up dragging its feet more often than not which really hurts the game. I don't really feel the broken doorknobs were something that should have been kept, especially when they don't serve anything other than to stall the player. I don't feel the courtyard and the basement layers needed as much as was added to them. I thought the guardhouse however and the aquatic underlayers were a great addition.

So what i'm ultimately left with is yeah, this is a good game, it's pretty great honestly, and I really do think the way it expands on the traitor storyline, the way it sets up barry and the writings he leaves you. I think Lisas storyline all are the best part of this game. When it actually comes around to expanding the map and the actual game, it usually falls into a trap of making itself more tedious rather than a clever maze. I think the greatest highlight of this is the fuel cell necessary 
to power the elevator. This wasn't in deadly silence or the original, what happens is that they now added a spot to travel to in order to slot in a fuel cell that's unfilled when you find it. Upon filling the fuel cell at another location, the compound is considered so volatile that running or using any weapon other than the pistol or knife will set it off and cause it to explode. In order to reasonably get past this area you have to put it away, or die and not pick it up, and then slowly kill every enemy between the point you refill the fuel cell and slot it in and then check a few times to take care of the crimson head that will spawn. Then you can go back, fill up your fuel cell, then walk the whole way back. This didn't add tension, this didn't add to the experience, all this did was add a section that took longer than necessary and annoyed me. Then you get back to the actual exploration and puzzle solving and resource management and it's a good time again. Well that's near the end so at that point you have a few boss fights and that's it but my point is stuff like this happens all over this remake. 

I think the positives far outweigh the negatives, and if you already knew what to expect from a classic resident evil style game, you would be forgiven for not noticing the added tedium that's distinct from what's actually effective at delivering a sense of anxiety and tension. It's especially outweighed by the expanded cinematic story moments. 
One final issue I do have though is just a personal preference. While the visuals are impressive for the time, I can't help but feel that a lot was lost when switching the art style from what feels closer to a 70's manor in the middle of the woods that's a little run down, but has this garrish yellow wallpaper with the clashing deep colored wood. It's colorful, it's bright but it still feels unsettling from simply being outdated, and feeling like a genuine home that's gone empty. By switching it out for marble floors, pillars, ornate wood carvings and expensive furniture layouts. I really do feel the game loses something. It changes the tone, you already know this manor can only exist from absurd amounts of wealth. It doesn't make any sense at all that an abandoned manor this well maintained and ornate is something you'd just stumble upon. You can already guess that it has a secret lab and military backed testing aquarium in the backyard and it would make perfect sense. Having the original dingy playboy style house. Even if the background for the manor is the same, it being a secret facility, you aren't immediately clued in to the fact that there weren't people living here. It genuinely feels like something terrible happened that you just stumbled across and the further you go the worse it gets. It's only when you reach the guardhouse that the manor is more than it appears.

So yeah there's me being an old better than new ass about this game, but yeah no, games good, felt it took up more time than it needed to.

In my top 3 games of all time. The 1996 release of this game shot the survival horror genre into the mainstream and was absolutely revolutionary to the gaming industry. The pre rendered backgrounds allowed for insane detail at the time and the fixed camera angles make you feel like you're in control of a horror movie protagonist. The voice acting and cutscenes, although maybe cheesy when the game was first released mostly due to awkward translations from the Japanese version, are now iconic and add so much charm when replaying just to here those iconic lines (who doesn't love being reminded Jill was almost a Jill Sandwich). The slow moving controls really make you feel vulnerable when in danger and limited ink ribbons can create some really stressful situations if you find yourself running out and then having to trek around the map with a full inventory looking for whatever you need. The atmosphere is a whole thing on its own and the most memorable part of the experience of this game for me. The creaking floorboards and eerie silence which suddenly gets interrupted by a zombie moaning in the distance really make the world feel alive in the mysterious estate. The Resident Evil HD Remaster on Steam is not just a polished throwback—it’s the definitive version of the game that birthed a genre and remains, to this day, the pinnacle of the franchise. While later entries veered into action-heavy territory, sacrificing tension for spectacle, this remaster preserves the essence of survival horror: a science fiction nightmare set in the eerie, labyrinthine Spencer Mansion where every bullet counts and every decision could be your last. The game punishes recklessness, demanding players conserve ammunition, manage limited resources, and navigate with deliberate caution—an ethos that’s been diluted in many modern titles. The fixed camera angles and tank controls, once divisive, now exude a nostalgic charm that countless indie horror games try to emulate, proving their timeless design. It’s a shame that despite the flood of Resident Evil movies, none have dared to faithfully recreate the original game’s slow-burn terror and intricate pacing; instead, they cram too much lore into a single film, missing the magic of the mansion’s creeping dread. The remaster beautifully showcases the franchise’s signature dual storytelling, with Jill and Barry’s emotionally grounded arc contrasting Chris and Rebecca’s more procedural survival, creating a layered narrative that deepens the experience. The game builds to a fever pitch in its final act, descending into the underground laboratory where grotesque chimeras stalk the halls and the climactic Tyrant battle delivers a perfect capstone to the journey. The addition of Crimson Heads—reanimated zombies that return faster and deadlier if not properly dispatched—adds a brilliant layer of strategy and fear, elevating the tension beyond the original. This remaster doesn’t just honor the 1996 classic—it refines and enhances it, making it not only a masterclass in horror design but also my personal favorite in the entire series.

I had a really hard time getting into the Resident Evil Remake at first. I dropped it more than once — controls felt off, the pacing was slow, and I didn’t really get what the game wanted from me. But after finally pushing through and finishing it twice (with Jill), I get it now. And looking back, I think my biggest mistake was using the alternate control scheme on my first playthrough.

The alternate controls seem more "modern," but they honestly just make the movement weird and frustrating. Since the game uses fixed camera angles, when you try to move based on the camera direction, it often ends up confusing — especially when the camera changes mid-move. It messed me up constantly. Once I switched to the original tank controls, everything clicked. They're more consistent: forward is always forward for the character, no matter what angle the camera is at. It actually made movement easier and less annoying.

That said, exploration wasn’t always fun. The mansion design is clever in theory — rooms loop back and unlock shortcuts — but in practice, the amount of backtracking can get really tedious. Sometimes you go through five rooms just to find out you need a key you won’t get for another hour. And the item management makes it worse. You’ve got super limited inventory space, so you're constantly juggling items or running back to item boxes.

And the ink ribbons... I really don’t get the logic there. Not only do you need them to save, but they take up an actual slot in your inventory. A consumable that lets you use a basic feature — saving your progress — and it punishes you by using up space you could’ve used for healing or ammo. That part just feels unnecessary and honestly kind of dumb. It adds fake difficulty without any real payoff.

Crimson Heads, though, were a nice touch. I hated them at first — until I realized they force you to think about whether it's even smart to kill a zombie. That kind of tension is great. Enemies overall aren’t that varied, but they’re placed well. Every room has you thinking about positioning, especially with the camera angles and tight spaces.

The puzzles are decent — mostly logical, not too obscure. Nothing mind-blowing, but they do a good job breaking up the combat and keeping things from getting stale.

By the time I finished it the second time (even did a speedrun on Normal), I had gone from kinda hating it to genuinely appreciating what it was doing. There’s still stuff I think is outdated or just frustrating — especially the save system and inventory limits — but the game does a lot right if you’re willing to meet it halfway.

Of the two first gen 6 installments in the series, this is the twin that paid attention in school while RE0 was the one that ate glue and jacked off in the bathroom. 
Ostensibly carrying the strength of the game its remaking, I think like the other remakes later in the series this one wasn't much of an uphill battle since they didn't change a lot other than some QoL and the graphics. This one pretty handily captures the same feelings of grotesque peril the original does, and while graphically I personally prefer the raw, harsh gen 5 look most of the time, this is pretty fresh paint for something a generation newer. More importantly, it of course resolves the one major flaw the OG had: those god awful tank controls. Call em intentionally clumsy all you want, bad controls are bad controls and the only place I want to see that kind of fighting with the fixed cam is in hokey tributes, not official remakes. This one is solid all the way through and thoroughly, quintessentially resident evil, not losing any of the charm in adding some arguably needed polish to a cultural touchstone. As I went on and on about in my RE0 review, I think this one is better seen in reference to that one than the original 1996 game, since they came out the same year (2002, these HD remakes in like 14 and 16 I think) and have the same graphical fidelity and gameplay with an important change echoing other games in the series: a damned storage mechanic, making inventory management a small challenge instead of a total hassle. The story beats are all there, the tension is great, and unlike many of the other games in the series, I think there are some genuinely scary moments, especially since the schlockiness is toned down quite a bit here compared to several of the other games (including the original) - but not so much it takes itself *too* seriously. The iconic cast is of course the main source of brevity, and while the performances overall are nothing to write home about (some great some mid some terrible) they are a huge improvement over both the original (obv) and 0, and are more importantly a great balance of cheesy and sympathetic. The core gameplay loop is the same as the rest of the series and frankly I have no complaints about it. This is the touch up of the game that invented it, after all, and it feels particularly well done here, with a much stronger balance of puzzles, management and action than a lot of the later installments that pivot more headlong into action. Storywise it really is a good setup for the more profound horror 2 and 3 bring to the table, and while I think the majority would agree the series peaked with Code Veronica or 4, this is more than serviceable as a fresh face for the strong start the series as a whole had. I can't recommend it enough. Great for players trying to get into the series in the first place, regulars who have done themselves a disservice by not going back to the beginning and would rather have something a little cleaner than just emulating the OG, and even the masochists who run through all of the games now and again - I think this one is particularly good for speedrunning and challenge runs compared to the easier or more tedious later installments. I'd dare say it's more than enough content to justify the sticker price, too.

[h1] [b] || Timeless and Terrifying || [/b] [/h1]
Even as a fan of the game, it is still hard to believe that [b] Resident Evil (Gamecube) [/b] is even a game that came out 20+ years ago. I am not just saying that because of its stellar art direction and oppressive atmosphere that can still put a lot of modern horror games to shame, but also because of how it's gameplay ,even at its simplest, can so effortlessly engage players. From the inventory management, puzzle solving, planning out what routes to take within the mansion when you are about to leave a save room, and so much more. And even if the stories on offer aren't anything that'll wow anyone in particular, the early 2000s B-movie charm and inherent cheesiness surprisingly compliments the main gameplay really well.

[h2] Pro tip: Start with Jill [/h2]
When starting the game you are given a choice to pick between two of the game's main playable characters: Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield. The first time this menu shows up, Chris will be be the character that the game defaults to. While Chris does have certain benefits over Jill such as more health and always having a lighter at all times, his smaller inventory size compared to Jill's just makes him less desirable for a lot of players especially if its on a first play through where you would spend most of your time learning the quirks of game. 

Getting into the gameplay flow proper, it mainly consists of exploring the environments, finding items that act as resources help you progress by using them in other rooms on the map, solving puzzles, avoiding and/or killing zombies along the way,  rinse and repeat until you reach credits. Like I said in the beginning, a lot of these gameplay elements are simple but its how they interact and effect the other gameplay aspects that manages to create a tight and engaging gameplay throughout.

For example, if you want to kill or stagger zombies you will have to shoot them with bullets which will then leave you with less resources to defend yourself. But if you do kill the zombies and you don't burn their bodies with fuel, which is also a limited resource, after a certain amount of time they will come back as Crimson Heads which are much faster and hit harder. So you are left with a choice of killing zombies and having the right amount of fuel to burn their remains or avoid the zombies while you keep exploring which doesn't expend any resources but it will mean that you'd have to constantly maneuver around them when entering their specified rooms. There are a several more of these types of decision making moments with the other gameplay elements that help keep you keep guessing the best way to approach the game.

[h2] Terrifying, yet gorgeous [/h2]
What Capcom managed to do here with Resident Evil's art direction and visual design is something that is still worthy of praise even up to this day. It was achieved by continuing the RE staple pre rendered backgrounds and static camera angles which then let's the developers use the extra horsepower on rendering characters and enemies. Add to the fact that although being pre rendered the backgrounds are filled to the brim with so many details and smart color choices that they are often mistaken for actual rendered environments.

Besides just making the game look great, these elements are also a major factor of the game's tense atmosphere. The fixed camera angles can add to the feel of danger when entering a brand new room for the first time since the lack of control would mean that enemies can be obscured by design. And the environment designs and layout were made with this limitation in mind where you can have big, open, and grand spaces to run around in or even smaller, cramped rooms with damp and moodier tones usually with a single enemy or two just around the corner punishing players that aren't cautious enough.

[h1] [b] "Wanna see STARS? I'll sho-" eh wait wrong game [/b] [/h1]
It really can't be said enough of just how great this generation of games was and [b] Resident Evil [/b] is easily one of its hallmarks. Tight gameplay, brilliant map design, dark and palpable atmosphere, and a consistently engaging experience makes for some really fun yet scary times especially if you intend to play the game again and again for those faster clear times and bonuses.

[h2]Quick Verdict[/h2]

Resident Evil remains an atmospheric masterpiece, delivering a level of tension and dread that very few games have ever managed to replicate.

[h2]Score: 4/5[/h2]

[hr]

[h1]The Review[/h1]

Resident Evil is still an absolute masterclass in atmosphere and pacing.

What struck me most during this playthrough was the constant, oppressive sense of dread. The game never lets you feel comfortable. The mansion feels hostile from the moment you step inside, and that feeling never fully goes away. Every corridor, hallway, and room feels like a potential threat, even after you have passed through it multiple times.

The limited save system plays a huge role in this. Saving requires a consumable item, which forces you to think carefully about when to commit progress. That single design choice adds an enormous amount of tension. You are constantly weighing risk versus safety, asking yourself whether you should push forward a little longer or retreat to save what you have accomplished so far. Failure always feels costly.

The puzzles are challenging without being obtuse. They require attention and thought, but they rarely stall momentum. Solving them feels satisfying rather than exhausting, and they integrate naturally into the environment instead of feeling like arbitrary obstacles. The game keeps you moving forward while never letting you feel secure.

This balance creates a constant push and pull. The game urges you onward, but simultaneously makes you fearful of what lies ahead. Entering a new section of the mansion is genuinely intimidating. I never knew what to expect, and the game is so densely packed with detail and horror that every new area feels dangerous.

There is a sense of powerlessness here that I rarely experience in games. Combat is deliberate, resources are scarce, and running away is often the correct choice. The tension does not come from overwhelming enemies, but from the uncertainty of what you might encounter next and whether you are prepared to deal with it.

I also have a real affection for the characters and the famously cheesy dialogue and voice acting. Rather than detracting from the experience, it adds to the game’s identity and charm. It feels earnest and confident in its tone, never apologetic for what it is.

I loved my time with Resident Evil and will absolutely be coming back for another playthrough. It is a game I think everyone should give a chance, even if it ultimately is not to their taste. Few games make you feel this vulnerable, this tense, and this engaged for so long, and even fewer do it with this much confidence.

My assumption before playing this game was that its reputation had likely clouded its quality over the years. I was very happy to be proven wrong. This is a fantastic game that captures some of the best survival horror has to offer. 

For its time the visuals are impressive, and Spencer mansion is my new favourite horror setting. The music and sound design really helps maintain an eerie atmosphere. 

The fixed camera took some adjusting, but added an element of horror I had not experienced before. Not being able to freely check around corners made me rely on sound and added to the experience. 

The number of puzzles surprised me, and how they often posed a challenge compared to modern games (even within the same franchise). I do wish there was an easier way in game to remind myself of certain objective locations.

Zombies have never been scarier than in this game. They are slow of course but never seem to die, and when they do you might get an even more dangerous enemy. Most of the bosses are puzzle related which I think allowed them to age better than other games.

Inventory management is possibly the most difficult part. The first half is so limited in storage locations that it can feel tedious alternating back and forth constantly while exploring. This can turn to frustration combined with animations when entering any door.

The combat has not aged well for me, but its thankfully not the focus. It's about managing your resources and choosing when to fight, kite, or run away.

You often get thrown surprising encounters or new enemies after completing major objectives, which stops things from getting boring whilst backtracking.

If you love survival horror then this is more than worth playing over 20 years later.

I am DNF'ing this game. I was excited to player REmake because I wanted to play one of the (relatively) old school versions of the Resident Evil games since I am a big fan of the remakes for Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4. I do like how you have to keep track of where things are on the map and plan out route strategies to avoid damage and using ammo. 

That being said, this game frustrates me to no end. I started out by playing on Expert, because of my familiarity with Resident Evil 2 Remake's expert difficulty. This may have been a mistake, but most of my frustrations have little to do with enemies doing more damage and being spongier. My most major issue with the game is that combat sucks. It is not intuitive where you have to aim to be able to do a hit head shot or hit enemies low to the ground. There were many times when I was fighting the zombie dogs, in particular, when I had to die multiple times through tedious trial and error to figure out when and where I could shoot them. And then even when I did, this only staggered them briefly with the handgun so that they could get a free hit in. 

The zombie dogs particularly suffer from being far too fast in a game where Jill moves like she is just learning to run for the first time. You could say that I should just dodge the zombie dogs but there is one part where you HAVE to kill one of them to receive a key necessary to continue in the game. On my second try at the game after having to restart, I quit after being killed by the two dogs over and over again. I only had one shotgun round so I had to muddle through with the handgun which has the problem I just mentioned. 

My second major issue is the save ribbon system. In theory, I like how you have to parse them out so you can't save scum. In practice, especially on expert, it is impossible to know how many more tasks need to be completed to get the next set of save ribbons so I would end up using them too frequently when I thought it made sense. By the time I had gotten to the part where Jill has to head in to the woods, I had none left. I could go back to previous saves but re-doing a lot of what I had already done wasn't rewarding since I would inevitably end up finding the most optimum way to do something and then just doing that over and over. If there was a better way of knowing how long you need to save them, it would still allow for strategy without leaving the player to essentially have to make wild guesses. When I got to the part with the boss fight in the cabin, I restarted the game because I had to backtrack so much every time I lost to her. 

I was having fun re-playing part of the beginning with the knowledge I had gained in the first run, but there were too many frustrations for me to want to keep soldiering on. This is a "skill issue", but why is that relevant? A game can be "hard" without being intuitive or fun. Not only a prime example of survival horror, but a prime example of how to do a remake. 

It still looks incredible, despite the resolution of the backgrounds showing some age. The way each angle is framed and lit, it's just gorgeous. They use the fixed camera angles to great effect a lot of the time, normally to create mood and atmosphere, but some times to setup reveals or surprises. You just can't do that with a free camera and I grew to love the fixed angles very quickly. 

It didn't take long at all to get used to the controls, and I think the slower movement & action is really a positive. It's genuinely refreshing to slow down, soak in the atmosphere, and explore a location freely. You're not led around by the nose, the game isn't throwing stuff at you constantly to keep your attention. It's not afraid to be quiet for a while, and build tension. It can feel a little obtuse at times, but figuring stuff out for yourself is so much more satisfying. 

I love the sense of permanence the game has. You shoot a zombie, it's still lying on the floor when you come back later. Items are fixed and finite. Occasionally, the game will refresh the mansion with new enemies, but it's always an event. Something happens to trigger it. You never backtrack and find a room repopulated. It's very deliberate and carefully orchestrated.

I won't go into spoilers, but, I loved how grounded things felt. There's none of the wacky stuff from later Resident Evil games. The mansion feels like a mansion, and subsequent areas feel like real places, not fantastical or overly sci-fi. There's no grotesque, shocking stuff here really either, it's all pretty safe for people (like me) who don't like gore and would walk away if it got too visceral.

Honestly I could gush about this game for a lot longer, I strongly recommend it. I didn't play the original Resident Evil on PS1, and I didn't play this when it released, but even as someone completely new to this style of game, I had a blast. It's fantastic.

[h1]Review[/h1] 
The remake of the original. The legend. What people miss and long for but we will probably never get again.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Comparing to the original the remake is probably even more hard. Although if you finish the game once it’s not a really difficult game aside the first section of the game. There are two new features that I think cancel themself out in greatness. You now have defensive weapons that protects you against one zombie grab. 
Chris being a worse character has the best one, a flashbang that one shots enemy when they grab you. Additionally, his lighter is now useful. You can get a can of kerosine, and it has two charges to burn zombies. Zombies that did not die from headshots have a chance to get up again and revive as a very fast crimson head zombie. In theory this feature looks nice, but just gives you more backtracking and walking. Some rooms you think you will never come back to? No need. Frequent hallways with still looked doors? Burn those zombies, run back to the chest and put that lighter/kerosine away. Just adds unnecessary walking, would have been fixed if it’s not an item that takes up inventory space.

Generally, the gameplay otherwise is still the same. Dodge or kill zombies, try to save ammo and health, pickup items and try to use them in the correct way to unlock a new path. It’s a puzzle game that is never testing your sanity with obscure puzzles and rather gives you good a good dopamine rush when you find out how to use that gem or emblem you found.
You can switch between tank controls and modern ones, but there is a reason why you should use tank controls due to the fixed camera angles.

[u]Story[/u]
The story is less B horror movie jank, although characters still talk like they are in one making it less offensive but also less memorable. There is new story sections included that just feel on point and completely fitting to the game. Overall, an improvement, depending on your opinion on the trash factor.

[u]Sound[/u]
It would have been awesome to choose between original ost and new one, although no matter its still atmospheric and the shotgun sounds punchy. Some tracks are just fantastic like the underground lab. Enemies still sound like they are skeletons or walking while dripping wet.

[u]Graphics[/u]
This is where im divided. The drab and bleak look is pulled off fantastically. Especially outside at night times or in small rooms. I just feel like that the colours of the original had more charm to it. Games like dino crisis had a perfect mix between dark areas and colourful but deadly looking rooms.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
The remake adds new content without changing too much. Puzzles are also slightly different but the game is still in spirit the same. It’s the perfect example of a remake that is more accessible to new players but also new (and same) enough for people who enjoyed the original. Highly recommended.

Resident Evil 1 is the bible of survival horror. This game is the blueprint, the sacred text for what the genre is and should be. The atmosphere is dense, haunting, and unforgettable. The Spencer Mansion serves as a character itself here. Every hallway, locked door, and distant creak contributes to this oppressive feeling that something isn’t right. This game is extremely obtuse and unapologetically old school. It does not hold your hand, and I respect that. Your save files, ink ribbons used at the typewriters, are a limited currency. If you don’t use them wisely, you might have to restart your entire playthrough from the beginning. Yes, this has happened to me, and no, I’ll never forget the heartbreak. Even though I’ve played this game multiple times over the years, I still lost hours and hours of progress during this playthrough. That risk adds to the tension and forces you to think. You need to plan your routes, manage your inventory, and really learn the mansion. This isn’t a game you zone out to, it demands focus and rewards careful, thoughtful play. It’s the ultimate escape room game. Every door leads to another riddle, every statue, key, and crank has meaning. Solving its puzzles under pressure, with limited health and ammo, is pure survival horror gold. The backtracking through the mansion is one of the most special things about this game. Because of how often you revisit areas, you slowly memorize the layout until you know the entire place by heart. I can recall every hallway, every safe room, every shortcut. That kind of familiarity with a game space is rare. The mansion itself is brought to life through subtle atmosphere, the creaking of old wooden floors, the echo of your footsteps, the strike of lightning through a distant window. The Spencer Mansion feels real, and the fact that I could confidently navigate it by memory is a testament to how iconic and thoughtfully designed it is. I’ll never forget the first time I saw a Crimson Head. I thought I had dealt with a regular zombie, moved on, and then out of nowhere it came tearing back to life, faster, meaner, and absolutely relentless. I shot out of my chair without thinking. That moment completely rewired my understanding of how dangerous this game really was. I also need to mention how awesome the normal zombies are here. Their groans and their labored gait is so iconic. And yes, of course the characters are cheesy. The story is cheesy. But that’s just Resident Evil. It’s part of the identity and it only adds to the charm. It’s like a B-horror movie that knows exactly what it is and leans into it. The real value of this game isn’t in the plot twists or the dialogue, it’s in the feeling you get after a long day where come late after spending all day mapping your path in the mansion, picking up where you left off on your last save, turning off the lights, and letting yourself sink into the tension. The real value is how cathartic it feels when you’re critically wounded, haven’t saved in an hour and a half, and you finally make it to a safe room. That moment when the door shuts behind you, the danger fades, and you hear that calm, beautiful save room music, it’s some of the best music you could ever hear in your life. That relief, after all the tension and horror, is unforgettable. Even though I don’t replay it as often as I’d like because of how punishing it can be, I will always respect this game. It shaped my taste forever. Survival horror is my favorite genre of all time, and Resident Evil 1 is what made that possible. And most importantly, I have to give it its flowers. My favorite series of all time, Silent Hill, would not exist without this game coming first. Resident Evil 1 Remake isn’t just a classic, it’s the foundation. And the fact that it still holds up today is a testament to just how powerful and well crafted it really is. I know everything that I said has been said a million different way by millions of different people. Yes this is a beautiful classic game that has only aged backwards and still holds the gold standard for not only survival horror but for remakes entirely.

After playing through the game for the first time completely blind using Chris on Easy mode, I can say that the game is very good if you don't mind looking things up every once in a while. 

The game stayed pretty scary throughout most of the game despite being made for older hardware, and I found myself jumping every time a zombie showed up around the corner when I wasn't expecting them. 

The camera is fixed, which means it does feel very dated, and makes the game as a whole feel pretty clunky and hard to navigate, but it didn't really get in the way of my enjoyment of the game too often. I did find myself wishing for a usable camera by the end of the game though.

Even though I'm not the biggest fan of limited saves in a game, I feel like there were enough ink ribbons for a casual player to get through the game without losing too much progress whenever they die. I even had about 10 ink ribbons left by the time I finished the game, so it was generous enough, which honestly goes for all of the consumables in the game. I had plenty of healing, and lots of ammo by the end of the game, so I never felt like I had ruined my save file if an enemy took more resources than felt required. 

The puzzles were very confusing, and I did have to look up where to go next three or four times, but most of the time I could figure out where to go next myself. Usually it was just me missing some small detail or something, but there were a few puzzles that either didn't feel intuitive or it just wasn't made clear at all that I could interact with an object. So if you are either incredibly patient and don't mind checking everything around the entire map multiple times just to be safe, or just don't mind looking something up every once in a while, this will be a great game for you.

By now, you can get a much better experience from the more recent games in the series like Resident Evil 7, but this is still a fun game, and it's always nice to look back at the experiences that modern horror games are inspired by.

TL;DR
Hated the game at first (negative review below). Came back to it 6 months later, and now I love it but it’s still very hard, and not everyone will enjoy it. I recommend reading this or watching some gameplay before buying.

It’s not a perfect game. The main problems are still the camera angles, the poor controls that come with them, the Hunters, the inventory and item management (especially with Chris), and the non-special enemies (like snakes or crows).

The camera angles and the controls can cause you to get hit a lot and can even make puzzles harder.

The Hunters are horrible extremely fast and strong. They can kill you in one hit if they want, and if they don’t, there’s a 5-second delay before you can move again. (I ended up killing all of them with the grenade launcher after dying around 20 times.)

As for the inventory, the main issue is that you collect a lot of items and never know when you’ll actually need them. So you either walk around with a full inventory all the time, or you keep going back and forth to get a specific item you picked up 6 hours ago.

Now for the positives:
The atmosphere, the map, the plot, and even the notes are all designed and written so well it was truly captivating to play. There’s a lot of ammo and healing items scattered around, so that’s not really a problem.

Since you mostly stay in the mansion (or around it), you really feel like you’re in a linear, focused story instead of constantly changing locations and forgetting what you’ve done. Even the areas outside the mansion are creepy and weird in a good way.
The bosses are actually too easy I never died to any of them and only got hit once.
The puzzles aren’t that hard they’re just confusing (mostly because of the number of items).

Overall:
A great experience once you get the hang of it.
Don’t forget to burn the bodies, and don’t be afraid to shoot zombies there’s more than enough ammo. (I finished with 130 handgun ammo and 20 shotgun shells.)

Resident Evil was my first introduction to the series, so I had no particular expectations going into it. 
I decided to play this because RE9 was announced and all I can say is: wow! It was a fantastic game. 

I don't usually play or enjoy single-player games but this game has been able to keep me on the edge of my seat and engaged all the way through.

Capcom did an incredible job at creating a tense and suffocating atmosphere. Through various ways, like music, enemy placement, and level design they were able to create and maintain this sense of dread and anticipation, something I consider essential to horror. The fixed camera positions enhanced that feeling tremendously, adding to the immersion. I was a big fan of that!

The puzzles aren't inherently complex but require you to pay attention to small details and take mental notes of whatever things or areas you've encountered. Sometimes, progress relies on combining specific items in ways that aren't immediately obvious.

That being said, if you missed out on any hints, [b]there will be a lot backtracking.[/b] Considering your inventory is as small as it is and with there being no way to drop items, you'll often be placing items in your item box in order to pick up new items along the way. Because of that, there are going to be many, many moments in which you need to cross the entire map again to reach an item box and retrieve said item which you just so happened to need for the next puzzle.
It was a bit tedious and sometimes frustrating for me, but from a different perspective could add to the feeling of methodically working through the mansion.

I spent a lot of time exploring, interacting with the environments, and reading parts of the lore that was available (or that I found) which helped me piece together bits and pieces of the story. There isn't a lot of story going on, but for what was there I enjoyed it thoroughly. Its good foundation building for the later installments of Resident Evil.

I managed to beat the game in roughly 14 hours, getting stuck on some puzzles because I had forgotten about a certain area, or overthought a certain part of the puzzle. 

[b]As a closing thought:[/b] a definitive recommendation to anyone looking to get into the series. Even though this particular game may feel a bit dated in comparison to the remakes that have recently released and has some minor drawbacks previously mentioned, don't let that stop you from experiencing what is truly a classic gem!

Before zombies became overexposed, before third-person shoulder cams took over, before “survival horror” was even a term… there was Resident Evil. Capcom’s original Resident Evil wasn’t just a game—it was the beginning of something massive. A blueprint for fear, tension, and atmospheric storytelling that left a permanent mark on the industry.

Sure, by today’s standards, it’s clunky, campy, and occasionally ridiculous. But beneath the awkward tank controls and “Jill sandwich” dialogue is a game that masterfully builds suspense and rewards players for thinking, exploring, and surviving.

Set in the outskirts of Raccoon City, you play as a member of the S.T.A.R.S. team—either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield—investigating bizarre murders. You end up trapped in a sprawling mansion, only to discover it’s crawling with undead horrors, mutant beasts, and Umbrella Corporation’s shady bioweapon experiments.

The plot, delivered through grainy cutscenes and scattered files, unfolds like a low-budget horror film—which is exactly the point. The bad acting and stilted dialogue (“You were almost a Jill sandwich!”) are part of the charm. Behind the B-movie shell, there’s a surprisingly engaging mystery that slowly pieces itself together as you explore.

At its core, Resident Evil is a game about resource management, puzzle solving, and deliberate pacing. Every decision—whether to engage a zombie, conserve ammo, or use a precious ink ribbon to save—matters. It’s a constant balance of risk and caution, and that’s what gives the game its unique thrill.

Combat is clunky by design. Tank controls and fixed camera angles make every encounter feel like a threat. You’re never fully comfortable, and that’s what builds dread. The camera may obscure your view, but it also creates anxiety—you hear the enemy before you see it.

Puzzles are a core part of the mansion’s layout. Expect everything from crests and keys to statues and shotgun traps. Backtracking is necessary, but the level design is tight and rewarding.

The Spencer Mansion is iconic—an eerie, gothic labyrinth full of creaking doors, flickering candles, and hidden terrors. The pre-rendered backgrounds still have a haunting charm, with lighting and angles crafted for maximum tension. The ambient soundtrack is minimal, allowing you to focus on every footstep, growl, and distant thunderclap.

Enemies are limited in variety but effective: standard zombies, infected dogs, giant snakes, and the terrifying Hunters all make their mark. It’s the kind of horror that lingers—not from gore or jumpscares, but from dread and disempowerment.

With two playable characters—Chris and Jill—each offering unique weapons, routes, and NPC interactions, Resident Evil encourages multiple playthroughs. Your choices affect the story’s ending and who survives, giving you plenty of incentive to return to the mansion’s horrors.

Resident Evil is a foundational horror experience. Yes, it’s aged in some areas—controls are stiff, voice acting is infamous—but it still accomplishes something few games can: it makes you afraid to open the next door. It’s not just nostalgia that keeps this game alive—it’s the sharp design, eerie pacing, and groundbreaking atmosphere.

A creepy, clunky classic that defined a genre and still delivers true survival horror when played on its own terms.

Pros:
-Incredible atmosphere and environmental design
-Tight resource management and puzzle solving
-Iconic enemy encounters and boss fights
-Two distinct playable characters for replayability
-Genuinely scary—even decades later

Cons:
-Tank controls can be tough for modern players
-Dated voice acting (though it’s part of the charm)
-Inventory management can get tedious

Rating: 9/10

Title: “Ink Ribbons Gave Me More Stability Than My Father Ever Did”
 
Resident Evil (HD Remaster) is a claustrophobic masterpiece. The Spencer Mansion is a maze of death, mystery, and atmospheric dread. It’s survival horror at its purest—low ammo, cryptic puzzles, and a creeping sense that something is always watching. The moment I first entered that dimly lit hallway and heard the soft, wet footsteps of an unseen creature, I was transported. Not just into the game, but into a very specific memory from 1999, when I hid in a linen closet to avoid hearing my father come home drunk again.

The game’s pacing is genius. Doors creak open slowly—just long enough for the tension to become unbearable. You never know what’s behind them: a zombie, a crimson head, or worse—sometimes, nothing at all. That nothingness is louder than any jump scare. It reminds me of the way our house went silent during fights. You'd wait behind your bedroom door, listening for footsteps, bracing for the sound of breaking plates—or your name, said in just the wrong tone. Resident Evil understands fear like that. It doesn’t shout. It waits.

The save system—with ink ribbons and typewriters—felt like a mechanic designed specifically to trigger my anxiety. You don’t just save when you want to. You save when you’ve earned it. It’s punishment and control, in digital form. Much like the rigid schedule of chores and “quiet hours” I had growing up, where freedom was rationed like bullets. One misstep and you'd lose everything—progress, safety, the illusion that things might be okay.

There’s a strange comfort in Jill Valentine’s stoic determination. She never complains. She just moves forward, unlocking doors and shooting monsters, even when the odds are stacked against her. I admired that. I used to imagine myself like her—silent, capable, walking through halls filled with danger like it didn’t matter. Of course, Jill gets a grenade launcher. I got a broken Game Boy Color and the inability to cry in front of other people.

What elevates Resident Evil above simple nostalgia is its restraint. It doesn’t over explain. It leaves room for silence and dread. It lets you sit with the horror. When I finally unlocked the door to the lab and saw the truth behind the virus, I wasn’t surprised. I already knew monsters are made, not born. Sometimes they wear lab coats. Sometimes they wear flannel and smell like whiskey and gasoline. Capcom nailed that part, even if they didn’t mean to.

In conclusion: Resident Evil is a brilliant, haunting survival horror experience that’s aged like fine wine… or an unresolved memory. It’s not for everyone, especially if you don’t like being alone with your thoughts. But if you want a game that makes you feel like surviving is both a victory and a punishment, look no further. 10/10. Also, Dad, if you’re reading this—don’t.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (The blueprint for survival horror — timeless and terrifying)

This isn’t just a remake — this is how you remake a game. Resident Evil 1 Remake (REmake) takes everything from the 1996 original and elevates it into a near-perfect survival horror experience. Even today, over 20 years later, it’s still one of the most atmospheric, tense, and iconic horror games ever made.

The setting is simple: a creepy mansion, limited resources, and something very, very wrong lurking in the shadows. But the execution? Masterful. Every hallway is a threat. Every zombie is a problem. And every decision — whether to use ammo, heal, or save your progress — feels like it matters.

Capcom didn’t just slap a coat of paint on the original. They reworked environments, added new areas, introduced the terrifying Crimson Heads (seriously, these things change how you think about killing zombies), and expanded the story with subtle but meaningful new lore. And the visual upgrade still holds up — the pre-rendered backgrounds look gorgeous, and the lighting and sound design create pure tension from start to finish.

The fixed camera angles and tank controls might feel dated to some, but in this context, they work. They make you feel vulnerable, disoriented, and on edge — exactly how survival horror should feel. And if you’re new to the series, there are modern control options included, so you can ease in without losing the fear.

Whether you play as Chris or Jill, the experience is tense, smartly designed, and brutally unforgiving in all the right ways. It's a slower, methodical game compared to modern RE titles — but that's what makes it so rewarding.

If you’re a fan of horror, this is essential. If you’re a Resident Evil fan and haven’t played this version? Fix that immediately.
This is the game that proved survival horror can be beautiful, terrifying, and thoughtful — all at once.

REmake is still the gold standard. Accept no substitutes.
