Arguably the best Resident Evil game ever made from an objective standpoint

A fantastic remake. I'm personally more fan of the oldschool RE games, and this makes the original more accessible for newer players while still maintaining what made it great: Atmosphere, limited resources and dangerous enemies. There is also a new control scheme that lets you pick from a more modern playstyle that's more snappy and easier to maneuver with. Though if you want to stick to the tank controls from the original, that is still in there as an option!

For one, it adds new content. If you've played the original from PS1, its familiar, yet fresh as there's new puzzles, and some items and events may be different from how they were in the PS version. Then, there's a new difficulty system, with a new Very Easy setting for those who want to take it, well, easy, or are not so experienced with this kind of a game. It does go the other way as well, letting you pick harder difficulties to challenge yourself!

Still just two campaigns, for Chris and Jill (first time players should pick Jill, by the by!). Beating the game unlocks bunch of new goodies to change up the experience though, so there's plenty replay value!

My biggest gripe with the game would be the camera. Moving around to certain spots on the screen changes the camera to a new, preset viewpoint. When it does this, it also flips your controls accordingly, which can sometimes be frustrating as the moment you let go of your movement button, the same button may now move you in a completely opposite direction. Likewise, the camera angles do occasionally allow for enemies that are JUST off the frame to ambush you, which is admittedly a little bit cheap. But, its something you can get used to after playing for a bit.

Overall, highly recommend, especially if its on sale as these days it goes down to like 5€ or smth. Absolutely encourage you to try it out!

TL;DR: Super well done, faithful remake. New content, familiar yet fresh, several difficulty levels to tailor your experience, limited resources and dangerous enemies. Lots of unlockables for plenty replay value. Wonky camera at times.

I imagine that every time a new Resident Evil game comes out, there will be new fans wondering if they should play this remake of the game that started it all. Considering how low the percentage is on some of the mid and late game achievements, it’s evident that it’s not easy for everyone to stick it out to the end. So why is that? 

Put simply, the game is very unfair on the first run and I even considered giving up out of frustration. I put the game down out of annoyance the year before too, so this was a pattern. I made the mistake of playing as Chris for my first run on Medium (what it considers easy) knowing that it would be harder so I could do a victory lap with Jill on the hardest skill available afterwards. While my thinking wasn’t entirely terrible, playing as Chris for the first run is an absolute chore. The backtracking became ever constant, and I say this as someone that has had experience in all the other RE games and some indie survival horrors. Only take what you need and don’t bring extra ammo unless you’re going to a boss fight. Combat itself is not difficult once you get used to the controls. 
Even when I played as Jill on the Normal difficulty - adding many more zombies and kerosene necessities to the run, I only died maybe twice across both playthroughs to actual combat. Once was getting knocked off a ledge by Lisa Trevor, and another was getting pecked to death by crows when I was low on health. You are much more likely to die from the stressful puzzle sequences that will result in your demise if you don’t do something or just press a random button out of curiosity. 

So don’t be ashamed to look at a walkthrough, because I certainly needed the help every once in a while. Like I didn’t understand the need to stop a waterfall, or have the patience to do a chemical mixing puzzle with lots of math. I’d say if you’re also wanting to go to the original RE to witness another fun, fleshed out story like some of the other remakes - just watch a lore recap on YouTube. The script in this game is terrible and left me pretty disappointed as a fan of all the games, even the bad ones. It might not be PS1 levels of hilarious, but now it’s so stilted, inconsistent and borderline nonsensical. 

It might sound like I hate this game, so why still put it in Recommended? Well there’s something to say for a game still being interesting, despite its faults. Not going to praise it in tongue baths like some of those old survival horror gatekeepers love to do, but I’m not going to burn down its house either. I’m not really wanting fixed-camera survival horror to come back, I think the indie scene has that covered if you want it. Just go in with the expectations that it’s going to suck for at least the first 30 minutes as you get used to everything. Aim your shotgun up for the head when a zombie gets close, always do the kind thing and help out your fellow S.T.A.R.S. members, and maybe play as Jill first.

I've been playing through the series remakes since I never got a chance to when I was younger, and right now I am part of the way through 5. I have to say that so far RE1 has been my favorite and its no wonder that the series gained so much popularity. So long as you understand that the first game is more of a puzzle game and less of an action game like the later titles I heavily recommend it. Sure there is combat, but that is more about resource management and preparation than skill. 

I haven't played any of the original versions but from what I have seen the remake seems to be not just faithful to the original,  but an upgrade in most areas: 
Better graphics allow for more detailed textures and models throughout each area lending to the creepier atmosphere that wasn't entirely captured by the clean and often empty walls of the original. 
Enemies are much more dangerous across the board and cannot be stagger chained. This is complemented by the newer camera based controls that allow you to be more reactive, but the original tank controls are still available if desired. Where this tends to hurt is the bosses, many of which relied on their mobility compared to the player to create a challenge, but now they seem more lack luster receiving little to no upgrades.
Most of the puzzles have been expanded, either requiring more steps, pieces to complete, or more traversal of the map. This may initially sound like a bad thing but many areas of the map have also been upgraded to change, often based on how many times the player has been there or how long a player spends in an area. This adds a great sense of unease and uncertainty to the first few runs where you are unsure if an area is safe even after you've been there. 

If you truly want the original experience, I know that GOG has preserved the original trilogy and you can easily get it there. But for old and new fans alike I think this is both a great game and a quality remake so it's worth giving it a try.

[h1]Resident Evil (2002) Review[/h1]

This game remains the gold standard for how a remake should be handled. Shinji Mikami didn't just update the graphics; he fundamentally changed the rhythm of the game.

The introduction of Crimson Head zombies means you can no longer just drop an enemy and forget about them. You have to burn the bodies, or they come back stronger. It turns a simple zombie shooter into a tense game of resource management and strategic routing.

[h2]The Good[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Atmosphere[/b]: The pre-rendered backgrounds and lighting effects still hold up and create a perfect B-movie horror vibe
[*][b]Crimson Heads[/b]: The mechanic of zombies reanimating if not burned forces you to make hard choices about using kerosene
[*][b]Unlockables[/b]: Modes like Invisible Enemy, Real Survival, and the infinite ammo Samurai Edge give this huge replay value
[*][b]Level Design[/b]: The mansion is a masterclass in claustrophobia and the new areas feel like they always belonged there
[*][b]Classic Charm[/b]: It retains the cheese and spirit of the 1996 original while modernizing the controls and visuals
[/list]

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Resource Scarcity[/b]: The limited kerosene and strict inventory slots can be incredibly punishing for new players
[*][b]Backtracking[/b]: Retreading old areas becomes stressful when zombies break through doors you thought were safe
[*][b]Learning Curve[/b]: Mastering the defensive items and movement canceling takes time and can lead to early deaths
[/list]

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Resident Evil (2002) is the definitive way to experience the mansion incident. It respects the source material while adding mechanics that make it genuinely scarier than the original. It is a masterpiece of the genre and the benchmark against which all other remakes should be judged.

I went into this game pretty much blind, and I can confidently say that the experience holds up. I started the series by playing Resident Evil 4 (2005)  which I really enjoyed, so I decided to play through all of the Resident Evil series on Steam after a great sale for the franchise came up. I plan to go for 100% of the achievements for all of them and this game was of course the first on the list. 
To those who are new to the series like I was, this is actually the remake of the original Resident Evil game which came out in 1996 for the PlayStation. This version was released in 2002 for the GameCube, and just looking at images of the original, the leap in graphics is impressive. This game does not look like it came out in 2002, and I was very impressed with the visuals. This is partially owed to the fact that all of the environments are pre-rendered, something that the developers clearly were able to take advantage of with the fixed camera angles. The first area of the mansion you explore in the entryway looks amazing with the flickering candles and reflections on the stone tiles. 

The fixed camera does make controlling your character awkward, not just because it uses tank controls, but the fact that your character moves based on the direction they are facing, rather then relative to the camera. I am of the opinion that the awkward controls contribute to the gameplay rather then take away from it. It is genuinely frightening when your character is “frozen” in fear and you just cannot get them out of the way of impending danger. Choose the original controls in the options if you want the experience intended by the developers. 

Speaking of which, this is not an easy game. You are presented with 3 difficulties initially, each described in a sentence by what kind of hiking experience you prefer. I assumed the middle one would be the equivalent of “normal” but this is not the case. The first three options available to you from top to bottom are considered normal, easy, and very easy. If you want to unlock additional game modes/difficulties, you will need to beat the game on normal mode.

You also get the choice of two characters, Jill or Chris. I chose Jill for my first playthrough, which I believe was the right choice. Inventory management is important in this game, and Jill having two extra slots makes your initial playthrough much easier (each character has benefits and drawbacks, but most consider Jill to be the easier character to play as). The inventory is also my only complaint about the game. Most people I think would agree that the inventory system is what really highlights the games age, but I was ok with it for the most part. There is a level of strategy to choosing what to bring with you. What I dislike is how key items that are used in puzzles to progress the story take up space. You will consistently receive items that you initially have no context for when it will need to be used (it is a puzzle horror game after all) so you feel torn between carrying an item on you that you have no idea will be useful anytime soon, or leaving it in your item box in the safe rooms. What usually ends up happening is making the long trek somewhere, realizing you needed an item, then backtracking all the way back. It takes a while to move between locations so frequently forgetting things can become tiring. 

To finish on a positive, the soundtrack and sound design is a big highlight for me. They have some truly memorable background music for the various rooms you will explore. My favorite is definitely the save room music though, it’s so simple but so cozy! They are not afraid to use silence as a tool as well, leaving you with just the footsteps of your character or the sudden cracking of thunder (I would be lying if I said it didn’t make me jump a few times). It’s used in the gameplay as well, listening closely once you enter a room for the first time has definitely saved my character’s life a few times.

My final verdict would definitely be a recommendation. Especially for someone who has never played survival horror before, I think this would be a great introduction to the genre. I myself am not a huge horror game fan, but I had a lot of fun playing this and would encourage anyone on the fence to give it a shot, as you may actually end up enjoying yourself!

If you are still unsure, Dunkey made a good review a few years ago, although there will be a few minor spoilers -> https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GduwxBZAxs4

A masterclass in survival horror. It’s atmospheric, it’s slow-paced, it’s campy. It’s also a game you should absolutely play, especially if you’re a fan of the Resident Evil franchise.

You have the choice of playing the campaign as one of two main characters: Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Each character has their own items, weapons, and support characters that lend them a hand as the story progresses. Essentially stranded in an abandoned mansion, you must investigate first to secure an escape route and second to get to the bottom of the strange happenings—and strange things—that plague the house and surroundings. 

I enjoyed the story quite a bit, especially having already connected with these characters in later games. Cutscenes are augmented by the voice-acting, which can be cheesy but is always enjoyable, in my opinion. The character models and environments have a distinct artistic style that complements the tense atmosphere. 

Do not write this game off for its use of tank controls and fixed camera angles. It took maybe an hour for me to feel comfortable with them with no prior experience, and from there, I was able to appreciate how it added to the game play. The fixed camera angles make exploring new areas deliciously intense. You have no clue what’s hiding around the corner, or even a few steps in front of you, because the camera angles dictate what you see. You have no choice but to steel yourself and press forward. I was pleasantly surprised at how effective this was in making me feel scared.  

What stands out to me in this game how important your choices are. I’m not talking narratively, though there are a few paths you can take that dictate which ending you get, but within gameplay. Resources are scarce. Inventory space is scarce. Save rooms and item storage boxes are scarce. It’s an amazing implementation of survival horror.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a pinnacle of both survival horror and remakes. It has become the definitive way to experience the original game, instead of removing most features like the remake of Resident Evil 3, it adds some of the scariest elements of the game such as new enemies and a boss. The game improves the controls and adds new defensive capabilities.
The Spencer mansion was reworked to look much better, and the game is darker while looking better, which makes the horror elements scarier than the original. The puzzles are well crafted, often requiring tedious backtracking and inventory management. 
While I admire the charm of the live-action cutscenes and sub-parr voice acting of the original game, the pre-rendered cutscenes and (mostly) better voice acting make the game feel more professionally designed.
The Crimson Heads are a terrifying addition to the game, the threat of previously dead enemies coming back to life as faster, stronger, and harder-to-kill enemies paired with the limited amount of kerosene leaves you questioning whether to burn or not to burn every zombie you kill.
Speaking of terrifying additions to the game, Lisa Trevor is one of the most tragic Bio-weapon enemies in the series. Her lore and terrifying stalker encounters made Lisa Trevor instantly iconic. The ability to add a completely new character, story, and boss fight into the game without breaking the pace is a true testament to how much care and detail went into the production.
The extra modes the game provides are also great additions, they add more challenge and terror into the game as you have to play the game with added challenges like invisible enemies, zombies wearing bombs that kill you if you shoot them, and unlinked storage boxes. In addition to extra challenge modes, there are unlockable costumes such as casual, military, R.P.D, and BSAA outfits for Chris and Jill.
The multiple endings and additional unlockables in the game add a lot of replayability to the game, and the new game + adds new enemy placements and lets you start with your unlocked weapons, adding more enjoyment to a second playthrough.
If I were to find a negative it would be that the voice acting can be flat at times, it's not goofy like in the original, but it definitely can be distracting at times.
Overall, the Resident Evil HD Remaster is one of the greatest survival horror games of all time. It is a prime example of what a remake should be and by no means does it lie when it tells you to "Enter the Survival Horror"

Y'all ever heard of this indie franchise, Resident Evil? A month or two back, I bought RE4 and enjoyed my time so frickin' much that I decided to make my way back through the franchise in release order—minus the spin-offs for now. I grabbed RE1 for PC and fell in love about as fast as a teenage boy seeing a cute cashier at the grocery store. The thing is old-school, brother, through and through. You will die, again and again—hell, they even name the achievement for dying the first time, "Get Used to This."

This is perhaps where my appreciation for the game really bloomed. There is very little handholding. They drop you in that sinister-ass mansion and tell you to ♥♥♥♥ off. Teaching the boy how to swim by throwing him in the pool, if you will. Because of that, my every advancement was a victory, each puzzle a rewarding experience, and even figuring out how to grab the shotgun felt special. It wasn't just a gun I bought with credits; I EARNED it.

Oddly enough, the tank controls didn't take that long to click. I knew through cultural osmosis that they're a big point of contention in the older games, but for me, they're pretty neat. Just like the level design itself, there's an exhilarating feeling when you master the controls and start dodging zombies like Michael Jackson doing a moonwalk with ants up his ass.

What else? Oh yeah, the game is a masterclass in horror. The fixed cameras bring a level of tension that just isn't possible to replicate with 3D cameras. Is there something beyond that corridor I can't see, or is my mind playing tricks on me? Even the slow door animations on the loading screens startled me because I always kept thinking they'd sneak a jumpscare in at some point.

All in all, a terrific experience. I might go back and replay as Chris one day to see what changes in the story.

after playing RE 2 3 and 4 remakes, and not having played any resident evil games prior, this game initially felt very alien and uncomfortably unstructured. the luxuries you have in the later remakes, such as items being marked on the map, doors on the map showing what key they need, infinite saves, etc. are not present here, which made my initial hours frustrating despite enjoying the story and atmosphere of the game. i played on easy difficulty, which is the 2nd easiest, and in those initial hours the game felt very challenging due to its fixed camera angles and slow combat animations.

however, once i got past a certain point something clicked, and i was able to make consistent progress with the game's common usage of backtracking and vague puzzle hints. the combat started seeming less and less foreign, and now i can admit that most of my current nitpicks after finishing the game on both Jill and Chris's playthroughs are mainly due to my preference of "modern video game" conveniences.

Resident Evil HD Remaster : By Triple F

"Resident Evil HD Remaster" is a faithful yet polished adaptation of the 2002 GameCube remake, which itself reimagined the 1996 classic that defined the survival horror genre. This remaster enhances the already stellar visuals, improves accessibility with modern control options, and retains the tense atmosphere, intricate puzzles, and resource management that made the original such a masterpiece. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer to the series, "Resident Evil HD Remaster" stands as one of the finest horror experiences in gaming history.

The game follows S.T.A.R.S. operatives Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine as they investigate the mysterious Spencer Mansion, only to uncover a nightmare of biological horrors unleashed by the Umbrella Corporation. The story is simple yet effective, drawing players into a web of corporate conspiracy, grotesque creatures, and claustrophobic terror. The game’s nonlinear exploration encourages backtracking and discovery, making the mansion feel like a puzzle box full of secrets. With multiple endings depending on player choices, the narrative offers strong replay value.

Graphically speaking, the remaster breathes new life into the GameCube remake’s already impressive pre-rendered backgrounds. Every room in the mansion oozes atmosphere, from flickering candlelit hallways to rain-soaked exteriors. The high-definition textures enhance details like bloodstains on walls, rotting flesh on zombies, and the grotesque designs of bosses like the Crimson Head and Lisa Trevor. While some background elements can appear slightly outdated due to their pre-rendered nature, the overall presentation holds up remarkably well, making it one of the most visually stunning survival horror games ever made.

Gameplay remains faithful to the original, with classic tank controls and fixed camera angles preserving the tension. However, Capcom added an alternative control scheme, allowing smoother movement for players unfamiliar with traditional survival horror mechanics. Combat is deliberately slow and methodical, emphasizing careful aiming and ammunition conservation rather than run-and-gun action. The introduction of defensive items like daggers and flash grenades adds a layer of strategy, giving players a fighting chance against enemies without making the game feel too forgiving.

The enemy design in "Resident Evil HD Remaster" is superb, with standard zombies becoming an ever-present threat due to the terrifying Crimson Head mechanic. If not burned or decapitated, defeated zombies reanimate as faster, deadlier versions of themselves, forcing players to carefully plan their kills. Boss fights remain tense and memorable, from the grotesque Yawn snake to the relentless Tyrant, each requiring a balance of preparation and resourcefulness. The game's limited inventory system also adds to the challenge, as players must make tough decisions about which weapons, healing items, and keys to carry at any given time.

Sound design plays a crucial role in the game’s horror experience. The eerie silence of the mansion is punctuated by distant moans, creaking doors, and unsettling ambient noises that keep players on edge. The remastered sound mix enhances these details, making headphones an excellent way to experience the game. The voice acting, while significantly improved from the 1996 original, retains some of its B-movie charm, fitting the game's blend of campy horror and serious tension. The orchestral soundtrack, particularly in the save rooms, creates an eerie yet oddly comforting atmosphere that perfectly complements the survival horror aesthetic.

Overall, "Resident Evil HD Remaster" is the definitive way to experience one of the greatest survival horror games of all time. It maintains the brutal difficulty, intricate level design, and haunting atmosphere that made the original so iconic while offering enough improvements to appeal to modern audiences. Whether you're a veteran revisiting the Spencer Mansion or a newcomer experiencing it for the first time, this remaster is a must-play for any horror fan.

The Resident Evil remake is the perfect bridge between the old RE games and something that you could enjoy in the present day because it doesn't look too goofy to be scary (like the PS1 original) and has a few quality-of-life improvements. However, what sets this remake apart from those like RE2's is that it does not change itself to suit modern gameplay at all. 

The game maintains almost every aspect of classic RE design that you can think of. Item boxes are rare, resources are very scarce, you can run out of save ribbons, you can softlock yourself if you waste too much ammo, there are time-sensitive events that you can't reverse, and the limited item slots force you to spend a lot of time figuring out the simplest things.

It's a perfect representation of a time when developers didn't mind making the game extremely confusing because they expected you to have access to a guide. A lot of puzzle solutions or needing a specific item at a specific time makes you go "how was I supposed to know that?!" - and I wouldn't just chalk it up to a case of skill issue. When inventory is limited as hell and puzzle items have to be carried manually, keeping a specific item with you at a specific time because you MIGHT need it is something that requires a lot of trial and error - and reloading your save files.

Besides the puzzles, the combat in the game feels very intense because zombies (especially their alternate versions such as Crimson Heads) are a force to be reckoned with and you're always trying your best to save ammo when fighting them. You will have to leave a lot of them alive in random places to ensure you have enough ammo for boss fights, and that makes backtracking a challenge every time you have to go back for something. The game keeps you on the edge of your seat and feels rewarding to complete.

All in all, Resident Evil 1 Remake is a great game that I think everyone should experience at least once - and don't shy away from checking out a guide sometimes because the game is built in a way that if you don't use a guide, you'll spend weeks trying to check where every single item goes.

Back in 2002, Capcom has made a great decision to re-visit one of their most influential and genre-defining games - the very first Resident Evil - to remake it into something more fitting to the size and grandeur that the series has grown into by that point, giving the fans of the franchise a new way to experience the original king of survival-horror shooters and luring new players in. In 2015, this remake got an HD remaster, which is what Steam now offers, and is, without a doubt, a definitive and by far the most enjoyable way to both get into the series and get back to where it all started.

[h1] [i] “Overcome your fears and survive.” [/i] [/h1]

I don't think I need to beat around the bush - RE1 Remake is as close to perfection as a game in this constantly re-inventing franchise can get. Unlike the later, pre-RE7 titles which went more and more in a Michel Bay-esque direction, putting action and spectacle front and center, the first game shines through by being very compact and contained, with the characters being confined to the Spencer Manor as a singular area, and is honestly all the better for it. This is because this allows RE Remake to really make each area shine in its own way, be it through cinematic camera angles, memorable soundtrack, or unique enemies or items. 

Additionally, the remake makes a lot of improvements and much appreciated additions to original which expand it to be more enjoyable, and also be more in line with the lore established in the later titles. While not everything is necessarily for the better, the vast majority of it helps making it the masterpiece of survival horror it is today. 

While I can easily recommend RE Remake to anyone who either is into the survival horror genre or, more specifically, the RE franchise, you should also understand that it still retains some (nowadays) more "archaic" mechanics such as very limited inventory, scarce items needed for saving the game, or a instant game-over scenarios if you aren't careful. This can make it frustrating for some, but also all the more rewarding for others. That being said, you'd be hard-pressed to find a more well-rounded, perfected and modernized survival horror with a capturing atmosphere and intriguing story.

*Spoilers Ahead*

This game is the purest Resident Evil has ever felt. Having played through almost all of the mainline entries, both old and new, I can confidently say that among all the remakes, this one stands out as the best. It faithfully retells the original story while refining its core elements, making it a perfect example of how a remake should be done.

It’s easy to see why this is a top pick for many Resident Evil fans. The game is absolutely dripping with atmosphere, from its haunting lighting to its eerie soundtrack. Enemies feel more vicious than ever, and the introduction of Crimson Heads adds an extra layer of tension, making every encounter feel like a true struggle for survival. The addition of defensive items is also a welcome improvement, addressing some of the frustrations from the original where enemy grabs could feel relentless. The puzzles have been refined as well, making for an even more engaging experience.

Resident Evil has had its fair share of tragic and unsettling moments, but Lisa Trevor’s story stands among the most heartbreaking in the entire series. The moment you open the coffin and reveal her mother’s skull is utterly devastating. What follows—Lisa clutching the skull before leaping into the abyss, calling out "Mother"—is one of the most hauntingly tragic scenes in any Resident Evil game. And when you realize that she’s essentially immortal, doomed to spend eternity at the bottom of that pit with nothing but her mother’s remains, it hits even harder.

That said, the game does have one major flaw: the camera. If you opt for the updated control scheme over the original tank controls, the sudden camera shifts can make movement frustrating. Pressing forward can suddenly send your character veering in an unintended direction when the camera angle changes, which can be especially annoying in tense moments. 

This is peak Resident Evil, and I highly recommend playing it. If possible, I also suggest trying the original—it’s fascinating to compare the two and see how they differ. This remake is one of the standout entries in the entire series, and playing it only makes me prouder to be a Resident Evil fan.

To beat this game, you need to be resourceful. You need to be careful how to use your ammo, whether you should kill enemies or not and know when and where to save. If you try kill every enemy in this game, you won't make it past the halfway point before you have run out of ammo and have to fight a boss. Even worse, dead zombies can come back to life as "Crimson Heads" which are much harder to kill and get around. Zombies only stay dead permanently if you burn them, but you have a limited amount of inventory slots as well. This game is set up to give you a hard as time as possible. Things that I don't like:
-It feels like there's no point in using the handgun. I have however never fought any bosses or any other enemies than the regular zombies so I'm not convinced that it's useless.
-Dodging zombies feels really inconsistent. I know that you're supposed to get close enough for them to lunge at you and then run past them while they're in "recovery". This works, but only sometimes. Every once in a while they just never enter recovery mode so you're forced to take a hit anyway or waste a defensive item.
-The fixed camera angles make it difficult to understand where you are and where you're going as well as the dimensions of the area that you're currently in. A video game remake done right.

It is a shame that it has been over 20 years, and this game still holds the crown of how to properly remake a game.

For one, if you played the original 1996 game, you will feel very familar with how this game plays. There's extremely minute changes to the gameplay and as such, veterans will be able to sink right in. I cannot stress how important this is for remaking a video game. DON'T ALTER THE CORE GAMEPLAY!

Secondly, the additions that were made didn't subtract from the experience. For example, you can now hold self-defense items that can save you from being chomped on by a zombie - a tool mostly meant for newbie players that may have difficulty juking through enemies. 

But then there's the Crimson Head mechanic - if you put down a zombie, after a certain amount of time, they will reanimate into a redder, faster, and more dangerous zombie. Now, if you know anything about the pre-RE4 Resident Evil games, killing monsters is secondary to the main gameplay of just getting from A to B. The monsters are just mere obstacles in your path, so you shouldn't really be spending resources killing them. The Remake decides to punish players who do with Crimson Heads. Again, mostly there for newbies. 

Veterans of the original game will have little trouble with this Remake albeit for maybe Lisa - one of the other additions of the Remake, and I would argue its worst one. With Lisa's addition came a few brand new areas and the boss character herself. I personally feel it needlessly elongates the game a bit (not anything too severe. You can still beat this game in less than 2 hours if you know what you're doing). While I don't like Lisa's addition, at least it doesn't overstay its welcome and most of all, it doesn't radically change the gameplay mechanics to something that the original never had you do. 

I of course recommend this game without question. If you liked the 1996 game and want to see it graphically enhanced, experience tighter controls, and hear better voice-acting (alas no meme-worthy Jill Sandwiches this time), pick this game up. 
If you're new to the series or have never played this specific entry before, I also recommend it if you are looking for a fun little maze/puzzle-box game to solve. While the tank-control movement may take getting used to, you can also use the Altermate Controls (but take heed: whenever the camera angle switches, you might need to jerk your analog stick in a different direction for your character to move correctly). Just know that the enemies you encounter (especially early on in the game) aren't worth wasting your ammo on. It's more about just getting from A to B: use this item to unlock a door so you can get a new item to unlock another door somewhere else.

I really wish Capcom would look back at this Remake and use it as the guide on how to make their future remakes, because... good lord. Those new remakes are so half-assed and barely even capture what made the originals liked to begin with.

Resident Evil HD Remaster remains a visually impressive and surprisingly fun game with its wonderfully gruesome and goofy story, beautifully pre-rendered backgrounds, and neat character designs. Unfortunately, the gameplay feels quite janky by modern standards. The game features a variety of atmospheric locations, several puzzles, and lots of interesting items to collect and utilize. If you can stomach the fixed camera angles and all the quirks, I highly recommend giving this game at least one playthrough.

The environments are both beautifully crafted and at the same time eerily dark, damp, and deteriorated. The mansion can feel like a maze during your first playthrough, which adds to the sense of mystery. The audio design significantly enhances the mood—squeaking floorboards, dripping water, thunder, howling wind, and moaning zombies evoke classic old-school horror movie vibes.

I played through the game for the first time without any guides or mods, but I recommend installing the door animation fix as soon as possible. Those unnecessarily long door-opening animations clearly don’t belong in the remake. The game also has some frustrating issues with colliders. For example, you might aim at a pickup or point of interest and miss it, leading you to think it’s not interactable. This can be especially frustrating since the game doesn’t provide visual highlights for interactive objects. Some doors are also hard to spot, and at least three gave me trouble during my first playthrough.

A couple of puzzles stumped me, and I had to get help. The waterfall puzzle was particularly frustrating, and another one failed simply because of a collider issue—it turned out my aim wasn’t precise enough. The story, however, turned out to be much longer than I expected, which was a pleasant surprise.

Both tank controls and the alternative control scheme are clunky, requiring too much concentration to be enjoyable. These can be of cause learned, but the controls are far from being intuitive. Many of the horror moments come not from atmosphere but from the difficulty of aiming or navigating. You’re often forced to aim at enemies outside the static camera view, which can be frustrating and unintuitive. Overall, combat is the weakest part of the game. Despite being a "survival horror" title, combat often feels more like a test of patience. It’s largely about maneuvering around enemies and trying to get a shot in without getting hit or bitten. Newer Resident Evil remakes handle this aspect much better, so if you’re new to the series, consider starting with Resident Evil 2 Remake instead!

I never played the original game back in the day (despite owning Capcom/RE art books and always liking the series’ concept), nor did I try this version when it first came out. However, it’s easy to see why this game remains so beloved. There are small variations in the story depending on how you play, multiple endings, and the option to start with either Jill or Chris, each offering slightly different gameplay experiences. The game also features three difficulty settings. I naturally started with "Very Easy" to focus on experiencing the story. Completing playthroughs unlocks additional content, like new difficulty modes and alternative costumes.

So if you can look past these issues, RE is still mostly very enjoyable, fun old-school game at its core. Simply don’t expect anything too serious horror stuff, but this game has its share of scary moments.

[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster breathes new life into the original survival horror masterpiece that started it all. [h1]A Return to Survival Horror’s Roots[/h1]
[b]The remaster revisits the classic story of Resident Evil, where players step into the shoes of either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, members of the elite S.T.A.R.S. team, sent to investigate mysterious murders on the outskirts of Raccoon City. What follows is a horrifying descent into the heart of the Spencer Mansion, a labyrinth of secrets, puzzles, and grotesque monstrosities.
The game stays true to its roots, focusing on tension, resource management, and environmental storytelling. Even after all these years, the mansion is as haunting and enigmatic as ever.[/b]

[h1]Enhanced Visuals and Atmosphere[/h1]
[b]The updated graphics in the HD Remaster are a standout feature. The pre-rendered backgrounds are beautifully remastered, with enhanced lighting and textures bringing the creepy atmosphere of the Spencer Mansion to life. Shadows flicker, lightning illuminates the dark hallways, and every creak of the floorboards feels more immersive than ever.
The game’s sound design is another highlight, with eerie background music and haunting ambient noises adding to the tension. It’s a game that demands to be played with headphones for the full effect.[/b]

[h1]Refined Controls: Old and New[/h1]
[b]One of the biggest improvements is the addition of modernized controls. The tank controls of the original, while still available for purists, are now complemented by an alternative control scheme that feels more fluid and intuitive. This makes the game more accessible for new players while preserving the challenge and suspense that defined the original.[/b]

[h1]Puzzles and Exploration: Engaging and Rewarding[/h1]
[b]The remaster retains the intricate puzzles and exploration that were a hallmark of the original. From cryptic riddles to hidden keys, each discovery feels satisfying and rewarding. The layout of the mansion itself is a puzzle, with shortcuts, locked doors, and secret pathways that gradually reveal themselves as you progress.[/b]

[h1]Survival Horror at Its Best[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster captures the essence of survival horror. Resources like ammunition and healing items are scarce, forcing players to make strategic choices and manage their inventory carefully. Every encounter with a zombie or monstrous creature feels tense and consequential, with death always lurking around the corner.
The addition of Crimson Heads, zombies that can resurrect into faster, deadlier versions if not disposed of properly, adds a new layer of fear and strategy, ensuring that even areas you thought were “safe” remain a source of dread.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Stunning visual overhaul: Pre-rendered backgrounds and lighting effects look gorgeous and atmospheric.
[*]Refined controls: The addition of modern controls makes the game more accessible.
[*]Classic survival horror: Maintains the tension, resource management, and puzzle-solving that define the genre.
[*]Improved sound design: Creepy ambient noises and music enhance the eerie atmosphere.
[*]Faithful to the original: Captures the essence of what made the original Resident Evil a masterpiece.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Fixed camera angles: While iconic, they can feel dated to some players and make combat tricky.
[*]Limited inventory space: Adds to the challenge but can be frustrating at times.
[*]Pace may feel slow: The deliberate pacing and backtracking might not appeal to players unfamiliar with older games.
[*]No major story changes: Veterans of the original may find little new content in terms of narrative.
[*]Lack of accessibility options: Limited features for modern accessibility standards.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil HD Remaster is a masterclass in remaking a classic. It preserves the charm and terror of the original while improving on its visuals, controls, and overall presentation. This is survival horror at its finest, with a haunting atmosphere, engaging puzzles, and relentless tension that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

First, let me clarify: This is just another port of the RE HD Remaster, so there’s not much to critique about this specific version. It runs smoothly and still looks gorgeous, even after all these years. And the modern controls still break this game similar to how Full Active Mode breaks the combat system in Star Ocean 3. That’s about it. Instead of reviewing this particular release of REmake1, I’ll share my thoughts on the game as a whole:

Obviously, REmake1 is a must-play for anyone who enjoys classic survival horror. Personally, I’ve played, completed, and 100%-ed this game countless times since its original release on the Nintendo GameCube. It’s a prime example of how to remake a game, and also of how to do classic survival horror right. At least, that’s what I thought.

However, when I played it again on Steam, I started to notice its weird pacing. The game feels somewhat stretched out in parts - if you know what I mean. Some of the improvements are great, but the game often has you running back and forth between two points way too many times. I’m not talking about returning to the mansion with a new key - I’m talking about literally running between two locations that are only four or five rooms apart. Then there are other annoyances, like not being allowed to run while carrying the nitro. There’s the broken door handle, the repetitive trips in the underground tunnels to get that broken flamethrower, and the frustrating statue puzzle to get the cylinder shaft. Overall there are just way too many slow and repetative parts, where you have to push stuff. And none of the puzzles requires any real thinking either.

Usually, in RE, after collecting all the trophies, I do one last perfect run with each character, gathering every item along the way and putting them in a nice order within the item box. But with REmake1, I skipped doing that with Chris because I was already fed up with the game’s odd pacing. I even had to resort to outfit mods and mods that skip the door animations to make the nine playthroughs a little more tolerable.

The survival mechanics of Resident Evil are rock solid. The game takes place in an enclosed space with limited resources which are often dangerous to obtain, especially if you haven't cleared the enemies or, worse yet, killed the zombies without burning them or destroying their heads.
Backtracking is not only dangerous but necessary due to the limited inventory and manual saving system so there are real choices to be made when it comes to moving around the mansion, what enemies to avoid, which ones to kill, and, perhaps most important of all, when to save.
This last aspect is what prevents me from saying that Resident Evil is perfect (the game is that good) because a new player has no way of knowing ahead of time how often they should save. 
For those who don't know, saving is a limited resource in Resident Evil because it requires ink ribbons that the player needs to find like any other item. This helps enhance the tension but it also promotes exploring as far as you can go, making notes of what you need to do and then reloading to try and maximize how much you do with each save. This is clearly overkill since you can save pretty comfortably and with ribbons to spare every 15-20 minutes (probably 5 on very easy) but I had no idea as a new player. Perhaps this says more about my own personality, but I digress.
The rest of the gameplay is quite good. Even the original tank controls have been retouched with the ability to do a quick turn and I think I prefer them over the modern setting for playing on a keyboard. There isn't much to say about the combat since aiming is largely automatic, it's more about the resource management aspect (ammo and inventory space in this case).
The presentation is nothing short of fantastic. Even the rejected concept art for this game was great, the mansion is beautiful and I love the sound effects.
To conclude, it was hard for me to get into the game but I'm glad I stuck around because it's totally worth it.

The biggest tips a new player can get are to avoid killing enemies that aren't in the way, and to not pick up everything you see unless you know for sure you need to. I actually remember playing the OG ‘96 version on an emulator on my phone a veery long time ago – pretty sure it was a Jill playthrough. I thought it was dated in every way and dismissed as a bad game. Now, I see I was only half wrong. It still has that dated gameplay – cause its a remaster, not a remake – but it’s definitely not a bad game. It holds up surprisingly well, whether in gameplay or the cheesiness. 

The first thing I understood when opening the game for the first time is that this would be a campy game, with a silly storyline and cheese lines like “Jill Sandwich” or “Never believe the liiiiiessss”. I truly wish they had kept the original intro because it really sets the tone for what kind of game this is. The new is more in tone with a game but I miss the B-movie aspect.

As for the story, the only way for you to even know there’s one is by reading the documents/diaries laying around. It’s disconnected at best, and connecting the dots is left entirely up to you. Thankfully, those documents/diaries are short and straightforward with little fluff. I’ll be honest, the story sucks. Later entries is where Resident Evil (henceforth RE, with this entry being RE HD) really begins with this one being little more than an introduction, a set piece for the rest. I still recommend reading those docs though.

As for the gameplay, I chose Chris purely because I still have ten other RE games to go through so I didn’t dwell on it or look into any gameplay differences between him and Jill – and, boy, do I regret it. Because Chris has only six empty slots in his inventory, the ungodly amount of backtracking I did was surreal! I’m convinced half my total playtime is just from that. He also gets more enemies spawn and has to do a lot of backtracking! But he’s not without good points. Unlike Jill, he has higher health and can tank more damage, has better crit chance (zombie heads explode) and, IMO, he also gets the better guns and defensive weapons. Overall I’d say he’s more action oriented. I didn’t play with Jill since Chris’s backtracking really killed my desire for a replay. But yeah, backtracking. Lots of it. Don’t forget.

As for the graphics, Capcom tried to upscale the textures resolution and they do look nice but nothing that’ll make you stop at any point and take a screenshot. Overall, they’re okay and nice looking.

As for the soundtrack, this is where the game truly shines. It plays pivotal role in creating the atmosphere, and it’s done exceptionally well. From the eerie silence to the hauntingly creepy songs on a loop, they do their job masterfully and when paired with the fixed camera angles, it kept me on edge through out. Several times, I walked from a quiet room to a corridor, only to be greeted by a chilling track and immediately tense up as a result. Even when there wasn’t any zombies around, that suspense lingered, with that constant “what if they are just around the corner?”. Absolutely brilliant!

As for the cheese, well… It’s everything really. From the puzzles’ silliness to the over-the-top boss fights, I often found myself laughing out loud at how ridiculous some parts of the game were. It’s a horror game the same way The Cabin in the Woods is a horror movie – self-aware and unapologetically campy. Of course, I don’t mean its a bad thing or that I didn’t like it; far from it. RE HD has that B-movie feel to it and is not ashamed of it, and to me that makes it a better game.

So, do I recommend it? Yes, I very much do! RE HD is an excellent remaster that fixes and updates several things—notably the graphics—but retains the core experience. It’s a game that doesn’t shy away from its identity, and that makes it all the more enjoyable.

P.S.: I do think that if Umbrella had given the budget to hiring Architects to “Safety and Security” instead, the outbreak would never had happened. Just a thought.

A great game with poor quality-of-life features.

The fixed camera angles, inability to drop items, rigid aiming mechanics, and lengthy door-opening animations in older games were "limitations" imposed by the technological constraints of their time. These features don't inherently hold nostalgic or classic value. If the developers from that era had any choices of getting modern technologies, I am sure that they would choose to fix these. So, instead of blindly praising these issues for their "classic" status, it’s important to critically evaluate them and acknowledge their shortcomings rather than excusing them simply because they’re part of an older era.

Resident Evil 1 HD remaster is my first Resident Evil to play and I found it to be a great starting point for the series. The game gives you an option of using the classic "tank controls" or a modern control scheme. The static camera initially something to get use too but soon after it was never a problem. 

You can play as both Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield who have their advantages and disadvantages, they also have different people show up in their playthroughs. There is different difficulty settings which you can choose from. These settings determine enemy and resource placements as well as the amount of ink ribbons you will find in your playthrough which are used to save your game. I did the easy difficulty and I had plenty of ink ribbons left over by the end; I never felt like I was going to run out of them. I played Jill, who gets a good variety of weapons throughout the story. I found the first area the most difficult. After moving past the first area, the game became a lot more manageable.

This game coming out in 1996 would have blown people's minds. The art and the atmosphere are insane. The horror doesn't come from the zombies themselves, but the scarcity of materials for you to survive. 

I would recommend following a guide for this game, the puzzles are very esoteric and knowing where you need to go is an immense help. There is the IGN guide or under the Steam guides for this game, there is a non-spoiler version where you have to use your brain a little more.

I recommend this game, while it's different to most other Resident Evil games with the static camera and optional tank controls. There is a lot of love put into this game, the difficulty was perfect and it's a great starting point for getting into the series, despite it's differences to the rest of it. I hope this game gets a remake, similar to Resident Evil 2's where the puzzles are less esoteric where you don't need a guide in order to finish it in a reasonable time.

[h1]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/h1]
[h3][Overview][/h3]
Resident Evil (or Resident Evil HD Remaster) is a remaster of the 2002 GameCube remake of the 1996 PS1 survival horror classic. You play as either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield, both members of S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team, investigating a mansion overrun with zombies and mutants from Umbrella’s T-Virus. They must survive with limited resources, solve puzzles, and uncover Umbrella’s dark web of secrets. Jill’s lockpick and extra inventory slots make her the easier starter for beginners; Chris packs more health for combat but has his own disadvantages.

[h3][Recommended Tweaks and Tips][/h3]
- [url=https://github.com/ThirteenAG/WidescreenFixesPack/releases/tag/re1]Resident Evil Fusion Fix (Door Skip + other fixes)[/url]
- [url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B4GQBygqK9jIMGFYSFAxUmYyMFU/view?resourcekey=0-f2HRH11eobZN1slyNSIe5w]Normalized/Fixed Music Mod[/url]
- [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/residentevilbiohazardhdremaster/mods/102]RESCALE[/url]
- Use the original 4:3 aspect ratio. The 16:9 mode zooms in, cropping details and ruining the cinematic framing.
- Use original tank controls. The alternate controls clash with the fixed camera angles, making movement clunky.
- Though it may be tempting, avoid killing zombies as much as possible. They will respawn as powerful Crimson Heads if they aren't burnt or killed with a headshot.
- Save across multiple slots (at least three) to avoid being stuck if you mismanage items or hit a tough spot.

[h3][Positives][/h3]
- Incredible atmosphere. The art style and audio design are great and add immersion.
- Intense survival horror gameplay. Success requires planning, strategy, and resource management.
- Very iconic map and environments. The Spencer Mansion is great, and even expanded upon in this remake compared to the PS1 version.
- Memorable characters. Chris and Jill are solid protagonists, Barry and Rebecca are great companions, and Wesker is an enjoyable villain.
- Great music. This game has tons of iconic tracks.
- Good puzzles. Very memorable and usually not too abstract.
- Great additions to the game. This version, being a remake of the PS1 game, adds in new locations and characters like Lisa Trevor.
- Interesting story and lore. This version of the game expands upon the story of the original.
- Multiple endings to go for. The best ending isn’t super complicated to achieve, which is appreciated.
- The ability to play slightly different campaigns as Jill or Chris adds replay value.

[h3][Mixed][/h3]
- The game offers minimal direction, on a first playthrough it can be hard to remember what you need to do. You don't want much hand holding in a game like this, but it can make it rough for new players who didn't play the PS1 version. Once you learn the game, this isn't too much of an issue though.

[h3][Negatives][/h3]
- The door loading animations are tedious and no longer necessary given modern hardware (see the Recommended Tweaks.)
- There’s a bug where some of the music will play faster than intended (see the Recommended Tweaks.)
- The final boss is very easy provided you didn’t waste all your ammo.
- All of the endings are very short and none of them are 100% canon either.

[h3][Conclusion][/h3]
Some of it’s design may feel antiquated, but there’s no denying that Resident Evil is peak survival horror. The mix of strategic gameplay and incredible atmosphere makes for a great time.

Resident Evil HD Remastered faithfully preserves the core experience of the original game while updating its visuals and controls for modern audiences. It's a must-play for anyone who loves survival horror and wants to experience one of the genre's defining titles. 

Story: You take on the roles of S.T.A.R.S. members Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine, tasked with investigating a series of gruesome murders on the outskirts of Raccoon City. The investigation leads you to a creepy mansion where things quickly spiral into chaos. Unraveling the dark secrets of the mansion, you encounter zombies, mutated creatures, and sinister bio-experiments gone horribly wrong. The story is filled with twists and keeps you on edge as you discover more about the infamous Umbrella Corporation.


• Atmosphere: The eerie corridors, the constant tension of not knowing what's around the corner, and the brilliant use of lightning and shadows create a creepy, immersive environment.

• Controls & Gameplay: While the tank controls might take some time getting use to, they add to the nostalgic charm. For those who prefer a more modern experience, the alternative control scheme is a welcome addition, but the original controls are still available for that classic feel.

• Difficulty & Puzzles: The game strikes a great balance with its difficulty. Resource management and puzzle-solving keep the tension high throughout. Every corner you turn feels like a gamble, and the satisfaction of solving the mansion's legendary puzzles is still just as rewarding.

• Graphics & Sound: The visual upgrades are outstanding. The remastered version captures the dark, haunting atmosphere of the Spencer Mansion beautifully. The sound design and music perfectly complement the setting, pulling you deeper into the game's world.

While this remaster does justice to the original, I can't help but feel that Resident Evil HD deserves a full remake treatment, just like Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4. A remake could elevate this masterpiece to new heights while keeping the soul of the game intact.

[h3] In bullets, I'd say: [/h3]

[h3] Now for my longer thoughts probably no one would read ;) but - [/h3] 
For some context, I've always had my eyes on RE, and naively assumed this would be somewhat spiritually similar to the Silent Hill series in terms of gameplay. I have played most of SH back in the day and remember completing the games mostly on my own without that much help of walkthroughs (could also be due to being younger and more patient :D ).

So, I've finally decided to take my steps into Resident Evil's mansion. I guess at this point I don't have much new stuff to say. Despite the release on steam being about a decade ago I think the game still looks pretty great visually and at first I was really pulled in.

As appropriate to remasters, gameplay remained largely loyal to the original (as far as I know), so that means late 90s mentatlity. The game is not ashamed to not explain to you everything, to have clunky control scheme, and to be extremely unforgiving, even on easy difficulty.
This are in facts some of the aspects that also make this a great horror title, though, as I was always very freaked out to make any error, and there are many reasons to be -
You have to manually save the game in some very specific save points.
You depend on save items which you have to find and manage carefully.
You have (very) little slots in inventory, so must decide carefully what are you carrying around with you, and pretty much everything requires inventory space: weapon, ammo, healing items, puzzle items.
Puzzles are cool but are potentially deadly as well.
You kill enemies (which requires not too little bullets!), they're not really dead, until you burn them - for which you need a lighter and some oil (so two more slots in inventory!)
Enemies start out as dumb zombies but getting stronger and crazier over time (kudos for enemy diversity!)

So, after having finished around half of the game on Easy mode along with some help of trainers (yeah I'm that noob!) I have ended up with mixed feelings.

All these points, along with great atmosphere and well crafted scares and horror, make this a truly horror masterpiece as expected, keeping you on edge, and that's good, right?
Still, I found myself lacking the patience (and time!) to die again, retry my steps again, having to backtrack over and over because I realized I need an item which I LEFT IN THE FRIGGIN CABINET, dying again on the way to get it.

So back to my original point, I would recommend this and am certifying this as a great game, but for those of you who are capable of enduring the outdated gameplay mechanics.

One last point I'd like to mention is, that I found the story rather underwhelming, even though I came with very low expectations, knowing this is intentionally not the strongest suite of the game (and possibly the entire series). So, I got this would be the sort of a B Zombie movie plot, and still thought that the story execution, along with the scripts and cutscenes, was, truly, meeeh minus.

I've played many hours across the different releases of this, and I anticipate many more in my future. This game is incredible. The atmosphere, music, sound design, visuals, all fantastic. The only thing I need now is a way to explore the Spencer Mansion in VR.

The Resident Evil remake, originally released for the GameCube in 2002, isn’t just a simple remaster of the 1996 classic, it’s a full-on reimagining that elevates the series to a new level. Capcom took everything that worked in the original game and pushed it to its absolute limits, delivering a visually stunning and deeply terrifying experience that redefined survival horror.

The game transports you back to the eerie, labyrinthine Spencer Mansion that clearly has more hidden passageways and cryptic puzzles than it has functional bathrooms, but with more detail and atmosphere than you could have imagined in the PS1 days. Every corridor is steeped in tension, from the flickering lights casting long shadows to the disturbing moans of creatures you can’t quite see yet. Where every door you open feels like you're pushing your luck just a bit too far.

And then there are the zombies. These guys aren’t the slow, bumbling corpses you might remember, they’re more like nightmare-inducing marathon runners after they’ve finished carbo-loading. The game’s biggest innovation? Crimson Heads. Because apparently, regular zombies weren’t scary enough. Now, when you think you’ve dealt with one, it rises back up, faster, stronger, and with an attitude problem. Oh yeah, Capcom thought, “What if zombies, but on steroids?” Forget about a double-tap; now you need to douse them in kerosene and set them on fire. Just normal survival tactics, really.

The real villain of the game, though? Your inventory. It’s like they gave Chris Redfield the world’s smallest fanny pack. "You want to carry both ammo AND healing herbs? Haha, nope! Pick one, good luck with your choices." You’ll spend more time backtracking to the item box than actually solving puzzles, all the while hoping you don’t run into another zombie that you forgot to burn. Honestly, at this point, you’re more of a FedEx delivery person for your own stuff than a trained S.T.A.R.S. operative.

The puzzles? Oh, they’re still here, and they’re as ridiculous as ever. Apparently, the mansion's architect was a puzzle-loving madman who thought the best security system involved emblems, statues, and paintings that scream "Don’t touch me unless you’ve got three other bizarre items." It’s like an escape room designed by someone with a deep love of making you feel just a little bit dumb. But you will feel like a genius when you finally figure it out, right before you realize you’ve got three zombies chasing you and you still haven’t saved.

The Resident Evil remake is more than just a nostalgic re-release. It’s an exemplar of how to handle remakes, honoring the original while vastly improving upon it. The enhanced graphics, expanded lore, and refined gameplay mechanics make it feel like a fresh experience, even for those familiar with the 1996 version. It sets the bar for what a survival horror game should be: atmospheric, terrifying, and deeply immersive.

In the end, Resident Evil Remake is a game where the biggest enemy is probably your own panic as you try to manage your item slots while running from zombies who just refuse to stay dead. The mansion may be filled with horrific monsters, but nothing is scarier than the realization that you left the one item you need across the map in a chest.

Resident Evil Remake 2015 HD Remaster

Story 8/10 - This game is a remake, which very closely follows the plot of the original 1996 PS1 game, with updated voice acting and dialogue. If you've played the original game as much as I have, you may be sad to see some of the classic lines have been omitted (one in particular), but objectively speaking, this is a vast improvement. The story itself isn't exactly Shakespeare, as most of your time spent in the game is more-or-less about surviving and escaping, but there are enough twists and turns to keep players invested in potentially determining the root cause of the chaos in Raccoon City. While the lore of the Resident Evil franchise has become bats*** crazy nowadays, keep in mind that this was the story that started it all, with "Outlandish reports of families being attacked by a group of about 10 people. Victims... were apparently... eaten"

Visuals 10/10 - Having been originally released on the Gamecube in 2002, this game had some of the best graphics on the console at the time. Despite being nearly a decade old at this point, the 2015 HD Remaster continues to impress, as the fixed camera angles allow for a highly cinematic experience, with every frame carefully crafted to increase the tension as you navigate through the mansion. With the help of the modding community, there are ways to further increase the visual quality, allowing for the characters to sometimes look like real-life 3D models on your screen.

Mechanics 9/10 - If you don't know by now, the classic Resident Evil games contained a tank-style control scheme with the above mentioned fixed-camera angles, where pushing 'Up' will always move the player forward, regardless of where they are facing on the screen. While I believe the 'Tank' controls is the proper way to play this game, this will admittedly be disorienting for new players, but can be switched to 'Modern' in the options menu. The game also has no auto-save feature, which again will be highly frustrating for some, but these are some of the features that once understood, make this game so memorable. It may seem too hard at first, as ammo and health can be scarce if not used correctly, but just remember that people can complete this game on the hardest difficulties with only the knife. It can be done!

Sound 10/10 - Although sound and music are arguably the most subjective topic of any game, Resident Evil Remake is filled with amazing tracks, which are indigenous to certain areas of the game. These tracks perfectly tie together all of the above mentioned features to provide an incredibly atmospheric experience. Like the dialogue, the game contains many of the same tracks from the original PS1 game, with some welcome updates. If you play this game enough, some of these will stick with you for life, most notably, the 'Save Room' theme. Even if you never play this game, I highly recommend listening to it at some point. 

Overall 10/10 - For long time fans of the series, or new players looking for a classic survival horror experience, Resident Evil Remake is absolutely incredible. This might be the best game in the series, as well as potentially the entire survival horror/zombie genre.

[h1]Zoinks Scoob, there sure’s evil in this bit.ch![/h1] 

The remastered remake of the game that pretty much paved the way for the genre. A classic, atmospheric survival horror experience and a perfect way to witness the incident that spawned the entire franchise. 

A series of bizarre murders took place around Raccoon City – families assaulted and eaten. You are part of the local police S.T.A.R.S. Alpha team investigating the weird occurrences. During the operation you are attacked by a pack of murderous dogs and forced to take shelter in a nearby creepy mansion. Little did you know that this place giving you a brief moment of respite is actually a death-trap. Fight your fears though, and maybe you’ll discover what is wrong with this entire evil residence. 
The story gold of RE games and a lot of survival horror games really, doesn’t lie in dialogue writing, voice-acting or characters’ behaviors – let's be real, apart from the bad script translation and poor acting, we still cringe whenever after some horrifying experience caused by not sticking together, the gang decides to split up once again. 
The story value of these games mostly lies in scenarios they present – “the incidents” that you find yourself in and must persevere through. Resident Evil establishes a very effective formula for such stories, one that could be summed up by its Japanese title – Biohazard. You get stuck in a biologically contaminated area, filled either with mutants, zombies, big predators or viruses. Add interesting environments such as big mansions with underground labs underneath, filled with puzzles and bizarre architectural designs. Sprinkle some tragic lore of characters, evil corporations, shadow governments, people trying to escape the nightmare the same way you do, but yet not successfully. Maybe add additional campaigns/perspectives that explain what other characters were doing in the meantime. And there you go – a great game with wiki pages of incident reports.
Despite some dry dialogues from the characters, I still liked them. Chris and Jill are cool protagonists, unique from each other, Barry is my boy and Wesker is a great villain. Different endings are a cool thing, but I wish there was more to them to make them unique – instead we pretty much have 2 with others just swapping characters. 

RE1 really isn’t anything like the newer instances of the franchise. It’s more of a puzzle game instead of an action, shooter game. Surprisingly, a large part of this game revolves around inventory management. You collect weapons, ammo, heals and key/story related items. You choose what you’ll need to take with you. Should you use the slots for more ammunition or healing items? This puzzle requires 3 slots, what should I leave? Should I travel light to collect more items on the way – but what if I go underprepared? This can affect the way you move around the map, the routes you take. This game is all about planning your moves and actions. 
The gameplay focuses on exploring the mansion and getting the items required to progress through various puzzles and challenges. Along the way you need to deal with enemies – some you can evade completely, some will be trickier and some need to be taken care of with your precious ammunition. Firing in this game is not so shooting by yourself, but rather feels like you’re telling Jill/Chris to shoot. You can also collect defensive items such as daggers and stun gun batteries to break out of enemies’ grabs. 
Health in this game not being represented as a bar or a percentage makes it somewhat hazy when you’re about to die. There are 4 health states. Fine is green, Caution is yellow/orange, Danger is orange/red and it makes you move slower. There is also Poisoned. To heal you need to use the first aid or herbs found around the Spencer Property. Mixed herbs have different effects – green plus red gives a full heal, same as three greens. Blue herbs heal poison. Obviously, once on red, anything can kill you, but there were also instances when I was insta-killed on Caution. The health system is another factor supposed to keep the player on edge – another thing to constantly worry about. 
RE brought a lot of pretty unique stuff to the table. Zombies can fake dying and get up. Then, even when dead and not properly disposed of, they can later morph into a crimsonhead which is faster and much more deadly. To get rid of them for good you need to either score a critical attack (head-go-boom) or burn the body with a lighter and kerosene. So, you can make it easier for yourself later, but the trade-off is to carry two additional items. Also, kerosene is a limited resource. 
Resident Evil introduces my favorite Save Rooms. Places offering a moment of respite accompanied by a calming yet still oppressive melody. An eye of the storm. A place in which you can safely save your progress using a typewriter (assuming you have an Ink Ribbon to spare), reload your guns and stock up on resources from your Item Box. All item boxes are connected (surely, they got inspired by the famous Minecraft Ender Chest) so you can hoard supplies for later. 
The game offers two main protagonists. Jill is better for beginners as she has two more inventory slots, a lockpick and my boy Barry. Chris however, has more HP, deals more damage with weapons and can get healed by Rebecca <3. Without a lockpick though, he has to carry special keys to open certain doors, and also –2 inventory slots is a nightmare. At the beginning I hated Chris, but after so many challenge playthroughs I’d say both characters are really nicely balanced to suit a playthrough’s specific needs. RE is really replayable, it rewards learning the game and playing it in different styles.
There are a few things that some people consider “part of the classic horror experience” and some just plain BS. The 7-second loading screen doors in each room could be considered part of the atmosphere on a 1st playthrough, but for real, after that just download a door-skip mod – at this point I don’t think wasting your time on doors is going to enrich your experience any further (unless you’re trying to unlock the speedrun weapons, skipping doors actually shortens your time, so do with that what you will). 
Another thing is the fixed camera angles and the control schemes. The original control scheme is less chaotic and it’s easier to navigate through sudden camera changes. The alternative scheme however, allows you to be much more flexible with your movements and bait zombies to evade them easier. It is also really easy to run like an absolute idiot around the room because how the camera changes the way you want to move. In my opinion the fixed camera angles are part of the design for this old game and just require some getting used to – I am glad though, that most games today decided to abandon such perspective. 

The game looks amazing despite its age thanks to a little trick we in the industry call “pre-rendered HD backgrounds”. It uses high-res images spliced together on which your character walks in front of. It’s some great atmosphere and it aged very well. The sound design along with music seem kind of old, but they also have their charm as well. 
Most of the enemy designs are just zombies and large animals. They look scary sure, but I think the most terrifying foes are Lisa and Tyrant. 

There is something alluring in exploring a creepy mansion, braving new horrors at every corner, discovering strange puzzles and following in the footsteps of others who failed. RE1 is a vastly different game than its later action-focused sequels. The combat is ass, especially with some bosses, but it is not the focus. This game puts emphasis on the atmosphere and mystery. It requires the player to carefully plan his actions, make compromises – always keeps him on the edge to not make him feel too confident. 
First and foremost however, it is one of [b]The[/b] Survival Horror Games – the OGs that set trends for years to come.
