[h1]Resident Evil (2002) – A Homage to the Survival Horror’s Roots[/h1]

This is the first Resident Evil remake that I ever played, and in the best possible time. After playing the action trio of RE4, RE5 and RE6, a return to the true form of Resident Evil’s survival horror that made it a remarkable franchise, was a breath of fresh air. If you weren’t happy about the genre change that RE4 started, you know exactly what I’m talking about.


The director of the original Resident Evil (1996), Shinji Mikami, wasn’t pleased with the hardware restrictions some years before, so he was determined to fulfill his creative ideas with this remake. And oh he did us justice, as a matter of fact, a lot of RE fans consider this title to be the top 3 or even the best title in the series, and rightfully so. It’s an example of a remake done perfectly well.

Same as in the original Resident Evil (1996), you get to choose 2 characters – Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine. A cool addition to this remastered version of the remake is that you can play with their models from RE5, but I don’t recommend using them on your first run, because some of the cutscenes always use the original ones.
The character selection will affect your gameplay, as you will be meeting different characters and also using different tools. While Chris gets to use his lighter, Jill has her lockpicks; I find lockpicks to be way more useful since you can enter some of the locked rooms without having to find a special key as with Chris. There are also differences in health points and also some of the weapons. My advice is to finish the first playthrough with whoever you feel like, then in the second one do it with the other one. 

Although it’s done in the “old-school” manner of the original RE trilogy, the game implemented new things to refresh its mechanics. 
In addition to the ordinary zombies that you are familiar with, the big addition is the introduction of the Crimson Head zombies. After you down an ordinary zombie, his body won’t disappear and will stay in the same place for some time, and after a random amount of time, he will rise into the upgraded form that is a Crimson Head (usually the second time you pass next to his body or after that). These zombies are much faster and deal more damage to you. Because of this, you have an option to use the kerosene fuel to burn their corpses so that you don’t have to worry about being ambushed. Of course, this will take an additional slot in your inventory (or even two if you are playing Jill), which adds more of the survival planning into your gameplay.
The other great addition is the defense items. There are a total of 3 types of defense items – daggers, tazers and flash grenades. Tazers are exclusive to Jill and flash grenades are only used by Chris, while both can use the dagger. Those items are scattered around the map, and the great thing is that they take up their own inventory space, so you don’t have to worry about not having enough slots to pick them up. These items can come in handy when trying to dodge hallways full of zombies, where it’s natural to get grabbed.

After 41 of playing this game and achieving the 100% completion (all in a week or less), I can say that I had loads of fun beating this game multiple times. The knife run was insanely tough to do, maybe one of the most challenging things I’ve done in any of RE games, but it proved to be a really fun and interesting playthrough. There is also the Invisible Enemy mode, which further adds up to the replayability of the game.

The ambience is just amazing, it resembles how real survival horror is meant to be done, and is something that the RE franchise was always famous about. The addition of new areas like the Graveyard and the Forest were done perfectly.

Graphics are obviously a much needed upgrade from the original game, meaning that some of the areas, most notably the Aqua Ring and the Laboratory parts are much more polished, bringing more immersion to the whole experience. I know this is the remastered version, but even so, the first release of the remake still looks so great, and the game is often hailed for its good looks.

The story is basically the same as in the original, showcasing the first appearance of Umbrella and its creations, but with some additions, now having the side story of Lisa Trevor and her encounter with the Umbrella Corporation. One other thing that was upgraded from the original version is the voice acting. Sure, as with all the RE titles, this one also has its cheesy moments, but well, that’s the soul of this franchise.

This is an amazing game honestly, even if you already played the original Resident Evil, don’t skip this one. Same goes if you don’t enjoy the older, original version, you should play this to fill in the gaps that were left empty by skipping the story of the first game. 

Tier list update until I finish all the Resident Evil main titles:
RE2 (1998) > RE4  > RE (2001) > RE (1996) > RE5 > RE3 (1999) > RE: Code Veronica > RE6 > RE0

The following is a review from someone that played the original, the remake when it was actually released and now this remaster for the second time. I'm not someone that clings to nostalgia so you can expect some kind of objectivity on that side of things at least. Everything else is subjective of course, as is every review ever.

• Surprisingly nice graphics.

• Fantastic atmosphere with sound design that's sometimes immersive, other times goofy. The mansion has this very sinister feeling about it and I am not talking about the entities that inhabit it, just the place itself feels malicious.

• Awful writing, plot. Itchy-tasty! People (rightfully) whine about RE6 giving zombies guns, this game made them writers. Truly ahead of its time.

• Immersive soundtrack - tense, scary, mysterious and even serene when the situation/ circumstance calls for it.

• As far as content is concerned, this game has plenty of it and none of it feels like filler. Plenty of locations, enemy variety, set-pieces and puzzles which I enjoyed, even if some were a little counter-intuitive.

• As for the gameplay, it is a mixed bag. The game has obviously aged a lot, some parts of it worse than others:
-- The worst one by far is the fixed camera as it compounds the issues of tank controls and sluggish movement. The imprecise aiming doesn't help either. It is the perfect recipe for quite a bit of frustration.
-- Something that I am definitely mixed on cause the game would not be the same without it is the restricted inventory space - it is so overly restricted that it becomes overbearing, creating way too many frequent gaps in progression and action to have you go to your safe-box to juggle inventory space. When they inevitably remake this game again, it is the one aspect I am most interested in seeing how they handle - my expectation is something like RE2R and my hope is that they don't just retain the current system and call it a day.

• Difficulty is another thing that might sour first time players. This is a game from an era where developers were not afraid to really mess with you. Saves tied to a limited consumable + you can only save at specific locations, the aforementioned extremely limited inventory system + you can't drop stuff to come back to it later, tricky encounters + one shot traps that will send you right back to the main menu as there's no such thing as "autosaves" and "checkpoints". It can definitely be a test in patience, as most games used to be back in the day, so just keep that in mind before you get into it.

In every way but the gameplay, Resident Evil Remake has aged quite well. It is well worth buying at full pricel.

Resident Evil teaches that cinematic doesn't mean uninteractive.

In the current zeitgeist of the videogame artform, the current standards call for a certain kind of game design. Filling your game with scenes, linear segments and a certain feel that the interaction was an afterthought. Games are trying to become movies and in such process, they simply forget what made videogames so special: interaction.

I'm not implying that such games shouldn't exist, or that such games are inherently bad — I'm a Metal Gear Solid fan, for F's sake. But I also do think that there's a model where they apply such elements without putting any thought on how to properly make the experience justifiable as a game. "Cinematic" became a really marketable adjective, but I don't think any of these recent cutscene focused games are the prime example of this quality just because they have a lot of dialogues and film-like photography. If I'm honest, the most "cinematic" game I have ever played is the one you are looking for opinions right now: Resident Evil Remake.

Due to the fact this title doesn't force you to watch Hollywood inspired scenes, some people might question my statement. And these people should maybe take some time to watch more films, especially Sam Raimi, Alfred Hitchcock or George Romero's films. Resident Evil Remake is the master of gamifying the experience of watching a horror thriller film through the clever usage of a philosophy the title coined: the so called "survival horror" experience. Akin to the classic Evil Dead, you are forced to explore an uncharted, lethal environment full of uncertainity. You have limited inventory slots, limited resources and the enemies you are facing are quite relentless. This game will show you how people in the 2000s viewed zombies: flesh dolls that hunt you regardless of how many shots you fired at them; it takes a lot of resources to effectively deal with them.

If you take the wrong choices, you might probably need to restart the game rather early... because even the saving system requires you to use a limited item. It never gets frustrating because the only part of the game you are given full player agency and freedom to experiment is the early segments (it gets linear and less likely for you to screw up in the last levels). Still, you are always exploring, room after room, with a gun in your hand and a lot of fear of what will appear next. This game hides surprises and plays around with making you familiar with ambients to subvert this notion later, while presenting challenges in unexpected ways. Resident Evil isn't as disturbing as Silent Hill or Fatal Frame, but it's constantly a despair fest, where you are always picking resources and planning your inventory so you can travel through corridors without falling into the mansion's deadly traps. It's the apex of the classic "haunted mansion" trope, even if it avoids supernatural explanations.

This is the first part of the "survival horror" experience, and it's where you might feel frustrated and overwhelmed. However, do not give up! The second part is where you find some kind of overpowering resource, which you can abuse to dominate the game and show those zombies what you are made of. Do you remember when Ash found the shotgun in Evil Dead? You'll feel just like him when you find RE1's shotgun. You will become an overpowered action hero that is throughly able to deal with the threats that oppressed you for so long; that is, until the game throws at you new enemies, traps and puzzles. It's a constant dance of being underpowered and overpowered and it's addicting. It's a masterclass on building tension, giving you consistent pay-offs and surprising you like a classic horror film.

One might ask himself about the replay value, due to the fact most of the surprises won't have the same effect if you know the mansion. Resident Evil answers this by rewarding players who know the layout with unlockables, new game modes and the fact you have two campaigns. While you are exploring the same basic environment, choosing between Chris and Jill alters a lot of the resources, gameplay elements and choices you are forced into. Playing at least two times to witness different situations and twists is totally worth it — Chris being the pure ludonarrative path, where you are given total agency of how you explore the mansion, and the game is tougher; Jill being the more "linear" path, where you have more resources and you don't need the same amount of backtracking and inventory management, thus making the exploration a bit more of a traditional videogame since you won't need to clear your path or worry about coming back all that much.

And as a remake, it plays around a lot with the idea of surprising the hardcore fan who has played the originals, changing a lot of the surprises and mixing a bit of the mansion's layout. New mechanics are added and they make the game even harder than it originally was. They also fix a lot of the issues the first game had, such as the underwhelming cave segment, the awful shark "bossfight" while adding a bit more of narrative to spice things up. I'll just say a name: Lisa Trevor, and you'll know what I mean when you get there. It also improves a bit on the controls, allowing you to use the analogue stick and giving you an option if you are not a fan of tank controls.

I'm more of a Chris fan because of how it plays out more akin to "living" a horror film, but both campaigns still feature the same core experience to some degree. Resident Evil Remake is a true masterpiece and I feel very compelled to play this until there's no more content to be found. I already have +20 hours, and this game lasts like, 10-12 hours in your first run. Your run can be optimized up to 2 hours or something if you do play it a lot, and it's just joyful. If you enjoy game design and haven't played this, I don't know what you are doing. This is a purchasable evidence that you can take movie elements and translate into a truly interactive and immersive game. Play it right now!

Resident Evil 1 is an absolute classic that changed the game (literally) for survival horror—but wow, it hasn’t aged well. Playing it now is like stepping into a time machine that takes you back to an era where controls were intentionally designed to make you suffer. The tank controls? Slower than a grandma on ice. The fixed camera angles? Frustrating, disorienting, and sometimes headache-inducing—like the game wants you to suffer for daring to play it. And the gameplay? Oh, you like backtracking? Good, because this game will have you running in circles like a dog chasing its tail.

Let’s talk item management, because boy, does this system make you feel something—and that something is rage. Your inventory space is so tiny you’ll wonder why your character didn’t think to bring a backpack. Can’t pick up that key item you need? No problem! Just hoof it all the way back to a storage box, stash your stuff, and then run all the way back to grab it. And good luck figuring out what the key item even does because the game tells you nothing. Trial and error, baby! It’s like solving a puzzle with no picture on the box.

Saving the game is another delightful pain in the neck. You need ink ribbons, which are limited, so you better pray to the zombie gods that you saved recently because this game loves to throw surprise one-shot kills at you. Nothing says "fun" like losing an hour of progress because you got mauled by a mutant dog that came out of nowhere. Oh, and the puzzles? Sure, they’re iconic, but they’re also cryptic as hell. Unless you have the brainpower of a Mensa member or a walkthrough open, you’re going to spend hours wandering aimlessly.

And yet, despite all of this, the atmosphere is chef’s kiss. The creepy mansion, the haunting vibe, the little details—this game is still a masterclass in creating tension. It’s so good at setting the mood that even modern games like Resident Evil 2 Remake and Resident Evil 7 can’t fully replicate it. They come close, but the original just hits different.

Now, would I recommend it? Eh, only if you’re really into old-school games or you’re a die-hard Resident Evil fan. Otherwise, you’re probably better off watching a walkthrough on YouTube. Honestly, playing this game feels more like a history lesson than an actual fun experience. I’ve beaten it multiple times, but that’s more about collecting achievements and soaking in the atmosphere than enjoying the gameplay.

So, should you try it? Maybe. It’s worth playing once just to see where the series started, but if the idea of clunky controls, endless backtracking, and surprise insta-deaths doesn’t sound fun, don’t force yourself. The mansion is iconic, but so is your time—don’t waste it unless you’re up for some real old-school frustration.

Resident Evil was undeniably influential, but playing it post-2020 required a fair amount of historical generosity. The controls were clumsy, the door animations sucked away all the pacing, and the general lack of quality-of-life features meant you had to actively embrace the jank rather than just grit your teeth and ignore it.

What held up better than expected was the fixed camera. It brought a strong mood, framing encounters as if they were being staged by something hostile and unseen. The occasional awkward angle was part of the deal - and not always to the game’s benefit - but the effect mostly worked.

As a remaster, it was competent but overpriced. Charging modern indie-game money for lightly polished, very dated assets felt hard to justify when [i]Age of Mythology[/i] tried it and it felt hard to justify here. Still, this was a solid way to revisit an important starting point for the genre - even if it never really outweighed the hardware limitations for me.

The game looks fantastic, and at the start oozes atmosphere. But it's soon ruined by the gameplay itself.
There are two big issues with the gameplay, which both compound into one bigger issue.
1. Artificially limiting saves.
2. Crimsonheads.
I don't mind limited saves when they are done in a checkpoint style, but being able to save at any point but having the amount limited makes you question each save, and if it's worth it. If you have somewhere to go in real life, then you can't just drop in, play some of the game, save and drop back out again, the game demands a good chunk of your time. It also leads to me losing LOADS of progress, then having to restart because I don't want to run out of saves, so need to get as much done as possible.
The Crimsonheads are zombies that come back to life after a certain amount of time, but faster and stronger. The only way to prevent them is by getting lucky with a headshot and decapitate the zombie, or to use the limited lighter fluid to burn the body. The thing is, headshots are unlikely and lighter fluid is hard to come by/takes up precious inventory space. So instead you end up playing most of the game trying to avoid the zombies rather than fighting them, because you don't want them to come back even harder, BUT the corridors are so tight you end up taking loads of hits. Instead of the game feeling scary the zombies just become an annoying chore.
Really, chore is the right word to describe this game. The two aforementioned flaws with the game compound to make the game just not fun to play. You have to plan everything to far ahead that you can screw yourself over hours on by making a minor mistake earlier. People will argue that this adds to the tension or horror, but it doesn't. Instead rather than allowing you to become immersed in the horror atmosphere, it just reminds me that I'm playing a game, a very annoying and tedious one at that.
I'm glad RE4 changed the gameplay style, and that RE2 and RE3 were remade in that style. The 30th anniversary of this game is coming in a few years time, and I really hope it gets remade in the RE4 style.

One of the best survival horror games ever made, also arguably the best remake of a game of all time, pioneering the genre and then coming back to reclaim its throne six years later with an almost squeaky clean remake.

A timeless classic, a game dear to me as it released in the year I was born, and there isn't a better entry-point into the genre than this. 
By itself, it's very meticulously-crafted and dense with detail and puzzles and lore tidbits, bundled with proper atmosphere and a soundtrack that keeps you on your toes. 

Story-wise, the events unfold in 1998, in the fictitious Arklay Mountains at the outskirts of Raccoon City. You play as two members of the Raccoon City Police Department (RPD) Special Tactics and Rescue Service (S.T.A.R.S) division, an elite squad tasked with investigating a mysterious series of murders going on in the wilderness outside of town. They run into a pack of feral dogs that chase them into an old and conspicuous mansion, infested with the undead. They have to find both a way out of the estate and the truth about the strange and grisly happenings. 

Resident Evil is a 2002 Gamecube remake of the older Playstation 1 game from 1996. It faithfully recaptures most of the music and visuals while reimagining them from the ground up to be more dense in detail. Nearly every area, save for some newly-added ones, is recreated shot-for-shot and modernized with newer technology without losing much of the original charm. It still uses the same technique of rendering a 3D character over 2D pre-rendered backgrounds, but it's noticeably more detailed this time around thanks to the more powerful hardware the Gamecube could offer. 

The gameplay is what really marks it as survival horror. You have limited inventory space and have to manage your resources (healing items, ammunition, key items) to progress through the mansion's many rooms and sections while defending yourself from threats and carry around important story items to solve puzzles. The enemy designs here are slightly readjusted from the original, with the T-virus-infected zombies being able to mutate further and get back up after being downed unless cremated or beheaded. There is also a new addition that wasn't present before, a new, undefeatable enemy you only encounter a few times, but is important to the story.  The game's split into two campaigns, Chris' and Jill's, with both of them having one permanent, slotless item as a unique tool to each character (lockpick for Jill, lighter for Chris), as well as having some difference in item slots and damage numbers. The game introduces 'defense items', like knives and flash grenades that you can use to save yourself from zombie grabs once only, as the item gets used up. Puzzles here are more difficult than in the original, marking it as the only remake in the series that actually makes the puzzles harder. 

As said previously, nearly the entire original soundtrack returns, recomposed with additional instruments and reimagined to fit the grimmer tone of the remake, but the voice acting is also significantly improved, from being memeably cheesy to being.. slightly less campy but only serviceably. Still memorable, though. Visually, the mansion has had a huge facelift, though noticeably darker than the original's rather well-lit halls. From the chandeliers, to the paintings, to the guest lounges and main dining halls, every section here is beautifully remodeled and prerendered. It is probably the biggest loveletter you could give as a remake to any game.

Spencer Mansion is absolutely a new favourite videogame locale of mine after finishing Resident Evil for the first time this January. An amazing realisation of a Gothic manor house, the muted colours, the sparse and strangely orderly interior convey just how haunted and uninviting it is. The sombre soundtrack exceptionally augments the art direction, constructing this palpably evil and mysterious atmosphere. The integration of the pre rendered backgrounds is still magic to me, they are just so incredibly detailed even by today’s standards. Character models look just as good, comparable even to late seventh generation titles, which is unbelievable. Yes, sure I did play the remastered version, but these are still the bones of a game that released twenty-two years ago.

Aside from the egregious door-opening cutscenes, which in hindsight I should’ve just modded out, exploring the mansion was always a thrill. The game has you slowly unlock distinct parts of the mansion, tying progression to exploration and puzzle solving which is excellent. The structure of Spencer Mansion is masterfully thought out, a true bastion of level design. Furthermore, I love the quality of deliberateness in Resident Evil’s gameplay, every choice feels important. For example, do you risk postponing saving to make the most out of your Ink Ribbons, decide to torch this corpse in anticipation that you will have to come here again. Occasionally the limited save system can lead to frustration as using your Ink Ribbons unwisely can lead to the player having to replay significant stretches, but at the same time it is fundamental in preserving the aspect of tension elicited by the gameplay. Manoeuvring around the zombies was also fun, as it can either be done by smartly directing them to the sides of a room or corridor so that you can out space their grab entirely, or for skilled players you can actually dodge these grabs by moving backwards when it is telegraphed which is extremely useful in tighter areas, when you are low on ammo or can’t warrant the usage. This again plays into resource management as it is entirely up to the player to decide whether they risk being grabbed, and wasting a healing or defensive item, or on the other hand wasting precious bullets which are essential for clearing boss fights later on, each scenario is like a puzzle in itself, leaving you to find the optimal way to overcome it.

On another note, during the early hours of my playthrough, I found myself being a bit discombobulated by the controls. This was because the default modern controls while easier and more responsive i.e. turning speed, aren’t seamless, as they don’t possess a direction that always corresponds to forward and in classic survival horror fashion the camera changes position constantly, with your directional input being dependent on this. To fix the problem that would arise from this it was made so unless you take your thumb off the stick you will keep moving in the direction you were before the camera change, however this causes the controls to be inconsistent, as it locks slightly, so repositioning Jill can become difficult. Unfortunately, I found the tanks controls even worse as they are so unbelievably stiff, in comparison to Silent Hill 2, therefore I was forced to make a compromise with the new controls which are ultimately okay for the most part once you become adjusted.

In conclusion the amalgamation of decision making, resource management and engaging exploration through a memorable locale makes Resident Evil truly special. I’m look forward to working my way through its future entries.

This review will be focused less on the quality of the game itself, and more a documentation of what to expect if you play it on Steam Deck. For the game itself, it's an absolute classic and 100% worth a play. Still unbelievably gorgeous to this day. Some people say that this is not an ideal remaster -- and I will get into my feelings on that in a second -- but even a serviceable-at-best remaster doesn't hold back the magic of this game.

Now, onto the Deck Experience. This game... has weird issues. For starters, there is no proper 4:3 mode that fits natively on a 16:10 display, so if you choose to play in 4:3, you will have black bars at the top and bottom. This is such a bummer considering how nicely native 4:3 fits on the Deck screen.

Secondly. this game has WEIRD issues with its FMVs. I believe this is specifically a Proton issue, as Resident Evil games seem to have their fair share of FMV playback issues on Deck (encountered similar issues with Village). The main issue seems to be in regards to what your resolution and textures are set at. If you're playing on the Deck itself with High textures at 720p resolution, FMVs will not play correctly and you get color bars. If you play with textures set to Medium or below, they have a better chance at playing, but not guaranteed. In MY experience, when I play this game at 1080p on a TV with textures set to High, most FMVs actually played back correctly, with one or two occasional glitches. This really is a YMMV type problem that Windows players probably don't have to worry about. I do take issues with its Verified rating when the game has these technical flaws, however.

Finally, holy cow this game eats so much battery life. I can't tell you why, but it's one of those games where you will get like an hour and a half of battery. It's not as dire as games like God of War or Ghostwire Tokyo on Deck, but it's pretty bizarre for a 2014 remaster of a 2002 GameCube game to have poor battery performance like this. You can mess with TDP wattage to get this lower, which I do recommend outside of the house, but just know that going in if you plan on playing on the go. Thank God it doesn't need an internet connection to start, at least.

Now with all that said, I had a wonderful time playing Resident Evil Remake, and am so glad I gave it another chance. And in spite of all my issues, I still think that playing it on Deck was worth my time and gave me many more chances to play the game than if I just played it on my Windows rig.

And I feel obligated to mention that from my light research, there are indeed mods that are supposed to help alleviate a lot of these issues, and perhaps different versions of Proton that can be used to get around the FMV issues. Mods can also help improve some of the graphics if you wish to pursue that. I chose to play vanilla and mostly do not regret that, but I would go into this game on Deck as Playable, not Verified.

“Resident Evil: A Retro Horror Jam That Still Slaps”

Introduction: Alright, my fellow survival horror aficionados, let’s rewind the clock to 1996 and dive headfirst into the Spencer Mansion. “Resident Evil” is like that vintage vinyl you found in your grandma’s attic—scratched, a bit dusty, but oh-so-iconic. So, grab your ink ribbons and let’s chat about this B-movie masterpiece.

Zombie Tango: Picture this: You’re strolling down dimly lit corridors, and suddenly—bam!—a zombie lunges at you like it’s auditioning for “Thriller.” These undead pals are the OGs of the genre. Sure, their polygonal faces might be a tad blocky, but their hunger for your brains? Still top-notch. And those Crimson Heads? They’re like the surprise guests at a party you didn’t invite. Every time they rise from the grave, it’s like a jump scare wrapped in nostalgia.

Resource Scarcity Ballet: Now, let’s talk survival. Ammo? Scarcer than a unicorn riding a rainbow. Ink ribbons for saving your progress? As precious as grandma’s secret cookie recipe. “Resident Evil” isn’t just about shooting zombies; it’s about resource management. Every bullet you fire feels like borrowing from your future self. And those inventory slots? More precious than a golden ticket to Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory. Choose wisely, my friend, or face the consequences.

Tank Controls vs. Modern Swagger: Remember those wonky tank controls? Yeah, the ones that made your character pirouette like a confused ballerina. Well, fear not! This remaster lets you switch to modern controls. No more moonwalking into zombie hugs. But hey, if you’re feeling nostalgic, stick with the OG setup. It’s like dancing the Macarena with a shotgun.

Visual Rollercoaster: Look, I won’t lie—the graphics have aged like fine wine left in the sun. But here’s the deal: The wonky visuals are part of the charm. It’s like watching a classic horror flick on VHS. Sure, there are moments when you squint and wonder if that’s a zombie or a cardboard cutout, but who cares? The atmosphere? Still chilling. The creaky doors? Still haunting. And that eerie save room music? Chef’s kiss.

Final Verdict: “Resident Evil” isn’t just a game; it’s a time capsule. It’s the reason you double-check your locks at night and side-eye your houseplants. So, whether you’re a veteran or a fresh-faced gamer, give it a spin. Just remember: When life hands you ink ribbons, save like your survival depends on it. Because in Raccoon City, it does. 🧟‍♂️🔥

A fantastic Survival horror experience! So I have never played the original Resident Evil (something I will one day remedy since the game is on GOG), so I wanted to play this remake since I played it on PS4 but never finished it. So far I’ve finished the game with Jill and am wrapping up a playthrough as Chris.

While the other RE remakes seek to modernize the series, this remake keeps most of the classic elements from the series such as the famous opening door animations, needing ink ribbons to save etc… I liked a lot of these elements as it makes this feel like a true classic survival horror which it is, and it gives me nostalgia from when I watched my parents play these games when I was a kid. Plus this remake features the crimson head zombie mechanic where after killing a zombie, it will come back as a Crimson head after enough time has passed. This was also a nice mechanic as it adds some strategy to the gameplay loop, as making sure to burn a zombie that's outside a save room is essential. It's a mechanic that has only ever been used again in Signalis and I wish more games used this mechanic.

Otherwise the horror is still pretty great, it doesn’t scare me as much as some other games, but they preserved the original game's atmosphere from what I’ve heard. Between playing as Jill and Chris, I definitely enjoyed playing as Jill more since she's just more fun to play with and who I’d recommend for a first time playthrough. Chris is meant to be the more challenging of the two in more ways than I originally thought. I knew he only had 6 inventory slots which I was willing to work with, but he gets less weapons overall and can’t even do some of the game's puzzles without another character's assistance. I mean I know people make fun of Chris because of his boulder punching shenanigans, but this doesn’t help his case!

Otherwise, not much else to say other than this a great entry in the series and scratches that classic survival horror itch.

Take a trip back to where it all started.

Resident Evil (2015) is an HD remaster of Resident Evil (2002) which is a remake of Resident Evil (1996). In short, it's the HD version of the original Resident Evil story, following Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine as they uncover the secrets behind a mysterious virus's origins at the Spencer mansion. Functionally the beginning of the survival horror genre as a whole, you'll carefully manage limited inventory space and resources to solve puzzles around the mansion while avoiding death from the various creatures that haunt its walls.

Despite being a nearly 10-year-old HD port of an over 20-year old remaster of a nearly 30-year-old game, Resident Evil holds up surprisingly well in the modern-day. Seeing where it all started and the origins of these iconic characters was quite fun, and I gained a lot of appreciation for the mechanics of Resident Evil 1 that would go on to become series-staples throughout many of the other games. I played one playthrough on "Easy" of both Jill and Chris, and while I liked the Jill playthrough more from both a story and gameplay perspective, I still felt that both were unique takes on the story despite encountering the same puzzles and enemies. At first the game was a little difficult, but once you learned how to play around fixed camera angles and tank controls and the limited inventory space it almost felt like playing through a classic haunted house horror movie, especially with how cinematic some of the environments were. Even with how cheesy some of the dialogue and action sequences are, you can't help but smile at the charm that this game carries throughout your playthroughs. 

My couple of gripes that I have with this game basically boil down to it being a bit dated. For one, the tank controls can be a bit of a hassle to work with, especially when shooting some of the more mobile enemies or when the camera angle just barely doesn't fit the combat environment you're in. Secondly, I have a 165hZ refresh rate monitor and unfortunately wasn't able to fully utilize this, understandably because the game wasn't designed to run at that pace. Finally, again because of the way the older game works with modern RAM I would frequently encounter "memory overload" errors (especially when loading a fully-rendered cutscene) which would close my game entirely, so saving often was a must in order to avoid losing a large amount of progress to sudden errors.

Despite all those gripes, I'd still recommend playing Resident Evil (2015), as it's a great experience to play through one of the classics of the horror genre. This is also arguably one of the better remakes of an older game, so there's a lot to appreciate from that standpoint. With Resident Evil (2015) frequently going on sale for very cheap, there's very little reason not to check it out for a playthrough or two.

After playing at least one of the more recent entries (RE6, I think) many years ago now, I decided that I would start from the beginning of the series (mainly for the lore/story and characters - really that's the whole reason I even play games). 

I expected the weird camera angles and some sluggish gameplay that requires some patience but what we have here is a whole other level of tedium. 

I mean, I just wanted to shoot zombies, get chased by Nemesis (because that's the big dude I remember when I watched my mum play RE as a kid lol - I guess he's not in this one but I haven't finished the game yet) and enjoy the story - get to know the OGs and how it all began. 

I didn't expect the game to be an opening doors simulator (thank god for the mod that remedies that) and feel like a chore with all the running back and forth with absolutely zero guidance as to what I'm supposed to be doing and having to solve a thousand puzzles around every corner - Jesus H Christ! [i] The puzzles. [/i] I hate them in any game. I would've thought twice if there'd been a tag or something about that in the product description. 

There's also the annoying inventory management game you have to play because you can only carry eight items at a time and you can't even drop items to be able to pick another one up instead. 

The enemies stun lock you all of the time (the crows are especially annoying) and combat is scuffed. You're constantly fighting with the controls and weird camera angles. Most of the time you can't even see the enemies because of the camera angles. The enemies also spawn randomly, even in places where you've already been.

You only get a limited amount of saves and can only save in designated save rooms so if you die and haven't saved in a while or something then have fun doing whatever you did all over again.

The map is garbage and doesn't say what any of the rooms are like, 'library' or 'dining room', etc. So have fun getting lost in this huge ass mansion while you're trying to figure out where that one, specific room is that you're looking for.

The voice acting and dialogue is pretty bad like a English dubbed Japanese anime. 

There's at least some good things and that's Jill's plump ass and that you can choose between Jill or Chris at the start of the game - there's also alternative costumes you can use or unlock for each of those but I'm not sure how much of a masochist you'd have to be to play this game multiple times for that. Apparently, Jill and Chris have somewhat different experiences (mostly the same but Chris has even more limited inventory and a few other differences that might qualify the game for a +1 in replay value - I read that Chris is basically hard mode for various reasons like less inventory space and that unlike Jill, he can't skip some puzzles and gets less help). 

Performance-wise the game was good apart from a weird slow-motion issue I had. Probably something to do with the frame rate. There were no crashes. I couldn't alt-f4 at all (like when I got soft locked after dying with god mode on lol) and sometimes if I alt-tabbed I'd be unable to click anything like my Google tabs or file explorer, etc, as if the game locked them.

I honestly think that the game is made more for people who have played the original game. [i] Nostalgia. [/i] It's a complete fail for anyone new to the series but if you're like me and enjoyed a more recent RE then the story is about the only thing worth experiencing here but that's something you can just watch on YouTube. The game is a mood I guess. The atmosphere. The music in the save rooms is good for falling asleep to. 

Overall, there's more pain than gain and personally, the experience has been a nightmare for me. I'm now finished with it thank ♥♥♥♥ clocking in at around 12 hours in total (the other hours are from when I went to bed while farming the trading cards or AFK) but I'm exhausted and therefore, NO. I wouldn't recommend it, especially if you value your time and sanity. You'll probably need a guide open for pretty much 100% of the game too (it goes way beyond no hand holding).

If you're still thinking about it though then know that you can at least use WeMod to make the game less of a chore with unlimited ammo, saves, etc. 😉

This game's design ethos is squarely a product of its time and is very hard for newcomers to get into. For example:
- Camera perspective changing 3-5 times running down a single corridor.
> Third-person is superior.
- Janky aiming. You aim high, middle, or low, but you still won't hit the enemy unless your character is precisely facing them.
> Again, third-person is superior.
- No objective. You start the game and are told absolutely nothing about what you need to do or what item(s) you need to find.
> In RE2, you get to RPD and right in front of you is a PC where you see another officer fighting zombies. You go to rescue him and take his notebook. On the way back to the Main Hall, you're attacked by zombies and Marvin saves you. In the ensuing cutscene, it's established you need to find the three medallions to open the Goddess statue. From there, you explore RPD and solve puzzles to complete the objective. The next objective is to obtain the parking permit, and again, you explore the area & solve puzzles to complete the objective. Nothing of that sort exists in RE1.
- Limited inventory (this is okay on its own) with no way of discarding items.
> RE2 allows you to discard any item out of your inventory and find upgrades to expand the maximum slots. Huge QoL improvement.
- Saving is tied to consumables, which ties to the last point. If you die and your last save was ages ago, yet you couldn't save because your inventory was full ergo had no room for an ink ribbon, you've lost a lot of progress. Or maybe you can't pick up a key you need to progress, thus you're softlocked. You'd have to purposefully get bitten by zombie, to then waste the green herb, which allows you to get the key needed to progress.
> RE2 saving is not tied to consumables.

One of the best games I have ever played.
But there is one issue. Its very unforgiving and different from most modern games. Here are some tips
Tip 1: Don't use alternate controls. (Its default setting so make sure you change it) In a basic way alternate controls are based on camera position meaning if the camera changes you will likely slam into a wall or go back to the other screen then go back and again and again being stuck in a infinite loop (Which could get you killed if you are being chased) But tank controls are based on the character meaning if the camera changes you will still be moving in the same direction. The trade off is pressing A or D will make you turn instead of moving in that direction making your movement slow (Press Q for a 180 turn it will be very helpful for faster enemies)
Tip 2: Make sure you select the right character and difficulty. At the start of the game you are given two choices. Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Chris is a tank he can take a lot of damage he handles weapons better and carries a lighter in a side pouch meaning it doesn't take any inventory slots but there are a lot of disadvantages. Chris only has 6 inventory slots he doesn't have a lock pick meaning he has to pick up old keys to unlock some doors. He doesn't have Barry to help him and he doesn't get the Grenade Launcher. Jill gets 8 inventory slots a lock pick a grenade launcher and Barry to help her. The only disadvantage is a lower health amount but the rest make up for it making Jill the better character for first time players. The difficulty select is a bit weird. It is presented like a survey not giving you any solid answers and what is what. I think this is purposeful because you are given three difficulty options very easy, easy and normal. The goal of this is to make new players click easy. The problem? Easy is extremly easy. You are given a ton of ammo and health some enemies are removed from key areas. Pick the max difficulty if you want a balanced game. (SAVE OFTEN you are given enough ink ribbons for consistent saving also use multiple save slots if you make a big mistake you will have to reload a save also there are some instant kills the worst is the dogs jump attack that will kill you if you dont have a defensive item spam A and D and you might get out but its very inconsistent)
Tip 3: Conserve resources.  Don't kill everything you see especially zombies. Zombies are tanks taking a ton of pistol ammo but can be one shot with a well placed shotgun blast. Zombies can easily be dodged simply bait a grab then run past their shoulder. Most other enemies can be killed quite consistently but be very careful. If you are playing Chris use strong healing items more due to his high health amount. If you are playing Jill try and use lesser healing items more as most of them can send her health to max pretty quickly. Explore EVERYTHING nearly all weapons can be missed the best weapon (excluding rocket launcher) requires you to solve two unrequired puzzles.
Check out some of the guides if your still having trouble but a lot of them contain spoilers.

Resident Evil Remake is one of my favourite game ever made, my favourite RE, and the best remake ever made. It’s classic Survival Horror in its purest form. This Steam version is an HD remaster of a port of a remake. Yup, Capcom’s obsession with rehashing old stuff isn’t new – but this Remake is special.

See, RE1 was already dated by the early 2000s, so Mikami and crew decided to remake RE1 using the at-the-time powerful GameCube hardware. This allowed them to make the most refined iteration of the classic Resident Evil formula to date, and fully realize the vision they had back in the mid-90s. They went back to the survival-focused approach instead of the more action-focused one of RE2/3/CV, and what we ended up getting is a timeless classic that outright replaces the original game – a rare feat for a remake. It really does feel like the game they wanted to make from the beginning.

Gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds, stellar sound design, fantastic level-design, oppressive atmosphere, tough enemies, inventory management, puzzles, limited saves, strategy – it’s all there and it all feels like RE1. There’s just about enough changes so that veterans can’t rely on their knowledge of the original game alone. The game even plays with that to catch experienced players off-guard. The story is more or less the same but the script was re-written entirely, and the voice acting redone (No more Jill Sandwich but oh well). 

It’s a fairly hard game on a first play-through and it can feel overwhelming, but do stick with it and you’ll find a game that rewards skill as well as wits, is endlessly replayable and doesn’t really age. It works just as well today as it did in 2002. 

There is but one blemish: this HD Remaster is inferior to the GameCube original in a couple aspects. Sadly, Capcom lost the source assets so the background could not be re-rendered. They opted to upscale them instead and replace the animated backgrounds with real-time 3D. It doesn’t do justice to how impressive this game was back in the day.

This HD Remaster takes what was good about the original PS1 version and gives it modern conveniences, such as updated graphics (not 4K, but still playable) and the most important for me, the updated movement system. The original movement in the PS1 version has your movement mapped to the direction the character is facing (i.e, the character's perspective). This means that when you press the walk forward key on your controller, your character will walk forward, no matter which direction the character is facing in relation to the "camera" or you. The updated movement allows you to move in relation to whichever way the joystick is pushed in relation to the perspective of the camera (your perspective as the gamer, I guess?). This is such a game changing update. And if you want to use the old way of moving, my Stadia controller has that mapped to the D-pad too. I find the old way of moving in PS1 Resident Evil to be counter-intuitive and limiting, whereas the new (they call it "Alternate") way is intuitive and freeing. Have fun.

There's something inherently beautiful about horror media. Finding the courage to face the unknown despite the odds being stacked against you is an experience which I constantly find myself being intoxicated by. Yet horror is a slippery slope, many horror entertainments lose their fear factor the second time around. You’ve already seen the monsters, shot the zombies, and turned on the metaphorical lights, most horror medias have nothing else to offer in a second playthrough or viewing… Resident Evil Remake is different. 

Atmosphere is the most important part of any horror experience, when done right you can get the feeling you’re never in control, that someone- or something is always watching you. Resident Evil Remake uses all of its tools to create a dark and unnerving atmosphere. The game uses the classic horror staple of a “fixed camera” to show players their environment. At the time of release, this method of presentation was scrutinized for limiting the players understanding and control of combat situations, in an oversaturated market of games whose implementation of the system wasn’t natural. But in a time where this kind of AAA horror is rare if not non-existent, I now understand this only adds to the experience allowing the game designers complete control of what the player needs to see, and what they shouldn’t. Gameplay is clunky for a reason. Moving Jill and Chris feels like piloting a tank instead of a special agent, but when considering the situation they are in, would you be so nimble? People tense up when scared, and take time to convince themselves to act in the face of the unknown, despite their training I doubt either of the playable characters were prepared to fight the undead. This clunky movement was chosen to push this feeling of tense and intentional movement. The enemies that you will fight range the gambit from vanilla zombies, mutated reptiles, to hellish undead creatures who look as though they were pulled through a steel grate. Each creature fights differently forcing players to count their bullets and rethink their strategies when entering rooms. The levels are cramped, dark, and tightly connected to the point I would consider calling it Metroid inspired, Almost all rooms hide something useful, whether that be a key or a few rounds of ammunition. And very few rooms will only be visited once, as hallways and living quarters believable lead into each other. Resident Evil is known for its music (especially its save themes) and Remake provides one of the best soundtracks.in the series. Using deep strings and wind instruments, the soundtrack is able to disarm the player's sense of belonging. Most instruments play single drawn out sounds to keep tension rising before finally silencing at the opening of the door, or intensifying with the entrance of an enemy. A resident evil game is only as good as its save room theme, and by God… this game has the best of the series (in my opinion). The slow use of piano chords in a repeated melody do provide the closest thing to comfort in the entire game, but never enough comfort to let you forget about the horror outside the locked door. And the story is… not great. Though the backstory or the mansion and its inhabitants is smart and well told, the story of STARS is not. Bland voice acting and very generically obvious villains do dampen serious scenes, but environmental storytelling and a subplot about a girl in the cabin do make the script enjoyable.

Whether it be your first, second, or fifth time running in the Spencer Mansion there seems to always be something new to appreciate.

For many the best remake, and objectively it is possible, and so the Re4 remake is probably very close to this, although for me it is the best because I adore Re4, but let's talk about the Re1 remake.

Amazing gameplay, great atmosphere, creepy music; the plot is the same as in the original, but sounds less cringe-worthy but just as iconic.

Very beautiful locations; the mansion itself is like one huge puzzle that you have to explore and solve. When I first played through, I probably got lost in this mansion a million times, and it's great!

In this game, you have 2 characters: Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield (Claire's big brother).

I personally like Jill more because she has a larger inventory (jiggle physics). In general, playing for Jill is a kind of easier mode since she has 8 inventory slots, a lockpick, and she can make poison against Plant 42 and play Moonlight Sonata. She also has access to a grenade launcher. She gets an assault shotgun earlier as well (Chris gets it much later, and instead of a grenade launcher, he has a flamethrower), and at the same time she is physically weaker and more vulnerable to damage.

In turn, Chris has only 6 inventory slots, and instead of a lockpick he has to collect small keys, and he cannot create poison against Plant 42 and cannot play Moonlight Sonata (since he is stupid, I think, well, I couldn’t do this stuff either, so I don't blame Homeboy). But Rebecca can help him with this; at the same time, Chris is stronger than Jill, can take more damage, and always carries a lighter with him to set fire to corpses (Jill’s permanent item was just a lockpick instead of a lighter).
In general, on the first playthrough, I 100% recommend playing as Jill!

The game also has 2 interesting difficulties that unlock after certain conditions of playthrough, such as "Real Survivor" and "Invisible Enemy." The first difficulty sets the game to Hard, and you do not have auto-aiming, and also the item boxes are no longer interconnected, meaning that if you left your stuff in one specific item box, then they will remain there, and the second difficulty offers you a game where all enemies are invisible (just as the title suggests), and all these difficulties are quite an interesting challenge!

And, as for the HD remaster itself, it is also wonderful, with its own features such as alternative controls. But I have two gripes with it. The first one is the resolution of backgrounds and UI. Yeah, the quality is better than the OG GameCube release, and also, I'm not a big graphics guy, but let's be honest, the quality of backgrounds and UI could have been better. And the second gripe is the inability to skip door loading animations; that was interesting back in the day, but this remaster should've been implementing that feature (even though OG RE1-3 PC ports have this feature; I don't know why they didn't bring it on this remaster), but gladly we have community mods for all that stuff.

Overall, it's an amazing game; every survival horror fan MUST play it at least once!

For remakes/remasters I like to do 2 separate review sections, one for the game itself and one for the remake/remaster.
Since I haven't played the original, my take on how good it is as a remake/remaster isn't very strong, but I do gotta say this...
This game was released in March 22, 2002, and the game looks fantastic.
These being the graphics for an early 2002 is very shocking, everything about it looks great. You may the newer remakes/remasters look better but... Duh, those are made like 5 years ago, this one was made over 20 years ago.
The quality of it is a massive improvement.

For the game itself, the gameplay is pretty good. It's a more of a traditional survival-puzzle game, where you have to go through a lot of places, getting different items for different object and solving numerous puzzles to keep going and making progress.
You have to do this while also avoiding the different monsters (which range from zombies, to giant spiders, to sharks and more), and also managing your inventory for carrying these different items that you get through the game.
These items can be weapons, ammo, key objects, healing items and some more.
And trust me, these 2 are essential for playing this game.
You also get to choose between playing Jill or Chris, each character with their own "traits" and unique stuff on their stories through the game.
I only played the Jill campaign, which gives you 8 inventory slots but you shoot slower with less powerful bullets or you play as Chris, which has more powerful bullets and faster shooting but less inventory slots, being only 6.

As for the monsters, this is one of my favourite parts of the game, because you encounter a lot of them in very tight places, and you really have to pay attention about them and what you want to do.
Zombies for example take a decent amount of ammo to kill but are very slow and their attacks arent very deadly. But if you do kill them, later on you will find their bodies in that same room, after a while turning into Crimson Heads.
Believe me when I say this, Crimson Heads are a pain, being a much faster and much stronger versions of the regular zombies.
In order for them to not turn into Crimson Heads, you either have to destroy their heads or burn their bodies. Burning their bodies takes 2 of your inventory items for them to just not come back as stronger versions of themselves, and as I said, managing your inventory is extremely important.

Gameplay is really where the game shows it's age, with fixed camera angles and tank controls really testing your patience if you aren't accustomed to them. However, it is absolutely still worth playing even now due to the engrossing atmosphere, likable characters, and heavy focus on puzzle-solving. This is actually my first time playing a Resident Evil game. I have to say, it's tough for newcomers like me. The constantly changing camera angles make aiming a real challenge. But nothing could stop me! I survived until the end, and the feeling of accomplishment after battling the controls (not the undead, of course) is amazing. There were times I got lost in the mansion a few times due to the confusing layout. Regardless, I'm incredibly proud of myself. This game is definitely one of the best I've ever played. It's a great introduction to the survival horror genre for anyone looking to jump in, just like me. Resident Evil is a fantastic place to start your horror gaming journey.

However, here's the pros and cons of the game:

Pros

1. Spine-tingling atmosphere: The mansion you explore is seriously creepy. Creaky floorboards, flickering lights, and the constant groans of the undead make you jumpy throughout. It's like being trapped in a bad dream.

2. Resource management challenge: Ammo and healing items are scarce, so every bullet and herb counts. This scarcity creates real tension. You gotta think strategically about every fight because you never know what's around the corner.

3. Puzzles that fit the world: Unlocking doors and progressing requires solving puzzles, but they make sense in the context of the spooky mansion. You're not just solving random riddles; you're piecing together the mystery of what happened here.

Cons

1. Saving anxieties: Saving is done at specific typewriters, and there aren't many of them. One wrong move and you might have to replay a big chunk. This can be super frustrating.

2. Limited ammo: You're constantly having to make tough choices about what to shoot and what to avoid. Running out of ammo in the middle of a zombie horde is a heart-stopping experience, but can also be annoying. 

3. Puzzles can be tough: Get ready to wrack your brain for some of these. They can be clever, but also confusing at times.

Lastly, I whole heartily recommend to play Resident Evil and I'm looking forward to playing the remaining Resident Evil games. Thank you for reading!

I never played the original in 1996 but I did play the 2002 GameCube remake. This is that 2002 game with some minor tinkering. The game was absolutely beautiful in 2002, and due to its prerendered nature, it still holds up in 2024.

The static camera takes some getting used to, and the controls can be weird. Instead of the old 'tank controls', it defaults to a more modern control scheme, and that feels better, but it's also disorienting every time the camera changes. So the controls aren't ideal, but they get the job done.

The story is decent, the voice acting is fun but corny, and most of the puzzles are a good balance of being challenging without being unfair. There were a couple I looked up, like the armory. The action was decent as well, but this is not an action game like later titles in the series are.

The real star here is the ambiance.

I'm not a big horror fan, so I set the difficulty level down because I don't enjoy the feeling of potentially dying at every turn, however the game still offers a fantastic feel and ambiance, especially in the Spencer Mansion segments. Just note that the 3 difficulty settings are Medium/Easy/Very Easy, NOT Hard/Medium/Easy. So if you want Easy, choose the middle, not the lowest. Hard opens up after you beat the game.

Even though this is a 22 year old game that is a remake of a 28 year old game, it holds up really well and I'd give it the same score I'd give it brand new in 2002: 85%.

Grab your Beretta and Load that shotgun, prepare for a long night of spooky third person horror. Resident Evil was and is in any form the finest survival horror game to ever be made. Resident Evil (1996) was a quirky and campy take on a fairly serious subject matter that didn't always hit the mark. Over a few years, and games, CAPCOM took all of the learnings and upgrades in technology and decided to take the Original survival horror game in for a remaster and re-polish. The result is the perfect survival horror game.

Resident Evil centers around the elite Special Tactics and Rescue Service of Raccoon Cities police department and their fight to survive in a zombie infested derelict mansion. Unfortunately, as the members of S.T.A.R.S explore the estate in an attempt to escape, it becomes abundantly clear that a greater scheme is at hand, and that some of their members may not be comrades after all.

The REmake (as it is affectionately called) takes all the good from the 1996 original and enhances the graphics, soundtrack, atmosphere and tension that made the original a staple and then dials it to 11. The mansion scenery is bleak, lighting effects are used to their fullest potential, and the camera angles will keep you guessing what lies around the corners of the mansion. The soundtrack has been completely overhauled and the eerie tunes can be heard while exploring the mansion, keeping the player alert and their hairs on end. The ambience of lightning and pained moans of the undead serve as an uneasy reminder that you are never truly safe, and in the distance the clicking of claws foreshadow deadlier beasts. 

While it is easy to forget about the Resident Evil remake when other giants of the series have entered the fray, we should not forget, that this is the perfect way to remaster any game. CAPCOM nailed it, the story is intact, and the core gameplay remains the same with major enhancements. For these reasons alone, Resident Evil Remake is the best of the series, and deserves its place as king of the survival horror franchise.

Resident Evil Remake (REmake) stands as a testament to the timeless brilliance of the survival horror genre, and this reimagining of the iconic 1996 title sets a new standard for what a remake can achieve. From the moment you step into the ominous halls of the Spencer Mansion, it's evident that REmake is a labour of love. The visuals are stunning, with meticulously crafted environments, atmospheric lighting, and chilling details that breathe new life into the familiar setting. The attention to detail is awe-inspiring, and the game's use of the RE Engine delivers an immersive experience that pays homage to the source material while feeling refreshingly contemporary.

The core gameplay mechanics have been refined without sacrificing the deliberate pacing and tension that made the original a genre-defining classic. The updated controls strike a balance between accessibility and maintaining the deliberate, anxiety-inducing movements of the original. Combat has been revamped, adding a layer of strategy with improved aiming mechanics while still emphasising the scarcity of resources and the importance of careful decision-making.

The audio design deserves special mention, as it contributes significantly to the game's overall atmosphere. The haunting soundtrack and spine-chilling sound effects enhance the sense of dread, while the voice acting, though faithful to the original, benefits from modern technology to deliver a more immersive narrative.

Resident Evil Remake doesn't just rely on nostalgia; it reinvigorates the narrative with additional lore and surprises that will keep even seasoned veterans on the edge of their seats. The pacing is masterfully orchestrated, with each encounter and puzzle feeling purposeful, leading to a crescendo of suspense that culminates in a truly satisfying experience.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Remake is a shining example of how to respectfully revive a classic. Whether you're a longtime fan or a newcomer to the series, this game manages to capture the essence of survival horror while embracing the advancements of the gaming industry. It's a must-play for anyone who appreciates a well-crafted, spine-tingling journey into the heart of horror.

This review is after finishing the Jill play through of the game with an xbox controller. I played this game for the first time as someone who has only played Resident evil 2 and 3 remake, 4 original, 7 and 8. I like this game overall but there are certain caveats to features that are also present in later entries you'll want to be aware of before starting this game.

I'll start with my one major grip with this game. You have limited times you can save throughout the game (in later games you can just use save points as much as you want). You have to collect things called Ink Ribbons (usually given in packs of 3) and then carry them in your inventory until you find a type writer to save the game. This can make playing the game a challenge if you have to get up and step away from your PC a lot due to a busy life schedule since you'll have to use an ink ribbon anytime you want to save. This problem can probably be sidelined if you are playing on PS4/PS5 or Xbox one/Series X since those consoles let you suspend the game at any point and come back to them when you turn on the console. Just be wary of going long periods without saving. You'll be backtracking your progress a lot of you don't save at reasonable intervals and die.

It took some getting used to the camera angles in this game since you are not able to view your aim from first person perspective or over the shoulder in 3rd person. With that said, the game does feature an autolock on button that will rotate your character in the direction of the nearest enemy. This made the combat experience much better than I thought it was going to be. You just can't guarantee you are getting headshots on enemies due to the way the aiming system works. 

The fixed camera angles this game uses can also lead to some confusion while trying to navigate. You may be pressing up on your joystick to run forward but then the camera angle shifts and suddenly you need to switch what direction you are pushing to keep going. This led to a lot of my character suddenly turning around and shifting back to the previous hallway (requiring me to shift my joystick repeatedly until I am running in the correct direction when I get back to the next hallway). 

The environments look good. Unlike later resident evils, this game seems to use pre-drawn or painted backgrounds that the 3d model characters walk through. It gives the game a really unique art style that you simply can't have without the fixed camera angles like this game uses. Some of the backgrounds I saw were blurry but this could potentially be fixed with upscale mods if this bothers use. I did not play with any mods but from what I saw on Nexus there are mods out there that will upscale parts of the game. 

For the horror/action encounters, this game feels like they are a bit more spread out. You'll spend a lot of time running back and forth through empty hallways once you clear them of enemies (especially if you burn the bodies to prevent them from coming back to life after enough time has passed). When the encounters do happen, it's often enemies that are hidden right around a corner due to the fixed camera angles. You won't see them until you go around the corner and they are already very close to you. Enemy variety is also a little limited compared to later resident evils but this is a remake of the first game where enemy types had not been fleshed out like later games.

The story is just kind of there. Maybe it's better in the Chris campaign. Anytime a cutscene played it was essentially Jill finding a coworker who just said "I'm gonna hang out in this room to check things out for a bit" or a zombie appearing in a more cinematic fashion than just standing in a hallway.

Puzzles are pretty good. There's not a lot of hand holding like modern games in general but it's not impossible to solve the puzzle either. If you are reading notes you find in the game or pick up on context clues related to the puzzle you'll solve most of them with no issue and feel like you had a decent challenge figuring them out.

With all the above stuff said, I do actually like this game. If you like the gameplay after trying it for an hour or two, keep with it. I stuck around mainly for exploring the environment and the puzzles throughout the game. There were also some good jump scares thanks to the camera angles. If you like resident evil the series I think it's definitely worth giving this one a shot. Just be aware it will be a different experience if you are coming from later entries in the series.

Resident Evil! I finally crossed this one off the list. Idk how much it differs from the original, but this game was pretty good.

In terms of design, it's nigh flawless. What I mean by design is not how the levels look or how hallways and rooms are laid out. Though that does add to the design -  what I mean is the engineered experience that a group of people have constructed, curated. What you're doing, how you're doing it, how the game unfolds from your actions, how it directs you, how it informs you. THE WAY IT PLAYS. 

That being said, the game is in fact NOT flawless. The vision and execution of this game are really tight and I'm certain what the devs intended it to be at the time, but the game has aged. Though it stands the test of time, I'd be lying if I said I'd change nothing about it with the advancements technology has brought us.

The largest issue, and by far the "easiest" to fix is the story/writing/acting. The world building through logs, journals etc is fine, old hat, over used, but fine. But more dynamic environmental story telling can be implemented. Anything from the Souls games for instance. For the actual story telling? Well, we have the Remakes of 2, 3, and 4 to look too. Though there was some charm to the B-horror cheese from the original games, I think the presentation of the Remakes is just better. More serious and grim, but more importantly, far more cohesive. The acting in video games of course has simply skyrocketed in quality over the years.

Past that, there are some design choices that have aged. Stiff controls, lo res visuals, surface-level combat. The save system I feel can also be updated. Though immersive, I feel it offers more frustration than fun. The tank controls are interesting but so clunky and unintuitive. I can see a case for keeping them but they can be updated to feel a lot better. The fixed camera presentation is also interesting but more infuriating than fun. I never advocate for mechanics that take away control from a player, and how you see the world you're in is one of the biggest. A free camera is paramount, but there could still be interesting ways to play with that. The combat could stand to be improved the most. You barely have to aim, going from standing to shooting state is pathetically slow. Weapon swapping, reloading, changing guns, items, anything with the inventory is painfully clunky.

But why do I bring all this up? Well, it's because this game is definitely going to be remade. And it seems the most contentious because of its strong identity and design. Modernizing it could prove disastrous. But I'm confident that if the devs stick to the soul of the game, they can make something truly compelling that also freshens up the worst parts of the game. Besides we still have the "original".
