This is the definitive version of one of the best video games ever made.  The original Resident Evil, while not the first Survival Horror game, was the first game to coin the term and really popularize the genre.  Now, to be clear, this is not the original Resident Evil.  Rather, this is the 2002 GameCube REmake of the game, remastered in 2015 for Steam and Consoles.  The Remake is more faithful to the original title than Capcom's more recent RE REmakes, but still has numerous differences from the original.  The Graphics are completely redone, the cheesy voice acting of the game has been replaced with much better (but arguably less iconic and memorable) voice work, and both the gameplay and story have been greatly expanded with various new elements.

One of the biggest changes lies with Crimson Heads.  Zombies you've killed can come back to life if you haven't either decapitated them or burned their bodies (and fuel to do so with is very limited).  You really have to carefully consider which enemies you'll fight, and which ones you'll want to avoid because of this, and while it makes the game more stressful, it also adds an additional level of strategy and depth to the game, and makes the already tense ammo and resource management even more challenging.  This is true Survival Horror, through and through.  To make the game a bit easier, there are also a new type of weapons known as defense items, which can be used to protect you when grabbed by enemies, and also deal some damage.

There are many other changes too.  Most rooms have been completely redesigned, or feature entirely new puzzles in place of the old ones.  Enemy and item locations have been changed around, and there are new surprises around every corner.  There are also a number of jump scares designed to catch returning players from the original RE1 off guard in particular, making certain familiar areas (like a certain iconic hallway) terrifying all over again.  It's amazing how this particular REmake straddles the line between old and new perfectly, acting as both a faithful REmake of RE1, and also throwing more than enough new elements into the mix that it can consistently scare and surprise RE Veterans with a fairly fresh experience.  The story has been expanded and improved upon as well, and without any spoilers for those who haven't played the game, it's great stuff, expanding RE1's plot and lore in compelling ways, and also better connecting it to it's sequels.

The Spencer Mansion is an still an incredible setting.  It's probably the best and most well realized setting in the entire series.  Every room is interesting and brimming with atmosphere and ambience.  The level design and pacing is incredible, and easily the best of all the old-school (Fixed Camera and Tank Control) RE games.  Learning the layout of the Mansion and the surrounding areas, figuring out the best routes to take to avoid enemies and limit backtracking, and solving clever puzzles, all while fighting (or avoiding) the undead and other monstrosities roaming the Mansion makes for a great time.  The original RE1 provides a brilliant foundation as it is, and all of REmake's many improvements just make it an absolutely incredible experience to this day.

There are also two different characters to play as, each bringing something unique to the experience.  Chris has higher health, and is a weapon expert who has slight advantages with various weapons, and has Rebecca as a partner, for some free heals throughout the game.  Playing as Jill, she has lower health and isn't quite as good at using most weapons, but gets a very powerful Grenade Launcher, has two extra inventory slots to make item management a bit easier, and gets Barry as a partner, who is more directly helpful throughout the game (saving you from traps, giving you hints and ammo, etc.).  Of the two, Jill is still the easier character to play through the game with the first time, but the two characters are much better balanced than in the original game, where Jill pretty much had every possible advantage Chris, and his game was intended as a Hard Mode is sorts.  Having two playable characters with various differences, as well a dozen different endings, and numerous extra modes and unlockables means the replay value here is extremely high, even in a series known for being highly replayable.

For the Remaster in particular, there were a few new additions.  Beyond improved visuals and completely redone character models, there is also a new widescreen mode. Now, REmake used pre-rendered backgrounds (which were essentially static 2D backgrounds) and 3D models to allow for a greater level of detail than was otherwise possible at the time of it's release.  While the results were amazing for the time, it also meant that the game couldn't easily be transferred to a 16:9 aspect ratio, as the backgrounds were designed for a 4:3 ratio.  Whilst you can still play with that ratio, the new 16:9 mode works well.  It essentially zooms in the screen, cropping off the top and bottom 25% or so of the screen, and then panning the camera up and down as the character moves through the environment.  It's a great solution that generally works well, and allows for a more immersive widescreen presentation.  And then there's the controls...

REmake was originally designed around Tank Controls, where you can only move forwards and backwards, or turn left and right, and with the remaster, there are now also more modern analog controls that allow you to simply move in the direction you press the stick. The original control scheme would understandably feel dated for anyone not used to this style of control, but it allows for consistent control across the game's fixed camera angles.  You don't actually control the camera in REmake, and instead move from camera angle to camera angle as you reach the edge of the current screen.  This allows for some incredibly cool and cinematic moments, with some incredibly cool looking camera angles, but these camera angles are often going to change your perspective frequently, for example putting the camera in front of, behind, above your character, or even at various other angles.  

This means that with the new analog controls, your controls have to change with each new angle, because they're tied to the current angle of the camera and the perspective, rather than the character.  So you might be running towards the screen away from a zombie, and then have to reorient your controls because the camera changed to be behind your characters back, forcing you start pressing up on the stick to continue moving forward, when before you were pressing downwards on the stick.  You can also continue holding the stick in one driection to keep running that way across camera angles, but it will lock you into that direction and prevent you from turning until you let go of the stick.  It's awkward at times.  

The original controls are tied to the character and thus consistent across the many camera angles (up on the stick always moves you forward, for instance), making moving through the environments much easier, and more natural and consistent feeling.  For this reason, while the game is playable with the new controls, I highly recommend giving the Tank Controls a chance.  They just feel better and work better with this style of gameplay.  The combat was also balanced around the original controls, with the new controls making things feel a bit too easy at times.

Finally, it's worth noting that the PC release is by far the best way to experience this game.  The ability to play at 60 or even 120 FPS is transformative (Console versions are locked to 30 FPS, sadly), making movement more responsive and also the camera scrolling in the new 16:9 mode much smoother looking.  Resident Evil REmake is one of the best games ever, and one of the best video game remakes of all-time, and the PC release is by far the best way to experience this Classic.  Highly Recommended!

DRM is not always a bad thing, if used correctly, it protects initial sales. Then good publishers will remove it later on allowing for better experiences. I am upset when DRM harms performance, which it often does (like Jedi Survivor). I find that inexcusable, poor performance that screws over the paying customer should always be frowned upon. Recently, denuvo was removed from RE8, which is good. But, when it was first added the game suffered many problems which modders had to remedy until its removal. Enigma seems to be capcom’s replacement for denuvo.

Denuvo a very good DRM, since there’s few who know how to crack it, even then it’s tough. Denuvo itself costs ~$5,000 per month for the license, ~$60,000 a year. A game’s sales can’t keep up with the fee forever, and the DRM has to be removed/replaced to salvage income. 

Enigma is $59,920 cheaper. It costs about $400 for initial purchase, and $80 annually for upkeep. Title: A Nostalgic Return to Horror Excellence - Resident Evil Remastered

Rating: ★★★★★

As a devoted fan of the Resident Evil franchise, experiencing the remastered version of the original Resident Evil was nothing short of a nostalgic and thrilling journey. Capcom has successfully brought the classic survival horror title into the modern era without compromising the essence that made it a genre-defining masterpiece.

Graphics and Atmosphere (5/5):
The graphical overhaul is nothing short of breathtaking. The eerie Spencer Mansion, once hauntingly pixelated, now comes to life with stunning detail and atmospheric lighting. From the creaking doors to the haunting echoes of footsteps in empty hallways, every element contributes to an immersive and spine-chilling atmosphere. The updated visuals seamlessly blend with the original design, capturing the essence of the 1996 classic while offering a fresh and visually striking experience.

Gameplay and Controls (4.5/5):
The tank controls and fixed camera angles, while divisive among modern gamers, stay true to the original design. Purists will appreciate the choice to retain these elements, but newcomers might find a slight learning curve. The addition of modernized controls is a welcome compromise, providing accessibility without compromising the tension of the original gameplay. The inventory system, a hallmark of the series, remains unchanged, adding to the strategic depth and resource management that defines Resident Evil.

Story and Narrative (5/5):
Resident Evil's gripping narrative of corporate conspiracy, bio-terrorism, and a mansion filled with unspeakable horrors remains as captivating as ever. The remastered edition doesn't tamper with the core story but enhances it with improved voice acting and subtle tweaks to dialogue. The lore is still as engaging, and the intertwining paths of the characters maintain their suspenseful allure.

Audio and Sound Design (5/5):
The revamped audio design is a standout feature, creating an atmosphere of dread and anticipation. The haunting score and meticulously crafted sound effects elevate the horror experience to new heights. From distant moans of zombies to the ominous echoes of footsteps, every sound contributes to the tension, making the auditory experience an integral part of the overall immersion.

Conclusion:
Resident Evil Remastered is a masterclass in preserving the essence of a classic while giving it a contemporary polish. It serves as both a love letter to longtime fans and an invitation for new players to explore the origins of survival horror. With its improved visuals, atmospheric design, and timeless gameplay, this remaster successfully proves that the horror of the Spencer Mansion is as potent today as it was in 1996. Whether you're a series veteran or a newcomer to the genre, Resident Evil Remastered is a must-play that stands the test of time.

There's something inherently beautiful about horror media. Finding the courage to face the unknown despite the odds being stacked against you is an experience which I constantly find myself being intoxicated by. Yet horror is a slippery slope, many horror entertainments lose their fear factor the second time around. You’ve already seen the monsters, shot the zombies, and turned on the metaphorical lights, most horror medias have nothing else to offer in a second playthrough or viewing… Resident Evil Remake is different. 

Atmosphere is the most important part of any horror experience, when done right you can get the feeling you’re never in control, that someone- or something is always watching you. Resident Evil Remake uses all of its tools to create a dark and unnerving atmosphere. The game uses the classic horror staple of a “fixed camera” to show players their environment. At the time of release, this method of presentation was scrutinized for limiting the players understanding and control of combat situations, in an oversaturated market of games whose implementation of the system wasn’t natural. But in a time where this kind of AAA horror is rare if not non-existent, I now understand this only adds to the experience allowing the game designers complete control of what the player needs to see, and what they shouldn’t. Gameplay is clunky for a reason. Moving Jill and Chris feels like piloting a tank instead of a special agent, but when considering the situation they are in, would you be so nimble? People tense up when scared, and take time to convince themselves to act in the face of the unknown, despite their training I doubt either of the playable characters were prepared to fight the undead. This clunky movement was chosen to push this feeling of tense and intentional movement. The enemies that you will fight range the gambit from vanilla zombies, mutated reptiles, to hellish undead creatures who look as though they were pulled through a steel grate. Each creature fights differently forcing players to count their bullets and rethink their strategies when entering rooms. The levels are cramped, dark, and tightly connected to the point I would consider calling it Metroid inspired, Almost all rooms hide something useful, whether that be a key or a few rounds of ammunition. And very few rooms will only be visited once, as hallways and living quarters believable lead into each other. Resident Evil is known for its music (especially its save themes) and Remake provides one of the best soundtracks.in the series. Using deep strings and wind instruments, the soundtrack is able to disarm the player's sense of belonging. Most instruments play single drawn out sounds to keep tension rising before finally silencing at the opening of the door, or intensifying with the entrance of an enemy. A resident evil game is only as good as its save room theme, and by God… this game has the best of the series (in my opinion). The slow use of piano chords in a repeated melody do provide the closest thing to comfort in the entire game, but never enough comfort to let you forget about the horror outside the locked door. And the story is… not great. Though the backstory or the mansion and its inhabitants is smart and well told, the story of STARS is not. Bland voice acting and very generically obvious villains do dampen serious scenes, but environmental storytelling and a subplot about a girl in the cabin do make the script enjoyable.

Whether it be your first, second, or fifth time running in the Spencer Mansion there seems to always be something new to appreciate.

I have never played a single Resident Evil game before, only watched a playthrough of RE VII and RE VIII, so I was interested in checking out the original experience for myself.

The start was veeery rough. The controls were extremely clunky and the camera angles crazy! Barely managed to kill the first enemy with my knife. After a couple hours of game time I still considered restarting and lowering the difficulty.

Then I read a few tips that encouraged to change the movement controls to [i]Classic[/i], which helped a lot – didn't feel as dexterous in fights, but exploration was much more pleasant! Bit by bit I started getting enough resources (and skills) that I wasn't constantly running around with only 1 % health and two bullets.

The limited saves were also a bit scary/annoying at first, but the amount of saves you get was pretty balanced in the end. Overall, I had more than enough of all resources towards the end of the game. The ending was almost too easy even, while the learning curve was a bit too steep at the start, and the middle part was probably the best balanced and it felt like you were starting to make solid progress.

The story was okay, but the main focus was heavily put on the gameplay – especially exploration and solving semi-simplistic puzzles. Running around was sometimes made more annoying than necessary by doors that broke down so you couldn't use them anymore and had to take longer routes, which felt completely unnecessary. There was quite a bit of backtracking, which I didn't find too bad, except when it was only to manage your teeny tiny inventory by picking up or putting away some items. The constant going through doors would have driven me crazy if it wasn't for a mod that cut off five seconds from the transitions – I highly recommend that you download it!

Jump scares were a bit less prevalent than I expected and usually easily spotted ahead of time. The horror element wasn't as strong as I had imagined, but the atmosphere was still great.

The achievements are very well balanced: you'll get around half in one playthrough, and getting the rest will motivate you to try playing as the other protagonist, whose story and gameplay experience differ a bit and offer good replay value. Though I feel that if you're going for a 100 % completion, you'll have a very rough time...

All in all, the classic Resident Evil experience was occasionally clunkier and more aggravating than I had hoped, but at the same time very polished and atmospheric. Very well-made for a game originally released in 1996!

As a longtime fan of the Resident Evil series, I'm disappointed in myself for taking so long to revisit REmake and play it all the way through. As I kid I had borrowed it from a friend but was too dumb and scared to finish it before they wanted it back and I never got back around to playing it myself. Now that I finally have I absolutely loved it. This game does a fantastic job of building a tense atmosphere. Left alone zombies can sometimes move between rooms on their own. Defeated zombies, if not defeated with a headshot, will eventually become even more powerful and rise again even more dangerous than before if not defeated with a headshot or burned. This turns every zombie from a standard enemy encounter into a series of decisions where you never really know the right answer. Do I try to avoid them, or is it a better idea to clear this hallway out? If I kill them do I use my precious shotgun ammo and hope for a headshot? Or do I use my limited supply of kerosene to burn them? Should I carry my lighter and fuel canteen with me just in case? Or do I run back to the item box whenever I may need them? The tension that this generates ensures that you never feel safe in the mansion even as you become more familiar with it. I've always loved the classic Resident Evil games, and I've played the original more times than I can count, and now that I've played REmake all the way through I can't believe how much better it is. This game will for sure be one that I revisit many times in the future.

A window into what Resident Evil could/should have been. A slow tense game where you have to plan your path and how much ammo to use ahead of time. You feel constantly in danger, scavenging for clues and resources with danger always lurking around the corner.

The fixed camera position is a well implemented mechanic in the game better than the free camera. This coupled with the slow pace everything moves really creates tension. You have to collect items in the world to progress which are scattered through the world. It is scary when you hear a zombie that you can't see and you have to think if you can spare the ammo to shoot or run. I prefer this over the dumb action mechanics future games take. 

The boss battles are suprisingly good again due to the mechanics of the game. You feel like fighting stronger enemies but you have a fighting chance. There is a large variety of enemies to fight.

The story is OK. It's mostly told through notes that I prefer. It's very low key compared to the craziness the rest of the RE franchise is. In the Witcher Gerald says he likes his horse because it has the perfect trait every horse has, it doesn't talk. There's so much in this game that may immediately turn off new players. Here's an incomplete list: The fixed camera angles and clunky controls. A save system restricted to set locations and requiring the use of a consumable item. A million doors that take 7 seconds to load. The extremely small inventory size. The slow firing guns. The cheesiest dialogue and voice acting. The dated graphics (even in this remake).

Yet, it's difficult to fault a lot of these pain points, as many were intentional design decisions chosen to make the game that much scarier. And hot damn, [i]they worked[/i]. It's these design elements that have made this game such a classic. It's difficult to describe how the changing camera angles, for example, unequivocally add to the tense atmosphere of the game. It's something you'd have to experience to understand, and there's joy in that experience.

Furthermore, the sense of frustration on player death, losing up to 20 minutes of progress, is always quickly overshadowed by the realization that it'd probably take less than 5 minutes to catch back up. Once you [i]learn[/i] the game, it becomes a bit of a playground. There's a sense of progress, not just from progressing through the game, but from understanding and mastering it. A remastering of a remake of a classic game that is a ton of fun to play. REmake is probably one of the best ways to experience the classic RE formula with manual, limited saves, limited inventory and resource management.

RE2make does something similar with its Hardcore difficulty, but I'd argue that Hardcore is too hard for a first blind playthrough, and Standard difficulty can be a bit easy with infinite saves and larger inventory space. REmake offers 3 difficulties of Very Easy, Easy, and Normal from the start, with unlockable higher difficulties after game completion.

It's an excellent starting point for those new to the series since it's the first in the timeline (besides RE0), and a lot of the games derive from the basic formula presented here. I have played REmake years ago without playing any other RE game prior, and the first 2 hours can be pretty confusing if you haven't played other games in the franchise, or old-school point-and-click type games. If you're concerned about struggling in the early-game, Jill's campaign is definitely the easiest out of the 2, and Easy (hiking) difficulty can still provide a decent challenge.

Unlike the newer RE remakes, this game does use tank controls with fixed camera angles, but you can use an alternate control scheme that allows either Jill or Chris to rotate and move freely. I would recommend playing with a controller since you have the ability to control with tank controls using the d-pad for precision, and then move freely with the analog stick. You can also stick purely with the original control scheme, which all the enemies and encounters were originally designed for.

Like a lot of RE games, there's a lot of replay value with the 2 campaigns, different difficulty modes, unlockables, etc.

After going on a marathon this year starting with RE2Make, RE3Make, RE4Make, replaying 5, finally trying out 6, playing Revelations then going to this is such a refreshing experience after the bloated noise that is 6. It's back to basics, an actual survival horror game in a really spooky setting that in itself is a giant puzzle to be solved.

Having played video games since the 90s, the fixed camera and controls did not bother me since I've played my fair share of point and click adventure games and games with similar setups (Devil May Cry 1, Grim Fandango, etc). The aesthetics of the Spencer Mansion really work well with all the odd camera angles, giving it an even more spooky vibe along with the excellent sound design. And regardless of how you think you handle horror, the game will eventually get you at some point or another with how well made the atmosphere is in the game.

It does get obtuse at times (like getting the item needed to unlock the Magnum), but  all the puzzles that are needed to advance the game has enough hints placed in the mansion, usually in the same room as the puzzles. Or are easy enough to solve via trial and error as those rooms are usually devoid of enemies. It is recommended to play as Jill first for newcomers as she has more inventory slots than Chris and has the very useful ability of unlocking some of the locked doors with her lock-pick.

The backtracking can get tedious at times, but eventually you figure out your own preferred safe paths to get from one point of the mansion to the other. If you play on Hiking difficulty, there is enough challenge but the game is chill enough for the most part (with less enemy placement and more resources you can get) so even the more horror (or fixed camera) averse people can play it at a leisurely pace.

If you are into horror games and is interested in the series, this is well worth a shot. If you are intimidated by its reputation as a hard game with limited saves, playing on Hiking should provide an optimal experience, although they added an even easier Walking mode if even Hiking is too much. If you look at the clear percentages on Steam, only around 27% managed to beat the game on Walking/Very Easy, and even lower for the other difficulties. If you persevere with this game, you'll be part of the proud few who beat it on Steam.

TLDR:  Reworked classic definitely showing its age.

Despite the Resident Evil series being a juggernaut in the gaming scene, I had never played any of the games before now, so I decided to give the franchise a shot and start with the first one. I had no idea what to expect.

(Slight spoilers below.)

For anyone unfamiliar with the scenario, several members of the elite STARS police team are trapped deep in the woods, in a mansion filled with zombies and other beasts. The player can choose to act as Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield and it's not a cosmetic choice; each character has strengths and weaknesses (for example, Jill has a bigger inventory and Chris can take more damage), and has different interactions with other characters. Even some of their cutscenes, at critical plot moments, are different. Changing the game experience depending on one's character is a nice feature that adds replay value and I wish more games would do that.

The mansion is incredibly spooky and creepy, as is the background music and overall sound scheme. I watched some gameplay of the original game. It's much brighter and cheerier and honestly looked a lot less chilling than this remastered version. Here, the environments are darker, dirtier, and more cluttered. The monsters (and cut scenes) are rendered better, sound much more intimidating and are--in a word--scary. (Yes, there are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ zombie sharks in the game ...  in a mansion in the middle of the woods. Always with the sharks ...) This remastered version includes a shambling monster threat (that can't be killed) that isn't in the original and that threat is ugly in every sense of the word. In terms of hitting the player in the visceral spot that taps your innermost fears, I haven't encountered many games that punch this hard.

Resident Evil is known for its creepy environment but at its core, it is a puzzle game, requiring the player to search for objects and information to solve traps, reveal critical information, or open new areas. A lot of these take brains and guesswork and players are unlikely to simply stumble on the answers without some exploration and pondering. I will say, it feels like nearly *every* object has some use, if you just keep looking around. This applies to limited inventory space too, as choosing the items to carry can be just as big a puzzle as anything, as well as balancing the use of limited heal items, ammo, and typewriter ribbons (to save game).

Unfortunately, when it came to to the gameplay itself, I had real problems. For one, fixed cameras in this style of game are one of my least favorite mechanics. Not being able to see what the character is looking at is annoying as hell--and there is no real reason for it, as games like the original Tomb Raider (released the same year as the original RE) had mastered an over-the-shoulder camera. That also played into the directional movement controls (relative to the view), as a sudden change of camera angle might send the character scurrying in the opposite direction. Neither of the game's control schemes felt intuitive or comfortable, which was a real issue when monsters attacked or in timed puzzles with moving walls and such. It was a consistent detraction that dragged down my enjoyment. I take it that preserving this style was probably a nod to nostalgia for the original game but updating it (as RE2 and RE3 evidently did for their remakes) would have gone a long way to making this game more accessible.

Other than using the knife, regular combat is overly simplistic. Pointing guns anywhere near the mobs will hit them and on any other the highest difficulty, aim was automatic. On the other hand, combat against the boss mobs felt unforgiving. That would be fine, except the stiff controls and flip-flopping camera often meant blundering into an attack without meaning to. Just kind of cheap and frustrating. The story is fairly boilerplate, though files scattered around the mansion provide some needed background. While light years ahead of the original, the voice acting is still only average and the dialogue is still incredibly cheesy and eyeroll-worthy.

Despite these detractions, I found the gameplay addictive. For some reason, stalking through the mansion, dodging mobs and trying to figure out the puzzles, kept bringing me back for another session. I'm not sure why and after a while, I stopped worrying about it. Sometimes, you can't pin down exactly *why* something is enjoyable. It just is.

I didn't have any glitches and crashes. This version of the game loaded smoothly and ran well enough. Steam achievements look do-able for someone really enjoying the game, though it will take multiple playthroughs. I played twice--once as Jill and once as Chris--and got about three-quarters of the achievements.

Resident Evil is one of those games that really made me wish Steam had a "Neutral" option for ratings. It's eerie as hell. I see the core appeal, and I cannot argue RE's influence on the modern game scene. At the same time, the camera and controls meant this was one of the most frustrating I've played recently.

In the end, I will give it a thumbs up because despite those negatives, I enjoyed my time here. The gameplay and iconic nature of the series are enough that I've already picked up RE2 and 3.

Pros
- Incredibly creepy setting, sound/music, and ambiance
- Thoughtful puzzles that take effort and exploration

Cons
- Gameplay, controls, and camera angles all very dated
- Cheesy dialogue and voicing

Final Score: 6/10

After decade, I revisit the Resident Evil remake.

Having played both the original and the GameCube remake in the past. My impression of both versions is that they differ, but both are commendable.

Initially intended as a GameCube exclusive, the 2002 remake later expanded to other platforms like the PS2. Remarkably, despite its 2002 origin, the game has aged gracefully. Even after two decades, it manages to keep up with contemporary graphic demands, securing its position as one of the best survival horror games. The controls pose no issues for me, but the occasional abrupt change in control due to map-switching can be a minor hiccup for speed runners. Aside from that, I have no complaints about the game and experience.

Regarding the story, I didn't expect much, as the focus is on introducing and exploring the origins of the RE outbreak. Emphasis is placed on game-play, replay value, suspense, and inventory management.

Differences between the original and the remake (if my memory serves me well):

Original Version:
[i]The original game features larger maps with more zones and rooms to explore. Some rooms from the original were omitted in the remake, such as the hidden room behind the glass of the greenhouse area. In the original, players had to mix various chemicals to eliminate a plant (not Plant 42). Navigating the original RE can be challenging, with the outdated map system. What I particularly enjoyed about the original was the abundance of diaries to collect and read, a feature somewhat lacking in the 2002 version.[/i]

[b]However, the strengths of the remake includes:[/b]

1. An improved and intricate map system.
2. Stunning graphics.
3. Numerous selective options.
4. Multiple endings.
5. A more in-depth exploration of the Spencer family and their discoveries.
6. Partner assistance.
7. Self-defense support.
8. Diverse enemies, including crimsons and bees.
9. A range of available bosses, such as the Elder Crimson and Lisa.

In conclusion, my Resident Evil game play provided a satisfying blend of nostalgia and enjoyment. For newcomers to the series, I highly recommend starting with the first Resident Evil game.

[h1]7/10[/h1] This game is awful and I hate so many of the design decisions the devs made... and I really enjoyed it. The requirement to use a consumable resource for saving progress is honestly genius and forces you to save only when it is absolutely necessary. The game actively encourages you NOT to use ammo; killing a zombie takes like 20 pistol bullets and they respawn even stronger and faster.

To get rid of 1 zombie you need to first kill it (ammo gone) and burn it (find fuel and lighter). This makes backtracking, which there is a lot of, excruciatingly painful but forces you to carefully plan routes and burn zombies in certain areas, while saving your lighter fuel in others. You also have to git gud at evading enemies. Finding new items also means backtracking to a safe room and depositing items into the chest as you've basically no inventory space. The puzzles are solid even if a lot of the time it's basically "slot the square crank into the square hole" type stuff.

None of this is helped by the fixed camera angles and abrupt transitions when going from one part of a room to another. Some of the camera angles are right in your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and so you can't even see zombies come at you - and it's great, it creates tension and makes you listen for enemies and carefully survey your environment. "Resident Evil HD Remaster" is a polished update of the game that established the survival horror genre in the gaming world. Here's an extensive review detailing why this game remains a must-play:

Historical Significance:
"Resident Evil HD" brings players back to the roots of the survival horror genre. It preserves the original game's groundbreaking elements while updating it for modern audiences. The game is a piece of video game history, showcasing how the genre began and how far it has come.

Graphics and Atmosphere:
The remaster significantly overhauls the graphics of the original 1996 game, with updated textures, models, and lighting effects that enhance the eerie atmosphere of the mansion. The fixed camera angles, a signature element of the original, add to the tension, often hiding dangers just out of sight. These angles, combined with the detailed environments and improved visuals, create a sense of dread and anticipation that few games can match.

Sound Design:
The sound design in "Resident Evil HD" is exceptional. Every creaking floorboard, distant moan, and ambient noise contributes to an immersive horror experience. The game's soundtrack is iconic, with haunting melodies that linger with players long after they've turned off the console.

Gameplay Mechanics:
While retaining the deliberate, tank-like controls of the original, the remaster offers an alternative control scheme that can make the experience more accessible to newcomers. The game's pacing is deliberate, forcing players to consider each action carefully, from managing limited resources to deciding when to fight or flee. Puzzle-solving remains a core aspect of the game, requiring players to pay close attention to their surroundings and think critically.

Storytelling:
The narrative of "Resident Evil HD" is classic horror. As members of the elite S.T.A.R.S. team, players unravel the mysteries of the ominous Spencer Mansion and the secrets it holds. The story is filled with twists, betrayals, and the kind of campy dialogue that has become endearing to fans over the years.

Character Choice:
Players can choose between two characters, Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, each with unique storylines and challenges. This choice adds to the game's replay value, as each character's experience differs in inventory space, available weapons, and support from other characters.

Survival Elements:
The game's inventory management and save system (using a limited number of typewriter ribbons) are integral to the survival experience. Players must constantly make decisions about what items to carry and when to save, which adds to the game's tension and difficulty.

Replayability:
"Resident Evil HD" has high replay value due to its multiple endings, hidden items, and unlockable modes. It rewards thorough exploration and mastery of its mechanics with new challenges and content, encouraging players to revisit the mansion again and again.

Impact on the Genre:
The remaster not only stands as a testament to the original game's impact but also influences the modern survival horror games that followed. Playing "Resident Evil HD" is not just about experiencing a great game; it's about understanding the evolution of the genre.

In conclusion, "Resident Evil HD Remaster" is an essential play for both fans of the series and those who appreciate the horror genre. It skillfully balances nostalgia with modern enhancements, making it a definitive version of a classic game. Whether you're in it for the scares, the story, or the history, "Resident Evil HD" delivers an experience that has stood the test of time and remains as compelling today as it was at its inception.

I thought I came to know the horror genre in gaming with Resident Evil 4 and how its atmosphere and game design evoked a foreboding sense of tension, but I realize now that was only child’s play compared to Resident Evil 1’s true feeling of claustrophobic terror. This game was fun, but more than it was fun it was spooky. So spooky, that I couldn’t play for more than 2 hours per session without needing to take in between as I’d be exhausted from the tension created from its eerie sound design that is determined to get me in cold sweat with the percussions and screeches it utilizes in scaring me . 

It is incredibly visually distinct. The use of a limited color palette is fantastic in portraying Spencer’s Mansion as this grand yet haunting area where you’ll never know what could be at the other end of the corridor. This game doesn’t have jumpscares but it really does feel like anything can pop up at any time. Considering this is a remake, I liked that they kept the door transitions despite not needing to as that added pause transition between rooms create this sense of dread as you enter a new room. 

Narratively, Resident Evil 1 is a lot less goofier than what I expected after playing Resident Evil 4 as the urgency of finding a way out of the terrifying mansion is a lot more felt compared to strolling and taking your time in saving the president’s daughter. However, the choices some of these characters make truly baffle me as it all falls into the same cliches I’ve seen over and over in horror movies. “Let’s split up” and “you go on ahead” will be common in tilting me as I just find it so convoluted that they’d want to be on their own despite being in near death scenarios multiple times. The worst part is when a certain betrayal happens but the victim never ends up asking why and what’s happening. Otherwise, the story was still pretty gripping up to the end where they use a grenade launcher to kill the big bad. The characters aren’t really much to speak about since Jill is really just a stand-in for the player and I can’t say a lot about their personalities or character traits besides me finding Jill hot, but that's okay.

Do I like the gameplay? Yes, but only to a certain extent. The fixed camera angles don’t bother me as I thought it would as I quickly got used to them and learnt to appreciate how the chosen framing can actually help a lot in setting up the creepy atmosphere. Having scarce resources also added to the overall horror experience and considering how simple it is to aim at zombies and also being unnecessary a lot of the time, things were relatively easy. Despite that, it was still overall incredibly enjoyable in solving the puzzles while navigating through the corridors of the mansion and running away from zombies. I did have a major issue with the very start though with how little it guides you in some of the mechanics like combining and examining items you get, but that's just probably old games am I right? 

Overall, Resident Evil (2002) was another great experience as part of my horror binge and is so far the most I have been scared of with a video game. Beyond some hiccups in the early parts, I thoroughly had a smooth playthrough of constantly getting exhausted from the tension and needing breaks every 2 hours or so. 8/10, the spooks are for real.

[h1] Resident Evil HD: A Haunting Masterpiece Remade for PC! [/h1]

Resident Evil, originally released in 1996 and remade in 2002, is an iconic survival horror title. Its recent PC release marks the return of director Shinji Mikami to the genre he helped shape. This isn't just a piece of gaming history; it's a brilliantly designed and claustrophobic masterpiece.

I must admit, I initially expected a more realistic zombie-infested survival experience - barricading windows, collecting supplies, and dealing with infections. But that's not the path Resident Evil takes. Instead, it offers a mansion filled with abstract puzzles and campy dialogue, which at first left me somewhat disappointed. I was looking for a deep survival experience and psychological thrills, not an intricate item hunt wrapped in a Sci-Fi Channel storyline.

The moment a Resident Evil game delves into its extensive backstory, it risks losing me. I've never been particularly invested in the series' narrative, so it's the actual gameplay, scares, and set pieces that pull me back in. Fortunately, Resident Evil Remake delivers in these areas.

The main plot is relatively tight and engaging, drawing inspiration from mad scientist B-movie narratives and comic book conspiracies. The subplots, including the one added in the 2002 remake, provide intense moments of terror. But what really shines is the game's design.

While it might not be the complex simulation I expected as a teenager, Resident Evil's layout is nothing short of a masterpiece. The mansion and its surroundings form the foundation, its intricate map transitioning from black to red to green as you progress. The entire location remains claustrophobic, even as you explore its darkest corners. There's a sense of purpose in almost every scene, with even seemingly empty hallways offering some challenge.

Management is the name of the game, whether it's handling combat, rationing ammo and healing items, or planning a route from a safe room to a problem. Resident Evil is a slow-burning experience, always offering a thread to follow or a puzzle to solve. Applying the right pressure – finding the correct item or using it in the right place – allows the mansion to unfold and unravel before you.

However, not everything is perfect. The lack of direction can be frustrating, leaving you stuck or unsure of your next step. The game's first couple of hours can be particularly bewildering as multiple paths open up and then lead to dead-ends.

Even the boss fights, while requiring different strategies, essentially operate on the same principle as the puzzles. They're about bringing the right equipment to the fight, more about calculations than reflexes.

The beauty of Resident Evil is in its resource management. You'll constantly weigh the risk of going down a certain corridor, contemplating if it's worth the ammunition needed to deal with lurking zombies. As you progress, healing items become scarcer, and ammunition runs low. The save system and limited inventory space may seem irritating at first, but they're core to the design, encouraging players to plan ahead.

As for the story, it's as cheesy as ever, though thankfully without the labyrinthine mythology of the later games. It's enjoyable in the way that Roger Corman's Poe adaptations are, offering moments of fear amid the campiness. The standout is the Lisa Trevor subplot, which debuted in the Gamecube remake. It's genuinely unsettling, making it all the more shocking in contrast to the rest of the narrative.

In terms of visuals, Resident Evil Remake is impressive, although some textures look dated. The increased resolution doesn't completely remove the game's VHS-like quality, and that's a good thing. It looks beautiful but maintains its original gritty atmosphere.

While the remaster lacks some extras, I wish there was more information about the game's design and development. Nevertheless, playing Resident Evil Remake has been a revelation. It may not be as bold as it was when it first launched, but I've come to appreciate its intricate design. What might have initially disappointed me has become a delightful and intriguing experience.

This release is a chance to revisit a classic, meet Lisa Trevor, and for those who've never played Resident Evil, it's the perfect time. It's a piece of gaming history that has shaped the survival horror genre. When a game is crafted this meticulously, the shortcomings of imitations become glaringly obvious.

The game that laid the foundations of survival horror deserved to be remastered, and they overdelivered with one of the greatest games of all time with Resident Evil. This version is the HD version of the 2002 remaster and the gameplay is phenomenal. You are trapped inside a zombie filled mansion, but combat is difficult because of the claustrophobic setting and a tight inventory system that makes you question if you should really pick every item you find. Amazingly, the remaster goes the extra mile to bring new areas to some levels that improve on the original game.
This gameplay cycle scales really well as the game story develops. It's all about the reason of a zombie outbreak, and how main characters Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine explore the mansion, each with their own story and small gameplay tweaks. The remake tries to maintain some of the campy charm of the game its based on, to my personal delight.
Resident Evil is visually breathtaking, it was for its 2002 release and it is today with this HD remaster, using the old technique of pre-rendering its graphics to use with fixed camera angles. The result is used to enhance the game performance with improvements such as real-time reflections and a remarkable use of light sources. 
The soundtrack is very well suited for this horror game, and can even be listened on its own, but some songs in this HD version are sped up. It is still a perfect rendition of the original soundtrack. The sound design is great, since there always are scary background sounds to keep you on your toes. Monsters can be distinguished by their cries and moans, which is really cool. 
Once you beat the game, based on your performance you will unlock new gameplay modes with even harder rules, new costumes for the main characters to wear and new weapons, encouraging you to finish the game faster each time. Not much more content is offered, but the game honestly does not need it.
Overall, every element of the game elevates the horror that you will experience the first time, with a gameplay developed to scare your eyes, ears, hands and mind, and will haunt you until you finish it again, and again. The original PlayStation game was really good, but this one? Simply one of the greatests.

The quintessential remake, yet to be surpassed by any other in this medium. Incredibly detailed visuals, astounding soundtrack, corny, yet well-delivered dialogue, near perfect gameplay and substantial replayability define it. Capcom set the bar so high, that no other game remake might ever top this work. It makes the original wholly superfluous, outside of pure nostalgia or curiosity. REmake is one of the best games ever made and it's king in its series for these reasons.

This port has some flaws to note. The resolution of many textures is sub par and shows that Capcom fought against their own art design when upscaling it for the HD era. The OST was sped up, but there's a mod for that as well. The faces and models were retouched, and look different from the GC ones, some more drastically than others. In general however, it's nothing that cannot be fixed with some mods. There are also some optional toggles, like original aspect ratio and modern controls, which break the game by the way, allowing one to dance around enemies freely. I must admit that I enjoy tank controls and this game was meant to be played with them, which contrary to popular belief, are not counterintuitive at all. After a couple of minutes, you'll adjust to them.

Resident Evil was, without exaggeration, a masterpiece, and while the HD version is not without caveats, it's the best way to experience REmake next to the original disc and hardware, if you can stomach such low resolutions.

[h1] The Game That Started It All [/h1]

Resident Evil has always been one of my favourite franchises, in fact I'd probably say it's my favourite overall if I had to pick one, ever since my Uncle gave me the "Claire Disc" for Resident Evil 2 for the Playstation 1 back when I was just a kid.

However that's where it started for me, Resident Evil 2, I'd never actually played Resident Evil 1. So after about 18 years of putting it off, I decided to finally give it a go after completing all of the other mainline games.

The remake is great, definitely the definitive way to play this game although there are some problems but there's a lot of fun to have here.

Firstly, the setting and sound design is great. In this Resident Evil, a Zombie feels like a genuine threat that you need to decide whether it's worth skipping round him or taking care of him. I think that's what makes this game enjoyable, it really is true survival horror, you need to decide when to use your bullets and when to know to save them.

The puzzles are good if not a bit convoluted at times, it might seem obvious when you've figured it out but there will be times when you've got absolutely 0 idea and will take a little peak online just to nudge you in the right direction. Although what I will say is that when you figure out a puzzle on your own, it feels amazing.

Combat is okay, it's a little rough and a bit tank controlly, but it is what it is, I'd say this is just a product of time and age.

Camera angles, they do take a bit of getting used to, but it's really not as bad as everyone makes it out to be, in fact I quite enjoyed it when I -wasn't- in combat. In combat it's a nightmare, but running around from place to place, it really makes the game feel movie like. I didn't mind it as much as I see other people complaining about it.

Story and dialogue is a bit cheesy, but the files are where the game shines. The spoken dialogue feels quite robotic but when you're reading through the jarring files of the whole scenario, it makes the world feel more alive. I always like it when the game feels bigger than the protagonist, that there was something going on during your mission and way before it. To me, the story's are the ones where you're just a smaller role in a bigger world who can make -some- difference but not completely resolving the problem.

Overall, Resident Evil 1 for me is a solid 6/10, it's enjoyable and possibly replayable on harder difficulties where the puzzles are apparently more difficult; camera angles are a bit of a nuisance at times and inventory management can feel like a chore. Definitely a good one and done.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a lovingly crafted resurrection of the classic that kickstarted the survival horror genre. This remaster is more than just a fresh coat of paint; it's a testament to the enduring brilliance of the original Resident Evil. On the positive side, the game's visual overhaul is nothing short of stunning, breathing new life into the iconic Spencer Mansion and its ghastly inhabitants. The meticulous attention to detail elevates the eerie atmosphere, making every shadow and creaking floorboard feel genuinely foreboding. The gameplay retains the tension and resource management that made the original a masterpiece, creating a sense of vulnerability that is often missing in modern horror games. The iconic puzzles and memorable encounters remain as captivating as ever, and the revamped control options make it accessible to both classic fans and newcomers.

However, Resident Evil HD Remaster isn't without its minor drawbacks. The fixed camera angles, while essential to the game's original design, can sometimes lead to awkward perspectives that hinder navigation. The voice acting, though charmingly nostalgic, may come across as campy to contemporary ears. Some players might find the backtracking and puzzle-solving a tad frustrating, but these elements are fundamental to the survival horror experience.

In summary, Resident Evil HD Remaster on Steam is a hauntingly beautiful return to the roots of survival horror. Its visual enhancements, faithful gameplay, and unwavering commitment to dread-inducing atmosphere make it a must-play for fans of the genre. While it may have some quirks related to camera angles and voice acting, these are minor blemishes on an otherwise flawless reimagining of a horror classic. Whether you're reliving the nightmare or stepping into the Spencer Mansion for the first time, this remaster is a spine-tingling journey into the heart of fear, and it stands as a shining example of what survival horror should be.

Have played through Chris' timeline and just started a new game as Jill. This game really ups the "Survival Horror" aspect it so gloriously created back in 1996. It's dark & finely refined extra attention to detail is mind blowing. Anyone not familiar with the 1st, 2nd or 3rd Resident Evil games (referring to the original from the 90's, not the remastered versions) will have a hard time adjusting to how this game doesn't hold your hand, once you're playing you are on your own. The added usage of defensive weapons, more pros & cons on which character you decide to play as and having to either decapitate or incinerate Zombies if you decide to drop a few, are great additions to the game.

Exploration, health & ammo management and a bit of patience are a must for this game, there's a lot of backtracking throughout the Mansion & for some that will get tedious. Thankfully, a majority of the game's puzzles don't take long to figure out & are a lot more straight forward compared to the original game's puzzles, there has been a few puzzles & things to do added that I've never seen before which kept me wondering & frustrated (why exploration is key), but after you get that "Eureka" moment you'll laugh at your mistakes or breath a sigh of relief in satisfaction. There is a lot of replay-ability. 

My only complaint is I found the control layout if using just the keyboard & mouse is pretty difficult to work with & I'm sure many will find it a lot easier using a control pad when playing this game, it makes character movement (Alternative or in it's Original setting), Aiming & Shooting a lot more smoother & just easier to manage when your thumbs are doing all the work & you can just focus on what's happening in game.

Would I recommend this? Absolutely! Like the remastered Resident Evil 2 & 3 which followed this is an example or how to revisit previous projects & remake them right. No bugs, glitches or performance issues. If you're a fan of the Resident Evil franchise & still haven't bought this, it's more than worth the price it's dropped to.

[h1] Brilliant formula, frustrating execution [/h1]
[b]Progress at the time of this review[/b]: 18/44 Achievements, finished one Chris playthrough; this is my first RE game
[b]Rating[/b]: 6/10
[b]Verdict[/b]: Somewhat of an acquired taste for me. The execution is so chock-full of immersion-breaking paper cuts that I was left feeling pity for the vast wasted potential of the core mechanisms. I probably would've given it a 5/10 and a thumbs-down if I weren't cautiously optimistic about playing the sequels.

[b]Positives[/b]:
[list]
    [*] Perhaps controversial, but: the camera angle and the character movement. I've taken for granted when games offer players plenty of freedom for camera control, and I've never thought about the ramifications of the camera angles being fixed. For me, this is the biggest factor behind the horror atmosphere and the game's unique charm to me.
    [*] As someone more familiar with FPS than survival horror that requires inventory management, I love the sense of scarcity of the ammunition. The combat also feels surprisingly engaging.
    [*] Related to the previous point, the placement of enemies and the map design work extremely well in conjunction to incentivize me to make strategic fight-or-flight decisions during each enemy encounter.
[/list]
[b]Negatives[/b]:
[list]
    [*] The storytelling and the characters are so forgettable and uninspiring. When I started, I was eagerly interacting with everything in the surroundings because I wanted to take in all the lore of this sinister mansion. I soon realized how bland the writing is and started avoiding unnecessary interactions to spare myself all the cringe. If you need an example, here's one I wish I could forget: when you interact with the shelf in the west side storage room, the game says something along the lines of, [spoiler] "The shelf is full of pills you've never seen. Many of them have changed colors." [/spoiler] Yeah, that's how bad the writing is.
    [*] The game sorely lacks respect for the players' time. Don't get me wrong, backtracking can be very rewarding if done right, but the way it works here frequently made me want to pull my hair out because I constantly found myself doing uneventful fetch quests or juggling items between my inventory and the item boxes, all while watching the unskippable animation of doors sloooooowly opening for the 300th time. No, Capcom, those don't impress or scare anyone anymore in 2015. (Thankfully, [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=378357950] door-skipping mods [/url] are a thing.)
    [*] Related to the previous point, I found it incredibly frustrating that I frequently could not identify on the map which room I should backtrack to. The way the rooms on maps are color coded to show the exploration progress does help, but not nearly enough for me. I would rather replace this feature with room labels on the maps (or some other variants, e.g. limited number of markers players that place on the map), so that at least I can more easily locate a room when I need to backtrack to it.
    [*] The puzzles are a mixed bag. Even the best ones are merely OK (e.g. the [spoiler] V-JOLT solution [/spoiler] puzzle), while the worst ones are convoluted wastes of time (e.g. the [spoiler] Pharmacy door code [/spoiler] puzzle).
[/list]

There are rarely sequels, remasters, or remakes that get the job done and get it done right.  When you want a game to give you the same feeling that the original did, but with up-to-date quality of life improvements, new and more impressive graphics, and better sound quality... you rarely get all of those things together.  Most of the time you get improved graphical fidelity, and everything else is either 'meh' or just bad.  Thankfully, Resident Evil HD Remaster is not one of those games.  This is a game where everything was done exactly as it should have been.  It's better, and it feels just like the original game does.  Never before has a walk down memory lane felt so good, while the nostalgia was the icing on the cake, and not the rickety supports holding the entire structure up.


More:

This is how a Resident Evil game should be remade... or remastered... or whatever.  When you want to revisit a game, but you want that touch of 'newness' so that you feel like you're experiencing it for the first time, you should look to games like this.  Games like Resident Evil HD Remaster should be the bar by which games redone are measured.  It's good... no... it's great.  I couldn't have asked for more.

The pre-rendered backgrounds are one of the staples of the Resident Evil series.  Well... they are if you grew up when I did, and you actually remember Resident Evil as it was in the past.  It felt like watching a scary movie just as much as it felt like you were playing a game.  Better yet, it felt like you were playing a character in a scary movie.  I guess you had to be there to really get the idea that I'm trying to convey, or perhaps you had to have played the games since then.  

When I played the Resident Evil 2 Remake, I did not feel like I was playing a Resident Evil game.  I did not give the game a good review, for various reasons, but I can totally see why people love the game.  It's not lost on me that the game can be viewed by some people as being amazing.  I get it.  I didn't like it that much, but more importantly... it did not capture the feeling of what a Resident Evil game is... at least not the way that I'm trying to convey it.  It was scary... yes.  It was gloomy... yes.  But that's not all Resident Evil is.  That's a surface level understanding of why Resident Evil was popular and why it basically laid the foundation for a specific type of survival horror game.

I don't remember disliking anything in this game.  I played through the game with both characters, and it was exactly what I expected it to be.  There were some new additions that weren't in the original... but it still felt like the original.  I wish that Resident Evil 2 Remake was made in the same style as this game.

Usually I touch on all the aspects of a game in a review.  I try to talk about the graphics, the sound design, the controls etc.  I'm just going to say that in this game, everything is great or good.  It is exactly what it needed to be.  It does the Resident Evil name proud.

My Review:
Resident Evil 1 holds an iconic place in gaming history, and after playing it, I'm reminded once again why this game is a true masterpiece. This title perfectly captures the essence of survival horror, blending atmospheric tension with challenging gameplay in a way that keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.

The mansion setting is meticulously designed, creating an atmosphere of suspense and unease that's hard to match. Every creaking floorboard and distant moan of a zombie adds to the sense of impending doom, making exploration a heart-pounding adventure in itself. The pre-rendered backgrounds, despite their age, still manage to convey a hauntingly immersive experience that draws you deeper into the mysteries of the mansion.

The gameplay mechanics, while they might feel somewhat dated to newcomers, are integral to the game's charm. The limited inventory space and resource management add an extra layer of tension, forcing you to think strategically about every decision. Puzzles are both intriguing and satisfyingly challenging, making you feel accomplished as you piece together the clues and unlock new areas.

The character development and storyline are engaging, with a cast of memorable and diverse personalities, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. The dynamic between the characters adds an extra layer of depth to the overall experience, making you feel invested in their journey.

Resident Evil 1 is a testament to the fact that great game design and storytelling can stand the test of time. It's not just a nostalgic trip down memory lane; it's a genuinely compelling and unsettling adventure that's just as captivating today as it was when it first released.

If you're a fan of survival horror, or if you're new to the genre and want to experience its roots, Resident Evil 1 is an absolute must-play. It's a piece of gaming history that every enthusiast should have in their collection. So grab your trusty handgun, brace yourself for the unknown, and step into the nightmare that started it all.

Maybe it's because I am a fan of Resident Evil series, but it was a quite fun and nostalgic experience for me. The oldschool style of the game is so much nice that you can enjoy the sweet taste of old games from both the puzzles and the general lines of the game. The lore and story are kept quite simple, like a typical 90's game, as the game is probably not expected to develop that much in the future. I highly recommend you to play the game with Chris, if you want to get the pleasure of old games again. But if you don't want to tire yourself with inventory management, just go with Jill.

First of all, I must say that the fixed camera in the game is sometimes bad and annoying, and sometimes it can reflect the atmosphere in a good way. You die directly due to a mistake you made due to carelessness in the game and you start from the last checkpoint. Actually sometimes I think this is a good thing because you usually can't die that way in new generation games, but almost every scenario that can kill you in real life also kills you in this game, like using a gunpowder gun or just running while keeping a chemical bottle in your inventory blows you up. It's hard to see that before dying once, but I like these small details.

Your checkpoints are limited in the game. Only in rooms with typewriters, you can save the game if you have an ink in your inventory. Because of that it's so risky to save the game too often. And I think the real fun of the game is based on decision making. When you play with Chris you have 6 slots. And throughout the game, inventory and saving the game becomes your main enemy.

Old-style puzzles, small inventory, limited saves and checkpoints, getting rid of all kinds of monsters gives you a very sweet experience. I think it is very nice that the game forces you in this way because it is almost impossible to find a game like this nowadays.  What I said may be a disadvantage of the game according to some, but I think it's a very good thing, in my opinion at least. Because games nowadays don't restrict players in this way anymore. More precisely, they are afraid of making the gameplay so challenging, so they put difficult bosses to make the game harder. Because they are afraid that the players will get bored with the game when they die and start over. Now everyone has a library of hundreds of games and when they are bored, they can easily switch to another game. But when Resident Evil first came out, everyone had very few game and they had to finish the games they had in the end by trying over and over again. Once you complete it, you would feel very good. This game gives that old completion pleasure to the player. 

Of course, there are cons of the game, such as boss battles are not more difficult than any normal zombies, or the fixed camera is sometimes so annoying... There is also a bug that the character starts to spin for no reason when you focus on somewhere. But I think the reasons I mentioned above compensated for them for me a little.

It pains me in a way to have to leave a thumbs down here, but I offer a warning that other potential players coming from a similar place that I was when I tried playing this should hear. I am not at all saying that this is a bad game, obviously the vast majority of folks enjoy it based on reviews; but Steam is asking if I recommend this game, and the answer to that is definitely no. I find it hard to fathom that I would be completely alone in my reasons for not liking this, so I offer this review as more of a caveat than trying to outright say you shouldn't buy it (TL;DR at bottom).

First, I totally understand what an important game this is. The action horror genre is alive and well today, and this 27 year old game is an enormous reason for that. There's not a lot of games that have ever spawned an entire gaming category, let alone a series of movies, comics, and probably other media as well. Despite all this, I hadn't actually played any of the games. RE7 and Village look really good and I'm gonna get around to playing them, but I'm the kind of player that likes to play through entire series. So, I figured that the one that started it all is worth taking a look at.

This, of course, is not that game exactly. It's a remake. My best guess is that the parts that were re-done are done quite well. It looks nice, that's for sure. Not modern graphics exactly, but not 1996 graphics either. The control scheme/core mechanics of the game are though, and that made this totally unplayable for me. I have 3 specific major gripes which add up to being a total deal-breaker, and they're things I imagine would be major turn-offs for some others wanting to jump into this series here as well. They are the following:

[b]1: Limited Saves.[/b] Saving is tied to a consumable item that you come across in the mansion. Since bag space is extremely limited, it's enormously cumbersome that your ability to save the damn game takes up a chunk of it. These items are only usable in specific locations as well. I get that saving this way is a design choice and a mechanic that some probably enjoy about this game. Elements of it persist on through the series, but it's not something I like at all in a game like this. It's something I do like in some games too; it feels great to finally get to that next bonfire and feel safe for a second. In this game though, I found it extremely frustrating that chunks of time and progress were just totally lost because I couldn't get back to the typewriter after having to backtrack because I couldn't pick up something else I needed because of that f!(#^ng ink ribbon in my inventory.

[b]2: Fixed Cameras.[/b] Again, this is a design choice and one that works sometimes. It makes total sense in a game like this that devs want you to see it from the angles they choose. It adds tension and atmosphere and surprise and is something that's actually done well in that respect, but I found having to navigate this way extremely frustrating as well. If you keep holding the button through a camera transition you'll keep moving in the same direction. As soon as you make any kind of adjustment after the transition, you'll begin to move relative to the new camera position. Even in the calmest of moments, I found myself accidentally turning the wrong direction over and over again, even some times when I knew the transition was coming. Having this issue when attempting to run for my life was something I found completely untenable.

[b]3: Combat.[/b] I found the aiming system totally unwieldy. The fact that you can't move while aiming alone feels totally wrong to me. Once your gun is up you can only turn left and right (camera relative, of course) at enemies that may be moving around you or even off-screen. There's very little in the way of feedback as to if your shots are even hitting the target sometimes, plus ammo is of course very limited. Add in the fact that you can only get hit 3 times before you die (and you better hope you used one of your precious save items recently if you do!) and it makes combat a terrifying experience for all the wrong reasons.

There's probably some very strong arguments for why these things shouldn't be deal-breakers. There's some workarounds for some of them too, probably. I only tried one of the control options and I'm sure I could have improved at both the combat and navigation if I played more (truthfully though, I figured that with the trouble I was having with early enemies that I couldn't possibly be able to get through any fights with any real complexity later). I got to this point where I [i]had[/i] to get by this one cerberus dog. I had full health and enough ammo to kill it, but it just kept getting me over and over and it just felt like whether or not I could kill it was more of a crap shoot than anything resembling skill. It took 5 attempts before I finally managed to get it down, and I managed to die before I could get to a save point so none of it mattered anyway. It was at this point that while Steam will say I played for 2.3 hours, I had only actually made like 25 minutes of game progress and had 0 minutes of fun in the process.

Let me reiterate that all this is wholly a personal matter for me. The things I've described are all things I can get over in some games but really made trying to play this impossible. I like playing retro games and especially love the nostalgia blast of playing one from my youth. This game does not scratch that particular itch for me though, and as such I had no desire to slog through some archaic design as I have with some other games. If you happen to be somebody like me though and want to finally give Resident Evil a try starting at the beginning, heed my warning and skip this one. Do what I did: watch a story synopsis for this one and move on to the RE2 remake, it's superb. I've gotten considerably more than twice as much time into that one now, have loved every minute, and can still feel like I did my due diligence to the series.

So in conclusion I suppose: the odds are, if you're gonna buy this game you probably will like it. Even in the frustration I was experiencing, the elements of what made this series persist are clearly there. They were buried under what I personally found to be some unplayable systems that anyone looking to replay a game they once loved (or possibly anyone simply with more patience than me) could probably get over. This concludes my warning, thanks for sticking with me this long.

TL;DR: A masterpiece from 1996 that spawned an entire genre, but unfortunately still plays like a game from 1996. Skip it and start playing the series at the RE2 remake.

Resident Evil is a classic survival horror game that defined the genre and spawned a successful franchise. The game follows the members of a special forces team who are trapped in a mansion infested with zombies and other horrific creatures. The player must explore the mansion, solve puzzles, find weapons and ammo, and fight for their survival.

The game was originally released in 1996 for the PlayStation, but it was later ported to the PC in 1997. The PC version features the uncensored American version of the game, which has more gore and violence than the Japanese version. The PC version also has improved graphics and sound, but it suffers from some compatibility issues with modern computers.

In 2015, Capcom released a remastered HD version of the game for various platforms, including PC. The remastered version has enhanced visuals, audio, and controls, as well as new modes and features. The remastered version is widely praised as one of the best remakes of a classic game ever made.

Resident Evil is a must-play game for fans of horror and survival games. It has a gripping story, atmospheric environments, memorable characters, and tense gameplay. It is also a challenging game that requires strategy and resource management. The game has multiple endings and scenarios depending on the player’s choices and actions.

I would rate Resident Evil 1 on PC as 4.5 out of 5 stars. It is a masterpiece of horror gaming that still holds up well today. However, I would recommend playing the remastered HD version over the original PC version, as it offers a smoother and more immersive experience. You can buy the remastered HD version on Steam for $4.99 until July 13.

Pros:

A faithful and enhanced remake of a classic game that preserves the original gameplay and atmosphere

A stunning and realistic visual upgrade that makes the game look like a modern title

A crisp and clear sound design that enhances the horror and immersion

A new control scheme that allows the player to move in the direction they want to go

A new widescreen mode that expands the field of view and adjusts the camera accordingly

A new mode called Wesker Mode that lets the player play as the famous villain of all games Albert Wesker

Cons:

The game still has some of the flaws and limitations of the original game, such as limited save points and inventory space

A thoroughly enjoyable experience. The fixed camera angles help enhance the horror, though at the detriment of character movement if you're playing with the alternate controls (the default setting). Supposedly, this isn't an issue when playing with the original controls (toggle-able in the settings), but I spent my entire playtime using the alternate controls and turned out just fine, so it's just a matter of getting used to it.

A few things to note when playing this game:

1. The initial difficulty selection menu consists of the choices "mountain climbing", "hiking", & "walking". This is equivalent to Normal, Easy, and Very Easy respectively. Hard, Real Survival and Invisible Enemy modes are unlocked later.

2. The choice between playing as Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine is an important one as they both play differently. In general, Chris is slightly more difficult to play compared to Jill, so most people recommend playing as her for a first playthrough. That being said, my first playthrough was Chris on Easy and it was fine.

3. For achievements that require multiple playthroughs ("We're in This Together", "Starsenal", "Passion for Fashion"), I believe that you need to complete them in the same save slot. When saving, remember to Overwrite as Cleared Data.

4. After completing the game with both Chris & Jill on Normal difficulty or higher in a single save slot, One Dangerous Zombie mode is unlocked. This change is permanent and irreversible on that save slot unless you delete the save itself, so plan repeated playthroughs properly if you do not wish to experience this mode every single other time you do so.

Lastly, whenever you enter a different room, an unskippable cutscene of the door opening plays. I was fine with it since it helps me compose myself, especially when trying for the speedrun achievements, but some might find it annoying, so just a heads-up to those who care.
