Non-spoiler tips for anyone new to these games: 
[list]
[*]Even though the camera switching may be jarring, don't let that intimidate you. If using a controller, the tank controls on the D-pad are your friend, as odd as that sounds. Hold forward on your d-pad and don't let go until you need to turn or you reach your destination. 

[*]Running past enemies *is* an option.  It took me a bit to get used to not killing every enemy in sight, but it's a crucial skill for survival horror (and Soulsborne games, but that's not what this review is for). Experiment with your controls and.

[*]Read any files you come across. You'll get hints, answers, and some chilling lore that wasn't in the 1998 RE for PSX/Saturn.
[/list]
My only complaint is a nitpick related to nostalgia more than how good this game is. [spoiler] I don't like that they patched out the infinite grenade round glitch. That glitch saved me when I was new and was great for casual runs with no unlocked weapons. [/spoiler]

All in all- It's a great remake of possibly the most influential game in the survival horror genre, given a fresh coat of paint to show it's still got it. It stays faithful to the game it was based on, while expanding on it in a meaningful way. If you want a Certified Classic™, look no further. It stands tall among the greats of its era.

[And if you feel like it when you're done with this, check out the original 1998 version. It's awful in so many wonderful ways and great where it counts. A casual eminder that jank can be a feature. And like movies, you can be bad and fun at the same time.]

The remake of the original iconic title that became a runaway success back in the PSX days, thus becoming a hit on the Nintendo GameCube. It's a game that improves on the original on most things, yet it surprisingly does away with some things that were really cool on the original.

The visuals and the iconic Spencer mansion layout received quite the overhaul, so returning vets from the PSX version had a lot of new surprises to face. The acting was much more improved over the campy, B movie style of the original (I don't really know whether to consider this an improvement or not, since the goofy voicework and corny script of the original were indeed half the fun!) The soundtrack was a remixed version of the original game and not the one used on the third version released (Resident Evil Director's Cut: Dual Shock Edition), I would have preffered Capcom had used both soundtracks and gave the chance to choose which one you would preffer on any given playthrough..., too bad.

Content wise, the game featured a new and intriguing side plot to the original game's storyline in the form of one of the new bosses you face: Lisa Trevor. Aside from that, as well as some rather surprising changes regarding Richard Aiken, the game's story doesn't really deviate much from the original. However, I do have to point the fact that the game's story now encourages a set route and order to do things, unlike the original where if you wanted to mix things up and go to places you hadn't gone earlier in previous playthroughs, you would discover additional cutscenes that changed slightly the game's story. However, new mechanics are available such as the defensive items which can save you in a pinch!

All in all, the game's pros are more numerous than its cons and I love to play this often along with the original. Just do not expect an easy challenge, for that is what defined the original survival horror genre back in the day!

Resident Evil HD Remake: Zombie-Slaying Timelessness... with a Side of Crispy Graphics
Ah, Resident Evil, the game that taught us all the valuable life skills of surviving a zombie apocalypse. And now, it's back in all its HD-remastered glory! Get ready to revisit the Spencer Mansion, where the undead roams, puzzles abound, and the ink ribbons are as scarce as a decent haircut during a quarantine. This game is like a fine wine—it stands the test of time, leaving you equal parts terrified and tickled.
First things first, let's talk about those crispy HD graphics. Gone are the days of pixelated zombies that looked more like angry Tetris blocks. Now, you can behold the zombies in all their decomposing glory, with every festering wound and hungry groan lovingly rendered in high definition. It's like a terrifying art gallery where you get to shoot the exhibits. Who said the violence can't be beautiful?
But fear not, fellow zombie slayers, for this remake remains faithful to the classic Resident Evil experience. The tank controls are back, reminding us of the joyous struggle of maneuvering our characters like drunken ballerinas. You'll find yourself running face-first into walls, attempting a simple 180-degree turn, and accidentally firing your shotgun at the wall while a zombie chews on your neck. Ah, good times!
Of course, we must remember the iconic dialogue. The voice acting in Resident Evil HD Remake is a true masterclass in unintentional comedy. Each line is delivered with such dramatic flair that it's hard to keep a straight face. Who can forget the iconic "You were almost a Jill sandwich" line? It's a gourmet feast of cringe that keeps on giving.
Now, let's talk puzzles. Oh, those glorious, brain-teasing puzzles that will make you question your own sanity. Resident Evil HD Remake brings back the joy of finding obscure keys, deciphering cryptic symbols, and rearranging statues like you're trying to win a demented game of interior design. Remember, when in doubt, examine everything, combine everything, and pray that you don't run out of ink ribbons right before a boss fight.
One of the joys of this game is the sense of dread it instills. Every door you open, every shadow you glimpse, and every distant groan sends a shiver down your spine. The atmosphere is thick with tension, and the jump scares are as effective as ever. You'll find yourself nervously inching forward, holding your breath, and then promptly screaming like a banshee when a zombie bursts through the window. It's cardio and a gaming experience all in one!
Resident Evil HD Remake is a testament to the fact that a game can stand the test of time. It captures the essence of the original while adding a fresh coat of HD paint. Whether you're a long-time fan reliving the terror or a newcomer experiencing the game for the first time, there's something undeniably special about the survival horror masterpiece that is Resident Evil.
So, grab your herbs, load your trusty shotgun, and prepare to embark on a journey through the Spencer Mansion that will leave you both frightened and entertained. Resident Evil HD Remake proves that even in the world of zombies and cheesy dialogue, there's a timeless charm that continues to captivate gamers of all generations. Now, go forth and make those zombies wish they had stayed buried!

I've actually struggled with myself on whether I should give it a thumbs up or down. The game is not terrible but it also hasn't aged very well in various aspects. Let me go through the core aspects of the game and what I see as positives and negatives.

[u] Graphics [/u]
The game overall in this HD version still looks pretty good. The backgrounds are well drawn and the lightning flashing in the background gives it a pretty good atmosphere. The character models are also still pretty good. Still sometimes you also find some pretty low resolution background where it will be difficult to identify things. The CGI video sequences are okay in terms of quality.

[u] Sound Design [/u]
The sound design is pretty good. You can hear your own steps on the different undergrounds pretty well as well as recognize enemies based on their sounds which is pretty important due to the fixed camera positions. The music also provides a decent atmosphere and the game also knows when to tone down the music to build up anticipation. The voice actors are doing an okay job. It's better than the original but still overall just mediocre.

[u] Map Design [/u]
The basic layout in many aspects is similar compared to the original but adds some new areas and modifies some existing ones. The remake has changed some of the older puzzles and introduced new ones. The remake is overall a bit bigger than the original I'd say and the new areas are well implemented into the overall design. Nothing feels out of place.

[u] Enemy Design [/u]
We have the classical enemies from the original and some new ones as well. In addition they've added some new mini bosses. The enemy design overall is fair. It's intended to provide a challenge while at times you have to consider whether fighting is the correct choice or running the better alternative.

[u] Story and Characters [/u]
The story and characters outside some minor tweaks have mostly stay the same compared to the original. It's a campy and goofy story about a zombie plague outbreak with some conspiracy in the background. They added some new information to build a connection to Resident Evil 2 and added some background story on the new minor bosses. It's servicable but shouldn't be taken to serious. This unfortunately affects the horror factor of the game in a negative way as you cannot really take any of it serious.

[u] Gameplay [/u]
Here comes the big issue for me as the gameplay of Resident Evil 1 has aged poorly in various aspects. Compared to the original it is now possible to use knifes and grenades to push enemies away from you and possibly land a one hit kill. In addition zombie corpses will not just disappear but if the head is still intact they will just drop to the ground and may re-awaken later. You can burn the corpses though to block that. It may be a good option in areas where you have to walk through several times. This is necessary as during your first playthrough players will be backtracking constantly and EXTENSIVELY. If you do not know where everything is located and where items have to be used you will walk/run around a LOT. Over 60% of the game is basically just running through areas of the mansion where you may to do something you couldn't do ealier or getting items into the storage room for later use as well as then taking items later again. This will be necessary as Chris for example has only 6 item slots in his inventory. If you carry a weapon + ammo you already lose 2 slots. If you add another more powerful weapon then half of the slots are already gone. Now add maybe a health recovery item and it leaves only two slots. Often you have to carry a key that leaves one slot to pick up new items. This is just poor design and a restriction to artificially stretch out the game length. Inventory management and memorizing the map layout become essential parts of the game. You really have to keep the inventory load to a minimum to ensure you can get as many relevant items as possible from your target locations.

The constant running around with backtracking where not much actually happens also causes the RE to become boring after a while. After the initial excitement and basic layout exploration the game basically comes down to:
1. Lighten inventory in storage room
2. Go to next room you haven't explored
3. Pick up relevant items
4. If inventory is not full go to next room you can open and pick up items
5. Return to storage room to lighten inventory
6. Repeat

Once you find riddles and specific key locations you will then take relevant items with you to unlock the next mystery but then it basically returns to the principle from before. Something that really annoyed me was while I was playing with the controller the stick by default always made my character run. At some point I had to pick up an item that would kill my character randomly if I started to run. So I purposely had to completely change the way I controlled the character as the standard controls would kill my character. I have no idea why anyone thought this was a good idea...

Anyway the combat controls are pretty straight forward. You go into a room and look at the door again. You hold the aim key and see if your character turns around to focus on a target. If he does an enemy is there and you can decide on whether to shoot at him or not. you can point guns up or downwards but outside of potenially knocking an enemy to the ground or blasting its head immediately when they are close it doesn't do much. The game aims at the enemies automatically and there is no skill involved there. So pretty basic combat.

The game got me a few times on jump scares (zombie behind a corner for example) but outside of that it's not really scary to be honest. Maybe I've just numbed down to much in the last few years to horror but for me the experience overall was mild.

Finally I think it's fine to buy the game when it's on sale but I wouldn't buy it at a price higher than 10€.

When I originally learned of the Resident Evil series many years ago through Resident Evil 4, I was always hesitant to go back and play the first three games due to their fixed camera & (more importantly) the long door animations. After the release of the Resident Evil 2 remake I was interested in comparing and contrasting it to it's original PS1 version from 1998. I ended up loving the fixed camera and the door animations didn't bother me as much as I expected. 

That was a few years ago; cut to present day and I decided to try out the remake of the very first Resident Evil game. While most modern gamers™ may be trepidatious to try out a game like REHD Remaster, I had heard over and over from old school fans how this is the definitive classic RE game. So I went in with high expectations, fully embracing the fixed camera (that I had grown to adore) and hesitantly accepting the punishingly long door animations. 

[h1] THE GOOD [/h1]

[b] STORY/CHARACTERS [/b]
Going in I had no expectations for this game's story beyond knowing the basic plot. However I quickly fell in love with the different characters the game had to offer. The game perfectly balances having the player feel lonely as they explore the mansion while simultaneously having recurring appearances from the cast. As the game goes on you run into the different characters, and while each interaction is short, it's expertly written to endear you to each character enough to that you genuinely care to see their story through and achieve the "best ending".

[b] REPLAYABILITY [/b]
During my hunt for 100% of achievements, I probably went through the entire game from start to finish about 6 or 7 times. Each playthrough was radically different than the previous one, due to the game masterfully increasing the challenge with each run. Modes like "Complete the game with only your knife" or "Invisible enemy mode" are gimmicky and seemingly present an unfair challenge, however the moment to moment gameplay during these modes is fun throughout, and never is there a challenge or fight that is truly insurmountable.

 The most satisfying mode by far is "Real Survival" which presents a challenge so hard I didn't dare even try it till my final playthrough. In this mode the game is set to the hardest difficulty, item boxes are disconnected (this is a huge change from the regular difficulties & modes) and auto aim is turned off. Completing this mode was truly hellish, however the satisfaction felt from seeing the credits at the end made the 37 hours~ I had put into the game to get up to that moment made it all worth it. 

[b] GAMEPLAY [/b]
The fixed camera in this game is masterfully placed, making you feel like you're watching a film throughout. There are 1 or 2 angles that most players (including myself) struggle to orient themselves around, however for the most part the angles are great. 

There isn't much variety in the weaponry, however the weapons that are available feel very satisfying to use. Especially the grenade launcher which is hilariously overpowered for a game like this. 

Boss fights are all great. 

The puzzles are all satisfying and challenging, though sometimes they can be a bit slow. 

[h1] THE BAD [/h1]

- Door animations are too long (can be fixed with mods)
- Some cutscenes are very low quality due to not being remade
- Some puzzles/boss fights have unskippable cutscenes 


[h1] CONCLUSION [/h1]

REHD Remaster is a great and satisfying game with plenty of variety to offer anyone who's willing to give it a chance. Highly recommended.

All the Resident Evil games are different. Through all the years this franchise existed the developers tried new formats. But this game is closer to the PS1 retro era. Except for the controls. You can use a more convenient control scheme. This makes game easier to dive into for newcomers.

Nowadays, there are remakes of parts 2-4 with modern 3rd person camera so you may not like being unable to control the camera and properly aim. This is ok. As for me, I like that style. The camera takes spectacular angles picked by the developers themselves to present you a certain scene in the best way possible. Combined with the absence of the interface while controlling the character and thorougly drawn static lighting on the levels, that brings to the atmosphere and gives you a cinematic feeling, like you're really watching a good horror movie. Even though this camera was used just because of pre-rendered backgrounds, it made the game better and unique.

And yeah, this game is really scary. Not only because of some jumscares. I advise you to play it blind and figure it out totally on your own. That's the most proper way to play it. The first playthrough will be the most thrilling. You never know what events will be triggered by your actions. You never know if the next room will have enemies or not. And your ability to save is restricted. This makes you feel uncomfortable and paranoid. You have to manage your resources and take risks. That's why the developers called this game a survival horror. I believe games should give you emotions. Resident Evil I definitely delivers you strong ones.

The puzzles here are harder than in the subsequent games of the series. They test your memory, intuition and logic. And yeah, you have to be really observant and attentive to solve some of them. You need to search in every nook and cranny and read some important notes to figure out what to do.

I noticed that people who like Dark Souls play Resident Evil games as well. These series have a couple of things in common. Strong enemies that you have to avoid, even stronger bosses, metroidvania style of level design with searching for keys, backtracking and opening shortcuts. I could say that Dark Souls is just Resident Evil with swords and armor. But the most important feature these two share is the feeling of great accomplishment, whether it comes from taking down a strong enemy, figuring out a complicated puzzle or questline or discovering a powerful weapon in a hidden location. The main trait of that aprroach to game desgin is uniqueness of each such event. You see, every dungeon in TES or Diablo, every outpost in Far Cry or Assassin's Creed, every quest in World of Warcraft is not much different from another one. These games are repetitive. With each accomplishment, they don't give the feeling that you really reached or achieved something. Your every action is just a tiny drop in the ocean. They don't have enough value to make impress you with what you just did. Whereas in DS and RE, each action is meaningful, you feel each one of them affecting your laythrough a lot.

Of course this game is not perfect. There are some frustrating moments. For example, the camera is good for the horror, but not for the combat. Sometimes you won't even clearly see the enemy you're shooting at. Thank the character automaticallu turns to the enemy. But it doesn't work good if there are several enemies attacking you.

Some puzzles are hard to solve because you didn't find a clue because you didn't notice somewhere on the level just because it didn't stand out much and blended into the backgorund. Also there is a moment when you have to remember a note you've read a 1/3 of the overall game time ago to proceed to a new area. Some items and notes are hard to take or read for the same reason. Some of them are hard to reach because of the controls and hitboxes even if you know their locations and stand right in front of them.

Your inventory is small and there is no way to extend it. This leads to a lot of backtracking, especially when you play the game for the first time and don't know what stuff you need to take to pass certain area and what stuff you will find there. Chris has even less backpack slots than Jill so put him away for a second playthrough.

For the conclusion, I would like to state that this game deserves a playthrough, and even more than a single one. But only if you don't mind its format. It's awesome, but it's not for everyone.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

[h1] Favorite Game of All Time [/h1]
Resident Evil Remake is not only one of the best Resident Evil games, but one of the best games of all time!  It has an excellent atmosphere, satisfying game play, and great exploration.  You play as either Jill or Chris and experience their night in the Spencer Mansion.  Each character's journey is masterfully designed with many story and game play changes.  The Spencer Mansion is one of the best locations ever developed in a video game.  It is not only scary, but well designed with plenty of doors and areas that unlock as you play.  Its level design encourages not only exploration, but memorization of enemies locations and room layouts .  This is also the first game in the story, and doesn't have the issue of being unbelievable like future games.  The characters introduced are iconic and very likable. 
The issues a player may face with this game are small, but present.  The tank controls may push some people away because they function very differently from modern control schemes.  Also, as this game is over twenty years old, you will notice some places where it shows its age.  Some of the backgrounds can look a little blurry, especially in the aqua ring and a few of the cutscenes are compressed.  These issues are minor though, and the game has aged very well.
Overall, this game deserves its place as a classic.  It is the gold standard, not only for survival horror but horror in general.
TLDR  An all time great game with excellent atmosphere, gameplay and characters.  Some may take issues with controls or backgrounds, but these are minor and shouldn't stop you from play this excellent game.

I've played a lot of survival horror games, and this one is by far the best. 

Many people seem to say that nostalgia is why this game is so well-regarded; however I can say I played it for the first time in 2023 and I'm still seriously impressed with how great it is. I don't find any mechanics or controls to be outdated, maybe the lack of automatic box sorting is the one exception. The optional tank controls will feel strange at first if you're not used to them, however it only takes a few minutes to adjust, and I do recommend them. They work much better with the fixed camera angles.

The initial difficulty levels as presented are 

1. Normal (mountain)
2. Easy (hike)
3. Very Easy (walk)

I'd recommend sticking with normal, although easy isn't a bad choice either as this game is more challenging than modern games. I'd avoid very easy as this will trivialize the experience. I also recommend choosing Jill Valentine as your character for the first run - she has a larger inventory and a lock pick. Chris Redfield can take more damage and has a lighter, but Jill's benefits are much stronger.

I'd rank this as tied for best entry in the series along with RE4 remake. This is the best of the survival horror RE games, RE4R is the best of the action entries.

I hope that Capcom will consider making some more survival horror entries in the mainline series, they're truly something special.

This game reminds me of an escape room. Often there's things you won't understand the significance of, or just won't have the key for, and you're meant to chain the puzzles together into a series of gameplay strings taking you on winding paths across the mansion and its grounds. The puzzles have some interesting logic to them sometimes, and the new horrors crawling through the area make you treat the map like a secondary puzzle, asking if you can safely make it between two places in these winding halls without expending your ever more limited supply of ammunition. While my first run on (what turned out to be) easy difficulty had me never outright run out of ammunition, I did come alarmingly close.

A side note on the difficulty selection, I did appreciate that it just asked how you like your games in terms of difficulty and focus on narrative or gameplay, similarly to how some games call their easiest difficulty a "story mode". It presented me with three options, I chose the middle one and the game accepted with no remark. No shame in choosing that way to play, just how you want to experience a game that's held up incredibly well (as long as you don't mind tank controls, but even then there's an option to use a different control scheme). Add into that a graphical upgrade that helps the atmosphere far more than any visual on the Gamecube could, and you have a remarkable piece of history brought forward for modern gamers to experience. Anyone that's a fan of the remakes would do well to experience this first remake of the franchise too.

[h1] Resident Evil teaches that cinematic doesn't mean uninteractive  [/h1]

In the current zeitgeist of the videogame artform, the current standards call for a certain kind of game design. Filling your game with scenes, linear segments and a certain feel that the interaction was an afterthought. Games are trying to become movies and in such process, they simply forget what made videogames so special: interaction.

[b]I'm not implying that such games shouldn't exist, or that such games are inherently bad[/b] — I'm a Metal Gear Solid fan, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake. But I also do think that there's a model where they apply such elements without putting any thought on how to properly make the experience justifiable as a game. "Cinematic" became a really marketable adjective, but I don't think any of these recent cutscene focused games are the prime example of this quality just because they have a lot of dialogues and film-like photography. If I'm honest, [b] the most "cinematic" game I have ever played is the one you are looking for opinions right now: Resident Evil Remake. [/b]

Due to the fact this title doesn't force you to watch Hollywood inspired scenes, some people might question my statement. And these people should maybe take some time to watch more films, especially Sam Raimi, Alfred Hitchcock or George Romero's films. [b]Resident Evil Remake is the master of gamifying the experience of watching a horror thriller film through the clever usage of a philosophy the title coined: the so called "survival horror" experience.[/b] Akin to the classic Evil Dead, you are forced to explore an uncharted, lethal environment full of uncertainity. You have limited inventory slots, limited resources and the enemies you are facing are quite relentless. This game will show you how people in the 2000s viewed zombies: flesh dolls that hunt you regardless of how many shots you fired at them; it takes a lot of resources to effectively deal with them.

If you take the wrong choices, you might probably need to restart the game rather early... because even the saving system requires you to use a limited item. It never gets frustrating because the only part of the game [b]you are given full player agency and freedom to experiment is the early segments[/b] (it gets linear and less likely for you to screw up in the last levels). Still, you are always exploring, room after room, with a gun in your hand and a lot of fear of what will appear next. This game hides surprises and plays around with making you familiar with ambients to subvert this notion later, while presenting challenges in unexpected ways. Resident Evil isn't as disturbing as Silent Hill or Fatal Frame, but it's constantly a despair fest, where you are always picking resources and planning your inventory so you can travel through corridors without falling into the mansion's deadly traps. It's the apex of the classic "haunted mansion" trope, even if it avoids supernatural explanations.

This is the first part of the "survival horror" experience, and it's where you might feel frustrated and overwhelmed. However, do not give up! The second part is where you find some kind of overpowering resource, which you can abuse to dominate the game and show those zombies what you are made of. Do you remember when Ash found the shotgun in Evil Dead? You'll feel just like him when you find RE1's shotgun. You will become an overpowered action hero that is throughly able to deal with the threats that oppressed you for so long; that is, until the game throws at you new enemies, traps and puzzles. It's a constant dance of being underpowered and overpowered and it's addicting. [b]It's a masterclass on building tension, giving you consistent pay-offs and surprising you like a classic horror film.[/b]

One might ask himself about the replay value, due to the fact most of the surprises won't have the same effect if you know the mansion. [b]Resident Evil answers this by rewarding players who know the layout with unlockables, new game modes and the fact you have two campaigns.[/b] While you are exploring the same basic environment, choosing between Chris and Jill alters a lot of the resources, gameplay elements and choices you are forced into. Playing at least two times to witness different situations and twists is totally worth it — Chris being the [b]pure ludonarrative path[/b], where you are given [b]total agency of how you explore the mansion, and the game is tougher[/b]; Jill being the more [b]"linear"[/b] path, where you have [b]more resources and you don't need the same amount of backtracking and inventory management[/b], thus making the exploration a bit more of a traditional videogame since you won't need to clear your path or worry about coming back all that much.

And as a remake, it plays around a lot with the idea of [b]surprising the hardcore fan who has played the originals, changing a lot of the surprises and mixing a bit of the mansion's layout.[/b] New mechanics are added and they make the game even harder than it originally was. They also fix a lot of the issues the first game had, such as the underwhelming cave segment, the awful shark "bossfight" while adding a bit more of narrative to spice things up. I'll just say a name: [b]Lisa Trevor[/b], and you'll know what I mean when you get there. It also improves a bit on the controls, allowing you to use the analogue stick and giving you an option if you are not a fan of tank controls.

I'm more of a Chris fan because of how it plays out more akin to "living" a horror film, but both campaigns still feature the same core experience to some degree. Got around this one because I really wanted to try 4's remake, which means I rushed through the original PS1 Resident Evil and then decided to rush through this one too. But I couldn't just rush this, because [b]Resident Evil Remake is a true masterpiece and I feel very compelled to play this until there's no more content to be found.[/b] I already have 50 hours, and this game lasts like, 15~20 hours in your first run. [b] Your run can be optimized up to 2 hours or something if you do play it a lot, and it's just joyful. If you enjoy game design and haven't played this, I don't know what you are doing. This is a purchasable evidence that you can take movie elements and translate into a truly interactive and immersive game. Play it right now![/b]

Since this game launched on the Gamecube back in 2002, we have received a lot of RE games. Some of them ok, some of them bad, some of them good and some of them very good. Just a couple of things I don't like, such as too much back tracking compared to OG RE2 and OG RE3; and a couple of QOL updates that are missing from previous titles such as being able to use green herbs without needing inventory space and a dodge mechanic like OG RE 3. Other than that, this game is amazing.

I recommend playing it on a 4:3 aspect ratio instead of 16:9 Widescreen resolutions, as the pre-rendered backgrounds (Which yes, this game still uses, hence why it looks so good) will get stretched when playing on 16:9 resolutions.

While I appreciate certain things about this game, the gameplay unfortunately didn't age well imo. The inventory system and backtracking with constant door animations turn most of the gameplay into a boring slog. (There is a mod for doors though, which is essential if you want to stay sane. At least something.)

Also who thought it would be a fun idea for key items to take up the already limited inventory space as well? There is absolutely nothing enjoyable about constantly running back and forth to your storage box, it just adds even more to the backtracking and tedium. 

The atmosphere is superb, but overall I am glad the series eventually evolved past this formula.

To honestly rate this very classic and unique horror game, I would give Resident Evil 1 somewhere between a 7.5/10 to an 8/10.

This game was truly unique and eerie in many ways, and the fact that it's also a horror game, it also brought many fun and dashing values besides constant scares. The design and graphics for this game, especially for the time it was released (in 2002) is extremely impressive. The atmosphere, the creatures, the characters, the story, the music, the places to explore, and the other elements give a true insight of what a Resident Evil game should be. 

Through my gameplay, I had lots of fun playing this, and I enjoyed the story a lot. I think the best part about this game wasn't just the horror. but the VAST exploration and unique creatures and monsters you encounter.  This game at times would go from being extremely eerie, distorting, and unnerving, to mystical, comforting, and humble. Exploring the whole premises of the mansion was truly fun and engaging. The only downfall of this game I could say, is some of the control aspects. It can be a little janky at times and many of the controls just seem very old like antiques, but it's easy to get used to and deal with. It took me like 20 minutes to get used to and then I just forgot about all of that. STILL GREAT.

If there's something I also haven't really talked about it's the SCARES. This game at times was horrifying. When it came to the Crimson Head Zombies, the sharks, Lisa Trevor, and DON'T FORGET ABOUT THE GIANT SNAKE, I found it scary as hell. Lucky I had a gun in my hand or I actually would've shat myself.

Last but not least, the characters and the story. I really liked the main characters and their future stories and games, but the voice acting and character development was a little lackluster and silly at times. Like I mean SILLY ASF. The story mixed with the development of the characters is solid by itself, and really helped build all of the other games in the future, but DAMN I can't keep mentioning how goofy a lot of the story aspects were. Well, I can't blame the story and characters for being like that, especially the fact that the game was originally released in Japan by CAPCOM in the early 2000s, with the type of action in some of these CAPCOM games being extremely serious and intense and just a little silly in general.  Other than that, the story and characters were still solid and I really enjoyed it but...this game would've been soooooo much different if it were remade in 2023.

Other than that, I recommend this game to anyone who wants to try the Resident Evil series for the first time. It's not the most perfect game, but it's definitely a great game.

Though the limitations in movement/control may put some people off, if you treat it as just a gameplay mechanic it shouldn't hinder you from having a blast. The fixed camera will rarely create unfair situations since the encounters have been designed with it in mind, and the aim-lock provides a good (and necessary) fix to the fixed camera.

The backgrounds are a little blurry with modern higher resolutions and could use an upgrade at least to 1080p if Capcom had the originals with enough detail since they were first created for low definition TV screens, but otherwise the game still looks good thanks to its great art direction.

Just go into this conscious about what you're getting: this is not an all-out action game and expects you to advance carefully, conserve your ammo, avoid enemies altogether where it makes sense and even limits your saves (so space them out!).

I recommend starting in Normal difficulty ("Going on a hike") with Jill if this your first time and you want it a bit more challenging, or at Easy difficulty ("Taking a walk") if you want it a bit easier (easily enough ammo to dispose of every enemy). Also if you don't find vertical black bars intolerable I recommend playing in 4:3 as I find the pan-and-scan method the game uses if you choose widescreen pretty distracting. Also, read the game manual as it'll contain the kind of information that you'd otherwise get from an initial tutorial section in modern games.

Wait... a Negative Review??  Well I had little choice, but don't get me wrong either, the GameCube Original is a PHENOMENAL GAME, I love it, I even did Invisible Mode on Hard as a Let's Play.  Resident Evil 1 Remake is a masterpiece that really should be played by everyone, it's one of these games that you almost never get tired of on repeated playthroughs, it's very seldom these days.

But oh well, my goal here isn't really to go in-depth with the base game itself for now, and I want you to understand that any Version stemming from the GameCube will do, HOWEVER my point with this Review is I'm comparing between the GC Version and this HD Remaster, as this HD Version is SUPPOSED to be a further improved version of the GameCube Original, and while HD is pretty faithful to GC, almost like a Port, well by evidence of my score, I would rather recommend you the GC one, if you can get it that is.

The changes and even additions for HD are what I actually take issue with.  It really doesn't add much to the Original, aside from Leaderboards that I believe don't even work due to hackers, and there is 1 new Costume for both Chris and Jill, they get their attire from RE5, but I think they were very lazily included in RE1; Chris isn't meant to be as old and experienced-looking as he does in RE5, and while I get Costumes are supposed to be a bit silly at times, I feel the RE5 skins miss the mark, they do not really follow the aesthetic of the Original's, and Chris is pretty much getting a SECOND military outft.  I still appreciate though that I can choose a Costume before starting a New Game, rather than going to the Closet every playthrough.

The backgrounds have been re-rendered or upscaled and, for the most part, they do have more details for larger resolutions than if you would put GC on an Emulator, plus there isn't the slight loading lag between each screens (not rooms, screens in a single room), so HD actually saves time on the loading times.  However, this is where hell breaks loose, the backgrounds were never made wider from what they originally were to fit the new 16:9 Aspect Ratio, they are sliced at the top and bottom edges of the screen to fit horizontally, and to make sure the S.T.A.R.S. don't disappear at the top or bottom, the camera can moves up or down to follow them, but this is [b]freaking awful[/b], I tried it for a while and it's just making me sick, and you're still missing crucial information offscreen wherever you go.  So, word of advice, play on 4:3 (which isn't even the Default), because then you'll see everything and the screens stay still, you're not going to get vertigo with that.

I also hinted at upscaling, which yeah, some backgrounds don't look that great, for example the Knights Room looks pixely in certain parts, and they even removed smaller details like a bug that was in GC, on a tree as you're about to enter the Lab, so I gotta wonder if even more details were lost in the HD transition.

Other aesthetic changes and this is where the changes hurt me the most; some of the musics on GC were altered in HD, like Rush of Horror and Concrete Bound, which were my favorites.  I... really don't like these new versions, they're not bad, but they were much better on GC IMO, felt more moody, and there is no way to revert these changes.  I do not understand why they did it.

Then, the addition of "Modernized" Controls (Alternate), as people seem to loathe the Original's Tank Controls, which for sure they need some getting used to, but they're perfectly fine for the most part, the Resident Evil Series tend to be at its best when the characters are very restricted in their movement, and if anything it has always stayed CONSISTENT.

When you use the Alternate Controls, the characters no longer have to turn sideways to then move forward, they simply Run towards wherever you aim the Control Stick at, and that makes navigation go "slightly" faster.  However, Alternate really breaks the game, it's very easy now to bait enemies to attack you and run past them when they miss, it really trivializes a lot of the base game and goes against the roots of the series, but eh I can't hide that it was somewhat fun to psyche out the enemies so often, but I still take issue that it breaks what made the OG special in its own way.

Where ♥♥♥♥ hits the fan again is when the screens change, because remember the characters move towards where you're moving the Stick, meaning that if a screen is orientated to the East, then the movement is no longer true as the next screen shifts towards the North.  The band-aid to this issue is that, as long as you keep the Stick in place when screens change, the character will keep going in that direction, so it doesn't always happen where you end up accidentally going back to the previous screen, for the most part you're able to reorient yourself.  However, notice my wording, because yes, there are still problems that arise from this system regardless; I would go down an hallway, and as I'm about to make the turn, I want to go left, but then the screen changes, meaning that I'm going left from the new screen's perspective, MEANING I'm going back to the previous screen!  And this happens REGULARLY, so much so that you'll often have no clue WTH Chris or Jill are doing, you'll end up doing circles as you fight with the Controls and this might allow a cheap shot from enemies.  Even in spite of said band-aid, this can get maddening.

Lastly, my other problem with Alternate is that there is no dedicated Run Button; of course you may Walk by tilting the Control Stick only slightly, and there is "almost" no reasons to walk (aside from maybe stealth?), so what is it then?  Well again notice I highlighted "almost", in the Original, if you mash the Run button when you're going up or down stairs, you actually climb them MUCH faster, and you may not think about it, but there are A LOT of stairs.  Well, you may finally realize that doing it with the Control Stick is impossible, and the Dead Zone for Walking is so small anyway you wouldn't be able to Walk in normal context.  There is also a part where you need to move an item to its destination purely by walking, meaning once again that fine-tuning movement on Alternate would be unwise.

The Original Controls never encounter these Modern problems, and so, I must say that, even if you activate Alternate, you can still play with the OG Controls at any time when using the D-Pad, and THAT has a dedicated Run Button.  So say Chris and Jill start having seizures due to screen changes, you can play with both Alternate and Original Controls at all times, depending on the situation.  The problem here isn't that I need to change my Options, but rather I would've preferred to Walk with the Control Stick as is, then use the Run Button to run.  Maybe you don't like holding a button all the time just to do something so trivially simple as Running, but... I just want my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Run Button, it's awkward going from Control Stick to D-Pad just for when I go up or down stairs as I need to stop for a second.

Still though, if you want to avoid any and all problems I've encountered using Alternate Controls, you can simply use the Original instead, meaning you'd be always on Tank Controls, but everything will stay consistent.

So afterall, I have many issues with this HD Remaster, which is kind of a shame because the 60fps and some of the Higher-Res Backgrounds would almost make it worth it, but there are some parts of the upscaling that look ugly, some of the musics are worse now, and then there are the many problems of the Alternate Controls.  The HD Remaster isn't worth it when put against the GameCube Version, so if you can get GC, just get GC (not sure about Wii).  However, in this day and age, it may be hard for you to get your hands on the GameCube Version, let alone the hardware, so you can still enjoy Resident Evil 1 Remake thanks to this HD Remaster, it's just not going to be my Version of choice.

“You have once again entered the world of survival horror...”

Resident Evil is a great remake of the iconic original version that shares the same name, you play as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, two members of the elite unit S.T.A.R.S. that have been sent into the Arklay mountains from Raccoon City in order to investigate a bizarre string of murders and the disappearance of their fellow members in Bravo team. After encountering monsters in the mountains and having their pilot take off without them, they seek refuge in a mansion in order to survive.

Both Chris and Jill have a unique scenario with different encounters and gameplay differences, choosing when to use certain resources like ammo and healing items is a major part of the survival horror gameplay, sometimes running past a zombie or cerberus is a better decision than using ammo so that you can save it later when you face a more dangerous encounter. You’re surrounded by monsters. Your only weapon is a handgun. The only people left to fight are your fellow survivors and the relentless, bloodthirsty hordes. The desperate need to survive is all that keeps you going, even if you’re terrified of your own shadow.

These are the facts. Not the fun of surviving on a post-apocalyptic, zombie-infested Earth, of course. The rest is window dressing. This is pure survival horror, a genre defined by the necessity to pay off some nameless, frustrating threat with your heart, mind, and soul. The genre calls on you to prepare for conflict, endure pain, and endure fear – in order to live a life worth living.

Survival horror is defined by the main character being bullied, put in a position where they have to survive on their own. The relentless AI and difficulty of beating a level make the mechanic of surviving seem simple, even boring. But it’s not. It’s just more challenging than most people want it to be.

So it goes with the Resident Evil remake, which is a game that tries to create a slow burn of terror, following you from room to room as you rescue other people from hordes of enemies. It tries to make the player feel uncomfortable, and to make the action-focused combat satisfying, but you don’t feel threatened or heroic or feared or like an exceptional combatant. Instead, you’re just relieved to make it out of a room alive.

There were a few different games to choose from, but one cover stood out: a haunting image of a ghoul peering over its shoulder at you, that struck me with fear and curiosity. We popped the CD in, turned off the lights, and with my cousins spectating all around me, I dared to venture into the Spencer Mansion for the first time, and discovering the horrors within. It was that moment I became a Resident Evil fan.

Being 8 years old, and not having access to the internet or any strategy guide, I didn't get far. The mansion was [i]massive[/i] and honestly it took me minutes to muster up the courage to see what was on the other side of every door I found myself in front of. I don't think I got much further than discovering the back gate to the courtyard before it was time to go home.

Cut to Christmas, quite a few years later: I get a Gamecube, and the Resident Evil remake that had just released on it. I was [i]ecstatic.[/i] Finally I was going to return to the Spencer Mansion, and it was going to be even scarier. And holy hell, was it scarier. I owned that game for years, and even then, I still couldn't get further than the courtyard. The crimson head mechanic alone gave me so much anxiety and terror that playing the game was an exercise in self-abuse. I've made many attempts--even on the easiest mode! But I still. Could not. Beat it.

Now, these games are classics. If you're on the fence of trying this game out, whether it be the fixed-camera, or the puzzles, or the anxiety: I urge you to play and beat this game at least once. Explore the world within: read the documents. Unravel the mystery of [i]what the hell happened here.[/i] And reach the satisfying ending.

Resident Evil released in 1996 for the PS1, then Capcom gave it a proper remake in 2002 for the GameCube, the same year Resident Evil 0 released. Both the REmake, and RE0, received HD remasters and were ported to modern systems 1/19/2015 and 1/19/2016. There are QoL updates, but for the most part, they're the exact same games from 02', making them 20 years old at this point, nearing 21 years. I just replayed it to confirm that I still enjoy it. The alternate controls make it possible to strafe and will be more familiar with modern/new players, but don't make the mistake of using the keyboard like I did. Use a controller as the game was created for it analog sticks. 

This era of RE is much slower pace, more puzzles and backtracking, and just thorough exploration of the Spencer mansion. References of characters, like Ada, are made, and it's nice to notice these small details and thinking, "oh, right, Ada from RE2 with Leon and RE4." The same thing is true for WIlliam Burkin and the G-Virus and other notable characters, even a slight reference to an arm wrestling competition from a poster and the winner becoming the Police Chief, who you see in RE2. The game is definitely more focused on terror and feeling uncomfortable, rather than repetitive jump scares. It's immersive and almost suffocating playing it for the first time, in the dark, with the music cranked up. It appealed to veterans who played the original. The infamous "dog jumps through the window" scene happens, but in a different way. When you think it's going to happen, and the camera angle in a certain hallway is practically telling you it will, something hits the window and the glass cracks, but no dogs jump through. This sort of appreciation isn't possible for new players, but it still provides a lot of tension, as many camera angles make it feel like you're being watched or something will jump through the windows. This will often turn out to be the case at some point in the game. Right before fighting Yawn the giant snake, it looks like something is watching you through the window. When you backtrack, it shows that he shattered and made his way through that very same window. The attention to detail in this game still amazes me, and even though it is 2 decades old, I had a lot of fun. I really hope it receives another remake, one comparable to RE2R, to really feel the game in a modern take on the RE engine. 

If you like to work your brain a bit, explore and immerse yourself in a dark mansion, take in the story, and even have a lot of replayability, buy this game. It's $4.99 right now, and so is RE0.

This review needs some backstory, so bare with it if you have the time to read. Otherwise, just skip to the actual review part.

Ever since I watched the first Resident Evil film staring Milla Jovovich, in my good old teen days, I realised three things. One, I had a mad crush on the celebrity ([i]don't worry, I got out of it[/i]). Two, zombie movies and games are kick-ass. Three, I really needed more Resident Evil in my life.

When I learnt that there was a Resident Evil game, I was stoked and couldn't wait to actually get hold of one of the titles. To my disappointment, it wasn't available on PC, I wasn't going to own a PS at the time, and none of my friends actually owned a copy, not to mention... no Alice as the main character.

My first actual entry to the game was Resident Evil 4 and although it wasn't nearly what I expected and it featured way less horror and zombies, it was actually a great game and I thoroughly enjoyed playing through the game and learning that the films are actually not even close to what the originals on PS were set out to be, so of course I started doing some digging and realised how much I've been missing out. After the release of the RE3 film, things just mostly went downhill in quality for me and overall the films just mostly suck and are completely over the top getting worse with each entry after RE2. The worse the films got, the more interesting the games became, but the problem remained that I didn't have a console to play on. Fortunately, the remaster came to Steam and it would take until now for me to actually play the game and I have to say that my mind has been blown by how much I actually missed out on over the years.

[b]Now we can actually start with the review![/b]

Are you in the mood for gaming as they were in the good old days ([i]or maybe you need to just experience it for the first time[/i]? A time when games didn't tell you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ other than throw you into the deep end and expect you to figure things out for yourself. Where there was no such thing as press F to salute, or sudden hints when the game realises that you're taking too long to solve a puzzle. Well, Resident Evil HD is definitely the game you're looking for!

Although I never experienced the original, I can tell that they've stayed true to the time period it was created. You're literally thrown into this mansion where you know ABSOLUTELY NOTHING! Not a single hint about which character you should start with for beginners ([i]Jill is the answer[/i]), not that knifes are basically completely useless throughout the game and especially not telling you where you should go or how to solve puzzles or trap rooms. It's brutal, but goodness me is it some of the most engaging and fun experiences I've had with a game in years! 

The funny part is, the game is actually easy to play and very straightforward. The camera angles might take some getting used to, but it's mostly as simple as aim in direction and shoot. It'll hit the target... maybe not where you want it to, but it'll hit the target. Repeat until collapse and enemy is done... or is it? Having a tough time finding your way? Are there too many locked doors? Have you truly explored all the nooks and crannies? Have you examined your items? These simple features are what makes this game golden in my view. The developers trusted that the players would be able to figure things out for themselves without giving them too many flashy screen hints, or some voice hints or whatever modern games do nowadays, even if it meant hours of running in circles, the player would eventually figure it out. Now I have to admit, I "mostly" did the game by myself. I never used a walkthrough on any of the puzzles, but when wanting to save time, it helps knowing which items you should carry, because your inventory is pretty small, but I swear almost everything else was my own work. Not that I'll judge casual players for using walkthroughs during hard times, because some of the puzzles, or at least navigating the map at times requires a pointer or two, but again as mentioned, the game doesn't really give that much and your memory plays a big role in progression.

The graphics is nothing impressive in modern standards, but it's definitely an awesome art style that had me pausing a few times just to see the view of a room. It has a somewhat realistic feel to it and it's very eerie at times being in this mansion with zombies that at times jump at you from corners you couldn't see because of the camera angle. You can definitely tell the game is dated, but I think it's one of those masterpieces that will continue the test of time.

If you play as Jill, you'll experience her cutscenes with her partner, giving you the best story experience of the game, while Chris is meant for the more veteran players with less story cutscenes ([i]if at all since I only did the first zombie with Chris[/i]. In both cases, you'll learn more about the game by collecting files and reading notes explaining the origins of the zombies, what happened in the mansion, why your team got sent there in the first place and probably how all the events spilled over into RE2.

There aren't many negatives for me with this game, especially keeping in mind that it's a remaster of a very old game, but if I had to criticise, I'd say that the inventory at times even with Jill felt too small and Chris has two slots less. On normal, I picked up way more ammo than I ever needed and honestly, I mostly conserved because I expected something that'll force me to use most of my ammo, but that never happened. I'm sure on harder difficulties it gets worse. Finally, the voice acting is pretty bad :D but honestly that's just trying to find fault, I don't really care about that all too much. Probably the most annoying feature is when every room or area you enter, it always has to play a slow scene of you opening the door, or climbing the ladder, or taking the elevator up and down. I'm sure there were reasons back then, but it's frustrating when backtracking.

I'm happy that I finally got to play the first entry and I'm now ready to continue to RE2, a game I've been looking forward to playing since release but left it off because I wanted to get through the whole franchise. No doubt I'll reinstall this game in the future and attempt to gain the rest of the achievements. It's just one of those games that deserves to be replayed!

[h1]Resident Evil has captured a unique form of horror only video games can achieve.[/h1]
My experience with the Resident Evil franchise is a new journey I set myself on toward the end of 2022. I was always aware of the series, but I couldn’t go as far as to name a character or describe the games past shooting zombies. While my personal opinions on each entry generally align with the average fan, the franchise’s roots hold the strongest grip on me. The original 1996 release is widely recognized as the pioneer of the survivor horror genre. Spawning hundreds of sequels, spinoffs, and adaptations, RE1 itself was remade in 2002 as REmake and that’s the version that was ported to Steam. Discussing the game is rather difficult as I simultaneously think this game is both one of the best and worst I’ve ever played.

Despite starting its own genre, REmake plays most similarly to a traditional point-and-click adventure game. The primary focus is on exploring the map and using the items you find to solve various puzzles. Even the enemies can be simplified as a form of puzzle interaction as effectively eliminating them resorts to spending the right resource or seeing them as just an obstacle to dodge. Sounds simple enough, but this game is a nightmare to play, and I don’t just say this because it’s scary. REmake has some of the worst design choices you will ever see. There are well over a hundred items and your inventory is confined to a mere 8 or 6 slots depending on which character you play. The maximum carrying capacity might as well be lower since you're going to have to play with 1 or 2 empty slots so you can even pick stuff up. This issue is exacerbated when you realize key items aren’t exempt from this rule. You will have no idea what you should bring unless you have a guide or have played the game before. An especially egregious example happens minutes after starting the game. You’ll find a blue gem from shoving a statue off a cliff and if you carry it with you until you need it, it’ll be in your inventory for half the game. Other items you wouldn’t expect to take up inventory space still do. Few items beside ammo are stackable, and if you want to bring more ammo than your magazine can fit it’ll cost you an item slot. Even something like SAVING requires an item. And every resource in the game is finite, meaning not only can you screw yourself up to the point where you’re out of bullets, but you might also have to start a save file from scratch simply from wasting your saves. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2904216363
Exploration is the other key component of REmake’s gameplay, and players are going to be incentivized to look around more when the environments look amazing. For what was natively a GameCube release, the Spencer Mansion looks absolutely stunning, and I find how they achieved this to be really interesting. The backgrounds are pre-rendered static images which lets the game look gorgeous while taking only an ounce of performance from the actual hardware. Think of how cutscenes look way better than the actual gameplay for games from the early to late 2000s. The art direction is phenomenal and the mansion you find yourself trapped in for the entire game felt like a real place because of it. Navigating areas and scrounging for resources never felt like a chore because every frame was a painting. Even the loading transitions were somewhat more immersive than what you’d see back in the day. It’s just a little cutscene of a door opening to cover up the load time. However these genius artistic decisions have had irreversible damage on the actual gameplay. Since the environment is static, the camera angles are fixed. Fighting a zombie in one room could have you repositioning through several camera changes, which makes seeing the enemy much more difficult. Larger rooms with zombies to fight are frustratingly hard when the camera is not in your control. And those cute lil’ door cutscenes I mentioned earlier? They’re completely unnecessary with modern hardware and aren’t skippable without the use of mods.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2904216520
Usually, these problems would be written off as bad game design and make for an awful experience, but in REmake’s case it actually somehow improves the experience in a completely different way. While the game is pretty clunky, that also makes it infinitely scarier. I think my favorite problem is with the ink ribbons. I find that a lot of horror games lose their scare factor when I can trial and error my way through a tough encounter by loading from a quicksave. When you die too much in a horror game, you lose immersion. And despite the mechanics actively working against you at times, it’s not really that difficult. This is something I feel like the later games don’t replicate as they’re either significantly harder or completely lack the feature. My death counter was only just about to leave the single digits and only one of those involving a plant would I call unfair. Dying in REmake was genuinely scary to me because there were actual consequences to it. And the enemies being oftentimes obscured by the camera worked towards the spook factor as well. There are several moments like when you enter a bathroom where the sound design alerts you to an upcoming threat that I don’t think could be found with a free camera. Combat in horror games generally has to be clunky or else I don’t think you’ll fear combating the numerous enemies. The camera is the factor that makes fighting harder, and in a weird way, I enjoyed that. That aforementioned horror REmake captures so perfectly was only achievable because of its faults. And a quick note about those aforementioned problems although I rarely like mentioning it in reviews, modding is a solution. Especially for skipping the door animations.

As for some final notes on the soundtrack and story. Horror games usually don’t have songs I’d listen to outside of the game, but REmake is a notable exception. The save room theme is the biggest highlight. It’s an incredibly soothing track with some distant howling playing in the background, a perfect representation of temporary safety. Guardhouse 1 and Neptune Tank are some other personal favorites that aren’t focused on the fear factor alone. That’s not to say the rest of OST isn’t fitting for quaking in your boots. One song has a nearly inaudible moan that most people won’t even actively pick up on. As for the story, don’t expect REmake’s writing to be the selling point for you. Like plenty of other older games, it’s there but it’s not really fleshed out. Spoilers I guess, but I doubt anyone doesn’t at least know about the series’ big bad. I really like that the zombies are man-made. RE’s zombie viruses have possibly my favorite lore and origins for undead infections. I find the idea of researchers creating zombies more in the realm of realism than them just appearing or any supernatural explanation which would be much less interesting. 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RRQI9GlGjsE
Resident Evil Remake, despite its numerous and very glaring flaws, is something I would change next to nothing about. It’s a game that I think everyone should at least try playing at least once. You don’t have to beat it, but at least give it a shot. This game is one of the scariest I’ve played and I highly recommend it because of that. [b]I’m giving the game a 7/10, but do not let that score trick you. While I have played dozens, if not hundreds, of better mechanically put-together games, none of them are going to stick in my head as long as REmake undoubtedly will.[/b]

[h1]Welcome To Survival Horror[/h1]
Resident Evil is a survival horror video game developed by Capcom Production Studio 4 and published by Capcom. Resident Evil (on Steam and Gamecube) is a Remake of the 1996 PlayStation game Resident Evil, the first installment in the Resident Evil video game series. The story takes place in 1998 near the fictional Midwestern town of Raccoon City where a series of bizarre murders have taken place. The player takes on the role of either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, S.T.A.R.S. agents sent in by the city to investigate the murders.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/ATReviews]Follow My Review Group Here![/url]

💾Graphics - Resident Evil Remake is a huge upgrade from the original. With a darker and scarier atmosphere, you will feel dread in every room with the haunting presence of a scary and haunting past the Spencer Mansion holds. With every hallway and room keeping you on edge, the map design is something truly special and I would go far and say near perfection. Some issues do occur such as some blurry textures that feel more rushed than others, but luckily there is a HD texture project you can install to improve them, but not too worry since most of the areas look really sharp and stunning. Not to mention the incredible lighting this game delivers. A true masterpiece in terms of a Remake in the graphics department. Just look up the original and compare it to the remake, it’s insane!

🎮Gameplay - This is what Survival Horror is all about! The inventory management is so good here. Having to plan every trip you take is well balanced. The safe room is your, well, safe haven. Being able to store items is a great feature Resident Evil has brought to the table. The storage box even transfers all items to every safe room so no need to go to the old storage box (except for “Real Survival” Game Mode), an amazing idea that has aged so well even for today. Both Jill and Chris have their own pro’s and con’s that makes them both feel unique from each other, even though their story lines are different in some ways which is really cool to see here. Taking down zombies and other terrifying enemies will put you through one crazy experience not many games capture well today. The gunplay is simple, but works well here. The movement can be kinda tricky, but you adapt pretty quickly. Beating the game will grant you unlockables, such as weapons, costumes, and new game modes. The game is unforgiving and the only way to save is through ink ribbons, which you only have a set amount in the game so save wisely. Also there are no checkpoints so if you haven’t saved in a while, prepare to make that long journey again! Honestly there is so much to talk about here in terms of gameplay, but I can promise you that this is peak survival horror from my experience (Resident Evil and Silent Hill respectively).

📜Story - The story is basic, simple, but actually really good. It’s a fun story that makes it so easy to understand and follow without getting lost. This is probably my favorite RE story since it’s the first that created the franchise, and it makes sense and can be somewhat believable. Reading all the files in the game really puts you in the experience and they are just so extremely fascinating to read and trying to imagine their situation they went through. Top tier storytelling in the files I must say! I won’t spoil the story, but it’s pretty predictable, but still a blast to play through.

🕛Playtime - With a healthy amount of unlocks and gamemodes, the replayability is high here. My first game took around 10 hours (that’s including checking every area and file). The game modes even bring more playtime which can change the game drastically, making it harder and a different experience. Each character has a different story as well (to a certain degree). Also you can install a randomizer mod that can really make the game feel challenging and can provide a unique playthrough, with each run being different and possibly harder than the last (links will be below).

🎧Sound - The sound design is perfect. All from the ambiance outside, hearing the crows and bugs in the night adds a calm, but eerie feeling. The zombie noises in each hallway, adding dread and fear to the experience. The sound track and safe room is absolutely incredible. The voice acting is better than the original, but still feels awkward in some areas.

❗Bugs❗- There is one music score that is sped up for some reason. Not sure if it’s a bug, but if you heard the original than the remaster it’s noticeable. It’s not a huge deal if you haven’t played the original. There is a patch for this luckily which will be linked below. The game can crash if you ALT+TAB too many times as well.

🔅Performance - The game runs smoothly on my system. Having no frame drops or slowdowns. Besides the crashing issue, it’s pretty good! Just don’t ALT+TAB if possible since you will have a risk of crashing.

This is the HD version of the GameCube RE, which is a remake of the original PS1 Resident Evil. Having played this game in almost all its ports and remakes (including the DS version), I can say that this is the definitive way to experience it. This version has practically all the extras present in the GC version, and updates the graphics to modern monitors. They definitely feel a bit dated, but are beautiful nonetheless. Movement is basically the same, which can be good news to purists, but not very attractive to those who don't like "tank" walking.

The atmosphere, on the other hand, is still intact, or even better, as the old mansion is still a very good scenario for a horror game, and it looks more terrifying than ever. The new mechanics introduced in the GC version are present, such as new rooms and zombies that are harder to kill. The game is still a blast to play through, if you can get past the outdated controls.

All in all, I recommend this version for anyone who enjoys survival horror games. Resident Evil is as fundamental today as it was in 1996.

For those playing for the first time, I offer a few tips to help you have a better experience:
- use the map. The house is not that big, but it's definitely confusing the first time;
- save ammo, especially the best ones. When possible, evade zombies, although it's not always possible. If you know you're going to pass through a room only once, maybe it's a nice trade-off to lose some health and not shooting anyone;
- on the other hand, if it's a corridor you're using constantly, remember to properly dispose of the bodies, burning them.

A great game that is unfortunately hampered by a terrible remaster.

The 2002 GameCube original was a good game. Unfortunately, this 2015 HD remaster really hinders the experience by making some ugly changes to the game's graphics and artstyle. This remaster also introduces some bugs that were not present in the original game. This review will go over some of the problems that are fixable, and some that are not.

[h1]The good news [/h1] 
[b](things that are fixable with mods)[/b]

For starters, CAPCOM lost the original renders for the backgrounds in this game, which means that the pre-rendered backgrounds in this remaster are upscaled versions of the GameCube assets. However, the actual upscales are very muddy and full of visual artifacts due to having some kind of sharpening filter applied to them. The sharpening was probably applied to make the muddy upscaling appear better, but it had the opposite effect of making things look aliased and blocky. This means that despite being stuck in 480p, the original GameCube backgrounds actually look better and have more visual clarity than the remaster’s upscaled backgrounds. [b]Fortunately[/b], you can circumvent this issue by downloading the [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/residentevilbiohazardhdremaster/mods/102]RESCALE[/url] mod. Even though I’m not a huge fan of AI upscaling due to some of the visual artifacts it produces, this mod is easily a hundred times better than the upscaled backgrounds that CAPCOM produced.

One other problem this remaster has is the audio. The original GameCube release uses MIDI tracks with custom instruments, so the HD remaster opted to convert these MIDI tracks into music files. However, during the transfer process CAPCOM really screwed up somehow. Some of the background tracks have really low volume, and some of them are just sped up, like the “Gallery” theme or the “Lab” theme. You can download the [url=https://residentevilmodding.boards.net/thread/3149/fixed-background-music]BGM Fix[/url] mod to fix the music. If you feel like the audio volume in general is too low, you can also try the [url=https://residentevilmodding.boards.net/thread/3533/normalized-music-mod] Normalized Music[/url] mod, which also fixes the aforementioned issues. Neither of these mods are perfect since they don’t 100% accurately replicate the audio mixing of the original GameCube release, but they are still essential fixes.

[h1]The bad news[/h1]
[b](things that are NOT fixable with mods)[/b]

Great, so all of the issues this remaster has are fixable with mods? [i]Oh boy…[/i] I wish. There are some visual changes that this remaster has made that are unfortunately not fixable with mods. I will go over some of the major ones that impact the game’s artstyle.

- The new color filter/black crush filter. This is probably the most significant change the HD remaster makes to REmake’s visual style. Someone at CAPCOM really loves the color black for some reason, because everything in the HD remaster is darkened heavily, and the warm color palette has been sucked out of the picture. All of the shadows in this remaster have had their contrast increased, meaning that any visual information that was previously present has been completely blacked out due to the harsh color filter. This makes some of the dark areas in the game like the Crypt, Courtyard, Graveyard and Aquarium extremely ugly, especially when combined with the badly upscaled backgrounds.

- Lighting changes. The remaster has a completely different lighting system compared to the original game. This change also affected how shadows from 3D objects are casted onto the backgrounds. This is most noticeable in the birdcage corridor, where the birdcage is not casting a shadow onto the wall when it’s supposed to. The lighting changes also added bloom to the game. Sometimes it looks fine, sometimes it looks jarring and makes it pretty obvious that it was added into the game after the fact.

- The remaster gave the game this weird radial fog effect that makes certain objects in the foreground look more washed out. Like with bloom, this effect ranges from being completely harmless to just looking slightly jarring.

- Noise filter. Overall harmless, but its inclusion is still puzzling, especially since you can’t disable it in the options.

Because of all of this, I would not recommend playing the HD remaster over the original GameCube version. This version of the game has cool inclusions like the RE5 costumes, but they don’t really make up for all of the changes this remaster made to the original game. I didn’t even mention all of the issues the PC port has, I only discussed the differences between the original game and the HD remaster. If you can’t play the GameCube version, just emulate it.
