Phenomenal horror game. The atmosphere and model designs really add to the game. There are some "issues" with it that hinder it. The first and most notable, 7 second door screens (loading screens) which really shouldn't take so long. The largest issues people talk about are item management/ limited saves and fixed camera angles. I don't have an issue with the fixed cameras, even when I'm in a tense situation (combat is hugely affected by the cameras and can make some fights a complete guessing game as to where an enemy is. I feel that the cameras actually add to the tension, which is why I don't see them as an issue. As for the inventory, thats a different story. There is no indication what so ever as to what you are supposed to do. This game forces you to really use your head. Confused as to what to do with this book? thats right, you had to go to it in your inventory, turn it halfway, then examine it, where you find a button which unlocks it. Stuff like that. You may feel softlocked if you have a full inventory and haven't unlocked any areas with item boxes, but believe me, you aren't. EVERYTHING you find has a purpose. The final issue is one I'm very mixed on. Limited saves, and no autosaves. While the idea of using ink cartridges at a typewriter to save is a cool idea, having only 30 saves for your whole game seems limiting. I think new players would find it limiting to not be able to save as often as in other games. There were probably many who hated this as well, as by RE4, limited saves were removed, so you could save all you wanted, but still had to get to a typewriter. The idea only returned as a harder difficulty in RE7, which is what this game should do. There should be an available mode for infinite saves so that players get a feel for the game before being limited. No auto saves is another issue, as once you die, you must load your most recent save, which can mean tons of progress lost. But thats where the true horror of Resident Evil comes into play. Its not just that there are zombies roaming the halls, giant spiders in the library or an unstoppable killing machine is waiting for you, its the fear of losing it all. You feel less scared after recently saving, but as you progress, the further and further you go, the more fear creeps up on you. What if I forgot about burning the zombie in the next room? what if a hunter shows up? Thats where Resident Evil gets its horror, its the fear of losing it all.

I will warn those not used to fixed cameras, it may be a bit of a learning curve and annoying for a while but nothing you can’t get used to. 

This game is such a breath of fresh air compared to modern survival horror. The door animations that play each time you enter through a door make me so giddy, it’s such a small thing but so cool to have that creepy, mysterious feeling of the unknown behind the door. Things like this just feel so refreshing after playing more modern Resident Evil games. 
These are things that you can’t find in the newer remakes that I’m thankful are preserved in this remake. 

If you take a look at the original Resident Evil, you can see what a truly phenomenal job they did in this remake. This remake did come out in 2002, but I wouldn’t say it’s dated at all, it simply modernized the original game and still definitely holds up to this day. 

Playing through this game, I’m absolutely glued to it. The determination to find out more information regarding the story and unlocking more doors to uncover the secrets of the mansion kept me absolutely enamored. I just kept wanting more and more resulting in many hours passing by feeling like minutes. This is one of the first games I’m actually planning on playing through multiple times. 

One more thing to add, if you are a veteran of classic survival horror, I recommend playing hard difficulty. I played through with normal difficulty and honestly, it was quite easier than I had expected. That’s really my one gripe with this game.

Resident Evil 1 Remake could actually be one of the fastest remakes to come out. with the original been released in 1996 and the remake coming out in 2002, there is just a six year gap but what Capcom delivered to us with without a doubt, the absolute gold standard on how to do a remake!

RE1R follows the original game almost beat for beat while adding its own unique story elements and sections that flow so smoothly with the whole of the game that you wouldn't even notice unless you were a hardcore fan of the original. And at the heart of it all is still the survival horror element.

You are gonna be running around the mansion non-stop, desperately trying to remember what room is where, what key goes to what door, where you last saw that zombie that bit you, if you got enough ammo and inventory space. Seriously, I've played this game a lot across different platforms and I still have to use the map to remember where some rooms are or what the best route to take is. Ammo and supplies are not in vast quantity here, so choosing which enemies to kill across the mansion is more vital than you realise. Slaying a zombie or something worse on a path most walked would be the ideal tactic but since you don't know what is in that room you finally got a key for, would it be worth back tracking for extra supplies or facing the danger head on? Sometimes, if the room is large enough, it is wiser to just loop the zombie and save your ammunition.

The game gives you the option of tank controls or a new updated system but here is the thing, using a mouse and keyboard, tank controls are actually super easy but the same input with the new control scheme is actually a nightmare, it was designed more for a controller but the gripe there is the fixed camera angle system does not compliment the new control scheme, so I highly suggest you use tank controls with a mouse and keyboard. You also have the option of playing the game in its original 4:3 ratio or a widescreen view, I guess if you really wanna feel like you are living back in the 90's or early 2000's then 4:3 is a good choice for you.

The pre-rendered backgrounds in this game, despite being from 2002 still hold up remarkably well as do all the character and enemy models, it could make a game or two from today blush! Each environment is packed full of rich detail and simply bathing in atmosphere. Granted the odd area or texture really doesn't hold up as it's either painfully pixelated or just doesn't look right at the angle the camera is at but these areas are few and far between. The sound design is absolutely top notch here, the sound of each enemy is distinct so if they are off screen, you know exactly what is coming, some rooms have no music at all and just the sound of the wind blowing outside, combined with the howl of dogs in the distance and it is some of the best atmosphere I have ever experienced in a video game, it's right up there alongside DMC1, which started out in life as RE4 and as a result is bathing in just as much atmosphere as this game is. The safe room under the stairs is swiftly going to become a favourite spot and not just for the respite.

You have two campaigns to choose from, both of which follow a similar plot but never fully tie into create one whole and continuous narrative as certain events just don't line up, just like how in RE2/R both campaigns/games never fully work off one another, Jill Valentine is the right choice to make for first time players as it is definitely the easiest. Jill has the advantage of having a larger inventory and carrying around a lockpick, with Barry Burton occasionally showing up to save you or offer you some supplies. Chris Redfield however has the advantage of being able to take more damage and a greater chance of getting that sweet critical headshot. Jill's campaign is definitely the must play out of the two of them just because the story seems to flow way better on her side and it gives me the sense that is where Capcom spent most of their time, while Chris' campaign, while I wouldn't say they did it like an afterthought, you would be forgiven for thinking that. Think of his campaign as Capcom using the leftovers, what you do get is good, don't get me wrong but Jill has the superior campaign, no question.

While this may be a remake, it is still a Resident Evil game and one from the early 2000's. You may be aware that the original has the record for worst voice acting in a game, it's more hilarious than anything and sort of adds a charm to it. Now, whether or not carrying over that into the remake was intentional or not, I don't know but this game also doesn't have the greatest of voice acting either. It's good but the delivery is sometimes just not correct and the result is kinda funny. This was also before Capcom found its favourite voice actors for certain characters for a while, so don't expect Chris to have his grim voice in this game.

If you think of the main Resident Evil games as trilogies, it makes it easier to pick a starting point in the series. You can easily start right here with RE1R or start with RE4, you could even start at RE7 but I highly suggest you make this Resident Evil your first one. This is one of the best, if not the best remake of a game you can ever play. Everything about this remake is done right and offers a fantastic introduction into the series.

Obviously the tank controls suck, and so do the fixed camera angles. But, the game was tactfully built with these in mind. Aiming/shooting is fairly lenient, the camera is usually placed in a spot where you won't get jumped around a corner (or there's a mirror showing you what's around the corner), and the alternative control scheme is workable.

The remaster evidently also includes several gameplay differences, such as expanded areas/sections, a couple new enemy encounters, and defensive items. Which, as far as remakes and remasters go, is really good! An exceptionally die-hard Resident Evil fan [i]might[/i] dislike the changes, but none of them feel out-of-place to me personally. The game is a rather backtrack-y (not necessarily bad, but can be off-putting to some people), and the difficulty is a bit inconsistent at times, but for the most part everything comes together well.

[hr][/hr]
Ideally, I'd love for them to do another modern remake similar to Resident Evil 2 and (the upcoming remake for Resident Evil 4), but with a first-person perspective similar to Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil Village. [h1]This isn't a remaster that was actually made in 2015.[/h1]

Don't go into it expecting that, as you are bound to be disappointed.

[u]Mini-review[/u]

I was very confused when I initially played this game. I couldn't understand it at first. It was clear that they went for a complete graphical overhaul, as the game doesn't look similar to the 1996 original at all, and yet the graphics seemed incredibly dated for a release in the 2010s. But that was fine by me, since I had expected that from the get-go, seeing the graphics in the thumbnail. Also worth mentioning that I recognise the fixed camera framework as iconic and a hallmark of the game, so I'm okay with that staying too.

What I [i]did[/i] expect, however, was QOL improvements and a UI that would match something that I'd expect from 2015, removing a lot of the frustrations that would come with playing older games today and make for a more streamlined experience instead of being a clunky mess. Assuming that a remaster would adress these frustrations, I was severely disappointed to see this was absolutely not the case. Controls were wonky, UI was dated and annoying, and overall the experience was bogged down due to a lot of aspects that a remaster was supposed to remove. 

So I wondered whether it was truly a cheap lazy product, and decided to look it up. And then I realised that what seems to be a remaster listed on steam in 2015 was actually made for the Gamecube in [i]2002[/i] and received a console port in 2009, and then was finally ported to PC in 2015. So yeah, this is still actually an incredibly dated game, don't let the release date fool you. This information is conveniently never mentioned in the description for the game and most of the reviews don't mention this either, so consider this a PSA of sorts to manage your expectations if you're still interested.

Now, to add on top of that, it's not even a good port. It's a lazy one that doesn't bother with thinking of how a shooting system that could work fine with a controller would feel absolutely horrid with KBM. So not only is it misleading, it's also just actually lazy as well. I wanted to enjoy it as an introduction to the RE franchise, but this just soured my experience beyond the point of being able to enjoy the game. If you're a first-timer, chances are you'll find that it's just a clunky mess. Just going to start from RE 2 and go from there. 

Now, there's still a good chance you might like the game if you're aware of how much of a mess it is from the standpoint of jank and gameplay, in that case from what I played the core of the game seemed fairly intact, but hopefully my experience can help newer player anticipate the issues you'd run into beforehand.

To this day, this game still looks beautiful. The static backgrounds are so detailed and the characters do not feel out of place. They feel like they are part of the environment, not pasted in. The best way to play this game is NOT in widescreen but in the original 4:3 aspect ratio. The reason being is because in widescreen, they stretch the width a bit but also cut off the top and bottom of the scenery. Because of this, you lose a lot of detail in the environment, along with the background not being as sharp and crisp as it is in 4:3 mode. 4:3 mode lets you see the original scene as it was intended.

The story is great and very engaging. And for those that played the original game before the remake, the main story is there but enhanced with new stories that add to the lore, add to the story, and make the game even more engaging. Many puzzles from the original are there, but are enhanced so that those that know the solution still have to figure them out.

Puzzles are not overly difficult nor too easy. They are intriguing and fun to figure out. As much as I like the RE2 Remake, this game definitely is tops of all the Resident Evils out there in my humble opinion. Some may not feel that way, but you can feel the love and compassion the developers put into this game; how they fleshed out the story, how the architecture of the environments feel so organic and not out-of-place, how the game-play is fun to do and feels "just right", and the music and ambient sounds just create such an environment of tension. Since you move from scene to scene, it "hides" zombies on purpose, making you have to possibly move slowly rather than trying to run through each room because there could be zombie right around the next corner you turn at and move onto another scene. You as the player need to be aware of the environment, the sounds you hear which give clues as to where zombies are at, and just so many other factors that the developers and writers ensured made this game fun to play, over and over again.

Hi, I am doing a series play-through of almost every game in the Resident Evil series. I am making a Tier List called: "Resident Evil Games by someone who has actually played them"

Here's my review of this game, the first in the series and the first I have played:

Tier: B

I grew up with games such as Silent Hill and Haunting Ground so the fixed camera angles and backtracking were nothing unfamiliar to me. However, the amount of backtracking in particular was pretty excessive when compared to other horror games of this caliber for the time. Having to actively run all the way from the mansion to the underground/cabin/residence and then BACK was a lot. It certainly made the game feel padded at times. 

I personally drew a map on paper in order to recall which doors took which keys as well as point-of-interests so that way I could methodically progress. I actually really enjoyed that and felt it made the game special/immersive. It was SO helpful that the map made note if I picked up every item in a room. I wanted to get every bit of lore possible and it helped me achieve that goal for sure.

The bosses did not feel as significant as I would like, being rather easy to take down. I do like that if you were clever, you could end some boss fights without ever firing a shot. 

The ink ribbon mechanic was initially intimidating as I am a chronic saver, but I found it less frustrating than I thought it would be. As long as I was actively trying to make progress, the supply of ink ribbons never got too low. In the process of getting all the achievements, I even ran the game without saving at all which pushed my limits and was surprisingly fun!

As for the crimson head mechanic, I did feel like it was harsh until I realized that the game promotes replayability and adaptation to the game's in and outs. Definitely a game I had to start over a few times before I got the hang of how things worked. This is just how difficult games were at the time. This game was not hand-holdy, that's for sure!

The narrative was okay, though some aspects of the story had me scratching my head like; "How did you not see that?" or "That was an awkward interaction". That being said, I do believe that is also part of the game's charm. Very horror movie-esque. I do wish that Chris or Jill (depending on who you play as) had more of an appearance in the story when playing as the other.

All in all, It was a very solid experience that was intimidating at first, but with time and perseverance, I was able to 100% the game and have fun while doing so. A bit dated and long-winded in some areas, but nonetheless a challenging classic that had me coming back for more.

 I think Chief Irons had made a good boss, imagine a boss-fight with a human who isn't infected by some kind of virus, blasting away with a hunting rifle, and setting off traps (he enjoyed hunting) during the fight. We were late to the Console Wars. We were conscripted (willingly, I might add) by our dad's mom one Christmas with the N64 around the time this game was released. We were still on the fringes until consoles moved from game cartridges to CDs: Dreamcast, Wii, Xbox. That whole time, though, I don't think I played a PlayStation. But I had heard people talk about PS games, and RE probably most of all. This sometimes took the form of quotes from the game. Like the (in?)famous "Jill sandwich" quote, which I didn't get to hear this time. And also pop cultural references, like the mention in Eiffel 65's song "My Console," the one where they spell out P-L-A-Y-S-T-A-T-I-O-N in the chorus.

And so when I saw (on Google+, I think) that there was a remaster for the PC -- my gaming platform of choice -- I leapt at the chance to see what it was like. A "shot in the dark" for me, but ultimately a good one. Some games I avoid researching so as not to spoil any surprises. When I bought it, I think I had tried a demo of one of the games on the Wii. Had a little trouble with the camera angles on that demo, and in this game as well. (They're disorienting, especially when going from one to the next. But then, I'm naturally disoriented, so I don't think it would bother most people.) Controls are simple but the camera angles put a kind of timer on them, to where W was forward at this angle but backward for the next one.

Despite my navigational handicap, this game brought a new level of immersion to me. You spend so much time in the mansion, seeing each screen always from this one fixed-camera view, that I began not just to feel like I [i]was[/i] at the mansion but also that I [i]had been[/i] at the mansion. I felt I could visualize or extrapolate what the room looked like from other angles in my head, as if the mansion were a place I had really been to. Which is saying something because I'm not a geospatial thinker normally. The environment was highly immersive and level design top-notch.

The camera and its angles would sometimes be frustrating when doing things timed. These events were rare, and you're usually given plenty of time. At least in the mode I played. Which I thought was normal difficulty because it was the middle one, but I guess they had a "Very Easy"-"Easy"-"Normal" scheme. I don't think "Easy" mode was difficult; I think I would rank it as a fairly standard Normal difficulty: I died, but not a lot; enemies could be overwhelming, but not a sticking-point; I ran low on items like ammo, but found a way out. I think I would only offer a few hints:
[spoiler]
1. Read the manual
2. Examine everything you pick up and check it from all angles
3. It can be difficult to tell what you can interact with (e.g., use/climb) and what you can't. You also have to lined yourself up correctly. Don't talk give up on interacting with something until you've tried it several times
4. May be worth it, if like me you don't have the head for it, to screenshot maps and write your own notations on them: what keys to what doors, where kerosene jugs are, etc.
[/spoiler]

Puzzles I would describe as [i]obscured[/i] rather than [i]obscure[/i].  Thinking back to [i]7th Guest[/i] in particular, whose challenges like chess-based Knight's Tour may be too well-known to be esoteric, but may also be less difficult to solve if you're "in" on the solution... from a math class that showed formal ways of solving this sort of thing, for example. (I've been meaning to revisit that game. Can you tell?) In contrast, I feel just about anyone could solve RE's puzzles; the very rewarding challenge is in figuring out what the puzzle [b]is[/b], because you're not given very many explicit instructions.

Camera angles aside, many other design decisions that make the game more challenging I thought were very clever. One is the saving mechanism. You save by collecting ink ribbon items, and there are only so many, and they can only be used at typewriters in specific rooms. This made me play more carefully than I usually do. I would sometimes think things like [i]I'm near a typewriter. Have I made enough progress to justify a save?[/i] or [i]Is this bad idea so bad that I wouldn't want to start over?[/i], which doesn't happen for me in games when I can save an unlimited number of times by pressing quicksave.

Another mechanism is the map. You reveal the map by exploring or by picking up map items. Rooms are color-coded based on if you've visited them or if they still have items to pick up. Doors are also color-coded based on if they're unlocked but unopened, locked, or open. So a process of deduction happens in place of needing explicit instructions on what to do or where to go next. There's a manual in the game, but I found some things I discovered more by accident, observation, or experimentation. The map lured me a few times into thinking I was almost done with the game, but then a new area opened up. There's a lot of game in RE! There are 4 distinct multi-floor areas that are pretty self-contained; you don't have to run back-and-forth between them very much, which is good because you're already doing that to get to the checkpoints.

Limited inventory is good too. You can only carry 6 items and given that the house is zombie-infested, one should be a weapon. Keys, ammo, medicine -- these all take up inventory slots. You can save every item you pick up in a chest, but they're few and far between, usually near the typewriters. So I would find myself strategizing my path, using the map and inventory, at these checkpoint areas. While the game world is closed in the sense that you're confined to a mansion and its grounds and you must open this area before that one, I would say this game is also fairly open in the sense of how big the player's decision-making space is.

I played as a special operations detective of the STARS agency named Chris. I think there are at least three other ways to play the game. I got roughly half the achievements this way. I would play the game over to get the rest, especially since I get the feeling playing as the other character Jill probably is like playing a whole new game (same map?). Voice acting was ok, but the story was better and the character development was great! I really got invested in the characters. Story is revealed to you piecemeal, and there's a really thrilling feeling when you start to unravel a story thread -- a sort of "the game/chase is afoot," "the plot thickens," "we're cracking the case" feverish compulsion to keep playing.

Sound effects are well-chosen. The creaking of doors is distinct but not tiring even when I did it for the zillionth time. Music is also done well, especially the checkpoint area song. That song and many of the sounds, especially water trickling, felt soothing. (Odd word to use when describing a zombie game, I know!)

As far as influences, RE reminded me of several "haunted house" games of the era, like [i]7th Guest[/i] and a [i]Casper the Ghost[/i] PC game we had based on the movie. Playing it also made me think of the [i]Arkham[/i] Batman games.

Closest thing to a bug I think I saw was my cutscenes' visuals would get out of sync with the sound. Game sometimes got a little skippy but not in critical areas. These might be unique to my machine.

It took me 18 hours to play the game -- you get a scorecard at the end that tells you play time -- which is right in my expected range of 11-20 hours. At the risk of sounding more like the [url=xkcd.com/606/]Cutting Edge xkcd guy[/url] than he himself does, I'd encourage you to try RE if like me you hadn't already. In fact, I have half a mind (sorry, zombies got to the rest) to make a tradition out of it and play an RE each year around Halloween.

Resident Evil is a really good game, but it may not be for everyone.
I played as Chris Redfield in my game, and it was a good experience! It got a little frustrating at times with the fixed camera, but I easily look past that. Plus, that's just part of the experience!

I'm sure you know, Resident Evil 1 plays from a fixed camera, which means it plays from a specific viewpoint in every room, and changes whenever you move in specific areas of said rooms. This kind of camera style, as opposed to Over-The-Shoulder or First Person, makes the game a little more difficult. Finding items in this game is by seeing a shine, but sometimes can be easily missed due to the fixed camera, at least for me. It frustrated me a few times, but that's just part of the experience I think! RE is full of puzzles, and what would puzzles be without frustration?
Fixed camera is definitely not for everybody, but if you can enjoy it, I am sure that you will enjoy this game despite some frustrations!

Just as a reminder: this Resident Evil is a remaster of the 2002 remake of the 1996 RESIDENT EVIL. Quality is not amazing, as environments are pre-rendered and come out really low quality a lot of the time, especially compared to your character model & interactive item models, which are high quality placed on a pre-rendered environment. It didn't take away from my experience so I hope it doesn't take away from yours either!

Voice acting is not exactly great. I'm not a voice-acting critic, but the dialogue in this game, mainly from Chris, sounds very inexpressive, and boring. Again, this flaw doesn't take away from my experience so I would hope it doesn't take away from yours.

As someone trying to finally get into the RESIDENT EVIL franchise after so long, this was my third game. I started with RE7 and that game really went back to the franchise's horror roots and took a great amount of inspiration from RE1. You can really see the shine of RE1 within RE7, and I love that.

Overall, RESIDENT EVIL is a good game. Yes it gets frustrating, and yes it has some flaws (as all games do), but it is still a very good game and started a great franchise. Is it perfect? No. Does it need to be? No. The game is great and definitely worth a play. Some may be turned off by the fixed camera (I was too!), but you get used to it and once you do, you are in for a ride. This game captured many people's hearts in it's beginning days, and it caught mine today. It truly is a timeless classic.

That's it! Next up is RE2...

This is a great survival horror game and a wonderfully done remake of the original 1996 Resident Evil. The graphics and sound design are great. There is a more modern means of character control or you may play with the more standard 'tank controls. The puzzles are not ridiculously complicated and combat is fluid. You must manage your resources including key items, weapons and ammo, and healing items to successfully investigate a mansion you find yourself stuck in. You can choose to play between Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Jill has more inventory slots and gets a lockpick, and Chris has more hp and has a lighter. The main story plays out basically the same regardless of who you choose but each character does have their own stories and unique supporting characters and plot points. New content has been added in the remake and some things have been changed around so even those familiar with the original can experience something new.
You can use fluffy manager for mods if you are so inclined, and the game still works just fine on windows 7.
I strongly recommend this to fans of survival horror games.

My first time playing this game (not the series for say, whereas I have played and beaten RE2 original, RE2 remake, RE: Code Veronica, RE: Dead Aim, RE4, also just "recently" RE: Zero right before now beating this one... and well, any others I only played demos of or what have you). Nonetheless though, here's my breakdown as well as my thoughts about this game...

[h1] Need to know bases for beginners: [/h1]

To any first time player of this game (such like myself... or at least was before I just now beaten it), I think it's worth noting that it's easy to find yourself confused about where to go and where to even start, being that it isn't very clear coated in the sense of things (whether it be to check the rooms on the left or to the right, etc)... Though it does get lesser confusing as you progress further through the game (perhaps a few hours later?).

Furthermore, what's even frustrating is that you can be roaming around for a while, before you find your first room with an Item Box, to put away your currently unneeded Items at the time (like seriously and as a free tip, don't pick up the Emblem in the dinning room too early on.. you won't need it until it's time to solve the puzzle in the room with a Piano... [spoiler] also about the Piano, I think Billy would have solved it more quickly than Rebecca *cough* *cough* ...you'll see what I mean if you play the game, also assuming if you know whom Billy is from RE: Zero... not that he's in this one of course, cause he isn't [/spoiler] ).

Also like I noticed in other peoples comments, it's probably a good idea to start with Jill first as a beginner, being that what I notice is that Jill can carry 8 Items, whereas Chris can carry only 6 Items. Also playing as Jill perhaps makes it a little more clear coated about what rooms to checkout first.

Note: [spoiler] don't shoot the female zombie (Lisa) in chains that you come across, inside the cabin in the woods; it's a waste of ammo and she will only keep getting back up like a terminator, no matter how many times you put her down... just run like Forest Gump and leave the Cabin. [/spoiler]

[h1] My Rating and such [/h1]

Resident Evil Remake is a perfect example of a remake – it keeps story, gameplay, characters, and most of all, charm of the original game, adds new visuals, QoL gameplay improvements and content to expand the RE universe. Everything is done with great care and love from the developers and I simply can’t recommend it enough.
[h1] Overview / Positives [/h1]
RE1 is a somewhat difficult game to get used to on first playthrough. It expects the player to fully experience survival horror – be attentive to your surroundings at all times, examine items for hidden surprises and anything that’s lurking around the environment – which are key for piecing together ideas on how you can progress and complete the game. The only guidance you have is basic info on area completion noted down on all maps, otherwise you must mark down important information on your own (specific locked doors, items and puzzles you need to come back to later), similar to any difficult PS1 era game. And most of all, the game expects you to learn from mistakes, load your previous save once more to retry and succeed.
Along with fixed camera angles, limited ammo, defense items, tight item management, OST – the game keeps a tense atmosphere at all times. Although it can deliver a few surprises that might seem unfair and get you killed, learning from mistakes gradually makes for a more satisfying experience, especially when replaying it flawlessly later. Repeat playthroughs will reward you with more gameplay variety options.

The game is simply beautiful to look at. High-quality models, aesthetics of all locations and cinematic fixed camera angles bring attention to a lot of small, nice-looking details of the environment, it’s as if you are inside a movie. Playing this game on repeat at night is such a great experience, it is so visually satisfying.
[h1] Positives – charm [/h1]
The game is rather simple in concept. A team of police officers got lost in the forest and another team goes to investigate, they get attacked by dogs and flee to a nearby mansion, now left to wander on their own to investigate and discover details on the case. Characters, story and dialogue are also rather simple and not really too special. But I think many will agree that this simplicity makes this game extremely charming and lovely. I kept going back to it for these reasons alone. Unique colours of police uniforms emphasize character personalities, and subtle, optional character interactions make each one of them and their simple appearances and personalities stand out. The OST keeps the atmosphere as silent as possible and this perfectly captures the anxious feeling of facing the unknown, making the situation these characters are in seem real. Cheesy and at times ridiculously unfitting PS1 character dialogue was altered to fit this idea well. This charm carried perfectly from the original and makes characters seem more real, human and make you believe that they are professionals who truly never encountered a situation as bizarre as this.
[h1] Negatives [/h1]
I can’t think of much I didn’t like aside from upscaled visuals looking unfinished/rushed, and zombie AI at times being inconsistent. Almost all areas of the game look like they were either left untouched or weren’t upscaled properly. Once you leave the mansion, you’ll notice a lot of what looks like just original GameCube visuals. This makes HD character models look out of place and sadly doesn’t make the game look too impressive on HD monitors. There’s also a strategy of forcing zombies to miss a lunge attack and that opens you a window to go past them, yet when you do bait it out and go past, zombie AI can still flip the bird on you, register an unexpected grab and bite a chunk of your health. But this is more of a minor issue, can be encountered only after you learn how to bait zombie attacks often.

Aside from obvious rushed visuals, RE1 Remake along with the PS1 original remain as one of the best in survival horror category. It’s possibly the best game to get as your first survival horror game and as an entry title to the RE universe. You know it's easily one of the best remakes ever made when the game rewards you with unlockable developer messages, which make you appreciate love and care put into the game even more.

Enter the Survival Horror  

A phrase that would coin a genre and a game that would define a generation. Resident Evil, a classic that needs no introduction and a rare example of a game that transcends past that of a simple game and has been the source of many multimedia projects from films, toys, TV shows, comics and books to name a few. At this point your Nan has probably heard of Resident Evil. 

So how do you go about remaking an absolute classic? A monumental task that could not only upset fans but could then also tarnish the legacy of the original. Somehow Capcom not only managed to make a REmake worthy of the original but in my personal opinion, surpass the original in almost everyway (well perhaps not the dialogue). 

Just in case you're not familiar Resident Evil Remake (I'll just refer to it as REmake going forward.) is a remake of the original Resident Evil and features the same fixed camera angles, inventory management, puzzles and combat - but with radically updated visuals, remixed puzzles, new weapons, enemies, music and probably other stuff I can't remember. It's a drastically different game but also the same game and the balance capcom made with the old and new is near god like. 

Look I don't like full on remakes that change the original game too much and I much prefer remasters or ports (the irony of this game being a HD remaster). I'm more of a Demon's souls remake person rather than a FF7 remake guy if that makes sense? I think when a remake changes too much or alters gameplay drastically it can lose something from the orginal to the point it may as well be its own separate game or a sequel. This is why I'm scared for the RE4 remake because the original RE4 is one of my most favourite games. But - and this is controversial - I think the resi games on ps1 are basically unplayable at this point and do drastically need remakes, now that's not to say every remake has been amazing (*cough* RE3 *cough*) but in REmakes case it has not only seen improvements but also new content which doesn't tarnish the orginal vision but if anything enhances it. 

Anyway rant over - let's get on with the review. 

Pros 

I love this games graphics and atmosphere, absolutely nails the horror and I love the angles for the camera, the pre-rendered backgrounds are stunning and the character models are perfect. For a twenty year old game it's seriously impressive how much this game holds up. 

Perfect survival horror gameplay. Juggle inventory management and horrific monster encounters whilst solving puzzles that are only somewhat obtuse. Modern controls help alleviate the pain of tank controls but they are still present if you like pain. 

Two iconic characters to choose from resulting in two quite different gameplay experiences, meet different characters, use different weapons and use each characters different strengths and weakness. 

Multiple branching paths and choices keep replays fresh, make hard decisions or save a comrades life. The choice is yours. 

Crimson heads, why did they never bring them back, an incredible way of making dead zombies more terrifying and it really plays on your paranoia, having to waste extra resources is an amazing addition and I cannot believe it never came back. 

God tier ost, one of the greatest. 

I'm not a RE lore buff by any means and this game still has that RE cheese but it's simple and effective, good enough story to keep you going. 

Cons 

My only complaint is that some of the best meme-worthy lines have been re-written and the live action intro was replaced by cgi. This is legit my only complaint 
Conclusion 

This is quite possibly the best remake ever made and is almost the best resident evil game, if I didn't have so much nostalgia for RE4 it might possibly be my favourite. It is such a testament to capcom that they've not only managed to make this absolutely god tier masterpiece but they did it again with RE2. Simply outstanding. 

Now go make a Jill Sandwich.

As a big fan of the Resident Evil series, I'd never played the real original from back in the day, so can't really say how this compares to it. From a modern perspective, it's still a great game in my opinion especially if you are a fan of the series, but it has numerous clunky/old mechanics lingering. I believe it is a less trans-formative remaster compared to 2 and 3 remake, but things like the searched/complete rooms on map and additional modes/unlockables available are welcome additions. The number one thing I would recommend is to start out using the D-Pad or whatever keyboard control allows the tank movement. The game maintains the old style of fixed camera position that you switch to as you traverse areas. Although tank movement is clunky and sometimes annoying, if you are using the joystick, you will constantly be getting into awkward loops of running the wrong way during camera transitions as the slightest change of held direction will take into account the new angle and send you off in a different direction. Getting used to the tank controls and D-Pad right away make it much easier to move quickly through multiple transitions.

Also make sure to download a door animation skip mod at least for subsequent playthroughs since it saves SO much time as the animations are far longer than the loading time required.

The game has great atmosphere and the exploration is tense but enjoyable. You go through some areas a few times and can never be truly sure if there will or won't be new enemies added or maybe some that you thought were dead actually aren't...

Two different perspectives are included for the campaign - Chris or Jill - and they do have a decent few differences to make playing through each a fresh experience. There's also several unlock-able difficulty modes which can be fun to replay, including a mode that makes all enemies INVISIBLE which is quite the challenge. Overall, I would recommend the game to anyone who is a fan of the series and wants to experience its roots, or if you're interested in survival horror and want to play one of the original classics

I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a good horror game. Considering this is the 2011 remaster, the only thing I would say is particularly dated are some of the graphics in regards to the 3d models and fmvs. The character models are still good for their time and even now the pre-rendered backgrounds are a beautiful selling point.

If the thought of fixed camera angles and tank controls puts you off, you can think of it as part of the fundamental challenge. I didn't even use tank, as there was a 2d fixed camera control scheme I used for the entirety of my playthrough that worked relatively well. Moreover, game had what I felt were extremely generous aim assist and hurtboxes for weapon spread. So for as infamously bad or janky this style of gameplay can be where in the sudden moments of combat you might presumably take cheap damage, it does its best to give you a reasonably winning chance. Also, once I had the shotgun most times I'd come out unscathed in those situations. Most of the core gameplay then comes down to strategy in exploration and resource management. Planning and running routes to carry necessary items around was fun. Then once I had a grasp of the area and wasn't doing blind exploration, routing just functioned as a form of stress relief, as puzzle solving tends to be.

That relief becomes sweeter in context when you factor in this game's best feature is its atmosphere. Again, the pre-rendered backgrounds are still gorgeous and the sound design matches its quality. Being a bad (or in an ironic sense great) B movie in video game form, I wouldn't describe the game as immersive but instead as a playable scary movie. It just wants to show you something well-crafted that is tonally scary. This has a few traditional jump scares, but it's the buildup and suspense the playable characters endure that even allows you to faithfully buy in to the idea of that's there is anything worth being fearful over. Later in the game when this scare-factor does wane as you actually start to feel unthreatened with your cleared hallways and powerful with your new resources and confidence in skill, the atmosphere itself is still deeply appreciable as flavor for running through the game.

Honestly, even if absolutely nothing about the gameplay entices you, this game is worth playing just for the atmosphere alone. That thick, almost dreamlike ambience that old video games were so incredibly good at that, an art that has seemingly been lost in the never-ending chase for photorealism and graphical fidelity. Don’t get me wrong, the modern RE games are great and the remakes are very impressive, but there’s just… [i] something [/i] here that can’t be replicated. The complete desolation of a quiet mansion mixed with the tension of not knowing what’s hiding around the corner. The dark, foggy forest outside. The creaky doors, the unsettling decorations, the elaborate death traps, the dimly lit corridors – it’s like being trapped inside of a painting. And the fixed camera angles only add to the cinematic feeling of it all – sure, they can be annoying sometimes, but the gameplay is slow enough that I don’t think they’re too much of a problem, so it is a worthy tradeoff.

And all that without even mentioning the gameplay itself, which simultaneously defined a genre and yet still managed to be better than basically all of its later imitators. Ammo, inventory space, healing, even the ability to [i] save [/i] – everything is limited. But every single item, every single enemy has been placed so meticulously that this intended scarcity achieves a perfect balance of being tense and stressful without ever becoming actually frustrating – as long as you play by the game’s rules, obviously (this is [b] not [/b] a third person shooter). And sure, the camera and the movement and the shooting mechanics all clash with modern game design principles – but it all feels so intentional, it all adds to the tension and pulls you into the game’s world so hard that it feels unfair to call any of it “clunky”.

TL;DR: If you're new to this franchise like I am, be ready to deal with some old school, out dated mechanics.

I've never really played the Resident Evil series, but I'd heard great things about the remakes, so I decided to finally start playing them, but felt like I needed to at least understand the story of the first one before playing RE2 remake. Full disclosure, I wanted to get through this as quickly as possible so I could get to that game, so I used a guide and I have no regrets on that because this game is confusing and annoying even with a guide, and life's too short to have to keep loading every time I enter a new room, realize it's the wrong room, then load again and get lost some more.

I still found this game to be fairly fun and interesting. The mystery around the mansion and the atmosphere of the game is where it excels, and I can see it being a big deal back in the day when it released. But kind of like going back and playing any older game, there's a lot of stuff that just hasn't aged well.

The biggest culprit in this game is the stupid camera angles. They got me all turned around at times, and when being chased by something they really threw me off and often got me hurt or killed. Hands down it was my biggest gripe of the game. The second were the ink ribbons, which are required to save your game. Not only do you need to go and find a typewriter to save, you also need an ink ribbon in your inventory (which is limited in space), and there are limited amounts of ink ribbons in the game. This means there is an actual cap to how many times you can save your game. This is meant to make the game more challenging, but I found it difficult to find time to sit down and play for just a few minutes. Each save matters, and so you have to plan it all ahead.

The voice acting is crap. I mean, it's just awful. Key plot moments of the game had me laughing because the delivery is so clunky and flat. 

Overall, I did enjoy going back in time for this one, as frustrating as it was. But I can also see completely skipping this and going straight for the RE2 remake. I beat this in 8 hours with a guide. Without a guide, I'd still be playing it and would never see my family again. If you're interested in knowing the full story of this series, give it a try, just be warned of the frustrating, old school gameplay mechanics you're getting into.

The apex of the genre.

If there's a more nerve-wracking game, I haven't played it. I've played Resident Evil start to finish at least half a dozen times in the twenty years since this remake was released on GameCube, and it still manages to catch me off guard and leave me rattled. But the appeal goes far beyond the thrill of grotesque monsters lurking around dark corners. At its core, Resident Evil is an adventure game. Even if one were to strip out the action elements, replacing the direct controls with a traditional point-'n'-click interface, this would still rank among the best work from Sierra, Lucas, Cyan, and the like.

However, it IS a horror game. It does require quick acting and careful planning to conserve ammo, recover from attacks, and run from fights you can't win. Horror games are defined by the dread influences your every action, and that sensation has never been more effectively delivered than it is here. When watching a horror movie, we yell, "Don't go in there!" In Resident Evil, we make the choice to push through that fear.

In 2002, this was, hands down, the best-looking game I had ever seen. I can't say that's true of this HD remaster. My understanding is that the original assets were lost, and that the backgrounds here were simply upscaled from the standard definition GameCube files, with a few shaders slapped on top. The result is still phenomenally atmospheric, with magnificent artistic direction and bespoke camera angles. Yes, real-time rendering means modern games can now come close to the fidelity of these pre-rendered backgrounds, but it's still rare to see a game where every shot is framed with this intentionality. It's a shame the modern presentation isn't just a little better. Resident Evil deserves it.

Fortunately, there are other fans who care about this stuff even more than I do, and I encourage you to take advantage of their efforts. It's not hard to find packs of higher quality backgrounds, made by modders with access to newer AI upscaling tools than Capcom had in 2014. Better still, there's a mod that skips door animations, which does alter the pacing and tension a little, and I am all for it. I also spent some time tinkering with ReShade, which is certainly isn't essential, but I'm happy with all the silly little ways I've changed the lighting. Between the new look and the quick transitions between rooms, one of the best games I've ever played is now even better.

Some of these issues include cutting to a door opening animation every time enter/exiting a room, clunky movement controls. Admittedly, its some of those limitations that add to the dread and made survival horror what it is today, i.e. severely limited inventory space, limited number of saves, etc...But in this game some of these elements are so severe that they could be considered obnoxious by today's standards.

If you can get past some of these technical issues, the game does an extremely good job of rewarding perseverance and where progress is made by overcoming these challenges through solid inventory management and a deliberate approach. I still had fun, but I don't recommend it. Here's what I think about this game after completing it:

- The mood and ambience is scary and it fits great but the dialogue and cutscenes are bad.
- The difficulty modes were confusing and many people play on the wrong difficulty because of this.
- The number of times you can save are limited. You save by using 1 unit of ink on a typewriter, which is found in some rooms. If you need to stop playing for any reason, you have to run back to a safe room where a typewriter (save spot) is. This can take a while because the gameplay and running speed are very slow. Otherwise you'll lose your whole progress since the last save. Now imagine you used up all your ink and now you can't save until you find more... but you have to stop playing - that's what happened to me and I had to leave the game running multiple times so I wouldn't lose progress.
- Way too much backtracking and then waiting for the animation/cutscene that plays when you move from one room to the other. I wish I could skip it.
- Not much is explained. I had to google around quite a bit. For example, I found out I needed to mash the movement keys to escape when I'm being bitten or grabbed.
- Just as bad as all the backtracking: the inventory management. I had to walk back to the closest safe room (where the safebox is) all the freaking time, in order to get whatever item was needed to progress in that section because it's impossible to know what you are going to need, and you cannot carry everything with you. Even more often that that, I had my inventory full and I had to go deposit 1 item (you can't drop stuff) so I could pick up another item I had found. Even the typewriter ink takes up an inventory slot. And every time after saving the game you need to go to the safe box to deposit the remaining ink so you can free up that inventory slot (again, you gotta wait for the opening and then closing animation to play out, etc etc - it's all very tedious and boring). They should have the limited saving either optional or apply it just to hard mode, for example.
- This game felt like a (very slow) walking simulator with jumpscares. Spending hours looking at the same slow animations of doors opening didn't help. 
- This game is not for everyone and if you look at the achievements you'll see a lot of people quit playing before they even kill the first zombie
- There are timed story events that you don't know about unless you google around and know about them before they are scripted. For example, I was locked out of a better weapon because of this. 
- The camera angles could be better. In some places there are zombies waiting for you right off camera (where the camera angle cuts off) so it's almost impossible to avoid getting hit if you don't know about it. 
- I am supposed to be an elite police force member or something like that, but my character can't aim to save his life. I got bitten a few times because my character takes too long to aim and shoot or to start running. Zombies also take like 10 bullets to kill, so you gotta shoot a few times, turn around and run to gain some distance, and then shoot some more. I don't know how many times I shot a zombie dog in the face with a shotgun and he just shrug it off and jumped on my face again before I could shoot a second tme. It's like everything my character does, he does in slowmotion.

The original game might have been amazing when it came out, but times change and standards do too. Die-hard fans might like this kind of thing and they'll tell you off "git gud" style saying "you don't know how to play" and "you're not good enough" and "this is not a shooting game, it's a survival game" etc, but different people have different tastes, and I found this game not be worthy of all the praise it gets.

I personally do not recommend it, especially for its full price. I'd say only play it for nostalgia and only buy it on sale.

This 20 something year old Resident Evil game is not only a horror classic, but also an example of how to make a good remake of something which started a franchise. Even if you played the original 1996 version a million times, the remake (or in this case, the remaster of the remake) still feels like a whole new game. Some puzzles are old, others new, and the same goes for certain plot & gameplay elements, plus the music. Be prepared though, this game can get very hard very early. Unlike a lot of present day games where the start is always about tutorials and learning, this game throws you into hot water immediately. Despite that, it's not an unfair game, and if anything, it really does make it feel like you play a survival horror game where you can't just go Rambo. Resident Evil 2 and its remake did the same thing, and it worked there too. 

As for the elephant in the room, the fixed camera angles, it usually doesn't cause much trouble. If you played any of the older RE games which used the fixed camera angles, you'll know what to expect. If anything, it only becomes annoying on hard difficulty when it is neccessary to fight with knives due to your lack of ammo. Despite the scariness, the zombies can be easily outmanouvered unless you are in a tight corridor (and 90% of the time, you are going to be in a tight corridor :) ) ... If you are able to run behind a zombie, they pretty much become useless and you can just keep knifing them, because by the time they turn around, you can already go behind them again. Now though, if you do this in a place where the camera switches angles, it makes it more difficult. Why? Because your direction input can (and will) change together with the camera. When you pressed up earlier, it can now change to down, and a left can change to right. In this regard, the controls & the camera is the weakest in this entry in the entire franchise, and the only thing I disliked about this game. I know every toxic diehard 60 years old fanboy and their grandma who all still live in 2001 will attack me over this opinion, but I don't care. And yes, before you fanboys throw hate comments on me for this and say I'm not a real fan and just not used to classic controls, I did grow up on the old RE games. Probably finished them more times than you do as well. 

This game can also be very rewarding. The Chris & Jill campaigns all have enough differences to feel separate, and finishing the game under certain conditions can unlock extra weapons. Some story elements can also change depending on choices you made, which, of course, also means there are multiple endings. You can also unlock extra game modes, and they are all great. You found it silly that you can put items in the item box, and they magically transfer to all the other item boxes? There's a game mode where they don't. Or you already finished this game a million times, and unlocked almost every achievement? Or you want to impress your nerdy girlfriend / boyfriend? Try invisible mode, where all the enemies are invisible. 

In short, it has enough twists & improvements to the original to feel even better. Overall, what's new:
-Dead zombies have to be incinerated with fuel + lighter, otherwise (depending on the difficulty setting) they will get up after a while as Crimson Head zombies.
-A new boss, Lisa Trevor
-Some new locations: a cemetery, the forest outside the mansion & a cabin
-If you finished the game once, a new zombie will spawn in certain places called the Bomb Zombie which you can't kill (or you blow up)
-Achievements
-Extra modes

9/10

Of all the Resident Evil games, I'm not at all surprised that this outing, alongside its Gamecube brothers Zero and 4, are the most readily available and remastered of the older games. Because not only is it the best, most refined Resident Evil game from an objective standpoint (tied for that spot with 4 and its more aggressive style of action horror gameplay), but because it is, without a doubt, the greatest video game remake of all time and greatest survival horror game of all time (often battling with Silent Hill 1 in my opinion).

It takes an influential, yet flawed first entry and revisits it with all the gameplay enhancements made in 2 classic, 3: Nemesis, and Code: Veronica, whilst adding in new surprises to catch the older players off guard and new elements to create a tight-knit package. Gone are the days of waddling around with aim assist disabled in the western version in a brightly-lit mansion whilst listening to voice acting that's more fun to meme on than hear; IN are terrifying zombies and monsters, gothic archetecture, puzzles that will boggle the mind, genuine frights that still hold up even today, an atmospheric soundtrack that retains iconic themes from the original and features new disturbing ambience, and genuinely good voice acting. 

In this game, you choose from two characters: Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine. Chris has six inventory slots, but is able to score critical headshots more frequently, whilst Jill has eight and starts with a gun in her inventory. Both characters are balanced and a joy to play as (though I'll admit Jill is far more welcoming to new players), and the story deviations alone give this game replay value.
Not only that, but this version gives me hope they do the same to the other classic entries for the 30th anniversary, with costumes from the Lost In Nightmares flashback depicted in Resident Evil 5, support for higher resolutions, and even a modern, directional control scheme taken from RE's action adventure sister Devil May Cry and Resident Evil: Outbreak.

Over all, you can't go wrong with Resident Evil. It's the most refined, most fantastic ResE game of them all, and it's a must-play for any gamer. It's atmospheric, tense, endlessly replayable, and will keep you coming until you've saved all your fellow STARS members and gotten the good endings...

The five senses. 

A flawed concept, a misconception, a fallacious simplification. Like many a concept, you can only cut away so much fat before you start cutting actual meat, that is, before you start generating falsehoods and misunderstandings. 

Tangentially, it can go the opposite way too; this statement is an example: ‘left-brain people are more organized and systematic. Right-brain people are more creative and intuitive.’ It is a generalization, yet in doing so it misses the mark, this is a false statement. Add too much fat and you no longer see the meat. Back to the subject matter at hand.

Our senses are not five.

To identify the actual number of senses, we must define what a “sense” is. Let’s compare our nervous system to a computer; the central nervous system (mostly the brain) is the central processing unit of this system; nerves are the periphery. Based on the direction of signal transmission, we have two types of nerves: Afferent fibers, carry signals toward the brain, meaning they carry sensation, they are the input. Efferent fibers, carry signals away from the brain, meaning they carry motor command, they are the output.

Let’s focus on the sensory fibers. Everything you “sense” is carried by these fibers, the optic nerve carries the vision stimulus, the olfactory carries the smell stimulus, the cochlear the auditory, the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves the taste, and many nerves carry the tactile stimuli. These sensations are conscious, which simply means that they reach the cerebral cortex, the outermost layer of the brain.

Not all sensations reach there, however. Some sensations are subconscious, they are processed elsewhere. Do you “sense” the increased glucose concentration after you eat, do you “sense” its decreased concentration when you don’t eat for long? You don’t, your body DOES. The point is this, there are many other sensations that exist, yet you are not conscious of. The number is more than five.

That is not all, we can still work towards the original statement. Yes, our senses are way more than five, but what about the special senses? You see, a special sense is one that only one organ is responsible of. Only the eyes see, only the ears hear, only the nose smells, and only the tongue tastes. What about touch? Touch is what skin senses, however, not only the skin has the tactile receptors responsible for touch, but some internal organs also do. More importantly, the skin is not regarded as an organ, it is a system, the integumentary system, thus touch is not a special sense.

Our special senses are four. This statement is surprisingly, still false. The special senses are not four, they are five.

That fifth sense is equilibrium. Its why you keep your balance, its why you can stay standing up without falling flat on your face, in brief, a vital sense. But if it is a special sense, which organ is responsible of it? the vestibule of the inner ear, while the cochlea of the inner ear is responsible for hearing.

Our special senses are five. A true statement yet when simplified to: “our senses are five,” is incorrect for several reasons as previously discussed. Two similar statements, one true, the other false. The missing word carries the entire context, but even with it not omitted, one can still be mistaken if one assumes that touch is one instead of equilibrium, which is not an uncommon assumption, in fact, it is the most common one.

One can hide falsehoods in the truth. The truth, when presented in a simplified, generalized way facilitates the creation of misunderstandings. It is context that determines whether the actual truth is reached. In one’s field of expertise, one can forgo the detailed explanation because that explanation is known. However, when discussing the same explanation with a layman, one must strike a balance that ensures the information is easily understood while also being understood correctly and not misinterpreted.

Context matters, oversimplifications and generalizations are a double-edged sword, the information reaches much more people at the risk of it being misunderstood or being completely incorrect.

I should stress that this style of Resident Evil is a major turn off for some. Fixed cameras and a stronger focus on planning paths through areas against item management as compared to any test of reflexes or aim might turn people away. That said, if you're willing to give fixed camera Resident Evil a shot either this entry or the original Resident Evil 2 are likely the best places to start. 

This is ostensibly a puzzle-box game in which the entire map is one large puzzle-box with resources growing/dwindling the more it is explored and the more time and backtracking is required to get through it.

The major upside to having a fixed camera-style of Resident Evil is that it can be surprisingly relaxing to not have to land crucial shots through good aim and instead take in the atmosphere which is bolstered by the unique camera angles. It still manages to be horrific, but arguably more in tone and feel rather than in producing sheer terror. 

The major downside of this era of Resident Evil is how doors and item boxes combine to waste a lot of time. If an item needs to be used in an area far away from an item box (item boxes being what allows you to change out items from your limited storage space), then you will need to enter a room with an item box (triggering an unskippable door opening animation), go the item box to get that item, leave (triggering that same unskippable door opening animation), go to that area to use the item, then potentially realize that you needed a different item, run back to that room with the item box (triggering another unskippable door opening animation), change out the item, then leave again (triggering another unskippable door opening animation). If you realize immediately after leaving the room that you forgot to put away a save ribbon or that you took out the wrong item, two more unskippable door opening animations will be repeated for every time this happens.

While that is a major nitpick as that time wasted will add up over the course of a single run through, the game is short enough that this added up time isn't too frustrating. Overall, a great game which you will have to meet halfway in terms of accepting its slower pace as compared to its own franchise's later additions but which is still very much worth it for its own unique feel of survival horror. It's also worthwhile from a genre lineage perspective given this is a remake of one of the progenitor's of survival horror, so it can allow for a stronger feeling of completeness when appreciating the genre as a whole.

I understand this is a remake of the original Resident Evil game which was released around a quarter of a century ago. It holds up quite well however and the graphics in this version are impressive. It's not an action-packed game - the emphasis instead is more about solving puzzles and exploring the map searching for key items whilst carrying out your investigation. It actually reminded me a little of Metroid Fusion, in the way that you feel the whole game is essentially a labyrinth and it's your goal to escape.

Good points:
- Impressive audio-visual design. The game looks great and the creaking doors, rumbling thunder, moaning zombies and cawing ravens all create an atmosphere that is consistently creepy.
- The various journals you collect throughout the game provide an intriguing and human story that will immerse you.
- You have a choice between the original 'tank' controls and a less old-school option.

Bad points:
- Too much back-tracking for my liking, although admittedly some of this was due to trying to figure out the game's quite challenging puzzles...
- I'm not keen on the inventory system. I know some feel this adds another dimension to the game-play, but you just don't always know which item you will need at what point, and there were times I'd rather have just got on with playing the game rather than having to back-track to an item box. Prefer the (still limited) but more generous RE4-style inventory.

7/10 - Well worth playing, particularly if like me you've never played this on any other format.

okay, so. the first run i had with this game took me a whole 12 hours, iirc. my friends were watching me stream it the whole time, and later i found out that apparently most people took 6 hours to beat the game. which was kind of embarrassing, but i think that's kind of a testament to how much this game scared me.

firstly, the fixed camera angles! i've heard from some people that the fixed camera angles make the controls a bit janky, and while i sort of agree, i personally had an extremely easy time adjusting to it! the fixed camera angles, however, honestly instilled more fear into me than anything else. no, the zombies didn't scare me, but what did scare me was the fact that i had no way to truly check if a zombie was in my blind spot - i have to actively move over there myself. i'm not a regular horror player, tbh, but i've found that those fixed camera angles instill more fear in me than jumpscares ever will.

secondly, the gameplay! i love the art direction, i think the controls are a tad janky, but the guns you use lock onto your target and you can shoot - if needed, really. i think that makes up for the fixed camera angles, but what really gets me even more than that is that this game discourages combat. your goal isn't to kill everyone - should you do that, you might be faced with something even worse along the way for recklessly wasting your ammo. [b]your job is to SURVIVE, not KILL.[/b] 

your job is to learn about your surroundings, be smart with your ammo and resources, and at the end of the day, make it out of this mansion without having run out midway. sure, the save mechanics are extremely annoying should you want to play the game in small increments - say you're busy, there's only 39 save ribbons in normal mode and if you don't make much progress, you're bound to run out easily - but if you do have the time, there are ways to beat this game in 3 hours and even less. the gameplay is really built around the lore, your time, and remembering what you can go back to, as well as making sure you searched every room that you might need. it's really about being smart with your time, which can be frustrating, but - for what it wants from you, i think it works. 

just remember to set aside time to properly finish puzzles and the like, so you don't waste ink ribbons in the game. i don't recommend playing the game for like, 10 minutes and saving, unless you get through the game extremely fast! a recommendation i've heard is to save after a big puzzle, or after a boss - tho there aren't too many bosses, and it takes a bit to get there, so. the game's all about trial and error, learn from your mistakes and previous playthroughs, so don't feel too bad about having to start over should you realize you made a major mistake.

thirdly, the lore. god, i severely love the lore in the resident evil games and they've had me hooked even when the game started to shift over to action - but even in this game, they add quite a bit of lore to the original's lore that makes the actions of the antagonists in this game sink in even harder. i could rave on and on about how interesting it is, how it definitely deserved it's spot as the founder of survival horror franchise, and how it makes sense that people were interested in zombies all over again because of this game - because it offers such an intriguing insight into zombies, an alternate version of classic undead monsters, and not only that? it's horror doesn't lie in gore, it doesn't lie in jumpscares.

it lies in the horrors of humanity, of reality - and the fact that you're unaware of what's going on, hidden facilities and experiments for which you are now unwittingly a piece of. it's so cool, it plays off the fear of the unknown, and resident evil seriously makes me reconsider reality and life as a whole. i totally recommend, and reading the original game's lore has been so fun too.

basically!!! this game's my favorite out of the entire franchise, and i think you should play it too. 10/10, even if the controls get janky and confusing! though if that does get you frustrated, a playthrough would be nice too. either way. its a nice look into a different perspective that chills me to the core, and it's a terrifying plotline. though it can hit a little too close to home with the current political climate, it's definitely a thinkpiece and a fun game all in one!

[h1]Resident Evil (2002)[/h1]

[i]Enter the survival horror.[/i]

It's no lie that this game still holds up to today and is one of Resident Evil's best titles for good reason: being the remake of the 1996 game, it improved on every level imaginable. While it still has some of the ills that people mention like the clunky tank controls and the classic mechanics compared to more recent RE titles, this game is still top tier for not just Resident Evil fans, but those who like horror games in general.

Despite being twenty years old now, Resident Evil Remake is still a gold standard for the survival horror genre and remakes. Even with other Resident Evil remakes being made, none can hold a candle to its reputation.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

Investigating the cannibal homicides that are occurring in the Arklay Mountains, S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team is sent to investigate the case, but after their disappearance, Alpha Team is dispatched to search for them and to also continue the investigation but a desperate situation forces the remaining four members of Alpha Team: Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, Barry Burton, and Albert Wesker into a large mansion in the middle of the forest where their investigation into the mysterious mansion begins.

[spoiler]The story isn't anything too thought-provoking or deep, but it's definitely a solid plot that accompanies a survival horror game like Resident Evil decently. While both scenarios with Jill and Chris are plausible, I'd say Chris' Story is the canon version since Rebecca was present in this one and it marks the beginning of his conflict with Wesker. Resident Evil also includes a pretty sad subplot about the Trevor family and their tragic fate as victims of Umbrella.[/spoiler]

The voice acting is definitely a step up from the 1996 version, as it feels less like a B-rated movie and more like an actual horror setting. but even that has its own charm. There are still some cheesy iconic lines that appear in the Resident Evil Remake though, which are just too good to leave out honestly.

[u]Gameplay[/u]

Resident Evil's gameplay challenge comes less from the strength of enemies, but just having enough resources to get around. Item & Resource management is a big part of Resident Evil; sometimes picking everything you see will prevent you from picking up key items which'll result in you having to go back through a potentially dangerous hallway filled with enemies just to get to an item box to put your items away.

Not going to sugarcoat it: this game can be [b]hard[/b] for new players even on Very Easy. Early on, you will constantly be looking for ammunition and trying to shoot every zombie you see because it will appear as if you can't bypass them but learning running patterns to bypass enemies in RE1 is very important if you want to get through without having to use a First Aid Spray occasionally. Enemies aren't bullet spongy, but you still need to make sure you have the resources in your limited inventory space to deal with them.

As for puzzle solving, the game does not hold your hand; you won't have an objective list to tell you what to do next so you'll have to meticulously check each door to see what key unlocks it, manually use key items on POIs (like an arrow shaped slot), and examine items to interact with them. Paired with the size of the map, you need to have a good plan in your mind on what your path is, what items to pick up, and find clues for solving puzzles.

Resident Evil allows you to choose whether to play as Jill or Chris. They both have their pros and cons but Jill is recommended for beginners as she has more inventory slots and has Barry to get you out of sticky situations, but Chris can hold his own better on harder difficulties due to the fact that Rebecca can heal you at certain moments in the game and has more health than Jill.

Controls can be a little clunky given that this game is almost twenty years old now, but you can get used to them quite easily. Included in the remaster, the alternate controls are a bit weird to use because your character can sometimes just spin out of control if you turn the left analog slightly and that could get you grabbed or hit by an enemy (but it is easier to dodge with the alt. controls).

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

Resident Evil's pre-rendered backgrounds made Resident Evil Remake one of the best looking games at the time when Gamecube came out. With the release of remaster, these graphics have been improved greatly but I did notice that some of the backgrounds looked grainy and it was quite clear that they were definitely not made to hold up for a remaster. But regardless, Resident Evil Remake improved massively on graphics compared to the 1996 version, which helped a lot to highlight its horror atmosphere.

Almost the entire soundtrack from this remake are remastered versions of the original game's music, which is some of the most memorable music (along with it's "Save Theme") in the series because each track played matches perfectly with every area/room you enter and monster you face against. Just a great combination with the atmosphere.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Even after twenty years, Resident Evil still holds its own as one of the top survival horror games out there and can be a terrifying experience for newcomers. It is an absolutely solid buy for anyone who likes horror games and has great replay value with unlockable rewards, costumes, and additional modes. Don't miss out on the game that defined survival horror.

This remake is a brilliant reimagining of an old classic. If you’re even remotely interested in the Resident Evil story, I highly recommend playing it. Backtracking always lead me to take the safest route, even if that meant a longer path. The fixed camera isn't the worst, but it can definitely make things inconvenient if you don't play super carefully. With regards to the control scheme that makes you feel like you're driving a car, I actually enjoyed it.
