I thought I fell in love with the series when I played those standing arcade games with the vibrating fake SMGs that made a cheap "pew pew" sound when you shoot the zombies and a huge blob of pixelated blood  splatters on the screen when you lose. Since then I had played a tiny segment of RE4 at a friend's house, and watched Youtubers play RE7 and 8 on Youtube. When I invested in a gaming PC recently, the first thing I wanted to do was binge-play the series starting from scratch. It was time to get serious about this ridiculous franchise.

Introductory lore in this game is fascinating, the ambiance was properly suspenseful and kept me on my toes. The overall subtlety of the horror was phenomenal, and the remastered graphics were pretty pleasing, too. I really enjoyed getting immersed into the story of the Umbrella Corps, Raccoon City and S.T.A.R.S. It's not even that it's really deep, at least it wasn't at this stage in the series, and yet it was so satisfying to slowly unravel hints of the mysterious backstory as a reward for solving puzzles. The tidbits became more disturbing the deeper into the game I delved, and I became obsessed with finding every item in every room thinking I could get even more details of the story this way. 

The biggest flaw of the game is the control system and  fixed camera. It's a shame, because this was a common style of old school games. Still, it can get tedious, irritating, and downright disabling. Learning what they call "tank controls" is like learning a new language, and it took me over two days just to get the basics down, let alone become fluent. Good luck to you if there is a movable box that you want to run past. If you are not facing the exact direction you need to run, with zero margin of error, you will not be able to keep your two hands off that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ box and will keep trying to push it. Oh, and when some puzzles need you to act quickly (again with virtually zero margin of error) and the camera cuts angles abruptly to another stupid angle as you're scrambling with the controls trying to get out (AND there's a push-able item)? Yeah, not the most fun time, I'll tell you that. 

There were other tedious aspects of the game that I did grow to really appreciate, though, as they were well-designed and clearly intentional, unlike the dumbass fixed cam and tank controls. I don't want to spoil it if you don't know what to expect but let's just say you will exercise your management skills in unique ways and suffer consequences of poor management in unique ways as well. It is only tedious because you are forced to slow down and actively think about your next moves to ensure you do not make a mistake that would cost you unnecessary effort. It's easier than it sounds.

Don't get me wrong, failing a puzzle or absent-mindedly approaching something can have heavy repercussions, especially if playing on hard-mode. But I guarantee you will not want to go straight into this game on hard if playing for the first time, or you'll probably end up doing what I did and- after getting f*cked by the cam and movement mechanisms several times, restart in normal mode.. and then get f*cked again and start in easy. Maybe that last part is just me, but it is apparently common for players to begin this game hard mode and bump it down a notch or two. I think it's because there's really no point to playing a mid-level difficulty on the first run, since you can't see what specific advantages and disadvantages are in any mode. You might as well then take all the easy-mode perks so you can even learn what they are. Then if you replay as a different or same character, you will be used to the controls and be ready to find out what helpful features you're about to get stripped of for the sake of a novel replay experience.

There is a whole lot more content than I would've expected, and this was a pleasant surprise, up to a point. After a while it became tiresome because I kept thinking I was close to the end after 100%-ing the rooms, only to discover a whole next chapter. And I got completely stuck on about five puzzles total. After looking up answers, I'd say three of the five times it was due to poor user interface mechanics. Two out of the five times I realized I was just getting impatient. Either way that made me waste plenty of time running back around the huge map over-analyzing what was often a non-intuitive prompt or glitch on something I already tried until it almost drove me to insanity. And when I kept thinking I should've been close to the end anyway, this started to become slightly more frustrating than enjoyable. But, personally, I still think it was all worth it.

Lastly, if you know little to nothing about Resident Evil games, please don't mind the dialogue. It's corny. This game is old, the logic is silly, and the characters act kinda stupid. It's endearing.

Played this back around 2005 on the GCN. Since I've been running through the classic games recently (including playing through the original RE1), I decided to give this one another spin. 

	It's as good as I remember it. Looks just as good, too. It's wild how such an outdated technique (even by 2002 standards) has kept this game from growing outdated: the pre-rendered backgrounds. Some areas legitimately look like they'd fit into any modern game with how well they look. It helps that lighting and shadows were now a thing; used to be that they were 'baked into' the textures to give the illusion of their existence. 

	Whats interesting is that some effects are actually video footage coupled with particle effects. I think the fireplaces are actually just videos of fire instead of real-time fire. It's an evolution of pre-rendered environments that would've been interesting to track had Capcom continued on this route.

	What helps the environments stand out are the character models. Characters now blend into the areas, with shadows and lighting hitting them from areas dictated by the scenery. It's actually difficult to disassociate the characters from the places they are in, which was always an issue in the older games. Characters stuck out, and whilst CRT's did a decent job at hiding it, modern monitors make it obvious. With REmake, the characters seamlessly blend into the mansion. Which gives a stronger illusion of real-time environments.

	Also helps that the pre-rendered pictures are no longer blurry or grainy. The camera panning and moving around is a nice touch, too.
	
	You can praise the graphical presentation both for how well it's kept up, and for what a huge leap it was at the time. Remember, RE1 and REmake were only 6 years apart. That's the same length of time between Metro:Last Light and Exodus. RE4 and 6 were 7 years apart. Compare the graphical improvements, because they do exist. But do the same comparison between RE1 and REmake. And yes, there was a sizable leap between PS1 and PS2 games, but it wasn't typically this large. REmake goes beyond typical expectations of the time.

	But graphical fidelity aside, REmake is just a straight improvement over the first game. Areas are slightly tweaked or expanded. New areas are introduced. Lore is expanded with either new notes or characters (Lisa Trevor). The dialogue, whilst I appreciated the camp of RE1, is now more professional. And the general atmosphere is more frightening due to a reworking of the camera angles. The game doesn't carry over all of the camera angles from RE1, and it plays with perspective more than it did before.

	Even if you've never played an RE game before, this is just a good game period. REmake was actually my first classic RE game (I played 4 before this). With no connection to the PS1 original, this still stood out when I initially played it. It's really hard to nitpick faults with this game, because it does nothing wrong. And that's expected, given that it's basically a second shot at a game; that gives the developer time to perfect their creation. Especially after 4 previous games. 

	REmake is typically called the best classic RE game, and sometimes the best game of the entire franchise. It enhances the original in virtually every way possible, while adding more to it. That's not always a guarantee with remakes, as The Twin Snakes (another GCN remake of a PSX game) showed; it can be praised for virtually the same reasons as REmake, but it failed to provide the same flavor. I'd call very few games a 'must-play', but this definitely stacks up there.

Remember that time all of the big games journalists and critics said that Resident Evil 7 was a return to form? Prove them wrong by playing this game; a faithful remake of the classic Playstation game! 

Going into this game it's important to understand that there is a heavy emphasis on puzzle solving, item management, and just general character navigation to contend with if you want to be successful with this game. The static camera can be an issue from time to time, but there are enough control options (and the ability to rebind keys) present here to make character movement more comfortable than it had been in the original version of this game from so many years ago. 

The puzzles in Resident Evil are fairly intuitive, but a minor issue I ran into came from not knowing where exactly certain assets actually were and what exactly I could interact with. The Aqua Ring and Residence in particular gave me some issues in that regard, 

Remember when I jabbed at Resident Evil7 earlier? Here's another one: This Resident Evil has a significant level of replay value. Even if you don't consider New Game+ and unlockable difficulties, there are major differences between Chris and Jill's experience in this game; including a different supporting cast, different weapons, different amounts of hit points, and different puzzles, including an optional means to skip a boss if you play as Jill. Playing as Chris instead of Jill also limits your inventory and as a result, makes the item management in this game that much more of a challenge to overcome. There are even alternate endings depending on whether or not you save the supporting cast you meet in this game, or leave them to an untimely fate. 

When it comes to the difficulty of this game, it definitely feels like it's somewhat front loaded. The first portion of the game that require you to collect the four death masks and begin your search of the mansion. This is from the point of view of someone playing on Normal and as Chris, but even my first playthrough (as Chris and on easy) had a couple of very noticeable peaks in difficulty after that early portion of the game. I can't say exactly how easy the "very easy" difficulty is because I don't plan on touching it, but similarly I don't know if I'll be good or patient enough to unlock the highest levels of difficulty either. 

It's worth pointing out real quick though, that the way you select the game difficulty in the beginning is vague. Instead of a standard prompt asking if you want to play in very easy, easy, or normal mode, you're asked to chose one of three descriptions that represent those difficulties. If you, like me, didn't know there was a 'very easy' mode, than you, like me, might feel a little silly and a little intimidated to find out that Resident Evil's easy mode is very capable of killing you if you make to many errors. What's really annoying is how you select a difficulty setting in New Game+ : You're asked flat out if you would like to play very easy, easy, normal, or the newly unlocked hard mode (or hard modes depending on how quickly you finished your first playthrough). That would have been helpful 9 hours ago before I started my first playthrough Capcom!

I've tried playing this game before on console, but it didn't click with me then. It's definitely a game that demands more out of a player than other Resident Evil games, and the rewards don't seem to be as game breaking for subsequent playthroughs aside from the Rocket Launcher you can earn if you're able to beat the game in under 3 hours, on normal or a higher difficulty. 

I'm really glad I gave Resident Evil R another chance. As demanding as it is, it's ultimately a lot more satisfying than what I expected, and despite having finished it once, I still have a lot more game to actually complete here. Definitely give this one a chance if you walked away from 7 or 8 feeling dissatisfied.

As a newcomer to the RE series, I knew I had to play this game first to see how the series kicked off. It's a survival horror set in a fictional city in America with zombies and infected creatures destroying the last vestiges of humankind. I love the inventory management in this game and how the game encourages you to be smart about your actions. At times, you may need to conserve ammo for other enemies or reserve space for key items. It's all about thinking about what you need now and what you need later. The item boxes give players the chance to store or take items, meaning that they are key to surviving in the game. The way most people these days remember the original Resident Evil from 1996 is pretty skewed. Most folks see the "classic" Resident Evil games through the lens of this 2002 remake, which was stark tonal re-evaluation of what the series was at that point: Action-Horror.

I know some of you are rolling your eyes right now thinking "Nah, RE was always SURVIVAL HORROR bruh" or something along those lines but two consider these two things:

A. "Survival Horror" is just a marketing term that Capcom made up. It's not a real genre, and no one agrees on what actually counts as a TRUE SURVIVAL HORROR GAME™ or not because the term is so vague. 

Do Survival Horror games need fixed camera angles? Because the classic Silent Hill games (1-4) do not employ them for 90% of their runtime.

Do Survival Horror games need inventory and item management? Because once again Silent Hill and even Fatal Frame eschew limited inventory in favor of a more streamlined method of item management.

Do Survival Horror games need tank controls? Because Fatal Frame and Obscure dropped them completely and Kuon, Deep Fear and Silent Hill 2-4 gave you the option for a 2-D control style.

So miss me with that "UM, AKSHULLY IT'S SERVIVUL HURRUR" ♥♥♥♥...

B. Consider how fast-paced, action oriented and unabashedly goofy RE1 is compared to other horror games from around that time.

Yes, some of that goofiness is due to age, but there were horror games that came out before RE that were a lot more serious, more tonally grounded, and didn't give you a small military arsenal to deal with any and all problems in your way.

People just seemingly forget there were horror games  that came before or around the same time as Resident Evil (Alone in the Dark, Doctor Hauzer, D, Enemy Zero, just to name a few) that were better at nailing the horror experience than RE1 did in 1996. That's not to say they were better games than RE1 (Enemy Zero was, though), but they actively tried to be straight horror, unlike RE1.

Resident Evil since day one has always loved goofy action ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You use a bazooka to blow up kung fu lizards and annihilated a buff naked dude that a weirdo who wears sun glasses at night was trying to steal with a big ♥♥♥♥-off rocket launcher, all before the mansion itself self-destructs. Ya' bro, that's straight horror right there...

The series would only get more bold with that sorta thing as it went on, even before Resident Evil 4. RE2 went hard on it's action, raising the stakes through the roof, and RE3 doubled down on that even harder by adding dodges, a 180 degree turn and ending with a you using a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ RAIL GUN on a blob and saying "You want S.T.A.R.S, I'll give you STARS!" before Raccoon City gets nuked. And you know what? It's cool! It's really cool that Capcom knew that the action element already embeded in RE1 was key to the series going forward.

But that's the funny thing about 2002 remake, it has all of the goofy ♥♥♥♥ that the original had. All of it! But it's presentation is flipped, as it plays everything with a straight face. Now blowing up the kung fu lizards and the big naked dude feel tense and even scary, so much so people forget that all that actiony meat is still there in underneath the surface. 

Now because the remake and the original are so very similar, and the fact that this version of the game is more readily available to play, newer fans who've never played the original before, old fans who haven't played the original in a while and old fans with little context as to the horror gaming landscape at the time think "Ah, this is what RE1 was trying to be all along!" and then ask "Why did RE4 turn RE into an action series?" when it always partially was one. I've done it myself, and I know a lot of you have too.

RE Remake is a good game, a great game even. I personally prefer it over the original by a fair margin myself. But it isn't really the best representative of what classic RE was either. It's its own thing, and that's cool, but it and the original trilogy (and I'll through CV in there, begrudgingly) set out to do things a bit differently from one another.

TLDR: Good game. Play it. Stop being Survival Horror boomers cause you have no idea what you are actually talking about. Good bye!

My tastes find delight in classical video games and systems, the PC has been my passion ever since I was old enough to afford a crappy Gateway PC (anyone remember Gateway?!) - the Smiling Anus on the phone promised me it would be GREAT for gaming! (It wasn't...) But luckily, that crappy computer that my roommate taught me the ways of electronics and computers and I bought my first video card! I think it was an nVidia 4800TI or something and it kicked ASS in TFC (the original!) Sims Online, AVP2 and Wolfenstein 2!

It's been years, and I wanted to revisit one of my most cherished games from my awkward sex years... Resident Evil on Playstation! Sadly, this is not a direct port of that jagged, blurry, blocky and lovably cheesy 32-bit classic - but holy kittens does this game stand as a perfect example of a "remake" done to perfection!

First off - the graphics are FANTASTIC. They are sharp, but also the pre-rendered backgrounds are phenomenal - definitely a strong vintage feel however - but these visuals have ages wonderfully! Personally, I am a big fan of the Haunted House setting, and coupling that with the haunting still imagery really works wonders in pulling you into the game! Yes, the TANK CONTROLS remain, but that's for the best given the horror-inspired camera angles that snap from frame to frame. The camera system feels like an artistic choice and I do miss it being missing from RE2 (which dashed my hopes after this wonderful game!) Resident Evil 2 drops the cinematic style horror camera angles in favor of an over-the-shoulder 3rd person mode like Skyrim only RE2 works. But I am just too much a fan of the presentation of the environment, the chaos and destruction literal tell the tale of a last stand and desperate struggle and it's marks are left all over that Raccoon City Police Station... but I don't ever get to take them in! I'm forced to run every where! Bumping and biting my way through rabid lickers and annoying zombies that I can never dodge! I am so much more in favor of the First RE Remake's slower pace and style! Makes it all the more heart-pumping when the monster go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the later parts of the game! (i.e. those cracked-out Red Zombies and that scary - but tragic - hunchback she-monster!

The gameplay thankfully remains quite honest with the original Playstation game. All the items have been scrambled around, but all your favorite locations are here! The monsters are all great - although I do wish some of the later monsters got a little more embellishment... I was always fascinated with the lesser known biological specimens Umbrella had been cooking up out there in those dark woods!

The MUSIC is spot on! Haunting and ambient - always a great mix! After running around dodging stupid zombies while juggling an inventory smaller than my bladder of items between getting eating by snakes and chopped in half by lizard people, hearing those soothing melodies of the sanctuary rooms literally heal away sickness in real life. Thanks to a few moments of rest and relaxation in the sanctuary rooms, I no longer have the Bends!

There's a few negatives and mostly minor ones... The running around zombies seems solid enough, though some of those lunges would make Dark Souls monsters narrow their eyes. The boss monsters are a little awkward, aiming bullets vertically or along a trajectory is difficult as you have only 3 directions in which to aim: your feet, the enemy's groin, or the ceiling...

Over alls, a 9/10! I recommend playing with a glass of Jameson, one cube! It'll help with those shakes of panic and fear while trying to figure a way through those darn caves with that hunchback, or the water parts!

Original:

Having never played a survival-horror game before now, I decided the best place to start would be with the GameCube remake of the first [i]Resident Evil[/i]: a wildly successful version of arguably the most important survival-horror title in history, ported and preserved on nearly every modern system you can think of. Since this was my first foray into the Spencer family mansion and all its glory, Jill's campaign took me 17 (in-game) hours to complete. This is a terrible finish time for the bulk of the RE fandom - many of whom played the PS1 original when they were kids - but as is typical for Capcom games, repeat playthroughs are of course heavily encouraged, and I plan to do exactly that (re: my hours in [i]Devil May Cry 3-5[/i] across multiple devices). Chris' campaign will be waiting for me when I'm ready.

I cannot recommend this game highly enough. Your first zombie encounter immediately sets the tone for a significant portion of the experience; the anticipation and tension both contribute to a fantastic gameplay loop that is hard [i]not to[/i] draw inspiration from. Even when you start hording a bunch of powerful ammo and health items like I did, you'll always be kept on your toes from beginning to end as you plan your routes in between saves.

I must unfortunately admit that near the end of the game, I looked up a guide on how to use certain items (e.g. the wooden mount) and solve a late-game puzzle in the mansion (the eagle room). The solutions just weren't immediately clear to me. However, I can say that if you're new to RE like me and you're unsure of what to do next (and you stubbornly refuse to look at a guide), then the best advice I can give is to [b]pay very close attention to the doors and red areas on your maps[/b]. They'll save you a tonne of headaches.

I enjoyed [i]Resident Evil[/i] so much that I'm probably going to double-dip and buy a physical copy sometime in the future. And any game that gives you such a feeling in this all-digital age is a very special Jill Sandwich indeed.

EDIT (31/03/2022): So I bought the Origins Collection on PS4 and was disappointed to find that it only runs at 30fps. If you like physical media then any version will suffice, but you're better off playing the PC version.

EDIT (07/10/2022): Fixed up the syntax in my review. Finished Chris' campaign in under ten hours. Ready to play at a higher difficulty next time.

Resident Evil is a classic game, but when most people hear "Resident Evil 1", they think of the original PS1 version. While that is certainly the version of the game that everyone knows, the version of the game that the Resident Evil community and myself love is the remake of the game for GameCube. Resident Evil on Steam is a remaster of the GameCube remake, and it's even better than other releases of this remaster for one reason: 60 FPS support.

Other versions of this game, even the ones on PS4 and Xbox One, are locked to 30 FPS for seemingly no reason. Add to that the fact that this game is moddable on PC, and you've got the definitive version of the game right here. The textures don't look that great, as the originals were lost, but just add the REupscale project, a texture mod, to the game, and things look instantly better.

As far as gameplay goes, be prepared for a challenge. Even on Easy, the game is no cakewalk. Good inventory management and save management are the names of the game here, and you won't last long if you waste all your ammo or never use any of it.

The zombies in this game aren't the biggest threat. Not even close. Without getting into too many spoilers, you have dogs, snakes, large reptiles, further-mutated zombies, and more to deal with in the Spencer Mansion and its vicinity.

The map is a challenge in and of itself, with the entire game being a puzzle box that you have to figure out in order to progress. There's no shame in finding a slightly-annotated map (or making one yourself), as you can quickly get turned around in the sprawling halls, and a wrong turn could mean getting chomped on by a zombie you weren't expecting or purposely left alive... or even worse.

While I personally prefer the newer Resident Evil games, with 2 and Village being my favorites, I will say that this is a phenomenal experience, and depending on your tastes, it could very well be the best in the series and the pinnacle of survival horror.

[h3]Full Circle[/h3]
Finally, it has come full circle! The original game made me who I am today - a compulsive hoarder. Only in virtual worlds, thankfully. I was so traumatized by all the panic and creature horror, but most of all - the inventory horror! Unprecedented for the time, the scarcity angle caught me off guard, and, for better or worse, it was never repeated to the same degree within the main series. To this day, I always have oodles of consumables left unused in any RPG, boast Amazon storages of ammunition in shooters, and I've beaten Silent Hill 2 into submission by primarily using a nail board. Bless your shivering, shrieking core, PTSD! Here I am, sinking my teeth into the necrotic pudding once more. Rich and creamy.

In the light of what I just said, it may sound weird, but RE sort of calms me down. There's no other way - you pull yourself together or get pulled apart. Collected, I tune in to its rhythmic pacing and calculated tension. I soak in the atmosphere, flow with the ambiance, and appreciate how the game treats its ripe horror tropes. While my love for Silent Hill is high-functioning, cerebral, what I feel for this franchise is visceral, almost carnal. Undeniably, I'm a die-hard fan. The last time I could call myself a fan happily, I was playing Fallout 2 while listening to Chocolate Starfish and the Hot Dog Flavored Water. But it's coming back now, it's coming back. Happiness, not Limp Bizkit.

[h3]Story & Puzzles[/h3]
I suppose I need to start this thing off properly with the game's story? I don't even think I need to give you my take on it. Who gives a crap about my thoughts on Mozart, for example? Okay, here you go: virus bad, Barry is my hunny bunny, mansion traps, monsters Cronenberg, your inventory is full, Salieri was falsely accused and then the fallacy was sung by poets for drama points. Not that sophisticated of a premise by modern standards, but a trendsetting classic nonetheless. I would never think of adding or subtracting anything like I wouldn't change a thing about a cat. Here, the golden cheese of outlandish voice acting got fixed, however, the old one remains out there forever, so I don't mind.

With a few notable exceptions, backtracking-intensive puzzles boil down to "I can't wait to get rid of this thing to save up some inventory space" kinds of entente. To boot, every so often, you're welcome to die after failing to figure out the logic behind a strict sequence of steps to perform on the double. No hard feelings though. Each time I inserted another object into another slot and heard the satisfying *click* or took the right course of action, it echoed inside my weary soul. I made some progress, I freed up some space, I lived, after all! Indulging an important relieving pause, my mind starts racing again, I'm on the move. I definitely saw a herb and some sweet shotgun ammo during my last impetuous scamper through the eastern wing.

[h3]They See Me Turnin', They Hatin'[/h3]
The remake has added an "Alternative" movement type as an option, but I initially went for tank controls anyway. The keyboard lends itself fine to this scheme, this is how I played the original. Yeah, yeah, you can't just lounge back and enjoy yourself while playing, but I'm okay with hunching like a true nerd. Tank controls have their charm, even some nostalgic value to me. Besides, horror only gets juicier the more uncomfortable it makes you feel... so I told myself until I finally found a spare mini-USB adapter, plugged in my gamepad, and tried the alternative. What can I say? Nothing beats instant turning, tank controls have no chance against such an obscene advantage! Although, they deserve to be honored for serving us faithfully - like horses before the age of cars or spittoons before the age of swallowing our phlegm.

[h3]I Love Fixed Camera Angles[/h3]
Speaking of paradigm shifts, they did a number on this remake's presentation. The competent use of dynamic lighting and crisp shadows makes certain moments even more dreadful than before, and locations - even more memorable, despite being somewhat drained of color. The detailed body horror of smooth models, headsplosions, and grimy pre-rendered backgrounds look fantastic, getting emphasized by the cinematic camera. In professional hands, dramatic camera angles really tie it all together! Nothing can set things up and create meticulously controlled experiences for a player quite as they do. And thanks to them, the perfect 80's horror sets that are this mansion's intricate, interconnected environments are the scariest character in the game.

Remember the room where you see a zombie around the corner in a mirror or these infamous hallways with cracking windows? Such well-manipulated scares! And you don't always need a threat for things to get eerie - like with these menacing staircase shots snatched directly from Alone in the Dark. Creating tension where there isn't a thing otherwise (as yet) and sustaining it is high art where, needless to say, the masterful sound design does half the job. Sure, clutch angles also cause such jarring issues as obstructing your vision when it's least appropriate, ending up with you getting blindsided by something that your character should've noticed from a mile away. I brush it off by saying that beauty requires sacrifice and sometimes it's chunks of your face.

[h3]On Curve[/h3]
You know what would be dakka? To just push-kick a zombie. Could one possibly catch your foot? Then again, hit too hard and you'll get stuck in its rotting guts. Zombie theories! Many of us are wired to always loop back to those in moments of respite. Anyway, it took me a while to learn how to evade properly, and even then, I wasn't exactly a floating butterfly, so I died a lot. In RE, however, losing a whole hour of progress is not a huge tragedy since redoing everything in a more efficient way is a treat in itself. To a degree. It's a genuinely hard game full of devious beginner's traps. After 3 hours of rapidly snowballing collapse, I swallowed my pride and restarted on medium difficulty, amply lubing the inverted difficulty curve.

Even with the new controls and the addition of defensive items seen in recent remakes, the game stays challenging, which is appreciated by veterans and amateurs alike. As for me, I'm happy with my humble "easy" victory for which poor Jill had to die a thousand deaths. I can't say I'm dying to experience an even smaller inventory, so, Chris, my apologies. Jill is the one who's packing. But enough about dying! Killing here is pleasant... and punitive. So cathartic, gory, fairly gratuitous, though simultaneously discouraged by sensible ammo shortage and fast Crimson Head zombies who start spawning later in the game from the bodies you made, but didn't burn or decapitate. It sounds like a nuisance, but no enemy is worse than dogs and birds anyway, trust me. The same goes for their in-game counterparts.

Being restricted and weak lends itself to the genre perfectly. Resident Evil knows how to play these cards expertly, it's confident enough to make you cooperate on its terms. I loved every predicament that it put me through! Making someone enjoy a thing they predictably would is admirable, but to think up mechanics that are repelling on paper and make them work in that someone's best interests I call pure brilliance. Every time you have to leave the safe room, you feel the taste of iron in your mouth, lick your lips that suddenly went dry. Thrilled, you tense up, wondering if you have the willpower for the constricting adventure howling in the corridors beyond. Inhale. Clench that shotgun, focus your senses. Turn the knob. Exhale. Run back in because you forgot to put the damn ink ribbons into the box.

Seeing as I wrote a recommendation for the RE2 Remake, I thought I should write one for the one where it all started for me.

The entire Resident Evil game series was always one of those where I had heard mixed opinions but I always wanted to find out for myself if it was worth all the attention. I love horror and Resident Evil aka Biohazard is deemed to be the pioneer of survival horror within the mainstream gaming community.

I was pleasantly surprised by how much this game toyed with my expectations in terms of gameplay. This was my first time playing this game. Many years ago, I attempted to play Code: Veronica on the Gamecube. The controls were terrible. Like nothing I had ever experienced. Granted I was more used to JRPG games at the time rather than shooters. I was worried that those god-awful controls would be in this game too. Thankfully, no. This version comes with two options. The original "awful" control style and an updated, new user-friendly style.

My favourite aspect of this game was the surprisingly gothic ambience of Spencer Mansion. A beautiful, traditional old house, full of art, sculpture, marble floors and sweeping stair cases. The mansion itself was a joy to explore, a haunting labyrinth full of hidden passages, booby traps and locked doors. (SO MANY DOORS). Especially with the storm blowing outside. But I also knew this game was a sci-fi so I was looking forward to finding out how that would be worked into the "haunted house" theme.

Being non the wiser, I ran my first playthrough as Chris. I'd heard Jill was the popular choice, but mostly because a lot of people chose her just so they could stare at her bum. I had no idea it was because she was the easier character to play as. I thought both characters had their own unique stories to tell and it didn't matter who you started with.
Anyhoo, I chose Chris. And yes, it was tricky. A lot of running backwards and forwards to the safe room due to a lack of pockets to carry resources (which is something Jill has plenty more of). I liked his moments with Rebecca.
But I think I enjoyed Jill's playthorugh a little more, purely because I was used to the game style at this point and her story was a bit more interesting with Barry and the more colourful arsenal of weapons. Somehow I managed to miss the infamous "Jill Sandwich" dialogue.

Overall, the game was loads of fun and a unique experience. I appreciated the pacing and that it felt like an actual horror experience and not all guns-a-blazing and explosions. In the earliest areas of the game, you learn quickly that enemies DO NOT go down easily and your ammo is limited so you have to play economically and learn to run circles around them to avoid using precious ammo. Also, because it takes place on a dark and stormy night in a creaky, old house and you don't know where anything is yet, you want to move slowly through corridors, just in case you draw attention to yourself and something jumps out at you. The camera angles really help to maintain the mystery of new, unexplored rooms and keep tensions high, but sometimes they can work to your disadvantage when you're running low on health and trying to find the nearest safe room. It's quite panic-inducing when you're not used to the gameplay style. When you get attacked, you feel the weight of that walking corpse trying to overpower you. It makes you feel vulnerable. When you're used to the zombies of Left4Dead2, which feel light and flimsy like ragdolls, this game makes zombies feel genuinely threatening, especially when you've been raised to believe that a single shot to the head will drop them. It doesn't. Unless you have bigger, better weapons, which you don't find until you've explored a lot of the house.

20 years on, still the greatest Resident Evil of all time. Not nostalgia. The gameplay here is RE at its most concrete, cohesive whole. From studying your map, pre-planning routes around enemies, resource management, atmosphere, characters, enemies, virtually everything about it is perfect. Slap FluffyQuack's door skip mod for a faster-paced experience, and the gameplay remains as engaging and as fresh as it was in 2002.

That being said, this remaster is a little dodgy. While the character and item models are gorgeously rendered, and the animations are silky smooth, there is some low-res texture work, and the pre-rendered backgrounds could have used a good smoothening up. There are also some technical aspects of the remaster that feel a little unpolished. However, we owe a lot to the success of this remaster for giving Capcom a wake-up call, granting them the confidence to take the series back to how it was in the beginning, and giving us not only Resident Evil 7, but the masterful Resident Evil 2 remake that was cancelled after the initial failure of this game upon launch.

Voice acting, while considerably improved compared to the original, retains some of its B-movie charm.
Notably, some of the game's features may seem quirky to newcomers. Specifically, controls can feel stiff, camera angles disorienting, loading times and backtracking a bit tedious.

Still, for old acquaintances, it's a delightful trip down memory lane.

After playing quite a few RE games I finally decided to play the 2002 remake of the First Resident evil game and while this is a great game, Ironically I don't recommend it as your first Resident Evil game. I'll get the more negatives stuff out first, then the positives in a different paragraph. Some elements in this game (strangely enough in this remake and the original) haven't aged too well like; the completely fixed camera angles with pre-rendered backgrounds. These 2D images then have 3D effects layered on top to give very detailed environments for a 2002 gamecube game. The problem with that is you are forced to use a still camera since its not a 3D rendered environment, and the camera perspective makes it very disorienting when moving between camera shots as you are still controlling your character relative to the previous angle which can be annoying. Not to mention, some items, which are 3D objects can be hard to see with the pre-rendered environments. This game is still very much a classic Resident evil game and with that comes limited saves. There are NO checkpoints in this game whatsoever, you save by using a consumable item called an "ink ribbon" at a typewriter, in a save room, in order to save progress. There are a limited number of these ink ribbons in the game so saving is a resource which can be intimidating to new comers. Although I will say having the option between tank controls and more modern feeling analog controls is a great upgrade the original didn't have, even if the analog controls feel a bit wonky due to the camera changes. Honestly my biggest complaint is the 5 second door opening animation that acts as a cheeky loading screen, it can be such a pace killer, and especially annoying when you forget and item or when you have to backtrack, which you are doing often in order to progress. 

Now that all of that junk is out of the way, this game is still great and holds up great too. The Enemies and environments, as well as level design are all great, and the puzzles are just the right amount of difficulty to be fun and engaging. The game does have cutscenes, but the bulk of its story is told through files that you find around the game giving detail to the horrible things going on in the mansion and the people, both in charge and normal employees and their families, suffering through it, and it does remain interesting till the very end. The voice acting, while different than the original, still has that B-Movie Resident Evil cheesiness that seems to make it more endearing. Definitely would recommend if you are already a preexisting fan due to its more outdated gameplay mechanics, but if your a new comer that doesn't mind the game showing its age very much, then this is still a great survival horror game. I suppose it should be considering Resident Evil 1 created the term "survival horror" and this game is well worthy of that title.

The original Resident Evil is a great game, but it is a little rough around the edges. Although it has aged rather well, a remake was warranted. However, how does one remake Resident Evil, especially after a relatively short period? You hire Shinji Mikami as director, of course. After all, who would know more about Resident Evil than the original's director? Capcom intended for REmake to be a darker, scarier, and overall more realistic interpretation of the original, and I'd say they leaped above and beyond expectations, creating what I'd argue is the best survival horror game of all time.

The plot, originally written by Kenichi Iwao and Yasuyuki Saga, is relatively unchanged, so I won't be going into specific details. If you've played the original, you know what to expect here. The original game had quite a good story, but it was marred by haphazard execution. Said execution is mostly improved here. Plot reveals are set up much better and character motivations are explored in more detail. There is a genuinely interesting mystery here and if you're not familiar with the original you'll find yourself invested. Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield are still somewhat flat protagonists, but it's more than made up for by the supporting cast. Barry Burton, Rebecca Chambers (my favorite), and Albert Wesker are all great additions to the cast and remain memorable over two decades later. The only outright new plot element is Lisa Trevor, and while I will not spoil the mystery surrounding her, she adds to the story's emotional core in an effective way.

While the central narrative involving the STARS members is certainly good, I found the environmental storytelling much more interesting. The bottles of alcohol lining a scientist's bedroom. The swaying zombie corpse hung from the banister. The letter to a lover, pleading her to forgive him. It feels like you've stepped into a world where you don't belong, that you're intruding on the personal lives of everyone who used to be here. It feels like this whole area used to be filled with people, but they all just up and left. It helps to flesh out the world in a masterful way.

Capcom was not simply content with remaking Resident Evil with better graphics and narrative tweaks. Instead, the entire game has been redesigned from a gameplay perspective, forming the ultimate survival horror experience. Not only do you have to struggle with limited health and ammunition, but also kerosene. In REmake, zombies do not die. When defeated, their corpses will reanimate later on as a crimson head, which is faster and stronger than the average shambling husk. To prevent this, the player must burn the corpses using kerosene. However, there isn't much of it, and not every corpse can be burned. In addition to carefully planning which zombies are worth killing, one now has to consider the potential dangers of doing so, which adds yet another layer of strategy to a game already so mechanically complex. The game is also incredibly difficult but in a way that comes off as ridiculously satisfying. When I died, it is because I had poorly planned a run rather than Capcom pulling out some unperceivable trick. You can't take very much damage, and enemies deal a lot, which helps make every encounter terrifying as even the lowliest zombie can end potentially 20 minutes of progress. If you play your cards right, and properly plan for any potential encounters, you will eventually become a survival machine that can handle any encounter, though the game does not lose its difficulty even then. Puzzles are also moderately improved. While they may not be particularly challenging they are creative and are satisfying to complete. They add to the sense that you are not just exploring the Spencer Mansion but slowly unwrapping its layers.

Another thing I enjoy is the playable characters. Unlike most games, where choosing a protagonist tends to only affect the story, there is an inherent gameplay difference between Jill and Chris. Jill may be more of a glass cannon, but she has two extra inventory slots, which goes a long way. Chris on the other hand is a bit tankier, but he is missing two slots and this makes backtracking to safe rooms a more frequent endeavor. Jill also has a lockpick which can be used to open simple locks throughout the mansion. Instead, Chris has to locate a limited number of old keys to open these doors, putting additional strain on your resource management. Chris, needless to say, is the game's hard mode and should be reserved for second playthroughs. Nevertheless, I still find his campaign particularly rewarding and I enjoy how Capcom went out of their way to make sure each character played differently.

REmake is a visual masterpiece. From the art direction down to the technical elements, every single visual element of this game works perfectly within intention. The dark, cobwebbed corridors of the mansion are beautifully rendered via pre-rendered backgrounds, providing significantly more detail than the GameCube's hardware could ever hope to provide in real-time. The backgrounds are impressively dynamic and layered, too. Dynamic lighting bounces off the walls and 3D models pass beneath pre-rendered elements. Even when rendered at 1440p, the effect remains convincing. Character models are detailed and while facial animation isn't mindblowing it's better than a lot of games at the time. Monsters are realized with disgusting fidelity and remain disturbing even today. REmake is probably the best-looking game on the GameCube and reaches levels of realism unparalleled by even other 6th generation visual masterworks like Silent Hill 3.

The original game's voice acting is infamous for being hilariously bad, ruining a lot of the tension in cutscenes. Naturally, REmake being a more realistic interpretation of RE1, redubbed the voice lines to be more natural. The voice acting in REmake is still not great, though it is an improvement. There is not a single line of dialog that is nearly as bad as the original's, but it can still be spotty at points. Joe Whyte, Ed Smaron, and Hope Levy do a decent job with their roles despite occasional iffy line delivery. I found that Heidi Anderson-Swan, Jill's actress, was the least convincing with her performance. I wouldn't call her bad necessarily but she could have been cast better. Peter Jessop gives the game's best performance, portraying Wesker as a truly manipulative and evil man. Overall, not bad, but not fantastic either.

The only major criticism I have isn't of the game itself, but rather, the PC port of the HD Remaster. It's a bit of a mess. Firstly, the port is unnecessarily demanding on lower to mid-end hardware, leading to an inconsistent framerate on those machines. Secondly, despite supporting 120 FPS, the game forces your monitor to output in 60 hertz in fullscreen mode, causing screen-tearing. The game also has no borderless fullscreen mode, meaning that when alt-tabbing, the game has to not only defocus the game but also change the refresh rate back to your monitor's default. This is incredibly inconvenient. Some music tracks even play faster than they're supposed to. These issues can all be fixed with relative ease, but shouldn't exist in the first place. Nevertheless, the PC port is the only way you can currently experience this game in 60 FPS or greater, so it's worth it if you're willing to spend 20 minutes downloading some fixes.

Shinji Mikami's Resident Evil Remake is a survival horror masterpiece. Everything that matters in this game is done perfectly. From the atmosphere to game design, to horror, to visuals, it accomplishes it all. It even expands on the story in a meaningful way, which I greatly appreciate. Insanely difficult, incredibly terrifying, and unfathomably gorgeous, REmake is a game everyone needs to play.

Overall:

A groundbreaking horror game remade by its original developers and improved upon in every conceivable way. A modern classic in every sense of the word, a game which defined survival horror and still reigns as the greatest game in the genre, all these years later.

10/10

The good:

The original PS1 version of Resident Evil from 1996 was a fantastically designed game, held back by the low quality of its presentation. The voice acting was atrocious (although pretty funny), the graphics (being early 3D) were unrefined, and it generally felt cheap and dated, even by the time its sequel came out, 2 years later. In 2002, the game was remade from the ground up for the Nintendo Gamecube, and that version was later remastered and ported to Steam (henceforth refered to as REmake). REmake keeps the vast majority of what made the original game great, while improving on almost everything. Its main gameplay loop involves exploring the environment, solving puzzles, and killing zombies, while managing limited inventory space and surviving with scarce resources. The player is required to strategize, and make efficient plans to progress while spending as little ammo, health, and save tokens as possible. This design philosophy, coupled with the fantastic level design are the basis of the game, creating tense gameplay full of meaningful and consequential decisions. Spend too much ammo, and you may not have enough for the boss later. Keep too many zombies alive in the narrow halls you will constantly be backtracking through, and you may get bitten, wasting precious health items. Pick up too many consumables, and you may not have space in your inventory for key items. Mastering this gameplay is very rewarding, and along with the two campaigns (one for each character), extra challenges, and unlockables, makes the game very replayable. REmake's environments are pre rendered backgrounds, which are viewed through fixed camera angles. This gives the game a very unique, cinematic look, and really contributes to its excellent atmosphere and scares. The music and sound design are great, and the voice acting is pretty good too. While the story is nothing to write home about, it is excellently paced, keeping the player intrigued about the mysteries behind the Spencer mansion, the zombies, and [spoiler] Lisa Trevor and her family (a subplot not featured in the PS1 original) [/spoiler].

The meh:

Tank controls are kind of a dealbreaker for many modern gamers, and may push others toward the alternate controls option, which allows the player character to move relative to the camera. While that addition is nice to have for those who want it, it can break the game, allowing the player to move in and out of zombies' grab range with ease, and trivializing a lot of the challenge. Also, the two campaigns start quite differently, with Chris having 6 inventory slots instead of 8, and not having access to a lockpick, thus needing to find some extra keys that Jill doesn't, who has a little less health to compensate. However, after the first third or so of the game, the path ahead becomes more linear, and the two campaigns start to have more and more in common. I understand that this is how the original played out too, but they could have improved this aspect somewhat in the remake, to add to the replayability.

The bad:

As this is a remaster of a game from 2002, heavily featuring 2D elements (namely the pre rendered backgrounds), one would expect that they are re-rendered from scratch to adapt to the modern display standards. However, it seems that Capcom simply took the original, low resolution backgrounds and upscaled them to modern high resolutions. In many rooms it looks fine, but in many others [spoiler] especially in the residence, aqua ring, and caves [/spoiler] the upscaled image looks very compressed, muddy and blurry, clashing horribly with the 3D models, and really detracting from the player's immersion.

[b]Positives[/b]

+ Graphics look really great and photo-realistic.
+ The design of the mansion and other areas is top-notch and highly memorable.
+ The atmosphere is creepy and well-done.
+ The story is simple but effective.
+ Huge mansion to explore, very believable and lots of different ways to tackle the mansion.
+ You can play through the game as Jill or Chris, both offering different experiences beyond gameplay differences.

[b]Neutral[/b]

/ The set camera angles are both good and bad. On one hand, visually it leads to a great cinematic experience, and I know the fixed camera angles are a big part of why the game looks as good as it does. On the other hand, from a gameplay perspective it means you can’t see very far and you can get caught off guard a bit unfairly.

[b]Negatives[/b]

- Some of the dialogue is a bit silly e.g. Jill challenges a potential traitor, a monster appears, they chase it off, and she suddenly drops her accusations entirely as if she’s had a memory reset.
- The inventory limit is an absolute pain and constantly leaves you not knowing what to bring and what to leave behind. A key taking up as much space as a shotgun seems stupid.
- Puzzles frequently make little sense and often require elements on completely different parts of the mansion that require a lot of travelling back and forth and trial and error.
- Long load times between rooms (although I guess some kudos for so many lovingly recreated and varied door opening animations?)
- Saving is limited to a consumable meaning you are forced to save sparingly and get overly punished if you go too long and get killed.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

There are some core fundamentals to this game that make it very punishing. I appreciate this was remade faithfully outside of a few tweaks, so this is a game of its time.

I ended up following a guide as I haven’t played Resident Evil 1 before and it was overwhelming to a newcomer. I initially stubbornly stuck to Normal difficulty as I wanted to play the game as it was meant to be played, but if you’re a newcomer to this too I would recommend either Easy or Very Easy to reduce how punishing it is. The punishment doesn’t come from the moment-to-moment gameplay, but to the attrition you will experience over time from backtracking between locations without the ability to negate a lot of the enemies in your path:

1) You don’t have enough ammo to take down all enemies you come across.
2) The zombies that you do manage to take down will come back as stronger, hardier, faster variants after a set amount of time unless you burn them with kerosene.
3) Kerosene is a limited supply and you can only carry 2 charges at a time.
4) Also, you need the lighter as well, so if you want to burn a zombie, that’s 2 inventory slots to do so.
5) You need to make sure you burn zombies in locations that you will commonly visit (which you probably won’t know on your first playthrough), or else you’ll waste your limited kerosene and not have any left for the zombies you should have burnt.
6) If you don’t know where to go, which specific items to bring, or how many inventory slots you’ll need free to gather the necessary items, you’re going to end up backtracking a lot.

Despite criticisms of some obtuse and punishing mechanics, I’m still recommending this because the mansion really is fantastic to explore and looks great - it isn’t hard to see why the game is iconic. I would describe my feelings on the game as glad to have experienced it, but didn’t necessarily have lots of fun with it. I think next time I play it I’ll have more fun by putting the difficulty lower and having more knowledge on the layout of the mansion which is why I’ve written the guidance I have above as knowing is half [or more] of the battle.

Are you a Resident Evil fan? Then this game is a must for you in case you haven't played it
New to the franchise and want to start with the first game? I wouldn't suggest doing that. "Why?" you may say. Please read on

!! CONTAINS SPOILERS !!

You start off in a mansion with no introductions as far as gameplay or controls go, so if you haven't played any RE titles before, it will most likely leave you thinking "what the *beep* do I do now?" 
The mansion is MASSIVE, or at least it feels that way because it's structured like a fricking maze. No matter how many times I've walked down the same halls going from A to B, I manage to get lost along the way. This could also be because of the camera angles this game offers. Yes, ladies and gentlemen, we need to talk about the camera angles.

If you have played any of the newer RE titles whether it's first-person or third-person over the shoulder view, you WILL have a hard time getting used to the fixed camera angles you have in this game. So, basically, you see your character as if you were watching a CCTV footage - I'm not kidding. Once you enter a room you will see the room (and yourself) from e.g a corner. Now, as you move further into the room, the camera may change to the opposite corner of the room. Because the camera angles keep changing all the time, I tend to walk in a loop where I will walk forwards then the camera angle changes to let's say that opposite corner angle I was talking about, thus I invert my joystick (that is if you are playing with a controller, but I guess it's the same with a keyboard) which then leaves you walking backwards and this loops until you realise that the controls get inverted once the camera angle changes. It's not easy to explain and I don't expect you to understand how the view angles work by the way I phrase it. Let's just put it this way: it sucks. It took me hours getting used to, and quite frankly, it's still not ideal. Especially not when you're running away from a monster or a huge boulder. 

The game also has two different controls options to choose from. I decided to play with the new controls since the original tank controls felt unappealing to me. I won't get more into that, that's for you to decide if you end up buying the game.

As far as the gameplay goes, it's actually pretty good once you get a little further into the story. At first, it feels like a door opening simulator. I have never seen so many locked doors in my life and it feels a bit overwhelming at first, that is until you obtain the keys you need to unlock them. Depending on IF and then WHICH resident evil games you have played before, this game is heavily puzzle-based. Dare I say you're doing puzzles 90% of the time? There's not a lot of action or boss fights (I'll get to that later), it's mostly you walking around trying to figure out how to open that one fricking door. [i]You've been at it for six hours now, you can't figure out how to get that door open, ugh... You're starting to get tired, you want to look it up on the internet but at the same time, you want to figure it out yourself. It leaves you thinking "What am I doing with my life?", [/i]sounds familiar? No? Okay, so I got a little carried away....

The graphics are average. They're either good or bad, just average. For its time, being released in 2015, I think the game looks all right. If you compare the graphics to the 1996 original, I think we can all agree that they did a good job. Audio-wise, the game shines. Scary ominous music 10/10. Something that caught my attention was the footstep sounds - they sound absolutely amazing! Voice acting on the other hand made me laugh a few times. Yup, it's that bad. I get that it's a remaster which heavily focused on improving the graphics, so I won't pick too much on it. The lines are also pretty laugh-worthy and goes somewhat like this, using each other's names in most sentences:
Jill - "Barry!"
Barry - "Jill!"
Jill - "Oh, barry!"
Barry - "Jill, I'm so glad you're alive!"
Barry- "You were almost a jill-sandwich!"
Jill - "You're right, Barry"

Boss fights! They have to be good, right? Meh, most can easily be killed with a few shots. Nothing special, to be fair. The first time you encounter the snake, Yawn, you can just grab the death mask and leave the room. You're not forced to fight the epic snake boss, whether that's a good or bad thing is for you to decide. However, you will encounter Yawn later on, and then you'll be forced to kill it. I believe I killed it with three shots from the grenade launcher if I remember correctly. It was fairly easy, despite the snake being highly intimidating. 

Another boss you will encounter two times is the Tyrant. During my first encounter with him, I shot him four times with my revolver and he died. It felt way too easy, but wait, "didn't you say two encounters?" oh yes, I did. You will fight him again shortly after. Without spoiling the whole scene, it goes pretty much exactly the same way that the Resident Evil 2 remake does. Taking a step away from the *weak* bosses, this game has all the evil creatures you could think of: Zombies; sharks; bees; snakes; spiders; plants; crows; dogs and other creatures I can't put a name on.

[H1]Conclusion[/h1]
[i]Is it a good game? Is it worth it?[/i]
Very much so! Absolutely worth it in my opinion [b]IF[/b] you have played RE before or you're a hardcore fan. Otherwise, the puzzles are way too hard for your average player to figure out on their own. Most of the time you have no idea what you're even looking for or where to even remotely look.
This is a great remake/remaster, and kicks off the franchise strong.

This game absolutely deserves its place at the pinnacle of the survival horror genre. It's the type of game that you can really master over time. Not by improving you execution of specific mechanics, but by building an intricate mental map of the excellently designed environments andgameplay systems. 

Tips:

For a fist play through, play as Jill on the middle difficulty (the hike) even if you like hard games. Your ability to play on hard is less dependent on skill and more dependent on knowledge and planning which you won't have for your first play through. 

Avoid killing enemies whenever possible. Almost all enemies in this game, even the really scary ones, can be maneuvered around and this is almost always the best way to approach situations. Killing to many enemies will deplete your limited ammo and may also have other consequences. The exceptions to this tip are the areas around save rooms, which are usually best to clear out since you will be revisiting them frequently. 

Play with the modern controls but make use of the tank controls as well. Using the modern control scheme places typical 360 movement on the analog stick and the original tank controls on the d-pad. Both of these control schemes are useful depending on the situation and it's good to be able to quickly switch between them. 

Explore every single room and keep your eyes open for ammo and puzzle items.

Was Resident Evil misclassified? Returning to the game that popularised the genre term 'survival horror' 19 years after its original release invites the question.

Sure, Spencer Mansion's warren of corridors and alcoves is riddled with tenacious horrors. There are hardy zombies that won't stay down unless you drench the corpse in gasoline and take a flame to its rags. There are rabid Doberman that round corners at full pelt. There are mad bees and hellish crows not to mention terror snakes and spiders seemingly imported straight from Greek myth.

Yes, the game makes good on its horror promise. Meanwhile, ensuring the survival of your protagonist - you choose between local special force operatives Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine at the start - is an ever-present theme (albeit no more than in any other video game). But 'survival horror' is not the game's principle theme. Rather, most of your stay here is spent solving puzzles. Resident Evil has the appearance of a lost George A. Romero classic, but the function is pure Myst.

There are some games out there which take years for you to truly enjoy or even understand. To be totally honest, I spent so many years trying to play the original Resident Evil, but I just couldn't.

Well, after a long time messing around with other titles and making no real progress, I finally beat Resident Evil and discovered why its so beloved. As a massive fan of the Resident Evil series it hurt me to take so long with this game, but now I can finally assess my thoughts on it.

The story takes place in the 90's in the Arklay Mountains on the outskirts of Raccoon City. After a series of group killings involving cannibalism occur, the Raccoon City police send their best cops, S.T.A.R.S out into the mountains to investigate. Not long after however, they lose contact with their Bravo team, and Alpha team is sent in to find out what happened. After arriving at their helicopter's wreckage, they are attacked by zombie dogs and retreat into a nearby mansion for safety. This mansion is not as safe as they think however, and this winds up being the catalyst for the entire Resident Evil series. The plot is fairly simple overall. Most of the detailed backstory and such is placed within the various optional documents strewn throughout the mansion grounds. There is plenty of additional info for you to dig through if you're interested, but it is optional. To summarise, it is a mystery story line. There are double crossings, conspiracies and themes of overindulgence and greed harming the innocent. Many of the characters present go on to become some of the most iconic in the series. Jill Valentine, Chris Redfield, Albert Wesker and Barry Burton are all likeable and unique characters that push the story along smoothly. It's no story telling masterpiece, and the dialogue is mostly just fine, but it kept me hooked the whole way.

On a technical level, it sits in a unique position. This version of the game is actually an HD remaster of the Gamecube remake from 2002. It is a massive improvement on the original PS1 title, however it does show its age when compared to more modern titles. For its time however, the game definitely had its impressive qualities. Character models still look really good and despite the pre-rendered backgrounds, the environments still drip with atmosphere and look appropriate. The PC port itself is also very solid. I played the game with a PS4 controller and the controls work well for the most part. The default tank controls are far from amazing, however the game is designed with these controls in mind, and they're not hard to get used to. The alternate controls work fine most of the time, but they can have issues with the changing camera angles.

Sound design is also very good for the most part. As I mentioned already, the voice acting is passable, but everything else is really nice. Guns have very punchy sounds, making even the weakest of weapons sound powerful. The enemy sound effects do repeat often, however they are quality, and this does help with identifying them when off screen. The music isn't always present, however it is very appropriate when it does appear. The save room theme in particular is a standout.

The gameplay for Resident Evil is ultimately where you either fall in love, or fall off completely. This is a classic game, not just culturally, but also in its very design. This is a true survival horror experience. On the normal difficulty, all of your resources are scarce and must be used correctly in order for you to survive. The mansion is huge, and you will spend most of your time simply exploring and opening up more and more sections. Combat is not the main focus here, not even close. Enemies are frequent, they take lots of damage and they can kill you quickly. There are a lot of moments where you will need to run past enemies instead of fighting to save your resources. There are puzzles sprinkled throughout the mansion that you must solve to get key items in order to progress. All main items take up space in your inventory, and the space you have is incredibly limited. A huge factor which will determine your enjoyment, is backtracking. There will be an innumerable amount of time where you will be forced to trek back through places you have already been. Sometimes this will be to go a newly unlocked area and other times it will be to grab some items you may have missed. The puzzles are not too difficult for the most part, however progression is sometimes obtuse. In your first playthrough, it is quite likely you will get lose at some point. The final thing to note is the pickable characters and difficulties. At the start, you will be asked to pick your difficulty and character. Out of the difficulties on offer, normal is by far the best. Very easy removes all challenge from the game and is extremely boring, and easy gives you so much ammo it makes combat a joke. If you can, play the game on normal, it can be difficulty on occasion, but its without a doubt the way the game is meant to be played. As for characters, you should always pick Jill for your first playthrough. Chris may be tougher and better in combat, but his smaller inventory means way more backtracking overall. If you beat the game as Jill and enjoy it, then give Chris a try.

Beating the game as Jill took me around 8 hours. I then beat the game again as Chris in about 6 hours. There is definitely some solid replay value here, especially when going for fast times. All in all, its still a great game after all this time, but its not perfect. Those tank controls haven't aged well, and the backtracking could definitely get on your nerves after a while. Even still, this is a classic game that still plays well today.

If you've played the game before, but haven't been able to get into it, I encourage you to give it another try.

I enjoyed revisiting this game after all these years. I played the original on PS1, and then this remake on Gamecube when it first came out, along with RE0. I enjoyed slowly unlocking the mansion and solving daft puzzles again. Combat and inventory management are solid and compelling. It's a little clunky by today's standards, though there is a smoother and more modern control method selectable for those who don't want to use the original tank controls. It's not a straightforward action game, so avoid if you don't like puzzles and backtracking. If you've enjoyed the sort of puzzles you might find in a point-and-click adventure, you'll be right at home. I'm not great at action games, so I lower the difficultly to make combat easier. I only died once (darn boulder!). On easy I was able then to focus on exploration and puzzle solving, which was a great time. If you like the recent Resi 2 remake - especially the first half in the police station - you'll enjoy this too. Especially on sale it's an easy recommend.

The only downside is the tatty pre-rendered graphics. As someone who uses Photoshop for a living, I can tell that they have simply been enlarged from the GC version and then the smart blur - or similar - filter has been applied to mitigate the distortion. At worst, some backgrounds can look like low quality jpegs. It's such a shame that Capcom didn't create the assets at a higher resolution in the first place, future-proofing them. Was it so wacky to make game art at 1080p or higher in 2002? Instead of redrawing the backgrounds for modern systems, they have simply blown them up, and it shows. There are places where in-world text is illegible (nothing puzzle critical, so don't worry). Could they not have retyped it with a fresh font? It takes seconds. But the background art is still atmospheric and 'good enough'. I had no problem buying into them as real places and most of the time I wasn't aware of them as low quality flat images. The 3D models on top are wonderful and full of detail. They have aged very well and even compare favourably with more recent remakes. I really feel, though, that if Capcom were to release this game again they would need to recreate those backgrounds. If they do, for goodness sake draw them at 4k, not 1080p! That way, you can release this game for the next 20 and not have it look like a finger painting in 10.

For example you might enter a room and the camera will be pointing directly in the face of the player's character, then you take a step and the camera is looking down on the top of the player's head, and then you take another step and the camera is now looking at the player from below and to the side.

This makes traversing the game a chore since what was moving forward turns into another direction every time the camera changes. The game also uses this to throw you into the arms of enemies that are waiting just around the corner which you can't see due to the static nature of the camera.

For the combat it's not so bad since you basically just have to broadly be aiming at the enemy.
For puzzle solving it can be very annoying since there are a lot of pushing objects around puzzles and often the camera will change to a completely different static view whilst pushing or even worse, just as you reach the object you want to push meaning you run off into a different direction instead of pushing said object.

The audio is fine.
The music is creepy, the guns go bang and monsters make non-sexual moaning sounds.

So would I recommend it?

I had finished remakes of RE2 and RE3 before I started playing this remaster. Therefore, I'll be comparing it to remakes. Maybe this can be helpful to those of you, who have already played remakes and now are thinking about giving the original game a try.

Firstly, I'm surprised how long it is. According to the game stats, it took me about 12 hours to finish it vs 8 hours in RE2. Steam counter says 18 hours! This six hours difference is caused by the fact that to save the game, here you need an ink ribbon (literally, to use a typewriter). Ink ribbon is a limited resource that you find lying around just like everything else. If you'll use all ink ribbons, you won't be able to save the game!

As a result, you don't save as often as you'd like. When you die, you lose some progress. For me, it was about 20-30 minutes on average. Though it's faster to catch up, because you already know where to go and what to do.

Secondly, even though it's similar to RE2 (a mansion, a bunch of puzzles), RE1 is subjectively bigger and the mansion is more complex and entangled. You need to collect more items, there are more puzzles, keys, etc. Given that the inventory is small, you have to make a lot of runs from points of interest to storage boxes and vice versa. This takes a lot of time.

Thirdly, this game feels less dangerous, it's almost relaxing sometimes. I guess it's probably different on hardest difficulty levels, I played on the second difficulty level. But I spent more time running alone and solving puzzles rather than actually fighting and trying to survive. RE2 felt harder than that even on the easiest difficulty! Maybe I'm simply more experienced with these games now.

Fourthly, it's outdated. I understand this is a remaster, not a remake, but sometimes it's painful to play in 2021: character's reaction to your inputs can be unpredictable (you want to run one direction, they run another), fixed camera angles don't show much. The situation is not terrible, but be ready for this. Visually it's acceptable. Plot and some behavior of characters are very questionable too, but you're not here for the plot, right?

To sum up, I can't say I enjoyed RE1 as much as RE2 or RE3. Regardless, it kept me engaged! I could play for 2-3 hours straight, which is a big achievement in my eyes for a single-player game.

Reports of cannibal attacks on the population are coming from around Raccoon City. The Bravo police team head to the forests of the Arklay Mountains to investigate the matter, but disappear without a trace. A second expedition follows, which reveals an abandoned helicopter in the middle of the woods. Just a moment later, the S.T.A.R.S. attacked by a pack of undead dogs and he has to make a nearby mansion a temporary refuge. But that's where the real problems begin…

At the very beginning, you can choose which character you want to play for. Jill Valentine is more suitable for newcomers because she can carry more items and has a jewel box available from the beginning. Chris Redfield (who breaks the rocks with his bare fist in later works), on the other hand, has a lighter in his pocket, which then does not take up valuable space in a very limited inventory.
The choice of character not only affects the progress of the game, but also determines who you will meet.
