I have played through Resident Evil many times and each time I am always reminded about why I love this game so much. The game is just the perfect amount of creepy and funny. First, lets start with why this game is creepy. The game takes place in this lone isolated mansion in the middle of the woods and the mansion has some very evil residents (get it, Resident Evil?). Obviously, the zombies are bad, so try to avoid them. But seriously, even a single zombie can be a little scary, especially since the game is pretty picky about giving you ammo. So you can't just go around shooting every zombie in the face. You have to conserve your ammo for when you desperately need it, so you'll often have to dance around zombies to save some bullets. And the music in this game is pretty good, I wouldn't say it's master piece mode, but it does a good job helping the game feel a little more creepy. Now, lets get on to the funny parts of Resident Evil. The voice acting in this game teeters on the "so bad it's good" line. If you're playing the game for the first time, I 100% recommend picking Jill as your character. Not only are there many advantages she has over Chris which greatly improve the overall experience (like more inventory space), Jill's story has the best character in all of video games in it, Barry fricken' Burton. He has so many iconic lines, and every time he talks with Jill it's like watching two aliens try to mimic humans, it's amazing. One negative I have for this game is that the puzzles can be a bit confusing at times, at least for my tiny monkey brain. And I'm not proud of this, but I did have to look up a walk through to help me a couple times. I know, I know, you can revoke my gamer licence if you want, but I'm just letting you know that if you have an impatient tiny monkey brain like me, you might get a little frustrated with some of the puzzles. A lot of people talk about the infamous "door cut scene" were when you open a door you have to watch a cut scene of the door opening. Of course, when this game first came out this was a way of sneakily hiding a loading screen, but now these door cut scenes really aren't necessary, and it would have been nice if there was an option to turn them off. If you have lower end PC, beware, because this game might not run well on it. I'm not very knowledgeable on this technical stuff so I'm probably not the best person to explain this, but basically Capcom locked the pre-rendered backgrounds at 1440p, so some lower end PCs might have trouble running the game, even though this game came out in 2002. Capcom really should have given people the ability to change this. Instead you're going to have to  download a mod which allows you to change the resolution so it can actually run decent. This shouldn't really be a problem, but I guess it is. Resident Evil overall is a great game and a very influential game on the survival horror genre. While the dialogue may be a bit cheesy, I honestly like that about this game and think that it's really funny. I definitely encourage everyone to give this game a try, just make sure your computer meets the required specs, or maybe get it on a different platform.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

This "game" is the antithesis of fun.

Starting off with what I like, I absolutely adore the atmosphere and design of the mansion, it's one of the reasons why I so deeply wish that this game was more accessible, exploring an enormous mansion in a thunderstorm while steadily unlocking more areas as you progress is phenomenally designed. The story is still relatively grounded in seriousness while maintaining the classic Resident Evil charm that makes these games so enjoyable to experience. Despite Chris and Jill's goofy and over-the-top line deliveries being removed, the game still maintains a sense of humour, albeit more subtle than the original.

Okay now onto the bad stuff. I won't drone on about tank controls and fixed cameras and door animations since you've heard it all before. Don't get me wrong, they're really bad, but what I hate is the fundamental design principles that set this game and the rest of the original trilogy (not including remakes) apart from the others in the series. This is not a survival horror game. This is a puzzle game designed with the sole purpose of pissing you off and wasting your time. You will spend at least five times the amount of time backtracking as you will actually making progress since you only get eight inventory slots (six if you're playing as Chris, do not play as Chris) and you cannot get more. Key items take up inventory slots and you will never know what items you'll need at any given time, meaning you'll be sprinting from item box to item box (watching door animations countless times) as you attempt to solve obtuse puzzles with absolutely no direction from the developers. Unless you have a guide or have already beaten the game before, you will NEVER know where to go next, and despite the fact that you never have any ammo to shoot the zombies, I honestly wish there were more enemies to make up for how mind-numbingly and downright depressingly BORING these runbacks are to the item boxes. Trying to progress in this game is nothing short of miserable, even following a guide is hard.

Resident Evil is a game with so much potential to be a horror masterpiece that is completely squandered by the most atrociously outdated design philosophies I have ever witnessed in my life, and I truly want to love this game but I just can't. If this remake gets remade, they'd have to do a lot more than fix camera angles and movement controls to make experiencing it anything other than a complete misery. I'll give it a 0/6, reminiscent of how many inventory slots I have free at any given time.

EDITED REVIEW:

Have you ever been wrong about something?

I've been wrong about something before. Turns out you should actually finish games before reviewing them. The fact that I hated this game initially can mostly be boiled down to the fact that I played as Chris, who is better at combat but far worse with exploration, generally better saved for a second playthrough. Replaying the game as Jill with the knowledge of where to go and what to do was far more gratifying than I thought possible. Once I beat the game, I found myself beating it again the very next day as Chris, and I was having fun.

The first playthrough was extremely rough, but it gets better for those persistent enough. I'm glad I gave the game a chance again, and I honestly understand the appeal of survival horror at this point.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a remaster, of a remake, of the first Resident Evil game released in 1996. Gameplay is considerably different from the newer RE games, most considerably because the game is played from fixed camera angles, not in third-person like most REs or first-person like the newer REs. The other big difference is that there are no autosaves, and saving is limited. You have to collect items called ink ribbons, and you can only save via a typewriter in certain rooms. Don't worry, there are quite many of those, and you'll probably end up with more than enough, unless you save very very often.

In this game you play as either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Both characters have advantages and disadvantages, like Jill has more inventory slots and weapons, but Chris has more health and stronger defense items. During some parts you may run into and work with the secondary characters, Barry Burton (Jill) and Rebecca Chambers (Chris). And of course, both will meet Captain Albert Wesker, as they try to find a way out of the scary Spencer Mansion. Sadly, other than the cutscenes, most of the story and gameplay are the same for both characters. There are no special locations that can only be visited by one of them. I still recommend playing at least once with each character to get the full story, though.

RE1 focuses more on inventory management, puzzle-solving, and survival rather than combat. To progress, you will have to find certain items to use, while still stocking your (very limited) inventory with weapons. You can use item boxes to store items, and it carries over to all item boxes. Combat is very simple and automatic, you just have to press the aim button when an enemy's around, and shoot. Kinda like the older Tomb Raider games. Combat is not a strong point in older TR and RE games, it focuses more on puzzles.

My problem with this game is a controversial one, the save system. Call me a "not real RE fan" or whatever, but in my opinion this game should at least have autosaves, even if it reduces the tenseness a bit. I have no problem with ink ribbons (even if it takes up 1 inventory space) being the only way to make a manual save, but it can get bad, like maybe you had a power outage, game crash, or accidentally activated a death trap. Your progress will be lost, even if you are well-equipped. Luckily, this game never crashed for me.

THE survival horror game, remade!

The classic Resident Evil when released back in 1996 made a real impact on release, everyone knew it was a game about zombies and had seen it either in a demo, in a magazine or perhaps watched a someone play it and got drawn into it in some way or another, but what made it have such an impact? I mean, Alone in the Dark was technically the first of this type of game that became a commercial hit, just what made Resident Evil stand out?

Well, the genre "survival horror" wasn't a thing back then, anything after Resident Evil was considered a Resident Evil clone because the genre contained the tropes that Resident Evil became famous for - static camera angle (or focus on the room you are in), hunting for items that enable you to progress through the game, a control system that handles like a tank (adding to the fear, like in a bad dream when you try to run but its like you are running on sand). All of these things, bad voice acting included, made the game very iconic.

The game is survival horror because of the staple gameplay mechanic that is a puzzle within itself, the whole game is like a puzzle you have to manage and solve and the jump scares come at just the right times to make you think again, like when the dogs smash through the windows in the original game - nothing truly shocking happens until this point and you know that this corridor is the only way forward and so the game knows then to throw the dogs at you (and ramp up the tense soundtrack) so this moment is very memorable because of this.

With the remake, originally released on the gamecube, they have carefully looked at what made the original game work and fine-tune it to perfection. For example, when you have already played the original (which a lot of us have back in the day), when this remake came out it was playing to new gamers but also fans of the series so when you get to the corridor with the dogs - you know that they are going to jump through the windows.. but in the remake they just hit the glass, not break through, so instantly fans of this game were thrown a curve ball, did they just take the dog corridor scene out?
No - this is what the remake does best, it carefully remixes these scenes up, especially in the first half - so just when you get the right items, and have to travel back through the corridor again THIS is when the dogs break through, genius.

Everything about this game preserves the original, the old story texts and the classic item management gameplay and extends the experience further with the death masks and the lisa trevor portion of the game.
The music is familiar, the puzzles are extended, it is the perfect survival horror game.

The trouble with it though is that its the type of game that seems a bit old fashioned by todays standards, Resident Evil 4 and 5 (and 2 remake) always seem to be the most popular so people know about Resident Evil because of those games so when they play this one it feels hard to get into, the deliberate slow pace and item management can be a real drag for those that want to explore a mansion and kill zombies.

The beauty of the game can be appreciated though if you forget all other resident evil games (even resident evil 0) and just know that this is where it is at, and what fans of the series really ask for, it is that deliberate slow pace, limited controls, really exploring the environment and the items you pick up - all of this really help draw you in to the world it is set in and this is why this game is the best survival horror there is.

SIlent Hill is great and all (big fan here) but with its many locked doors and abstract puzzles - it is more of a psychological horror treading in resident evils shoes rather than just being its own thing.
Resident Evil (after code veronica) began changing direction, becoming more action packed and started to ditch the puzzles making them easy and making the controls more involved with combat rather than conserving ammo. Resident Evil 4, in my opinion, has got this nailed as it has that purposefully awkward over the shoulder camera that really brings you in to the scene and hides enemies from your sight until they lunge at you at the last second, but after that - they lose the original game completely, a subtle mention of Umbrella and hardly any puzzles at all.

This game will bring it all back for you and make you read all of those notes left by the people who had died because of umbrella, and the many cool secrets that the mansion has to offer.

You just have to stick some headphones on and figure this game out because when you do, it will reward you with classic Resident Evil style that will stick with you through the whole series and all of the others games that have tried to emulate it.

The definitive version of a classic with tastefully enhanced lighting and improved positional audio... just be sure you take the time to install a bunch of mods first.

At absolute minimum, everyone will want Fluffy Manager 5000 to install and manage their mods, masterotaku's real time graphics mod, and either Mr. Bunny's BGM Fix (UPDATED) or zeikar's Normalized Music Mod.

Additionally, CRT users able to run the game at 512x448 (the real resolution of the backgrounds underneath Capcom's low effort upscale) will want  to use atom0s' REHDHook (to force the game to run at true 1920x1440 without pillarboxing) and Durante's GeDoSaTo (to force the game to run at 1920x1440 downsampled to 512x448.) Based on my comparisons, the aforementioned upscaling doesn't appear to have caused any noticeable quality loss compared to the GameCube originals when running at 512x448

LCD/Plasma/OLED users will instead want to use Shiryu's REupscale Project. In my opinion, the results aren't as stunning as downsampled 512x448 on a CRT (i'm not a fan of AI upscaling in general honestly), but it's *infinitely* preferable to Capcom's own ugly upscale when running at higher resolutions.

Other noteworthy mods include:

reaccount's UI Improvements (I consider this one to be essential, but i suspect that the HD font is more readable for some, so ymmv.)

Bloodyhunter's Retcon Pack (I don't love all of the changes personally, and i made some rather extensive edits and alterations for my personal installation, but the Jill default costume recolor is *fantastic*, and the retextured gloves are also pretty great.)

EvilLord's STARS Vests for Jill and Rebecca (For those of us who always thought it was a smidge silly that Jill had a completely different, utterly inexplicable uniform because boobs.)

LeigiBoy's Classic Costumes series (Lovely interpretations of every alternate costume from the PS1, Saturn, and PC versions of the original game.)

Alkimical's REalistic Weapon Names (As you may or may not know, up until this remake, the series used actual real life weapon names. This mod brings back some of that 90s "lol, who cares about copyrights and trademarks?" energy.)

EVERGREEN's Resident Evil to Biohazard conversion (I maintain that Biohazard is a much better, more descriptive name for the franchise.)

The fixed cameras bring a lot of tension and foreboding to the environments whilst the controls are tight and responsive. Limited inventory forces you to get tactical with how you engage with resources whilst the new Crimson Head mechanic makes every Zombie killed a potential problem later on, forcing you to really consider when to fight and when to flee. There's all manner of endings, unlockables, and extra modes for the completionist out there to extend playtime too!

This is the quintessential video game remake—a gold standard in all aspects of game design. There may never be another Resident Evil game like it again; whilst this may be an unfortunate casualty of the modern video game landscape, what we have here is a testament to what heights the genre is capable of reaching.

As someone who only got into the Resident Evil series (and survival horror in general) with the RE2 Remake, I had no nostalgia for the series at all. 

That said, this game is an absolute masterpiece of the genre. The atmosphere of the Spencer Mansion is superb - the prerendered backgrounds are beautiful even so many years later, and the dread / terror of the place seeps out of every camera angle. The fixed camera angles can be a bit to get used to, especially if using the non-tank controls, as your momentum can change rapidly and have your character spinning in circles. It will probably lead to some frustration in your first playthrough, but it absolutely will not detract from the tension of the game. 

The game is also highly replayable. With the True Survivor mode (item boxes aren't linked together), Invisible Enemies, and a whole slew of unlockables, I came back to this game at least 8 times, and thoroughly enjoyed it every time. 

As a survivor horror game, REmake is unparalleled in the genre, and I highly recommend it to anyone who has the slightest passing interest in the genre.

[h1] Must-play Classic, even for 4Heads [/h1] 

Up until now I'd only ever played Resident Evil 4 and the games that came after. I always kind of assumed that the slower, clunkier pre-4 RE games, with their standard-issue zombies, giant snakes and spiders and spooky halloween mansions, were kind of pointless in a world where Silent Hill also exists. How wrong I was...

Resident Evil the 1st is an enduringly relevant, incredibly atmospheric and mechanically nerve-wracking horror classic. The way you slowly unlock, clean out and master the creepy Spencer estate, going from scared and underequipped rookie to skilled and loaded survival beast is unrivalled (outside of maybe 2D Metroidvanias, immersive sims and Dark Souls).
Everything you do has some kind of consequence or resource cost, even saving and opening doors, which makes every step forward extremely tense. This uncertainty and anxiety caused by constant decision-making is what makes the otherwise hokey and kind of lame story, setting and enemies genuinely scary. This is one of the few pieces of media to make the common zombie genuinely frightening.

The only weakness is perhaps the logarithmic difficulty curve. I started the game on the highest (i.e. "Normal") difficulty setting, got eaten a couple of times while wandering the manor not knowing where to go or what items to pick up, got frustrated and restarted on the medium difficulty. This was perfect at first, but by the end of the game I was so loaded on ammo and healing items that nothing posed any kind of threat. The game starts out a bit too hard for newcomers and ends up too easy by the end...

Visually, the game is still stunning. The prerendered backgrounds and creepy camera angles create a rich, gooey gothic vibe. Every room has a unique personality. 
The locations of this game are so memorable that after just one playthrough you could probably draw a map of the manor from memory.

If you have any interest in horror games and want to experience a stone-cold tense, mechanically-driven, survival horror classic, treat yourself to this one. It rules OK

[h2]Survival horror... perfected[/h2]
📌 Many people compare this game (hereinafter referred to as REmake) to its slightly younger sister, Resident Evil 0 – both were released in the same year (2002) and for the same console (Nintendo GameCube), so the comparisons make a lot of sense; it is also much easier to understand and appreciate the merits of REmake when it's juxtaposed with its misunderstanding of a sibling, [i]okay[/i] by itself, but laughable and inferior in every single way whenever the two are brought up together in conversation. 

So... Let's keep comparing.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2596034224 
[h3]The horror aspect[/h3]
😨 I'm going to go right ahead and admit that this game has made me scream out loud on multiple occasions. The overwhelming atmosphere of helplessness and utter vulnerability created by an extreme scarcity of resources (if played on Normal or Hard) multiplies the dread tenfold and makes what would be simply traversing a zombie-infested and puzzle-riddled mansion into a survival horror experience like no other. After all these years (nineteen years, to be precise), it is still widely regarded as one of the scariest – if not [u]the[/u] scariest – iterations of the franchise, and deservedly so.

[spoiler]I didn't want you to know anything about Crimson Heads before you actually started playing, but since you seem to enjoy spoilers, here's one – killed zombies come back to... "life", now more vicious and threatening than ever. Keep a pair of clean underwear nearby – you'll need it.[/spoiler] 
 
🙄 Resident Evil 0, on the other hand, excels as much in [i]annoying[/i] the players as REmake excels in scaring the bejesus out of them. 

[h3]The story[/h3]
😟 It would [i]not[/i] be an exaggeration on my part if I said that REmake has one of the best stories across the entire series – and I am not speaking about the main plot, which is as self-absorbedly puerile as usual – but about the subplot, featuring poor Lisa Trevor and her mother. Suffice it to say that nothing else in this game has made me feel so horrified, appalled and... sorry – all at the same time. The wild rollercoaster of emotions this [i]subplot[/i] (!) takes you on has surpassed any other major story development in the franchise by a wide margin, and it's worth getting the game just to experience this alone. 

🙄 Resident Evil 0 features an anime villain who sings opera to control leeches, laughs like an evil genius and – as per tradition – wants to burn the world to exact his [b]RRREVENGE![/b]

[h3]Music and gameplay[/h3]
😌 None of REmake's background music made me want to cut my ears off with a bread knife and fill the wounds with super glue so I may never hear a sound again. This game also values your time; no matter what you do, unless you walk around in circles like a terrified toddler who lost his mum in a supermarket, you'll be making progress.

🙄 Resident Evil 0 is not ashamed of pushing the same content down your throat via obnoxious amounts of backtracking to perform the most boring, menial tasks imaginable.

[h3]Actually using your brain[/h3]
🤓 REmake will have you looking at the map and planning the route 30 minutes in advance because the mansion is very much alive here; you wouldn't want to go through some corridors twice – a couple of them are deceivingly empty, only to become nothing short of [i]murder halls[/i] once you've finally let your guard down. Moreover, killing zombies will not be your first instinct anymore – if you hovered over the spoiler tag at the beginning of this review, which you shouldn't have done, you already know why. Lots of careful consideration and thought go into planning what enemies to dispose of and whom to ignore and evade for the rest of the game.

🙄 Resident Evil 0 engages as many brain cells as taking a catnap on a somnolent Sunday afternoon, and what cells it doesn't engage it kills altogether 💤

[h3]Okay, wait a second... RE0 is actually better at something[/h3]
😳 This something is the graphics. Especially after the facelift of the remasters that both games got, Resident Evil 0 just looks a lot prettier. The visual splendour is everywhere – on the train, in the mansion, even in the dark underground passages, while REmake sports somewhat dated textures that stick out like a sore thumb and spoil some of the most important cutscenes. Unfortunately, it means that RE0 is eye candy and nothing more – all fur coat and no knickers, tricking you into liking it just because it pleases you with its aesthetics. Once you scrape off the gold veneer though, you'll be left with a 60-year-old homeless drunk who's got a grand total of 3 teeth, smells like death itself and wants to kiss you. Run.

This one is interesting. First off, I'm a really big fan of the Resident Evil series (videogames, not the movies), so I do have a little bit of bias going into it, full transparency. That being said, it's drastically different from most of the other titles in the series I've played so far. While writing this, I haven't had a chance to play the original Resident Evils from the early PlayStation days (like the original RE2 and 3), Code Veronica, or even the newest one, Resident Evil 8. I have however played all of the other ones in the series, even the iffy ones like Operation Raccoon City, the Wii motion zapper Darkside and Umbrella Chronicles, and even Umbrella Corps. The reason I say that RE1 is so different from the rest is that the others are, more or less, combat heavy with doses of puzzles. This is the flip side of that really. Anyway, let's get into the review itself.

I want to start with the negatives. The inventory management system in this game is kinda irksome. I get that the idea of your character being unburdened by hauling around what would realistically be an incredible amount of weight in equipment and weaponry (a la RE4, RE5, etc.) would be unrealistic, but wow, I mean you can carry sometimes an embarrassing little amount of stuff in this game. Chris Redfield, one of the two playable protagonists, has only six inventory slots. And EVERYTHING in this game counts as an item to take up one of those slots. A dog whistle takes up a sixth of your inventory, as can a lighter, a piece of sheet music, a single herb, and your weapon and ammo count as two separate items. In short, there is a tremendous amount of backtracking in this game as you go from room to room trying to figure out what you need to progress. You figure out you aren't carrying the right things, you run all the way back to an inventory chest, grab the right stuff, lug it all the way back to proceed. It gets old after a while.

The character dialogue is cheesy and goofy and you can tell it's got that old time horror game feel to it, but I hesitate to even put it as a negative because honestly, it entertains me. My only other complaint is more minor, but the fact that there is a door opening loading screen every time you want to go into a new room also gets tiring. 

I know it seems like this should be a negative review so far, but hear me out, because here come the positives. True to form with most Resident Evils, this game has parts that scare the living ♥♥♥♥ out of me. It isn't done so much from the actual horror of the enemies you fight (though there are more than it's fair share of those kind too, especially for a guy with arachnophobia let me tell you), but it's done from the excellent atmosphere of tension and dread that Capcom was able to build. Everything from the music that plays as you creep down a dimly lit hallway hoping not to be attacked, to the design and layout of the mansion that makes it visibly clear it has a disturbing and violent past, to even the camera, which to me, adds to the fear of the combat.

On top of that, the graphics in this game are out of bounds. I mean, if you compare this game to most other shooter games or really any kind coming out of this era, I sincerely bet that this one is at least better than it. It looks damn amazing, from lighting, to the details of each room, everything. To sum it up I suppose, despite some gameplay that gets repetitive, it's a hell of a fun game with plenty of scares in between, and a classic of the horror videogame genre.

[u]Gist:[/u]
The not so elite Bravo team of professional task force S.T.A.R.S. lost comms somewhere in the vicinities of the Arklay Mountain. It is up to Alpha members, most notably Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield to put them in their place! Unfortunately, once there; the cavalry gets picked clean just as fast by some doggies and now they must reconsider their careers. Before that can materialize, their chickenshi* pilot leaves them for dead and so they have to apply themselves to survive the night~ 


[h1]NARRATIVE[/h1] 
Let’s get this out of the way, the story has ‘amateur’ splayed all around or a throbbing bite mark. And it never makes you forget it! Which used to be much “worse” or unrecognized genius in the 1996 OG. So, got to give it credit, for that much. 

It has its sob moments for some of the victims, but then Alpha team decimates it, presumably with Barry’s .44 magnum with lines so dry the zombies can understand them! Everything is spun around to be as obvious as possible that there is no fun or anticipation in the story… Though I doubt people play RE games for the lore~

[b]6.5 / 10[/b]


[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
Despite having experienced both the OG and console version of the remaster, I still gasped in terror and awe! Why? Because my memory’s about to go- also, I discovered encounters, hidden items I simply didn’t before… Granted, the aiming and inventory management mechanics could use some updates but that would defeat the purpose- legacy of this survival horror classic which still puts up a fight surprisingly competent today! 

And man did it; even on Easy was I already running on fumes and developed a tolerance to “medicinal” herbs!! I don’t recall it being this challenging, at all or maybe the later RE titles softened me. It establishes its difficulty unlike any other, from the moment you are prompted on exercise preferences and then predicated on which character you play as! Of course, depending on your arrogance/ignorance, you could turn the tables on yourself before the zombies do you in… 

It’s not unfounded to say the puzzle design is on a level all its own! Simple but methodical, short yet variable though it’s just as easy to be bamboozled if you’re not a careful reader or investigator. I would go so far to say exploration is a puzzle too; which routes to take, object to carry and enemies to bypass.

There is just a ton to do, with multiple playthroughs to get the 12 endings! Either character’s campaigns differ enough to be replaying worthwhile what with their respective strengths, perks each partner can offer or even initial routes. I’d estimate 30+ hours or more, for both newcomers, returning players and completionists~

[b]TIPS:[/b]
1. Some enemies/deaths can be avoided entirely. Just don’t startle them or make mistakes in puzzles.
2. Jill’s campaign may be “easier” a.k.a damsel-in-distress” but Chris is tougher with enhanced attributes. 
3. Reload weapon by combining in inventory
4. Mash WASD or whittle L3 to break free of grab and shove enemies!

[b]8.5 / 10[/b]


[h1]VISUALS[/h1]
The mansion is iconic, it's a museum with exhibits that pop out... Need I say more? Fine, much like the zombies reanimating, the setting is equally thriving! I’m talking moth-to-flame heat rays, smoke in your eyes and out of the barrel effects, enigmatic shadows and splash-worthy water particles. Really, goes without saying- a vast improvement from the Gamecube version and not merely having undergone up-res processes. Even if it did, nothing wrong with that! HD remasters can go awry too, just check out the [b]Silent Hill HD Collection[/b], or rather DON’T! 

Yeah, textures still appear mucky and the FMV garbled hot garbage on widescreen but you could always opt for the “4:3” which helps sort of. Not that I was hung up on them for they further give REHD that antiquated look. The character models are yummy and suave, it’s refreshing to see what they “actually” look like. Our eyes are so trained for crisp, polished looks that it’s overall a nice touch-up to ease that itch AND we get to play with old-school tank controls. What more do you want~

[b] 8.5 / 10[/b]

[h1]TONE:[/h1]
Notwithstanding some of the up-tempo soundtrack butchering the more exquisitely-paced OG orchestral arrangements. It remains a delight to hear- luckily the save room music was left alone and I go there to do my philosophy. But the unsung praises go to the background noises of howls, buzzes and wind whooshes to remind you of life outside, that for all you know has not been infected. 

Then the groans, thuds to situate you back here in ground zero along with other ear-gasmic sound effects. The irregular clapping of thunder, doors creaking open or the sound of your teammate meeting their end when you save yourself… 

[b]9 / 10[/b]


[h1]CHARACTERS[/h1]
Not their greatest suit but I’ll be damned if they aren’t funny! I’m serious, every line of dialogue regardless of situation at hand, had me cracking up and downright hysterical as if I were a crimson head! I’d bet it’s the writing but the delivery is probably the nail in the coffin!! Whether it was intentional is up for debate but it does go smooth with the b-movie filter the game has.

Resident Evil Remake is one of the few games in the franchise that can make me scream like a baby. Despite being a Resident Evil fan, I did not have the heart to pick this up because I thought the fixed camera would put me off (I only played the newer installments before this). Then my friend gifted the game to me and I thought, it is finally time to try this out. And after  25 hours playing both campaigns, I absolutely adored it from beginning to end.

[u][b]Things that Resident Evil did well[/b][/u]

• [b]The atmosphere in this game is simply perfect.[/b] I love the night setting, the dark hallways, the occassional thunders, even the jumpscares. Everything is just flawlessly put together.
• [b]Fixed camera angles and the tank controls are back from the classics.[/b] The angles would cause me so much anxiety, with enemies could appear in the corners without me knowing. This, combine with the tank controls, makes it harder to fight against zombies and other enemies. And if you don't like the tank controls, the game will let you pick the alternative controls that is closer to the modern controls (which is what I did).
• [b]Inventory management is amazing as usual.[/b] Given that this is a classic Resident Evil game, it is to be expected. In this game, you cannot discard or drop any item, you either have to use it up or put it in the item box. This makes managing your stuffs more tedious and requires a lot of backtracking for a casual player.
• [b]Death actually means death in Resident Evil.[/b] If you die, all your progress is lost and you must load the previous saves, if not you have to start the game all over again. I'll admit, this used to frustrate me because sometimes I forgot to save then got reset so further back when I died. But then, it grew on me, like it's a way of the game telling me to be careful and be more cautious of the environment.
• [b]Awesome characters.[/b] I especially love [spoiler]Barry[/spoiler] in this game, he's sweet and caring just like a father. Jill is a bit wimpy at first, being overwhelmed by the situation she is in, but as the story progresses you can see her grow into a braver person. Chris and Rebecca, well, they're the same as ever, though Rebecca does have a few character development. There is a standout enemy that you only know the backstory of if you read through the files, but I'm not gonna name her (spoilers!)
• [b]Puzzles can give you a really hard time.[/b] This can be a good thing or a bad thing, but for players who want difficult puzzles then this is for you. Personally, I had to get help from the Wiki occassionally because some puzzles can be super obscure. [spoiler](How the hell can you do the fireplace puzzle without help??!)[/spoiler] Despite that, it can offer a bit satisfaction once you figure it out on your own.
• [b]Enemies make you sweaty, even the regular zombies.[/b] Zombies in Resident Evil is unsurprisingly a bullet sponge, so you have to make quick decisions either to kill them or leave them. They can also come back stronger and faster if you do not burn them, so that is another thing to worry about. [spoiler]Cerberus[/spoiler] are annoying and can kill you if you aren't quick enough. [spoiler]Hunters[/spoiler] waste a lot of your ammunition and can insta kill you if you don't deal with them. There are lots of other freaky enemies such as the [spoiler]yawn, black tiger, chimeras, etc.[/spoiler] but I'm not gonna spoil them all. Go discover them yourself!
• [b]Level design in Resident Evil is intricate and full of mysteries.[/b] The Spencer mansion is so gigantic, you have to spend at least 5 hours in your first playthrough to discover every nook and cranny in there. Apart from the Spencer mansion we also have a lot of other locations such as the dormitory, laboratory, etc.
• [b]It has multiple routes and endings.[/b] There are two campaigns to select from (Jill and Chris), and each campaign has many routes and endings depends on the choices you make. Some route also earn you special weapons, which is cool in my book.
• [b]The soundtrack can give you goosebumps.[/b] I can't praise the soundtrack enough, because it contributes so much to the atmosphere of the game. The save room music always give me so much relief after a long run.

[u][b]Things that Resident Evil did not so well[/b][/u]

• [b]Some cutscenes are not remastered, resulting in blurry graphics.[/b] It's a little bit distracting to have a few cutscenes in SQ quality in the middle of other remastered ones. I don't mind much since they're short, but it's worth pointing out anyway.
• [b]The voice acting is hilariously bad.[/b] I kinda feel bad for putting it here, because the bad acting actually captures the charm of the characters and the game, so it is an accidental plus for me.
• [b]The difficulty is quite rough, even on normal.[/b] I played Chris on normal, and they gave very little ammunition. It can get quite stressful and annoying when you're almost out of everything.
• [b]Sorting the items is time consuming.[/b] If you want your item box to be neater, then it's gonna take a long time to sort everything out. If you want to switch an item's place with another, you got to move them to the inventory and back.

[b]In short, Resident Evil is a faithful remake, offering quite a survival horror experience that keeps you on your toes.[/b] It might not be a good entry for newcomers due to how difficult it is, but it is a fulfilling game once you get the grasp of it. If you have played Resident Evil 2 Remake or Resident Evil 7, I absolutely recommend you to play this game. It is challenging, terrifying, fun and satisfying - a must have for every Resident Evil enthusiast.

EDIT: Forget what I said... it was only a blast at the beginning, now that the difficulty has ramped up, the arbitrary limitations I mentioned at first, mainly the limited ink ribbons that you need in order to save my progress, are really preventing me from enjoying this game. Most fans defend this limitations on the fact they make the game harder, hence the survival horror aspect of it. True, but that's called artificial difficulty. 

Did you just picked an item that you don't need right away and now you have no room left for the item you do need to pick?? Too bad!! Either load your last save point, or go all the way back to the nearest storage box (which is probably pretty far away cause there is only a handful of them), drop the items you don need, and come back... oh and try not to die in the process cause there is probably a good deal of enemies on the way that you can't afford to kill cause you don't have enough bullets. This is some real BS!! And of course think 3 times before saving cause you don't want to run out of ink ribbons later on with the harder enemies, and there is no way for you tell when/if you will get anymore.

Case in point is, you can only really do "resources management" if you know what's coming, if you know exactly where to go next, what enemies to expect, which ones are worth killing and which ones are not, what areas to avoid, and most important, what items are worth picking now, and which ones you don't need just yet, because 99% of the times you encounter the item BEFORE you find the place where you need it, so you will have no idea what it is for and when/where will you need it.

So my 2 cents for newcomers is, play it on easy, at least the first time so that you can memorize the layout and figure out the puzzles (which is the real fun of this game) and leave all of the BS for your second run, when you actually know what the hell to do!

I'm gonna start my review by saying straight off the bat, If you absolutely are against tank controls, this game is not for you. This particular RE title mainly operates at its best when you're using its traditional tank controls, however, you can play this game using free movement controls if you desire to do it that way. Just know that doing so plays against the games shifting camera angles, and it can make for an awkward and cumbersome experience. This is mainly because the original release of this remake never had free movement controls, and were added in only for this modern release to appease a broader audience. Reality is, this game was made for tank controls and does play at its best that way, but there is a place for free movement if you don't mind adapting a hybrid play style. This game's controls are designated D-pad as tank, and left thumb stick as free movement. I had the best experience using the D-pad for exploration and the thumb stick for maneuvering enemies.

With that controller disclaimer out of he way, this game is an absolute classic, and in my own personal opinion, one of the best Resident Evil games ever made. Even the graphics hold up well, which is impressive given that this is a 19 year old game. From up close, the character models can show their age a bit, but in the motion of gameplay, the characters and environments actually look pretty great.

One thing that a lot of horror games tend to do is lean towards an identity. Am I going to be a hair raising spine chiller? Or a jumpy scare fest? The best horror experiences hit a balance of both, and that's what this game does. The music is foreboding at all times, the environments are very scary and memorable, and the jump scares don't feel cheap. Even your decisions regarding the way you'll handle enemies might have you second guessing yourself, as they tend to surprise you later on... I don't want to say anymore than that because I'd be spoiling the fun, but just know that the AI is a winner here.

Overall I do love this game, but one flaw that really came up much more than I liked was its puzzles. Quite a few of them are too simple and tedious. Some puzzles make me wonder why they're even there at all. By example, a puzzle in this game could ask of the player to push a series of large crates into water until he/she forms a bridge. It isn't fun to do, it's tedious, and it isn't challenging the player at all. Including these types of menial tasks into an otherwise superb experience just goes against fun, and drags the games pacing down. Is it all like that? No. Most of the games puzzles will involve the player figuring out what to do with certain items found in different rooms in order to advance the story, and that's done very well here. But every once in a while, they'll throw something so easy at you that it might as well not even be there. This isn't a major flaw by any means, but it is much more prominent during subsequent run-throughs of the game, and this game does have very high replay value.

Overall, this is actually one of the scary Resident Evil games that really put the franchise on the map. If you're used to Capcom's more action oriented renditions of Resident Evil games, know going into this one that it's radically different beast altogether. This game focuses on puzzle solving and tension. It's a cult classic for a reason, so if you're looking for a good starting point for the series, and the controls aren't an issue for you, this is it. The tension and scares are fantastic here, and what this game does right outweighs it's few flaws. An easy recommend for horror fans of any kind.

A preface: Despite the 3 hours of play time it shows on Steam, I did beat Jill's normal mode on the Gamecube version before I bought this and started Chris' campaign.

Anyways, the first thing that everyone NEEDS to know about this game before playing is that Resident Evil Remake is a VERY difficult game. If you've played the original RE1 or 2 (not 3, that game is also really hard), avoiding zombies and taking them out wasn't too hard when you got the hang of it. This game however feels MUCH harder to evade them and to top it off, you die QUICK. 3 zombie bites will kill you, and there are many rooms with 3-4 zombies at a time. For these reasons, I cannot recommend normal mode to a first time player (in case you didn't know normal is "climbing a mountain", easy is "hiking", and very easy is "walking". It's a dumb way of naming difficulty but whatever.)

I could talk about how fun the game is when you start to get into the "flow" for multiple paragraphs but honestly who cares. What I do need to address are the absolutely garbage criticisms of tank controls. Every single time I read a review of an old RE game, the very first thing I see is "the controls suck and I'm glad I don't have to use them in the modern games!" When I see these I seriously have to wonder if they played the game, and more importantly, how LONG they played the game. Sure, everyone who plays a classic RE game for the first time might struggle with the controls for a little bit. Key words: a little bit. I had a complete grasp of tank controls after like an hour and never struggled with them after that. They produce predictable results and are the only way that the game COULD work with pre-rendered backgrounds. I want you all to think for five seconds about how the game would work with normal controls... DONE! Now, hopefully you see the problem that the camera changes angles and therefore changes the reference of what your control stick direction means. If you hold right down a hallway with a camera at a side angle, you'll walk down it fine until the camera turns to be inside the hallway and holding right pushes you into the wall. After it changes, forward has become the new right, leading to an EXTREMELY frustrating control scheme where you DON'T get predictable results with your movement. Let's say you're trying to dodge a zombie but you have to go past a camera transition plane. That action of dodging becomes nearly impossible because you don't have that consistent reference that tank controls give. This review is now a review of idiotic commenters who don't think through their arguments before complaining. But regardless, this game is really great if you are up to the challenge. My playthrough took me 12 hours in game time, so probably about 16 hours in real time, making it a pretty long game, but I felt really satisfied when I finally finished it.

Yikes. I'm glad I was able to finally play through the game that started it all...and boy am I glad to be DONE with it. A horribly annoying inventory system, a tedious maze of environments you'll be backtracking through countless times, and a camera system that DOES make the game scarier - but more difficult to control, really shows the game's age and the inexperience of development. However, this title became a gem for good reason. It really defines the "survival horror" genre, where everything is spooky, most of it can kill you, and most of the time, you'd be better off running away than firing some lead into the problems in your path. OH and did I mention the SAVE system?? It's one thing to have "save points" where you can only checkpoint your progress in designated areas. It's another thing to not only have "save points" but you can ONLY save if you have a special item that LETS you save. Have to quit playing 'cause you've gotta get up early tomorrow? Mom's on her way home and your room is a mess? Too bad: you gotta run through 15 doorways (THAT HECKING SUCK WITH THEIR SLOW ANIMATIONS) and pray to Umbrella Corp that you have an Ink Ribbon in your inventory or item box. This is quite literally, "Inconvenience: The Game". Not meant for casuals. But that's okay. If I had played this when it came out originally, I would've just chewed on the controller at 1 year old, but I might've accepted the mechanics as revolutionary, instead of ridiculous. It's a game you should play as part of your gaming education. Experience what the people before you had to deal with, so you can appreciate the efforts of today's developers a bit more. Having tried this about a year back and quickly putting it away as it was very intimidating (limited saves, inventory slots etc), I am very glad I decided to give it another go. I've been going through the games in the series for the first time since a few months ago, started with 5>6>7>8, so am relatively new to the series.

I would put this game up there with 7/8 which are some of the best games I've ever played. Less said about 5/6 the better.

The most obvious thing to comment on in this game is the atmosphere. It really is haunting and probably on par with RE7 in that regard. Resources, saves, and inventory space are limited in this game, so you have to move with intent the whole time. You will be required to think carefully about what you need to have on you at any given time, in stark contrast to the expectation in modern games of having an endless inventory at your disposal that ends up meaning anything coming your way, you know you can deal with then and there. Not having that luxury really heightens the fear factor, as opening any new door could lead to your death if not prepared for correctly, which given the way the save system works could mean you are sent back a long way. So the stakes are high at all times. There are times when travelling light is necessary, so leaving behind weapons and heals and going into the unknown gives a feeling of untethered and fearful isolation like no other game I have played.

The gameplay is very satisfying, everything feels very intuitive. Things you expect to work, do, and the puzzles are just hard enough to be satisfying, but easy enough that they don't provide any big challenge, so the pace of the game moves along nicely. Even the finer details in the game (that you might miss entirely if you aren't paying close attention) seem very worked on, from cutscenes changing slightly depending on what side of a room you might be coming from so there is no jarring shift in continuity, to simple things that give the game an overall very polished feel.

The story is simple, but still engaging and interesting, and opts more for revealing events through the environment, found letters and memos etc which I really like as a storytelling method. You will want to explore every nook and cranny just to find out more about what this place is and what is really going on.

Overall, this is the game that made survival horror what it is today, but it doesn't feel as primitive as you might think when you really get into it. It might seem overwhelming at first, but it absolutely rewards patience. If I had played it back then I would probably have given it a 10/10. It's a strange mix now between showing its age, and timeless classic that holds its own against any modern game.

I'm a big fan of the RE franchise from a story perspective and the gameplay in later games. That said, this game is nearly intolerable, personally.

I started on the "hiking" (easy) difficulty as Jill, since that seemed reasonable.
- First zombie encounter can be killed by the player even though Barry will kill it in a cutscene shortly after. May cause players to waste precious ammo.
- Camera angle switches are jarring and lead to disorientation, walking in circles, or walking back towards enemies. Cameras are fixed, so that is also a tedious adjustment.
- Aiming may as well not exist. You just point the gun at a zombie and pray that it doesn't take the whole magazine to kill one. Headshots are extremely rare. 
- The combat knife may as well be a soggy noodle as it does minimal damage and is nigh impossible to use without taking ridiculous amounts of damage.
- Dead zombies don't stay dead. Unless you find the lighter, the fuel canteen, and one of those ever rare kerosene jugs, then burn every body 2 at a time, the dead zombies will turn into crimson heads. They are faster, hurt more, and, from what I can tell, sponge up even more ammo that a regular zombie. So have fun killing every zombie whose body you couldn't burn in time, twice.
- [spoiler] The zombie dog on the balcony [/spoiler] will kill you in one hit since you can't escape the tackle. Took 2 shotgun shells to the head to die.
- Most of the "puzzles" are elongated fetch quests that usually have you picking up items and then running back to a room, or running to a storage locker a lightyear away and the back again.
- Door animations seem quite unnecessary, and I say this as a Skyrim player.
- So many keys...
- There are rarely any hints as to where to go next and what to do next. You either figure it out over many hours, look up a guide, or don't.
- Ammo seems painfully scarce for how many shots it takes to down a zombie.
- The saving mechanic is a limited resource, and only allowed at very certain spots. This often leads to being set back about 20-30 minutes every time you die. Kills any joy the game had to start with.
- Limited inventory space: everything takes up inventory space. Your gun, the knife, the ink ribbons (save item), every single god forsaken puzzle piece you pick up, extra ammo, all of it. The only exception is defensive weapons which stack, from what I can tell. You only get 6 inventory slots with Chris, or 8 with Jill.

Overall, the game shows its age in its mechanics. It becomes mundane and frustrating to the point of downright agitating in a hurry.

I think that this game can be pretty complicated when looking for games to buy. Its the first in a long series of pretty expensive games, and its mechanics are outdated... to say the least. To me this game is absolutely worth the money. 
- First of all this series (at least what I've played and seen so far) is amazing. The story is spectacular and it really hooks you in. 
- As for the mechanics. I think that the hardest one to get around is the camera. A lot of people are put off from this game because the camera is fixed (It is in one spot of a room that you move around, rather than it following you or being first person). At first this makes movement strange, and it does take a while to get used to. I believe that the fixed camera can add a lot to the horror/suspense of the game. There are moments that you'll hear things close to you, but its not as easy as turning to see them; you have to get close. I think that adds a really interesting dynamic to the game that makes it feel a lot more scary. It's certainly something to get used to though. 
- Finally I'll just talk about the game play a bit. I feel like this game combines some fun aspects from a lot of different genres; mainly horror, puzzle, and shooter. The horror aspects of this game are what makes it so iconic. Every scare feels just different enough where it never gets old. After playing nearly 20 hours in this game I have still come dangerously close to needing to change pants. The puzzles in this game are really fun and rewarding, and they can span across different parts of the story and different areas. Sometimes you'll get pieces to a puzzle that you haven't even come across yet and you'll just have to wait and keep an eye out. I think of the three genres shooter is the weakest for this specific one. The fixed camera angle (though it lends really well to the horror aspect) does not lend itself to shooting. With a bit of practice and patience it will get much easier. (The shooting aspect does get better in the future games if you decide to stick with it). 
This game is probably one of my favorite solo games, and the series is shaping up to be very promising. I hope this review helps someone who's on the fence about the game :)

Getting the hill I will die on out of the way first: I hate the fixed camera angels. It's disorienting and makes me nauseous. Also, I hate how small the inventory is but I know that's also like a hallmark for RE so I can forgive. 

The Good: The atmosphere is top notch. I can definitely see why so many people feel in love with the game and how groundbreaking it was at the time. The Meh: While the sound design is good, the music is mediocre at best. The graphics look pretty good but I personally think that they're starting to show their age, especially the backgrounds. The voice acting is leagues better than the original PS1 but it's not top tier.

Resident Evil HD is a classic horror experience, as well as a shining example of what a remake should aim to do. A spooky atmosphere along with the players' weak tools to combat enemies, tight resource management and manual saves make for a terrifying combination that is sure to make the player permanently uneasy to enter the next room.

The age of the game is a slight detriment, as some aspects are clearly far from user friendly. Fixed camera angles make for movie-shot like views that do wonders for the atmosphere, however they greatly hinder the player in fighting the enemies, in many cases an enemy will be out of sight and by the time you see it, they have gotten too close to be taken out safely.

PS: I recommend everyone to play on the hardest difficulty and to pick Chris on their first playthrough, as Chris is a lot harder to play than Jill and the difficulty is the main reason why the horror works in this game.

In the March of 1996 I went to a local video game store and began to peruse the PSX titles that were on the shelf. i was pretty young then and I only had enough money for one game, so I asked the clerk behind the counter for a recommendation. He told me a new game called Resident Evil had just come out the weekend before and if I wanted solid gameplay and a good scare, I should check it out. So that was my introduction the Resident Evil Series.

Four days ago, a Steam Summer Sale kicked off and on a whim (maybe because I recently played through RE4), I decided to pick up the Resident Evil 1 Remaster. I haven't played this game in over 20 years and the nostalgic in me decided to revisit with improved graphics and gameplay.

The Good:

Literally everything in the game received a visual upgrade. The character models, the scenery, the cut scenes. Everything was far more appealing to look at, even it was dated by modern standards. In addition to better visuals, the controls were also greatly improved. They still proved to be infuriating at times, but if you've played the original version, you will appreciate the new handling. Seriously, turning Chris and Jill with the right stick in the original was sort of like waiting for your luggage to rotate on the conveyor at the airport. By then, the Zombie behind you probably already got a hit in. Despite the visual upgrades and the new control scheme, the core of the story and the puzzles were there. it still felt like the original game and allowed me to sip from the fountain of nostalgia for a while.

The Bad:

This game has a number of the same flaws as the original. Infuriating item management system, camera angles that leave considerable blind spots, and the changing camera angle is the worst. Nothing more frustrating (there is, I'm exaggerating a little) than holding the left stick up to make a character run forward, only to have the camera angle change so that forward is now down and up is now back, so your character spins right around and runs back the way you came. That scene with the closing walls and the statue was maddening.

The Ugly:

Zombie dogs. Introduced early and hide their hit boxes from the pistol. Like seriously. They ripped out my throat in ways that made the end boss wish he had four legs. Literally the only enemy in the game that killed me. I guess at least they weren't Cliff Racers.
Good puzzles, good boss fights, possibly the best learning curve in the franchise. If you like old school RE games, this is a must buy.

What should a Remaster really be? Should it be ultra faithful to the original even if it's painful? Or should it "modernize" the game, including some quality of life changes?

If you're in the former category then this game will be for you, if you're more like me and expect a bit more for such a price then I wouldn't recommend it.

Like Resident Evil 0 this game suffers from rose tinted glasses vision. The game mechanics are horribly outdated, the story is barely existent and held together loosely by documents strewn around and the overall graphical presentation is obviously leagues ahead of the original, yet still muddy as hell. It's got a nice atmosphere, and the sense of exploration the first time around is generally pretty nice. It also introduces the player to some of the "big shows" of the franchise, but that's about it.

Gameplay consists of fighting the terrible fixed camera, shooting in the wrong direction, watching about ten thousand unskippable (and unnecessary) door animations (which you supposedly can fix with a mod that didn't work for me, but that would save you at least an hour of game time, as one animation easily takes 5 seconds), and backtracking for the umpteenth time, because your inventory consists of only 6 (8 with Jill, omg, so much better) spaces and in your first playthrough you don't know when you will need what item. Just as an example: In the very first room you can get a crest... naturally a player will pick it up and wonder what to do with it. Well, you need it several hours later. Hours! Until then it either takes up precious space in your inventory (6 spaces = 2 slots for a weapon and some ammo, maybe 1 slot for a healing item, leaving you with 3 slots, while you're running around the place finding 10 times that number until you reach another save point). You could also put it back and hope to remember where it was. You can't simply discard items like in RE 0 (perhaps the only good thing about that game).
Rooms stay red when there are still items in it. The game doesn't differentiate between vital and non-essential items though and since you also have no way of labelling a room (or a door, because you need 10 different keys in this game) you're often left wondering if you can open a specific door with the new key you've found or if that redlit room just has some unnecessary items in it or a key progression item.

Saving is only possible in certain safe rooms with a "ink ribbon" item. Depending on difficulty mode you might find more or not so many, which further prolongs the game time needlessly if you die (especially to one of the few insta death scenarios), because you have to do everything again, pick up every item again, watch every door animation again, etc.

That's what I mean by quality of life. The aforementioned systems do not make RE 1 difficult, they just make it tedious, so you don't beat the game in 2 hours. My first playthrough was over 9 hours...my 2nd under 5. Now subtract another hour for door animations and maybe another hour for pointless running back and forth.
The puzzles aren't worth mentioning either for the most part. I've seen reviewers complain how easy the puzzles in RE 8 are...and I'm like, well they can't be easier than these. The only puzzle I've had trouble with was one where you were supposed to note down (or really remember) certain previously thought unconnected things you needed later on for a door code. And I don't mind that per se. It's a horror action game, not so much a puzzle game.

Sound and music are good though for the most part. Of course this is a more than 20 year old game, only remade with better graphics. But that's just it: It's still wasting your time to be honest. It could have been more. Like RE 2 and perhaps 3 remake.

[h1]Quick Summary [/h1]
A game franchise that has a wide array of quality and style of games and the first game hasn’t aged well as its old designs fixed in later entries hold it back for me. The actual fear of dying in this game makes it a blast for those looking for a challenge, it’s unique and very ominous yet simple horror elements feel fresh for someone that has played the franchise in reverse order. I would love to see a remake like RE2 got with the improvements it made to all my complaints but keep the core intact, and then you get a game worthy of being a horror masterpiece. That said it’s still worth a go for anyone looking for a unique horror game as there is nothing like this and couldn’t imagine how epic this was when all came out over 20 years ago

 [h1]More in depth: [/h1]
[list]
    [*]The STORY is what you already know if you’ve played or seen any of their games or movies; passable at best. Here the VOICE ACTING IS LAUGHABLE. People speak like they don’t know what they are trying to read from the script with no range of emotions, Barry is nice, mean or almost dies, Jill sounds the same. I don’t know who is at fault, the original or the remaster, but overall the writing and story is not the reason to get invested in this game.

     [*]THE UNIQUENESS IS THE CLEAR GREATEST PART and clearly the biggest thing this game has to offer. The angle of the fixed cameras gives handpicked encounters and is still never been done and I really enjoyed it along with the movement controls that felt easy to pick up;  coming from a person that has played more games than anyone. There are very few actual good horror games still to this day even in its own franchise. All the others lean way more into action and I finally understand the love this game gets and why the dislike of the new entries if this was the first game played, or like me prefer this unique style.

[*]In terms of LEVEL DESIGN THE MANSION IS ONE OF THE BEST in horror games, following after RE 2 police station. With the tight corridors and windows making it tense at times when to avoid or kill the zombified creatures. The placement of said enemies with mirrors and corners to obscure and give me a person that never gets scared in any horror game freak out twice one was a spider on a similar colored wall; their look might even give people with arachnophobia panic attacks. The other was a jumping lizard creature right in front of me. Planning routes are important and learning the layout isn’t that hard and having most of the map not required to enter to beat the game is a nice touch. Save locations and spacing apart along with limited in game saves that makes dying actually scary because of time. 

    [*]The PUZZLES and interconnected nature of the progression I can see has been a standard of the good games of the franchise and like that some rewards are optional and reward you with ammo and new weapons. The way they handle it at times is neat and can feel like you pieced things together organically through classic metroidvania and shortcuts similar to Dark Souls to ease probably my biggest issue with the game. 

    [*]The AGE OF THIS GAME SHOWS REALLY BAD IN TWO MAIN AREAS, FIRST THE LOADING, I get that back in the day they used the doors like this because of tech reasons, but we are 20 years later and like RE2 and others have shown this is terrible and I get fans will be nostalgic for; but really hurts the game overall pacing as there is a lot of backtracking itself which isn’t really a huge issue in itself. It’s the loading for each room that gets tedious, at least each door animation is unique and fitting the style of entry, it could of just been a generic door each time. You can solve this issue using this https://residentevilmodding.boards.net/thread/3092/door-skip-mod. Wish I knew about this before I started, but I did get the true experience which is what I wanted to go for. It is only like 10 seconds at most, but still something that could be fixed.

    [*]  The other major issue is the slow interactions; it is the slowest of any game I’ve played. Press a button and a prompt shows up to accept it and then put in in the slot, combining is twice as slow and transferring items from your box and saving is a nightmare, it’s a linear list that you need to scroll and you can’t take one ink to save so afterwards you need to put it back, and of course after playing the way better ones that fixed all my complaints of this game it was a tough pill to swallow.  Also 8 items with Jill without any upgrades was a huge letdown; I didn’t play as Chris because ONLY 6 SLOTS, I’M NOT A MASOCHIST. This issue was made more annoying with NOT KNOWING WHAT ITEMS I NEEDED AT WHAT TIE TO GO WHERE at times and to prevent taking 20 hours to beat I used a wiki guide to tell me when and what I needed to easy my suffering with this issue.

Resident Evil Remake captures everything the fans love of what defined this genre in the 90s.
Survival horror experience that involves several puzzles, decision-making and exploration, with fairly decent combat along the way.
Obviously, the cheesy dialogues couldn’t be forgotten in a Capcom game.

The graphics are beautiful and the fixed camera didn’t really bother me (most of the time) because I used to play a lot of Resident Evil Outbreak back in the early 2000s (although I do recommend a controller to play this game because turning around corners can be frustrating with keyboard & mouse, in my opinion).
The only downsides for me are the long character animations when being bitten by zombies or dogs, and the loading screens behind every single door. I obviously understand it’s not a modern game and all Resident Evil titles until 2004 had this door-opening loading screen. The nostalgic feel even made me smile a few times, but it’s terribly annoying to go through loading screens every time I open a door, especially in a game that involves plenty of back-tracking and exploration.
It removed much of the immersive aspects of the game (in my personal experience) and harmed the exploration that I value so much in a Resident Evil game.

Overall, really entertaining and nostalgic! Great scenarios, amazing storyline and unbelievably faithful to the entire franchise. It’s arguably the most accurate RE game out there.

Resident Evil is a classic survival horror game about a pair of cripples who overcame their physical handicaps to become STARS agents. Chris and Jill are geriatric special forces who cannot make sharp turns, aim within 90 degree angles, or carry more than a couple pounds worth of mundane items. It's a miracle they even passed basic training. They couldn't clear an empty room much less take on an undead horde. However, that's part of the game's genius. The horror is magnified by the fact that Chris and Jill aren't some stupid boring generic action stars like Leon.

Experience the sheer terror through constant epileptic camera cuts, which effectively heighten the tension by leaving players lost as ♥♥♥♥. Fight memorable nightmarish bosses like Big Snake, Big Spider, Big Fish, and of course Big Plant. Solve difficult mind-bending puzzles like, why does my uniform only have four tiny pockets, and why does a key take up the same space as a handgun or a houseplant? What's my holster even for??

But these answers won't be easily obtained, because this is extreme hardcore survival horror for grown-up adults. Don't even think of buying this if you're someone who needs their hand held by responsive controls, or reasonable inventory space, or a clear view of what's actually happening, or immersive gameplay that isn't interrupted by a thousand and one loading screen doors. This obviously isn't your kind of game.

[h1][u]A Brief Introduction[/u][/h1]
Resident Evil is the prized show dog of the survival horror industry. Every time somebody brings up the word “horror”, somebody also brings up Resident Evil. It’s an iconic titan of the industry. But does that mean it’s worth getting and experiencing in modern times? No. No it does not.

[h1][u]In-Depth Analysis[/u][/h1]
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Resident Evil Remake has a management style that can best be described as a maliciously neglectful parent. It does not “Hold your hand”, in the sense that it explains quite literally nothing about itself, including basic, necessary information such as how to shake off zombies, what the controls even are, or what your objective is at any point in time. RE1 will let its kid stick a fork in the outlet under the philosophy that their excruciatingly painful death will teach them not to do that again. 

[b][u]Resident Evil punishes.[/u][/b] It punishes you for picking up items with a brutally restrictive inventory of eight spaces, which is shared across ALL items, including guns, ammo, keys, mandatory progress items, and everything else. Picking up something you don’t immediately need punishes you by making it impossible to pick up something later. Yet, there is no way to know what you need in advance because of the comical, James Bond villain style of puzzles around the house. Yet still, the game also punishes you for NOT bringing the right item, even if you didn’t know you needed it. There are numerous points in the game where lacking a specific item will result in your death.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2504208174

And guess what? Resident Evil punishes saving. You can only save at specific times, in specific places, and with a limited amount of saves at that. This breeds paranoia as to when to save. Go too long without saving and die? Tough crap, replay it all again. 

Resident Evil even punishes you for daring to attack enemies. Any zombie you kill that wasn’t put down with a headshot or being lit on fire is guaranteed to come back later as a stronger and faster Crimson Head zombie. A new player can easily softlock their own game by having so many Crimson Head zombies pile up they can’t kill them all before they get mauled to death trying to get past them.

The enemies that aren’t zombies also heavily abuse the outdated and clunky shooting system, dashing into you and slashing you before you can fire another bullet. The best option is to try and run past them all, which doesn’t even reliably work, and also isn’t remotely fun. 

Resident Evil 1 isn’t scary. The zombies are laughable in nature, shuffling around like they are doing the conga with comical moans. I can clearly tell the zombie lying down on the floor is not dead, I’m not a child. It doesn’t scare me when it tries to stand up. Hunters equally shuffle around making weird noises and their only “scare factor” is it instantly killing you, which is no different than any other game.

Resident Evil is tedious. As people have pointed out, when you actually know where to go and what to do, you can beat the entire game in under an hour and a half. The gameplay consists exclusively of backtracking around a labyrinthian mansion and solving nonsensical puzzles while dodging, not killing zombies. Remember, killing zombies is punished. RE1 is a zombie themed puzzle game, not survival horror. A poor, outdated zombie puzzle game at that.

Oh, and don’t forget there’s a mandatory, unskippable seven second cutscene every single time you open any door in the game. I do mean ANY door.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You, either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield, have been stranded in a mysterious mansion after being chased there by zombie dogs while investigating cannibalistic murders in the nearby area. After that, there’s basically no story. A few, scarce character interactions occur, along with some lore and world building, and while it is interesting stuff, spending hours backtracking around a mansion to get it is hardly an ideal way to spend an afternoon.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
Finally, an area that isn’t all bad news. Resident Evil does look quite excellent, thanks to its unique combination of pre-rendered backgrounds that allowed for high detail. This was much more impressive back in 2002 when the GameCube and its 43MB of memory couldn’t handle all that much. These days, the same thing can be achieved with normal processing power. It does have an old time charm to it, which I did enjoy. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2504207827

However, the cost of this is the most infamously horrible game mechanic in all of history: Fixed. Camera. Angles. These can happen at any time, anywhere. Simply crossing a single room may involve four to five different camera angle changes. If you’re using the classic tank controls, this doesn’t affect you so much, except for the fact you’re using the objectively worst movement method in gaming, tank controls. If you are using the new controls provided by the remake, the instant the camera changes, if you change your walking angle in the slightest, you immediately re-orient to the new camera, often causing you to walk in between the same camera angle several times just trying to readjust. 

This camera is also used to intentionally obscure upcoming zombies and other enemies to provide sources of cheap scares or cheap damage. Imagine if Lakitu in Super Mario 64 refused to show enemies on the camera until they smacked into you and killed you. That’s the Resident Evil experience.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The audio is mediocre at best and bad at worst. Zombies, as previously mentioned, sound comical, like they recorded somebody snoring instead of anything meaningful. Everything else sounds like stock footage. The music is generic and unimpressive, if you even get music. 

Even with the Remake voice acting, it still sounds flat and completely lacking in motivation. The corniness and amusingly bad campiness of the original lines are actually more fun because of how ridiculous they are. 

[h1]Technical[/h1]
[u]GeForce RTX 2060 6GB | AMD Ryzen 9 | 16GB | Windows 10 [/u]

It runs fine. The keyboard keybinds are awful though, so its best played on a controller.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[h1][u]The Very Definition of the Word “Outdated”[/u][/h1]
Resident Evil 1 was once the pinnacle of survival horror. However, that time and that title has long, long, long passed away. It is punishing, lacks any decent reward for success, doesn’t look that good, sound that good, and has some of the most clunky, outdated gameplay I have ever witnessed. Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a better horror game. Dead Space is a better survival horror game. It has been surpassed twenty times over by history, and there's no reason for a new player to pick it up in the modern era with vastly superior alternatives available.

It reminds me of the old Sierra point and click adventure games. You touch anything, you die, for the crime of not being clairvoyant and not knowing that would kill you ahead of time. There’s no survival, there’s no horror. It’s a puzzle game with zombies placed around it to annoy you and waste your time.

It is the relic of a time long gone, held alive by the nostalgia goggled fanbase that had no better alternatives back in the 90s and have been playing it for so long they are blind to its blatant flaws.

Don’t believe the hype. Watch a playthrough on YouTube, it will be less painful and you’ll miss none of the experience. Some games just don’t age well. Resident Evil is a prime example of this lesson.
