Resident Evil(2015) is remaster of the Resident Evil(2002) which was the remake of the Resident Evil(1996). I don't think I need to explain what Resident Evil is and why it's so important for the gaming history. Resident Evil did for the survival horror genre what DOOM did for FPS or Street Fighter II did for the fighting games. That being said, I never played any of the original RE games (I know, not a "true fan" and a fake gamer), and this version of RE is the only one anyone can get without resorting to emulation or searching for the original hardware, which sucks for preservation, but it's not like companies ever cared for that type of stuff.
Anyway, if you never played original RE, bad news: this is your only option, good news: you won't get much better than this. REmake is one of the best games of all time and can be considered pretty much perfect in almost every regard, except for a few minor nitpicks.

The story of the game follows the Alpha Team of the Special Tactics and Rescue Squad, S.T.A.R.S. Player takes control of one the members of the squad: Jill Valentine, master of lockpicking and chemistry, and Chris Redfield, who burns corpses. Our chosen character gets separated from the rest of the squad and has to explore the mysterious mansion, full of zombies and traps, find your missing partners, uncover th reason why dead are walking the earth again, and get out of there alive.
The story and plot of RE is a wonderful mix of 80-s action and horror tropes. The characters are trying to be super serious, but talk and act in such unnatural manner it genuinely made me laugh out loud couple of times. Most of the time you spend the time in Spencer Mansion alone, so meeting another character alive and well is always a highlight. Even if it's Wesker, who is always, as kids this days say, very sus.

The presentation of the game is unique and a relic of the era long gone. The game has fixed cameras put in different places in the mansion and features prerendered backgrounds with 3D objects put into them. You would think that it's kind f jarring, seeing a 3D model of your character and enemies walking around in, what is essentially 2D still picture, but with clever use of said fixed camera angles and very convincing optical illusions, gives REmake sort of timeless look, which is very rare in the games from that era. And everything is dark, depressing and claustrophibic. In Resident Evil you never can feel like you are safe, something is always behind the corner, or just out of your field of view, or behind next door. The rare moments of piece and quite are only present in safe rooms with your item box and typewriter, and incredible, soothing musical theme. The soundtrack in general is very good and fitting, and used very sparingly in certain rooms. 

Playing Resident Evil for the first, you might be confused as to what the game actually wants from you. Usually everything we need to know about a game can be solved in first few minutes, but RE doesn't really hold your hand and gives you any pointers. You have to figure everything out yourself. But playing this game I realised one thing, at it's core, RE is a puzzle game with action elements. You see, most of the time spent in RE you will be searching for items, keys, puzzle pieces. That is your main motivation moving forward. Zombies, dogs and other enemies ar essentially just obstacles on your wayy t your next objective, and most of them can actually be avoided, and it is recommended for you to avoid them at all costs to preserve your scarce resources and engaging in combat if only absolutely necessary. But here is the thing, your main obstacle and main source of fear is not zombies or lack of resources or the situations you get into from time to time, it's your own characters limitations. The controls of the original RE are praised for being perfect for the game they are in. The fabled tank controls are universally loved by the veterans of the franchise, that desperately want the frachise to go back to it's roots, and they are probably your main source of problems in this game. Fortunately for little baby casuals like me 2015 remaster of REmake features alternative control scheme that gives you full 360 degrees of motion wth just one stick, but if you want true RE experience, you have to go with tank controls. Another limitation of your character is their invertory space. Chris has 6 slots in his invertory, while Jill has more pockets in her uniform, since she has 8 slots so she can carry her overpowered grenade launcher. Still, the invertory is very small, and if you fill it up with some garbage you have no way to drop unless you have access to item box or< in case of ammo or health items, just use them up, probably wasting them in the process. 
So yeah, even if you get used to creepy atmsphere and not very friendly inhabitants of Spencer Mansion, you will always be in constant stress, simply of how clunky the game feels to play. You yourself is your main obstacle in your survival. In other games I would call it stupid, but in RE it simply legendary how well it works with the themes and feel of the game. It is truly remarkable how you can turn bad game design into good game design by simply putting it into right context.
The game is also VERY addictive. Finding every key item and getting more progress little by little is a giant dopamine explosion, that hooks you and won't let you go till the end. You would feel that you need to stop, but just quickly, what's behind that door, or what does this item does, or just need to go back to that room and get that item that fits in that other room. Just a little more, little by little, and then it's 5am, you need to go to work in a couple of hours and you watching the credits, itching to go back and try it all over again.

Resident Evil is simply a masterpiece of a game and should be requred title for every single fan of videogames. The same way we learn about great classcs of authors long gone, we need to know about the work of Shinji Mikami and the whole team at Capcom that worked on this project. I simply can not recommend it enough. Just get it and go play it. You will not regret it.

The first time I ever played this game was way back when it first came out and I was staying at my cousins' house over the weekend. These two introduced me to video games early on but this visit they had a new one...Resident Evil!...and I wasn't allowed to tell my parents I played it because it's super scary and bloody and gory and stuff. I was petrified...immediately my mind raced with irrational thoughts of the basement becoming full of spiders, zombies, dogs and other horrible things. I could eventually hear them laughing so I calmed down, and kept playing.

Eventually the two of them came down and saw I was still playing, which I think impressed them. Then we all started playing together again but this time, in the dark. Playing this game in the dark changed my life in a huge way. It changed the way I thought about video game immersion. So I highly recommend playing in the dark with headphones on.

The tank controls are admittedly an unfortunate sacrifice but once you get over that the camera work shines, especially in REmake where the cameras where much more dynamic but still true to original game. This is one of those games that makes me wish Steam had a 'neutral review' option.  

I remember playing this on my Playstation (1st Gen) and it was my first delve into 'survival horror.'  I was terrified of this game when it first came out.  Now - it's more of nostalgia trip than actually scary.  The hours I spent getting lost and dying and trying to figure out the puzzles are all coming back to me now.  I never liked the save system so I ended up leaving the console on with the game running and my character in a save room after using up all the ribbons with panic saves.  Then my father turned it off when I was at work one day...and I never played again - until now. 

As for this remastered HD version - it's gorgeous and smooth and everything I expected graphically and atmospherically.  A perfect upgrade to the original.  I still hate the save system and the extreme limited inventory you can carry.  The amount of backtracking you have to do to the inventory box rooms is borderline maddening just like the original.  Had to re-adjust to the wonky camera and movement controls (keyboard, not controller.)  The targeting for item pick up is still just as bad as the original.  Things aren't always where the guides say they should be so I'm missing out on the 'green' completion of a location.

I still get lost.  I still die. I still get angry at the puzzles.

The hardest part to deal with is the two game-breaking glitches/bugs I've encountered.
I would leave the game running to conserve save ribbons - but this game has a nasty habit of randomly closing down every time I play with a 'fatal error' message which causes me to rage at lost progress. The constant anxiety of how much progress I can make between saves before the game will inevitably crash and close is difficult to tolerate considering the save system and amount of time spent backtracking you have to do. 

The worst bug is seriously the randomly clipping through the ground when you climb onto an object or jump down.  This is game breaking.  I fall halfway into the ground, the camera locks position and I can clip through the entire map - only I can't follow my character and I can't get back up to ground level without reloading a save.

Do I recommend it? Maybe, if you were a fan of the original it is fun for the nostalgia and the graphic upgrade.  Just be aware that it is far from perfect.  It has glitches/bugs.  Hopefully, I can complete a playthrough but as of 6.7 hours of gameplay - it has crashed on me at least once every hour of play time.  

So if you have the patience for nostalgia and puzzle solving weighed against game-breaking, rage-inducing random bugs...go for it.

I feel like everyone should know the original Resident Evil, but considering even this 2002 remake is old enough to drink there’s a good chance that there’s a whole generation of gamers below the age of 25 who may be completely unfamiliar with the classic RE games. This version of Resident Evil is generally considered the absolute pinnacle of the classic style games, and this rather lovely HD remaster is the perfect place to dip your toes in.

However if you’re not familiar with its particular brand of obtuse puzzles, inventory management and endless backtracking you may find the waters rather more biting than you might expect, and that’s before we come to the tank controls. It’s worth noting that this re-release does come with analogue controls that will likely make it more palatable to a modern audience, but the game was clearly not designed around them. Tank controls are stiff and awkward but are more suited to rapidly changing camera angles where regardless of what direction you’re facing up will move your character forwards. The analogue controls pitch a bitchfit in some of the more cramped corridors of the mansion, and if you can stomach them, I’d strongly recommend trying to get used to the tank controls. Try type E if you’re struggling, this is the type C of all the gamecube games and allows you to hold a trigger to move forwards like you’re driving a car. It sounds utterly insane but I found it strangely useable.

Even if you get used to the controls, if you’re expecting anything remotely modern in terms of game design I’d temper your expectations as this was considered rather quaint even in 2002. The game itself is much closer to an old style classic adventure game than it is a modern zombie shooter. Killing an enemy is less about “can I do this” and more about “can I afford to do this” – killing them is utterly trivial, but ammunition is extremely scarce and you are encouraged to avoid enemies if at all possible. 90% of your time will be spent going back and forth in the mansion plugging objects into their corresponding holes and solving rudimentary puzzles while managing your tiny inventory space. 

Speaking of which, I would strongly recommend new players start with Jill, as she has more inventory slots and gets to avoid the tedium of tracking down old keys. Chris is more of an “arrange mode” for those familiar with the game, and I cannot imagine how frustrating it is to play as him on a first run. I’m probably making this sound absolutely awful, and certainly on a blind playthrough progress can feel quite frustrating with endless trips back to the item box (how could you possibly have known that attaching the beard to the stone cat would release the obsidian buttplug?). 

However, it’s a game that’s utterly carried by its atmosphere, art and sound design and weirdly enough novelty. It’s strangely satisfying to click all the pieces of the mansion together while soaking in the spooky atmosphere, and even considering the clear return to survival horror that the series took with RE7 nothing really plays like these stodgy old games any more, and likely never will.

A good game. You can play with either alternative or original/tank controls, respectively. The Original has more rigid movement where "W" being forward and "S" is backwards while "A" turns left and "D" right. Alternative controls being up-to-date with modern games and allowing more fluid-movement where "S" and "W" can be either forward or backwards and vice versa depending on the camera angle or direction faced. 

Tank controls are a more archaic control system with the term deriving from the steering systems of old tanks or other continuous track vehicles such as Caterpillar's D9T Dozer, which allowed more restricted movement, hence the term: "tank controls". 

Tank controls were common in games from the 1980s-90s (Vindicators 1988). The original Resident Evil did not feature "alternative controls" and was designed with the older (tank) controls in mind. Alternative controls are arguably considered less difficult to utilize than tank controls because of its fluidity in movement. Although, the issue with alternative arises from the design-choice of the fixed camera angles when turning certain corners of the mansion which may leave the user disoriented. This issue is nonexistent with the original controls attributed to the reason that "W" is the only key that allows one to go forward. The game is playable with both controls and it is possible for one to learn to play with both.

The original PS1 Resident Evil was one of my favorite childhood games. And yet here I am, not recommending its remake to be played in 2021. This game is arguably the most faithful to the source material out of the Raccoon City trilogy of remakes. Everything you loved Resident Evil for is there, and then some. 

And that's exactly where the problem lies. Unlike the brilliant and acclaimed RE2make, this game fails to acknowledge the achievements in gamedev and the genre over the past 20 years. It's still the same game design and mechanics from the 1990th, and frankly, they aged terribly.

Constant backtracking because of very low inventory capacity which is not upgradable, meaningless filler tasks like "run to the other end of the map to grab the serum for a guy bitten by a giant snake and then do another run because why not", waiting simulator of looking at door opening cutscenes every single time (which made sense and even added flavour back then, but is just tedious now), and then even more backtracking. And puzzles, tons of non-obvious puzzles the game doesn't do the job of explaining well, so expect asking Google / Youtube for a walkthrough at regular intervals. 

Overall the experience is rather tedious than challenging or hardcore. Ammo and healing are in abundance, so you're more likely to die because of wonky camera / controls rather than because of failing at the "survival" aspect of the game. 

If you'd still like to sate your nostalgia, or are a newcomer looking to get acquainted with the origins of the series, the best advice I can give you is at least play as Jill. She has more inventory space and gets to skip a lot of annoying filler content, which will certainly improve your overall experience.

Resident Evil Remake Review:
[Story and In-game Item Spoilers Below]

TL;DR: Horror Good, Genre-defining game

	It says a lot about the significance of the Resident Evil franchise when a game from 2002 holds up nearly 20 years later. Resident Evil HD (2015) is the PC port of the HD re-release for the original Resident Evil remake (colloquially referred to as “RE Remake” or “Remake”). HD Remake does not add many features – the most notable of which being the inclusion of a more modern control scheme (3D/circular movement, as opposed to tank controls). This is the method that I played with, although the classic control scheme is immediately available to the player by using the D-pad on their controller. I heard suggestions from RE veterans that suggests this modern scheme makes escaping zombies easier, but a novice like me did not find that to be true. Other than the controls, there is now support for 5.1 surround. From a more “objective” view, HD Remake does not add much. However, I would posit that there is little in need of adding. [url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150120063823/http://www.gameinformer.com/b/features/archive/2014/10/17/dissecting-resident-evil-hd-remaster.aspx]The developers made the creative decision to not redo the pre-rendered environments into the modern 16:9 format and kept the old 4:3.[/url]  Instead, they opted to have the fixed cameras scroll in certain scenes. Personally, I think this adds to the game’s atmosphere, and is reminiscent of classic horror films.

Speaking of horror, this is probably the closest to true horror the franchise has been. Story-wise, it is a very typical setup. Your gang of characters are stuck in a mysterious house, and you need to find a way to escape before the zombies infect you. As the plot continues, you learn more about the estate, and danger creeps around every corner. This is peak 80’s and 90’s horror media, which makes sense considering that Resident Evil came out in 1996. There are technically 2 scenarios in this game, although they are only marginally different. The difference being so minor that the fan wiki refers to the “canonical” hero as “a member of S.T.A.R.S.”. instead of outright stating any names. I played through Jill’s campaign, and got the ending in which both Chris and Barry were alive during my final battle. This was my first playthrough, and I was genuinely surprised to find out that my NPC buddies could - die if I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. It was not until the last third of the game’s final act that I learned about this hidden feature. The game’s fixed camera angles certainly added to the mystique of each room. There were a couple rooms that held close on Jill’s face, and I kind of just got lost in those moments. The music is quiet, there are no monsters. I am just alone, staring at my character, and thinking.

	In terms of gameplay, this game is the most barebones of any other game in the franchise. Jill and Chris play very differently from one another. Jill has more item slots, greater weapon variety, but less health compared to Chris. Chris is faster, better defensive items, and has a lighter as a key item (more on that later). Enemy variety   is very lackluster but is excused by the fact that this is the first in a series of games. Later games that rely on the cliché “animal but it’s big” (see my Resident Evil 0 review) have far less excuses. Enemy placement is daunting, and I often found myself scraping by for resources until the very back-end of the game. There was a wide array of puzzles throughout that run the gamut of “a child could do this” to “You need to be a math wizard”. There is only one puzzle (the knights) that bothered me, and it was only because I needed to stare at a very muddy texture on the wall. Some may find it more difficult than others to determine the difference between a halberd and a sword. Otherwise, I found these puzzle segments to be very engaging and fun. Discovering the solution to V-Jolt on my own was great, but I felt like a fool when I discovered the game’s hint for it was on a wall that I had not examined. There is a frequent number   of hints given through examinable objects, so I would recommend anyone to peruse a room in its entirety before doing anything destructive.

	It is difficult to really disparage this game because it serves as the entry point for most people nowadays. With the recent erasure of the PS3, PSP, and PS Vita digital outlets, there isn’t a way to play RE ’96 without the use of emulators or expensive physical releases. However, Remake is widely available of PS4, the Xbox platforms (360, Xbone, and now Series S/X via backwards compatibility), and this PC release. I would highly recommend playing this game if you want to see what all the fuss is about. It is a great experience, and solidates itself as a shining example of true “survival horror”.

Pros:

-Gameplay: Game sells itself as Survival horror and feels it. At no point in-game did I find myself ever feeling fully at "ease" with my position. Constantly scrounging for items and worrying about Zombies or other assorted Horrors really helps keep the player in a constant state of tense dread. I especially like the Inventory system that really helps tie the games thematic pretensions into gameplay.

-Music: Excellent tracks that really help solidify the spooky atmosphere.

-Story: Very cheesy. This game's story will not be for everyone. But I personally found it enjoyable in a very "80's creature feature" way. Characters are fun if not exactly complex and the pacing of the uncovering of the background of the Mansion is done very well

Neutral:
-Graphics: Even this remake is beginning to show its age in my opinion. However, the game still has moments where it looks great especially in some of its late game environments.

Cons
-Occasional puzzle woes: One or two puzzles in this game are slightly frustrating to solve or might seem slightly unfair. This is partially a result of the inventory system I mentioned earlier. While I was a fan of the overall implementation of the system I can easily see how some players might get frustrated with how puzzles are used in the game. This is not a massive issue in my opinion but something worth noting.

-Controls: Occasionally the game seemed to actively wrestle against my inputs. Overall I would say the game controlled well but sometimes while attempting to aim the controls felt highly cumbersome.

Conclusion
This is a great game with a fun story and highly suspenseful gameplay

[h1] Intro [/h1]
An absolute classic of the survival-horror genre, and honestly a pretty interesting game to play through in the modern day.  This game is essentially an HD port of a GameCube remake of a PlayStation 1 game. That is to say it is a pretty old game, and some parts of it definitely feel like it. I will however note here that while nothing special by today's standards, visually this game has held up pretty well.

[h1] The Camera [/h1]
So important it gets its own section, the gameplay is a fixed perspective third person game. What this means is that unlike more modern Resident Evil games which have an over-the-shoulder perspective, the camera isn't controlled by the player and instead is in fixed positions that changed based on where the player goes, almost in a way like watching someone moving through a series of security cameras in a way. For the most part this is actually pretty cool, most of the time the camera work really helps toward building a sense of dread and anticipation, as the placement of camera angles are used to hide things like enemies and items until the most opportune, surprising, or cinematic of moments. However, it can also be somewhat clunky at times, as some areas have a lot of different camera angles in relatively small areas and from pretty different angles, which can make movement in certain areas really clumsy and even a tad annoying. They do also occasionally have some bad angles that do hide enemies too well, meaning that there will be some instances where you find out an enemy is there by almost running straight into them, which can feel slightly cheap. However both these issues are relatively uncommon, and in general the camera angles and positioning really do serve the atmosphere of the game.

[h1] The Gameplay [/h1]
This is a game about shooting, exploration, and item management. On most difficulties there is a sort of auto targeting, as long as you face toward the enemy you'll be able to shoot it. There is a strong focus of exploring every area possible, scavenging for key items and backtracking to progress through the game. Resources are pretty scarce, with ammo, healing, and even saving being fairly limited. This does emphasise evasion over combat, as trying to kill every enemy you encounter can be very costly (especially on the higher difficulties). You have access to a small selection of guns and other supporting weapons, and there are a selection of two different playable characters, each with their own gameplay and story differences. Jill has less health and a lower headshot chance, but has more inventory space and the lockpick, which makes it easier to access certain areas, Chris meanwhile has more health and a higher headshot chance, but has less inventory space and has to scavenge for keys, meaning a lot more backtracking compared to Jill. Honestly would advise playing as Jill for your first playthrough, the extra inventory space and the lockpick make her a bit easier than Chris.

[h1] Story and Voice Acting [/h1]
The series in general was fairly inspired by B-Movie horror, and that does translate a fair bit to the story and voice acting. Story is relatively simple, mostly just exploring the mansion and surrounding areas trying to figure out what happened and how to escape, all up it's fairly enjoyable, and the characters are mostly enjoyable. As for the voice acting, the original Resident Evil is infamous for how amazingly terrible the voice acting and dialogue is. This one by comparison is so much better. Not to say it's particularly great, and it can be pretty cheesy at times, but as a whole it doesn't really detract from the game.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Despite being around 19 years old as at the time of this review, this game is still surprisingly creepy, with the camera angles and sounds really working together quite beautifully to create a very tense atmosphere that makes you dread going around the next corner. In terms of the technical factors of the game, I didn't experience any kind of technical issues. It can definitely be quite clunky at times, but honestly as a whole I found it to be a really fun and creepy experience that I would recommend if you are into Resident Evil or older survival-horror games.

While I've never played the PS1 game that this is a remake of, I can tell that this must be a pretty faithful adaptation just because of how [i]oldschool[/i] the design is. This is the type of game where you have to read the manual just to know what the controls are and there's one or two small mechanics you just have to find on your own.. Resident Evil is [i]brutal[/i] to start out on, but the more I got accustomed to it's quirks, the more I came to appreciate it's unique brilliance.

This is truly a [i]survival[/i] game in every sense of the word. You simply don't have enough resources to kill every enemy and you need to conserve your ammo to take out the ones that really matter. Sometimes it's best just to let that zombie live and successfully dodging several of them while running down a hallway feels like you're some kind of football player trying to get to the end zone. Starting out is punishingly difficult but as you progress you start to get a feel for which parts of the mansion are safe, and finding multiple routes to get to the same room.

The simultaneous best and worst design choice is the fact that your ability to actually save your progress is also a limited resource. When you're starting out, this will punish you. You really have no feel for the game's pacing at first and about 6 hours in I had gotten to what I thought was a fairly far part of the game, but it turns out this was laughably early in the campaign and I had already spend so many of my saves that I realized that continuing further was going to be woefully impractical. I decided to restart the game, and knowing what I knew now I made up that 6 hours of progress in about 30 or 40 minutes, and that difference is at the heart of what made my time with [i]Resident Evil[/i] so compelling. Once I got a feel for the layout and how things worked, I kept trying to optimize my run through each part of the game. Sometimes I would do a section and think "Did I spend too much ammo? Did I use too many saves?" and I would reload from my last save to try and do the section more efficiently. I've never really been into speedrunning, but I became obsessed with trying to make more of each section while using as little of my resources as possible. Of course, the longer you go without saving, the more risk you run if you die, as you'll have to replay the game in larger chunks, which brings a brilliant tension to the gameplay. Death actually matters here in a way it doesn't in most games and every time you die is a legitimate punishment. Normally when I finish a game I'm ready to be done with it, but I'm excited to play the other character's story knowing what I know now to see how optimal a run I can get now that I've seen the entire game (Edit: the Chris campaign only took 9.5 hours and 22 saves).

Yet despite how tense and punishing the game can be, it's a surprisingly cozy game thanks to the fantastic atmosphere. [i]Resident Evil[/i] feels like a truly [i]classic[/i] Gothic horror with all the genre trappings: a big baroque mansion with statues and hidden passageways, cryptic riddles, and the slow reveal of a tragedy that happened long before told through a series of journals and snippets. While you don't get much characterization from the player characters, there's a surprisingly eclectic cast of supporting characters that inject some life into an otherwise solitary affair. [i]Resident Evil[/i] is dense with atmosphere and the beautifully pre-rendered backgrounds and carefully chosen camera angles convey mood in ways a fully-controllable camera just can't. It's a gorgeous game to look at and the music just seals the deal.

This coziness also lends itself well to the game's other large component: the puzzles. [i]Resident Evil[/i] is as much a point-and-click adventure game as it is an action game. Games from this era can sometimes have a problem with the puzzles being too obtuse, but the puzzle design here is excellent and I think the game is perhaps best when it's "Scary Myst" rather than trying to avoid zombies. It's a general rule of puzzle design that if you've got a lock and key puzzle, the further you place the key from the lock, the harder the puzzle is. [i]Resident Evil[/i] gives you tons of keys upfront and you really have to mentally keep them in mind because some of them only come up near the end of the game. There are no red herrings here and everything that looks important, is important. Thankfully you can stash your stuff in series of item boxes and whatever you put in is available at every item box. It was fun finding each clue and especially satisfying when I realized somewhere went, and in addition to the lock/key puzzles there are some wonderfully creative brainteasers that make you really think without entering the realm of unfair.

The only area the game really falls down in is you never really get a good motivation from the villain. You have a great idea by the end what happened at this mansion and the story up to then is great, but there's a cutscene before the end that's supposed to be the big reveal, but it's so badly translated that it becomes incoherent and kind of hilarious. The voice acting and writing are great for most of the game and some of it seems deliberately campy to enhance the B-movie feel, but that one scene is the only time it's really apparent the game was translated from Japanese and I was mostly left confused. In addition, while the game does perform very well, there are a couple of odd hiccups. You can't select every resolution from the menu, so you'll have to go into the config file and manually set it if you need, say, 2550x1440. There's also an odd glitch where if you try to set the game to fullscreen it crashes, so you have to just set it to a higer resolution, save yoru settings, then close the game, then [i]after that[/i] open the game up and set it to fullscreen.

Those little flaws aside though, [i]Resident Evil[/i] is a fantastic game and I'm looking forward to playing the other scenario and the rest of the series. It's much more of a thinking game than it lets on and if you enjoy strategy, speedrunning, or puzzles you'll have a great time.

You know of the grand Spencer Mansion in the Arklay Mountains, with its baroque dining rooms and gloomy, thunder-clapped corridors, even if you’ve never been there. You already know what monsters stalk its halls, even if you’ve never faced them. You know where they come from, even if you’ve never penetrated the secret research centre beneath its marbled floors and crimson carpets.

And you know [i]why[/i] all of the above exists, even if you’ve never confronted the Umbrella Corporation directly.

Of course, you might have been there and done that—back when there were [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYvCHm3Ov4&ab_channel=Aidan%27sThing]clowns farting in the basement[/url].

But let’s say you haven’t, with or without farts and clowns. You know what went down that night because you’ve likely felt the consequences.

When the virus inevitably slipped into that strange piece of Americana in the Midwest and sent a cop’s first day careening into a gnarled and bloody nightmare.

When the devoted sister pursued the truth to a secret island and then an Antarctic base, where that same truth, cowering before death, revealed itself to be incestuous and grotesque in the extreme.

When the cop-turned-secret-agent penetrated a decaying rural community in Spain to rescue the President’s daughter, only to be again confronted with the mysterious woman in a dress and her sinister employer in shades.

When the bland husband tracked his less bland wife to a bayou in the Deep South, and found another bio-hazard disaster waiting for him—one where the once evil corporation was doing the clean-up and not the instigating. For a change.

And on, and on, and on. There’s no end to the consequences of that night, not soon.

Not when it helped define the survival horror genre as we know it.

Not when Umbrella’s demented research crossed platforms and mediums and created a multimedia franchise that still entrances us with its monsters and melodrama.

I’ve written before about my problems with remakes and my lack of interest them, knowing there’s a glaring hypocrisy to it all: one of my favourite games is a remake, and one I would choose to play over the original if I had to make a choice (I don’t).

Shinji Mikami’s return to his 1996 classic resulted in something quite rare: the creation of another. As terrifying as it is beautiful, [i]Resident Evil: Remake[/i] was a bold statement on the efficacy of Mikami’s original concept and the strengths of survival horror.

It’s a second bat at a haunted house with zombies and monsters wrapped in an appallingly stupid narrative, yet [i]still[/i] it triumphs.

It’s a triumph encoded in the foundations of the mansion. This illogical nightmare of an edifice that only game designers could have built. To beat [i]Resident Evil[/i], remake or otherwise, basement or clown farts, is to beat the Spencer Mansion—to evade its traps, solve its puzzles, repel its assaults, and master its topography.

It makes no overtures to reality, existing only to conjure horror from the shape and colour of its halls.

In this it proves itself a master. It’s probably why you know about it even if you haven’t played it.

But you should. You should step inside where there's no turning back, face its monsters, penetrate its research facility, and confront what hides beneath it all—if only to set those consequences in motion.

For a long time, I used to think RE games were a complete joke for some odd reason. I played one and two as a little kiddy. I never got far in those games and I remember nearly browning my pants a few times. After a 30 minute session of Resident Evil 1 I used to watch my door when I went to sleep, just to see if it opens up by itself, and sometimes I thought it did. 

Long, long after that I started to truly appreciate what RE's are about. The gameplay is about making decisions, constantly. Where to go? Why am I going there? There might be monsters on the way, what should I bring along? What route should I take? Should I burn this corpse or save the fuel for later? Do I need to take healing items with me? Should I shoot or run and save ammo? Should I save or is this a bad spot? And it's so well done that it never gets boring. Things kill you really fast and nothing seems to stay dead. You're always on your toes, thinking about your next move. 

The story seems quite simple at first, but it won't be long until you start finding layers after layers of more complex ideology behind what's happening. You realize it's not just a game about zombies, it's a deep story that requires thinking and reading to uncover, and the greatest thing is that it spans through most of the whole franchise. [h1]Resident Evil[/h1]
[b]Review in one sentence[/b]:
"One word: Masterpiece".

To be honest it took me some getting used to.  Even though this game is a remake of the original, it's already showing its age.  When I first started playing, the controls felt clunky, the fixed camera angles were annoying, and I kept getting lost and confused.

Eventually I got the hang of it, and started enjoying the game a lot more.  I got used to how the controls worked with the angles, and figured out how the game worked.  Having now also beaten Resident Evil 2, I can say that I prefer the 3rd person perspective to the fixed cameras.  The fixed cameras do add something, though.  They can frame the scene to highlight certain spots, add to the atmosphere, and make things more scary.  It's tense when you can hear an enemy nearby, but don't quite know where they're at.  It can get annoying sometimes, though, when you just can't see what you're trying to do.  As I played, the controls began to feel more natural, and for me personally a controller smoothed the experience.  Camera and controls aside, Resident Evil definitely has a formula, and it can take some getting used to.  At first I would get lost in the mansion, forgetting where I had already been and missing stuff.  As I played, though, I began to pick up on more stuff and began to progress much faster.  It can be frustrating to get stuck, but in hindsight the puzzles are well made, and progressing is really enjoyable.

Overall, Resident Evil (REmake) was a lot of fun to play, leaving me confused as to why I hadn't played it sooner.  Even if I feel like this remake could use a remake, it's a lot of fun to play, and I highly recommend everyone gives it a shot.

I'd rather be eaten by a zombie in real life than play RE 1 again. I don't think I've experienced such tedium from a game before. It's a shame because the game looks good and has a great atmosphere.

Edit: I replayed the game (and actually finished it this time). Whether or not it has anything to do with me playing RE 2 through 6 or being a more competent person, but I actually enjoyed playing this game. However, I still really don't recommend. REmake is filled with as many technical problems as it has technical achievements. 

My favorite part of the game was allowing myself to get immersed into the atmosphere and subjecting myself to things I didn't want to do, like going down a narrow hallway when I know there's deadly enemies in there. In comparison to the other games, most of the puzzles were top notch and actually had me think. Additionally, even though I personally didn't like the stiff controls and camera, it somewhat made the game more exciting since I had less control of the situation.

Unfortunately, my likes end there. While I did like the control scheme for the atmospheric pleasures, I would rather have had a modern control scheme and camera for better flow. I didn't really have an issue with moving around, it's just that the camera constantly changing made it confusing for map recognition and finding certain items that were basically invisible to the human eye that could only be found unless you spammed the interaction button everywhere. The map does help to a degree, but I used it way more than I would have liked to in a horror game. Additionally, the map had a lack of reference points, like which doors require which keys which I think would have been a good feature so you don't have to try every locked door in the entire mansion. 

Additionally, traversing anywhere is a pain in the ass. It takes so long just to get from one part of the map to another, not because you walk slow or anything, but because of all the inconveniences you encounter along the way. For one, the doors. For second, pretty much every enemy you decide not to kill. Particularly in the first half of the game where ammo is limited to handgun ammo, you'll probably try to run around most enemies. However, every time you submit to fleeing just means there's another time you'll have to get around the zombie or dog or hunter since they'll still be there. What makes for a decent game mechanic turns into an annoyance real quick as you sacrifice health instead of safety which I think is kinda stupid for a literal zombie game.

Combining my previous gripes with the fact that your inventory is the size of a shrunken testicle causing you to backtrack to a safe room every time you find an item you want, and you find that RE1 does a good job at wasting your time. I think my play through would have been half as long if these issues weren't there. Like I said before, I still had fun with this game and possibly that's all that counts, but I would still deter people who are unsure if they would like the game. I recommend playing one of the newer games of the RE series if you're new to RE, or if you really want to see this game, go watch game play first and see if you like it.

Resident Evil HD Remaster Review

If you played this way back then, you are in for some fond memories and waves of nostalgia…

Please note that this Review may contain spoilers from the Original game 

Some key points that this Remaster offers:

1.	Nostalgia
2.	5.1 Surround Sound
3.	1080p
4.	16:9
5.	Enhanced Visuals
6.	Upgraded Controls

Remastered:

It’s the same great experience, just remastered for current Gen systems. They did a wonderful job with this remaster though! The game looks and feels beautiful! Every corner you take brings back memories of fear and dread… Wondering if it's here where it jumps out or killed you so many times in a row, over and over again! It’s amazing and rewarding just as it is punishing.

The game's age shines through and why wouldn’t it, it's practically 20 years old. It is thanks to the original that we have the horror genre that we have today. We owe a lot to this game and what it gave us over the years. It is a remaster of a remake and that can be taken as further proof of how incredible this game is and what it offers.
The Remastered version boasts a variety of improvements to the game.

We have 5.1 surround sound that will totally haunt you as you explore this seemingly unending mansion. What is a remaster without HD, RE1 sports 1080p now with updated visuals and textures! Character models were updated as well, and the lighting and shadow rendering was also improved. The game's world looks absolutely beautiful when the lighting catches it just right!

The control system has been given a slight upgrade to make it a tad friendlier to use, especially for new players. Those who played it back in 1996 will remember full well how taxing and unforgiving this game was. The save system, limited inventory space, and the camera control… All designed to stack up the difficulty to offer you one hell of a challenge, and it is still there!

To adjust the game mechanics with the updated visuals they had to improvise on how some mechanics work to keep the same great atmosphere ever-present. This is and was the birth of the Horror Survival Genre we have come to love… 
Those gut tearing puzzles requiring you crossing hallways full of undead to progress through the game are still here waiting for you. Don’t forget all those hidden keys and fun jump scares… They're right here waiting for you! 

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:

I loved every moment of it; however, I can understand how very few people who actually played either the original or the GameCube remake will enjoy it. As beautiful as the game looks, you can clearly tell it is old and very dated. If I look at it, I see memories of a much younger me playing this game having a blast winning or dying… 

Other than the aged visuals, is the aged gameplay mechanics. Games back then were incredible more difficult to play, and what better example than RE1. The limited saving, if you ran out of ink ribbons, there was simply no saving. The extreme lack of weapons and ammo. It is here where you were taught to rather save those bullets until you really needed them, or couldn’t run away! The difficulty itself didn’t really matter, even on lower difficulties, It only took a few hits for your character to die. 

This however was part of the charm and extreme fun that was gaming back then, life was so much simpler back then, and I thank this Remaster for reminding me of that and all the other fond memories it reminded me of…

This has aged surprisingly well for a game that's almost 19 years old. The pre-rendered graphics still look great for the most part (though the textures do look outdated in some cases) and the gameplay is as good as it has always been, with plenty of weapons to use and a good variety of enemies to fight over the course of the game, including some great boss fights. The fixed camera angles could put some people off, but I feel that it works very well with this game and it doesn't take long for you to get used to it. The level design of this game is really good, with a real sense of progression as you make your way through the Spencer mansion and its surrounding locations, though I still have a couple of problems with it that I'll mention later. The story is not very deep, though it does still manage to be enjoyable with cutscenes that give you a better understanding of what is going on, and serve as a good way to segment the game. 

The main way I think that this game has aged poorly is in the amount of backtracking you will end up doing, as you'll end up passing through the same areas dozens of times over the course of the game, and this is made far worse by the animation that plays whenever a door is opened. I know that this made sense at the time of the game's release to hide loading screens, but here it seems unnecessary to me, and it would have been good if the remaster included a feature to skip or speed up these animations to make the backtracking less tedious. 

Overall, I am impressed with how well this game held up over the years, and although the cracks do start to show, they shouldn't prevent you from having a good experience.

Resident Evil Remake (REmake) is the best of the classic style RE games (if you're not sure what a classic-style resident evil game is, I'll briefly give you a definition: a classic-style Resident Evil game is comprised of zombies, fixed camera angles, tank controls, limited resources, inventory management, and many puzzles to solve). Arguably it's the best Resident Evil game of all, and arguably it's also the best that the survival horror genre has to offer; while it isn't as scary as the likes of Silent Hill 2, the 'survival' aspect is much stronger in REmake. 

There are simply more factors pertaining to your 'survival' to think about while in the process of playing REmake than there are while playing any other survival horror title. It makes for a more interesting experience. For example:
-use of kerosene is important in REmake, but it's a limited resource. Where should you use it and where would it be a waste? Also, there's the matter of where you should take kerosene from first (your fuel canteen can only carry enough for 2 uses and there are multiple kerosene tanks in the game); for example, things might be relatively safe early on in the game in one specific area of the mansion that is quite far away from a save room, so might drawing kerosene from that particular tank be wise?
- then, if you're playing as Chris, there's the matter of whether or not you should use your Old Key (keys in limited supply which are single-use (Jill has a lockpick so doesn't need Old Keys)) or save it for later. For example, there's a door locked that can only be unlocked from one side with an Old Key, which leads back as a shortcut to an area that is immediately accessible right from the beginning of the game. Would it be wise to use your limited resource to open a shortcut when it might be used to obtain something better?
- then, there's single-use defensive items (Chris and Jill each can carry two different kinds, one of which being unique to that character), which, if equipped, can be used to break free from the grapple of a creature and completely avoid the damage they would otherwise have inflicted. Does this particular creature deal sufficient damage to make it worth using up a defensive item? 
- there's a door with a damaged doorknob, which you will be warned upon trying to use, that it might fall apart some time soon (rendering use of the door impossible). Is this side of the mansion otherwise easy to access, and is it safe?
- then, there's a few herb patches which you can use; is it wise to use this now? Is it easily accessible otherwise?
- there's a few instances in the mansion of rooms that are high-value in terms of resources, like healing, for example, that they have available; they're quite likely to contain more items than you can carry upon discovering them. Would returning for the items you can't carry be wise here? Have you got enough healing/ammo for it to be worth the trade?
- the Spencer Mansion has several different routes that you can take. Where are resources best spent? Which is the fastest route? Is the fastest necessarily the safest?

I've excluded a few other variables that come into play which would be major spoilers. On the final point there, ie, the interconnected nature of the Spencer Mansion; while I concede that there are other survival horror games, including other games in the Resident Evil series, which also have an interconnected level design, it's the fact that, in REmake, there's so many other variables in play that make the process of navigating the mansion so much more interesting.

Now, onto visuals: the game looks amazing, so eerie. It looks like a faded old antique painting that has come to life; this singular effect is achieved by juxtaposing faintly grainy textures with clear-cut animations like the reflections in the glass, the flickering candles, and the flashes of lightning. 

The puzzles are decent, requiring close attention to detail. Although, there's nothing too taxing on the brain. The objects involved in the puzzles have a pleasing gothic element to them. REmake is completely committed to the gothic aesthetic, unlike RE2 which, although fantastic in its own right, is a little strained in this respect, with its art-gallery-turned-police-station setting. At one point as part of a puzzle you even need to play on the piano a dreary part of Beethoven's 'Moonlight Sonata', which fits in PERFECTLY with the tone of the mansion. 

The story in REmake is incredibly basic and fairly forgettable, although, mercifully, there's nothing quite so painfully cringeworthy as the cinematic for the ps1 original. The unremarkable story is a matter of indifference for me because everything else about the game is so good.

However, as a nitpick, there is one thing that has always irritated me wherever it occurs in survival horror games, and that's when you encounter another character who is somehow already behind a door that was locked until the moment you just opened it, having gone through an incredibly obscure and convoluted process to first find the key. But, this isn't important and it certainly doesn't detract from the quality of the game in every other respect.

Strongly recommended.

[h1] “It’s a weapon. It’s really powerful, especially against [i]living[/i] things.”[/h1]

Oh RE1, how I love you. Playing you is like watching a classic horror movie. Much like Evil Dead, Dawn of the Dead, or [i]SCREAM[/i]. You don’t throw on the first Resident Evil game to watch a modern splosion-fest or deep plot with award winning acting. You put on any of those excellent, classic, and cheesy films to have a good time. That’s what the first Resident Evil is. A good time. It’s the loony grandpa telling crazy and fun stories to it’s grandkids like Evil Within and Dead Space. [i]“Back in my day we only had 6 inventory slots, 4 weapons, and had to save our progress on a god darned typewriter!”[/i]. Oh grandpa, you’re so wacky.

Okay, to be fair this isn’t [i][b]TECHNICALLY[/b][/i] that game I played as a 12 year old in 1997, getting my hands on it for the first time by renting it from a video store. I remember having to tell my grandmother “It’s not ACTUALLY Evil, it’s okay for me to play!”. I remember having it for weeks and weeks before they let me just keep the damned thing. I still have my original RE1 in it’s PS1 cardboard/plastic longbox. But this is not that game from 1996. This game on steam is actually the “Remake” for Gamecube, released in 2002. But, let’s be honest. It’s the same damn game with a smattering of 2002 paint and some added sections. I’m not sure I can tell the difference between the two anymore. My memory isn’t that good. 

[h1]Story[/h1]

Mansion has zombies. Zombies eat people. You’re a member of an elite local task force S.T.A.R.S… I mean, I have to think most people know the story of this game by now. If I say EVIL DEAD you think of a man with a chainsaw hand killing bad things in a cabin. If I say DAWN OF THE DEAD you think of a zombie outbreak and people trying to survive. If I say RESIDENT EVIL you think of Jill Valentine in a mansion nearly becoming a [h1] JILL SANDWICH[/h1] I truly can’t imagine anyone into video games and even slightly interested in this genre doesn’t know what this game is about in some form. Let me move on and get to the part most of you are likely wondering about.

[h1]Gameplay/Performance[/h1]
Now, before we go any further let me say something. This is an [b]OLD[/b] game. It doesn’t look bad for an OLD game though. Nor does it run bad at all. You have games like Max Payne, Fallout 3, or even the Still Life games which simply won’t run on modern systems without some serious patches or workarounds. I know, I’ve tried. Resident Evil runs like it was released yesterday. Well, that’s not fair, most games released these days don’t work this well. I installed it, booted it, and played it. It was that easy. No crashes, no bugs, no issues.

There are some caveats however. Let me tell you about those:

[b]Camera Angles[/b]
This game has fixed camera angles. Meaning, the camera does not follow your character. At all. This is about 99% obnoxious, but it works. Shinji Mikami [i](the director)[/i] uses these set angles to set scenes and instill fear. Fear of what's right in front of you [i]here: [/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2372105763

Or [i]what’s down this hallway? :[/i]

A classic horror game that has aged pretty well, and whether you are a new player, and old player, or someone who's played other RE games but not this one, you can buy with confidence. I remember playing the 1996 title on PC, and I instantly loved the game. When I heard that there was a new and updated version coming out on Nintendo Gamecube in 2002, I purposely bought the console so I can play the game. I've been contemplating it on Steam ever since its release because I remembered it being very good back then, but I didn't remember much of the story and the content. However, I was waiting for it to be on special because I also didn't know what to expect from it in 2020/2021 having played the latest graphically immersive RE7, RE2 and RE3. I thought I wouldn't enjoy as much and that it would be perhaps a little boring even, but let me tell you that I WAS WRONG ! This game is absolutely worth it, on special or not. It turns out I had forgotten a lot more of it than I anticipated, and it felt like a whole new game. It felt fresh, the graphics and visual effects are absolutely amazing for a game of that time, and it really doesn't seem so far behind even with modern standards. The way it's presented is quite unique as the camera angles are fixed for each area of the game, so you'll either love it or hate it, but hopefully love it, because that is actually what allowed this game to look so gorgeous for its time and make it even more immersive. It took me about 20 hours to complete it with Chris on a first run, which is a lot of game time for the money. I know, I know, you may complete it considerably faster depending on your level OCD and whether you have played the game before or not, but either way you can replay the game with the 2nd character as well for a different experience. I also recommend playing the game on the highest difficulty right away, which in the beginning translates to "medium", because I played it on easy thinking it was medium and I found it to be a little too easy, and I ended up with way more ammunition and healing elements than I could use, or at least don't be too conservative with your items, especially with pistol ammo and healing kits. Even though it feels like you may be short on them in the beginning, you'll start stacking them faster than you think. Finally, I recommend using a controller if possible as it helps smoothen the slightly clunky movements of your character.

Having never played Resident Evil before I decided to pick this up and see what the fuss was all about. I honestly wish I hadn't. This game plays like a badly designed 3D game from the late 90s PC era. In my 7 hours of playing this game I ran into the following:

-Bad camera angles. There is no excuse in this day and age to have the camera constantly flip on you like so that what was left is now up or down or whatever. 
-Inability to aim. Seriously I could aim shots better in most 90s PC games than I can this game!
-Way too dark. I know some are going to say that's part of the atmosphere, but making the game so you can't see your hand in front of your face in places is not atmospheric, it's also not realistic. There is such a thing as ambient light and we can see a little in the dark. Plus how hard is it to at least give the character a lantern or something?
-Limited saving. I'm sorry but limited saving by inventory items is a design choice that needs to go away. I don't care if it supposedly adds to the atmosphere as fans say. Some of us got limited time to play games and need to be able to save when we need to save without penalty, and penalizing players for saving by limiting it to hard to find inventory items is just bad design. Replaying sections over and over and over because you are out of save items is not fun.
-Limited ammo, but enemies come back. Yep you heard that right. I had new enemies show up in areas I had cleared out (even by burning bodies). Add this to the fact you can't aim worth squat means prepare to waste your limited ammo constantly.
-Enemies are HP sponges. Sorry but it really should not take me 11 shots from a pistol to drop a zombie. Ever. What are they wearing, bullet proof vests?

Overall this just compounded into a game I could not enjoy at all. What the company should have done is remake the game, but give players options to play it like the old version, or let new players play it with some changes. But as it is, I can see this only appeasing to fans of the original version of the game only, and not to new players trying to figure out what the big deal is of the series.

In 1993, a CAPCOM dev team led by Shinji Mikami (now known as CAPCOM Production Studio 4) started production on a new game. It was originally proposed to be a remake of a legendary Famicom horror game, Sweet Home. However the developers quickly abandoned the idea and instead decided to create a new IP named Biohazard which takes heavy inspiration from Sweet Home and is a spiritual successor to the game. Biohazard released in 1996 on the original Playstation and PC, under the name "Resident Evil" outside of Asia. The game was a success to the amazement of the developers who didn't expect a horror game to sell this well, which kickstarted the franchise that is still running to this date. However many of the developers were still not happy with the game including Mikami himself as they could not fully realise their idea due to the PS1 hardware limitations. Two more versions of the game were released on PS1 in the following years and the game was ported to Sega Saturn in 1997.

In 2002 as Capcom struck a deal with Nintendo, a series of Capcom games was coming to Nintendo Gamecube and among them was a remake of the first Resident Evil game. Taking advantage of the hardware, it featured updated graphics, new gameplay mechanics such as Crimson Head zombies, tons of new content such as new areas, bosses etc. and changes to existing puzzles. In 2014, this version of the game was ported to 8th gen consoles and PC. It's the version sold on Steam.

The artstyle is one of the biggest changes between the original game from 1996 and the remake. While the original version was very saturated, slightly cartoonish and well lit due to the graphical limitations of the time, the Remake is leaning more towards stylised realism and has mostly desaturated, brown-ish colours and a lot of environmental weather effects such as fog, lighting bolts etc. that enhance the atmosphere further. This is also the first RE game to have faces of main characters based on real people, most famous being the Canadian actress Julia Voth who is Jill's face model.

The story revolves around the S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team, one of the two police special operations teams serving in Raccoon City, a city in USA known for being the home for the farmaceutical company Umbrella Corporation. After numerous mysterious murders related to cannibalism in the nearby Arklay mountains, the Bravo Team was sent in to investigate. However the police department soon lost contact with the team and Alpha Team was sent to find out what happened to Bravo. They find Bravo's crashed helicopter and get attacked by zombie dogs, taking shelter in a nearby mansion. The mansion is however filled to the brim with zombies and mutants. The surviving Alpha team members, Jill Valentine, Chris Redfield, Barry Burton and Albert Wesker attempt to escape the mansion and find out who caused this mess.

There are two playable characters from Alpha team, Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield. Jill is the easier one to play as. She is often assisted by Barry, who helps her out of tough situations and provides items and additional firepower. Jill also has more inventory space and a lockpick, allowing her to open certain locked doors without a key. Chris on the other hand starts with a zippo lighter and has higher headshot chance with weapons.

The gameplay is very metroidvania-ish, you run around mansion, gather keys to open doors to allow you to explore new areas, complete puzzles to get important items to advance the story and avoid or fight the infected that are all around the environment, with occasional boss fights. The game features multiple save rooms where you can deposit your items and save the game without the fear of getting attacked. The camera view is presented in fixed camera angles and tank controls. A new mechanic in the remake that wasn't in the 1996 original are crimson heads. 

Regular human zombies transform approximately 15-30 minutes after death (depending on difficulty) into a stronger enemy type, Crimson head, which can run much faster and is incredibly lethal. The only way to prevent this is to  burn the body or land a headshot. Another notable new mechanic are the defensive items, which allow you to escape an enemy's grab immediately without losing health. They are usually in the form of grenades, tazers or daggers. The game encourages you to avoid attacking zombie humans at all cost unless it is neccessary (costing you much needed ammo and fuel), which ramps up the tension. Boss fights are rather simplistic.

Overall, the game is an excellent survival horror and I reccomend it.

(Based on the my experience playing the game for the first time as Chris on Normal Mode.)

Graphics:
I had to install a mod that lowers the resolution to make it playable on my potato laptop, but the game still looks phenomenal! The dynamic lighting and the cinematic angles really adds to the tense and dreadful atmosphere.

Audio/Soundtrack:
The soundtrack is amazing. I've been a big fan of atmospheric (video game) OST. If the setting does not make you feel a bit tense, the soundtrack will definitely do the job. My favorite song had to be the "Save Room Theme" because it was the only room I felt relieved to be in. There were a few audio glitches during cutscenes, but they are not game-breaking.

Gameplay:
The game used tank controls and fixed camera angles. It felt awkward at first, but after a while I got used to them quickly. For those trying to get used to them, I'd recommend playing with movement in the dining and opening area of the mansion. Controls can also be customized as well! You'll be shooting (or avoiding) monsters, scavenging, solving puzzles, and managing item inventory throughout the game. It's simple but effective.

Difficulty:
There's multiple difficulty options, but I thought the game was fair in difficulty at normal. The beginning of the game was the toughest part but it steadily got manageable.
 
Story:
Not the best story I've seen, but it gets the job done. I love the characters in the game though, they strike a balance between cheesy and good acting. Definitely has that (top-quality) "B-Horror" charm to it.

Others:
My favorite part of the game was actually the puzzles. They strike a good balance between thought-provoking and accessible; there wasn't a puzzle I felt that overstayed its welcome, and there wasn't a lot to drag the game either. Every time I solved a puzzle, I felt very accomplished.
As beautiful as fixed camera angles are, sometimes they can make an area feel disorientating. Thankfully, there's a map that shows your location.
 
Verdict:
Overall, I had a blast playing this game. I intend on getting that 100% achievement for this game! I'd say you should definitely buy this game if you're a survival horror fan. Definitely come into the game with an open-mind, the controls are not what I consider beginner-friendly. However, they add (in a positive way) to the game, and without it, the game would definitely not be the same. (There's an alternative control scheme but I don't recommend it personally.) 8/10

Resident Evil is a classic fixed-camera horror game, originally released for the Playstation 1, extensively remade for the Nintendo Gamecube and now re-released for PC. As a member of S.T.A.R.S., a special division of the Raccoon City Police, the player participates in an investigation of a series of gruesome murders taking place in the remote Arklay Mountains. After being ambushed and overwhelmed in the woods they are forced to retreat and take shelter in a seemingly abandoned mansion.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Throughout the game the player has to explore and navigate the many rooms of the mansion as well as solving puzzles and finding keys to progress. Outside of a map keeping track which rooms already have been visited and which doors remain locked, there isn't much explicit guidance which can lead to a lot of time spent simply exploring and picking up various puzzle items without immediately knowing how to use them. Examining an item from the inventory menu can often reveal greater insight into how to use it, but even then it may not be obvious until later in the game.
Much of the game is spent backtracking through the mansion. The player character's inventory is of very limited capacity and has to fit weapons, healing items and puzzle pieces alike. It's not possible to carry all of them at once, making it necessary to stash some in item boxes, which can be found in save rooms. The player has to decide what to make room for and what to leave behind in order to be able to pick up more items as they keep exploring or come back for them at a later point.
While slowly moving from room to room the player will encounter many zombies roaming the halls, who will attempt to grab and bite them. Combat generally is as simple as pointing a weapon at an enemy and shooting until they drop to the ground, however there are caveats. The amount of ammo to be found throughout the game is limited and sometimes a room may not be worth the expense to clean out for a variety of reasons, including that zombies could come back stronger if they aren't appropriately dealt with. It is up to the player to decide whether they want to clear out a route for good or if they only want to quickly pass through, possibly using up a healing item instead of ammo if they get injured. Room for movement is generally tight and claustrophobia-inducing, especially with the control scheme that a fixed-camera perspective enforces. Since the player isn't always able to see what's directly in front of them, some encounters might be difficult to gauge visually, so forethought into how to approach an encounter as well as sometimes just retreating pays off.
The game can be saved only at typewriters placed throughout the game, using up ink ribbons which can be picked up and stored like any other item. Enough of them are placed in the game to allow comfortably frequent saving, if spread out between every other point of progress.

[h1]Storytelling[/h1]
The game allows to choose from two playable characters who apart from having their respective gameplay differences, also have unique cutscenes and interactions with other characters. The main plot remains largely unaffected by this however.

Cutscene interruptions are fairly rare and usually only happen after major progress milestones. Most of the lore is conveyed through diaries and logs left behind in the mansion.

[h1]Remaster Differences and Technical Issues[/h1]
The original game used a tank control scheme (D-PAD Up = Walk Foward, D-PAD Left and Right = Turn Character), which makes moving around initially feel rather awkward and takes a while to get used to. However the game's encounters have been designed with this in mind and are decently playable after some adjustment period.
The remaster added modern omni-directional analogue stick movement, which generally is much easier to control, however due to the fixed-camera perspective the walk direction corresponding to the stick direction can suddenly change when transitioning between screens. Both control schemes can be used at any time by simply switching the thumb between D-PAD and stick on the fly. It should be noted however that using analogue movement controls can trivialize portions of the game, since they weren't expected to exist back when the game was originally conceived.

Widescreen support has been added with the remaster, however it may be worth considering disabling it. The original pre-rendered backgrounds were made for an aspect ratio of 4:3 and in order to make them fill the screen the game zooms in on them and pans the screen according to where the player character currently is visible. This can look very distracting because the perspective isn't properly preserved anymore. The game allows sticking with the original 4:3 ratio which will add black bars to the sides of the screen, but have the actual image remain in a static position, as well as allowing a wider field of vision, because the entire image is shown at all times.

Some people have encountered a "slow motion" bug, with the game randomly stuttering and playing poorly, it appears to not be known what causes this and how to fix it when it happens. I personally have never encountered it in my entire playthrough, but it may be something to look out for.

New costume options for the player characters have been added, one each, modelled after their appearances in Resident Evil 5. They can be selected before starting a new game.

[h1]Final Judgement[/h1]
I've only recently discovered Resident Evil for myself, and while you can certainly tell that it's a product of its time, it still conveyed an intriguing atmosphere as I was uncovering the mystery of the mansion. The fixed camera perspective might be somewhat frustrating to deal with at times, such as getting injured when you cannot really see what is moaning and swiping at you immediately in front, but it also brings a certain creepy mood to the environment that would have been lost if you were allowed full control over the camera.
Some of the puzzles can take a while to figure out, often because it can be a long time before an item actually becomes relevant or because you forgot to properly examine it, but the solutions themselves are not so otherworldly that it is ever a requirement to bust out a walkthrough if you pay enough attention to the hints that the game already provides you with.
The visuals of the environment have aged incredibly well. Although while under strict scrutiny you can tell that the backgrounds are pre-rendered and that live-rendered characters stick slightly out, it is practically never noticeable while playing normally (unless you play in the bad widescreen mode). This game made the most out of its old rendering technique back in the and still holds up rather well because of it.

Recommending at sale price.

[b]Full Review:[/b] I’m trying to finally take a  deep dive into the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise, having only played [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/drambiguous/recommended/254700/ ][i]Resident Evil 4[/i][/url] (which is often considered both a high point and a turning point for the series). [i]RE4[/i] has a stronger action theme throughout, while the original game was pure survival horror, pioneering the genre. Earlier examples of survival horror games were much more rudimentary, the most notable of which, [i]Sweet Home[/i], serving as a major influence on the original [i]Resident Evil[/i].

There exist numerous versions of this game (8 at the time of this writing), though in my opinion only 3 of note: The original from 1996, the 2002 remake, and then this one, the 2015 remaster, which is based on the 2002 remake, though with better graphics. I haven’t played the 96 original and I don’t really intend to, as the changes in the remake seem for the better.

The gameplay of [i]Resident Evil[/i] is slow paced, puzzle-centric, and for much of the game you feel as if you’re just scraping by in combat situations. This combined with the need to scavenge for weapons, items, and ammo does help to emphasize the survival aspect of the game.

The atmosphere is pretty great throughout, though I feel it shines strongest during the early game exploration of the mansion. I feel as if the atmosphere does taper off at some points throughout, though it’s never bad, just not always great.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2261974256
The game isn’t without its flaws and even with the updates from this remake/remaster some elements still remain dated. The original game featured tank controls, which I’m not a fan of, and while the game offers an option for more modern controls, they’re still not perfect. Aiming sucks, especially when trying to score headshots against zombies, which is integral to gameplay. You can’t move while shooting either. The camera changes can sometimes be a bit wonky when switching angles, though to be fair that 
works fine if playing with the games intended tank controls.

My biggest gripe with the game though is that much of the game comes down to trial and error, which combined with having a limited number of saves and only being able to save at typewriters scattered about the map (the checkpoints of the game), ends up being rather frustrating at times. I don’t mind some trial and error gameplay for my puzzle solving. Nor do I mind the checkpoint system, it can even work very well for survival horror, such as in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/drambiguous/recommended/214490/][i]Alien Isolation[/i][/url]. However there were a few too many times that failing a puzzle resulted in a death, requiring me to redo a chunk of the game, and being limited on the number of saves you have make you think twice about if you should save or try to hold out longer. Not to mention that some of the puzzles are rather obtuse in how you’re supposed to solve them. Eventually I settled on using a guide for the puzzles, which helped some, but I’d also rather just not play with a guide. It’s difficult to say if that was the right decision, but I digress.

That said, I can forgive a lot of the gameplay flaws simply because at the time this game originally released survival horror barely existed and 3D games were so new that many things that were revolutionary then are considered primitive now. I think approaching the game knowing this helps make the experience more enjoyable, especially for anyone -such as myself- that enjoys the history and development of video games over the years.
