That kind of response just feels like Capcom shat this port out with little regard to their PC audience, ♥♥♥♥ slapped us across the face, and then told us to thank them for it. There’s probably a way to mod that out, but I didn’t feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with it and just played with a controller. Thankfully, the game plays pretty well with a controller and I was able to hide the mouse just fine. Though I’m still annoyed that that Capcom can’t be arsed to fix what should never have been a problem.

The game also doesn’t allow you to set your resolution above 1080p in game, though it’s pretty easy to force by editing the config file. I can forgive this since I doubt 1440p was all that common in 2015. Check this Steam [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/304240/discussions/0/620703493312273360/]thread[/url] for how to force 1440p.

It took me about 14 hours real time to finish the game, and just under 10 hours of in game time. Most googling I’ve done suggest people finish this in the 10-12 hour mark, though I’m unsure if I was just slow, or if that’s based on the in game timer, which doesn’t factor in time spent redoing things after death.

Perhaps it sounds like I’m being overly critical of [i]Resident Evil[/i], but I still I enjoyed the game and I’m glad I played it. Given that it is somewhat dated it may not be worthwhile to everyone. Both the series itself and other more recent survival horror games have improved upon the genre immensely, and if you prefer the refinements that the years have brought us this will be a bit of an adjustment. Nonetheless, I would still recommend this game, though just with the aforementioned caveats in mind.

In this, the spooky month, I somehow always get it into my head that I want to play spooky games. I have a difficult relationship with horror—I love spooky games but hate actually being, well, spooked. It's a real conundrum and one that can be traced back to my weird childhood obsession with Resident Evil. Not the games—I played 2 up until the gun shop and that led to a few recurring nightmares. No, I was [b]obsessed[/b] with the campy, bizarre B-movie world of intricately connected lore. I had [b]game-changing theories[/b] about this long-running (and in hindsight very silly) story but I had to make do with scraps of pre-wiki forum threads and GameFAQs.

I moved on eventually and forgot my PhD-level knowledge of Umbrella. But when I was much older and [strike]far more dead inside[/strike] not so easily spooked, I took the opportunity a couple years back to finally play through the series that up till now only vaguely existed in my head. How did it compare to what I so vividly imagined?

I played the games in more or less release order, so by the time I reached REmake I was getting the hang of this whole survival horror thing. The trick is that the games aren't actually all that scary apart from a few, specifically crafted moments. They're more... tense, where you're constantly worrying about resources and long term planning, not the lizard monster jumping directly at your throat. Regardless, I had the knowledge from my run of PS1 Resident Evil. How different could this remake be?

Very different, actually, but in a very good way. REmake is one of the best examples of, well, remakes out there. It's not surprising the RE2 remake was so successful because this game set a precedent for excellent, thoughtful remakes that keep the feeling of the game you played while ditching the clumsiness or technical limitations of before. The stuff that stays the same is just better, like the devs took a mulligan and sunk it. Plus, there's tons of new story and set-pieces—my 90s trained lore background was pretty unprepared for Crimson Heads and Lisa Trevor.

It also looks real good, perfecting the borderline outdated pre-rendered background technique to its absolute maximum. This release is probably the best of the bunch since it includes every scrap of content ever appended to REmake. It also hacks together 60 FPS, a reasonable widescreen TV compromise and it offers a toggle for common sense controls. Listen, I know tank controls are better—my 1 thru Code Veronica runs taught me that—but giving the option opens the game up to players that would otherwise skip it. More options the better, right?

I have a soft spot for the PS1 original, because I love the campiness, but REmake is undoubtedly the better game (and much closer to what I had imagined all those years ago). It's just really fun and tense stomping all over the Metroidvania mansion, sussing out the silly puzzles and debating whether or not you have bullets to spare for that zombie in your way.

The HD remaster has some problems. From poor texture resolutions that clearly haven't been fully updated for modern monitors to some strange audio changes, this is not the best version of Resident Evil Remake (REmake) I have played to date. At least keyboard/mouse controls work reasonably well. For a game from 2002, it's more accessible than you might think, even if Capcom could have done more here.

Despite a slightly disappointing PC remaster, REmake is one of the most perfectly-paced and atmospheric horror games ever made. The lighting and design of the pre-rendered backgrounds still hold up incredibly well, aging far better than competing GameCube titles in 2002 like Eternal Darkness (arguably even better than RE4). The movement system, while taking some time to get used to, limits your options in a way that reinforces the moment-by-moment tension. Turning around to shoot a zombie while they inch closer towards you out of the camera's frame is one of the many ways REmake makes you feel like you're living a John Carpenter movie infused with the Gothic horror elements from Robert Wise’s The Haunting. Ammo scarcity along with limited saves reminds the player that their actions have consequences; failure is something to fear and learn from, not just an inconvenience. 

REmake's ability to make the player feel like they're in peril (not just being scared for the character on screen) through mechanics and game systems still surprises me to this day. That's not to mention the absolutely phenomenal score by Shusaku Uchiyama, Makoto Tomozawa, and Misao Senbongi, featuring iconic tracks like "Safe Haven" and "Main Hall". In many ways, the game is the pinnacle of its genre before survival horror took a backseat to 1st and 3rd person action shooters like Gears of War and RE4. Although, I'm really happy to see horror titles make a comeback over the past few years. 

Yeah, the voice acting and dialogue in REmake are corny and monotone as hell. Honestly, I kind of love that. They serve as a break from the tension of the rest of the game because the "off" localization comes off as somewhat endearing, not trite or uninspired. It's what distinguishes their performances from distressingly lifeless ones like Peter Dinklage in Destiny. In a way, the moments of hammy acting provide a sense of relief similar to the save rooms, even if they aren't nearly as hilarious as the original Resident Evil's most quotably terrible lines. 

Is REmake perfect? Well, that's kind of a silly question. No game is perfect. But for its genre, REmake comes damn close. If you love survival horror, this game is a must-play.

[h1]INSIGHT[/h1]

Resident Evil is a HD remastered version of the original remake of the first game that came out in 2001. Due to it being released only on the Gamecube at the time, along with RE:Zero and even RE4 at the time; its market sales were limited and thus not even got to experience what for me, is the definitive example of a remake done to its highest standard of remaking a game.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

With the High definition remastering, this remake looks remarkable, regardless of its old pre-rendered backgrounds that make it only look even more spectacular. The shadows, the lightning and the strategically placed camera angles help hone down the tense atmosphere this game provides.

And that’s right; this game was from the time where fixed camera angles were the staple of horror.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

Although it still maintains the old tank controls, the player has the option of opting for the newer control scheme; but any old RE veteran will wince and hiss at these aspects. Besides this, the game is largely dominated by dark and claustrophobic environments of limited manoeuvre leeway. Unlike the more modern Resident Evil titles, this game has a stronger emphasis on being tactical and thinking things through cautiously and carefully. Ammo is a serious consideration, along with health, item management and the way you precede forward in your search for progress and dealing with or avoiding enemies.

Dispatching enemies in the good old way is dangerous for several reasons, and of course one is for your ammo consumption. Whilst this will remove the threats, if you lock down on your dodging, you can save ammo, at worst, lose health – but it all comes down to skill and what you’re willing to lose. The game will throw more than just enemies at you: environmental hazards, boss fights and various puzzle that were more thought provoking back in those days than they are now.

You will rarely get a sense of power in this, and any sense you get will either be fear, tension or brief safety in the safe room. Any power earned will be your rewards for meeting certain objectives on normal or higher. But that’s if you can master the horror.

[h1]STORY[/h1]

The plot follows alpha team, an S.T.A.R.S. (Special tactics and rescue service) group who are sent to a mansion in the Arklay Mountains by Raccoon city to get back in touch with Bravo team, who were in turn sent to the area after reports of serious incidents of people being attacked and ‘eaten’. 

Of course, however; it doesn’t take things to go awry when their presence is felt, and the journey through survival begins.

[h1]AUDIO[/h1]

The game is strongly complimented by a re-worked score of the original soundtrack as well as new music. The ominous music fits well and helps build tension and set the tone for each environment. The voice acting in this series has always been an amusing topic; and although the voice acting has undoubtedly improved from this remake over its predecessor, it still has that lingering cheesiness and awkward writing and stiff acting usually conjured from good old classic Japanese culture and writing.

[h1]PERFORMANCE[/h1]
Whilst an old game, it will still require some oomph from your computer. It shouldn’t be too heavy for the mid-high range specs though. But playing on lower performance PC’s will result in slowdown in various areas and the cut scenes to sync out as the dialogue goes unimpeded but the visuals themselves lag behind.

[h1]REPLAYABILITY[/h1]

This remake offers a sizable amount of replaying, from the challenges the game gives you to the ones you can give yourself; such as knife runs, no saving, beating the game under a certain amount of time etc. But the game also offers classic horror gameplay alongside unlockables. Two new harder modes were added and two BSAA costumes for both Jill and Chris have been added from RE5.

You can choose to play as either Chris or Jill, whom both have their strengths and weaknesses. Jill has more slots and pick-locking abilities whereas Chris has stronger melee and a lighter off the get-go (you will also have the chance to play as Rebecca with Chris). Multiple endings can be achieved with each character and several weapons and costumes unlocked along the way as well as the aforementioned harder game modes such as ‘real survival’ and ‘invisible enemies’.

And as always, being on PC; allows for all kinds of modding shenanigans.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

[i]+ Strong replayability[/i]
[i]+ Classic remake of original title[/i]
[i]+ Powerful atmosphere and good sound design[/i]
[i]+ Good level and game design[/i]
[i]+ Superior to the original, surpassing it in all regards[/i]
[i]+ New enemies and bosses[/i]
[i]+ New costumes and game modes[/i]
[i]+ The pinnacle of remakes done right[/i]
[i]+/- Game does utilise tank controls but can be altered[/i]
[i]- Lower-end PC’s will be in for a nasty surprise. [/i]

Whilst the remake of 2 was exceptional and the remake for 3, whilst a good game in its own right, but lacked seriously as a ‘remake’ were decent continuations, the first and for the longest, the only RE remake still holds the bar high for not only respecting the original, but expanding upon it, improving the foundations on which it honours.

Faithful in every way to the 1996 classic whilst adding its own twists and turns to keep the game new and fresh for even returning veterans; the game solidified itself not only as a phenomenal horror title still bound to the old-school fixed camera angles, but also rose to the challenge and showed itself that despite being a remake of an older game, managed to surpass that older game and be the one that many people continue to play even now with great fondness.

This ladies and gentlemen, is the old-school horror that terrified as well as inspired a gaming generation alongside its younger brother Silent hill.

This is remaster of the 2002 Nintendo Gamecube remake of the 1996 PlayStation original game. But in reality, all you need to know is that this is a genre-defining awesome survival horror game worth your money.

While this game may feel a bit archaic in terms of controls and use of fixed-camera angles, these features make this game unique and up the level of tension all while adding to the overall eerie atmosphere courtesy of the beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds. The fact that this game still looks great after all these years is a testament on how well the game was remade. Replay value is high since you can play the game with two characters with slight differences in their stories and progression, as well as a number of unlockables and challenging achievements. 

Do note that this Steam version has some flaws. I noticed subtitles are usually not synched with the speed of the voice acting and that the "second disc" content (laboratory final area) has severe audio lag in the cutscenes. Maybe these problems were unique to my rig but thought they needed to be mentioned. 

Despite these issues this game still retains a masterpiece label in my book and it's a must have for any survival horror fan out there.

[h1]Plot[/h1]
S.T.A.R.S assigned Bravo Team to investigate a series of cannibalistic homicides conducted by an unidentified group of people near Arklay Mountains, after not hearing from Bravo Team, S.T.A.R.S decides to sent Alpha Team to search for them. Alpha Team finds Bravo Team's derelict helicopter on the ground and investigates, finding the body of its pilot, but no sign of the others. Soon into the search, Alpha Team is attacked by a pack of mutant dogs, Jill Valentine desperately tries to save her comrade from being eaten by the wild dogs, only to hopeless seen her partner get ripped apart. His comrades, unable to save him, are soon forced to flee from the dogs as well. In the commotion, pilot Brad takes off, stranding the remaining four members of Alpha Team behind, forcing them to run for a Mansion. 

Out of Alpha Team investigation force, only four members managed to reach the mansion - Jill, Cris, Barry and Wesker.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2179802434
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Unlike the previous game (Resident Evil 0), you can only play with one character at a time both have their pros and cons. Jill finds it easier with carrying things, opening things and with a few boss battles but finds it harder to use guns well and also doesn't have as much health as Chris. 

Chris finds it easier to aim, shoot, and has more health but has to use Old keys to open things and has less help from his partner during boss battles and also less carrying space. 

Most of the puzzles have been changed, and the player's character is now also equipped with a defensive weapon that can be used while being grabbed by the enemy. Jill's exclusive defence item is a stun gun, a weapon that temporarily floors enemies in the ground if they were at full health and Chris' defence item is a flash grenade, a weapon that can instantly decapitate most of the enemies. Another change is players can perform critical headshots on zombies using a handgun at any time. The camera position and movements are very pleasant. Resident Evil doesn't let you down when It comes to difficulty, out of all the games in the series, I considered this one the second on my list; the challenges and difficulty will actually make you think.

When it comes down to challenges the classic won't let you down. In every corner of the game, things can go really bad: a Zombie could bite you from behind, a dog could jump through a window, a Hunter could kill you in 1 FK* hit, a shark could rip you to pieces, a "dead" Zombie lying on the ground could bite your foot. Anyway, things could go bad so watch out. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2179802680
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The remake features all-new graphics, sound and also incorporates gameplay elements from the earlier instalments. Several new areas and rooms were added to the game, including a graveyard and a cabin in the woods. Other areas were are also condensed. For the HD Remaster, not only were the graphics and sound massively improved, but a new controller scheme was also implemented for those who do not want to use the classic controls. 

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
Now let talk about the real challenges. When you finish the game for the first time you unlock an extra mode called Real Survival; no Storage Box in this mode; including stronger enemies; NO auto-aim; less ammunition and herbs. 

You may be thinking: [quote=Rookie][i]Hmm, this mode seems hard, but I can beat it[/i].[/quote] Well, remember that I said challenge(s), after you beat this mode you unlock a new one called Invisible Enemy, yep, that's right the Zombies are invisible, including ALL the boss (Python, Tyrant, Plant42...) the whole lot. This mode is one the hardest I have seen in the series, It was not in the classic but I'm glad they put in the Remake. Ok, after days trying to beat this mode you finally did It! You will receive a reward for beating that Nightmare mode that won't let you down [b](Sorry, can't say what is it, find out for yourself)[/b] Congratulations! but that's not the end. There's one last mode called Dangerous Zombie, in this specific mode there's Zombie([b]s[/b]) that's carrying a bunch of grenades on its body.

[h1]Extra Mode[/h1]
The game also features many additional modes, secrets, and various endings over the original, as well as restoring the George Trevor sub-plot from the pre-release versions of the original game, while adding his daughter Lisa into the game.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Resident Evil is one of those games that changed the genre completely, one of the few survivor horrors who actually make you scared. It is you, the mansion, and your imagination. As it happens, that trio makes for a fine adventure, without the need for more monsters, more outbreaks, and more guns.

I get that it is a classic and I really tried to like it, but there are just too many annoying factors that make playing this game feel like a chore.

The most annoying is a combination of two things:
For one, your inventory size is ridiculously small. I started the game with Chris and he has six inventory slots. I constantly run past items that I cannot pick up because I lack the inventory space, because my inventory is already full with one or two keys, a weapon, some herbs and other random items that I found along the way and don't know the use for yet.
This results in constantly having to run to your storage box. I get that more experienced players will have less of a problem with that, but I'm on my first play-through and if I don't want to read spoilers, there is no possible way for me to know which items I currently have to carry with me to make progress. So I basically have to run back to the safe room every time I encounter a new obstacle and get the item to solve the puzzle or what ever.

The other thing are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ door animations. Every time you enter another room, there is a ~3 second animation of the door opening. Combined with the fact that you constantly have to backtrack because of your tiny inventory, this makes the game roughly 40% door opening animations. At a little less than 3 hours I am just done with looking at doors swinging open. 

I don't get why both of these things are necessary. I understand that limiting your inventory adds to the game play when it comes to resources like healing items, weapons and ammunition, but why do keys and other items relevant to the story progression share the same inventory limitation? It just doesn't make sense and is needlessly frustrating. "Hey I finally found a place to use the blue gem stone, now I just have to walk back to the nearest storage room, get the gem, go back to the room, use it and pick up the item that I get then go back to the storage room again to deposit it and I can get on with the game."

And these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ door animations make this ten times worse. Why do I have to wait 3 seconds every time I enter a room? The game is installed on an ssd, there should be no load times for those small rooms, it makes the game so annoying and I don't get why it has to be that way.

I might give the game another chance in a little while because there are definitely some very charming and fun elements and the atmosphere is incredible. I also read that Jill is a much more beginner friendly charakter than Chris. For now I really can't say that I enjoyed this game though.

A decent remaster of the original, but with caveats and concerns.

Disclaimer: I ran this game with a trainer which I deemed absolutely necessary after playing for 45 minutes and getting killed w/o saving. The trainer is the top mod for RE remastered and there's a reason why.

Having played the original back in 1996 I can say that the new version did it's best to keep most things the same with minor tweaks here and there. Unlike the RE 2 remaster which changes the game a great deal, you can more or less expect to play the 1996 version with incredible graphics.

There are a few things you should know before buying:

1) Camera angles will be the bane of your existence on PC. One room can have multiple (4-5) camera angles and they are not friendly to the W-A-S-D movement keys. They are quite infuriating, if you can't handle this I highly suggest using a controller.

2) Trainer is a must. As previously mentioned the game is so much more fun/better with a trainer. Zombies take about 6-8 bullets to put down on normal and the knife is laughably useless. I prefer slashing them once and being done with them. Healing items are plentiful but in true Resident Evil fashion there's not enough ammo, especially when it takes 30 9mm rounds to take down a pair of hunters.

3) The same stupidity from 1996 RE still exists here, you just have to accept it and live with it. What I mean by that is your character not being able to jump across a puddle to get to the other side, characters needlessly suggesting they split up like the Texas Chainsaw Massacre after seeing their friends killed and monsters roaming the mansion, and needing to spend half an hour of toiling to shut off a waterfall which has what would be considered a mild stream in order to go through it. They're all incredibly stupid situations you just have to laugh at.

Resident Evil is basically Backtracking: The Videogame™. You don’t “explore” the Spencer mansion; you develop a committed relationship with its hallways. 

You’ll pass through the same corridor so many times you start knowing the zombies by name. Every locked door is a promise that, in 40 minutes, you’ll be running past it again with one health bar, two bullets, and three regrets.

But that’s exactly why it’s one of the fundamental pillars of what we now call survival horror.

Limited resources, tight spaces, item management, routes you optimize in your head, and that constant feeling of “I could die in two hits if I screw this up.” 

RE1 turned backtracking, inventory stress, and map memorization into core mechanics instead of flaws. 

Without this game, half of the genre wouldn’t even know what it wants to be scared of.

Incredible game. I will say, though, that it has a learning curve. If "normal mode" (the 'mountain climb' difficulty) had a bit more time to ease you into the mechanics of dodging, killing, and negotiating the mansion's zombies, it'd be perfect. As it is, I switched to the middle difficulty--which turned out to be easy mode--after some rough deaths on normal in the hopes of getting acclimated. By the end, though, I was overflowing on resources and the bosses were mostly trivial. If I could've had something in between the two difficulties, that might've been ideal, or something which started easier but ramped harder by the end.

Also, this is NOT a game you should stop playing in the hopes of picking it up weeks, months, or years later. There are too many interlocking puzzle pieces to keep track of for that to be anything less than annoying. However, this is the same reason it's so engaging to binge-play that it only took me a few sessions. If, however, there were some way to mark or write on the map (i.e. "shield lock here," "clock puzzle," "dogs!") that would be a non-issue (and would make the backtracking a bit less tedious if you have a small working memory).

I put those points first because other than that, it's damn near flawless. The puzzles are almost never too tough or obtuse, the combat is simple but works, and the scares are there in spades. It builds them up, too. It doesn't seem too bad at first once you learn how to handle a zombie, but it constantly throws something new at you and finds ways to twist the mansion against you. And it only goes up from there, saving some of the scariest enemies and most thrilling moments for the final act. The main downside is that the boss fights aren't too challenging or interesting--assuming you saved your most powerful ammo for them--but that's a necessary consequence of the clunkier control scheme than modern games. The more awkward combat mechanics mean that a boss can't require precise aiming or navigation, just some basic dodging and the occasional puzzle solving, but that's fine. It's for this reason that Plant 42 is one of the standouts--you only need to leave and solve a puzzle to beat it instead of spamming grenades at it. The character of the bosses goes a long way, at least: Yawn's jump scare for the second fight, Lisa Trevor's stalking, and Neptune's... sharkiness. Still, the climactic fights don't stand out the way RE2make or RE4's more action-driven battles do, even if they have just as much personality.

These scares are all served by its atmosphere, with compelling sound design that always seems to know how to manage music, ambience, and volume to great effect. But the standout here are the pre-rendered backgrounds, which have a beautiful yet ethereal quality to them that only serves to make the mansion feel more like a waking nightmare. They would be nothing, however, without the fixed camera angles which are aggressively cinematic--even more so than most games of this type. Only on rare occasions does this make you accidentally run into a zombie out of frame, but that's an entirely worthwhile sacrifice. Few other games commit so hard to the control of tone and information that the fixed camera provides, and none do it so well.

Narratively, it's no Silent Hill 2, but it balances its intense spooks with an absolute charmer of a silly B-movie script (with some genuinely effective plot threads sewn into the background through lore items scattered about the world). 

Now let me entertain a theory. Resident Evil is basically the Evil Dead of video games: it starts out as a serious and deadly effective, yet campy, horror dream (Evil Dead 1=Resident Evil 1-3), but as the series progresses, it gets more self-aware, more campy, and more absurd before turning into outright action (Evil Dead 2/Army of Darkness=Resident Evil 4-6). Somewhere along the way, there's a serious but seriously overlooked attempt to call back to the series' roots that no one talks about anymore (Evil Dead 2013=Resident Evil Revelations). Eventually, years down the line, they return to form with a fan-pleaser that both moves the series forward and calls back to what everyone loved about it. (Ash vs. Evil Dead=Resident Evil 7).

This game helped lay the framework for, and coined the term, survival horror as a genre. This PC Port is an HD remaster of a remake of the original Resident Evil (the original being on the Playstation 1, and the remake being on the Gamecube). As such, it does have those gamecube-era graphical restrictions BUT the game designers and art team took some shortcuts to make this game one hell of a looker on the Gamecube, and it still oozes with atmosphere even in the year 2020.

In an attempt to retain the spirit of the original game, and to push the Gamecube graphics to the limit, the game has 3D characters moving over pre-rendered 2D backgrounds. These backgrounds are extremely detailed and beautiful to look at, though they can look a tad grainy. The game cleverly uses its static camera to swap between backgrounds to keep certain areas or monsters out of view until you explore further or the monster jumps out at you. The camera also uses many cinematic tricks, like showing a room's contents through a mirror, or showing the player character through a window, or using a dutch angle to make a hallway feel more eerie. The effect works wonderfully, and often leaves you feeling like an intruder in the Spencer Mansion and, surprisingly, is perfectly playable with tank controls even in the modern age.

The story is very interesting, but the dialogue doesn't age as well as the controls or camera effects. The dialogue is clunky and cheesy with mediocre acting. It IS better than the original, but you'll probably snort or roll your eyes through most cutscenes, but that's okay. Resident Evil has always had a layer of cheese and corn over it's more terrifying elements and that's what keeps the series fun for many of its fans. It also, thankfully, does not detract from the spooks within the game. 


Speaking of spooks, this game is not super horrifying and it's not YouTube/Twitch jumpscare bait. What it is though, is a moody, horror-themed adventure game where you explore and solve puzzles and fret over every wasted bullet and healing item. The game can push and challenge you, and there are several powerful enemies that WILL scare you, so I feel safe recommending it for horror game fans and adventure game fans alike. It's a classic of the horror genre, and with two characters with vastly different playstyles, altered stories, and multiple endings, its clear to see why this game is a classic. There's a lot to enjoy here, and while the game looks and feels a little old, once you get used to it, it plays very well. Definitely grab this game. You won't regret it.

PS: For your first time play as Jill and try to go through it as blind as possible.

[b]An Excellent Remaster Of A Pioneering Genre[/b]
Credited as being the game that created Survival Horror genre, Resident Evil 2002 is a remake of the iconic 1996 Playstation game with updated everything. Being a 18-25 year game, RE 2002 surprisingly still holds up in current year with good puzzles, great atmosphere, still good looking graphics while maintaining the cringeworthy charm of the original. 

No, it's not as dorky as RE 1996 "Jill Sandwich" level of cringe but RE 2002 doesn't stray too far from the original story and it adds a few details (such as Lisa, Jessie and Trevor side story) which, while not related to the main plot, still give the game a welcome extra content. The atmosphere has been greatly improved; the mansion looked suitably grand and dilapidated and the surrounding forest is dark and creepy. 

Controls is for the most part, good. I played using a Logitech F710 controller; the analog stick has standard controls while the D-pad has tank controls and trust me when I say you're going to need the tank controls in some puzzles as the camera in some instances gets in your way. Otherwise, you generally won't have a problem with the gameplay. 

If you're curious about where it all began, this is really a good place to start if you find the 1996 original too outdated for your taste.

Resident Evil is a survival horror game where you explore a mansion filled with monsters and solve adventure game style puzzles and I have to say that the game is quite good. Mansion is fun to explore, puzzles aren't too easy or hard and feel just right (well there are couple of exceptions) and while I didn't find the game to be scary it did a pretty good job at building a haunting atmosphere. Even the strict camera angles work since you don't usually see what is behind the next corner and have to rely on sounds to locate dangers.

Now while I think the game is good it should be noted that it is very old school in its sensibilities. The game usually doesn't tell you what to do and where to go and most of the time you have figure things out by yourself. There aren't autosaves either so if you die then you have to reload the previous save you made in a save point. 
Another old school feature is the strict inventory management. You can only carry certain number of items and you can't drop them either. You can only store items in a specific storage box so you'll be running back and forth quite a lot.  

So while I'm willing to recommend this game I'd also say that it requires certain amount of patience.

[h1] The original Resident Evil should be proud [/h1]

- GAMEPLAY
The game's difficulty relies on resource management and not so much on mechanics, except when maneuvering enemies. Is it worth shooting that zombie and risk wasting 7-ish bullets or try to go around it? Is it worth going through those zombie dogs to grab some fuel and save me from crimson heads? The game achieves this quite well, there are, most of the times, different aspects to consider when making a decision.
The puzzles are fun, albeit not very challenging, consisting mostly of finding an item and figuring out where it should be used, which is, for most of the time, quite straightforward.

 - AMBIENCE
For the first parts of the game you will feel just like the character, inside a maze-like mansion. You find a door but it's locked, just like the last 2 you tried to open. You feel helpless, as there's a zombie in the way and you're running out of ammo. There's a feeling of anxiety everytime you open a new door - will something pop out from behind the door? And let's not talk about the clinging chains and the moaning coming exactly from the place where you have to go to!

Anxiety, suspense, and unease are some of the feelings I got while playing through the game. 
Jumpscares occur, but are not very common, the game relies instead on it's environment and the resource management to make the player feel uneasy, which is to me a very positive point in horror games.

- STORY
Stays true to the original Resident Evil, with the addition of the story of Lisa Trevor, a quite disturbing and fleshed out [spoiler]Umbrella experiment [/spoiler] to discover. 

- TECHNICAL STUFF
Never crashed on me, didn't encounter any bugs, amazing pad support, graphics are beautiful.

My final veredict: [b] 8/10  would fit nicely into a sandwich [/b]

You want headshot the zombies, otherwise they come back: but you can't aim at all, headshots are random. Investigating the surroundings is a collection of bizarre puzzles. Door is locked - oh noes, I can't bust it. Pick up a gem, place it in a socket instead.

How come this ends up with a thumbs up?

I don't know why this game receives the overwhelmingly positive review, as I can list so many problems within merely two hours of play.

1. The game won't save automatically as we quit the program. If for any reason we must stop playing, we have to go back to a save point and consume a specific item which allows us to save at the save point. As such, if we save the game too frequently so that we run out of the item, then we can no longer save the game.

2. We only have 6 slots in our backpack, and we are not allowed to drop the items in our backpack unless we find a drop box. The game doesn't tell us this nonsense mechanism at all. While we are exploring the mansion, naturally we will pick up whatever we see valuable. However, we will reach the backpack limit (i.e., 6) very soon such that within a few minutes of gameplay we are unable to pick up any item which may be substantial to proceed the game (such as the keys). Does the developer really thinks it's fun to force the players to go back and forth to the drop box whenever the players picks up 2~3 items? 

3. The game only supports the 3rd person viewport, but the camera is not fixed at the back of the character. When the character moves around to explore different areas in the same room, the viewport adjusts automatically in an uncontrollable way, from time to time resulting in the disruption of the original intended movement. That being said, originally we may press the right arrow key to move the character to the right corner of the room. Nonetheless, after the viewport rotates as the character moves, the right arrow key may actually lead the character back to the left corner of the room (with respect to the original viewport).

4. What happens if we get bitten by the zombies? I don't see any HP bar at all. Does it mean it's okay to be bitten by the zombies as it seems the bite has no effect on the character? But will we turn into a zombie later in the game, leading to a bad ending? If I want to avoid the bad ending, do I need to load a saved game and retry whenever I get bitten? There is no clue to this concern at all, and we players need to Google to figure it out by ourselves.

5. There is no tutorial teaching the player how to fight the zombie with a knife (which is the only weapon in our backpack when the game starts). I mean, the game actually allows us to attack either the head, body, or leg of a zombie, but the tutorial only explained how to fire/attack with a weapon without indicating how to or even mentioning the possibility to aim at a specific part of a zombie's body using a melee weapon. 


During my 2 hours of gameplay, nearly half of the time was used in searching on the internet for the answers of the above questions. I've thus lost my interest in the game very quickly and requested for a refund.

A tentative thumbs down here. I had never played the original, this is my first playthrough.

There's a lot to like: the game is interesting from a historical perspective for its influence, the clever camera angles, sound design and tough resource management is creepy, and deciding to leave a zombie be knowing you'll likely have to backtrack there later is an interesting decision. The game's campy, cheesy story and acting are entertainingly silly, which makes for some nice relief in between the tension. 

Unfortunately for me the puzzles kind of killed it, I just can't get into it. There's kind of a an adventure game, metroidvania thing going on in the structure, but too often I just felt totally directionless and solutions to problems seemed a little out of  reach. There's a lot of trial and error thinking, and while some people might like just wandering around, exploring, tying to put two and two together, I found it a little tedious. I think also the game can be a little unfriendly to newcomers in its opening hour or so, I resorted to a walkthrough to advise me on the slightly arbitrary series of events I would need to pull off to grab the shotgun.

The game also uses this archaic save system where you can only save at specific typewriters throughout the mansion and even your save slots are a limited resource. It makes for some cool tense moments, but it's also kind of just annoying and impractical -- I'd have liked an option to allow some kind of checkpoint saving, even if it's only on quitting the game. 

Bit of a shame, maybe I'll revoke my thoughts on a later playthrough, and on sale at like three pounds, I can't really complain. I also seem to be a little outnumbered and most people love the game so, what do I know? But personally, a little too jarring to keep up with.

Resident Evil helped truly kickstart the popularity of survival horror games and this shows, for better or worse. This game is the 2004 gamecube remake of the playstation 1 release. Therefore, don't expect a full on remake, rather, this is an enhanced port with some added features. New costumes, controls, and a few more added things probably make this the definitive version of the game. I also believe this the only version of the game that runs at a full 60 frames per second, not that you'd need it for this game but it's nice to have.

That being said, the game holds up phenomenally well. Pre-rendered backgrounds often show their age in these types of games, but Resident Evil manages to mask it well utilizing all kinds of dark fillers and special effects that help truly create an unnerving atmosphere. Although it's nothing spectacular, taking into context this remake was made in 2004, it does look good. Despite the game taking place in one location, you'll have a variety of different areas around the mansion that slowly reveal the true nature of things as you progress. 

The delivery and acting of the characters can be really cheesy. This feels intentional in some areas considering the fact the original Playstation release went all out with the gritty live action FMV scenes. These aren't scary in any way, they're just really goofy. This remake doesn't have those live action scenes but some of the cheesiness is still in-tact and at times I feel like they run with it, embracing it roots while also staying original and new. 

It'll be made clear pretty early on that this game doesn't hold your hand. The amount of saves you have are limited, inventory management is small, puzzles can be confusing and even cryptic, and it's pretty easy to die early on. How you manage your resources, overcome the obstacles, and progress through the Spencer Mansion is where much of the satisfaction of this game comes from. I feel with how instantly gratifying a lot of newer games are, it'd take a special kind of patience for a newcomer to enjoy this game but if you can see past the few flaws this is a game really worth visiting. 

If you are going to try diving into this game, do yourself a favor and start off as Jill Valentine. I played as Chris Redfield for my second playthrough and it wasn't a super pleasant time. Although you have more health, your inventory space is even more limited with Chris, making it so you'll have constant visits to a safe room to swap out items in your inventory that sort of hurt the pacing of his playthrough. 

If you're indifferent, you can often find the game on sale on a lot of Capcom humble bundles, or you can wait for another steam sale.

I'm discovering the Resident Evil franchise. I finished RE2 remaster recently, you can read the review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/cecton/recommended/883710]here[/url]. My review of RE0 can be read [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/cecton/recommended/339340]here[/url].

First of all: don't get me wrong, this is a great game (just like RE2), I just don't *recommend* it for different reasons. Since I played RE2 recently, my review here will be a comparison of RE2 remaster and RE1 remaster.

In comparison of RE2, RE1 is not a remake, it's really a remastered version. RE1 HD Remaster has the exact same game play (afaik because I didn't play the original game) than the original game.

While in RE2, the story is the same but the gameplay is completely changed to a 3rd/1st person game with a camera sticking on the character. In RE1 the camera is fixed in a place in the room with a certain angle and when you get out of sight of the camera, the view changes to another camera that allows to see your character.

In RE2 the difficulty is adapted to the standards nowadays: you can save as many times as you want but the bosses are much stronger because the controls of the character is much better. In RE1, the character's control are difficult because they are based on the fixed cameras.

In this game (RE1), the bosses are ridiculously easy. The only difficulty comes from the control of the character. For example: [spoiler]the first transformation of[/spoiler] the last boss can be killed in 4 magnum bullets and that boss don't attack much.

The story of RE1 is much more complete of the one of RE2. In RE1 you read a lot more documents and they explain better the origin of the virus, etc... I was very disappointed about the lack of story in RE2. I think it is possible that I missed a lot of the story of RE2 because I didn't play with Leon. I will update my review later when I do.

RE1 is slightly longer than RE2 without knowing the game. I finished RE1 in 19h compared to 13h for Claire in RE2. But RE1 was also a lot more tedious.

What is great with RE1: graphics, ambiance, puzzles. There is more search to do in RE1 than RE2. RE2 scared me more though (maybe also because I played it first).

What isn't too good: fixed cameras with awkward controls, door opening animations (fortunately there is a mod to remove that), and the WORST of all: the amount of saves you can do is limited. You need to get ink ribbon to be able to save. I guess they did that to raise a bit the difficulty but it's a real pain in the ass. I re-did a lot more things because of that and I would probably have saved hours of gameplay if I didn't have to redo stuff over and over again.

When I played RE2 I kept saving in new slots because I felt that maybe I would miss something and I would like to load an earlier game (which never happened). In RE1 I kept saving because the resources are so limited that I felt that if I lost too much bullets or too much daggers I should reload otherwise I will get blocked. I never got blocked but I did reload 2 or 3 times because I felt I lost too much resources.

In RE2 the most valuable resources seems to be the herbs to restore your health. In RE1 the most valuable resources are the dagger: they prevent the damage entirely and damage the enemy at the same time. They are limited so you need to be careful with them.

Overall it was fun to play but it was also very tedious. If you have to choose between RE1 and RE2, you should consider this:

- if you prefer more story and are not afraid of the game being tedious: RE1
- if you prefer a modern gameplay and don't mind having less story: RE2

The other thing that might be an issue with RE1 is the controller you choose:

1. I didn't play with a gamepad with an analog stick but I think the controls are easier that way. I would recommend to play with a xbox-like controller (any controller with one analog stick).

2. Keyboard with mouse works if you use the "old" control types which are awkward (and the mouse pointer is totally useless)). It's fine but I think the old control types are really not for everybody. The way it works is: you press up (w) or down (s) to move the character forward or backward and you press left (a) or right (d) to rotate the character.

3. You CAN play with the "new" controls with the keyboard but it is even more awkward because it's impossible to move straight. I definitely don't recommend that and I don't believe anyone would play in such horrible conditions.

4. You can play with a gamepad without analog stick but you need to activate the "old" control types. (This is how I played. Works great. Controls are awkward)

5. Controls are very important for you? Play RE2, modern game, modern controls. DEFINITELY

[i]Resident Evil[/i] is the ultimate haunted house experience, yet the series is also one of many "classic" franchises that I have intentionally ignored for years. Not being a huge fan of the horror genre, I was expecting the series to be infested with cheap scares, gore, and hectic action sequences. And while it has plenty of each, it also has its share of puzzles and survival elements. I ended up enjoying the game quite a bit, and I look forward to replaying the game as a different character, before venturing into the countless sequels in the series.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
On some level, [i]Resident Evil[/i] is like a click-and-point adventure with a horror twist. The majority of gameplay you wander around a mysterious mansion looking for clues that might help you escape. Occasionally you encounter zombies and other beasts that do require you to pull the trigger. Combat is limited to using firearms or a knife; while there is no rolling or dodging, you do end up running quite a bit. There is quite a bit of inventory management, since you only have a handful of item slots to carry things. In a nutshell, there is not much else as far as gameplay is concerned, but the gameplay is not really the draw here.

[b]Characters/Customization[/b]
The game has two protagonists, Chris and Jill, who do have slightly different loadouts. For example, Jill has two more inventory slots and starts the game with a gun, whereas Chris just starts off with a knife. I have only played through with Jill so far, but from what I gathered there are also differences in their respective storylines. There is no character progression in the game, although you do acquire slightly more powerful firepower as you make your way to the end. One of the few weak points, when it comes to the protagonists and the non-player characters (NPCs), is the spoken dialogue; with an otherwise decent narrative, the dialogue is surprisingly superficial and not something you would expect characters to say given their current predicament.

[b]Story/Atmosphere[/b]
The story behind this first [i]Resident Evil[/i] game is pretty good, certainly on par with your better horror genre movies. And given that each protagonist has a slightly different story with slightly different interactions with NPCs, there is actually some replayability for what would otherwise be a fairly linear game. Increasing the difficulty setting also changes the game, by increasing the number of foes, their toughness, the availability of first aid items, and some other variables. The setting of the game is by no means vast, but to escape the mansion, you end up going back and forth through areas that you have previously visited, which makes the game feel even less linear. Some might find this repetitive, but as a huge fan of [i]System Shock 2[/i] which also involves a lot of back-and-forth, I enjoyed revisiting locations, particularly if those locations had changed even in the smallest of ways. [i]System Shock 2[/i] was also the first game with horror elements that I enjoyed tremendously.

[b]Graphics/Sound[/b]
The remaster does a fairly good job with the updated visuals, especially if you compare with the graphics from the original 1996 game. The character models look very good. The gameplay, with keyboard-and-mouse, can be little awkward at times, probably because the game is meant to be played with a controller. Camera angles are fixed in every frame of the game, so sometimes you find yourself running away from the camera, sometimes towards the camera. It can be disorienting at times, which is unfortunate, especially if trying to fight a boss or to avoid a hazard. 

As stated earlier, the spoken dialogue is average at best, and there is little music to speak of. However, the atmospheric sounds are very good and necessary as they serve as audio queues warning you of upcoming trouble.

[b]Replay Value:[/b] Surprisingly, yes. I definitely plan to play through again as Chris, on a different difficulty setting, and I might even consider additional playthroughs to complete some of the achievements. My first playthrough -- albeit with the help of an online guide -- went by rather quickly, around 10-11 hours, so the prospect of an additional playthrough does not seem particularly daunting.

[b]Overall Score:[/b] 8/10. For a game remastered in 2015, some of the gameplay elements and fixed camera angles seem a bit dated. However, the game still has character and oozes with atmosphere. If, like me, you enjoy good suspense but are not fan of horror, you may still want to give this game a try.

Resident Evil is not the FIRST Survival-Horror game, but it is probably the first popular one. Originally released back in 1996 for the PlayStation, Shinji MIkami's Horror Masterpiece hit all of the right boxes for players looking for a tough, but rewarding experience that didn't overtly rely on action, and instead offered a more scary and lonesome atmosphere.


The original version of this game is markedly different compared to this version, which was released in 2002 as "Resident Evil" for the GameCube, as part of Capcom's then "exclusivity" deal with Nintendo. The most stark differences between RE 2002 and RE 1996 is as follows:

-Killing Zombies does not take them out forever, unless you have performed an attack that destroys their head, or knees. "Killed" zombies, i.e. Zombies that have been incapacitated without destroying their head or knees, will eventually return as "Crimson Heads", which are far faster and more aggressive versions of the normal Zombies. The way this game determines this is random, every play through. The only constant in this mechanic is the fact that it takes a certain amount of time. The difficulty plays in how faster or long they take to turn into Crimson Heads, but it's not going to be the same every playthrough. To combat this, you can now burn Zombie "corpses" with the Lighter and Fuel Flask. Doing so, however, means you now need an extra item in your inventory. You refuel the Flask with Kerosene tanks scattered around the map, and there isn't enough to burn every Zombie so avoiding zombies now isn't just a save of ammo anymore, it also means you won't create more annoying monsters later one.

-Chris' and Jill's scenarios remain mostly the same, except there are small differences in the game world. For example, the method you get the Sword key is entirely different in this version compared to the PS version.
Some items are in different places and some puzzles were re-vamped to either be less annoying or just easier to complete.

-This is the only "remake" in the series that did not remove any gameplay mechanic or location from the game. Later remakes, such as Resident Evil 2 2019 and Resident Evil 3 2020 markedly cut down parts of the original games, instead of just adding content in

Resident Evil has remained Capcom's most lucrative and most popular franchise outside of Street Fighter. While there is still no official way to play the original versions of the original Resident Evil trilogy, this version of the first game has remained one of the most popular remakes ever created. While some aspects were changed, nothing was removed. Shinji Mikami simply added more to his original game, bringing it closer to what he originally wanted to do on the PlayStation.

If you've never heard of Resident Evil, or have and were never interested, this is still the original master piece it has always been. You will die a lot, so much to the point that your first death is an achievement in the game, but stick through it and keep playing and you will find plenty of reasons to come back to it. The story, unlockable rewards, and remixed item locations mode is enough for anyone that enjoys Survival Horror game play to keep playing this game forever.

[b][TL;DR][/b]

Absolutely get this if you played this on PSX and want to re-discover, consider it if you're a "Remastered" player and want to delve deeper, but prepare for some control struggles initially. A great legacy game to discover in the Series. Inventory managemant is a worse enemy than most Zeds.

[The Long and Hard of it]
If you are looking here because you entered RE through the "Remaster" period (2019+), be prepared for control/tech challenges due to the fixed camera angles. If you move and the camera suddenly "flips around on you" you can get confused. 
That said, the old Resident Evil/Biohazard do have a charm to them that is quite unmatched by any other offering.
Inventory management is still your actual worst enemy, the Zeds are kind of manageable, depending on your difficulty level.

[b][Story][/b]
The story is well done, considering some of the writing falls into the "Engrish" category. In the 90's they couldn't give two damns, or not even one, about well-done western market localization and there definitely is some cheese here in the voicework and in how the characters are basically blueprints from (bad) 80s action movies. The story itself is solid, and mainly lives from notebook entries you discover to see what happened in that strange mansion. That foreboding feeling of “something sinister” is there and the story has a nice culmination, also depending on your choices on how you handle some of the events presented.
 
[b][The Tech][/b]

PC iterations usually are (bad) ports of console launches. In this case, Capcom did a nice job of translating the gameplay to PC tech. The test of time when it comes to high res display is not weathered so well, with ugly, up-res'd Textures. It does play best at 1080p res, would not recommend to go higher.
The good: Any kind of modern PC can probably handle this low-tech game, so that's the good part!

[i]Controls[/i] are nicely mapped, using X-Input (ie. Xbox controllers or compatible) - but take getting used to as per the fixed camera angles bascially changing your direction while walking.

[i]Sound design[/i] does a nice job of putting that fear of the unkown in you. The game detects correctly if you have a surround setup, and directional audio works great to hear those Zombies shuffle around the corners or behind your back.

[b][Overall / Rating][/b]

I give the most classic of all the RE's a 6/10 (tech / gameplay) and an 8/10 for the story experience. You should not miss it if you're into RE remasters and are trying to delve to the origins. Then I played RE 7 and ended up really enjoying the more survival horror aspect of it. So I wanted to go back and bought this game initially on the PS4. At first I was really put of by the limited saves and the more traditional game design. Which is very unlike the modern quality or life features we have today like autosaves. 

But ultimately that is the fun of it all, the game is designed to make you feel constantly on the edge and the limited resources you do get will always feel precious and will make you rethink you decisions on using them. For example do you kill that zombie in the hallway only for it to become a crimson head later and proceed to use more ammo and heals on or do you find a way around it and not waste a single bullet, the decision is up to you.  

The puzzles are great and will get your head scratching. But please if your stuck just look up a walkthrough, but only as a last resort.

TLDR

Yes this game has fixed camera angles, yes this game has limited amount of saves and yes the story is pretty dumb and nonsensical. 

But it is and will always will be one of the best survival horror games out there.

Resident Evil and Silent Hill used this to an advantage, but it doesn't change the fact that it was infuriating. Walking a few inches and needing to change direction immediately and not being able to always see in front of you was not fun. It was scary, yes. Was it a good feature? Well if it worked out then we'd see it a little more often, wouldn't we? Same as with the system of limited saves. So if I'm taking the time to complain so much, why am I giving it a positive review? I'm hesitant to say this, but it's because the game may not be fun, but it is good. I don't believe I've played a game that made me be afraid of literally almost everything in it. Each time you pick up an item, each time you use an item, each time you walk forward, each time you shoot or even save the game, you're hoping you won't regret it. Everything you do in this game can ruin you. It's horrifying, it's tense, and above all it's infuriatingly made, but it's a feeling so unique to the game that I have to recommend it. You will be startled, you will panic, you will need to take breaks, and you will die. While I can't say that I believe this is a good game, when I'm asked whether or not I recommend it, I have to say yes. I can't say that it's a game everyone should play, but if you like horror and want something fresh, while still being pretty basic in function, then get this game. But before you get into it, let me list some things you may not like about the game:

1. To save the game, you need to use an Ink Ribbon item. These are limited. There are no autosaves, so it is completely possible to ruin an entire playthrough.
2. The camera cannot be moved and camera-based controls make it so that when it does move, you usually have to change how you control the character.
3. Every time you open a door, there is a 5 second or longer cutscene of the door opening. This is true for every door. Unless you mod the game, this cannot be avoided.
4. There is not an option to discard an item. If you pick up too many items, you will need to put something in the item box in order to carry more. Early in the game, picking up too many items may leave you unable to get to the first item box and you will have to restart.
5. The character you choose matters. They don't mention it, but both of them are different in stats and in some story aspects.
6. Zombies only actually "die" under certain circumstances. Zombies can fake death. Aiming will automatically snap to a living target, so it's easy to tell. However, even the "dead" zombies will come back to life. Unless you use the lighter and lighter fluid to incinerate a zombie's corpse, or you get a random critical headshot (which is unlikely) the zombie will come back faster and stronger as an enemy called a Crimson Head once you return to them. There are a few unavoidable Crimson Heads, and you will most likely not have enough lighter fluid to incinerate each zombie.

With all that in mind, if you think it's bearable enough, I say you should pick the game up (preferably on sale) and get ready to have a heart attack or five. Just remember there's no shame in getting scared.

Enter the world of survival horror!

PROS: The atmosphere in this game is on point.  It feels terrifying to walk through the halls of the mansion.  The entire place actually feels lived in, and the audio surrounding different areas amps up the fear.  The abundance of notes and journals scattered across adds to the terror, giving those fleeting final moments of those trapped inside.  The story is decently told, removing the heavy cheese from the original, while attempting to give it more of a significance to the horror part of survival horror.  The gameplay is, in my opinion, as crisp as tank controls can be.  The weapons pack a serious punch, and ammo can be a little scarce, making the player learn how to properly dodge incoming threats.  The new additions to the game, such as Crimson Heads, add an extra layer of thought when considering options on resource management.

CONS: The puzzles are still very lackluster.  With the exception of one or two, they're very uninteresting, with little to offer.  The game also feels like it starts losing steam in the guard tower portion, though it picks back up in the underground lab.

ACHIEVEMENTS: This will give you a run for your money.  Some of the challenge based achievements will require a great deal of memorization, map knowledge, and enemy management.  This list not for the faint of heart.

FINAL: This is an amazing remaster, and the kind that others should strive to be like.  The gameplay is solid, the atmosphere is tense, and it's just overall fun.  If you'd like to see where the term (not the origin, but the term) survival horror came front, look no further.

This is still the ultimate Resident Evil experience in my opinion. They took the classic RE1 PS1 game and completely remade it, with updated graphics, controls, animations, voices, sounds, and even added brand new areas, enemies and puzzles - as well as a more fleshed out story and characters.

The mansion is dark, eery, and you never know what's around the next corner. Easily the most atmospheric and creepy RE game to this day. Sound design is stellar, with ambient sounds, wind, creatures - and gutteral zombie moans. It oozes atmosphere at every turn.

Graphically, it holds up extremely well, thanks to the great pre-rendered backgrounds. They're limited to 1920x1080 (upscaled from the SD Gamecube assets), but the the artistry behind them is so good that they look good no matter what. I don't think I've ever seen a more memorable location; aside from perhaps Rapture from Bioshock. Every corner of every room has love and detail poured into it.

The 'tank' controls take some getting used to compared to modern controls, but once you familiarise yourself with them, this is the classic RE gameplay loop. You manage your inventory, pick up key items, and solve the many mysteries of the mansion, while also managing ammo and health items.

This is the best 'jumping in' point for the entire RE franchise, with a very basic story, that slowly unfolds as you explore the mansion and uncover its' secrets and read the undead residents' diaries and notes.

If you enjoy the RE2 and RE3 remakes, this is almost identical in gameplay; just from a different perspective. Thoroughly recommended for any RE or horror fans.

For the love of god, if you are not a potato at video games and especially if you have played a RE game before, make sure you're playing the game on normal. Rather than asking you which difficulty you'd prefer, the game asks you to pick which of the following best resembles how you like your video games:

I - Like climbing a mountain
II - Like riding a bike
III - Like walking

I picked "Like riding a bike", because 1) that was the most truthful answer to the question they were asking and 2) I assumed this was code for hard/normal/easy and the middle option would give me normal. Turns out, this was actually code for normal/easy/very easy.  You don't unlock hard mode until after beating the game.

I ended up unknowingly playing through the entire game on easy and getting pretty bored by halfway through because I was able to kill every enemy I came across and *still* have boatloads of ammo and healing items to spare. The puzzles became walking simulators through looted, empty rooms and I started getting really tired of all of the backtracking through loading door upon loading door... I had assumed the game was just easier than it should have been with modern controls until I finally beat the game and didn't get the achievement for beating it on normal. Currently about 27% of people have the very easy completion achievement, about 21% have the easy completion achievement, and about 12% have the normal completion achievement, so I know there are a ton of people out there who made my mistake. 

The game itself is surprisingly good - if you've enjoyed other RE titles it's a no-brainer and I could recommend this to anyone mildly interested - but you will not have a good time if the difficulty is not right. I'm assuming on very easy you start the game with a magnum and 100 rounds.

[h1] Resident backtrack [/h1]
Beyond a shadow of doubt Resident Evil is one of the most recognisable game franchises there are. In retrospect, the series’ beginnings all the way back in 1996 seem utterly distant - like a fairytale you’ve heard of, yet never quite read yourself. Nearly 20 years later, in 2015 Resident Evil HD Remaster was released, finally giving a chance to experience series’ humble beginnings on PC. Before you put your adventurer’s hat on and venture into the past, bear in mind that foundations for the remastered version were laid for Gamecube in 2002. RE HD Remaster is foremost directed at franchise fans and those with patience for the old games. If you are none of the above, you are probably better off trying one of the newer games instead.

That said, it’s endearing to see a very different Chris Redfield. Not the boulder-punching grizzled veteran who rampaged across the Africa in RE 5; but a confused rookie to whom even a single zombie poses a mortal threat. The veil of mystery has been long since lifted by the series itself, back in 1996 though, the intrigue was there. The T-virus or the Umbrella corporation were concepts yet to be explored.  You are a part of an elite police unit investigating strange reports of cannibalism on the outskirts of Racoon City. Suddenly your squad is being attacked by a pack of monstrous dogs and you barely make it into a mysterious residence in the middle of a forest. That’s it. What followed is history.

[b] Visions of Dread [/b]
Story has it that the most dangerous mutant stalking the halls of titular residence is the camera work. This is mostly true, RE HD Remaster is likely to be the very first game with a fixed camera you’ve ever played. Meaning that every environment in the game is a still frame with only the characters within moving. The technique allowed creating a functional illusion of a fully 3D environment without the need to actually model everything. It also means that you can get turned around while running down a straight corridor and not even realise. While you do get somewhat used to it over time it’s quite confusing.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2023306615 [/url]
This makes picking the right spot for a fight a genuine challenge. There are relatively few places in the game that allow you properly aim at enemies, meaning you either fight and point-blank range or shoot blind. Whichever you choose, better not miss, as bullets are a precious commodity in this title. Especially when you take into account that Resident Evil is the game that essentially introduced the idea of scarce resources into survival horror. Perhaps RE uses underhanded methods to achieve effect, yet the result is an absolutely choking atmosphere. Almost every fight is a tense experience and likely more than once, you will be frantically running your bloodied character into one of few saferooms in the residence. The only place where you can store away the items you just tore out from the jaws of a monster and use one of the healing items you hoarded away. 

[b] Preparing for the unknown [/b]
Nowadays it’s easy to forget how unrelenting the old game mechanics used to be. Resident Evil has most of them, making for a one steep learning curve. The game has no autosave feature, allowing the player only to save at specific locations, there is also a limited number of saves depending on difficulty level. On top of that, the player’s character has a very tiny inventory space that can be easily filled, forcing the player to stab their way through, unable to pick up a pistol clip lying at their feet. Luckily there are magical storeboxes spread throughout the mansion, which grant you vital extra storage room, accessible from any such chest. 

Alas, planning ahead and making the most of the resources available is what the game is all about. The trick is, most of the time you have absolutely no idea what are you going into. Instead, you will launch the game, brick your equipment, get killed by the very first zombie and after roughly 3-4 restarts actually get the hang of basic game mechanics. At least that’s what I did. 
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2023307734 [/url]
The frankly impossible task of preparing for the unknown is where the most of the game’s difficulty and an overall slow pace stems from. On top of that, while Resident Evil does drop some hints about how to progress, you are largely left on your own. The fact, that the residence was filled with puzzles by a literal mad inventor doesn’t help. Few of them are quite fun to solve and give the game a slight touch of the adventure genre. Then again, by the time you figure out the proper use for some of the key items, you will have learnt residence’s map by heart. There is a lot of running back and forth in RE, and the areas once cleared of enemies never quite stay so. The game will eagerly punish any player getting too relaxed.

[b] Once again [/b]
When you first start the game you get to choose one of the two characters – Jill and Chris. While the game at large remains the same for both survivors there are subtle differences in how RE plays. That’s why you should pick Jill for your first playthrough. She has 8 inventory slots instead of 6, has access to a wider range of weaponry and Barry – a partner eager to provide a Magnum-sized help early on. While Chris on the other hand... has got this. And Rebecca to occasionally aid him in the brains department. That said, having a second possible protagonist gives Resident Evil a surprisingly good replayability.

Once I’ve finally beaten the game after roughly 15 hours, I immediately had a go at it with a second character. The idea may appear silly given how much of a chore Resident Evil can be at times. Yet, I highly recommend at least trying to play the game twice. It is plain astonishing when you realise how smoothly you can progress through the residence when you are actually able to plan ahead. The 3-hours completion achievement suddenly shifts from being utterly absurd into a viable challenge.

In the end, playing Resident Evil HD Remaster was a quite tedious experience, yet I enjoyed the game for what it was. A piece of gaming history in all of its clunky splendour. This title’s difficulty gives a lesson in humility and fixed-camera gameplay was an experience I’ve never had before. Despite certain upgrades being made since Gamecube version, especially in resolution and character models, this is as oldschool as it can get. Whether it’s for better or worse is a matter of taste at this point. If you have that certain appreciation for old-school, necessary to fully enjoy such a title, this game is definitely worth your while.

[h1]Survival Horror[/h1]

This game has great atmosphere. The fact that you know there are a finite amount of healing items, bullets, and even saves in the game gives the game such particular feel. 

This isn't an action game. The only thing you gain from shooting an enemy down is that the enemy is down, and often not for long. Every bullet you spend is one bullet off the total amount of bullets you can get in the campaign. 
This isn't a survival game. You don't spend your time upkeeping your hunger or thirst. Finding items is often not the issue, but rather, rationing them. 
This isn't a horror game. This game does not revolve around making you feel uncomfortable. It doesn't want to fill you with fear all the time. 

This [b]is[/b] survival horror. You will have bouts of terror and peaks of triumph. You will manage your resources and wonder if you actually have enough. You might take risky strategies in order to save resources. Or play it safe by using them. This game has you survive despite the horror around you.

I think the best way to sum up my experience with RE1 HD is to say that I loved it, but that I was glad for it to be over. 

I missed Resident Evil as a kid, so the remaster was my first taste of the original. I came to it after absolutely loving the RE2 remake and wanting to dig deeper into the series and the story. In some ways, I think having played RE2 first got me excited for RE1 in a way that carried me through the game's sometimes frustrating spots. In other ways, though, the back-to-back runs just highlighted how outdated many parts of RE1 feel nearly 25 years later. 

Technically speaking, I was impressed (I played the game in 1440p at 120 FPS on a 2070 Super, 8700K @ 4.7, and 16 GB RAM). The game certainly won't be giving your graphics card a workout, but the prerendered backgrounds actually look pretty good in a quaint, throwback sort of way. The lighting and sound are very atmospheric, and a great old-school soundtrack round out the package to make everything feel super moody and dark. The character models look decent, too, and I never found the textures or animations distracting the way I do in some old games.

I loved exploring the mansion and its surrounding locales, but I quickly tired of seeing the same hallways over and over again as I endlessly returned to the item box to drop off healing items, ammo, and keys for later use. I know the inventory system is an important part of the RE series, but it feels particularly oppressive here--to the point that I spent a lot more time worrying about how many free slots I had than I did about zombies.

I also struggled with how opaque the game is about where you're supposed to go and what you're supposed to do. I know that's part of the "old school appeal," but I feel like I spent huge sections of the game without so much as even an objective to work toward. I'm not ashamed to say that I had to refer to a walkthrough several times when I tired of aimless wandering, or to say that at least a few of the solutions I found there were so ridiculously illogical and obscure (especially those that involved massive backtracking) that I doubt I ever would have figured them out without a nudge. Puzzles are fine, as are locked doors and key quests. But they do have to make some level of sense for players. Otherwise, all they do is frustrate.

I had some other quibbles, too. The limited save system seems unnecessarily harsh in 2020, especially given how few save rooms there are to start with. RE2 managed to maintain tension just fine with limited typewriter locations but unlimited saves, so RE1 felt like a major step backward. There were a few times where I didn't save for an hour or more because I was scared of running out of ribbons. You can imagine how I felt when I died at the end of one of those runs.

Finally, the story was a bit of a letdown. I had hoped to get some really cool insights into the origins of the virus and Umbrella's schemes, but I don't feel like that happened at all. By the end of the game, it was clear that a corporation was testing a terrible new bioweapon, and that something had gone horribly wrong. But... I already knew that. Aside from a mostly vapid plot about a team of yawn-inducing cops, one (predictable) twist, and a few interesting notes here and there, I honestly don't feel like I got much in the way of story at all.

This all sounds really negative, I know. But I actually DID enjoy my time with RE1, and I'm glad I played it all these years later. But having now experienced the original game, I think I'm ready to uninstall it, move on to games with more modern mechanics, and never look back.
