THE STANDARD FOR SURVIVAL HORROR. HOLDS UP ADMIRABLY FOR ITS AGE. EXTREMELY ENGAGING. I started my RE franchise with RE4 back in the day and played all subsequent games (op-RC, zero, rev1+2, and the DS titles included). This was my first go round at the"original" game. And I can say that it is obvious how much this game influences the genre, even to this to this day. I'd consider this game a near-masterpiece, not as good as 4 overall, but BETTER in a lot of ways. Replay value is its weak-point, an aspect that 4 nailed. And obviously game mechanics of the time were not as well fleshed-out. But one of things that made me most apprehensive to play the game all these years, actually ended up being one of my favorite aspects... the camera angles. They really change the meta of survival horror. The right camera angles are everything in this game. I also found a healthy balance between combat mechanics and puzzle-solving, something I have come to expect from mainline RE/BH games. The track is strangely monotonous yet mesmerizing at the same time. I love the repeated use of audio affects and sound clips across the early games as it brings a small sense of familiarity and comfort (reloads, door openings, and item pick-ups), which is sparse in this game. The map is non-intuitive but added an element of suspense, not knowing what keys open what doors and no linear path makes for a very interesting game experience. I recommend this game to any fans of classic survival horror games or any one looking for a gripping intro into one of the best franchises in gaming.

The survival horror classic that started the entire genre. But what is it exactly that made this game so great? 

Now I don't wanna talk about the story in case someone hasn't played this yet, so I'll be focusing on other things in this review, that being the actual gameplay. 

Well, first of all, the atmosphere. It's always there, starting from the first minutes of the game. The spooky dark ambient soundtrack, the first person door opening scenes. You'll never know what's lurking on the other side of the door and it can lead to your death countless times before you start to get the hang of the "tank controls". 

That leads to the next thing that makes this game the memorable classic it still is to this day, which exactly are the controls. Basically, you press up (W on PC, obviously) to go forward regardless of the camera angle, which keeps changing all the time and messes with your mind at first. Believe me, if you've never played this game before, you will have a hard time getting used to them at first, but once you do, it's not really a hard game, and it feels so rewarding to finally beat it. Now there is an alternate control scheme for this remaster, but imo, it just made it harder to play. Honestly, I couldn't really figure out how you're supposed to play the game with this new control scheme, even though I was new to the series. Everything was just the opposite from what it should be, or I'm just stupid. Whatever the case is, the only useful thing I found about the alternate controls was that you don't have to press shift to run, but that's not much so I'd rather play this with the og tank controls anytime. Besides, in a game like RE, running automatically can often lead to your death more easily, or that's how I felt anyway when I tried that control scheme. Not for me, that's all I can say.

Now the most important thing that makes this game the unique piece it is, and the number #1 rule of the game you could say, is that everything is limited: ammo, saves, item slots (prepare to use item boxes a lot, you only have 8 item slots), gas (you need that and the lighter to burn the corpses so they won't turn into Crimson Heads. Now what is a Crimson Head? That you'll have to find out yourself if you don't already know it, but a little hint for you: you might not want to find out, so I'd recommend to just burn every corpse you can). You use "ink ribbons" to save your game. These are items that can be found throughout the mansion, but like I said, they're limited too. So once you'll remember to not use too much ammo or too many ink ribbons, you should be fine (when you get used to the controls first, that is, whichever control scheme you prefer). Keep in mind that this is a remaster of the 2002 GameCube remake and not the original game. I've never played the original one and I had to restart this game once because I was wasting too much ammo and using too many ink ribbons on my first playthrough. 

And last but not least, the thing I enjoyed the most: The puzzles. Some of them are easy, but some of them really make you use your brain. I admit that I was stuck for hours multiple times during this game, but that's what made it an interesting experience for me. A lot of these puzzles require quite a bit of backtracking due to the limited item slots. 

So, my final verdict for this game, if you haven't played a lot of horror games and you want to start with the classics, here it is for you. A true masterpiece of the genre, I'd recommend this to anyone. Even if you're not into horror yet, who knows, it might change your mind? Give it a chance I'd say, I enjoyed it a lot and I can totally understand why it has such a huge fanbase. Highly recommended if you're even the slightest bit interested about the survival horror genre or zombie games in general.

A great remastering of the classic 1998 Resident Evil. Great puzzle/horror game with some action mixed in. I recommend anyone who enjoys horror games to play this.

THE GOOD:
- A really creepy atmosphere. Even if it's an HD remake, the horror atmosphere is still that of a '90s horror game. The narrow hallways and camera angles really contribute to this.
- Sufficiently hard on the Mountain Climbing mode (though this was my first survival horror for me, so opinion on this may differ).
- Encourages exploration and new enemies usually appear to shock you when you re-explore a room during a later section of the game. 

THE BAD:
- Saving should not have been as much of a resource as it is. The harder modes should provide more saving opportunities than easier modes to balance them out. I felt stressed out about playing a session of this game for too long since I knew there will probably be no opportunity to save easily if I press further on and have to risk losing enormous progress otherwise.
- Resource management. I understand the game probably would make no sense without it, but resource management as a mechanic is faulty and annoying at its root. "Oh, I can keep my lighter and as many daggers as I want attached to me, but no way can I carry these two keys in my pockets without throwing stuff away." The keys AT LEAST should not have taken up any slots.

Overall, I highly recommend it if you're mostly a noob to the horror genre like me. I think it's an excellent horror game to dip your feet in.

First, I want to say that I appreciate the nostalgia factor of this game.  When it came out, the games that were available at the time were completely different, and this was certainly a pioneer.  It paved the way for survival horror and opened up a whole genre.  But if you're like me and didn't play the original when it came out, it's pretty hard to really enjoy this game when it's compared to more modern games.  My first introduction to the series was Resident Evil 4 on the Wii and it's been years since I played it.  I was in the mood for a good zombie shooter, and decided to start the series from the beginning, to really experience the whole series.  Unfortunately I cant recommend this game to anyone who isn't playing it to re-live the original that they may have grown up with.

Here's the Bad:

It's very hard to get used to the controls, as the camera isn't controllable and instead sits in a fixed position and will "hop" to different vantage points as you move through a room, creating a sort of cinematic view rather than first or third person.  This means that moving through one room in the same direction (i.e. west across a corridor) may require you to push the control stick in one direction, and then a completely different direction when the camera jumps.  You end up constantly walking into walls, and getting confused on which way you were actually going.  It makes it hard to orient yourself, and at it's worst moment for me I got stuck in a hallway going back and forth instead of actually escaping while hoards of zombies piled in through the windows.

You can't save often. Saves work by finding a typewriter in the game, and using a roll of ink.  Which means you are limited in the amount of saving you can do, as well as where you can save.  There are no auto saves or checkpoints.  Worse yet, the spool of ink uses an item slot.  And you only have 6 item slots.  Your inventory fills insanely fast.  Your gun and your mag take 2 slots, a key (of which you need multiples) needs another, so you're down to 1/3 to 1/2 your inventory before you even pick up anything new.  Add health and any item you find and you're totally full.  I ran out of bullets and found a new mag, but couldn't reload my gun because the mag has to go into an item slot before you can use it to reload the gun.

You'll find yourself just running around all over the mansion trying to figure out what key or item goes into a sculpture or a certain door, but the map doesn't mark any of these items.  So you just get lost running around looking for something that you know you've seen but cant remember where.

And the worst part is the door animations.  Every. Single. Time. you go through a door, it's a 2-5 second ordeal where the screen goes black except for the door, and you wait while it opens.  Man does this slow down game play. 

It's obviously a game that was groundbreaking, but going back to play it after playing modern games is pretty tough, unfortunately.  I gave it a fair shot, 5 hours or so, before giving up.  I lost interest when I ran out of ammo and the game CLEARLY got harder with more zombies showing up and killing me about 15 or 20 minutes past my last save.  I wasn't ready to replay that section, so I guess I'll just read a plot synopsis and give Resident Evil 2 a shot.

The Good:

This game is very suspenseful.  Man, they really nailed that part.  It's genuinely frightening, and every zombie is a legitimate event, not just some ammo sponge.  I also love having to figure out the different puzzles and where the items are supposed to go.  It's awesome to unlock a new part of the mansion and keep exploring.

If you're feeling nostalgic, or really want to play the series all the way through and don't mind the stuff I described above, go for it.  But if you're just looking for a zombie shooter with jump scares, or think you might get frustrated with un-intuitive controls, a lack of a decent map, relentless door animations and a limited ability to save your progress, you might want to skip ahead to a more modern game.

Talking about how good Resident Evil HD Remaster is, it is like talking about how good was Bruce Lee’s “The Big Boss”: you might not like them, but you cannot deny how important and instrumental they were in advancing and popularizing their respective genres. 

The classic Resident Evil has stood the test of time: there are some aspects of the game that are great(ly terrifying) even today, such as the dread-filled atmosphere as you wait to see what horrors are lurking beyond the old wooden door of the next room, claustrophobic and limiting movement and combat system, nice puzzle sections to ease the player a bit before the next big scare, two overlapping single-player campaigns that flesh out the story (no pun intended), and who can forget the nerve-racking resurrections of crimson heads caused by your neglect, and undead pooches! There are also some duds in the game that time has run over like critics did over Stephen King’s drug-fueled first and only movie directorial debut: camera switching madly and constantly changing perception to add the additional element of fright to the player today seems more irritating than enjoyable, let alone scary; the story’s backdrop and how the T-Virus was created in the past are more interesting and serious then the entirety of the current campy story the game is showing. The first Resident Evil game never was perfect; it was created as an omage to the schlocky horror movie classics of the past by the original developers.

But, to their credit, Capcom has given it all and birthed a new remake of this survival horror classic that polishes the graphics and the dialogue, while leaving everything else in its pristine, antiquated condition. 2D backgrounds the player is traversing are looking better and chilling than ever before, 3D models of the protagonists and monsters have been greatly enriched and sharpened, while the corny dialogue of the original game was also overhauled with a more serious, if not easily forgettable note in mind. Heck, even the simple yet effective PS1 soundtrack got a nice and equally serious Botox injection. This has resulted in a strikingly beautiful and rugged game that exudes atmosphere of elegance and fear in every playthrough and screenshot the community makes. As for leaving the crutches the original game had, this is a beloved game among players so fiddling with the core, beating heart of this Resident Evil would not end well, but one cannot help and imagine what wonder or a catastrophe of the game we would get if Capcom had more faith and courage and reworked everything. Luckily, they showed their iron will with a completely reimagined Resident Evil 2, but that is a story for another time.

Some things age like fine wine, and those things are always in a vast minority and should be cherished. Such is the case with the Resident Evil HD Remaster (good lord that prolonged title though), a game that spawned a series that has been frightening players for more than 20 years now, with a varying degree of success. This game is and will remain a captivating shiny, red and imperfect jewel of the horror survival genre that everyone should play.

They mostly consist of you running into a corner and unloading your best weapon into the boss until it dies. The original Resident Evil didn't really have good boss fights so you could argue they were trying to stick with that for this game. However, with all the other improvements they made to this game, in comparison to the original, you'd think they would've improved the bosses. Even with the bad boss fights and mediocre voice acting, I'd still give this game an 8/10 and would say it's worth buying, especially for Resident Evil fans and fans of OG survival horror games.

I should confess now, that while I have seen the original 1996 release of Resident Evil, I have not had the personal pleasure of playing it myself.  Still, RE:HD remains cemented in my mind as a genre defining title in survival horror, just as RE(1996) did when it first coined that term.

Short Review:
Resident Evil begins with you and the STARS Alpha team investigating your missing compatriots after they went to investigate a series of disturbing murders and cannibalised corpses.  Things go from bad to worse, as you are left stranded in a nightmarish mansion, forced to enter the survival horror as either resident Action Guy Chris Redfield, or the Capable Jill Valentine.

Choosing the former is probably the harder choice for gameplay.  You'll have longer reach with your knife and better damage but have fewer inventory slots.  You'll have two more slots as Jill, access to one of the games most powerful weapons, and lockpicks to open certain doors.  Though, you'll have less health.  You'll also have slightly different stories with either character, with Chris being assisted by Medic Rebbecca Chambers, while Jill will have the always handy Barry Burton.  I suggest playing Jill first then maybe bump up your difficulty and try Chris.

Here begins RE:HD's brilliance as it blends story, atmosphere, and gameplay to create a wonderfully fear inducing experience.  With fixed cameras and pre-rendered high definition backgrounds the game is beautiful and full of dark foreboding character, while characters, items, lighting, and other effects are all of the highest grade.

Limited resources, even limited saves, make encounters tense and help bring you into a survival mindset.  The fixed camera angles shine as an example of great visual story telling, as well as making the entire mansion and other areas truly scary.  Without the ability to see where the gruesome and dangerous enemies are, we are forced into a state of panic as well as forced to careful hear and observe the environment.  Tanky controls take this even further, with movement being hampered making encounters feel more tense and claustrophobic.  All of which reinforces RE:HD's themes of horror, panic, and survival.

Slightly Longer Review (Slight Spoilers):
Apart from the base gameplay, RE:HD has some additions to its horror themes that truly make it a masterpiece in my eyes.  For one, despite them being quite strong, and you as a player being quite weak, the enemies themselves are not the biggest threat.  Your own fear is.

If you know where an enemy is you can fairly easily dispatch them (if you have the ammo) or avoid them (if you don't).  Most encounters are for the most part completely optional.  But if you try to kill every enemy you'll find yourself damaged and low on health and ammo.  This makes further exploration that much more fear inducing.  Further, fear of the unknown and the unseen is a palpable force in this game, and having enemies be off screen is actually more frightening.  Almost as if they are looming behind you always.

Even area's you have made "safe" will soon become anything but, as zombies move about the house, and unattended corpses vanish.  Entering a room then hearing a window break, or a door slam as an unseen horror now invades an area you thought safe is a masterpiece of horror game design.

As for flaw and critique, while I enjoy the campy action movie style and plot not everyone will, and certainly your going to need to suspend your disbelief.  The inventory is clunky and small, and if it didn't play an instrumental role in providing the survival aspect of the survival horror, I would certainly be voicing a lot loud complaints about it.  Keys in particular take up an entire vital space, making exploration somewhat of a chore if your having to go back to re-equip ever other other room.  Aiming is awful, but, once again, having to get close to enemies to hit critical areas further adds tension.

Still RE:HD is beautiful both graphically and mechanically.  It's sound design is superb, and it makes full use of its fixed cameras not only to guide but to obfuscate.  I have a hard time saying anything bad about RE:HD.  To me it is an enduring piece of art, and genre defining title, and one of the most fun games I have ever played.

The original Reside Evil was an incredibly impressive game, it engrossed players with an extremely stressful atmosphere that required them to constantly be on their toes. It had simple, yet satisfying puzzles, a wide variety of enemies, fun characters, an interesting world to explore, an atmosphere so thick that you could drown in it, and many memorable moments. This was one of the games that set the foundation for the survival horror genre, and after all of these years, it's still one of the top-dogs of the genre. When you experience a game like this, it leaves an impact on you, so naturally when a remake comes along a nervous excitement comes over you. So many remakes struggle with the balancing act of trying to reimagine the game, whilst simultaneously trying not to ruin what made the original so special. RE1 Remake is trifled by no such issue, every change it made only elevated the overall gameplay. The addition of new enemies, new sections, and the inclusion of new game modes made for a game that was not only more fun to explore but offered a fresh experience to series veterans. This is not only one of the best remakes I have ever played, but it's also one of the best games I have ever played.

Resident Evil HD Remastered is one of those games that was destined to leave an impact the moment it landed, and I'm happy to say that I finally understand why. I usually try to steer away from playing horror games because of how much they bored me; I don't find them scary nor particularly enjoyable to play for a multitude of reasons. Resident Evil suffered from almost none of those reasons. 

[u] What I love about Resident Evil [/u]

The biggest things going for Resident Evil are an incredible atmosphere, sound design, puzzles, and survival horror. I LOVE the feel of this game; Everything about it is just superb. The music, the eerie quietness, the sense of danger and conspiracy, lighting, and the ominous tone among various other factors contributed so much to this game's excellent atmosphere that I can say without hesitation that this is the reason why horror works so effectively for Resident Evil. 

While you're not shooting and evading zombies, you'll be solving fun and mysterious puzzles. I never found any to be particularly tricky; However, I will say for anybody who isn't willing to explore and going out of their way to observe contextual clues, I'm afraid you're going to have a few problems with the puzzles in this game. Just use common sense, and don't be scared to use guides if you're stuck, and I think you'll be fine. 

[u] A timeless classic with rough edges and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ does it have a lot [/u]

Every game has its flaws, and even this timeless gem is no exception to the rule. It is expected, after all, considering it is a remastered version of a game that came out in 1996. Resident Evil has fixed camera angles; While some may say it's needed because it adds an extra sense of uneasiness and anxiety because you can't see what's fully around you, I say this reason is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid and exactly why it's so annoying. No, you don't need a fixed camera angle for a game to be scary; All it does is frustrates the players by making exploration slower and more tiresome than it has to be. Most of the time, you can't even properly see what you're shooting at because the camera angle is in the way. The camera is far worse than any zombies you will have to deal with in Resident Evil. 

The second most annoying aspect is the ungodly amount of backtracking you can expect to do in this game. If you're someone who loath backtracking, I say skip Resident 0 and 1 altogether. And this is all thanks to the minimal amount of backspace space you get in Resident Evil. There are two reasons why its execution is so bad. Contrary to popular beliefs, No, it doesn't encourage critical thinking and good foresight. As you play, you'll come across several banks placed around the map that gives you quick access to storage spaces. So now, the question goes from whether or not I should take this to whether or not I have the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ patience to backtrack all the way to get it again and get back to my original objective. The second reason why its execution is so bad is because of how many plot-related items you're given and the inability to drop resources. Instead of having them take no room because it provides nothing beneficial to the player except furthering the plot and opening doors, the developers made it so it takes space in your backpack. And, as a result of this ridiculous decision, you will find yourself regularly, and I mean CONSTANTLY run into locked doors and puzzles only to find out the critical components in solving it are stored in your bank, so you'll have to backtrack ALL THE WAY to the nearest safe room and waste time again getting back to where you were. It makes exploration EXTREMELY time-consuming and frustrating to do. It takes all of the fun and excitement away from it when you always have to backtrack to get the necessary item you need to keep playing. Did I also mention you CAN'T drop items? Yeah, have fun with that. 

Third, You will see more loading screens than you'll see zombies. It's everywhere, and you'll have to sit through one and watch the door opening animation every time you want to enter a new area. Combine this fact with just how many times you'll be going back and forth to ascertain items and solve puzzles, and you have a game that is incredibly wasteful of your time as you spend hours of it in loading screens and backtracking. 

Lastly, aiming and shooting is just terrible. Your aim is automatic and manually aiming is a nightmare, and critical hit is entirely random. Essentially, all of the bad things about the old Resident Evil games can be boiled down to outdated mechanics and bad gameplay design choices made by the developers more than two decades ago.

[u] In conclusion [/u]

For some godforsaken reason, despite the game suffering from so many crucial problems, I still found myself enjoying it very much. However, I'm not blind to the fact that not many people are like me. So, as a formal warning, if you find overly excessive backtracking, the lack of control over camera angles, and the inability to accurately aim and shoot too tiresome, then I highly suggest you stay the hell away from Resident Evil. It will be a horrible experience for you, and you'll thank me for saving your sanity and time. However, if you're one of those that is willing to tolerate these issues like I was able to miraculously, then what you'll find is an unforgettable experience and a true classic to remember.

[b] TL;DR [/b]
It's one of the best survival horror games ever made, but please approach with caution. If you're the type of person who can't adapt to tank control, hate backtracking and seeing loading screens every few minutes, then you might want to consider skipping this and watch someone play it instead.

I used to judge the Resident Evil series a lot more for its silly plot and terribly written characters, but over time I've come to really miss 90's game design and how it had more bravery to challenge the player and force them to explore and think a little. (Not a LOT mind you, these puzzles are still pretty easy.) Tank controls, limited inventory space, key collecting, crimson heads, and typewriter saves are all a bit cumbersome, but without that friction you'd just mindlessly blast through and not really take in the amazingly well crafted sights. These mechanics make you feel like you are inhabiting the space and feeling the tension of the conflict a lot more than in most modern games where you just sort of blast through a lot of the time. Kudos to the RE2 remake for doing a solid job of keeping some of this stuff in when most developers are turning away from that kind of design. What I'd REALLY like to see is a game with the demanding mechanical richness of classic Resident Evil with the writing quality of a Last of Us or God of War 4, but in the meantime you sure could do a lot worse than checking out this iconic mansion and its still unmatched pre-rendered backgrounds. Despite the god awful writing, there is some serious artistry in the visuals and atmosphere department that still stands above most of the rest of the industry today, and the gameplay can still cough up the goods in tense moments of just barley scratching by. Check it out if you somehow haven’t already. Also: the RE2 remake. I know a few Resident Evil fans who still haven't returned to the series after 6 understandably killed their enthusiasm for new RE games, but guys, they're GOOD again. Seriously.

Riding off the back of the most recent Resident Evil 2 Remake, which had been my first real experience in the series, I decided to dive a little deeper into the RE universe and backtrack to the beginning...or as close to it as possible because I enjoyed the RE2 Remake so much. There just so happened to be a publisher sale on at the time so I was able to snag pretty much every Resident Evil game that steam had to offer for a fantastic price.

I remember many moons ago when I was but a small bab, my brother had RE2 on Playstation and I decided to wap the disk in and see what was what. Needless to say I had to ask my brother to open every door I got to because I was absolutely petrified of the door opening sequences and the possibility of jumpscares. I just couldn't handle it at that age so I never got very far at all before I stopped trying to play it. Years went by, I dabbled every so often as I grew up and got my first computer, eventually after many more years I picked up Revelations 2 on a deal...I tried it, completed a chapter or two but I wasn't in the right mindset to play it. I did a bit of RAID mode then uninstalled it. Flash forward to recent days and the RE2 Remake really re-lit that fire and helped me rediscover the series. Now a lot older and more open to different genres of games, I found it really easy to fully embrace the nature of what a Resident Evil game is about.

Even as a remake of the original this is still an old game, yet it stands the test of time quite well, even with its pre-rendered environments. One of the rare few games I've ever played that actually pull it off so well, honestly can't fault them for the effort...looked a bit crusty here and there, but again for its age its a great job.

One of the initial things that worried me was the control scheme...now i'm all too familiar with tank controls and I know for a lot of people it can be a deal breaker, honestly? a little frustrating for me especially in tight spaces with ♥♥♥♥ running at me...but have no fear! For they have an alternative movement scheme that gives you more freedom of movement with the WASD keys. I suppose adding this was a way to appeal to the more modern gaming audience and I honestly think it was a good move. It does generally make getting around a lot easier without trivialising everything. The only thing it really effects are the constantly changing static camera angles as you can easily spin yourself off in a random direction if you press another directional key after a camera transition and it isn't the right way. Accidentally ran back into the open arms of a zombie a few times from that...or span around during the short boulder escape sequences, causing Chris or Jill to run DIRECTLY into said boulder.

I'm well aware of the Chris punching boulders meme. Can't wait to play the game and see it for myself.

Quick note on the gunplay, its auto-aim and headshots are purely RNG based from what I could see...biggest chance to pull a headshot from personal experience was pretty much with a shotgun, pointing the gun up and waiting until they are within an inch of grabbing you. Even then though, a headshot is not guaranteed. Whats more is the number of rounds needed to drop something changes from enemy to enemy.

Decently sized map with multiple areas to explore and goodies to find...there no real rush unless you're a speed runner or there's an immediate event happening, like you hear someone getting attacked or have to rush to get a serum to cure someone of poison. There's an invisible timer on those things, if you fart about too much they WILL die. Besides that the only thing you have to worry about are zombies getting back up if you leave them too long and haven't either set them on fire or blown its head off. If its your first time, just kick back and explore to your hearts content, learn the lay of the land -- er -- mansion and be conservative with ammo and supplies until a little later into the game.

Having events play out in certain ways may or may not leave you at an advantage or disadvantage, it really depends on what type of ending you want or weapons/items you are after. The big one, the video game that defined them all, the magnus opus that created a standard still used today and inspired almost every good survival horror to come. The controls, the setting, the atmosphere, the annoying but carefully placed jump scares. It wasn’t the first of its genre but the original Resident Evil implemented what every horror game had to show at the time – from previous Capcom titles such as Sweet Home to the western Alone in the Dark – along with the movie culture from the 80s, from Shining to Romero’s movies. All of these inspirations combined created a frightful journey of horror but with an over-the-top plot worthy of the worst, best American B-movie. Despite the low budget, they utilized whichever mean they had to craft the most immersive experience as possible, the pre-rendered backgrounds and the doors opening that create tension but are ultimately there to hide the loading times are two examples of this.

What came was a revolutionary game that set the bar and defined its medium, and still today this HD iteration, an upgrade over the Nintendo Gamecube remake of the game, of the first Resident Evil still holds as solid as ever. The tank controls might be unfamiliar for some but it is a deliberate and necessary choice to truly delve into the narrow and unsettling hallways of the mansion, where at every corner a disturbing sound or a tough enemy could be in wait to eat the players’ necks and immediate response is required without feeling confused over where to turn. The fixed camera all the more reinforces this feeling of dread and helplessness because, despite being fully armed and distant from the enemies, there will be many times where the players won’t be able to immediately see the zombies, nor realise how far and safe they are from danger.

The enemies’ placement, the puzzles and the difficulty spikes are all still highly accessible and rewarding to overcome today as they were over 20 years ago, the game has only ever improved and it still plays beautifully on every system blessed enough to have a port of its own. The series might have had its ups and downs and many old fans might be only pleased with the second remake of the series now since it’s the only game in years that tried to replicate the original feeling instead of fully committing to action set pieces, camp entertainment or the reboot RE7 tried to do, but this first chapter is still a milestone under every department, and it won’t yield its throne anytime soon.

One of the greatest video game remakes of all time breathes new life to the legendary survival horror game and now, its HD remaster brings the genre back from the dead to magnificent results. 
A perfect starting point for newcomers but also highly recommended to veterans  of the series, RE-HD isn't just a pretty graphical overhaul but a whole new experience, with new puzzles, new enemies, new locations, new gameplay features and a rewritten more detailed script, a package that makes the game feel like a fresh Jill Sandwich again.  

But-just-take-a-look-at-this! Graphics are updated, with some new small touch ups, bloom effects etc. running in smooth 60fps and proving once more how great pre-rendered backgrounds can be - still looking good after all these years. My only complaint is that due to the game being originally designed with 4:3 format, the new widescreen option is a compromise, simply zooming the camera close and cropping out some details sinc eit would be impossible to implement a true 16:9 format unless they worked on everything from scratch. Also it's unfortunate that a few backgrounds look a little bit more grainy and blurry in some small parts  because they had to be upscaled to match our new resolutions. The blood still looks great though. I hope it' s not Chris's blood!
In my humble opinion, the 4:3 is the best format because of the extra details it offers, making your character feel smaller and really enhancing the sheer scale of the mansion (wow! what a mansion!) and the loneliness you face in its empty corridors.
But the great thing is that the game offers plenty of choice. You can switch between the display formats anytime during the game. And that also counts for the control scheme where you are given the choice of traditional tank controls or modern ones. Personally I feel that the tank controls are better, the game was designed with them in mind, so it offers a perfectly balanced challence (instead of easily zig-zagging your way past zombies) making it far more enjoyable to play. Modern controls felt a bit strange to use, causing some slight disorientation due to the constant camera angles changing, but again, it's wonderful that the game offers a choice so everyone can decide which method suits their tastes better!

Music is equally moody and full of dread, with many familliar pieces carryimg over the original game.
Finishing the game multiple times also offers plenty new unlockables, from costumes, weapons to extra game modes. And while it might seems a pretty daunting task for people who aren't used in the tropes of classic survival horror with constant inventory management and ammo conservation, don't be afraid, as the game offers multiple difficulties and with enough patience you too can be a master of unlocking.

Resident Evil HD Remaster is the crowing achievement of classic survival horror, a game that everyone should experience and for fans of the genre is an essential item for their game collection.

And this ladies and gentlemen is how to remaster a game!

I love the Resident Evil series. No, I adore it. I've played all of it and I consider myself a huge fan.

However, as far as RECOMMENDING goes, I can't recommend REmake to anyone nowadays. I did play it on Gamecube and had a lot of fun back then. It looks gorgeous and it's very hard in a good way.

But it's 2019 when I'm writing this, and it's very hard to have any fun with this game if you haven't played the original old Resident Evil games. Especially if you've played RE2 remake already. There are too many things about this remake that will feel very awkward and hard to get used to. Here's a short list:

* Tank controls. Obviously. That wasn't a problem for me, since I have a lot of experience with classic survival horror, even before RE (see Alone in the Dark 1992), but they'll feel very stiff and awkward nowadays.

* No markers of any sort. Considering this game is relatively non-linear, you'll at many points have 6-8 important "key" items in your inventory, and you'll constantly be going, "Hey, where did I see that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ door/lock/puzzle that I need this item for?" At least RE2 Remake did a smart thing by adding notes and markers to doors and puzzles on the map. Good luck trying to remember what should go where in this game, though. (Especially if make the mistake of taking a week-long break; you'll be completely lost when you get back.) Oh, and most of the time you'll have like 6 item slots. It's a huge pain in the ass.

* Last but not least: door animations. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, unskippable, slow-ass door animations. They'll drive you completely insane within an hour. Want to hear something funny? Original RE2 and RE3 actually were released for Windows in  the 90s, and both games allowed you to SKIP door animations. Because PC loads the next room almost immediately, obviously. And yet this remake somehow fails to have that feature. It literally takes about 8-10 seconds to open a door into another room, and let me tell you, Spencer mansion has A LOT of doors. About 10-15% of your gameplay time will be watching door animations. You can install a mod that will allow you skip door animations, though, which means running it all the time with the game _and_ having your anitvirus program go nuts whenever it's activated.

If you're going to play a Resident Evil game, this is the one to play. As the kickoff of a franchise that would have more ups and downs than a roller coaster at an amusement park, this is the game that truly defines the series and is what Capcom is trying to go back to through RE 7 and RE 2 remake.

The atmosphere of this game truly lives it up to it's horror name - the designated camera angles, the ambient sound effects, the terrifying sound of monsters looming in the distance, so many things in this game can strike fear into the heart of player. The game knows this too, always prompting you to "Fight your fears and survive." as you load into a game.

The puzzles in this game are not too difficult to complete, and are more than likely the easier part of the game. Most of them require some back and forth to pick up certain items, so on your first play through there might be some awkward moments, but all the others after, you'll be able to outsmart the game and know exactly what to expect. This is what helps the game have such replayability and why it's avid in the speedrunning community.

One of the only drawbacks this game has is the movement system because of the fixed camera position. However, the remaster version allows analog stick movement and has auto-aim that helps you to turn around much faster than the original, and this should help you get by. My recommendation is that you play with a controller and with a D-Pad (or on "original" controller settings, which the game automatically configures for you. It just sets the analog stick to behave like the D-Pad does) as this is the way the game is intended to be played. You also have to remember the game was originally created for the first Playstation, which has no analog stick at all, which is why D-Pad movement feels more natural with this game (D-Pad is character based - hitting left will ALWAYS turn the character left, while analog stick movement is camera based, where if the angle changes 'left' might become 'up'). It might feel strange and janky at first since the movement is not like most other games today (the RE 2 remake actually changed the system to make it more like RE 4 with over-the-shoulder free movement likely because this system is limiting) but with enough practice, you'll be able to dodge everything like a pro.

The survival horror aspect of this game is electrifying. You could play this game 1000 times and it would still be an intense experience every time, especially playing on higher difficulties. Things change as the difficulty goes up, such as less healing items and less save items (because yes, you need an item to save the game, and there's only a limited number of them, so you better be strategic about it!) which cause you to be more cautious about being careless around zombies and other monsters. Also, the amount of ammunition the game gives you is limited as well, which should make you think twice about unloading your clip when you should be saving it for times when you really need it. Not only that, but the game punishes you in other ways for using your precious ammo when it might be more beneficial to just avoid the threat in the first place. I won't spoil it, but let's just say if you use up too much ammo, you might be seeing red later ;).

Finally, the replayability factor of this game is amazing. Usually with console games, you might play it once just to say you played it, and then maybe again later in life to revisit it. Maybe you'll play a game a lot because you like it so much, or to achievement hunt and try to speedrun or 100% it, etc. The thing is, some games do factor in that you'll play again by adding some extra goodies that bring you back. This game is no exception to that. Not only do they add in costumes that make for hilarious encounters with these characters (as they transfer through most cutscenes) but they give you some extra things for achievements you've gotten (I won't spoil anything there either). Not only that, but the game has two distinct characters that you can play as who each have a different 'skillset' (hp pool, tools/items they start with) that make it just that much more interesting. You can beat the game as one character and then play again and have a completely different experience with the other character, even if you already know all the puzzles and strategy to get to the end. As soon as I beat the game, I started it up again as the next character and had a completely different experience following the same story and events, and it only made it that much more fun. It also lets you decide for yourself who you like playing as better, since each character has some advantages and disadvantages, and it's debated online which character is actually "easier" to play as. But this is Resident Evil, and nothing is easy ;)

All in all, this game is a masterpiece and the best beginning to a series that anyone could have hoped for. It is defining for Survival Horror and for the franchise as a whole and I highly recommend you play through it if you intend to become (or are!) a Resident Evil/survival horror fan.

Great game! It's nice to see where the series started. To those of you who don't know, this is a remaster of the 2002 Gamecube remake of the 1996 original game. Confusing? Don't worry, it's awesome. Let me break it down a bit.

Story: The story is simple on the surface but becomes more meaningful as you progress through the game. However, if you're looking for a game that explains the story through cutscenes then this may not be your game. Resident Evil relies heavily on notes and diaries for storytelling and background information, so I highly recommend you read everything to fully immerse yourself. But to put it simply, the story is about you going to a mansion and discovering why there has been a zombie outbreak. Pretty simple but still appealing.

Graphics: The graphics are still exceptionally good considering it's remaster of a Gamcube game. The game supports widescreen and 1080p with up to 60FPS. My only complaint is that CAPCOM only partially remastered the textures. This results in awkward moments where you see beautiful textures next to choppy, low-resolution textures. Despite this, the game still looks good and lighting is AMAZING.

Sound: The sound is great. Voice acting is generally good. Gunshots and doors sound clear and realistic. The zombies sound terrifying with their moans and roars. The music, while not entirely memorable, does a great job of making situations more horrific. The save room music is heaven to your ears and will most likely become the only tune you'll recognize by heart.

Controls: This game has tank controls. So if that's not your cup of tea, then maybe you shouldn't play it. But if you're up for a new experience the controls are definitely unique. You can only move one way at a time and you can't move while aiming or shooting, which is terrifying when you're fighting some other creatures like dogs and others I won't mention here. Other than moving and fighting, there is an interact button but that's pretty much all there is. It's simple to learn but hard to master, especially when exploring your first few hallways.

Gameplay: The gameplay is the best part of the game by far. You explore areas throughout the mansion. Solve puzzles. Unlock new areas and backtrack to old ones. Encounter new enemies and surprises. Collect items such as quest objects, healing herbs and ammo. You get new weapons that are all optional to use. You can literally beat the game with just your knife if you really wanted to. Several difficulties to attempt. You can only carry a certain amount of items at a time so you're gonna have to get well acquainted with the item boxes located in several save rooms. You're going to be responsible for making choices that can permanently kill a companion in the story. To make a long story short, the game is superb. It's diverse and dynamic.

Verdict: 8.7/10

This is a great version of the game that defined the original survival horror genre. It is a no-frills experience that is easy to pick up and play, complete with scares, a B-movie atmosphere, lots of puzzles and a unique mansion. Unlike in newer so-called "survival" games, there are no tacky features added to satisfy industry expectations. Every room has a distinctive "feel". The soundtrack, visual and sound effects, zombie placement, puzzles and fixed camera angles are instill a sense of mystery and isolation.

The player is always on edge, as every move requires planning. Dead zombies, if not burned, turn into much more aggressive monsters after a while. Resources like kerosene and ammo are found in small quantities and take up inventory space. Decisions have to be made on whether to kill zombies, go around them, fetch kerosene from an Item Box to burn them etc.

The mansion is filled with puzzles and hidden items, almost all of which are part of some combination or contraption, and the inventory is not very big, requiring the player to keep pieces of the puzzle and important locations on the back of their mind as well. Saves are manual and limited by Ink Ribbons, which can only be used on typewriters. All of this is in contrast with the simplicity of the gameplay itself: just move, try to aim (maybe offscreen) and shoot.

RE HD has high replay value, with Jill's and Chris' campaigns, alternate modes and special guns and costumes, unlocked by completing challenges. The modding scene is still active, although most changes are cosmetic or silly (except for the FPS fix, which is pretty much required due to game engine bugs.)

Truly a classic, and worth playing. That said, there are a few minor caveats that I'd mention. 

To newcomers to the Resident Evil ("Biohazard" outside the USA) franchise who have never experienced a classic RE game (meaning anything from RE4 onward, with the exceptions of RE:Outbreak & RE:Outbreak File#2), be warned that this isn't going to be quite like the 2019 remake of RE2.  

Like the RE2 remake, there are a number of fairly simple puzzles, some creepy environments, some minor jumpscares, back-tracking after gathering keys or clues, defense items (albeit, they're single-use, but they stack and don't take up inventory space), and you would be well-advised to conserve your stronger ammo by avoiding combat altogether whenever practical.

Unlike RE2 remake, however, it [b]is[/b] a classic RE game, meaning it has traditional "fixed-camera angles," (fixed camera angles were a bit of a common thing for early survival horror genre games and the adventure/mystery genres that they borrow heavily from - exploration combined with puzzles, keys, clues, and mixing items together all are fairly common things to these genres as well) and isn't particularly action-heavy (no QTEs, roundhouse kicks, or other fancy moves that you might see in the era of RE4-RE6; and combat equates to pressing and holding a button to raise your weapon, which also immediately turns your character in the direction of the nearest enemy, and pressing a button to attack it or another button to switch targets).

Probably my only real complaint, some of the textures are kinda hit or miss. Some look excellent with the new lighting effects and look like they got a decent retouch; others look a little blurry - like they were just stretched a bit - and actually look worse than the graphics in the GameCube and Wii versions of the game.There are some mods out there to fix the textures though, if you really want to mess with it, but it'll take up a few GBs of space in your PC to do so. On the upshot though, this version of the game doesn't have the awkward brief pauses that occurred whenever the camera switched between angles during cutscenes back in the GameCube and Wii versions, so the cutscenes will at least be smoother if you're trying to record a video to upload to Youtube or if you're streaming.

If you already have this game for the Wii or Gamecube, I wouldn't advise bothering with picking up this version. But, if you haven't played it, or if you're able to catch it on sale for a reasonable price (Steam sales happen often enough that I wouldn't recommend bothering with paying full price), go for it!

Upon I play Resident Evil 1, I only played the third-person shooter Resident Evil (4,5,6 and Revelations 1 and 2) and Resident Evil 7. It was my first time playing the classic Resident Evil and games with fixed camera. On top of the camera, I was not prepared for the complex map design that requires lots of exploration and backtracking. Only a single one of them would not be a problem, but when they combine, it is pretty deadly. I was lost constantly, particularly in the mansion session, as it is so hard for me to gain a sense of direction with the fixed camera inside a very complex map. To make the matter worse, lots of environments look similar, and each camera is placed in different angles, meaning you don’t see the character in the same direction once the camera switches and that made me so disoriented. This is my main problem with this game, I spent most of my playtime trying to figure out where I was supposed to go. After the mansion, as the map gets more linear, things get better, but that mansion part has already killed my patience so I did not really enjoy this game.

Another problem with the design is the “hints”, meaning the guidance the game gives on what should be the next. This game does not nail it as you would experience lots of times when you gather items or arrive at some places but unknowing what should be done to the items or places. It is probably due to the time it was made when people were still using walkthrough books to figure out game puzzles and maze (so the game did not have the incentive to explain things explicitly or it would impede the merchandise sales).

A couple of extra things centered around why this game is notoriously hard: it is a hard game itself with rare resources and unforgiving enemies that do not go down easily; you could die a lot because you can have a hard time seeing your enemies with the fixed camera; the control is clumsy and stiff impeding your movement and action; the very limited inventory slots and the frequent backtracking increase your chance of death a lot; there is no autosave and your save times are limited by the infamous ink ribbons, so get ready for redo sh*it tons of progress again and again. If you are about to play this game, prepared yourself mentally for lots of frustration.

This remake isn't ashamed of being RE1, it's not trying to be a different kind of game and bring a completely different experience. It is faithful to RE1's gameplay style and overall experience, but expanded and improved in almost everything. It nails the perfect balance between new and familiar that only good remakes can achieve, and is a great and highly replayable Survival Horror game, even more replayable than the original thanks to the different difficulty modes you can unlock, such as Real Survival and One Dangerous Zombie additions.

This game was something of a slow burn for me, but I'm glad I stuck with it, because it really is a great game and classic for a reason.

[b]First, the main reasons that I hated it in the beginning:[/b]

[h1]1. The Controls[/h1]
The game offers two major options for control schemes here. Alternate and Original. Alternate has a reputation for making the game too easy (because the game was designed for the Original control scheme), but I strongly suspect that everyone saying that plays with a controller. To put it simply, the alternate control scheme is god-awful with a keyboard and I really doubt the developers spent much time on that use case. 

The main problem is that, while your directional movement keys are relative to the camera angle, they will be INSTANTLY overridden if you press even a movement single key after a camera transition, jerking your character in a totally different direction (often in the OPPOSITE direction and back into the previous camera angle). The easy way to fix this would be to maintain the current movement axis as long as at least ONE movement key is being pressed. That would be more similar to the analogue stick behavior (because analogue doesn't require the same kind of micro-adjustments digital switches/buttons do).

I switched to Original (the tank controls) and it became vastly more playable. Even though they are still sluggish.

[h1]2. Fixed Camera Angles.[/h1]
I am not watching a movie, I am playing a game. Despite softening my position on this once I started enjoying the game, the general principle still stands: fixed camera angles are annoying and you should have a very, VERY good reason for forcing them on me.

[h1]3. Bullet Sponge Enemies.[/h1]
The BASIC zombie in this game takes 10 shots from the pistol to kill on Normal difficulty (unless you get a critical and pop their head like a grape). You start the game with 15 rounds of ammunition in your pistol. I can understand the rationale for avoiding one tap head shot combat in this game, but that is just excessive. I honestly love games that put you in a position of weakness and force you to use your wits to succeed (I love stealth games), but this is just too much for me and you don't have enough alternatives to kill them to make up for it. For reference, I think Easy enemy tuning is much better and I would rather have half as much ammo with that than the usual ammo supply with meat shield zombies.

[h1]4. Generous Enemy Grab Ranges in Tiny Rooms[/h1]
I'm familiar with most of the technique commonly used for avoiding zombies (including baiting a grab and then running past as they recover), but having dodging be one of your best option to avoid getting munched on in a game with slow tank controls and fixed camera angles that make it difficult to consistently judge distances is a recipe for frustration. If you don't dodge, your other options are to let them grab you and button mash to throw them off (still taking damage), use a counter item to instantly break out (and deal damage to them), or to stand still and empty an entire magazine in the their face. The only one of these that is particularly satisfying is dodging them, but it just doesn't feel consistent at all, especially in tight corridors.

[b]In spite of all this, I found myself having quite a good time with this game for a few reason:[/b]

[h1]1. Level Design[/h1]
The bulk of the game takes place in the Spencer Mansion, a creepy labyrinthine structure filled with puzzles and deadly traps. This area slowly opens up as you explore it, unlocking new areas, solving puzzles, and trying not to get smooshed, stabbed, or gassed to death. The area gradually opens up and as it does so, you get more and more comfortable with the layout. But they don't let you stay comfortable, reguarly changing the game by introducing new threats, bringing back old ones (like the new Crimson Head zombie that is apparently new to the remake), and even closing off routes to force you to take a different path. The game does a great job of keeping you on your toes.

This is also in part the reason I've soften my position on fixed camera angles... Somewhat. See, one thing that these shifting and obscure camera angles do in this game is mess with your sense of 3D space. Navigating a true 3D area with full camera control would be much simpler, but in this game, the camera shifts from front angles to rear angles to top angles to side angles and so on, sometimes in the span of a single room or a long hallway. It makes the already confusing mansion feel disjointed and almost surreal. You never really have the information you think you should have. Sometimes you have no idea what's directly in front of you. Sometimes it's a zombie. 

My thoughts on this are mixed, because I still find it annoying on a certain level, but the more I played, the more I understood the positive impact for this type of game or even just THIS game specifically. I still don't like fixed cameras in general and they need to be a very intentional and considered choice when used... but I don't think fixed camera angles are a mark against this game.

[h1]2. Resource and Inventory Management[/h1]
You can play as one of two characters: Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine. The biggest gameplay difference between the two relates to their inventory. Chris has 6 slots plus his lighter. Jill has 8 slots, plus a lockpick. In principle what this means as that each character has to pick up a particular item that the other doesn't need. Christ has to pick up Old Keys to open standard locked doors, while Jill can open these with her lockpick. Jill has to carry a lighter (in addition to the kersone flask for burning bodies), while Chris always has one.

A huge, persistent strategic element of this game is utilizing your extremely limited inventory space. A weapon takes up a slot. Additiona ammo takes up a slot. Each individual healing item takes up a slot. Keys take up a slot. Beyond that, it's often necessary to have one or more puzzle-related items in your inventory at a time. You can put items in functionally bottomless storage boxes (which share an inventory throughout the game), but these are only found at very specific points throughout the game.

[h1]3. Focus and Replayability[/h1]
The final major thing that I enjoyed about this game is a design philosophy that is less and less common in modern games: replayability. This game is clearly intended to be played through multiple times and in multiple ways. Players are rewarded for knowledge and mastery of the map layouts and game systems. Part of this is the presence of two different characters who, in addition to the different traits that actually change the game a fair amount, also have their own unique permutation of the narrative. Another is the difficulty modes which, in addition to the more simplistic damage scaling with is more common these days, also modify enemy and consumable placements. 

This game can be finished pretty quickly once you know where to go and what to do. It is nothing like the modern open world game that requires a minimum of 30-40 hours and then offers a bloated endgame of recycled content and collectibles to waste more time on. This philosophy is accompanied by a variety of unlockables, including weapons, costumes, and game modes.

With the release of RE2's remake and it having sparked my interest after having played the demo, I decided now would be a good time to haul the first Resident Evil game out of my colossal game backlog and give it a go. As it happens, aside from an abortive run at RE2 back in the late 90's, this is actually the first time i've ever really played a Resident Evil game. Needless to day, I am quite late to this party.

So how was my adventure into this "classic" mansion in this "classic" game? :o

Well, it showed its age quite quickly with its controls, which are clunky and was the cause of a few irritating moments. I played very few 90's era survival horror games (Silent Hill 1 was pretty much it), but this certainly plays like something from that era even if this is a remaster. The fixed camera and the sudden changes of perspective that often led to running in the opposite intended direction was not something I enjoyed. But... it is a really old game.

The rest of the gameplay actually came as something of a surprise for me. Despite being called a "survival horror" game (which it is), to me it felt like playing an adventure game as you roamed around looking for ways to solve puzzles and open doors. So much so that it seems to me like this was the gameplay Capcom chose for their game, and then decided to add all the zombies and freaky monsters to make things more interesting. The combat was hard at times, but that seemed to have more to do with the poor controls then it did with the enemies being rather tough and their tendency to not stay dead. Overall, I have to go back to what I said about the controls: I had some issues, but I largely let it go because of how old this game is.

Lastly, the story is... well its alright. I didn't exactly come into this expecting the next Nier: Automata or Yakuza 0. But it worked and all the little notes people left behind for you to read give you a pretty good idea of the sorts of people that inhabited the mansion. I played as Jill (so far), and did find it rather hilarious how my support character Barry seemed to come up with reasons to split up and for him to investigate areas already covered. My only real issue story-wise is less with the story itself, and more with a mechanic (or lack thereof). For those who don't want to see spoilers for a game over 20 years old, i'll tag the following part:

[spoiler]When facing the decision whether or not to give Barry his gun back, I opted to give it back. I got the achievement for "saving him", but the boss fight following this decision seemed to have gotten him killed without actually telling me. I didn't notice until much later in the game when it was far too late to go back. Didn't get the best Jill ending thanks to the game killing Barry off without telling me. :( [/spoiler]

Anyway, although I don't like the controls and ended up playing something more like an adventure game than the sorts of horror gams I'm used to... I did like this game. Sorta. It's alright. I do plan to play it again as Chris just to see that side of things, so at the very least I'm willing to play this more despite my issues. So i'll give this a "yes". Hooray.

Resident Evil Remaster is a port of the Resident Evil remake for the gamecube from 2002. I got this game on sale thinking that I wouldent like the game all that much, but it turned out to be my favorite RE game on steam so far.  It should be noted that the mechanics are antiquated in a sense,3D models on 2D backgrounds limited saves, tank controls(which can be enabled or disabled, though alternative isnt any better), static cameras, and backtracking. If you want to enjoy the game, you have adjust to these limitations in order to truely enjoy the game.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The gamecube version looked amazing for a 2002 game because of the high quality background rendering allowed more resources to go to the 3D character models. Here they took the background from the gamecube version, put some filters on, and called it a day. Its not distractingly bad per say, but you can tell what's 3D and what's a 2D background if you look hard enough, in a strange way it can help you beat the game cause the diffrence between 2D and 3D point out what you can interact with along with the glow that show up with important items in the envoirment.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You can pick from 2 characters each with their own advantages and disadvantages, Jill and Chris, though the story will more or less play out the same. Your squad gets ambushed by a bunch of zombie dogs when looking for missing teammates are are forced to retreat into the mansion. After that you have to go through the storyline of uncovering what happened to your teammatesthe dirty secrets in the mansion. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Gamplay is mostly the same, but a there are diffrences. Each character has their own special items and skills, for example Jill can pick locks, but Chris can light enemies on fire. The camera is static, ammo is limited, and you cant carry much items. It is smarter to keep a mental note of where items are instead of carrying everything you see, especially as Chris.  Its also better to save ammo if you have the option to avoid around the basic zombie enemies, cause if they're not burned alive or head is completely gone, they WILL come back and they'll be faster and tougher. I know for playing the game that picking Chris for a first time playthrough is the harder choice.For example Jill can mix a special chemical to help kill a boss, Chris can't do that, he needs help from a friend, but that friend can only help if certain conditions are met, so Chris really only can kill said boss by utilizing the Cyberdemon tatic of shooting at it until it dies. The game is also much more scarier as Chris cause you are alone for most of the game. The game is also puzzle heavy, though there not too diffucult to solve, its usually a matter of exploring every nook and cranny for anything that you need or for hints which usually makes the solution obvious save for a few exceptions.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
If youre willing to get your feet wet in older, argueably more frustrating gameplay design, you just may like this game.

[h1]A classic I liked and hated at the same time[/h1]
There are a lot of reasons why I personally disliked the RE1 remaster but most of them are very subjective to my tastes so I'm recommending it on the grounds that in its remastered form it's reasonably playable even if you're not into retro games and because RE1 is a gaming classic. It has a number of things going for it if you can get past the horrible controls and frequent loading screens.

If you enjoy modern games more than old ones and/or don't care much for the Resident Evil franchise this one won't be a lot of fun.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
However if you like the franchise (I got on board because I'm a huge fan of RE7 and because I like the movies, yea let's not get into the movies though...) there's a couple of good aspects to this game:
-Atmosphere is surprisingly good considering the fixed camera and grainy gif backgrounds from the last century.
-There's a bunch of neat bits of info and history regarding Resident Evil lore, if you value that anyway.
-Puzzles are rewarding once you figure them out (but are also unforgiving and I hated doing them but I just don't like puzzles, see negatives section further down).
–Shooting the weapons themselves feels satisfying, disregarding that the fixed camera makes aiming feel god-awful.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
And oh boy here we go with the things I disliked. Mind you this is a bit of a rant section rather than constructive criticism because I just need to vent after finishing the game):
-Did I already mention that the fixed camera feels terrible? I get it, it can't be any other way in this case because it's a remaster but it's still one of the worst things in gaming and an artifact of retro games I can't wait never to see again.
-The game doesn't care if you succeed or don't. Let me elaborate. RE7 subtly funelled me to the ending and I almost never got stuck anywhere. This game does nothing even remotely like that, I had trouble figuring out what to do on many occasions even whilst googling what to do. You might miss a subtle item's hiding spot and go across the entire map to only to be missing that item for progress and then unless you google it you might as well re-search the entire play area multiple times. I find this ridiculous and very frustrating. But it's and old game, I get it.
-The loading screens. Every single door in a huge mansion (and other areas) is a loading screen. Every single door. The animations are now stuck in my head and I guess they're kindof iconic? But you have to get around the map a lot of and with each trip to a different area the only thing I could think of were the dozen or so room seperator door animations. This might seem like nitpicking but the animations take about half the time of actaully getting anywhere.
-The inventory. I'm not complaining about the inventory size being small, I know there's a reason for it but I wish you could carry more of smaller items and that some quest items like keys wouldn't take up space. It serves no purpose and a key taking up as much inventory space as a granade launcher is silly. The small inventories only make you look at more door loading screens (see previous rant point).
-The sluggishness of figuring out the puzzles and looking at door loading screens feels out of sync with the narrative speed and so you lose touch with the story.

[h1]In conclusion[/h1]
I would never re-play RE1 but I don't regret having the experience of going through it once. If you're into the franchise or want a taste of gaming history give it a go but unless you're a masochist keep a google tab open.

This was a great game with a few bad design choices.
The positives are the atmosphere and the whole feel of the game. The puzzles are sometimes easy and sometimes a bit challenging and made sense most of the time. Only once or twice I felt a puzzle was not logic.
The action is not the best, but deciding what weapon and ammo to use is very fun. exploring a new room and finding new ammo feels great because your resources can become pretty scarce at moments.
Even if the story was cliche, I still enjoyed it and was executed pretty well. The mystery around the house builds up great.
I also like how close they stayed to the original game. Nostalgic feelings until the end.

The game does have some bad things which I can not leave unmentioned. The inventory size and the doors!
Let me start with the inventory. You can only cary 8 items at once (if you play with Chris it will only be 6).
In my opinion this is way to little. I had to backtrack soo many times just because my inventory was full. I don't dislike backtracking, I even like it, because it really makes you feel being part of the environment. But this was way too much.
Here is a key, but you don't have space. So go all the way back to that storage box to drop that inkribon you have and then come back here so you can open that door that is on the other side of the house. And once you are there you see this save point but you need an inkribon for that so you have to travel back to the storage box to get it and then go back so you can save the game. Also the gamedesigners decided to break one of the doorhandles that connected two pretty important parts of the house. So everytime you wanted to go to the other part you had to walk all the way around. It really took away the fun sometimes. Backtracking is also less fun because of the doors.

That brings me to the second bad point of this game:
The doors. In the beginning they make the game feel scary, because you never know what is waiting for you in the other room. But after a while they become very very tedious. To give you an idea look at the following calculation:

There are 266 doors in this game. Every single door you open will show you a door-opening animation. These animations take around 7 seconds. If it is your first playtrough you will most likely go trough every door. That is 266x7=30 minutes.
It doesn't stop there though. Most of the doors you will use at least twice. That is 1 hour looking at doors.
BUT... many doors you will use a lot more than twice. Especially when you have to figure out where to go next. I think many doors you will use at least 4 times if not 6 times. That is around 3 hours of looking at doors. Some paths require you to go trough several doors. So it ends up of you running an hallway for 3 seconds-->7 sec door opening animation-->running for 5 seconds-->another 7 seconds of a door opening animation-->1 sec of running-->7 seconds of looking at a door, and so on.
It took me 14 hours to complete the game. And I would not be surprised if at least 4 hours of them is looking at doors.
I decided to get some snack so I had something to do when I had to go trough all the doors.

It's just a very very bad design choice. I know the old game had loading times and they covered it up with the doors. But in these times that is not necessary anymore. For nostalgic reasons the doors are very cool and they do have their charme. But at least give us an option to turn them off. 

Overall I enjoyed the game and it felt satisfying to find new resources. The game challenges you to be wise in how you use them. It is just the doors and backtracking that are horrible. Maybe the backtracking would not be as bad if the doors were not so annoying.

Conclusion:
Game: Good
Doors: Bad

[b]Resident Evil HD REMASTER[/b] is a survivor horror with focus on exploration and puzzles. The story is pretty simple, the team is sent to investigate strange murders and they get attacked by zombie dogs. They run from them and arrive at the mysterious mansion. That's where the game starts. You can choose one of two characters to play as. They have somewhat different stories and some puzzles change depending on the character you choose. I would recommend finishing the game as Jill first, as she is more easier character, she has a bigger inventory and puzzles are easier for her. 

The gameplay hovewer is fun by itself, there is no need for a good story when you have a big mansion full of secrets and you just can't stop until you solve them all. Unlike in Resident Evil: Zero, there's no need to carry a lot of items from room to room, because you can put unneeded items in the item box and retrieve them later at any other item box. So inventory management isn't so tedious in this game. There's also another interesting feature, zombies in this game don't die from a full clip shot in their body, they just fall down and regenerate after sometime, sometimes they even become stronger after regeneration. The only way to take them out is to burn their bodies or remove the head. It makes you think twice either you should waste your bullets on zombies or just run around them, hoping they wouldn't be able to bite you. 

Moving on to the visuals, the graphics aren't Full HD, you can see the distortion in the background, like their rendered in 720p, nevertheless the game still looks wonderfull because of it's art style. The game has a certain unsettling mysterious atmosphere, that you rarely see in survival horror games. Soundtrack plays a huge part in it, it sets up the mood for each room, getting into a room and hearing this quiet peaceful music makes you instantly feel at home, because you've a safe room and can now relax for a bit before getting back into the action. Voice acting feels cheap, but not as bad as Resident Evil: Zero, just mediocre. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Dark mystery atmosphere
+ Interesting exploration
+ Engaging puzzles
+ Multiple ways to complete the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Quite a lot of backtracking on first playthrough
- Mediocre voice acting
- Backgrounds aren't HD

Overall this game is a great experience and I recommend it to everyone, who likes exploration and horror games.
