While I've never played any Resident Evil games before this I was interested with how the ResE2 remake was turning out so I decided to start with this since I've heard great things about it.  I'm a big fan of how detailed this remaster looks in comparison to the 1996 original, not only does the atmosphere look just as eerie but it controls great as well (I opted for the original "tank" controls).  The forced camera perspective lends itself well to the genre, giving you a sense of uneasiness as you navigate your way through the mansion in search of answers.  The way the game handles strategy is also very fun and rewarding, knowing the layout of the mansion and where enemies are located leads to saving precious ammo and health reserves.  In some areas you can even weave your way past an enemy that's right in-front of you given the proper planning, it's really fun to pull off successfully!  I also appreciated that the puzzles are (for the most part) straight-forward enough that the average player should be able to solve all of them without needing external help.  Lastly, it's great that in the map system you can find if any explored areas still have collectibles or not.  In my case it came in handy using it to clear a large area before moving on to another one and I'm sure it'll be a major help to players that are low on resources.

I did have some frustration understanding the examine system at first but after plenty of meandering around I eventually solved my problem which was simply/uneventfully orienting the object in the correct way.  Due to this, I went through roughly half of the game without being able to open first-aid-kits properly due to the aforementioned problem.  However, it is worth mentioning that it definitely increased the tension of resource-management which made for some fun nerve-wracking scenarios.  Thankfully they were surmountable regardless even on my first playthrough on medium difficulty but your mileage may vary.

Without a guide the game took me about 22 hours to beat, it felt really exciting to finish a section with the expectation of a finale only for the game to have plenty of meat left on it's bones to chew.  With another character to play as and achievements to unlock I'm sure I'll be enjoying the game for many more hours to come!

Like a few other reviewers, I have been priveleged enough to have played both the original and the remastered version. 

Honestly, this is how a remaster should happen. Not only is the unique gameplay replicated in a prettier environment, there is also new gameplay, locations and enemies to conquer. This is an absolute must-play for those that are interested in survival-horror.

The escalating gameplay is clearly mindful of people who have played the original version. Trust me, this will not play out the same way if you are returning to your outdated guidebook and trying to complete it. There are new puzzles, item locations and encounters alike. Were you expecting to be ambushed by dogs in the L-corner hallway? Instead, you'll be met with a jump scare of a dog bouncing off of the glass, giving RE veterans a nudge that "hey, this is still a new game." Even with passing knowledge of what has changed, that suspense is always kept through each new room. Not much is left over from the original, and the score alone adds new elements to the game that weren't present previously.

I do have one personal gripe, and it is with the optional control scheme. I know that this may be controversial for some of you, but giving players to ability to run freely in other directions without stepping to rotate the character definitely takes away the danger of some of the encounters. This makes dodging a lot easier and the combat gameplay a better experience for those that want to experiment. It's very easy to look at this and say that it doesn't matter, but this objectively affects the difficulty of the game and I felt the need to bring it up. For those of you playing for the first time that are anticipating tank controls, there is absolutely nothing wrong with the classic controls and I recommend playing once with them before moving on. I insist that nothing is actually wrong here, but be mindful of the difference.

The voice acting is much better (obviously), if a little uninspired at times, but many obvious remarks from the first iteration that were hilariously bad to listen to have been replaced with dialogue that is down to earth. It really helps with the atmosphere, as Jill is no longer the "master of unlocking" and the location is no longer "what a mansion". By today's standards, this game has a great story and good dialogue all around. There are a few lip-sync issues (which could easily be my hardware failing to keep up sometimes, as I have seen better sync with other people playing the game) but it's nothing immersion breaking. 

The new side-stories told by the environmental design and new locations in the remastered version definitely bring a lot more to enjoy even if you have never played a Resident Evil game before. Atmosphere is a heavy draw to these games. If you can appreciate the details, this classic will still have something to offer you.

The original Resident Evil released on the Sony Playstation and Sega Saturn in 1996, was a ground breaking experience. 
Never before had a horror game have such a sense of dread and fear.

Taking Infogrames's 1992 Alone in the Dark recipe and honing it to a sharp edge, Capcom created an experience that stuck with us since 1996, but how does it compare to today’s modern gaming standards?

Graphics:
The graphics in this HD remake are fantastic, from the pre rendered backgrounds to the character and asset models, it sets the tone and atmosphere perfectly.  Comparing the original to the remake, it is surprising how bland the original looks today and clearly shows how far the technologies have evolved during the last couple of years.  Overall it gets the job done, and really makes you feel isolated.

Sound:
An extremely atmospheric soundtrack and crisp sound effects from your footfalls down the corridors to the thunder booming outside the mansion, the sound design leaves nothing lacking and completely submerges you into the setting.  
I would suggest playing with headphones if possible. 


Gameplay:
And so we come to the biggest problem facing Resident Evil: HD.
The gameplay had not aged well.  We have been spoiled and hand held since those early days in 1996.
The limited Inventory slot system and opening door animations is what kills this otherwise great experience.  Although I do understand that the inventory management and door animations creates tension and pacing, it does get tedious and frustrating at times.  I would have liked to had been able to see how it would play, if you were able to carry more items with you, on the other hand it makes perfect sense as without it, there wouldn’t be a need to back track and a lot of the tension would be gone.  Is it the gameplay which is dated, or did we become spoiled and used to being coddled by modern games?

The puzzles are fun and not difficult.  You get an endorphin dose from your brain every time you figure one out.
The controls can be a little frustrating at certain points, but can be forgiven as the game simply would not be as effective without them.  Playing with a joypad which has an analogue stick and Dpad, gives you the option of switching seamlessly between the modernised and vintage control schemes as required, which makes life a little easier.  Using the analogue some times causes your character to appear to have seizures when the camera angles change on certain sections.

The voice acting is still garbage as you would expect, but adds to the nostalgia, I was however, disappointed that the live action scenes were replaced with CGI, although it wouldn’t be possible to use the old footage in this remake based on how much content was added, still, it would had been nice to have them viewable as bonus material.
(PS.  Would someone please explain to the developers the difference between venomous and poisonous, it's no wonder Richard got bitten, he tried to eat the snake, apparently...)

Now that i have finished the game on stream, it's time to review it.

Presentation:
It's slick, it feels good and everything flows the way it should. Like the name implies, everything got a visual rehaul. Sharper texture, higher resolution and an uncapped framerate makes this game not only look good, it also feels good. But not all is well in Resident Evil:ville. Some textures look very rough in comparison to the excellent character models. One very notable example is in the Aquarium ring. Most of the textures in here look rough in comparison to the character. To the point where i was wondering if the game was processing all textures right. I guess they couldn't clean up all textures. Some might've been a bit too tricky.

Gameplay:
There isn't a whole lot to say here. If you played the Gamecube original, you'll seamlessly transition into this port. It feels great to play. Now, it has the added new functionality of the "modern control scheme" that was established in the N64 port of Resident Evil 2 where instead of the traditional tank controls, you have direct control over your character with the control stick, like a third person action game. It's useful but it also breaks the game in many ways. Specifically, how the zombies work. With the new control scheme, you can just run a quick circle around the zombie, bait him and then run past them without any issues. You can also do some pretty interesting move like quick shooting. Basically, cooldowns are somewhat broken making everything interestingly easy.

In the end, should you buy it? 
Yes. Yes you should. Not only is it the best way to play it, it's also an excellent start point for people who might be interested in the series but have yet to dive in. In the end, i give it a solid 9/10, mostly due to the texture issues. It's amazing. Get it, buy it, enjoy it.

Don't let the short play time here dissuade you about this review - I've played Resident Evil on the PS1, and this remaster in full on the GameCube, as well as a bit here on PC.

The game is sadly only a classic for those who are blinded by nostalgia, and it hasn't aged well at all. The updated graphics and controls can't gloss over the fact that it is very clunky to play, and much of it's challenge comes from how flipping awkward it is due to it's roots in over 20 year old technology.

Prerendered backdrops give it a visual splendour that 3d graphics of the time (even with the gamecube release) couldn't match, but they also make it really irritating trying to aim at enemies since the "camera" doesn't move at all. Enemies can be hidden for cheap scares , but once revealed it is very fiddly moving around them even with the updated controls - which are still pretty stilted in their movement.

The basics are good - the survival aspects of limted inventory space meaning you have to play more carefully than the likes of Resident Evil 4, and environments are non linear which gives it that puzzle aspect. But those are the only ways in which this very outdated game is "better" than RE 4. The action by comparison is dire, and it is still an action game - which makes 50% of it's DNA horrible in this day and age.

It is also a prime example of Capcoms inability to do measured storytelling. The original ps1 game had one of the dodgiest FMV intro's you could see, and somehow they managed to make it even worse despite using pretty swish CGI. As a young'un I didn't notice how bad it still was when I played it on the GameCube, but even now Capcom can't tell a good story and always put style over any substance. Not that I'd expect Shakespeare from a game with zombies and monsters, but the writing and "acting" here are terrible. I've played RE 7 and they've not gotten any better in all this time.

This is a remaster, not a remake like they're doing with RESI 2, and it's just a case of putting lipstick on what is now a very ugly decrepit pig when it comes to the gameplay. If you've never played it then it might be worth a look dirt cheap, but know that much of it doesn't hold up all that well from a modern perspective. If you're adament that this is the "best" RE then those rose tinted glasses of nostalgia will be obscuring what are now glaringly obvious cracks. 

An ideal Resident Evil for me is one that has the action and setpieces of RE4, and the more intricate level design of Resident Evil 1 / 2. But this is not that game, and whilst RE4 still holds up well for what it is - this doesn't at all, so I can't recommend it. Not when something like Dead Space has the same horror, action, non linearity, and plays much, much, muuuuuuuch better. Anyone who wants to disagree would do well to remember this is 2018, and NOT 2002, things have moved on greatly since then and RE HD Remake is crap these days.

Resident Evil HD REMASTER is a remaster of a remake of original Resident Evil. It's also a survival horror. Albeit survival nowadays means actual surviving simulation while in survival horror genre it just stands for limited supplies. As in, you have less ammo than enemies. And it's also not as much horror. Well, it has an awesome atmosphere. But as far as scares go, this franchise is the most tame out of them all. I can assure you that as scaredy cat. Just that many people played it at kindergarden age. Oh, and because original was at the peak of technology. Stopped being revelant in horror once Silent Hill came out.

And yea. First there was original Resident Evil. On PSX. Got some ports around, such as nice Saturn one, that one having exclusive battle mode. Exclusive even to this day. Nintendo DS also had an enhanced port of original. But Gamecube got something else. It was called Resident Evil. But fans called it a REmake. This is the big deal, as it not only improved graphically but actually remade the game, adding new rooms, changing layout and puzzles, getting new mechanics. HD REMASTER is a Remaster of REmake, adding few things like widescreen support. Albeit widescreen just cuts background below and above, adding camera pan as character comes closer to those edges. I actually liked it, gave it a weird feeling, fits to this game. That, and heavily upgrade the qualities of backgrounds and textures and lighting. Yep!

Sadly, it's not a very good version for it has few fixable flaws. The first, is how brutal this is on low specs. Apparently, the game always renders at a certain high resolution internally, so I had to download a fan patch that forces it to render on same resolution as what you set. I also didn't find a resolution that fits to my laptop one in options. That, and game speed is directly tied to FPS, with original Gamecube running at 30FPS, so better fix the game, yea. The worst, however, is how they screwed up music. Some of the tracks play way too fast, giving it a chipmunk feel. You will feel it once you get to the residence. Once again, fan patch to the rescue.
I still recommend getting this version. Because I don't own Gamecube. Also, screw Nintendo.

By the way, preorder content sucked. Soundtrack was not complete and had tracks that play too fast just like in-game. Artbook turned out to be just a bunch of screenshots of the mansion.

As for control options, I recommend the following: If you got a gamepad, pick Control Type B, which is like classic RE games. Between Alternate and Original control, well, if you play on keyboard, pick Original. On gamepad pick Alternate. Alternate control is a new type in REMASTERED, it makes characters control like in 3D platformers. Or 3D action games. Not tank controls. However, as game changes cameras a lot and wasn't designed for that, not to mention that character turns instantly which doesn't fit to whole survival horror feel, it just doesn't work too good. Alternate controls on gamepad however allow you to use analog stick for new controls and d-pad for tank ones, so you get both. Between manual or auto defensive items usage, pick manual. You can use it the moment you get grabbed from the front and the timing is fairly forgiving, it's more fun to be in control.

[h1]Intro, Graphics and Music[/h1]

This game has a high place in gaming history. Resident Evil HD Remaster is the HD version of the 2002 Gamecube remake of the 1996 Resident Evil that came out on Playstation. The Gamecube version itself was beautiful visually and it was only in 480p. The HD remake is simply gorgeous looking. There are some blurry elements in the pre-rendered backgrounds but it takes nothing away from the visual narrative and I mention it only as nitpicking. The music is also really good, always creating tense and often jump scares. There’s nothing like finding a safe room and listening the series trademark calm piano music that assures your that you are safe, for now. 

The game runs extremely smoothly at 60fps. The CGI cutscenes however are both in low resolution and fps, but overall do not hurt the experience at all. 

[h1]Story[/h1]

You play as either Jill or Chris, two members of the special police force STARS that investigate a series of murders in a remote US mountain area where they come across a mysterious mansion which is infested with zombies and other abominations. The heroes struggle to survive while trying to make out what has gone down. 

I would suggest to every newcomer to take his or her time and read all the files that can be found in the game. The writers have put together some very tense background stories that fill you in on the bigger picture. 

The original Playstation game had a B movie cheesy narrative. Here they have changed a lot of that and now the game is more serious but still retains some corky dialogues from its past. The voice overs are also good. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Resident Evil or [b]REmake[/b] as it's known in the RE community is an old-school survival horror game with emphasis in puzzle solving, item management and tight corridor fights. The puzzles are cleverly scattered around the game. Big part of the game’s allure is to explore the mansion and other premises in order to find clues. In doing that the game offers you a thrilling experience via the fixed camera system which offers a cinematic experience. The camera system works better with the traditional tank controls but you also have the option to use modern controls that allow you to navigate in the direction of the analog controller. 

The second most appealing part of the game is the item-management. You have a limited number of item slots in your inventory (Jill has 8, Chris has 6) and you need to think really carefully about what to take with you when leaving a safe room. 

REmake offers a lot of action with the traditional variety of weapons you will find in a horror game, but remember, that conserving ammo is one of the main strategies here. In higher difficulties there are not enough healing items and ammo to keep you safe, so you will need to either skilfully avoid enemies or find alternative routes. Each one of the playable characters have different stats (attack, speed, vitality, item slots, etc), something you’ll need to take into account when choosing yours. 

After you finish the game you will unlock the higher difficulties which offer higher challenge (more enemies, less supplies) and some special costumes and weapons that will spice up your next runs. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Highly recommended. It’s a classic and currently the best in the series at least until the remake of Resident Evil 2 comes out. If you enjoy this one, you should also check out the remastered version of Resident Evil Zero, which is a prequel leading to the events of this title. Both games go as low as 8 bucks during Steam sales. Easy pick up. Cheers!

This is a REMASTER of a REMAKE of the unforgettable Resident Evil, a classic of the horror genre.
The remake is perfectly done. The visuals and other aspects of the game got upgraded to modern standards while keeping the original experience intact.
 
There are a couple of small problems with the control scheme though. The first problem is that the original game had tank controls, while the remake lets you choose between tank controls and a more modern camera relative control scheme. The problem is that camera relative movement isn't ideal in a fixed camera environment. 
Let's make an example: you're going straight down a corridor by tilting the analog stick UP with the camera pointing at the corridor from behind your back; halfway through, the camera goes on the other side of the corridor, so now it's in front of you; now, if you're still tilting the stick UP, you'll find yourself still moving forward, but not in a camera relative way, but if you ever so slightly tilt the stick a bit to left (or right), the character movements will go back to being camera relative and, in most cases, you'll find yourself going in a totally different direction from where you intended to go. 
It's not THAT bad, but it can get frustrating at first. 
So the choice is between facing this problem or choosing tank controls which, let's admit it, are a thing of the past.

Now, for the interesting part.
After all these years, Resident Evil remains one of the best horror games out there. 
From the first moment you'll be thrown in a hostile environment with no clue about what to do. You'll find a ton of doors and many things with which you can interact, but still don't know how. So you'll have to explore your surroundings while managing ammo and inventory space to slowly understand what to do and where to go. This, to me, is the strongest point of Resident Evil. At first, you'll have the feeling of being stranded in uncharted territory, but when your surroundings will get familiar you'll be able to navigate through them easily.

With its fixed cameras, the game's main focus is exploration and survival, not combat. This brings up another little problem with the control scheme: if you want to have the original experience, you need to choose tank controls. Even if they're outdated (and honestly terrible), tank controls add to this feeling of being helpless in an hostile environment. With limited mobility you won't be able to avoid enemies easily, so you'll have to make more tought choices: do I risk getting hit to preserve ammo or do I shoot? The original game was clearly built around this control scheme, that's why the modern one harms the experience a little bit, making you able to dodge enemies way more easily.

Another key aspect of the game is the puzzles.
The puzzles in RE are easy, you'll never find yourself thinking for an hour about a particular solution, but, at the same time, they are engaging and satisfying to complete. In some cases you'll find yourself racing a clock for the solution, in others you'll just feel the pressure of the menacing gaze of angry crows watching your every move. We could also say that you'll be always trying to solve a puzzle, even if it's just finding a key to open a door.

Finally, we need to address backtracking.
There's a good dose of backtracking in this game, but it's not as tedious as you might think.
First of all, you may actually WANT to do some backtracking. In the very first room you'll find various locked doors that you'll be able to open only much later in the game, so, for the whole time, you'll always have that voice in the back of your head reminding you about those closed doors and how much you want to know what the hell is inside. Even if you don't really want to revisit the same areas, the game changes them up a bit by adding new enemies or modifying some doors.

In any case, if you're a fan of horror games or you're just beginning to explore the genre, Resident Evil is a MUST PLAY.

I'd been trying to get through REmake for a while now, but the controls and camera always stopped me in the beginning of the game.  This time though, which has to be at least my third try, I think everything just clicked and I ended up actually enjoying a lot about the game.  Do I like the controls and camera now? Oh god no, this control setup, even with modern control options, is awful.  They are clunky and absolutely a product of the time.  There was never a point where I felt comfortable with them and would routinely make weird turns or get screwed by bad camera placement, and that lasted till the end of the game.  I'm not even truly sure why I was able to beat the game this time, but I think it's because I really wanted to experience the rest of the game.

In particular, it's the exploration and general puzzle aspects that kept me going, which is what initially got me interested in the series.  The puzzles are a mixed bag though, ranging from okay, to "This was just lame padding".  They really could've been more inventive at multiple points in the game, but took the laziest option design wise.  Despite that, I liked wandering around, finding a new room, getting a new item, checking it out to find a name or something hidden on it, that ended up being my favorite part.  That's the exploration part that I enjoyed.  Finally getting that shortcut opened was so good.

Combat is also a mixed bag, it's usually okay, but dogs are obnoxious and I don't know how many times bad camera placement screwed me on shots. If you want to enjoy the one game which started it all but you don't like eye cancer - then this remastered version Resident Evil is for you.

Visuals:

Resident Evil looks really good if you consider its age. Mostly due to the fact that the backgrounds are pre-rendered. Some of them look like they have to, others though seem to have been rendered on a lower resolution. At least it seems that way. Nevertheless, the backgrounds are beautiful. The characters are a bit different though. They look good while you're playing and even if you're forced to zoom in during cutscenes, they don't look bad. However, the characters seem have lost any kind of emotion because, no matter in what situation they are in, they always make the "question mark"-face. Excuse me, not all. Barry's face works to some degree - he can look angry. 
It works for Albert Wesker because he has sunglasses but Chris and Jill seem to have lost all capability of processing of what is going on. But hey, Jill has a tank-top skin which easily directs your eyes somewhere else. Also, her breasts jiggle. Nice attention to detail.

Sound:

Resident Evil has a great soundtrack and you can recognize  some tracks if you've played the original version on the PlayStation. Sound effects are fitting and the voice acting is decent. There are no brilliant dialogues here but on average, they're not as bad as in Resident Evil 0. As I pointed out in my review of Resident Evil 0: the story was basically the justification for the gameplay back in 1996. And since this is a remastered version, you have a remastered version - you know? They altered some dialogues and they are now not as cheesy as they used to be. But they still are to a certain degree. The dialogues basically evolved from a big chunk of cheese into a big chunk of Swiss cheese - the holes mean less cheese....
The game also supports surround sound but it is not that effective. At least not if you play on normal volume. 

Gameplay:

You have the option to play with the original controls (don't!) and the alternative controls which are very direct and make it much easier to navigate through all the rooms and dodge enemies. 
It basically makes the game easier. But then again, additional enemies have been added to the game who, to some degree, balance it out. 
You can also choose between Jill and Chris but there is no big difference. Some cutscenes are different, there is an inventory difference of two slots and as Chris, you don't have the lock-pick. That means, some doors (I think it's 5 in total) can only be opened with a small key which can only be used once but can be found in several different rooms. Basically, it narrows the amount of rooms you can enter in the beginning down and thus makes it easier to find the right way. Or the way to the next key item.
Compared to the original version, this version offers more more places/ rooms to visit, more and different puzzles, several events that allow you to achieve three different endings per protagonist and three additional difficulty levels after you've finished the game on normal (which I recommend for first timers - because you'll get a bit of a challenge). 

For those who have never played any classic Resident Evil: no auto-saves for you and real item-management is needed to complete the game. 

Verdict:

I can definetly recommend this one. In my opinion, when it comes to atmosphere and gameplay, Resident Evil HD Remaster is one, if not the best game of the series (Resident Evil basically died after Code Veronica X and Outbreak and then got revived with Resident Evil 7. Between those titles, it turned into a, at first enjoyable, but then really generic and boring shooter - looking at you, Resident Evil 6). It is also one of the best Survival Horror games. The only games that come close to a real survival horror experience like Resident HD Remaster are Resident Evil 7 (really good revival of the series) and The Evil Within (I haven't played the second one yet.). I don't want to include horror games like Alien: Isolation or Outlast because these games come closer to some kind of hide and seek than to anything else. And I don't mean that in a bad way. I just think it's hard if not pointless to compare those games to Resident Evil.

So yeah, 20 bucks? Sure. Less? Definetly!

[h1] Great horror game with tons of replayability, although flawed, but that doesn't detract from the experience.[/h1]

The first time exploring the mansion can be dreadful and intense, especially considering saves are limited. Normally you'd think limited saves would be a bad idea in a game but it serves to add to the tension here for a true survival horror experience. In order to save, you have to find "ink ribbons" and take them to a typewriter to save, forcing you to think about when and where to save, and you're always wondering when the game will give you a break and provide you some ink ribbons so you can relax and save. 

Your inventory is also limited by 6-8 slots, depending on who you choose to play as. You'll have to frequently go to a save room not only to save, but also to free up some inventory space by putting items you don't need into item boxes. It's more to think about with the limited inventory as you have to ask "what items do I need to carry with me, and where do I take them, to progress?" Luckily, the item boxes are linked so when you go to an item box in a new area, all your stored items will be there for you to access. All of this makes the game intense and challenging, the game wouldn't be as great without the limited saves and inventory slots in my opinion.

Once you get through the game once, you should replay it as the other character as each character has their own unique challenges, and new characters show up with new cutscenes and dialogue that add to the story. After your first play through, subsequent play throughs become less intense as you already know what to do and where to go, and I feel it naturally becomes a sort of speedrunning exercise because of that, at least it was for me. I just wanted to see how fast I could beat the game again and again. Replaying it allows you to unlock alternative costumes for the characters, including the RE3 costume for Jill. Beating the game under certain time limits unlocks new weapons, including a really fun and satisfying rocket launcher that one shots everything and has unlimited ammo if you beat the game in less than 3 hours. Replaying it can also unlock a challenging and fun "Real Survival" mode, which is hard mode but the item boxes are all unlinked which forces you to think about where to place key items in which item box. So there's a lot of replayability here.

There's a minor flaw that might take getting used to at first. Sometimes the changing camera angles and the alternative thumbstick controls clash - occasionally I'll move in one direction, the camera will change angles and at the same time I'll try and move one way based on the old camera angle but because the camera angle changed right then my character will go in a different direction than I wanted. Can be a bit frustrating at times. But once you get used to that, the game is a treat.

Before I get mauled by angry die-hard fans, I would kindly like to provide some feedback as to why I would not recommend this game.

I played the original game when I was little and loved it. I think it was essential in order for me to establish survival horror as one of my priority genres within videogames. I certainly think it was groundbreaking as it introduced a series of features that should justify the status of cult game it bears: the camera angles, the dark scenarios and the argumental framework the rest of the saga has drawn upon.

Of course that game had its flaws, but they could be ignored if you were as awed as I was at the aforementioned mechanics. Since then, a remake and a remaster have been released, which I think have barely touched or improved its most frustrating drawbacks. 

I would say the main reason why this game has managed to create such a faithful fanbase is the fact that it becomes more enjoyable as you replay it. However, as someone who hasn't played the remake and who certainly did not remember the puzzles, playing Resident Evil Remake has been a very underwhelming experience so far and I would say most people who play the game for the first time without using any walkthroughs or guides (like I did) would agree with me:

A great part of the the time is spent wandering from room to room trying to figure out where the items you need to solve the puzzles are. The problem is, as I was trying to find one of them, I ran into other key items that I would need in puzzles I could not yet access. This would not have been a problem if these key items didn't take up space in the inventory, but they do. Your best option is, then, to run back to the safe and leave them there. I understand that this is done to force players to go through corridors and make you fear that a devilish creature would jump into you from a window or from under a desk. That concept would certainly be granted the status of flawless, Harvard-quality logic if that happened the first two or three times you're forced to go through them. Yet, as it happens, you're bound to repeat the same path as many times as your inventory ends up filled up by key items or herbs you run into. Of course, the first two times you run through the same corridor, a certain event triggers which meant I joyfully saw myself having to deal with the anxious yet enticing feeling of adrenaline rushing through my blood vessels. After that, the following few times nothing happened and I could allow myself to relax and admire the beauty of the camera angles. By the time I was running through the same corridor for the sixth time, I was bored enough to grab my phone and browse Reddit while doing it: aaaaaand... there goes my survival horror experience.

Funnily enough, this would have been easily fixed by implementing two things:
[list]
[*] Let key items have their own inventory as implemented in many other games of the RE saga.
[*] LET THAT BLOODY DOOR KEEP ITS DAMNED DOORKNOB (and you know exactly which door I'm talking about). [spoiler] I know, I know it gets fixed, but by the time it did I was already too tilted by it. [/spoiler]
[/list]

Many other features have been improved thanks to the remake/remaster, that's for sure. For example, the shapes inside the mansion have never enjoyed that amount of detail. Yet I refuse to believe that it offsets the countless hours of mindless wandering and inventory-induced frustration.

Resident Evil is a big boy game, it is a game that expects you to not sniff your finger after scratching your butt. Unlike later games in the series, there are no real item drops, so everything in the game is finite. So if you use your ammo on everything and everyone, then you're going to run out real quick. You end up working out a system where you have to decide if its worth using your bullets to clap a fool or not, and even then you have to be careful.
Because they get back up.
And they're not happy with you. 

You work out in your head on how to move around, do you really need to kill that zombie, how to get from A to B with least resistance, what you should and shouldn't take with you, etc. There are some rooms that I only needed to to once or twice before I found the most optimal route from checkpoint to check point. (So yeah, I did miss the dog window scene. I got the fakeout, though.) 

The boss battles in the game are kind of push overs, especially when you realize you shouldn't be using your big guns on everything that moves. Some of the boss fights just kind of not happen if you know what you're doing. At least when you're playing Jill they do. 

For a game that technically came out in 1996, there's a surprising amount of replayability. Not only do Jill and Chris play differently, but the two experience entirely different events as well, even characters one would meet and not the other.

Jill can carry more, but I also want to know what her workout regime is. 80 pound lady can carry a grenade launcher that probably weighs more than her like its nothing. Breakfast of champions or maybe breakfast that doesn't involve peanut shells and spiders.

[h1][b]RE-enter the survival horror[/b][/h1]

[b]Though Resident Evil was originally released in 1996,[/b] this remaster is based off the 2002 remake, only released on the GameCube, and later, Wii. Thus, this HD version is the third time the remake gets released -- now on current generation consoles and PC, which means this gem is finally available to a much wider audience. Deservedly so.

As a survival horror title, you will be zigging and zagging through maze-like environments in order to gather resources, solve puzzles and avoid (or fight) zombies and other monsters. Knowing the ins-and-outs of your surroundings is essential, as you need to plan your route carefully -- most of the time the level design [b]is nonlinear and interconnected enough to allow you to take alternate paths to reach the same destination.[/b] After all, given the game's genre, it's unlikely your ammunition will be enough to allow you to waltz through every room and take care of every threat.

Zombies, while slow, may be a bit tough to dodge due to the tight nature of the hallways and rooms. Dogs, on the other hand, are faster than your character, but easier to dodge and deal less damage. You will come across many other biological weapons as you play, from slow passive-agressive creatures to agile deadly monsters, and once new enemies are introduced, they may start appearing in previously explored areas, messing up with your once safe route. 

[b]Another factor that can ruin your life (and resources) are the Crimson Heads.[/b] These powered up zombies can run (!), hit like a truck and take more bullets to go down. But there's a catch -- they are actually regular zombies the player eliminated and didn't dispose of properly. So, after killing a zombie, burn them with kerosene (which of course is a limited resource) or obliterate their head with a good shotgun blast, otherwise you may regret revisiting the place where you killed them later on!

On top of all these dangers ahead of you, you'll be mostly progressing through the game by solving puzzles -- and there are plenty of them, from simple riddles to puzzle boss fights. You will have to act logically, memorize codes, interpret files, investigate the environment in search of hints and so on. If it feels like you're missing something required to complete a certain puzzle presented in a room, there's no doubt you will eventually find the item needed to solve that when you least expect. And then, you will need to smartly backtrack your way back to said room only to be greeted with more key items, precious ammo and/or new places to explore. Rinse and repeat.

[b]The whole experience is backed by a great atmosphere from start to finish:[/b] the suspenseful tracks are there, the relieving save room tune is there as well; prerendered environments, though obviously upscaled from the original NGC release, still look very good, and [url=http://images.onesite.com/capcom-unity.com/user/brelston/remake/large/0afcc4cef926b233513450e036c0b23c.png] lighting reacts more realistically to character models[/url], greatly enhancing the look of the game while maintaining the core artwork.

Additionally, there are several unlockables that gives a lot of replayability to the game, such as outfits, new weapons and, most importantly, new difficulties. Beating the game more than a couple of times, for instance, rewards the player with the Invisible Enemy mode, which is exactly what it sounds like.

[b]All in all, Resident Evil HD REMASTER is an amazing title.[/b] Its smart design constantly challenges the player by making them adjust their routes on the fly in order to avoid threats and save resources, while travelling back and forth through zombie filled rooms and hallways to solve puzzles and progress through the story. Wrap that gameplay loop around a solid presentation that oozes atmosphere and you have a tense, yet gripping experience.

[h1][b][i]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/i][/b][/h1]

[h1]Recommended purchase point: [b]FULL PRICE[/b][/h1]

A remastered rerelease of the 2002 remake of Resident Evil, available for the first time on PC. Spoilers: It's great. The game's graphics and ambience were nothing short of astounding in 2002, and with only minor alterations still look incredible in 2018. Technically speaking, the port runs flawlessly. A new, alternative control scheme has been added for those that can't stand tank controls. There's no excuse not to pick up and play one of the greatest horror games of all time.

[h1]STORY[/h1]
Resident Evil's story is in a slightly surreal realm, its dialogue and occasionally bizarre character reactions treading the line of 'so bad it's good'. This is nothing new to anybody who's played any other Resident Evil game. In 1998, the S.T.A.R.S. Alpha team is sent to investigate the disappearance of the Bravo team, who themselves were investigating a string of cannibalistic murders. Finding Bravo Team's helicopter crashed in the forest and several of their number dead, our heroes quickly find themselves menaced by strange dogs and chased through the woods into a mysterious mansion. At this point the player chooses whether to play as Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, with the protagonist not chosen quickly becoming lost in the mansion.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
RE's gameplay will be familiar to those who grew up in the 1990s - you explore an undead-infested mansion with prerendered graphics and fixed camera angles, using either the original "tank controls" or the newly added relative controls, which allow for far more nimble control of your character. (Take note, the new control scheme allows your character to be so much more nimble that the game's level of fear and menace may be compromised. Whether that's a good or a bad thing is entirely up to you.)

Weapons are hard to come by and even harder to keep loaded - a very limited inventory space (even more so depending which playable character you choose) and scarce pickings for ammo in the game world ensure that clearing the mansion of zombies is basically a pipe dream. Running and skilfully dodging the undead soon become the norm, with killing relegated to zombies which are occupying major thoroughfares and shortcuts you find yourself travelling often.

Adding to the menace is the threat that killed zombies may resurrect, mutating into lightning-fast variants known as Crimson Heads after a certain amount of real-world time has passed, or after certain plot events. Crimson Heads are fierce and relentless, and their creation can only be prevented by getting a lucky headshot and destroying the head of the zombie or by burning its corpse. This of course requires kerosene (which is limited and takes up valuable inventory space). Many factors go into the consideration of whether killing any given zombie is actually a good idea or will make life harder for you down the road.

[h1]PRESENTATION[/h1]
This is where Resident Evil truly shines. The pre-rendered graphics are almost photorealistic, creating a real and constant sense of looming terror throughout the mansion. The sound design works hand in hand with the graphical fidelity, with mysterious creaks and thunderclaps piercing the eeriely silent night at all the wrong times. Generally speaking, Resident Evil games aren't exactly survival horror games anymore, in either the survival or the horror sense. RE1 is both, remaining to this day one of the scariest games on the market (thanks in part to its impeccable timing and restraint when it comes to actually unleashing jumpscares versus holding back and biding its time).

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
REmake is one of the great classics of gaming - one of those rare games that absolutely everyone with any interest in the genre should play. If you haven't already, rectify that. It's more than worth full price, so any discount you can get it for is a steal in my books.

With this is quite simple:

Did you like the original Resident Evil? Buy it.

Did you disliked the original? Don't buy it.

You haven't played the original? Only if you like the game scheme: carrying items back and forth, messy controls, fixed camera. I particularly don't like games in which the game mechanics themselves are my worst enemies, hence the negative review.

The first [i]Resident Evil[/i] game (known as [i]Biohazard[/i] in its country of origin, Japan, but they had to change the name to avoid problems with both an old DOS game and a metal band of the same name) is a classic, old-school third-person survival horror game.

I tried playing the game many years ago on Nintendo GameCube, but within minutes, I was put off by its clumsy controls and awkward, fixed camera angles. 

I recently played [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i], the prequel to this game. Although RE0 is basically an ancient game, too, I did enjoy playing the remastered version. Controls still felt somewhat clunky, despite an 'alternate controls' option that allowed playing without the original 'tank controls', but overall it was an enjoyable experience if you could deal with a few clunky old-school gameplay elements like that.

However, [i]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/i]'s controls still feel way too clunky, even with the same 'alternate controls' option enabled. Combined with its awkward camera angles, this game hasn't aged well at all despite being remastered.

It isn't just me. If you look at any gameplay video on YouTube, you'll see the player character constantly running into walls, furniture and other obstacles, looking like a drunk trying to find his way by stumbling from one solid object to the next, instead of the character just walking through corridors and rooms without running into anything in its way, like you can do in pretty much every other third-person game ever made.

So I can't recommend this game at all. If you're a long-time gamer and you loved the game back in its day and you can still enjoy it due to sheer nostalgia, that's perfectly fine. But these reviews are meant for people who don't know about the game and aren't sure about whether to buy it or not. Well, recommending [i]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/i] to that target audience would be plain wrong and deceitful, and I won't do it. 

That may sound defensive, but we're talking about a game that has fans who would actually kill people who voice their honest, negative opinion if they could. I mean, one of the most recent discussions on the Steam forums is literally an enquiry whether critical opinions about the game could somehow be silenced completely: https://steamcommunity.com/app/304240/discussions/0/3211505894136294244/. 

If you've played 2002's remake of the original game and you're just curious about the changes in this 'HD Remaster' version, it seems only the graphics have been upgraded. Backgrounds do look nice, but the other graphics like the characters, enemies and items don't look all that impressive, resulting in a noticeable difference in quality from the backgrounds. The graphical improvements to [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] were a lot more impressive and it looks stunning compared to [i]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/i]. Both remastered games come with widescreen support now, which is nice.

A final note on Steam's extra features: [i]Resident Evil HD Remaster[/i] has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game. Its 44 Steam Achievements are mostly very challenging and unlocking them all requires you to play through the game multiple times.

-Full Review (Some spoilers ahead)-
Plot: The year is 1996 and the arsenal forces of the RCPD known as S.T.A.R.S. is sent to an abandoned mansion to investigate the bizarre incidents that have occured in outskirts of Raccoon City. The branch consists of two, elite teams: Alpha and Bravo. Both teams enlist specialists that are proficient in the following areas: forensics, computer systems, weaponry, medical, vehicular and communications. Two characters can be selected before starting the game: Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. 

Jill is the B&E specialist of the Alpha team: a very charismatic and highly intelligent lady with an array of skills. She can also be assertive when it comes to serving justice and will align to her rightful morals. If Jill is selected, she starts off with 8 slots in her inventory and possesses the ability to unlock doors w/ her lockpick. Her partner is Barry Burton, a veteran & weapons expert of the Alpha team. He provides alot of help and tends to be quite protective of Jill in dangerous situations. Just like RE:Zero, there are some puzzles of the game require both characters to work together in order to reach the next stage. Even tho her gameplay is shorter than Chris, Jill's vitality is low because she can die within 3-4 attacks (depending on the difficulty, ofc).

Chris is the Sharpshooter specialist of the team: a strong-willed and combative guy that is level-headed when it comes to danger. He is very tactical and physically strong to overcome any obstacle. Although Chris starts off w/ very little resources, his health is greater than Jill's (about 4-6 attacks) and his speed is also much faster. He can only carry 6 slots in his inventory, but he contains his trademark lighter. His partner, Rebecca Chambers, is the Medic & biochemist of the Bravo team. A passionate and a critically alerted teenager, Rebecca's cleverness allows her to calm down in times of need and utilizes her fear to conquer any trouble. She is most helpful to Chris in sections where he lacks a particular skill or when he cannot complete a task on his own. Chris's route is tougher than Jill's as there are more zombies and hunters due to the timed events that occur in the game.

Overall, the RE franchise is the godfather of survivor horror that we take for granted nowadays. 'The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents. We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity, and it was not meant that we should voyage far.' - HP Lovecraft, The Call of Cthulhu

The king of survival horror for my money needs no introduction (Despite the irony of namedropping Lovecraft in the opening paragraph, but there you go). The revised controls make for a much more contemporary and arguably enjoyable experience over the classic tank controls, though there are more than a few times where this can be a pain (This was a game that was obviously not designed with this setup in mind due to the pre-rendered backgrounds and various camera angles changing - you'll find yourself on more than one occasion running in one direction, and then having to adjust to the new camera position and reorientate yourself accordingly). This can result in a few cheap hits from enemies, which can be fairly irritating. 

A beautiful game brought gracefully into the modern era; the gamecube's graphics still hold up to this day and the HD remaster just adds that extra bit of polish for a gorgeous experience. There are some downright pretty and artistic shots in this game. If you've never played Resident Evil 1, it is on the list of "Games you must play before you die" without a second thought - Newcomers to the franchise should count themselves lucky, you're in for a hell of a ride and there is no better place to start! The Spencer Mansion has plenty to offer still for returning veterans, like a fine wine this game only gets better with age, particularly with this iteration. 

The admittedly occasionally cheesy voice acting just drills home the B-Movie vibe, personally I love that ♥♥♥♥, if you don't, trust me; it's not a dealbreaker. I would be willing to bet that the ever-present dread which persists throughout the entire experience will invariably distract you from that, or trying to work out the solution to the obtuse puzzle in front of you will certainly occupy your mind. This game can be cryptic at times without doubt, but the majority of the puzzles, with a little bit of thought shouldn't trouble you too much.

The beauty of the whole experience I feel is that you're never quite sure when, if ever, you're truly safe. Just when you think you have a handle on things, or that you have it all figured out, the game will throw you a curveball in the shape of some unspeakable horror lurking in the dark. Suddenly you'll be wishing you hadn't blown that last clip on that thing you saw lumbering around on the west wing of the second floor, or that you hadn't used up your ink ribbons (Your currency for your finite amount of saves) when forced to confront that horrible noise you heard moaning under the stairs. "Item management" is the word of the day here - You cannot try to go postal on everything that makes you jump, otherwise you'll land yourself in a very unfortunate situation. This concept undoes many newcomers - The game will try to make you panic and use your limited resources at every turn. There are definitely more unsettling experiences available on the market in the modern era of gaming, but if fear is a turnoff, this probably isn't the game for you. 

As a side note, since I was a child I've owned every single version of this game on major consoles that I can think of - Resident Evil and Resident Evil : Directors Cut on PSX, Resident Evil : Deadly Silence on DS, REmake on the Gamecube and now REmake REmastered - and as a 28 year old man I finally got the stones to actually finish it for the first time! A couple of years of horror under my belt has finally made my composition into sterner stuff it would seem. It feels like a chapter of my life has finally been closed, in some insignificant fashion at any rate! Despite only just clocking it now after close to 20 something years, I absolutely adore this game, if you hadn't guessed already.

In summary, though not without its flaws, this game is what I would call an essential masterpiece, and it still remains my favorite in the franchise. Don't think twice! You owe it to yourself to play this game!

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a 2015 remaster of 2002 remake of 1996 classic Third Person Perspective survival horror game by Capcom. This one is very personal for me because I was dreaming of this game ever making it to PC or Xbox 360, but now also PS3,PS4 abd Xbox One players can enjoy it as well.

1998,"I will never forget it", that year Bravo Team of an elite unit of Racoon City police - S.T.A.R.S has been dispatched to Arklay mountains to investigate case of bizarre cannibalistic murders, but gone missing in the forest, a day later Team Alpha was sent to find them. Attacked by strange dogs our two protagonists, Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield were forced to hide in mansion not predicting what nightmare tgey have brought on themselves. On start we choose who do we want to play as, then our actual adventure begins and we can end it with one of five endings.
Gameplay remain unchanged over the years, from cameras set on walls we proceed from one room to another by solving puzzles, facing B.O.Ws (zombies mostly) and finding items required to survive, also our equipment is not unlimited so we must decide which ones are more important. Playing as Chris is harder as he does not have as many spaces in inventory as Jill and he must find a pistol and keys to some doors but have a lighter right on the beggining. His female counterpart is better in equipment management plus she use a lockpick on doors requiring old keys. To save our game we need to find the ink first, then use a typewriter.
After beating the game we unlock outfits and bonus modes such as One Dangerous Zombie, Invisible Enemy ir True Survivor modes.
Capcom upgraded graphics, remodeled some items, added customes from Resident Evil 5 and files unlockable by completing various tasks.
There is a large variety of weapons hidden inside the mansion, some are exclusive to certain characters, some unlockable by beating game on normal under 3 or 5 hours (Timer does not stop when you pause the game, only when you use a typewriter)
You are never alone, many types of mutants and bosses will wait for you in almost every corner of mansion, do not expect  too smart AI from zombies but the other ones are preety intelligent though.
Every location is climatic and force you to use your head, puzzles or tactics (sometimes it is better to run than facing our enemy), the mansion is not an easy place to plan next movements so you might need to see a guide on internet first.
Soundtrack does not exist when it is not needed (The only thing you need to hear are the footsteps of creatures walking nearby) but sometimes it will give you a moment to relax in save rooms or add a tense when it is necesarry.

So, how should I rate the game that defined survival horror for decades, gave birth to my favourite franchise and influenced my vision how perfect game should look like? Like I have said it is perfect, so 10/10 will be well earned note.

This is the first Resident Evil game I have ever played. I have never played the 1996 original, nor the 2002 Gamecube remake. I have never played any game from the Resident Evil series before, and I haven't watched or read very much about any of them (except for 7). Sure, I knew about herbs, and tank controls, and the fixed camera, and Wesker, and other assorted RE memes, but I honestly had very little knowledge about what this game would be like.

So, as someone who is new to RE, going in almost totally blind, and is completely untainted by nostalgia, my opinion on Resident Evil is as follows:

It's damn fantastic.

From the tense exploration, to the visceral combat, to the wonderfully brain-churning and subsequently domapine-pumping puzzles, Resident Evil is a highly enjoyable experience that pulled me in harder than any game has in a long time.

While it's certainly not particularly scary by today's standards, it often manages to conjure up a miasma of deliciously compelling tension, accentuated by the fixed camera and ever-limited resources. It absolutely made me jump more than a rew times. Hearing that zombie moan and shuffle, but having no idea where it is and how close it is to you, still still manages to put me on edge even though I've already killed dozens of the things.

The gameplay has two basic halves: killing stuff, and solving puzzles. Both are great. The gunplay is competent for a game like this, though it can be a little animation-lock-y at times. Perfectly lining up a point-blank upwards shotgun headshot and blowing a zombie's head to vapor, knowing that bastard ain't ever coming back, is one of the most satisfying things I've ever experienced in a video game. 
The puzzles are generally well done, often challenging you enough that you feel accomplished when you complete them, but not being so grueling as to grind the game to a halt. There are a few that are a little unfair, but if you get stuck on any, there's always the Internet to help you (Don't be ashamed! We all do it! And by "all", I mean "me").

The two distinct things this game has are obviously the fixed camera and the tank controls, both of which I found incredibly charming. The camera placement is is often used to great effect, creating a certain feeling with each new angle. The camera will linger at the beginning of a long hallway, creating a building sense of dread as you move towards its end. It will position itself behind a window, or a crevasse, or a fence, creating the feeling that something's watching you. Each new angle feels thought-out and intelligent, like a movie director controlling exactly what's allowed to be on screen. It's brilliant, and I wish more games had this feature and did it this well.
The tank controls (Which, by the way, are optional - you can switch to a modern "Alternate" conrol scheme, which I never tried) are interesting and unique, and work pretty well most of the time - which is suprising, considering how much I've heard people complain about them. They lend themselves well to the slow, deliberate pace of the game. It just wouldn't feel the same if you could instantly spin 280 degrees to get away from that monster chasing you.

Though Resident Evil is, by and large, a fantastic experience, there are more than a few issues I had with it, most of which are simply relics of its old age.

First of all, the door animations. Every single time you enter a new room, it plays a 3-ish second long animation/loading screen of you opening the door. This is a fun, sylish little detail at first, but when you're going back through the Mansion for the 10th time, going through door after door after door after door, it will make you want to rip your hair out. I understand why this was in the original game, and I also understand why people would want it in the remaster, but I would greatly appreciate it if there were an option to turn it off for those who are tired of seeing it for the 50th time.

That gripe folds neatly into my second and biggest issue: Backtracking. You will backtrack a lot in this game, going from save points, to items you couldn't pick up, to puzzle locations, again and again. While this is sometimes used as an opportunity to spawn new enemies and let you discover things you missed the first time, the slow pace, coupled with those damn door animations, can lead to hours of mind-numbing dullness as you move from room to room looking for the next thing to do. It is by far the worst thing about this game. If there was some kind of limited fast-travel, or, again, a way to disable the door animations, it might have been alright, but as it stands, it can be truly torturous.

Other than those two major issues, I have a few small others.
The ink ribbon saving system is a little bad. I understand the idea behind limiting your saves, but I often found myself in situations where I was effecively locked into the game because my last save was and hour and a half ago and I hadn't found any ribbons, which is kind of a ♥♥♥♥ move on the game's behalf. I think the resource-free save system that emerged 
in later games is a much better evolution of this concept.

MINOR SPOILERS FOR A THING 20 MINUTES TO AN HOUR IN THE GAME: [spoiler] The Crimson Heads are a little B.S. on your first time through. The game gives you absolutely no warning that the dozens of zombies you've killed are going to come back as far stronger versions and destroy you, so I got absolutely demolished because I didn't burn all their bodies, which, again, I was never told I had to do. All it would have taken was a dying S.T.A.R.S. member gasping "You....have to...burn....the bodies!" to convey this information in a fair way, but no. So that's a little uncool. [/spoiler]

And finally, there's the game's treatment of women. I played as Jill my first time through, and was struck by her consistenly poor characterization. Sure, when you're in control of her, she's a monster-annihilating beast, but in nearly every cutscene she's a whimpering, pathetic mess, always tripping over herself and cowering in fear until her helpless ass gets saved by one of her various beefy hunk teammates. It just really struck of old-timey game tropes that are better off staying in the past.

In relation to the overall gameplay experience, however, these issues are rather small, and I still had a fantastic time with this game.

----CONCLUSION----

Resident Evil HD Remaster is a brilliant game, a classic that started a genre (or two, or three), and a kick-ass experience that can stand against any triple-A game released today. I bought it on sale for dirt cheap, but I would absolutely say it's worth full price - if not more. If you, like me, have never played a Resident Evil game before, don't hesitate to hop on board with the one that started it all. It's made a fan out of me, and it will probably make one out of you, too.

Let me start by saying I'm not the kind of person who tends to play horror games. They're by and large too scary for me, and I really don't enjoy jumpscares, which seem to be a pretty popular method of horror these days. However, I could not put this game down once I picked it up, no matter how tense it got. Resident Evil is truly great at building a sense of horror where you never know what's going to be around the next corner, and that's intensely scary when you've got extremely limited supplies to work with. One of the true strengths of this game is its fixed camera--it may seem like an outdated relic of the past, but since the player is certain to encounter things from a certain angle, there's an element of cinematography present within this game that most other horror lacks. In some ways it feels constricting, but it really allowed the developers far more control over what they were creating in a great way.

As you progress through the game you'll become familiar with your enviornment, but never comfortable. Even in places you've been before you can't count on being safe, as there are constant surprises waiting for you around every corner. The only place you're truly safe is in the save rooms, but even those feel tense as each save costs you an item that only exists in limited amounts, making you question whether or not it's worth using before you venture out into danger. The whole game is commited to creating this atmosphere of unease for the player, and it knocks it out of the park in that regard.

This game does horror in a way that few other games I've played have, creating a game that's truly scary but also incredily gripping, even for someone who doesn't normally like horror. Really, everyone should try this game out at some point or another.

I greatly enjoyed this game, but there are a few things I'm going to talk about.

For anyone who doesn't already know: this is not an action game. The best way to survive is to avoid fighting more than strictly necessary, and several bosses can be bypassed altogether if you know what you're doing.

The path that you take changes the order and places in which enemies spawn and cutscenes happen, but some enemies will always appear in the same places at the same times.

Tank controls: one of the major difficulty factors in the game is learning to operate with the tank controls, once you've got that, the difficulty of the game goes down quite a bit.

Fixed camera: Adds to the horror, you can hear there's something there, but you just can't see it. The reason the fixed camera angle was there dates back to the days of the Playstation when this game was first made. The total number of polygons you could have on a screen at any time was very limited, so the environments were drawn in such a way that they were a single image to save polygon count and memory space.

Resident evil is one of the biggest named horror games. It used the idea of tank like controls and preset camera angles to add fear to the player of limited control and the unkown of what is ahead to be faced in the next camera angle. Does all of this make resident evil a good game as of today? I will be reviewing the game on a pro/ con style and end with my final conclusion.

Pro:
      The mansion and atmosphere is brillian. Large mansion like locations are excellent for a horror atmosphere because of how large it is and how closed end the hallways are. Added to that the game does an amazing job with sound effects like thunder and lightning in a few areas which helps aid the spooky nature that the game holds.

      The spooky moments that occure in the game are handled very well. Some moments that are ment to be spooky are simply sound effects followed by a adrinaline rushing music much like the moments when zombies open doors or when zombies break through windows. It is not easy to explain how well it is done but it is far better scares than the generic jumpscares that plague a lot of current generation games. Scares like these plays on the players mind.

      The game is full of replay value. That is a huge plus for the game as to how it has two seperate character stories which has some minor differences but enough that nets more than one playthrough. On top of that there is many endings depending on what characters survive till the end, many new modes which challenges the player like the real survival mode, and finally unlockable weapons with infinite ammo which are a major reward for those who can speedrun the game.

     Characters are very good. Each character besides their models looking good also have great dialogue. It is not super worth mention besides the point how originally when the game first came out somewhere in the 1990's had very cheesy dialogue which is ok in my book but how it improved with both the remake on gamecube and the remaster on pc, those changes are very much in need of acknowledgement.

     The saferoom music is a classic. Really that is it, the music is very soft and comforting, ment to inspire hope in a situation of fear or dispare. Definently worth a listen.

      ChrimsonHeads are very creepy. A new type of zombie never before seen in any other resident evil game exists in this one game, known as chrimson heads. They are mutated zombies that were killed and not burned. If left unburnt they take the time to mutate into these red zombies with sharp claws and run pretty fast. This is a warning to any future player to burn the bodies of dead zombies so they dont turn into chrimson heads.

Con:

      The initial first time player would be confused to what difficulty to choose. There options are very vague with slight hints as to what they are likely to be getting into. This is just a nitpick.

      Also when one dangerous zombie is unlocked, it is very scripted. When I say that I mean that he shows up in only a few set locations but he will always be there once that character is unlocked. There is no chances that he will show up in those set spot, he will be there everytime and that can be very frustrating making those locations where this zombie hangs around just a drag to visit. There really should be a percentage chance that he will show up in those set locations but within 3 to 4 playthroughs he always showed up in those same locations everytime.

Conclusion:

       There are so many good things about this remake of a classic game. It adds and fine tunes what made the original so successful without changing anything too much to allienate the game from fans of both the series and the original. There is some negatives and one if forgot to say was how in the later end of the game has more instant death situations which feels a tad unfair compaired the early moments in the game. That can be a tad annoying to experience 4 instant death moments within about a 20 minute time frame. That aside the game is amazing and I would reccomend it, definently worth a try and with practice and preparations any situation can be overcomed.

[h1]High Definition Nostalgia[/h1]

[b]The Good:[/b]
[list]
[*]Visuals worthy of being called a Remaster. Unlike other remastered games, just adding a few details here and there, this game actually updated and improved the overall appearance of the game. Better textures, reduced or more controlled colors, refined shapes of objects, this remaster was truely able to build its atmosphere.
[*]Game enhancements kept the suspense going. The developers added another type of zombie in the game, the "Crimson Heads". It made me think twice before walking close to any fallen zombie. If you're going back to this game, it should add enough tension and resource management to keep the game interesting even if you've been through most of the sequences. 
[/list]

[b]The Bad:
This is a list for those who are walking into this game for the first time. Beware! If you've played the original then maybe this won't be an issue for you, best that you skip to my 2nd complaint.[/b]
[list]
[*]Inventory horror. I don't know if I've been spoiled by most modern game's intventory system, but intentory management in RE Remaster is totally a rythm breaker. So you figured out which item to use, but you didn't carry it. So you have to run all the way back into the "safe room" to get it! You'll spend most of your time running back to the storage box to keep or take items. This game would be a lot shorter if you could carry all items at once. I don't want to ruin the inventory management as a part of a survival horror game, but maybe the devs could increase your storage capacity by at least 2 more slots.. (?)
[*]Slow Down Glitch. In my play through as Chris, I encountered sections of the game where instead of his usual running speed he would just slow down. I tried looking for solutions in various forums, but ultimately I just gave up on playing Chris and continued using Jill instead.
[/list]

[b]The Recommendation:[/b]
[*][b]If you're a fan of the original series, a collector of Resident Evil titles, then YES.[/b] This game is a must have and I would totally recommend it to you. At what price should you get this game? Well thats totally up to you, some would pay full price for their collection while others might wait for a sale. 
[*][b]If you're going to play this game for the first time, then I strongly recommend that you get it for 50-75% off[/b] at the very least. Glitches and Inventory management simply breaks the rythm and kills the mood that the game visuals built so well. Back tracking around the mansion can be mind numbing. 

Overall, this is a good game that deserves to be experienced at its improved condition if you have the patience to deal with its inventory issues.

What can I say? The game looks stunningly gorgeous 17 years on, playing this game 120fps versus 30fps makes it feel like an entirely new game.  It plays so smoothly, the jump scares still to this day make me jump and the hunters will always give me an uneasy feeling bypassing them as I open the door across the hallway.

This is technically the first game of the series (Resident Evil 0 is a prequel to this game so that's why I'd say this is the first main game in the series).  It's one of the best if not the best in my humble opinion.  Everything just works, the pacing from travelling through the tight corridors of the mansion, not knowing what's going to be around the next corner to little wooden hut out in the middle of nowhere where you meet what only can be described as an abomination living there.  The game just makes you feel uneasy from start to finish as everything is out to kill you and you never feel completely safe.  Your only respite is a save room and even then you have to eventually leave it to zombie invested corridors attempting to dodge most of them to save precious ammo on bigger more powerful enemies.

That is another thing this game does really well, it forces you to conserve your ammo which in doing so makes the game that much scarier as you have to attempt to dodge enemies in tight spaces without dying.  I can't tell you how many times I've been on red caution/danger health wise and just dodged enough to make it to a save room to collect a health item from the item chest and heal.  

Combine this with great voice acting (MUCH MUCH better than the original game which came out in 1996 on the PSX) and interesting characters and you really feel for your team whenever you meet them throughout the storyline.

You have a choice whether to play as Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield.  Each character has both pro's and negatives (Chris can run faster and has a lighter by default whilst Jill cannot run as quick but to compensate has a lockpick by default alongside being able to do other things Chris cannot).  Jill also has 2 more item slots than Chris does, has access to the grenade launcher which chris does not, has access to a lockpick which means she doesn't have to collect small keys to open doors like Chris does and finally is a lot more knowledgable on certain areas than Chris is which makes puzzle solving and one particular boss fight much easier.  For each character the gameplay is the same in terms of story progression, you need the same keys to open the same doors and the same objects to unlock the same items etc. but your interactions with your fellow Stars members are different and ultimately the game feels much different which gives the player an excuse to play through the game at least twice over, once with Jill and once with Chris.

Resident Evil's return to form before the 2017's RE7 came in the guise of the GameCube remake with a fresh coat of paint.

A lot could be said about Resident Evil, one of the most iconic horror video game series of all time. This remake of a remake (or remaster, rather) is the de facto best version of the original game. The game includes high resolution textures and supports modern controls, so there is no need to play with the old school tank controls.

A feature which was previously only present in the GameCube remake is present here as well, namely Crimsonheads. Killed zombies have the potential to resurrect themselves later on as deadly and fast crimsonheads which are really tough to kill. This feature is a great add on the already great game. The courtyard sections with Lisa Trevor are here, too. The HD remaster manages to retain its atmosphere right till the end, proving that the first game in the series is also one the best to date.

Veterans of the original game are able to run through the game with ease in a couple of hours, but for newcomers the game may take anywhere between 8-15 hours. 

Pros:
+ A fresh, new look for the best version of the iconic horror series' first offering
+ An incentive to play the game twice: Jill and Chris
+ Added features from the GameCube remake
+ Modernized control-scheme for those who want it

Cons:
- None
