The nightmarish game of my childhood, I remember sitting next to my sister while she was playing the game on a PS1. I have a vivid picture of the first time I seen the zombie in this game that caused me nightmares for days. I could not believe when I found out Capcom had made a HD remaster of this masterpiece. 

As an adult the first thing that caught my attention was the environment I found myself to play, a vintage mansion that I already knew I'd spend hours revisiting during the progress of the game, I've learned the locations of each room like my backpocket while desperately looking for a key or solution to a puzzle. That brings me to the puzzles of the game, I can't express how well done they are especially the Bee Puzzle which felt quite simple at first but the audio and setting that accompanied the puzzle made me forget my surroundings. The audio in this game is well designed because every time you visit an important location the music is drastically different to the regular audio, as the game progress and things get done, each time a new soundtrack plays the feeling of going forward is so well adapted in the players brain that I could call it a magic at times.  

I found the combat system to be in par to the original, at first I found it stiff and hard to adjust but with time I was able to pull off some nice headshots (much easier with controller). The one thing I didn't like about this game is the camera angles and how it affects the keyboard while moving from one angle to another, my character would change the direction of his movement if I pressed the same button on different angle, therefore, each time there's a new angle a 'go forward' button could be any of the WASD keys. 

The graphics are well done, each item of interest nicely highlighted in comparison to the background and monsters are easily distinctive. The music is absoultely fantastic, I found myself to be in trance while doing puzzles. Cinematics were ok at best, let's not forget this is a remaster so I didn't expect 21st century cut-scences. Story is well done although it didn't caught my attention all that much, I tend to forget different characters names and their significance except Albert Wesker because he was in the movie adaptation of the Resident Evil. The overall content of the game was fluid, I didn't find much items that were very situational or locations that would be non-significant in any way. The controls are fairly difficult to adapt but overall I'd say the game shouldn't be rated negatively solely based on one aspect. The gameplay is very compelling and after several hours - surprisingly, fluid. 

I certainly advice you to go pick yourself a steam copy of this game, as it might be just the best Resident Evil game to ever come out.

[b]A PC port of a remaster of a remake that was released in 2002 on the GameCube of a game that was originally released in the late 90s which already had a few different re-releases during the time.[/b] While the original may have aged considerably unlike its sequels & later games that share the same name, REmake–as called by many fans–updates pretty much everything about the original game as well as adding new content and slight changes to what was already there. 

Playing with a keyboard or a controller is entirely up to preference as they're both very much playable with this game. Keyboard and mouse controls are rebindable but you can only change controller buttons through pre-set control schemes like Type A, Type B, etc.

The plot starts off simply with a special forces team searching for another team that went missing. Killer dogs come around and the team escape to a nearby mansion and then the game begins.
Before all that, you can choose to start the game off as either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Each have different stats and you go through the story almost the same exact way solving the same exact puzzles.

Most of the game takes place inside a mansion full of claustrophobic areas. Every room you see is accessible at some point. It's a very non-linear game where progress involves solving puzzles in order to unlock areas to get items to unlock more doors to solve more puzzles and so on and so on. The entire game really is just one big puzzle box. The puzzles themselves aren't at all difficult and finding solutions is one way it encourages you to explore around to see where what item may go and such, but this also means there's a lot of backtracking involved whether a puzzle solution needs you to go to the same places again or you're just lost.
If you're pressed on gathering every item a room has, you can check the map to see if the room you're currently in still has items laying around somewhere.

Both a flaw & charm of this game are the fixed camera angles and tank controls.
The camera angles are meant to only show you what the developers want to show you (or hide from you), which can lead to some great "horror" moments that aren't necessarily [i]surprises.[/i] From a gameplay aspect, it can often be an incredible nuisance – for example, the enemy may be right in front of you but the camera just won't show it until you move to where the camera angle changes to view that general direction.
The tank controls encourage the slow pacing of the game. Trouble with that is you can't move & shoot, the speed when moving backwards is limited to only walking speed (which is already slow), and doing a quick turn-around can feel like ages during critical moments. You can use "Alternate" controls, which allows you to move around more fluidly like in most other 3D character action games such as Devil May Cry, but it's not really natural for this game as the camera will always change when moving around, thus forcing you to constantly reorient your analog stick or change the key you're using to move. If you're on a controller, using "Alternate" is only changed for the left analog stick, meaning you can use both tank controls with the D-pad and "alternate" controls with the left stick simultaneously.
Additionally, you can only aim straight ahead (neutral), upwards, and downwards, but precision isn't necessarily needed so long as your weapon is pointed in their general direction. There's an auto-aim to rely on anyway that aims towards an enemy when they're within the character's 360-degree sight.

All the backgrounds in-game are pre-rendered with very little 3D models actually being on-screen. The environment sometimes look blurry since all they ever did for this port was upscale the backgrounds as well as the FMVs. Regardless, the atmosphere portrayed and the 3D models on top are convincingly fitting with even the lighting and reflections having been focused on.
The music & sounds accentuate with the dark atmosphere. When there's a lack of either, it can make good on that "fear of the unknown" feeling.

Being strong on the [i]survival[/i] aspect in this survival horror game, resources are very limited – even saving is limited to the amount of a certain item you have. You've got to manage your resources and learn when and when not to waste bullets and health items. Your inventory is also very small, guaranteeing the need to leave some items where they are and making return trips to item boxes constantly to store unneeded items. All item boxes in the game are unrealistically, but conveniently, connected, so you can store items into one box in one location and find the same items in another box in another location. The difficulty chosen when you start the game also determines how many items will be in the playthrough as well as how many enemies there will be. There's only Very Easy, Easy, and Normal, though on a first run they're hidden as "Like climbing a mountain", "Like going on a hike", and "Like taking a walk". You get Hard mode after you beat the game once.
The most basic of zombies are often serious threats and can drain your ammo and health items fast if you're careless thanks to the slow pacing, the claustrophobic maps, and limited resources. Damage dealt is pretty random; one zombie may take up to 10 shots to kill with a basic handgun while the same zombie re-loaded from the same save file may take just 5. The same go for enemy damage against you, at least for the weaker attacks. Even headshots–which are actually just instant-kill shots as visualized by a head explosion–are incredibly random unless it's with a shotgun, up close, and aimed upwards, but even then that method is just "most likely" to grant a proper headshot. You can't aim up at the head, shoot with a handgun, and expect an instant or even faster kill. Even if you do manage to kill a zombie, it can come back as a stronger, faster version of itself usually after a certain amount of time passes unless you burn the "dead" zombie or get lucky with a headshot. You can't burn every zombie out there either as even the resources that allow you to do so are very limited.
The entirety of the mansion is designed so that you're creating your own routes, relying on you to know what paths are at least safe enough to backtrack through & not waste resources on, leaving it up to you to see what enemies you should just leave alone. Progress throughout the game can however trigger certain events in places you've run back & forth through several times, thus keeping up surprises in already familiar locations.
All that and more in mind, the entire game is all about surviving. There's action, but taking the action-route is obviously not always going to help.

The entire game is only really difficult on the first run and with little to no outside help whatsoever. A first-time playthrough may take up to 10 hours, but once you get to know how the game works and find out where items and even enemies are located, the "horror" is pretty much gone and the difficulty is tremendously lowered, making future playthroughs possibly take up half or even less than that of the first run, even if you decide to run through the game again with a different character.
You can unlock a couple of bonus weapons if you finish the game fast enough and a few extra costumes for finishing the game multiple times. You can also unlock a couple of bonus game modes that may make the game considerably tougher.
Some events only trigger if you do–or don't do–certain actions, like getting the infamous "sandwich" cutscene only if you didn't find a certain item by that point.
There are 6 endings for each character. They're pretty much the same for each other and are all pretty underwhelming.

Resident Evil, also called Biohazard in some countries, is a Survival Horror game in which you play as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, two members of a special task force known as S.T.A.R.S., as they explore a mysterious mansion and its surroundings and try to uncover the fate of their lost teammates. The game plays like a third person shooter, but the camera is always in fixed angles chosen by the developers. You must solve puzzles to acquire keys, items and weapons in order to open more rooms and progress through the mansion. The hallways are filled with zombies, but resources are extremely scarce so you'll have to decide whether to shoot, or to run.

[list]
    [*][b]The atmosphere is incredible:[/b] For a game that was originally on the gamecube (and before that the PS1), this game really knows how to scare the bajeezus out of you at times. It's less prevalent on repeat playthroughs since you know where the enemies are and are better at managing resources, but on your first attempt ? You'll be scared for your life, not knowing what awaits you around the next corner as your ammo supply goes down and you're out of healing items. 

    [*][b]So many reasons to come back:[/b] So many games don't know how to reward their players after they complete their first playthrough, so they'll never come back. Resident evil, tho ? Oh you've completed the game once ? Here's a new outfit and an extra difficulty mode. Completed again, but under five hours this time and with a different character ? Have more outfits, a pistol with infinite ammo and now the game includes a new enemy that poses a real threat even to an experienced player ! Oh, you've completed the game under three hours ? Here's a rocket launcher with infinite ammunition ! I'm not even counting the extra survival difficulty which makes the game really tough, and then the absolutely ridiculous difficulty where all enemies are invisible ! I squeezed 50 hours out of a game I can complete under 4 with ease now, to give you an idea of how much there is to do !

    [*][b]A story to die for:[/b] The game's plot and presentation are right out of a B series TV show, with all that it entails, including stupid decisions like splitting up, and cheesy dialogue and voice acting. Rather than hurting the game, this all serves to give it a unique charm that one can't help but love as they bite down on their Jibble sandwich.
[/list]

This HD port for the current generation was a great way for me to discover the series, even if the regular asking price of 20 bucks is a little high. Wait for a sale or for it to show up in a bundle, but if you find it or less than 10 bucks, it's well worth it. I recommend this to both fans of horror games and total newcomers like me, it's a game worth experiencing at least once in your life.

This game is known in the gaming industry as one of the pioneering games that defined the survival horror genre and the game that started it all. The first time I played this game was many years ago and was the absolute scariest ♥♥♥♥. Granted I was still a child but I can assure you this game is dripping with as much atmosphere and terror now as it was then. At its core it holds up ridiculously well despite the original REmake being over a decade and a half old now. This game is one of the only two that come to mind when I think of a pure 10/10 game, the other being Resident Evil 4. Huh, another Resident Evil game that began life on the Gamecube is my favorite? Maybe my age is showing. Even so the only games that come to mind being MAYBE 10/10 are Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater, Final Fantasy VI, and the original Legend of Zelda.

If you've never experienced this game or another Resident Evil in this style I certainly from the bottom of my heart recommend it, but with a big warning. This game though aged well is 100% a product of its time within its genre. Expect tank-like control of your character's movement (this can be switched on and off, but please play the classic style as the game was designed with it in mind and mastering it is incredibly satisfying), a sorta cheesy story, camera angles that are not controlled by you but are dependent on where you stand within a room to give an appropriate shot of the scene straight out of a horror movie, limited ability to save the game, and an overall great challenge.

With the risk of sounding like a backwards elitist I must say that this game is not for the faint of heart or those without an open mind who aren't ready to experience something like this. As I've just stated, death doesn't mean reloading a checkpoint, it means going straight back to the main menu and reloading a save. The number of saves that can make is limited by an in-game item known as an Ink Ribbon, which are used at typewriters scattered throughout the game. There are two different characters to play as with their own unique experience with one being able to carry more items at once for example, as well as story differences but between them is enough similarity to call beating the game with only one of the characters a full run of the game, which may last first-timers somewhere between 7 to 15 hours to pull off. Once you play through once though this time naturally gets shorter as you remember the layout of the mansion and where items are to be taken and placed, resulting in fast runs of about only 2 to 3 hours. In case you haven't caught on to what I'm trying to convey here, this game is gushing with replayability. Just this past week when I returned to the game for the first time in many years I played about 6 full playthroughs to get all of the steam achievements and even now I feel like it was well worth it.

For players who have already played REmake in some form or have at least played other classic RE games, this port of the game isn't perfect I'm afraid. The original game was clearly never intended for "HD" widescreen support and some textures look especially artificial compared to the original version of the game, some objects really standing awkwardly out against the pre-rendered background. The lighting also feels pallid, or flushed of color while I remember the original version of the game being a bit warmer and grittier. This could be imagined or a weird hang-up from experiencing the Silent Hill HD Collection. The biggest flaw I personally experienced was a laggy slow-down effect well below 30 fps seemingly at random, which I believe shouldn't happen for me seeing as my PC is capable of running a 60 fps tense battle in Overwatch at max settings. While I am by no means a stickler for muh fps below 30 is just bad, and the game itself slowing down is problematic. Especially considering the achievement/unlockables based on completion time where it's unclear to what extent the slow-down affects the in-game timer.

Whether this is your first Resident Evil game, you're looking to explore more of the series, or you just wanna return to this game on another form I have two last important things to say. The first is play with a controller (didn't try keyboard and mouse but I can only imagine how unnatural it must feel) and if it is convenient for you to just get a Gamecube and the 2002 Gamecube release of this game, do that instead of getting this version. If none of the problems I've explained in my previous paragraph bother you and you really want this version for the achievements/steam crap (like me) or the ease of access, then feel free to buy this version. I don't regret buying this version despite it being largely inferior to the Gamecube release.

The original game of 1996 inspired by alone in the dark (1992) and Sweet home (1989), that later become a huge and succesful franchise of videogames and even movies and novels, was remade in 2002 for the Gamecube with some changes to its gameplay and plot and that version was remastered in 2015 with HD graphics for the PC and current consoles. I will do a quick review of the PC remastered version now, yet half of it also belongs to the gamecube version.

Gameplay: 10/10
 
The basics of the 1996 title remain there, getting lost in a mansion, going all around getting the items you need to survive, kill zombies and other creatures that appear later while trying to conserve ammo, solve puzzles to get keys to unlock doors to make progress to the plot and reveal the next puzzle untill you finish the game. But there are some additions to it: a new place to explore, an unbeatable boss like Nemesis or Mr X will be chasing you a few times, defense items, a few more puzzles, some of them changed and actions needed to progress and the crimsom head mecanic. What else do you want? 

Visuals: 10/10 

Nothing wrong here. The camera angles are better than the original, the enemies and characters look scary (specially the jumping ones) and move very smooth on your computer, the rooms and places do look great as well, you will be inmered in your first playthroughs untill you can try to speedrun the game. HD does wonders. The next step will be in 4K :D

Sounds: 7/10

The music is very atmospheric and orchestral here, with dark tones and great quality. Still I prefer the original one, which is more scary, like in the old horror B movies. The voice acting and phrases did improve, though someone might miss the Jill sandwich and cheesy lines of the original, it was that bad that it was good. sometimes less can be more. Still there will be new funny lines here as well, which don't fit if this game pretends to be more serious than the original. The sound effects are superb, as expected.

Plot: 6/10

You should know the basic plot, the twists and secrets of the original game. It was considered great when it came out, thanks in part by the novelty of the technology it was running on back then, but now it shows its age. The only thing new is a change on Wesker's events and the addition of the Lisa subplot.

Replay factor / Achievements: 7/10

This game was short, and still is, even with the new additions. In the original game was only two characters with different endings each depending of the people you saved, the reward of the infinite rocket launcher for those that finished the game quickly, and later it was added an easy difficulty and arrange.

This version has the same as above and: 2 more difficulty settings, different costumes for each character, the invisible mode, the dangerous zombie you cannot shoot mode, the not interconnected boxes mode, the knife only achievement, the no save achievement and the samurai edge weapon.  All that while is a big improvement, you will manage to complete 100% very quick, one step at a time, and then it's over.

Overall score. 8/10

The game still has some flaws but it's improvements over the original will make you enjoy it once again, and the new modes will keep you busy for a while.

I do have negative things to say about this game, but almost all of them are about the story/dialog/characters and camera angles as the latter relate to controlling your character's movement in the game. Let's get those out of the way first. I would consider myself a fan of the Resident Evil franchise. When I was young and couldn't afford a Playstation 1 or N64, I used to read the strategy guides and stare at the screenshots from Resident Evil 2 longingly. However, as someone who doesn't have nostalgia issues when it comes to dealing with games from "back in the day," I can look at this remaster of Resident Evil and say that there are some serious flaws in my opinion.


[h1]Plot/Characters/Dialog[/h1]
I found the game's plot and characters to be very lame and uninteresting. Dialog is extremely rare, because you are alone at least 95% of the game (excluding feral monsters), and what little dialog there is I found to be either bland or terribly delivered. They do not use the original lines, either, so much of the meme fodder fo the original game's release is gone (no "Jill sandwich," but a similar joke is said in its place, nowhere near as enjoyable, in my opinion). Each character is just sort of there, without any nuance, character arcs, or even playing into fun tropes or archetypes. If a character is going to be static, at least play up the archetype, writers. The story seems like it's supposed to be a bunch of big twists, but almost everything seems plainly stated in the hard-to-miss documents, long before each twist or plot development comes up.

[h1]Camera Angles[/h1]
The camera angles are fantastic...if this was just a movie or a set of screenshots. However, as a video game, the camera gets yanked all over the place. You could be running toward the screen, then the camera angle changes to a view off to one side...or the other side...or behind your character...or at a diagonal. The angles themselves look great, but the slightest touch to a keyboard button or gamebad directional button other than a single direction being held consistently will result in your character running all over the place in the wrong direction, which can sometime lead to instant death. I was about ready to chuck my mouse at a wall while trying to push a statue into an alcove in between two crushing walls, because I kept getting insta-killed when the camera angle on the puzzle reset button kept changing and having my character run back into danger despite me struggling with controlling it.

I'm no stranger to tank controls, and have no problem with those. I've beaten all the numbered Resident Evil games with those controls before, and they work well enough, even if I don't think they're necessarily ideal. However, the camera angles make maneuvering in Resident Evil something that I do not enjoy. The new control scheme offered in the PC version is nice, though arguably worse since pressing up while using the old controls won't send you the wrong direction if the camera angle changes while you're moving.

[h1]Don't Play as Chris Unless You're an Expert[/h1]
I've beaten this game at least twice before beating the PC version, but it had been a few years. Unless you know where all the items are and what items you need when, do [i]not[/i] play as Chris. Aside from having a little more health and supposedly firing weapons a bit faster and possibly with more headshots than Jill, he seems to be inferior to her in virually every other way. Chris can't play the piano. Jill can. Chris can't mix chemicals. Jill can. Chris has to fight a boss that Jill can skip (no benefit for fighting it),and so on. OH. And he has 33% less inventory space that her. If you don't know exactly what you're doing, this is probably the biggest reason not to play Chris. 6 inventory slots SUCKS. It's rough all throughout the game, and requires tons of running back and forth from items to safe rooms to store my stuff. I was doing laps for 15-20 minutes straight, collecting stuff, and that's with me only carrying a pistol with no extra ammo at times.

[h1]Creepy Atmosphere, Cool Art Style, and great Audio[/h1]
This is the difference between making something that's just technologically good, and something artistically legit. The backgrounds in this game are gorgeous. Ten years from now, they will still be gorgeous.  The sound quality is nice, the music and sounds are creepy (the safe rooms have this lovely, haunting melody <3), and the game manages to be creepy even when I'm armed to the teeth. All my gripes about things before this topic...those are my issues with the game, but the atmosphere from the sights and sounds in this game are why I recommend it. These are so good that they gave me an overall good time despite those things I didn't like.

To reiterate, this game's backgrounds are essentially [i]timeless[/i] because they look so good. Supposedly, Capcom is going to make a Resident Evil 2 remaster someday. I hope that as much effort is put into it as this remaster. That said, although I know it would piss some people off, camera angles/perspectives such as either RE7 or RE4 would be preferable to me, due to the camera problems I had with the remaster here.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Then again, I wish a [i]lot[/i] of games would get the Resident Evil Remaster treatment. This is a good game, and I wish other games that have become dated and suffer for it could use this treatment. I was playing Soul  Reaver on Steam the other day, and everything looks so incredibly dated without "immortalizing" art style that graphical quality can't hamper. The voice acting and story is good, and it could use that sort of touch. Not only that, but just as the Resident Evil Remaster did, new story, locaitons, and events, could be added to the games to improve upon them (not just talking about Soul Reaver). If you haven't played the Resident Evil Remaster, I'd definitely give it a whirl when it's on sale. Just don't play as Chris, and get a refund if you don't like it in the first 2 hours.

[h1] Summary	[/h1]
Classic horror adventure game that is still entertaining after all these years. Took around 8 hours to finish the story. 
 
[h1] Review	[/h1]
I recently replayed this after not playing a Resident Evil game for at least 10 years. This is the Gamecube remake which completely updated the graphics, added new areas and story and re-recorded the hilariously awful voice acting. This remaster makes it available for modern widescreen displays and resolutions without adding (any?) extras.
The graphics are a mix, characters generally look good but some of the backgrounds and objects are very murky looking.
The set up is simple and as close to a coherent story as the series ever managed. There have been murders in the forest and you must investigate as a member of the ‘Special’ police (S.T.A.R.S). 
The mysterious mansion and claustrophobic environments that you investigate fit well with the exploring and puzzles that are really the heart of the game. The puzzles are fun to solve, they are not to cryptic but you will have to think where and how to use items. The homage to classic horror movies add suspense and tension. Jump scares are used sparingly and the sound design is wonderfully creepy.
My major criticism is that the inventory management becomes cumbersome if you are playing for the first time because it is so limited. You have to guess when you need certain objects or tediously back track to collect and store items. The door cutscenes can thankfully be disabled with a mod as they are really slow.
The game offers good replayability. The 2 characters have slightly different stories and a few item changes between them.
Overall this holds up well for an essentially 20 year old game and I would recommend it if you want a slower paced adventure game.

[h1]What is Resident Evil HD?[/h1]

Resident Evil HD is a complete remaster of the original Resident Evil released on Playstation 1 in 1996.  If you played the original way back when, are familiar with the more recent titles, or haven't yet taken the dive into the series, Resident Evil HD is definitely a game worth picking up.  The game looks fantastic, plays exceptionally well with updated controls, is a heck of a challenge, manages to strike an incredible balance between old-school and new-age, and it's an incredibly fun (and scary) experience!

[h1]So... Resident Evil is a "Horror" game, eh?...[/h1]

The Resident Evil series was built to be a horror genre, and - though some of the new-age games might leave your eyes rolling - the classic ones pull off the horror genre perfectly.  You won't find cheesy jump-scares, ear-piercingly loud noises, obnoxiously dark rooms or copious amounts of gore here.  The Resident Evil HD is about [i]real horror done the right way[/i]; constant suspense of what kind of enemies you will encounter in the next room, fear of death (and the resulting loss of progress), nervous planning for how to conserve your resources and ammo, and strategic use of weapons and ...[i] eh-hem [/i]... tactical retreats to make it to checkpoints and stay alive.  Resident Evil HD is a horror game because it truly immerses you in its world, keeps you actively engaged with its one-of-a-kind atmosphere, and does so with beautifully simple grace.  

That said, don't come into Resident Evil expecting a "modern 3rd-person shooter", because that's certainly not what Resident Evil is. While it has shooting elements as a core mechanic of its gameplay, at it's heart Resident Evil is a survival-strategy game, with heavy emphasis on puzzles and solving the horror-thriller mystery that your main characters find themselves in.  If I had to compare Resident Evil HD to a modern game, it's more of an "Amnesia" or "SOMA" with the addition of a limited amount of weapons than it is a Resident Evil 5 or Dead Space. 

[h1]But, how does a faithful reboot of a [i]20-year-old game[/i] actually [i]play[/i]?[/h1]

Breathtakingly well.  I remember all-too-well the shooters on first-gen consoles; they were clunky, frustratingly difficult to play, and not exactly the easiest on the eyes.  Resident Evil HD manages to strip its reboot of all the bad things I remember of those days while retaining what made them great.  Controls have been updated to make movement and aiming much more intuitive (I recommend a controller, but mouse/keyboard also works to satisfaction).  Visuals have been completely redone, from textures, to models, to levels, to in-game text and inventory.  Everything is identical from a mechanical and (level/game) design standpoint, but it runs smoothly, plays smoothly, and looks fantastic.  Don't let the simple movement/camera/aim controls fool you, Resident Evil is fun, engaging, and challenging in all of its own right. 

[h1]And the story?[/h1]

While admittedly the story itself isn't the most stand-out, that's not to say it's poorly written.  Resident Evil's story shares the same beautiful simplicity that defines its core gameplay.  You play as one of two main characters, whom you can select at the start of your game.  They find themselves trapped in a mysterious mansion with the undead (and other vicious creatures), with their friends lost, and looking for a way to escape.  Cutscenes are limited, dialogue is concise, and there's only as much story driving the game along as there needs to be; and that's just fine (preferable, even).  The real story here is how the characters are going to survive... or more accurately, how YOU are going to.  You must solve puzzles, explore the mansion, survive with limited resources, and ultimately hope to get the heck outta dodge before the evil there takes you down with it.  Who caused the horror at the mansion?  What is the purpose of this desolate building in the middle of nowhere?  You can only hope to find out as you try to escape.

[h1]Aaaaand the Verdict?[/h1]

[b]An absolute must buy, 9.5/10[/b] At $20 this game is some fantastic value for your dollar, is an experience unlike anything else you'll find, and will give you more than a few fun play-throughs. On sale this game is a no-brainer.  As I also mentioned above, the remaster is of the highest quality and it is one of the better optimized reboot/ports out there on PC.  Resident Evil HD is a game that's definitely worth picking up and giving a try for almost any category of gamer, and I have been very pleasantly surprised with just how great it is.

[b] Intro [/b]
Resident evil hd remaster is a survival horror game developed by Capcom and was released in 2015 it Is a remaster of the 2002 remake of the 1996 original resident evil.

[b] Story [/b]
In resident evil you play as Either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, a member of Raccoon City’s STARS squad which gets sent to investigate murders on the outskirts of town, the team gets separated and eventually you end up in an abandoned mansion in the middle of a forest, from then on you explore the mansion looking for the rest of your squad as well as finding a way to escape, as well as trying not to get killed by the numerous zombies roaming around the mansion. I won’t say much more about the plot, overall I thought the story was quite interesting, and there is quite a good sense of mystery going on that kept me interested.    

[b] Gameplay [/b]
Gameplay revolves around you exploring the mansion, avoiding zombies, picking up items and supplies and solving puzzles to progress forward. I’ve never played a resident evil game before and I’ll be honest, when I first tried it I didn’t like it that much. However after giving it a second try I learnt the controls, and I took my time to understand the game mechanics I actually really enjoyed it. If you play the game on PC I highly recommend using a controller, you can select between two different control layouts, one is the original tank controls and one is a more updated control scheme that feels a bit more forgiving, I decided to use the tank controls as I feel it adds to the tension of it all. This game is pretty tough for a first timer even on the easy settings, there are zombies and monsters scattered throughout the mansion and you have to deal with them, however at the beginning supplies are very limited so you have to be careful not to use up all your ammo and health items and you also have a very small inventory size plus you can die very easily, but there are item boxes scattered throughout the world allowing you to manage your inventory. Saving is done through the use of ink ribbons and you also have a limited supply of them, however on the easy settings the game is very generous with how many ink ribbons you can find as well as the other supplies including ammo and health. 

The game forces the player to think about their surroundings and make smart decisions on how to progress forward, avoiding zombies completely and trying to run past can be a better strategy in the long run as you might need that ammo for later when you really do need it. If you do end up having to kill a zombie, just be sure to actually kill it, you can do this in two ways; either scoring a headshot or burning the corpse, a headshot is never guaranteed however and the kerosene used to burn zombies is also limited. The puzzles in the game aren’t too difficult and is usually just a case of remember what fits where. All these gameplay elements work well together to create an intense and somewhat frightening experience that is also highly enjoyable, once I got the hang of everything and I took it slow and methodically I really started to enjoy the game.   

[b] Graphics [/b]
Graphically the game looks quite nice, with some very good use of lighting which adds to horror atmosphere of the game. 

[b] Sounds and Music [/b]
The sound and music of the game is fantastic. Hearing the groan of a zombie once you walk into a new room can strike a little bit of fear into you especially if you’re low on supplies. Hearing the ongoing thunderstorm outside the mansion adds to the atmosphere and the echoes of your own footsteps make the mansion feel like a real place. The music is quite dark and atmospheric adding to the tension of it all. Using headphones is a must in my opinion   

[b] Conclusion [/b]
Overall I enjoyed the game a lot once I figured out all the game mechanics. The game took me around 15 hours to complete. I wouldn’t say its Silent Hill scary but it is still very atmospheric and tense experience and a highly enjoyable one. I’d say this game is a must play, take your time and learn the mechanics and it is a blast to play. There is also quite a bit of replayability with playing as the different characters and playing on the higher difficulty settings. Let’s hope they do an HD remake of Resident Evil 2 and 3.

Resident Evil (1996) was the game that successfully continued the traditions of Alone in the Dark (1992) and strengthened the survival horror as a category. With simplified adventure elements and often dumb(ish) puzzles it concentrated on horror with lots of fighting involved. Using the same fixed camera view/angle as seen in AitD, the game managed to amplify the horror feel, but the fights were often unnecessarily hard because of this (and the scarcity of ammunition).

After some strange murders in the countryside, a team of S.T.A.R.S. (Special Tactics and Rescue Service) officers from the nearby town, Raccoon City are sent to investigate the area. Attacked by zombie dobermanns they run into a nearby mansion that's seemingly abandoned (even though all the lights are on) to seek shelter. Soon all hell breaks loose as they discover the traces (and results) of a secret experiment regarding a mysterious virus that threatens the whole world...

The surviving team members' presence depends on which character we picked at the beginning. We can choose Chris Redfield by default, who is strong, has a lighter and 6 inventory slots. To make things more entertaining, he doesn't have a firearm (he had one in the intro, but nevermind). The other protagonist is Jill Valentine, who can't take as much damage as Chris, her knife is weaker, but has 8 inventory slots so she can carry more stuff around (this involves both quest related items and weapons). She also starts the game with a handgun and soon acquires a lockpick as well (which is only useful for a couple of doors though), not to mention she has access to the powerful grenade launcher.
The game is slightly different depending on which character we chose, there are minor plot twists and additional information revealed, plus both of them meet different sidekicks (Jill - Barry, Chris - Rebecca) throughout the game. We also have to rescue our partner accordingly and there are certain situations where the 2 characters can act differently. For example Jill can attempt to kill the plant monster using a herbicide whereas Chris has to use conventional firearms to destroy it, but Chris can use a flamethrower later against a giant spider while Jill can't and so on. Also there are funny moments, such as the one with the zombie emerging from the bathtub, where Chris just watches and freaks out, while Jill quickly crushes the zombie's head by trampling on it then rushes to the toilet and throws up :)

There isn't much to praise about the plot as it's quite simple (the characters are even more so), but anyone who has heard about Resident Evil already knows this. There are 4 (or 12 to be precise) different endings depending on who we rescue and whether we blow up the secret underground lab or not. Don't expect huge differences though, I'd say the game gets rather boring after 2 (1 with Chris and 1 with Jill) playthroughs (you will need at least 4 if you plan on unlocking all the costumes, weapons and such).
The dialogues are hillariously and notoriously bad (just your average Japanese game), but they became a positive trademark of the Resident Evil games as time flew by. The "You were almost a Jill sandwich!" line for example became quite famous and it's a mystery why they removed it (!) from the game. Were they trying to even out this mistake and make the game more serious? Probably. Well, they could have left this one in for fun and for old times' sake.

Resident Evil HD REMASTER features a fair number of new elements (I'm comparing it to the original RE from 1996, not to the 2002 gamecube version). The most important one is the addition of an extra boss, Lisa Trevor, the daughter of a former employee of Umbrella. With it new areas were also added: the spooky cabin outside the mansion and her lair below. The encounter with the giant shark is also a highlight.
Another new enemy is the "crimson head", a reawakened zombie which is a faster, deadlier version of the shambling, twitching zombies we all know. They usually appear after leaving the corpse of a zombie (with its head still attached to its neck) on the ground and reentering the area. To prevent this from happening we can do 2 things: going for headshots (in a game where it's practically impossible to aim vertically, it's not an option) by lucky criticals, or using kerosene and burn the corpses. Yes, burning them is a new feature too, but for that we'll need a flask filled with kerosene (it runs out after 2 uses) and a lighter (which Chris has automatically, but Jill needs to find and carry around). And yes, this means we need extra inventory space.
We also receive close-quarter self-defense weapons (other than the terrible knife): disposable (because each one can only be used once - don't ask) daggers. Depending on which character we chose, Jill can find battery packs for her taser while Chris uses flash grenades (this one is lethal, because he places them inside the mouth of our foes and the resulting explosion blows their head apart, but it can injure us as well if we stand to close). We are definitely going to be needing these, because if one of the enemies manage to grab us, it'll start biting us immeditely, but with the use of these items, not only we can avoid taking damage, but can also injure or kill our attacker.

The game requires a controller (it doesn't, but it is recommended) and even with that it won't be easy. There are numerous layouts, but I found none of them exactly useful: autorun is handy, but sometimes walking and "tank controls" are more suitable to dodge the zombies' attacks (when they lunge at us and miss, they stand idle for a while which we can use to slip by). Later on as the enemies get quite fast though and we should use the autorun option again. Also, if we don't have any defense items (daggers, etc.) and the enemies grab us, we can only free ourselves by shaking the analog sticks (we're still going to be moderately injured after doing so) or we just simply die. I felt this is important to mention as I did not find any clues for that in the game itself.
The fixed camera angles - while providing the perfect atmosphere - also make our job harder: the game contains far too many action scenes for it to be easily overlooked and the sudden change of perspective can also be disorienting especially during a fight. This was a common problem in Alone in the Dark as well, but it wasn't as combat oriented as Resident Evil. Also the game punishes us for not following a certain pattern: if we venture somewhere we are not supposed to (yet or again) we can quickly find ourselves surrounded by 3+ zombies and this can force players to refer to walkthroughs.

The game is still trying to balance between action and adventure, but does so with little success, as I haven't seen anyone praising RE for its clever puzzles. Most of them are mediocre at best and serve as a bit of a relax period between 2 fights. Mostly we have to look for keys and push crates.

As far as graphics go, I'd call it a lazy port: the character models look good (especially the bonus costumes), but the backgrounds look just plain ugly compared to Resident Evil 0's crisp environments, the contrast between the characters and the backgrounds is visible. The audio is pretty good, but the crows still sound awfully wrong.

To be honest, Resident Evil 1 has never been amongst my favourites: I liked Resident Evil 2 better and now after having played Resident Evil 0 (which I loved and also [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/339340/]reviewed[/url]) I must say it exceeds this one in almost every aspect. That being said, Resident Evil HD REMASTER is still a very good game, but in my opinion its status in the series is overrated (blame nostalgia).

[h1]Short version: 93%[/h1]
Resident Evil 1 HD is an example of a game remake done right. Not only it captures all the elements that made the original RE1 famous, but also it ironed out most of the kinks, added new content that resulted in even greater experience, and made sure that this game, even after 15 years of release, is still the quintessential survival action horror on any platform. 

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
The Resident Evil series is far from perfect, but its infamous cheesiness is also its greatest advantage. No game on Steam can showcase this more than the HD remaster of the 2002 Resident Evil 1 REmake, which is considered to be the best in the entire franchise by many (at least until the RE2 REmake comes along).
The game’s secret is the perfect bland of several smaller and larger elements. It mostly takes place in an incredibly unrealistic, giant 1930s horror film mansion filled with ridiculous 1960s spy movie deathtraps. Its script and voice acting—while improving a ton compared to the 1996 original—just revel in the typical B movie cheesiness.

Still, the game is not a parody, and its straight-faced serious approach, interestingly enough, makes everything a lot better. The levels and enemies (chiefly zombies, with some gruesome biological experiments in the mix) are deadly and put most gamers to the test. Especially if you are used to modern autosaves, checkpoints, instant retries, replenishing health, and near-infinite ammunition; this game lacks all of these.
The difficulty also comes from the old-school control system, where the levels use fixed cameras (and stunningly gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds) instead of the more common over-the-shoulder viewpoint. It takes time to get used to it, but the reward is great, because RE1 offers unparalleled replay value within its genre, thanks to its wide variety of game modes, two selectable protagonists, and several paths and endings the player can take.

Resident Evil/Biohazard HD Remaster is a remastered version of the classic survival horror game developed and published by Capcom

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

OK, I had the original one for PSX back in the day, but I couldn't play it. Being honest, I was a kid and it scared the hell out of me. I remember watching that cutscene where the first zombie appears, turning and watching you. Yes, that was the point my dad said "Not for kids, not at all". So, from that day, I had this idealized idea of this game where it was the scariest one out there. 

But I think it would be fair to analyze the game without the nostalgia factor in mind. And, if you do that, man it is bad. Like, bad bad. Why do I say that? Let's summarize:

- Controls are bad. Even with the remastered ones, where you can use your controller sticks in a moder way, in which left means left, not just turn left, the control is confusing. Because the camera system is. So you push forward to advance, the character moves to the next part of the room, where a new camera angle is set and now you are running towards the camera, so left, right, up and down get all mixed up. And the shooting seems clunky for today standards.
- Transitions. These are a house brand. You click a door and a cutscene starts where the door opens and you expect something to be on the other side but it's never there. Well, there is a transition for EVERY SINGLE DOOR. And sometimes you have to go from one side to the opposite one of the mansion and, in the process, get through six or seven doors. I think the main reason for this is to make the game pace slow and to avoid the speedrun feeling. But man, it is way too much.
- Inventory. Six slots and that's it. And for the survival component is fine. I don't like games where you can carry an arsenal with you at any time. But this is plain frustrating. There are times where I shot to spend the ammunition so I could free a slot in my inventory to pick an item. Combined with the transitions nightmare, it is an unpleasant experience indeed. I mean, you are in a room with your inventory almost full. Find a herb and say "why not pick it up?". You do and then you find a quest item. And you can't take it because your inventory is full. So you say "OK, let's head back to the container with all my stuff to make some space". And that's four doors away, so you know it's going to take way too much time. So you curse, throw the controller away and quit the game.
- Bad story. And, if you don't agree, I am sure you have played (and loved) the original one. Because, let's be serious, it is not good. At all. 
- Cheap puns. This is the worst and it kills the mood.

But there were good things too, don't get me wrong:

+ The atmosphere. The horror is not constant, but I was tense the whole time.
+ Difficulty. It is a fair game. Even though hard was too hard for me, I think it was fair. It is just that it requires more focus on it that I was willing to give.
+ Eventually, it is over, and you could say "I finished that", and then you uninstall it and forget about it, just remembering the good parts when it pops up in a conversation with friends.

As someone who started the Resident Evil series at RE4, it was cool to experience the origins of the games.

Some of the puzzles are fun, and give you a good feeling of accomplishment when you solve them.

It is a lot more puzzly than a lot of the other games, and some of them have not aged well. A lot of puzzles rely on the player knowing whether or not they interacted with all background objects in the room, and later on in the game where there are multiple rooms with red zones (items not yet picked up), it gets annoying to run back and forth to check rooms.

Locked doors work nicely to limit your search area to check at the start of the game, and focus player exploration.

Another issue is early on in the game, when the game does not keep track of which doors on the map are unlocked by which key, and there are 4 types of locks or more depending on how you include them.

It's honestly one of the scariest RE games I have played. You run past enemies a lot and limited ammo/item slots is always a concern, so it makes just getting around the house incredibly tense. Enemies just off camera can lunge out suddenly, which keeps exploration really exciting.

Limited item slots, even for puzzle items and limited save items, does get frustrating at some points though, as it leads to a lot of backtracking to swap out items.

Overall, I would say that if you are a fan of any of the other RE games or if it is even your first entry into the series, it is definitely worth a try.

The graphics are still not very good, though certainly decent for their time. A bit like Final Fantasy 8 or so. Almsot everything is static like FF8, anyway.

The Resident Evil Remake (i.e. the original Gamecube version) is, without a doubt, a stone-cold, bone-chilling classic that has to this day remained my favourite game of all time (not to mention one of the greatest and most beautifully crafted videogames ever), so to be able to replay it on my PC in all its remastered gory glory is something akin to heaven.

The main backstory, told via a series of old notes scattered throughout the ominous Spencer estate, is that of the mansion's architect, George Trevor, and his family, all of whom fell victim to the sadistic Oswell E. Spencer's truly nefarious plot to eliminate George (tragically he knew too much) and use his beloved wife and daughter as live test subjects for Umbrella's extracurricular and profoundly immoral viral experimentation program.

The subsequent chain of events surrounding the ill-fated Trevor family (and in particular, George's then 14 year old daughter, Lisa) provide what is by far the deepest, darkest and most disturbing layer of this exceptional game that adds, along with the beautiful, chillingly atmospheric score, a whole new dimension and complexity to what might otherwise have been little more than a textual overhaul – albeit a very impressive textual overhaul – of the 1996 original.
 
Lisa Trevor's ordeal is a tragic, harrowing and intensely nostalgic account of an innocent child who was imprisoned, violated in the worst possible way by a viral onslaught and transformed into an abomination simply to serve the dark purposes of evil men with God complexes, before being thrown out with the garbage after the real monsters had extracted what they needed from her: namely the Progenitor strain from which the T-virus would one day be spawned. I simply cannot imagine a more grisly fate to befall someone. The fact that she, unlike her mother, somehow survived the horrific viral onslaught to live on in agony, torment, fear, rage, confusion and isolation for some 31 years is surely the most tragic aspect.

But I'm digressing as usual. Simply put, this remastered Resident Evil Remake is an even more stunning, visceral and immersive exploration into the dark, disturbing depths of Umbrella's original haunt; and in all honesty, you'd have to be a zombie not to play it.

I consider this game, specifically this one, to be close to absolute perfection... if it's not already perfect. No, it doesn't have the best emotional moments. When it comes to puzzles, design and threat... everything is married together in a way that most horror games... if not any horror games... wish to. We can all appreciate the Amnesia or Alien: Isolation or even the FNAF or Outlast... something about Resident Evil Remake makes it clear that it was built with effort, integrity and passion: the Crimson Head! Shinji Mikami loved his project, he loved what he did with Resident Evil despite the fact that Capcom has rushed the multiple ports including the "uncensored/Director's Cut" editions. The REmake is THE Director's Cut of any game, the ultimate REMAKE. It's more than a dumb remaster with graphics being the only upgrade yet having the issues of performances or controls. The Crimson Heads are the definition of Resident Evil. They are scary!

The second you go in the first cabin in the woods after discovering the secret from the Crypt, you know you're up against something creepy and... I can't say more.

Besides that, I'm happy that this game exists for others to appreciate. This is the BEST that Resident Evil ever got. Easily in my personal Top 5 games of all time. Resident Evil games always try to make traversing the levels interesting due to various mechanics: limited inventory meaning you have to choose which items to bring with you at any time, various locked doors forcing you to search for key items, enemies which you don't have the resources to kill, and doors which are close to breaking or are only usable one way. All those features combined makes traversing the mansion feel like a big puzzle, and this game handles that aspect much better than any other game in the series. It does become a bit too simplified in the later parts of the game, but the first half of the game has excellent level design.

This remaster of the game features a new rendering engine which makes the characters look a lot better, new costumes, a new very easy difficulty (which anyone wanting an actual challenge should avoid), and rather lackluster backgrounds. Unfortuantely, Capcom weren't able to re-render the backgrounds for this remaster, but they tried their best to find alternate solutions. So the result is that you've got some backgrounds which are simply upscaled from their original jpeg renders, some which are touched up by hand,  some which have specific elements replaced with 3D models, and a couple which are fully re-created in 3D. Unfortunately, the vast majority are simply upscaled. Despite this, the game still manages to look good overall.

The original version features slow door animations with a static speed which were masking loading times. Loading times in this version would be virtually instaneously if it weren't for the fact the door animations are still the same length and they're still unskippable. As a result, you'll be looking at doors for potentially hours throughout a playthrough. If this doesn't sound appealing, I suggest looking up steam guides to find a mod which lets you skip all door animations.
This is not just one of the greatest RE games, it's one of the greatest games ever, in general.

Back in the late 90's I remember this game releasing for PS1, and I was a huge fan of it. I purchased the original, the directors cut, every version I could get my hands on.

Fastforward to now, and I decided to tromp through some old stomping grounds. RE HD Remaster is a remaster of the Gamecube version of the game, which includes a few new and revamped areas, and much better graphics. Gameplay has remained unchanged from the original, other than a key fact that you can play without tank controls (hell yes!). Resident evil relies heavily on the "survival" aspect; you have limited inventory space, limited ammo, even limited number of saves. The puzzles in this game can be quite devious, and the game gives you hints, but rarely outright tells you what to do (I played the game with a guide because I'm old and don't have the same memory I once did). Zombies, dogs, every enemy in this game is deadly; a normal zombie can take as many as 10 bullets to kill on Normal. Its a lot more brutal than I remembered as a kid. Top it off that some enemies can follow you around the mansion, its constantly a harrowing experience, especially if you skipped enemies to conserve ammo. 

However, the game is not without its flaws. I really wish they would have edited out the "loading" animations of the doors, it adds a lot of unnecessary length. As well, the rooms are not labeled, so sometimes finding where you need to go next can be an absolute chore. I remember one time I was looking for a specific room and it took me 10 minutes combing through google pictures to locate the damn thing. Aiming is incredibly difficult, to score headshots you need to let an enemy almost bite you half the time. As well, inventory management is a real chore, and while it adds a lot of challange to the game it becomes a chore constantly running back to a storage box. I really wish they gave an option to discard things like herbs or ammo, especially if you accidentally picked something up. Lastly, the cheesy voice acting is still here, and the lip sync with the words is HORRIBLE. Its wayyyyy off... why the hell didn't they fix that, I can't fathom.

Pros

   In short: this port simply doesn't work for some people. MANY people. I used to be one of those people. Then I got myself a spanking new laptop about a year ago, and lo and behold: the game from 2002, itself a remake of a game from 1996, finally works! (Though granted, not the first time 'round. I'm suspecting that a recent NVIDIA or Windows update has now rendered it playable. On an expensive modern gaming laptop, no less!!)

   For the sake of posterity, I'll post my old review in the Comments below, just so you can witness the rage myself and countless others have felt - still DO feel, to some extent - towards Capcom's absolutely appalling customer service policies. (Oh-oh! Probably ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up this review's chances already, seeing what a bunch of butt-smooching apologists the average "loyal" Capcom fan appears to be. Go on, vote me down, you sycophantic bottom-dwellers.)

   Anyway, onto my review of the 2015 HD remaster of the 2002 Gamecube remake of the game originally released on the Playstation 1 in 1996. (Still with me? Good. Be thankful I haven't even mentioned the Playstation 1 "Director's Cut" released in 1997. You're welcome.)

   I adore this game. Beyond words. It is, simply put, the single most sentimental horror video game in all of history for me. Or at least...the 1996 version is. Though this remake is largely faithful, and mostly just improves on some of the shortcomings of the original, so...I guess I'm sentimental towards THIS, too. Though not quite as much. But you get the idea. The 1996 version is still the product I have the most sentiment towards, but I'm happy to pretend these two versions are the "same game". Which they're definitely not. Though they very nearly are, in a way; at least in MY head, and in my heart.

   Rambling aside, this is a game - and version, particularly - which still holds up well in this day and age. Sure, the manipulative (yet oh-so-effective) fixed camera angles remain, but we now have the option to change to a control system which is a tad less "tank-like" than both the original PS1 and Gamecube versions (though still potentially confusing, by modern standards). 

   The closest thing we had to a genuinely terrifying and highly cinematic horror game before this was Alone in the Dark, and that was...even more clunky to control, and considerably less cinematic and thereby significantly less scary. I also played this before any Alone in the Dark games, so it still seems like "the original" scary horror game set in a spooky mansion...to me, at least.

   Hey, ♥♥♥♥ it: did Alone in the Dark have any giant sharks in it? No. No, it didn't. Suck several fat, throbbing ♥♥♥♥♥, Alone in the Dark. Resident Evil got there first.

   It's actually very hard to explain to people who "weren't there" how significant the original version of this game was when it came out. The mansion was a truly amazing thing to explore, its denizens a true nightmare to behold. I have not before, or since, experienced anything quite so simultaneously terrifying yet compellingly unputdownable in a video game. Many games have since come close...but none could ever replace the unique place that Resident Evil holds in my heart.

   I love you, Resident Evil. I hate you, Capcom. I'm still not going to give this a perfect score, because of the troubles I know this ridiculously under-serviced port still causes for other people. The only warning I can give is: don't be surprised if it doesn't work on your computer, for no good reason whatsoever. A bit of a wonky recommendation I know, but it's regrettably the only one that I can give.

   Verdict: 9/10 (10/10, minus one point for the fact that Capcom have no morals whatsoever, and couldn't give two frigs about who their products do or do not work for).

[h1] [b] [u] Resident Evil / Biohazard HD REMASTER [/u] [/b] [/h1]

[b] A Classic Never Dies [/b]

[i] BY CHRIS [/i] --> As I creep though the familiar-yet-eerie corridors of Resident Evil, I can't help but feel terrified of Crimson Heads. Even 12 years after I first encountered them, it's genuinely frightening every time they spring back to life to try to tear a hole in my esophagus, but they're also a great example of why Resident Evil still holds up. While inconsistent art and persistent clipping problems give away that this is an update of a 1996 survival-horror game, the scares, puzzles, and atmosphere of the creepy corridors of Spencer Mansion are as potent as ever.

Ever since the tweaks made in the 2002 GameCube remake, Resident Evil has been a tense game of resource management. The makeover to the many rooms, puzzles, and monsters give it an edge that significantly surpasses the original game. Every zombie you spend precious ammunition to kill becomes a ticking time bomb that’ll turn into something much more deadly if you don’t dispose of them properly with fire or headshots.

That persistent danger is what makes the frequent backtracking through this labyrinth of locked doors something more interesting than typical busywork. As Resident Evil uses adventure game-style design to send you looking for keys and objects that have to be examined closely to solve puzzles, then brought back to the right location, you can feel the stakes rising as the chances of getting mauled or caught without the right resources increase.

Resident Evil is a gauntlet of twisted monsters and hard decisions. Make the wrong choice or take too long on some objectives, and sometimes you’ll pay for it with the death of a comrade or missing out on precious resources. It’s punishing at times, and managing the different inventories of two playable characters forces you to be smart and frugal with regard to what you carry with you. The constant pressure makes it a difficult game to play by design, but one that still manages to be fair.

This HD remastered edition of Resident Evil looks pretty good on the new-gen consoles, thanks to 1080p resolution and some nicely touched up backgrounds and textures, with the PC version offering the highest settings and a nifty option to switch between 60 and 30 frames per second. The biggest improvement across all versions is the ability to scale the experience the way you want to play it. You could choose between 4:3 or 16:9 aspect ratios, and you can swap the original “tank-style” controls for a more modern setup that moves your character in the direction you push the stick.

As an old fan I prefer the original controls, but the new controls help make Resident Evil accessible without sacrificing the tense nature of combat. You still have to stand your ground in order to shoot zombies and deal with the pressure of enemies getting closer. Since most face-offs happen in tight spaces, it’s not super easy to pull a juke move on multiple zombies, even with the new controls. Purists can have it the way the designers originally intended. Newbies can jump in and not completely break the game.

Dimly lit rooms with ambient effects like lightning or floating dust particles are some of the best to look at in this update. However, some backdrops look garish under a lot of light, and there are some noticeably blurry textures and pixelated art. I’m also disappointed that the major clipping problems still haven’t been fixed. Maybe in the next remake, Capcom?

Resident Evil (Remake) is a beautiful object of design which delivers a pleasurable and precisely managed play experience, but its mechanics and structure are stylized in the fashion of late 90s survival horror games. It's not for everyone.

The premise is a medium-length (i.e., the first playthrough is ~9 hours) single-player, linear 'survival horror' game played with fixed camera angles and set in a mansion populated with zombies and genetic aberrations. You need to kill a few things, understand the physical space, manage your inventory and use of items, and solve the odd puzzle. This game is very good-looking and powerfully scary. Fear here comes mostly from suspension of disbelief, and a very tense atmosphere, but there are a small number of contextual jump scares too. The hallmarks of later Resident Evil titles (quicktime events, over-the-shoulder cameras, fully rendered 3D environments, modular item management, and big action setpieces) are entirely absent. This game is much quieter and more delicate.

Like the many ornate keys the player accumulates in the game, this game feels bespoke and carefully produced. Every art asset is rendered lovingly, with an eye for detail. The mutated shark models have scars on their skin from where they have become aggressive with one another in their pool after having been abandoned. Each zombie's dress and injuries implies their backstory, and there are many zombie character models. The items the player collects are fetishistic totems, whose gorgeous polygonal models can all be examined closely in three dimensions. They include Yale lock keys, first aid kits, weapons (including a simulacrum of the Colt Python revolver), a large battery, piano scores, and X-ray scans. Every item has been crafted with obvious love and care. It has become a useless cliché to write of a game's 'fully realized world', but items, character models and lavish backgrounds are the core of Resident Evil (Remake)'s incomparable atmosphere. Because the game uses fixed camera angles, its backgrounds are pre-rendered textures, and there are relatively few 3D models on screen at any time. Spareness is presumably one reason for its high production values. The fixed camera angles give the level designers cinematic control over tone, which is rare in modern games. There is no capacity for the player to debase in-game suspense by constantly jumping or moving the camera during a crucial moment. A new room may open with the camera on the avatar, against the door, so you can't see what's ahead. In short, it looks great. This is a minor 'high definition' update to a game released in 2002, but the game has barely aged at all. Only graphics buffs or very superficial players will feel that they are playing an outdated title.

The controls and mechanics of the game are very much of their era. In this game, you control your avatar using so-called 'tank controls', which nominally resemble those of a traditional tank in that you cannot simultaneously turn and advance forward. Unusually for a 3D video game, pushing forward on the stick moves your avatar in the direction they are currently facing. This control system has always been controversial, and is now widely dismissed as a relic. There is an option to switch to a more conventional control system in the menu. Players will find their own most comfortable playing style, but the game was designed for tank controls, and I believe they are necessary for full enjoyment. This game is about suspense, ad hoc strategy, and uncertainty. The slight awkwardness and feeling of limitation which tank controls offer suit the setting. This game's fixed camera angles, which can switch between very different viewpoints, make conventional 3D world control systems unintuitive. The player can become disorientated easily as they move between screens. Tank controls alleviate this problem, because the player always has a sense of their current direction and momentum.

Plot barely features in this game. Cutscenes are minimal (although countless variations of scenes exist for players with different play conditions), and the optional backstory is explored mostly through text documents or exquisite environmental storytelling. You may find a couple of the characters irritating (personally I can't stand Chris, one of the playable characters), but what little dialogue there is can be skipped. As it is now fashionable to say, the story of the game is the story of your playthrough. I have found that I end up with a very particular relationship with certain rooms in the mansion. Ammunition and healing items are sparse, such that there are generally more zombies than you can kill in a given area, and unless they are properly disposed of (through fire or removal of the head), zombies will return, flush with their own blood and saturated with a more mature form of the plague virus, as the deadly 'crimson heads'. For these reasons, it is generally more desirable to avoid zombies than to engage them. But certain areas of the mansion are connected by narrow corridors, making escape difficult. The player therefore has to monitor their resources, managing ammunition, physical space, health and healing items, and inventory space, all of which are limited. Compromises must be made. That's a lot of the fun.

A few recommendations to maximise your pleasure: play it at night. Try not to seek help for the hard parts (unless a puzzle is totally stumping you, because a couple of them are very obtuse). Turn up the volume.

The HD Remaster is a delight. Every inch of curling wallpaper and dry rot is now visible! I just have a couple of complaints. A very select few of the master textures (such as the letter Wesker/Barry pins to the wall outside the East Wing save room) were obviously never designed to be seen at this resolution, and they really should have been replaced like other models have been. More inexplicably, great effort has been put into adding a 'physics boob jiggle' to Jill's walk. The effect is to dehumanize and overtly sexualize a well-loved character. Watching Jill animate is now an item of titillation for the presumed heterosexual male player. I think it's very myopic and dull of Capcom to add this feature. If nothing else, it is absurdly unrealistic. Jill's chest now undulates at a steady pace, independent from the rest of her body, whenever she walks or runs. It makes me more aware of the game as software, and harms its chief achievement: its extraordinarily tense atmosphere. This feature was missing in the 2002 release of this same game. Sadly, in every other way, this HD Remaster is the superior edition.

You have to look out for things whilst in game, such as the character looking hurt indicates low health. And you have to know when to shoot and how to aim the weapon without auto aim or crosshairs.

I also super appreciate them sticking with 3d models ontop of pre-rendered screens, the fixed camera angles and even the door transitions. It emulates the original perfectly making it a brillant remake, One of the best i've seen actually. 

The fixed camera angles is actually one of the core elements that make this game scary as it is. A lot of establishing shots of an area shows Jill/Chris facing the camera. You have no idea what's in that place until you move forward. It's a really good mechanic.

Great remaster of what was and still is the best remake ever, and one of the best games of all time. 

I owned and enjoyed the original on the GameCube, and I had just as much, if not more fun with this PC remaster. The character models got revamped with new textures as well as shiny new normal maps, and every area in the game takes advantage of that with nicer more-detailed lighting (on the characters) throughout.  Even though the pre-rendered backgrounds were just upscaled and filtered a bit (not re-rendered at a higher resolution), they still look convincing over 90% of the time. That eased my biggest worry with this remaster - that it would look dated in HD. I didn't end up feeling that was the case at all. It's aged surprisingly well.

I HIGHLY recommend playing this game how it was intended - with the tank controls. The game had the alternative, non-tank control option enabled by default when I first launched it, which I found odd. I guess Capcom is afraid modern-day gamers can't handle tank controls, but honestly, as long as you aren't playing on Hard, this game is pretty easy even with tank controls. I breezed through it on Normal mode with Jill, with dozens of healing items left over in my storage box. If I had such an easy time with it with tank controls, I can't imagine playing it with the new alternate control scheme. It likely makes the game WAY too easy to the point of being a snorefest. Do yourself a favor and play it with the original controls. It's a fantastic and enjoyable game that way, and one of the best examples of good pacing and game design in videogame history.

Brilliant game/remaster. As a long-time resident evil fan who played the first game shortly after it was released in the UK all those years ago, I was very happy with the remastered version which has managed to keep true to the originals story, play style and overall game-play.

I feel the best way to review the remastered edition would be compare it to the original, so that's what I've done. As many of us are aware, remasters these days are usually lacking on some of the key aspects of the originals, and somewhat loose the allure and appeal of their original counterparts due to badly made graphics, game-play, story modifications or additional content. This version however has managed to tick all the boxes a remaster should tick, and has brought forward many of the positives of the original game and delivered them in a very positive way. Many of the aspects of the game have been modified for the better, and all come together to form this masterpiece. Here is a list of improvements the remastered version has delivered.

# Kept to the original story and added content (for the better) that slightly expands on the original story-line in a non-intrusive way.
# Slight tweaks to character movement have been implemented, and alternate control setups are available. The original controls are also included if you wished to stick to what you know.
# A few adjustments and additions to the combat have been added, to bring the game up-to-date with newer modern-day resident evil titles. These additions are also very welcome and improve the game-play further.
# The atmosphere of the game has been kept as it was in the original, delivering that feeling which any decent horror game should deliver. This has been kept true to the original and deserves praise, as this was the part I was most worried about just before release.
# Graphical improvements. These are obvious even from the picture on the store page above. The graphics have been improved dramatically, and are delivered seamlessly with none of the bugs/issue many remastered version seem to adopt these days, (IE. bad texture mapping, lighting issues etc.)

All of these points above come together in harmony to bring you the end result, a very well made remaster of a timeless classic in the most efficient way possible, in my opinion. I couldn't have asked for anything more from a remaster of this game.

Any fan of the original series should play this game, and they will not be disappointed with this. I bought this game on pre-order at the time, at full price and was extremely happy with it. I personally think this game is worth more than the store price, when compared to other titles of the same price, so in my opinion even full price for this is a steal.

If I was to nit-pick at issues with the game, the voice acting is not the best, however saying that, the original had 'cheesy' voice acting, so keeping true to the original I don't think this is a major issue in itself. Some dialog has been added to the voice acting here and there, but it's only really minor changes that don't defect too far away from the original.

So in conclusion, this is a brilliant game, and well worth every penny. I cant wait for the Resident Evil 2 remaster to come out and I hope it follows the same steps as this remaster has.
